Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 1:

Page 74
(7 Surat al-A'raf)

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Hibban narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It is Meccan, except for the verse ﴿Ask them about the town﴾." Others said: "From this [verse] up to ﴿And when your Lord took...﴾ it is Medinan." Also, more than one narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that it is Meccan, and the two of them excepted nothing. Its number of verses is two hundred and five according to the Basran and Syrian reckoning, and six according to the Medinan and Kufan reckoning. ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad﴾ and ﴿and as He originated you, you will return﴾ are Kufan; ﴿sincere in religion to Him﴾ is Basran and Syrian; ﴿double the punishment of the Fire﴾ and ﴿the good reward for the Children of Israel﴾ are Medinan. All of it is muhkam (firm, unabrogated). It has been said: except for two places. The first is ﴿and I will give them respite﴾, which was abrogated by the verse of the sword. The second is ﴿Take what is easy of forgiveness﴾, which was abrogated by it too according to Ibn Zayd. He also claimed that ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾ is likewise, but there is scrutiny in what he mentioned, and the discussion of it will come, God willing, Exalted is He.

Its connection with what precedes it, according to what al-Jalal al-Suyuti (may God have mercy on him) said, is that since Surat al-An'am was for explaining creation, and in it is ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾, and He, glorified is He, said in explaining the generations ﴿How many generations did We destroy before them?﴾, and reference was made to the mention of the messengers and enumeration of many of them, and what was mentioned was in summary form, this surah was brought after it, containing its explanation and detail. So the story of Adam was expanded upon in it, the stories of the messengers and their nations were elaborated, and the manner of their destruction was detailed in the fullest way. This can serve as an elaboration of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And it is He who made you successors on the earth﴾. For this reason the surah opens with the creation of Adam, whom He made a successor on the earth. And He, glorified is He, said in the story of 'Ad: ﴿He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾, and in the story of Thamud: ﴿He made you successors after 'Ad﴾. Also, He, glorified is He, said earlier: ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾, which is a concise statement, and He expanded upon it here with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things, so I will prescribe it for those who fear God...﴾, etc.

As for the connection of the beginning of this surah with the end of the first, it is that there was earlier ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ and ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it﴾, and it opened this matter with following the Book. Also, because of what preceded: ﴿Then He will inform them of what they used to do﴾ and ﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to dispute﴾. He, majestic is His affair, said at the opening of this: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾, etc., and that is in explanation of the informing mentioned. Also, when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾, the verse, and that does not become evident except in the scale, He opened this with mention of weighing, so the Mighty One, the Speaker, said: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, then ﴿Those whose scales are heavy﴾, which means those whose good deeds outweigh their evil deeds, then ﴿Those whose scales are light﴾, which is the opposite. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned after this the people of the A'raf, who, according to one opinion, are those whose good deeds and evil deeds are equal.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad﴾. The discussion of its like has preceded, and the explanation of what it contains, so there is no need for repetition, except that it has been said here that the meaning of that is "the Fashioner." This was related from al-Suddi. Al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: "I am God, the Knower and the Explainer," and al-Zajjaj preferred this. It was related from Ibn Jubayr, and in another narration from the scholar [Ibn 'Abbas], that it and its like are an oath which God Exalted swore by, and it is among His names, glorified is He. It was related from al-Dahhak that its meaning is: "I am God, the Truthful." It was related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that the alif and lam are from Allah, the mim from al-Rahman, and the sad from al-Samad. It has also been said that what is meant is: "Did We not expand for you your breast?"

Some have mentioned that no surah opens with Alif Lam Mim except that it contains three matters: the beginning of creation, the end which is the Return, and the middle which is the livelihood. To these the allusion is made by its containing the three articulation points: the throat, the tongue, and the two lips. It is said that in this surah, in addition to that, the sad was added because of its mention of the explanation of the stories. This is, as you see, [a weak view], and God Exalted knows best His intent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 2:

Page 75

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿A Book﴾ — according to some of the possibilities, it is a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "it is" or "that is a Book." His saying, glorified is He: ﴿which has been sent down to you﴾ — i.e., from Him, exalted is He — is an attribute of it, ennobling its rank and the rank of the one to whom it was sent down, ﷺ. The verb is put in the passive form in accordance with the customs of majesty (al-kibriya'), and as an indication of dispensing with explicitly naming the agent, because it is extremely evident who it is; and this is the secret in omitting mention of the source of the sending down. The description with the past tense: if "the Book" refers to the Qur'an, then in terms of the common notion shared between the whole and the part it is evident; and if it refers to the whole, then, because its realization is certain, it is treated as if past. Al-Zamakhshari and those who agreed with him chose that what is meant by "the Book" here is the sura (surah), and in this there is an exaggeration that is not hidden, if we say that it is not applied to a part; and if we say that it is applied to that, as in their saying: "this ruling was established by the Book," then the matter is clear. Some people permitted making ﴿A Book﴾ a subject (mubtada'), with the sentence after it being the predicate, in the sense of "a Book, which has been sent down to you." But it is not hidden that the first is preferable, because this is contrary to the original and the omission of the subject is more than can be counted.

﴿So let there be no constraint in your breast concerning it﴾ — i.e., doubt, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said. Its original meaning is narrowness, and its use for that is a metaphor (majaz), as in al-Asas; its relation is necessity (luzum), for the doubter is overcome by constriction of the breast just as the one who is certain is overcome by its expansion and openness. The preventing indicator (qarina) is that the literal constraint and narrowness from the Book is impossible. And if you permit it, it is a metonymy (kinaya). In either case, it has become a conventional literal meaning for that, as one of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said.

It is also permitted that it remain on its literal meaning, but with an implied omitted element in the speech, such as "fear of non-acceptance and denial," for he ﷺ feared his people, their denial, their turning away from him, and their harm to him. The interpretation is supported by His exalted saying: ﴿Perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you, and your breast would be constrained by it, because they say: "Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?"﴾ — the verse. For the first (interpretation) there is His exalted saying: ﴿So you must not be of those who doubt.﴾ And it may be said: it is a metonymy for fear, and fear, just as it occurs with what is disliked, occurs with its cause.

The directing of the prohibition to the constraint, in the sense of the shirk (polytheism), though what is meant is the prohibition to him, peace and blessings be upon him, from that — it has been said: either for the sake of intensifying the purification of the Messenger's dignity (ﷺ) from doubt, for prohibition of something may give the impression of the possibility of the forbidden thing proceeding from the one prohibited; or for the sake of intensifying the prohibition, for the occurrence of doubt in his breast, peace and blessings be upon him, is a cause for his being described by it — far be it from him — and the prohibition of a cause is a prohibition of the effect by the demonstrative method, and a negation of it entirely, as in His glorified saying: ﴿And let not the hatred of a people lead you to transgress﴾. This is not of the kind of "lā arayanaka" here, for there the prohibition is directed at the effect, with the meaning of prohibiting the cause; so the result is his prohibition, peace and blessings be upon him, from engaging in what produces constraint. So reflect. End.

What the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) have gone to is that what is meant is the prohibition of the addressee from exposing himself to constraint by way of metonymy, and that it is of the kind of "lā arayanaka" here in that respect, because the absence of constraint in his breast is among the necessary consequences of the absence of his being exposed to constraint, just as the absence of seeing is among the necessary consequences of the absence of being here. As for the one who denies that it is of that kind: if he intends to distinguish between them on the basis that in one of them what is meant is the prohibition of the cause and what is meant is the effect, and in the other the reverse, then there is no harm in that, and for this reason some expressed it by necessity rather than causation. But if he intends that it is not metonymy at all, then it is false. Yes, it is permitted that it be metaphor (majaz). The well-known view is that the motive for this interpretation is that the apparent sense calls for prohibiting constraint from being in the breast, while constraint is not the sort of thing that is prohibited; and it has a sound aspect. So let it be understood.

The sentence, on the assumption that constraint is literal, as the Kashshaf's statement implies, is a metonymy for not caring about the enemies. In any case, the tanwin in ﴿constraint﴾ is for belittling, and ﴿from﴾ is connected to what is near it or to an omitted element that occurs as an attribute of it, i.e., a constraint existing from it. And the fa'
Page 76

may be a conjunction either with an implied element, i.e., "by a message, so let there not be in your breast...", or with what precedes it, with the report interpreted as an imperative, or the reverse, i.e., "its sending down from God, exalted is He, to you has been realized," or "constraint is not fitting for you." It may also be a response, as if it were said: "When it has been sent down to you, then let there not be..."

Al-Farra' said it is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya). Some shaykhs said it is for the ordering (tartib) of the prohibition or of the cessation upon the content of the sentence, if what is meant is: let there not be in your breast doubt about its truth, for that necessitates the complete removal of doubt about what has been mentioned and the attainment of certainty about it definitively; and for the ordering of what has been mentioned upon the report of that, not upon itself, if what is meant is: let there not be in it doubt that it is a Book sent down to you; and for ordering upon the content of the sentence, or upon the report of it, if what is meant is: let there not be in you constriction of breast from conveying it, for fear that they would deny you, or that you would fall short in discharging its right, for each of these necessitates proceeding to convey it and the removal of fear definitively, even if the necessitation of the second is through the first. The view in the middle of these divisions has its consideration, so reflect.

﴿That you may warn thereby﴾ — i.e., by the Book sent down. The verb has been said either to be placed in the position of an intransitive verb, or its object has been omitted for the sake of conveying generality. It may also be said that its object has been omitted for indication by what will come after it. The lam is connected to "has been sent down" according to al-Farra'. The prohibitive sentence is parenthetical between the cause and its effect, and this is the meaning, according to what is transmitted from him that it has the form of anteriority and posteriority. It was said: this is something that should be pointed out, for the earlier scholars make parenthetical insertion as anteriority and posteriority because it intervenes between parts of a single speech, and they do not mean that there is an inversion (qalb) in the speech. The reason for the interposition is either that the ordering is upon the sending down itself, not upon the sending down for warning; or the preservation of emphasis, together with what that contains, according to what has been said, of an indication that each of the sending down and the warning suffices for the negation of constraint. As for the sufficiency of the second, it is evident, because the one who warns should not fear the one he warns, so that he may be able to warn as is required. As for the sufficiency of the first, it is because the Book that attains the utmost perfection being sent down to him, peace and blessings be upon him, specifically among his brother prophets, peace be upon them, requires that he be broad-breasted and unconcerned with falsehood and its people. And from Ibn al-Anbari: the lam is connected to the complement of the predicate, i.e., let constraint not be established in your breast for the sake of warning. It was said: it is connected to the verb of prohibition, which is "being," on the basis of permitting the connection of the preposition to the defective kana, because it indicates a sound event. It was said: it is permissible for it to be connected to "constraint," in the sense that constraint is for warning, and narrowness of breast for it should not be. The second allamah said: it is an object of the demand or of what is demanded, namely the absence of constraint; and this is more apparent, not of the prohibited, i.e., the act to which the prohibition is attached, as was said, because of the corruption of the meaning. Al-Zamakhshari stated its connection to the prohibition without qualification, and it was objected that this cannot be sustained on the first interpretation of constraint, because the causation of the prohibition of doubt by what was mentioned, namely warning and reminding, together with its implication that it is possible for it to proceed from him, peace and blessings be upon him, indicates that the forbidden thing is not harmful in itself but because it leads to the loss of warning and reminding; at least it signals that this is the greatest of its perils. There is no doubt of its corruption. As for the second interpretation, causation by warning can only apply, not by reminding the believers, for there is no trace of fear in it, so that it could be made a goal of its removal. You know well that the prohibition of it being harmful in itself is as evident as the fire of hospitality at night upon a landmark, so its contrary is hardly conceivable. And the claim that at least it signals that this is the greatest of its perils is not corrupt, based on what the context requires, even if some of its perils in reality are greater than that; and that the verse is not an explicit text on causation of the prohibition by warning and reminding, as will soon become clear to you, God willing, so that the objection could be raised in view of the second interpretation. Even if we grant that it is an explicit text, we say: why could it not be that this is of the kind of His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you a clear victory﴾, ﴿that God may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what followed, and complete His favor upon you﴾, the verse, ﴿and a reminder for the believers﴾ (2)
Page 77

is in the accusative, by implying its verb, coordinated with "that you may warn," i.e., "and remind the believers with a reminder." Al-Zamakhshari, as transmitted from him, prevented coordination in the accusative with the position of "li-tundhira," reasoning that the object of purpose must have the same agent as the thing it explains, so that the lam may be dropped from it.

It is possible, as in the Kashf, to say there is no barrier to the reminding being the act of the Sender, the Real, exalted is He, except that the contrast between warning and reminding would be lost. Yes, the genitive by coordination with the position is permitted, i.e., for warning and reminding; and the nominative is permitted, on the basis that it is coordinated with "a Book," or is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a reminder." The difference between the two readings, according to the Kashf, is that the first means that this combines two matters: being a Book complete in its affair, reaching the limit of inimitability in the excellence of its exposition, and being a reminder for the believers, reminding them of the origin and the return. The second indicates that this, restricted to being a Book, has such-and-such characteristics, and is a reminder for the believers; and this is coordination of sentence upon sentence, so it indicates that it is independent with each of the two matters. This is more preferable in wording and meaning. The restriction of reminding to the believers is because they are the ones who benefit from it, or to indicate that warning is specific to the unbelievers.

The preposing of warning is because it is more important according to the context.

**"Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord"** (7:3). This is addressed to all those who are responsible (*mukallafun*). The relative phrase refers to the Book revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), as narrated from Qatadah. However, the explicit noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, and the revelation is described as sent down "to them" to emphasize the obligation to follow it. It has also been said that what is meant is that which encompasses both the Book and the Sunnah (the Prophet's teachings and practice). In that case, there is no placing of an explicit noun in the position of a pronoun. Choosing it is for the purpose of generality. This is an instance of *tashmim* (a subtle allusion), from the style of the saying of the woman from the Anmar tribe: "They are like a hollow ring; one cannot tell where its ends are." It is also a *tatmim* (completion) for *sharh al-sadr* (expansion of the breast), since when the command to follow all that he prescribes was made general to everyone, it would be more conducive to the expansion of the breast of the Prophet, upon him be peace, and the widening of his capacity.

It is not hidden that this interpretation is far-fetched. Yes, the Sunnah in all its divisions is encompassed by the ruling through implication (*dalalah*), not through direct expression (*ibarah*). The word *min* ("from") is connected to *unzila* ("was sent down"), with it being for the starting point of the action in a figurative sense, or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the relative pronoun or of its pronoun in the relative clause. Referring to the title of Lordship together with its attachment to the pronoun of the addressees conveys great kindness toward them, encouragement for them to comply with what they have been commanded, and an emphasis on its obligation after an emphasis.

**"And do not follow, apart from Him, protectors"** (7:3). The pronoun in the genitive refers to *Rabbikum* ("your Lord"). The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state of the subject of the prohibitive verb. That is: do not follow, going beyond your Lord, who sent down to you what guides you to the truth, *awliya'* ("protectors") from among the devils and the soothsayers, by accepting from them what they throw to you of falsehoods, so that they may lead you astray from the truth after it has come to you, and drive you toward innovations and deviant desires.

It is also permissible that the prepositional phrase be connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state of *awliya'*, placed before it because it is indefinite. That is: protectors who are other than Him, the Exalted. It is also permissible that it be connected to the verb before it, meaning: you turn away from Him, glorified is He, to other than Him. Since following what He, glorified is He, sent down amounts to following Him, mighty is His majesty, He followed the previous command with this prohibition.

It has also been said that the pronoun refers to what was sent down, with an omitted noun before *awliya'*. That is: do not follow, apart from what was sent down, the falsehoods of protectors. It is as if it were said: do not follow, apart from the religion of your Lord, the religion of protectors. This estimate is necessary because it is not fitting to describe what was sent down as being "apart from them." It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: do not follow protectors with a following apart from your following what was sent down to you. But this has a remoteness to it.

Mujahid read *tabtaghu* ("seek") with an unpointed *ghayn*, from *ibtigha'* (seeking).

**"Little do you remember"** (7:3). That is: a little remembrance, or a little time you remember, not much, since you are not affected by that, do not act upon its requirement, abandon the truth, and follow other than it. *Qalilan* is an adjective of a verbal noun or of an omitted time expression that has been put in its place, and it is governed by the verb after it. It has been placed before the verb for restriction (*qasr*). The particle *ma* is additional, to emphasize the paucity, because it conveys that meaning in such constructions as *akaltu akla ma* ("I ate a little bit of eating"). Thus here is paucity upon paucity. The apparent meaning of paucity is its literal sense, but it is permissible that by it is meant non-existence, as in His saying, exalted is He: "So little do they believe" (*faqalilan ma yu'minun*). It has also been permitted that *qalilan* be an adjective of a verbal noun for *tattabi'u*, meaning: a little following. It has been said that this is weakened because there would be no meaning then to His saying, glorified is He, "you remember." As for the prohibition against little following, it does no harm, since the other is understood from it by the demonstrative method (*al-tariq al-burhani*).

It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial state of the subject of *tattabi'u*, with *ma* being a verbal (*masdariyyah*) or relative particle functioning as its subject, as was said of His saying, exalted is He: "They used to sleep but little of the night" (*kanu qalilan min al-layli ma yahja'un*). The prohibition is directed at both the restriction and the restricted together. It has been objected that there is no point under its meaning, even if it were given a direction. It is also permitted that *ma* be a verbal or relative particle functioning as the subject, with *qalilan* in the sense of "a little time," and the verbal phrase functioning as the predicate. It has been said that *ma* is a negating particle, and *qalilan* is an object of what follows it. The Kufans permit the governing of what follows *ma* the negator over what precedes it. The meaning would be: you hardly remember, so how do you remember much? But this is not valid.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read *tadhkurun* by omitting one of the two *ta'* letters, with a lightened *dhal*. Ibn 'Amir read *yatadhakkarun* with a *ya'* (third person) and a *ta'* (second letter), with a lightened *dhal*; in an irregular transmission from him, it is with two *ta'* letters. The rest read *tatadhakkarun* with a *ta'* and a doubled *dhal*, by assimilating the voiceless *ta'* into the voiced *dhal*. The sentence, according to what many have said, is a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiradh tadhyiliyy*), brought to condemn the state of the addressees. The shift in person (*iltifat*) according to the well-known reading of Ibn 'Amir is to signify that the bad state of theirs, in failing to comply with the command and the prohibition, requires turning the address away from them and relating their offenses to others in a manner of rejection (*mubatta*). There is no proof in the verse for those who deny analogical reasoning (*qiyas*), as is not hidden.

﴿How many a town We destroyed﴾: this begins the warning and admonition regarding what punishment befell those before them because of their turning away from the religion of God Most High and their persistence in the falsehoods of their allies. "Kam" (how many) is informative (khabariyyah), indicating multiplicity, and is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'); the clause after it is its predicate (khabar). The "min" is the "sword of the orator" (sayf khatib), an emphatic extra particle, and "qaryah" (town) is a specification (tamyiz).

It is also permissible that the position of "kam" be accusative by way of the construction of the verb with its pronoun (ishtighal), and the pronoun in "We destroyed it" refers to the meaning of "kam," for the meaning is "many towns, which We destroyed." The intended sense of destroying them is the intention to destroy them, used figuratively, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When you stand up to prayer﴾ and the verse continues. Thus there is no difficulty regarding the sequence indicated by the "fa" (then) in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿so Our punishment came upon them﴾, meaning Our chastisement. Some of the scrupulous scholars objected to this answer, saying that it contains a fundamental (usuli) difficulty: if the intention is taken in the sense of its immediate effect (ta'alluq tanjizi), then the coming of the punishment is simultaneous with it, not following it and after it; and if that intention is not meant, then it is eternal (qadimah), so if the punishment were to follow it, the eternity of the world would be necessary, and if it came after it, the conjunction "thumma" (then) would be required.

It was answered that what is meant is the immediate effect before the event, i.e., We intended to destroy them. So reflect on this. It was also said: what is meant by destruction is abandonment and the lack of success (khidhlan wa 'adam al-tawfiq), and so it is a metaphor (isti'arah), or it is from the use of the effect to name the cause. Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement points to this. It was criticized on the grounds that it is a Mu'tazili (rationalist school) view, and that the correct formulation is: its meaning is that We created in its people wickedness and opposition, so Our punishment came upon them. It was also said: what is meant is Our decree to destroy them, so it came upon them. It was also said: the "fa" is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), like "he performed ablution, so he washed his face," etc. It was also said: the "fa" is for the order of mention (tartib dhikri). Ibn 'Usfur said: what is meant is that We destroyed them with a destruction short of total annihilation (istisal), so there came upon them the destruction of annihilation. Al-Farra' said: the "fa" has the meaning of "wa" (and), or the meaning is: so Our might became manifest and famous. It was also said: the discourse is inverted (qalb), and there is a transposition, i.e., We destroyed them ﴿by night or while they were resting at midday﴾ (4), so the destruction is in this world and the coming of the punishment is in the Hereafter, and so the discourse includes the punishment of both abodes. But what follows clearly rejects this, for it indicates that the punishment was in this world. Many have supposed in the noble text an elided noun, i.e., "so the people of it came upon them."

Some allowed that it be understood as a *istikhdam* (a rhetorical device in which a word is used in one sense and its pronoun in another), because the town is figuratively used for its people. Some supposed the elided noun in the first clause as well, though the town may be described as being destroyed, which is ruin. The word "bayat" (night-visit) is originally the verbal noun of "bata yabitu" (to pass the night), "baytan," "bitatan," "baytutah." Al-Raghib mentioned that "bayat," and likewise "tabyit," is attacking the enemy at night. Al-Layth said: "baytutah" is entering at night. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) by interpretation as "those who passed the night."

It was permitted that it be a temporal adverb (zarf), which is contrary to the apparent sense. The possibility of its being an object of cause (maf'ul lahu) in the accusative, as Abu al-Baqa' claimed, is not worth attention. The "aw" (or) is for classification, and what follows it is coordinated with the state, and it is also in the position of a state. The "wa" (and) was elided there, as Ibn al-Anbari said, for the meaning is clear. Because "aw," a conjunction, and "wa" are similar, they disliked combining two conjunctive particles, so they omitted the second. This is also reported from al-Farra'. It was objected that the "wa" of state is distinct from the "wa" of conjunction in every case; it is a category of the "wa" like the "wa" of oath, as shown by the fact that it occurs where what precedes it cannot be a state. If it were a conjunction, it would only occur where what precedes it is a state, so that one conjoins a state to a state. Ibn al-Munir said: this "wa" must be distinguished from the "wa" of conjunction by a special feature. Do you not see that it accompanies a nominal clause after a verbal clause? If it were a bare conjunction, its placement between two different things would be disliked, or the more eloquent would be otherwise. Since we see it placed in the middle of discourse and this is the most eloquent or the required form, we know that it is distinguished from the conjunctive "wa." If this is established, there is no wonder in their combination, even if it has the sense of conjunction added to that special feature. Either you deprive it of that sense because the conjunctive particle suffices for it, or it keeps it and combines with it, or it is like how the "wa" combines [with another], but in eloquent speech it is less usual, because of the added sense of contrast (istidrak). On this basis the combination is possible without any dislike. So if you say: "Glorify God the Exalted while you are bowing," or "while you are prostrating," it would be eloquent with no defect or dislike. This is contrary to Abu Hayyan, who claimed that the grammarians stated that when a conjunction enters upon a circumstantial nominal clause, the "wa" of state may not enter upon it, because of the verbal similarity; so the example is not correct on this basis. The apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's statement is that this "wa" was originally the conjunctive "wa," then it was borrowed for the state because of the connection it provides. It has thus departed from conjunction and is used with another meaning, but it has been given the ruling of its origin in not combining with another conjunction. On this basis, the words of these two imams must be understood. This is the view of both of them and of those who followed them.

Some grammarians said: the pronoun here suffices without the elided "wa," and relying on it is not anomalous, as has been said; rather it is more common than the sand of Yabrin and the gazelles of Filastin. It is reported from al-Zamakhshari that he returned to this view. The question is disputed and has detail. In al-Badi', the nominal circumstantial clause is either from the cause of the possessor of the state or foreign to it. If it is from its cause, it must have a returning pronoun and the "wa," as you say: "Zayd came and his father is departing"; "'Amr went out and his hand is on his head," except what is anomalous in their saying: "I spoke to him, his mouth to his mouth." If it is foreign, it must have the "wa" and it replaces the returning pronoun. It may be combined with both, as in: "'Amr came, and Bishr stood up to him." It has also come without "wa" and without a pronoun, as in the verse:

*Then we passed the mountains of Safd, turning away from the left,*
*and on our right are paths.*

For "the mountains of Safd turning away" is a state without "wa" and without a pronoun. From Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir: he divided this into two categories: that which requires the "wa" absolutely, which is what begins with the pronoun of the possessor of the state, as in "Zayd came while he was hastening," for repeating its pronoun requires that the clause be resumptive (mustanafah), so that the repetition is not idle. When the resumption is not intended, the "wa" is necessary. Anything other than this requires the "wa" in eloquent speech, except by way of likening it to the single word and interpretation, for then the "wa" may be omitted permissibly. It was said, and it is not accepted: the rule in this is that if the subject is the pronoun of the possessor of the state, the "wa" is obligatory; otherwise, if the pronoun is in what the clause begins with, whether as subject, as in "Fuhun ila fi" (a mouth to a mouth) and "Ba'dukum liba'din 'aduwwun" (some of you are enemies to others), or as predicate, as in "I found him present, his generosity and his nobility," then it is not judged weak, because it is the connective at the beginning of the clause. Otherwise, it is weak and rare.

Ibn Malik, followed by Ibn Hisham, and reported from al-Sakkaki, said: if the nominal clause is emphatic, the pronoun is required and the "wa" is omitted, as in "He is the truth, there is no doubt in it," and "That is the Book, there is no doubt in it." Ibn al-Munir preferred that what makes this clause suitable as a state without "wa" here is the conjunction, since it requires that the second clause share with what it is conjoined to in the status of state. Thus the "wa" of state is dispensed with, just as you conjoin to the thing sworn by and bring it into the ruling of the oath without a "wa," as in ﴿By the night when it covers﴾, ﴿By the day when it shines forth﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So I swear by the stars﴾, ﴿that run and hide﴾, ﴿and by the night when it departs﴾. The repetition of the oath particle is dispensed with by the conjunction standing in its place. So let it be understood, whichever it is. The sum of the meaning: Our punishment came upon them at times by night, as with the people of Lot, peace be upon him, and at times at the time of the midday rest (qaylulah), as with the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. The "qaylulah" comes from "qala yaqilu," so he is "qa'il," and it is said "qiylan," "qa'ilah," "maqalan," and "maqilan." It is, as in the Qamus, half of the day, or it is repose and ease at midday, even if there is no sleep with it, as in the Nihayah. It is cited as evidence for this His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their rest (maqil)﴾, since the Garden has no sleep in it.

Al-Layth said: it is a midday nap. The proof is rejected on the ground that this is figurative. The descent of the punishment upon them was specified at these two times because the arrival of what is hated at a time of heedlessness and ease is more terrible, and recounting it to the listeners is more effective in deterring them from being deceived by the causes of security and comfort. In the first state the use of the verbal noun and making it the very thing of the night-attack, and in the second state the nominal clause, which in the well-known view indicates permanence, together with the fronting of the subject which indicates restriction, carries what is not hidden of exaggeration. Likewise in describing all of them with the description of night-attack and midday rest, though some of those destroyed were far from either, is an indication of complete security and heedlessness, and in this there is a rebuke of them for their heedlessness of what they were facing. It was said that the two expressions were varied in form, and the second state was built on confirming the judgment and indicating the strength of their condition in what was attributed to them, for the midday rest is more evident in the intention of ease and comfort of life, since it is the habit of the affluent and the pampered, not of one accustomed to toil and fatigue. This contains an indication that they were people of insolence and arrogance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 5:

﴿Their only plea﴾ means their supplication and their calling for help, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their last plea﴾ [Qur'an 10:10]. It is also the saying of some Arabs, related by al-Khalil and Sibawayh: "O Allah, make us partners in the good supplication of the Muslims," or their claim (iddi'a'ahum), as is the well-known meaning of da'wa (claim). ﴿When Our punishment came upon them﴾, meaning Our chastisement, and they witnessed its signs, ﴿except that they said﴾, all together, ﴿"Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ (5) That is, except their acknowledgment of their wrongdoing in what they had been upon, and their testimony to its falsehood, out of regret, remorse, and hope for deliverance, but it is too late, and there is no time for salvation. Making this acknowledgment identical to that [plea] is an exaggeration, in the manner of his saying:

"Their greeting among them is a painful striking."

As for ﴿their plea﴾, it is permissible, as Abu al-Baqa' said, for it to be the subject of kana with the predicate being ﴿except that they said﴾, or for it to be the predicate and ﴿except that they said﴾ to be the subject. He preferred the second, because making the more definite element the subject is the common usage in their speech, and the verbal noun here resembles a pronoun, since it is described and it is more definite than the genitive construction. It was objected to this that when the subject and predicate are both definite and their i'rab is not apparent, one of them may be placed before the other, so the first is determined. This was answered by saying that this applies when there is no indicator, and the indicator here is that the second is more definite and the absence of feminine marking. Also, that rule applies when there is no restriction; if restriction is intended, what it requires is considered. In al-Kashshaf he preferred the second, saying it is the reading that matches its parallels in the Qur'an.

The meaning according to it is more fitting, because the premise is that another statement did not occupy this position, so the intent is to pass judgment on this specific utterance as being the supplication, and it is reinforced by the introduction of the particle of restriction. It is not a matter of fronting at all, because the restricted element should always be postponed. So reflect and take heed.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 6:**

﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾. This is an explanation, as al-Tabarsi said, of their otherworldly punishment following the explanation of their worldly punishment. However, as it has been said, it addresses the beginnings of the states of all accountable people, because this is more effective in inspiring awe. The *fa'* (the connecting particle) here, according to some, serves to order the otherworldly states after the worldly ones in mention, in the same sequence in which they occur in existence.

The Allama al-Tibi mentioned that the *fa'* is *fasiha* (an elucidating particle), meaning: "So their claim in the world, when Our punishment came upon them, was only that they said, 'So We cut off their last remnant,' then 'We will surely gather them, and then We will surely question them.'" On this reading, the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun for the sake of further emphasis.

Al-Kashshaf says: "Perhaps the more correct view is that this be connected to the words of the Exalted, *'Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow other than Him'* [7:3], and that His words, *'How many a town have We destroyed...'* [7:4], etc., be considered a parenthetical statement, urging reflection on the condition of those who came before, so that they will hasten to follow." End of quote.

The matter, according to those who hold that the preceding speech is in inverted order and claim that the coming of the punishment in the Hereafter is easy, as is not hidden, is this: "We will surely question the nations entirely, or these [people], saying, 'What did you answer the messengers?' And We will surely question the messengers: what were they answered?" The purpose of this questioning is to rebuke and reprimand the disbelievers.

As for the negated statement in the words of the Exalted, *'On that Day, no human or jinn will be asked about his sin'* [55:39], it refers to the questioning of inquiry (*su'al al-istila'*). So there is no contradiction between the two verses. Others reconciled them by saying that the affirmed questioning has one station and the negated one has another. The Imam said: "They will not be questioned about their deeds, meaning, 'What did you do?' Rather, they will be questioned about the motives that drove them to the deeds and the obstacles that turned them away from them, meaning, 'Why was it so?'"

It has also been said: the meaning of *'No human or jinn will be asked about his sin'* is that no one will be punished for another's sin. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "those to whom [messengers] were sent" is the prophets' peoples, and of "the messengers" are the angels who conveyed to them the messages of their Lord. This was narrated from Farqad, and it is, as you see, far-fetched.

It has been said: there is no need for reconciliation, since what is negated is questioning about sin, not questioning in general. This was refuted by saying that the non-acceptance of the messengers' call, peace be upon them, for the reasons mentioned, is what the reports attest to and the traditions indicate, and there is support for this in the Qur'an, for the Exalted said: *'On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?"'* [5:109].

Restricting the questioning of those to whom messengers were sent to what has been mentioned above is the view adopted by a group of exegetes.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan al-Thawri that it is said to those to whom messengers were sent: "Did the messengers convey to you?" and it is said to the messengers: "What did they respond to you?" He also related from al-Qasim Abu 'Abd al-Rahman that he recited this verse and said: "The servant will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about four traits. Your Lord will say: 'Did I not give you a body? So for what did you wear it out? Did I not give you knowledge? So what did you do with what you knew? Did I not give you wealth? So where did you spend it, in My obedience or in My disobedience? Did I not give you a lifespan? So how did you spend it?'"

He and others also related from Tawus that he recited it and said: "The Imam is questioned about the people, a man is questioned about his family, a woman is questioned about her husband's house, and a slave is questioned about his master's property."

[p. 82]

It seems apparent that the questioning of each of those to whom messengers were sent and of the messengers here concerns a matter related to its own party. This does not preclude that accountable people will be questioned about other matters too, and the stations of the Day of Resurrection are many. The Lord, Possessor of Majesty, will question His servants there about many aims. Blessed is the one whom good fortune takes by the arm, so that he answers with what will save him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 7:

﴿So We will surely relate to them﴾ It has been said: that is, to the messengers, when they entrust the matter to His knowledge, the Exalted, and say, ﴿We have no knowledge. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.﴾ Or [it means] to them and to the messengers sent to them, all together, [relating] all their circumstances. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the book of their deeds will speak against them ﴿with knowledge﴾, that is, knowing their outward and inward [states], or with what We know of them. The preposition (ba') in the first interpretation is for accompaniment (al-mulabasah), and the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (naqussu, "We relate"). In the second interpretation, the ba' is connected to (naqussu). ﴿And We were not absent﴾ (7) from them in any state of their conditions. What is meant is the complete encompassing of their circumstances and actions, such that nothing of them escapes His knowledge, glorified is He. The sentence is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to emphasize what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 8:

﴿And the weighing﴾ means the weighing of deeds and the distinguishing between their heavy and light, and their good and bad. It is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). His statement, exalted is He, ﴿on that day﴾, is related to an omitted khabar (predicate). His statement, exalted is He, ﴿is the truth﴾, is its sifah (adjective). That is, the weighing that is true and established is on the day when the questioning and the recounting will take place. Some of the grammarians (mu'rabun) chose this. It has been said: the apparent reading is that "the truth" is the khabar, and "on that day" is an adverbial complement of the weighing, so that a separation between the adjective and the noun modified does not occur.

Perhaps the reason for not choosing this is that it involves the operation of a definite verbal noun (al-masdar al-mu'arraf), which is rare. In al-Kashf: the meaning is not that the weighing is the truth, but rather that the true weighing occurs on that day. Do you not see His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾. Al-Isfahani mentioned in his commentary on Ibn Jinni's al-Lum'ah that "the truth" is a badal (substitute) for the pronoun hidden in the adverbial complement. This is a good view, except that the first view gave precedence to the meaning and was not concerned about the separation by the khabar, since it is one with the mubtada' in one respect, especially as the adverbial complement is treated with latitude.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "the truth" be the khabar of an omitted mubtada', as if it were said: what is that weighing? So it was said: it is the truth, that is, the upright justice. He also permitted that "the weighing" be the khabar of an omitted mubtada', that is, this weighing. And that is, as you see, [weak]. It was read ﴿al-qist﴾ (justice) [in the accusative].

As al-Raghib said, weighing is knowing the measure of a thing; one says "wazantuhu, wazna, wazinah." The commonly understood meaning among the general public is that which is measured by the qistas (balance) and the qabban (steelyard). Its manner on the Day of Resurrection has been disputed. The majority, as al-Qadi said, hold that the records of deeds are what is weighed by a scale that has a tongue and two pans, so that the creatures may look at it, as a demonstration of justice and a cutting off of excuses, just as they are questioned about their deeds, and their tongues and limbs testify to them. The nature of those records is not disclosed to them, and Allah the Exalted knows their reality best.

This is supported by what Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man of my ummah will be called out before the heads of all creation on the Day of Resurrection, and ninety-nine registers will be unfolded for him, each register as far as the eye can see. He (exalted is He) will say: Do you deny any of this? Has My recording scribes wronged you? He will say: No, my Lord. He will say: Do you have any excuse, or any good deed? The man will be fearful and say: No, my Lord. He will say, majestic is His affair: Yes, indeed you have a good deed with Us, and there is no wrong upon you today. Then a card will come out for him in which is written: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger. He will say: My Lord, what is this card with these registers? It will be said: Indeed you will not be wronged. The registers will be placed in one pan, and the card in the other pan. The registers will be lightened, and the card will be heavy, and nothing is heavy along with the name of Allah the Exalted."

This testimony, according to al-Qurtubi quoting al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, is not the testimony of tawhid (oneness), because the nature of the scale is that in one of its two pans something is placed and in the other its opposite. The good deeds are placed in one pan and the bad deeds in the other. It is impossible for one servant to be brought with both disbelief and faith together, so it is impossible that the testimony of tawhid be placed in the scale. As for after faith, the utterance of this good word is a good deed, so it is placed in the scale like the rest of the good deeds. This is supported by His statement, majestic and exalted is He, in the hadith: "Indeed you have a good deed with Us," without saying "faith." It is permitted that the intended meaning is this word when it is the last of his words in this world. Others permitted that it is the word of tawhid. The necessity of placing the opposite in the other pan was denied, so that the impossibility would not follow. So reflect.

Another report has come, narrated by Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Numayri in Kitab al-A'lam, also from Abdullah, who said: "Indeed Adam (peace be upon him) has from Allah, mighty and majestic, a station in a wide space of the Throne, upon which are two green garments, as if he were a tall palm tree. He looks at those of his offspring who are led to Paradise and those who are led to the Fire. While Adam is in this state, he sees a man from the ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) being led to the Fire. So Adam (peace be upon him) calls out: O Ahmad! O Ahmad! The Prophet (ﷺ) says: At your service, O father of mankind. He says: This is a man of your ummah being led to the Fire. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: So I tighten my waistcloth and hasten after the angels, and I say: O messengers of my Lord, stop! They say: We are the harsh and severe ones who do not disobey Allah the Exalted in what He commands us, and we do what we are commanded. When the Prophet (ﷺ) despairs, he seizes his beard with his left hand, faces the Throne with his face, and says: O my Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me regarding my ummah. Then the call comes from the direction of the Throne: Obey Muhammad, and return this servant to the station. So the Prophet (ﷺ) brings out a white card like a fingertip, and places it in the right pan of the scale, saying: In the name of Allah. The good deeds then outweigh the bad deeds. The caller calls out: He is blessed, and his grandfather is blessed, and his scales are heavy! Take him to Paradise! He says: O messengers of my Lord, stop, until I ask this noble servant regarding his Lord. He says: May my father and mother be your ransom! How beautiful is your face and how beautiful is your character! Who are you? For you have relieved me of my stumble and had mercy on my tears. The Prophet (ﷺ) says: I am your Prophet, Muhammad, and this is your salawat (blessing) which you used to send upon me; I have repaid it to you at the time you most need it." End.

Perhaps the doing of such a thing, if the report is sound, is an exaggeration in displaying the honour of the Prophet (ﷺ) before his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, among the first and the last.

It has been said that persons are weighed. They argued for this with what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed a fat, large person will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and he will not weigh the wing of a mosquito in the sight of Allah the Exalted." I do not know, according to this view, what is placed in the other pan of the scale if the sinner is placed in one of them. Placing one person against another person, I do not see it except as you see. The report is not an explicit text for the claim, as is not hidden.

It has been said: these apparent deeds in this worldly form, in an accidental form, appear in the next life in an essential form suited to them in beauty and ugliness. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and many declared it sahih, and said: belief in it is obligatory. In the reports there is what supports it. Ibn Abd al-Barr narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: A man's deed is brought on the Day of Resurrection and placed in the pan of his scale, and it is light. Then something like clouds is brought and placed in the pan of his scale, and it outweighs it. It is said to him: Do you know what this is? He says: No. It is said to him: This is the excess of the knowledge which you used to teach people. Ibn al-Mubarak narrated from Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman with a similar meaning.

It has been said: the weighing is an expression for the upright judgement and the just ruling. The use of the word "weighing" in this sense is common in language and custom, by way of metonymy (kinayah). This is the view of Mujahid, al-A'mash and al-Dahhak, and the Mu'tazilah went to it, except that some of them permitted the weighing in the commonly understood sense rationally, even if they did not judge that it would occur, like al-Allaf and Bishr ibn al-Mu'tamir. Others considered it impossible, because deeds are accidents (a'rad), and they do not last, and it is not possible for them to be restored. But they are accidents, and accidents cannot be weighed, since they are not described as heavy or light. Even if we grant the possibility of weighing them, there is no benefit in that, since the purpose is only knowledge of the differences between deeds, and Allah the Exalted knows that. What has no benefit is an ugly act, and the Lord, exalted is He, is far above doing ugly acts. Its answer is known from what we have already presented.

These [Mu'tazilah] interpreted the scale as justice and equity. Al-Amidi objected to this, saying that the scale is described as heavy and light, and justice and equity are not described thus. There are reports that clearly state that the scale is corporeal. Al-Hakim narrated and declared it sahih, from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The scale will be set up on the Day of Resurrection. If the heavens and the earth were weighed in it, it would contain them. The angels will say: O Lord, who will weigh this? Allah the Exalted will say: Whomever of My creation I wish. The angels will say: Glory be to You, we did not worship You as You deserve to be worshipped." In the narration of Ibn al-Mubarak and al-Lalika'i from him, he said: "The scale will be set up and it has two pans. If the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them were placed in one of them, it would contain them. The angels will say: Who will weigh this?" The hadith [continues].

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah the Exalted created the two pans of the scale like the heavens and the earth. The angels said: O our Lord, whom will You weigh with this? He said: I will weigh with it whomever I wish." It is also related in some reports that Allah the Exalted uncovered the sight of Dawud (peace be upon him), and he saw of the scale what frightened him until he fainted. When he recovered, he said: O my Lord, who will fill the pan of this with good deeds? Majestic is His affair, said: O Dawud, when I am pleased with a servant, I fill it with half a date which he gave in charity, and other things beyond counting in abundance. So the better course, as al-Zajjaj said, is to follow what has come in the hadiths, and there is no reason to deviate from that.

If it is said: the responsible person on the Day of Resurrection is either a believer that He, exalted is He, is wise and far above injustice, so His judgement regarding the qualities and quantities of deeds suffices him; or he is a denier, and then he would not accept that the outweighing of some deeds over others is due to particular features returning to the essences of those deeds, but rather he would attribute it to Allah the Exalted's making it appear to him in that manner. So what is the benefit of the weighing? It is answered: the state will be revealed on that day, and all things will appear with their realities as they are, with their attributes and states in themselves, of beauty, ugliness and other things. They will be stripped of the borrowed forms by which they appeared in this world, so no one who witnesses them will have any doubt that they are the same ones that existed in this world, and that each of them has appeared in this worldly life in its true form, following its attributes, and no contrary thought will occur to him. So said some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin). And Allah the Exalted knows the reality of the matter best.

﴿So whoever's scales are heavy﴾ is a detailing of the rulings that follow from the weighing. The mawazin (scales) is either the plural of mizan, although the well-known correct view is that mizan in general is singular, considering the plurality of the weighings or of the things weighed; and likewise if we say that each person's scale is one. In the statement there is an omitted modifier, that is, the pan of his scales. Or it is the plural of mawzun (the thing weighed), and its annexation is to the known (ahd), because success is consequent upon that. Then what is meant is the good deeds, and the plural on this view is clear. Likewise if we say that each deed has its own scale. ﴿Then those﴾ refers to the relative pronoun (mawsul) with regard to its being characterized by what is in the sphere of the relative clause (sillah). The plurality is with regard to its meaning, just as the singularity of the pronoun "his scales" which refers back to it is with regard to its wording. And the sense of distance in it [the demonstrative] is as has passed many times. It is the mubtada' (subject). ﴿They﴾ is either a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), by which the khabar is separated from the sifah, and it emphasizes the attribution and indicates the restriction of the predicate to the subject. And ﴿the successful ones﴾ (8), that is, those who win salvation and reward, is the khabar. Or it is a second mubtada', and "the successful ones" is its khabar, and the sentence is the khabar of the first mubtada'. The definiteness of "the successful ones" is to indicate that they are the people of whom you have been informed that they are successful in the Hereafter, or it is a reference to what everyone knows of the reality of the successful and their characteristics.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 9:

﴿And as for those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls﴾ through neglecting the fitrah (innate nature) of Islam, concerning which "there is no child born except upon it," or the fitrah of goodness, which is the origin of natural disposition.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿because they used to wrong Our signs﴾ (9) is connected to *khasirū* (have lost). The *mā* is verbal (*maṣdariyyah*), meaning "because of their wronging." The phrase *bi-āyātinā* (concerning Our signs) is connected to *yaẓlimūn* (they wrong), and it was placed before it for the sake of the *fāṣilah* (verse-ending rhyme). The verb *ẓalama* (to wrong) is transitive with *bi* (with) because it implies the meaning of *takdhīb* (denial) or *juḥūd* (rejection). The combination of the past form and the present form (*kānū* ... *yaẓlimūn*) indicates the continuation of wrongdoing in the world. The apparent sense of the noble text is that the weighing is not restricted to Muslims; rather, the deeds of the disbelievers are also weighed, those deeds that do not depend on Islam. Some scholars held this view. Al-Qurtubi claimed that the correct view is that their punishment is lightened by them, even if they are not outweighed, as was reported concerning Abu Talib. Most scholars, however, held that the weighing is restricted to Muslims, and that as for the disbelievers, their deeds are nullified whatever they may be. This is one of the two interpretations of His saying: ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and nothing of the punishment is lightened for them by them. As for what has been reported about the lightening of punishment for Abu Talib, al-Sakhawi said that the accepted view is that it is specific to him. In light of this, it is necessary to depart from the apparent meaning of the verse. In either case, the verse is silent about the state of those whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal, and they are the people of the A'raf according to one view. Hence some scholars cited it as evidence that this category does not exist. This was refuted by saying that they may be included in the first category, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad; perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness﴾. The *'asā* (perhaps) from Allah, exalted is He, indicates certainty, as they have stated explicitly. But this is open to scrutiny.

This is a commentary (tafsir) on the verse "And We had certainly established you upon the earth..." The passage that follows is the commentary of al-Alusi in Ruh al-Ma'ani on surah 7, verse 10.

﴿And We had certainly established you upon the earth﴾: this is an encouragement to accept the call of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), by reminding them of blessings immediately after an encouragement.

Al-Tibi (al-Tibi, Sharaf al-Din) mentioned that this is another type of warning, for it is a oath-clause (jumla qasamiyya) conjoined to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, on the assumption of the implied "Say: follow," and "Say: By God, We had certainly established you..." The meaning is: We made for you a place and a settlement in the earth.

It has been said: We empowered you to dispose of it, and in that case it is a metonymy (kinaya). Here the literal meaning is preferred. ﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood (ma'ayish)﴾, i.e. that by which you live and subsist, of foods, drinks and the like, or that by which you reach those things. It is originally a verbal noun of 'ash, ya'ish, 'aysha, ma'ash and ma'isha on the pattern maf'ala. The majority read it with the yā' explicitly written, "ma'ayish." It is transmitted from Nafi' that he read "ma'a'ish" with a hamza, but the grammarians, including Sibawayh, judged this to be an error, because according to them no hamza occurs after the alif of the plural except for a added (ziyada) yā', as in ṣaḥīfa and ṣaḥā'if. As for ma'ayish, its yā' is original, being the 'ayn of the word, since it derives from al-'aysh. Abu 'Uthman went further and said that Nafi' did not know Arabic. This was rebutted: this reading, although irregular (shādhdha) and not mutawatir, is taken from reliable eloquent authorities, and the Arabs may liken an original letter to a added one because it has its form; this has been heard from them, it is reported, also in maṣā'ib and manā'ir.

Sibawayh said that it is an error (ghalat), which may mean that it is outside the beaten path and analogy; the word "error" is often used in his book in this sense. The verb ja'ala here means "to create and originate." Each of the two adverbial phrases (ẓarfayn) is connected to it or to an implied element, and it occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its indefinite object, for had it been postponed it would have been a qualifier of it. Its placement before the object, although the proper place of both is after it, is, as some verifiers said, for the sake of giving importance to what is put first and creating anticipation for what is delayed, for the soul, when what should be first is delayed, especially when the first indicates the benefit of the hearer, remains awaiting the arrival of the delayed item, so it settles in it with a greater settling upon its arrival. As for placing the lam before fi, it is because it indicates the aforementioned benefit more completely, and hastening to mention it is more important.

It has also been said that ja'ala is transitive to two objects, the second of which is one of the two adverbial phrases, on the basis that it is a stable predicate (mustaqirr) placed before the first object. The adverbial phrase is either a superfluous complement (laghw) connected to ja'ala, or to the implied element occurring as a circumstantial clause from the first object, as has passed. This was objected to: there is no benefit worth considering in reporting that the means of livelihood were made attained for them, or attained in the earth.

﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾ (10) for that great blessing. This is a concluding clause (tadhyil) brought to explain the poor condition of those addressed and to warn them. Al-Tibi said: The concluding clause with this is because thanks is suitable to their being established in the lands and their disposing of them, just as remembrance in the preceding clause is consistent with distinguishing between following the religion of truth and the religion of falsehood. The rest of the discussion of this clause follows the patterns of what has passed concerning its counterpart, so reflect upon it.

[Page 87]

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Rabi', Qatada and al-Suddi said: "The meaning is: We created Adam, then We shaped you in his loins, then We said..." The discussion of who the angels commanded to prostrate were, and of what prostration means, has already passed.

Some scholars of verification (muhaqqiqun) mentioned that the apparent wording would have been: "Then We commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam." But it departed from this, because the command to prostrate was before the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, as His words speak of: ﴿So when I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration﴾. What follows his shaping is only His words, glorified be He: ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾. This is to specify the time of the prostration that was commanded earlier. The summary is that He, glorified be He, first gave them a conditional command, then gave them a second, immediate command matching the earlier one, and so He made this a report of it. In this there is clearly great regard for the status of Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿So they prostrated﴾, that is, the angels, peace be upon them, after the saying, without hesitation, all of them together, ﴿except Iblis﴾. This is an exception of the contiguous kind (istithna' muttasil), whether or not we say that Iblis was truly one of the angels. On the first view it is obvious. On the second view, since he was a jinni, singled out and submerged among thousands of angels, and characterized by most of their attributes, he was subsumed under them in ﴿they prostrated﴾, and then he was excepted as one individual from among them. It was also said that it is a disjunct exception (munqati'), on the basis that he was of the jinn and that they are not of the same kind as the angels, and there is no subsumption (taghlib). The first view is the one preferred.

As for the mention of His words: ﴿He was not among the prostrators﴾ (11), that is, among those who prostrated to Adam, peace be upon him, even though it is already understood from the exception that he did not prostrate. This is because what is understood from an exception is the absence of the generality, not the generality of the absence. The intended meaning here is the second: that prostration did not proceed from him at all, neither with them nor alone. This, it was said, is conveyed only by explicit statement. But it has been objected that the explicit statement mentioned conveys the generality of states and times, so what was said does not hold.

The verification of this position, according to what al-Mawla Sari al-Din mentioned, is as follows: the scholars differed as to whether an exception from a negation is an affirmation. Al-Shafi'i said: yes, so the contradictory of the ruling is established for the excepted party by way of expression (ibarah). The apparent wording of al-Hidaya agrees with him.

A group of the Hanafis held that it is by way of allusion (isharah). Others held that the excepted party is in the status of what is left unstated, and that the ruling is derived only by way of the inference from contrary (mafhum al-mukhalafah). The author of al-Bahr preferred that it is an explicit statement at times by allusion and at other times by expression.

Given this, it may be said in reply that since the context was the context of recording against Iblis his failure to prostrate, and of exposing and rebuking him for that monstrous vice, it was fitting for it to be stated explicitly and deserving of caution, because reliance on an indicator is weak and suited to full clarity and affirmation. So the Qur'an turned away from the method of omission, even though the speech indicates the omitted part, toward the method of mention and explicit statement. This is evident on the view of al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him, and al-Sarraj al-Hindi pointed to it in the chapter on exception in his commentary on al-Mughni. As for the remaining schools, the matter is even clearer, since the ruling on the excepted party with the contradictory of the ruling on the party excepted from is either by way of allusion or by the inference from contrary. In either case the context refuses to settle for something like that and requires explicit mention of the ruling.

Our master Ibn al-Kamal claimed that this clause was only brought in because the exception is disjunct, and that if the exception were contiguous, bringing it would be wasted, because Iblis's not being among the prostrators would be understood from the exception on the assumption that it is contiguous. What this contains is not hidden from one who has grasped what we have mentioned. Some also objected to it, saying that on the assumption of disjunction it would also be wasted, based on what he supposed. For the establishing of the contradictory of the ruling on the party excepted from for the excepted party is not specific to the contiguous exception. That is why we do not find them mentioning, with a disjunct exception, the contradictory of the ruling on the party excepted from, except rarely. And if what he mentioned were sound, it would be obligatory to mention the predicate with every disjunct exception. So let this be understood.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 12:**

﴿Said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), arising from the report of his not prostrating, as if it were said: "Then what did Allah, exalted is He, say at that time?" Based on this, as has been said, the shift to the third person (*iltifat*, a change of grammatical person) becomes clear, since there is no basis for supposing the question in the second-person form. There is another benefit in it, which is an indication that what is related does not concern the addressees, as in the account of the creation and the shaping. That is: Allah, exalted is He, said to Iblis when he was not among those who prostrate: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ It is well known that *la* (not) is superfluous (*mazidah*), based on His saying, exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ It has also come thus in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that the People of the Book may not know﴾, meaning, "so that they may know." It is, in that case, as many have said, for emphasizing the meaning of the verb it enters upon and confirming it.

It has been objected: how can it emphasize the affirmation of the verb while giving the impression of its negation? Al-Shihab said: "What appears to me is that it does not emphasize it absolutely, but only when it accompanies a negation, whether preceding or following, explicit or not explicit, as in ﴿not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, and as here. So it emphasizes the connection of the prevention to it." And for this reason they said: it serves to draw attention to the fact that what is being rebuked is the abandonment of prostration. It has also been said that it is not superfluous, by taking the prevention to be a metaphor for compulsion and constraint, so the meaning is: "What compelled you to not prostrate?" Al-Sakkaki took it as a metaphor for "moving/inclining" (*al-haml*), with no clear indication (*qarinah*) for the metaphor, meaning: "What moved you and urged you to not prostrate?" There is not much difference between the two interpretations.

It was also permitted that this be a case of *tadmin* (conveying the sense of one verb within another). Al-Raghib said: *al-man'* (prevention) is used in the opposite sense of giving, as in "a man who withholds (*mani'*) and is stingy (*manna'*)," meaning miserly; and it is used for protection, from which come "a fortified place (*makan mani'*)," "he has prevented (*mana'a*)," and "so-and-so has a strong position (*dhu mana'ah*)," meaning powerful, unassailable by whoever seeks to attack him. The prevention in the verse is of the second kind, meaning: what protected you from not prostrating ﴿when I commanded you﴾ to prostrate. And ﴿when﴾ (*idh*) is an adverbial clause modifying ﴿you prostrate﴾.

This verse is one of the proofs of those who hold that a command implies immediacy (*al-amr li-l-fawr*), because it is a reproach for failing to hasten. Were the command not for immediacy, the reproach would not have been directed at him, and he would have been able to answer: "You did not command me to hasten, and I will prostrate later." It has been answered that the immediacy comes from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then fall down before him in prostration﴾, and not from the form of the command itself. Yet some have denied that the conditional *fa'* (then) indicates immediate consequence without delay. Others have said that the argument rests on the consequence of blame for disobeying an unrestricted command, since He, exalted is He, said: ﴿when I commanded you﴾ and did not say: "when I said, then fall down before him in prostration." So reflect.

In the reporting of the rebuke here, with this wording; in Surat al-Hijr with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Iblis, what is the matter with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾; and in Surat Sad with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾, there is an indication that the accursed one combined, in one act of disobedience, more than one of those acts of disobedience, each sufficient for the rebuke and the invalidity of what he committed. The reporting of the rebuke has been entirely omitted in Surat al-Baqarah, Surat Bani Isra'il, Surat al-Kahf and Surat Ta-Ha. Allah, exalted is He, knows best the wisdom of each.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence, as has been mentioned, built upon a question that arose from the report of the rebuke, as if it were said: "Then what did the accursed one say at that point?" So it is said: he said ﴿I am better than him﴾. This is of the foolish style, for the answer that corresponds to the question would be "what prevented me is such-and-such." This is an answer to "which of you is better?" It contains an assertion of something that is, by his claim, necessarily implying the intended point, and it suggests that one of such a character should not be fitting to prostrate to one lesser than himself; so how could it be fitting for him to be commanded to do so? Thus the accursed one was the first to lay the foundation of arrogance and to invent the doctrine of good and evil as intrinsic causes (*al-husn wa-l-qubh al-'illiyyayn*).

His saying, exalted is He, reporting him: ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ (12) is a justification for what he claimed, that he is superior to him (peace be upon him), and its summary is: "I was created from a substance more noble than his substance, because my substance is celestial, luminous, strong in influence, and suited to the matter of life, whereas his substance is the opposite of that. And what is created from the more noble is more noble, because nobility of origin entails nobility of offshoot, so I am like that. And the noble does not fittingly submit to one lower than himself." The accursed one erred, for the claim that fire is nobler than earth is not established. Each of the four elements has benefits peculiar to it that are not found in others, and each is essential in this mode of existence, and each has its excellence in its own place and condition. So preferring some over others is prolix without benefit, for one who considers that earth provides more benefits to creatures, since it is their dwelling place and the place of their livelihoods, and it is characterized by steadiness, which is one of the requirements of forbearance and dignity; and that fire is below it in benefits and is characterized by lightness, which is one of the requirements of frivolity, arrogance and self-exaltation. Thus what is in the accursed one's words becomes known. Furthermore, nobility of origin does not necessarily entail nobility of offshoot:

*"The rose comes only from the thorn, and the narcissus grows only from an onion."*

It suffices in that the unbeliever may come forth from the believer. Moreover, he restricted nobility to what derives from the matter and substance, although a thing is ennobled not only by its matter and substance but also by its agent, its end and its form. And this nobility is found in Adam (peace be upon him) beyond that, for Allah, exalted is He, created him with His two hands, breathed into him of His spirit, made him a vicegerent on earth, as He related, and placed in him what He placed. Furthermore, what ugliness is there in the excellent serving the less excellent out of humility and in disregarding one's own share? Indeed, the service was in reality for Allah, exalted is He. To this Zafir al-Iskandari alluded in his saying:

*"You are the aim of the arrangement of every poem*
*that was built upon the purpose of exalting him,*
*Like the prostration of the angels of heaven to Adam,*
*while their prostration was to Allah in its true sense."*
