Then, the apparent meaning is that this answer from the accursed one was given while granting that he was commanded to prostrate; in that case his error is more evident than fire on a flag, since it amounts to objecting to the Wise Sovereign. Some have said: he did not concede that he was commanded, but rather removed himself from the general address through analogy (*qiyas*). The proponents of this view cite this rebuke as proof that a text (*nass*) may not be specified by analogy.

It has been answered that this is not specification, but rather a nullification of the text and its complete abrogation of it. And in this there is room for reflection.

Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* and al-Daylami narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, may Allah be pleased with them all, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to measure the matter of religion by his opinion was Iblis. Allah, exalted is He, said to him: 'Prostrate to Adam,' and he said: 'I am better than him'..." etc. Ja'far said: "Whoever measures the matter of religion by his opinion, Allah, exalted is He, will join him on the Day of Resurrection with Iblis, because he followed him by analogy." And whoever prohibits analogy absolutely has argued with this and similar reports.

It has been answered regarding that: what is blameworthy is analogy and opinion set against a text, or in cases where one of the valid conditions is absent. The verification of this belongs in its proper place. In the verse there is also evidence for creation (*al-kawn*) and corruption (*al-fasad*), since it indicates the creation of Adam (peace be upon him) and Iblis (may the curse of Allah be upon him), and their bringing into existence; and for the impossibility of clay and fire changing from what each of them was, in clayness and fieriness, into what is composed of them; and that Iblis and his kind are bodies that have come into being, not eternal spirits. It has been said: perhaps the attribution of the creation of Adam (peace be upon him) to clay and of his (Iblis's) creation to fire is in consideration of the predominant component, since otherwise it has been established that bodies are composed of the four elements; and some people hold back from denying this.

[Page 90]

﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (istinaf), as explained earlier. The "fa" in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So get down from it﴾, indicates that the command follows from the arrogance that became evident from him. The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ is said to refer to the Garden, and that he was one of its inhabitants is well known. According to some, the Garden meant here is the one in which the believers will dwell on the Day of Resurrection. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it was a garden in 'Adn, and that Adam, peace be upon him, was created in it. According to one view, it was on a raised place of the earth (nashz). The basic meaning of hubut (descent) is downward movement by compulsion, as in the falling of a stone. When it is used of a human being or the like, it implies belittlement (istikhaf), as al-Raghib said.

Some scholars did not require anything in hubut beyond moving from a noble place to a lesser one, based on His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Get down to a city﴾ [2:61]. The meaning of this is clear, even if we do not say that that Garden was on a raised place.

It is also said that the pronoun refers to the company of the angels, meaning: go out from the company of the honoured angels, for leaving their company is a descent, and what a descent it is. In Surat al-Hijr the words are ﴿So go out from it﴾ [15:34].

It is said that the pronoun refers to the heaven, and a group of scholars held this view. But it is refuted on the ground that his whispering to Adam, peace be upon him, took place after this expulsion, so it must be understood as one of the two earlier interpretations, definitely. His whispering, according to the first interpretation, would be by way of calling out from the gate of the Garden, as narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri. It is answered that it is possible that what is meant by that is the Garden, or also the company of the angels, on the basis that the first (the Garden) and most of the second are in the heaven. Or it may be said that the story took place on earth, and the Garden was in it, and after the disobedience the accursed one was barred from the heaven, which is his abode and place of worship. The meaning of the command to go out from it is a command to cut his ties to it and to take it no longer as a dwelling. This is like when you say to someone who has usurped your house, for example, in the presence of a judge or the like: "Get out of my house," although at that time he is not in it. You mean: do not enter it, and cut your ties to it. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the earth.

It has been narrated that he was expelled from it to the islands, and was commanded not to enter it except secretly. But this is far-fetched, because the specification in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So it is not for you﴾, that is, it is not proper, nor fitting, nor becoming of your rank ﴿to be arrogant therein﴾, does not appear to have a sense on this view, except in a far-fetched way.

As for the earlier interpretations, the meaning is evident, namely the great nobility of the place from which he is expelled, the exaltation of its rank, and the sanctity of its precinct. From this it is known that the verse gives no indication of the permissibility of arrogance in other matters, according to those who hold the principle of mafhum (implicit meaning). The clause is a reason for the command to descend. The subtlety of the expression "descend" rather than "go out" is not hidden, in contrast to his words ﴿I am better than him. You created me from fire﴾ [7:12], which points to the elevation of his element and the loftiness of his place.

Arrogance (takabbur), as has been said, is like pride (kibr), which is the state in which a person is distinguished by admiring himself, namely that he sees himself as greater and more magnificent than others. What is meant by arrogance here is either arrogance against Allah, Exalted is He, which is the greatest arrogance, and it is by refusing to accept the truth and submit to it in worship. Some scholars interpreted it as disobedience. Or it is arrogance against Adam, peace be upon him, on the basis of his claim that he is better than him and greater in rank. It has also been said that what is meant is something more general than this, including arrogance against the angels, since he claimed that he had a special quality that distinguished him over them and removed him from their general status. There is reflection needed on this.

Some claimed that the verse contains an indication that arrogance does not befit the people of the Garden. Just as he is prevented from remaining in it, he is prevented from entering it afterwards. And that He, Exalted is He, expelled him only because of his arrogance, not merely because of his disobedience. This is evident on one of the possibilities, as is not hidden.

The adverbial phrase ("therein") is either connected to what is before it, or to an elided element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal). His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So go out﴾, are an emphasis of the command to descend, following from it. His words, Glorified is He, ﴿Indeed you are among the abased﴾ [7:13], are a reason for the command to go out, implying that it is because of his arrogance; that is, you are among the people of humiliation and disgrace before Allah, Exalted is He, and before His friends, because of your arrogance.

Al-Bayhaqi related in Shu'ab al-Iman from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:
"Whoever humbles himself for Allah, Allah, Exalted is He, will raise him; and whoever is arrogant, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will lower him."
And from his hadith, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever humbles himself for Allah, Exalted is He, Allah raises his wisdom," and he said: "Rise up, may Allah raise you up." "And whoever is arrogant and transgresses his bounds, Allah, Exalted is He, will push him down to the earth."

It is said that what is meant by "the abased" is those debased in this world through blame and curse, and in the Hereafter through punishment, because of the disobedience and arrogance he committed. And the humiliation of the arrogant by Allah, Exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection is something the reports have spoken of.

Al-Tirmidhi related from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:
"The arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in the likeness of ants, in the forms of men. Abasement will overwhelm them from every place. They will be driven to a prison in Hell called Bulas, and they will be given to drink from the clay of corruption, the essence of the people of the Fire."

Some interpreted "al-sagirin" (the abased) as those content with humiliation, as is the well-known meaning of the word. The intended meaning is describing him as base in nature, lowly, and that he saw himself as greater than others while he was not great. Abu Nuwas composed excellently with a verse addressing him:

"You are a disgrace in the eye; you have robbed people of all of them through rage against them.
You went astray when you were commanded in the ancient age, and you parted from the company of those who prostrate.
When you said: I will not bear to prostrate to a likeness that You, my Lord, created from clay,
out of envy, since You created Yourself from the blazing fire, for the one who was the origin of the worlds.
Then you were made to lead, running to the pimping of the adulterers and the sodomites, O protector of fornicators and sodomites."

He also has, in other lines of his:
"He showed off over Adam in prostration, and became a pimp for his offspring."

Say (qāla) — this is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf), as mentioned before, built upon a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What did the accursed one say after he heard what he heard?" So it is answered: he said, "Reprieve me" (anẓirnī), i.e., grant me respite and do not cause me to die, "until the day they are resurrected" (ilā yawmi yubʿathūn) (14). That is, Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring. It is the time of the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thāniyah). By this he intended to find a space for seduction (al-ighwāʾ) and to take revenge (akhdh al-thaʾr), and to be saved from death, since there is no death after resurrection (al-baʿth).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 15:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as has been explained. ﴿Indeed, you are among those given respite﴾ (15). Its apparent meaning is "until the day they are resurrected," since it occurs in response to his statement. But in Surah al-Hijr and Surah Sad, the restriction is "until the day of the known time." There is disagreement about what is meant by it. The well-known view is that it is the day of the first blast (al-nafkha al-ula), not the day of resurrection, because it is not a day of death. Some have permitted that it means the day of resurrection, and it does not follow that he will not die; perhaps he will die at the beginning of the day and be resurrected with the creation within its span.

In the book al-Arais, it is related from Ka'b al-Ahbar that Iblis only tastes death on the Day of Gathering. He mentioned the manner of his death and the seizing of his soul by Azra'il, in a way that is astonishing. The virtuous al-Saffarini did not approve of that, and said in his book (al-Buhur al-Zakhirah): Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "They will not remain," meaning the people, after Gog and Magog, until the sun rises from its place of setting. Then the pens will dry, the scrolls will be rolled up, and no repentance will be accepted from anyone. Iblis will fall prostrate, calling out: "My Lord, command me to prostrate to whomever You wish." The devils will gather around him and say: "O our master, to whom will you turn for refuge?" He will say: "I only asked my Lord to grant me respite until the day of resurrection, so He granted me respite until the day of the known time." The sun will have risen from its place of setting, and this is the day of the known time. The devils will appear on the earth, until a man says: "This is my companion who used to be with me." So praise be to Allah who has disgraced him. Iblis will remain prostrate, weeping, until the beast comes out and kills him while he is prostrate. End.

From this it is known that what is meant by the known day is what the accursed one himself stated, and it is well before the day of the first blast. This is an opinion that we have not seen any of the exegetes mention, and it is what this virtuous scholar approved. He said: the report is in the ruling of the attributed-to-the-Prophet (marfu'), because it is not said from opinion, and Ibn Mas'ud is not like Ka'b al-Ahbar, who took from the books of the People of the Book.

You know that if the attribution of this report to Ibn Mas'ud is sound, then one should not turn away to an opinion that contradicts it. But concerning the soundness of its attribution to him, may Allah be pleased with him, I have doubts. It was said: what is meant by it is a time at which Allah, exalted is He, knows the end of his term, and that has been hidden from us, and likewise from the accursed one. On this view it must be before the second blast. Some have argued for it by saying: the accursed one was a mukallaf (bound by religious obligation), and a mukallaf cannot be allowed to know his term, because he would proceed to disobedience with an empty heart, until when his term draws near he repents and his repentance is accepted; this would amount to encouragement to sins, and so it would be repugnant. It was answered: whoever Allah, exalted is He, knows from his state will die in purity and infallibility, like the prophets, peace be upon them, or in disbelief and sins, like Iblis and his partisans, then informing him of the time of his term is not an encouragement to disobedience, because his state does not change through that information and notification.

The apparent sense of the noble verse, according to more than one, is that this is a response to his supplication, wholly or partly. In that is evidence for the one who said that the supplication of a disbeliever may be answered, which is the view taken by al-Dabbusi and others among the jurists, contrary to what al-Bazzaziyya reports from some, that it is not permissible to say that the supplication of a disbeliever is answered, because he does not know Allah, exalted is He, so as to call upon Him. The fatwa follows the first view, for the apparent meaning and for his saying ﷺ: "The supplication of the wronged is answered, even if he is a disbeliever."

Interpreting disbelief as ingratitude for blessings rather than disbelief in the religion is contrary to the apparent meaning. And answering does not entail love and honor, for it may be for the sake of gradual enticement (istidraj). Some verifiers said: the sentence is a report that he is among those given respite in the decree of Allah, exalted is He, without it being consequent upon his supplication. It was claimed that its occurrence as a nominal sentence, together with the reference to the inclusion of the others for whom the accursed one asked in a manner that indicates that the petitioner is a follower of them in that, is clear that this is a report that the respite mentioned for them was from eternity, not a fresh granting of respite specific to him in answer to his supplication. It is also known from this that his request for respite was a request to delay death, since by it his being among them is realized, not to delay punishment as has been said; and it is not without good. The wisdom in granting him that long period, despite what he is upon, the curse of corruption, is something whose knowledge should be entrusted to the Creator of the servants.

Al-Shahrastani mentioned, from the commentator of the Four Gospels, a picture of a debate that took place between the angels and Iblis after this event, which is also mentioned in the Torah. It is that the accursed one said to the angels: "I concede that I have a god who is my creator and originator, and he is the creator of creation, but I have questions about his judgment. The first: what is the wisdom in creation, especially since he knew that the disbeliever upon his creation deserves only the Fire? The second: what is the benefit of obligation, since no benefit or harm returns to him from it, and whatever returns to the obligated, he is able to achieve for them without the means of obligation? The third: suppose he obligated me to know him and obey him, then why did he obligate me to prostrate to Adam? The fourth: when I disobeyed him in abandoning prostration, why did he curse me and make my punishment obligatory, when there is no benefit to him or to anyone else in it, and for me in it is the greatest harm? The fifth: when he did that, why did he give me power over his offspring and enable me to mislead and lead them astray? The sixth: when I asked him for a long period of respite in that, why did he grant it to me, when it is known that if the world were free of evil, that would be better?" The commentator of the Gospels said: Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him from the pavilion of majesty and greatness: "O Iblis, you did not know Me, and if you had known Me, you would have known that there is no objection against Me in any of My acts, for I am Allah, there is no god but I, I am not questioned about what I do." End.

In the sixth question there is something that supports the first view in general. It is not hidden that these doubts are hard for those who hold the rational good and evil to answer; rather, al-Imam said: if the first and last of creation gathered and judged by the reason's assessment of good and evil, they would not find a way out of these doubts, and all would be obliged. And what is related pleases me: Sayf al-Dawla ibn Hamdan once went out to his company and said: "I have composed a verse that I do not think anyone will compose a second to, unless it is Abu Firas." Abu Firas was sitting, and he was asked: "What is it?" He said: "My saying:"

"For you, my body is afflicted, and my blood has not been pursued by you"
Abu Firas immediately replied:

"He said: if you are a possessor, then all the command is mine."

Al-Zamakhshari explained his granting of the request for respite by saying: in that is a trial for the servants, and in opposing it is the greatest reward; its ruling is the ruling of the adornments and kinds of diversions and pleasures that Allah, exalted is He, created in this world, and the desires He placed in the souls, by which He tests His servants. Al-Allama al-Thani critiqued him, as others did, saying that it is based on explaining the acts of Allah, exalted is He, by purposes, and on not attributing the creation of evils and corruptions to Him, glorified is He; yet that is nothing, because the reality of trial with respect to Him, exalted is He, is impossible, and its metaphorical sense does not remove the question. Also, the painful punishment in following him is many times what is in opposing him of great reward. Indeed, if He had not given him respite and enablement, there would have been of the servants nothing but acts of obedience and abstaining from sins, and there would be only reward, like the angels. And there is no hiding what is in it; except that his saying afterward: "It is better that the servant not delve into such secrets, and entrust their reality to the Wise, the Chooser," is among what we say, because knowing that is extremely difficult for the people of talk and the people of dispute.

This is it. The reason the timing was omitted in this verse is reliance on what occurred in Surah al-Hijr and Surah Sad, just as the call particle and the fa' were omitted in the request for respite and the granting of respite, relying on what was mentioned in them both.

If you say: there is no doubt that a reported speech, at the time of its utterance by the speaker, has a particular state that requires its coming in a specific way from the aspects of composition, such that if it lacked any of that, the speech would wholly fall from the rank of eloquence. So a single reported speech related in various ways: if the situation requires its coming in a specific way among those ways that come in that report, that way is the one that conforms to what the situation requires and reaches the rank of eloquence, not the others. We say then: it is not hidden that the accursed one's request for respite issued from him only once and no more. Its setting, if it required displaying humility and arranging the request upon what befell him of curse and expulsion, in the manner of seeking restoration in exchange for breaking, is as is evident from his saying: "My Lord, grant me respite," as reported of him in the two surahs. So what is reported of him here will be far from conformity with what the situation requires, let alone ascending to the heights of inimitability.

I say: Our master Shaykh al-Islam answered this question after stating it: the setting of his request requires what has been mentioned, namely displaying humility and arranging the request upon the deprivation indicated by the expulsion and stoning; likewise the setting of the granting requires arranging the report of the granting upon the request. The speech was applied to this in those two surahs, and each of the two settings, that of the reporting and that of the reported, was given its full share. But here, since the setting of the reporting required mere report of the request and the granting, the reporting was brought in a manner of brevity and conciseness, without addressing the manner of each of them in address and reply. It does not follow that this is not a transmission of the speech as it was, nor that it is not conforming to the requirement of the setting. What must be considered in transmitting speech is only the original meaning and the very signified content. As for the manner of conveying it, that may or may not be observed according to what is required. Stripping it of those does not harm the essence of the speech; rather, when transmitted, there are manners observed which the speaker did not observe at all, indeed may not even be able to observe. All the reported utterances in the verses are of this kind; otherwise most of them would not be inimitable. The criterion for conformity is the setting of the reporting. As for the setting of the reported, if its requirement agrees with that, each of the two is given its full share, as in the two surahs; otherwise not, as in this place. So understand.

﴿قالَ﴾ *(He said)*: a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), like its counterparts elsewhere. ﴿فَبِما أغْوَيْتَنِي﴾ *(So because You have led me astray)*: the *fa'* marks the sequence of the clause that follows, ("because You granted me respite"). The *ba'* is either an oath particle or a causal particle. In both readings *ma* is a verbal-masdar (*mas­dariyyah*) particle, and the prepositional phrase is linked to "I swear" (*uqsimu*). It has also been said that on the causal reading it is linked to what follows the *lam*. But this is weak, because according to the sound view the *lam* has the right of initial position, so what follows it cannot govern what precedes it. Some scholars allowed that *ma* is an interrogative whose *alif* was not dropped, and that the prepositional phrase is linked to *aghwaytani*. But its weakness is not hidden.

*Al-ighwa'* (causing error) means creating *al-ghayy* (error, deviation). The root meaning of *al-ghayy* is corruption. From it comes *ghawiya al-fasilu*, when the young camel's stomach is upset and corrupted. It also comes to mean ignorance arising from a false belief, as in His saying, glorified be He: ﴿ما ضَلَّ صاحِبُكم وما غَوى﴾ *(Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred)*. It also means failure, as in the verse:

*Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair,*
*and whoever errs will not lack a reproacher for his error.*

From this is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿وعَصى آدَمُ رَبَّهُ فَغَوى﴾ *(And Adam disobeyed his Lord, so he erred)*. It is also used metaphorically, with the relation of cause (*'alaqah sababiyyah*), to mean punishment, as in His saying: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يَلْقَوْنَ غَيًّا﴾ *(so they will encounter destruction)*.

For the People of the Sunnah there is no barrier to taking *al-ighwa'* here to mean creating error in the sense of misguidance, i.e. "by what You have misguided me." This is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Attributing *ighwa'* in this sense to Allah, mighty and majestic, is what the generality of His saying, glorified be He, requires: ( *the Creator of every thing* ). The Mu'tazilah refuse to attribute such a thing to Him, glorified be He. At times they said about this that it is a satanic statement and so is not evidence. At other times they interpreted it as meaning that *ighwa'* is the attribution of *ghayy* to someone, as in *akfarahu* when one attributes unbelief (*kufr*) to him, or that it means bringing about and causing the cause of error, which is the command to prostrate.

Some scholars said: *al-ghayy* here means failure, i.e. "by what You have deprived him of from Your mercy," or destruction, i.e. "by what You have destroyed him with Your curse upon him and Your expulsion of him." What led them to all of this is their not saying that Allah, exalted be He, is the Creator of every thing and that there is no creator besides Him, glorified be He. This did not suffice them, so they attacked the People of the Sunnah who affirm this. What can one think of a group that is content for itself with hidden forms of polytheism that Iblis, may the curse be upon him, did not precede them in? We seek refuge in Allah, glorified and exalted be He, from provoking His wrath.

Yes, *al-ighwa'* in the sense of encouragement toward that in which there is error, and commanding it, as is the intent of the accursed one in his saying ﴿لأُغْوِيَنَّهُمْ﴾ *(I will surely mislead them)*, is something that is not permissible from Allah, exalted is His state, as is not hidden. Then, if the *ba'* is an oath particle, the thing sworn by is an attribute of the actions of God. This is something that is sworn by in common usage, even though the jurists do not apply the rulings of an oath to it.

It is possible that the accursed one swore by both of them together, so that at times he related his oath by one and at other times by the other. If the particle is causal, then the oath is by His might, meaning: because of Your misleading me, for their sake, *I swear by Your might*, ﴿لأقْعُدَنَّ لَهُمْ﴾ *(I will surely sit in wait for them)*, i.e. for Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring, lying in ambush for them as highwaymen sit in wait for travellers, ﴿صِراطَكَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ *(Your straight path)* (16): the one that leads to Paradise, which is the truth in which is Your good pleasure.

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Sabrah ibn al-Fakih, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, Satan sat in wait for the son of Adam on his paths. He sat in wait for him on the path of Islam and said: 'Will you embrace Islam and abandon your religion and the religion of your fathers?' He disobeyed him and embraced Islam. Then he sat in wait for him on the path of emigration (*hijrah*) and said: 'Will you emigrate and abandon your land and your sky? The likeness of the emigrant is like the horse in its tether.' He disobeyed him and emigrated. Then he sat in wait for him on the path of jihad and said: 'It is exertion of the self and wealth; you will fight, and you will be killed, and your wife will be married off, and your wealth will be divided.' He disobeyed him and strove. Then he (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever of them does that and dies, or whose mount throws him and he dies, it is an obligation upon Allah, exalted be He, that He admit him to Paradise.'"

The Prophet (ﷺ) may have limited himself to these mentioned matters in order to give attention to their importance and to draw attention to their great worth, since the context required that. It is not for restriction. A parallel to this is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and others, may Allah be pleased with them, in explaining *al-sirat al-mustaqim* (the straight path) as the road to Mecca. The statement is from the category of metonymy (*kinayah*) or figurative representation (*tamthil*, an image drawn to illustrate a meaning).

The word ( *al-sirata* ) is in the accusative either as a direct object (*maf'ul bihi*), by implying in *uqa'dannna* the sense of "traverse" (*tadmin*), or by removing the preposition, meaning "on Your path," like your saying *darraba Zayd al-zahra wa al-batna* ("Zayd struck the back and the belly"), or as an adverb of place (*zarf*). The accusative of a place noun specific to this use is rare. Among such uses, the most famous is the verse:

*Ladun* with the shaking of the hand, its shaft is smeared in it,
as the fox smears the road.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 17:

﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and behind them, and from their right and from their left.﴾ That is, from the four directions from which an enemy is customarily expected to attack. The intended meaning is: "I will surely embellish (lu-usawwilanna) for them and lead them astray (la-udillannahum) as far as is possible." However, he (Iblis) has likened the state of his embellishing and whispering to them to the state of an enemy coming upon one who is hostile to him from whatever direction is available to him. For this reason "above" and "below" are not mentioned, since no attack comes from those two. Thus the statement is of the type of metaphorical representation (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah). And "I will surely sit in wait for them" (﴿la-aq'udanna lahum﴾), according to what has been said, is a continuation (tarshih) of this image. Some (scholars) did not take the statement out of the realm of representation, and they excused the omission of the direction of "above" by saying that mercy descends from it, and the omission of the direction of "below" by saying that an attack from it is frightening. The excuse regarding the first, as mentioned, has been transmitted by several (narrators) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father; it is also narrated from 'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi. The excuse regarding the second has been attributed by al-Tabarsi to the same scholar (al-Habr) as well. It is not far-fetched, on this basis, that the statement is also a representation, and the difference between the two explanations is that the omission of these two directions in the first is due to their absence in the thing represented by the image (al-mumaththal bihi), and in the second, due to their absence in the thing represented (al-mumaththal).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that ﴿from before them﴾ means from the direction of the Hereafter, because it is future and coming, and what is such is as if it were "before" (in front of) them; ﴿and from behind them﴾ means from the direction of this world, because it is past in relation to the Hereafter, and because it is perishable, left behind and abandoned; ﴿and from their right and from their left﴾ means from the direction of their good deeds and their bad deeds. The explanation of "right" as good deeds and "left" as bad deeds is because they place the beloved on the right side and other things on the left side, as the poet said:

"Buthayna, have you placed me on your right hand, so that I rejoice, or have you made me among your left (things)?"

Al-Asma'i said: It is said, "He is with us on the right (bi-l-yamin)," meaning in a good position, and "on the left (bi-l-shimal)" is the opposite of that. The statement, according to this, may admit metaphors, metonymies or allusions. A similar thing has been said: ﴿from before them﴾ means from where they know and are able to guard against it; ﴿and from behind them﴾ means from where they do not know; ﴿and from their right and from their left﴾ means from where it is easy for them to know and guard themselves, but they did not do so due to their lack of vigilance and caution; and from where that is not easy for them.

Some of the wise men of Islam said: In the body there are four powers. The first is the retentive power (al-quwwah al-khaliyah), in which things like sensible objects are gathered; its seat is the front ventricle of the brain, and the reference to it is in His saying ﴿from before them﴾. The second is the imaginative power (al-quwwah al-wahmiyyah), which judges, regarding non-sensible things, by judgments suited to sensible things; its seat is the rear ventricle of the brain, and the reference to it is in His saying ﴿and from behind them﴾. The third is the appetitive power (al-quwwah al-shahwaniyyah), whose seat is the liver, which is on the right side of the human being, and the reference to it is in His saying ﴿and from their right﴾. The fourth is the irascible power (al-quwwah al-ghadabiyyah), whose seat is the heart, which is on the left side, and the reference to it is in His saying ﴿and from their left﴾. The Devil, so long as he does not seek help from any of these powers, cannot cast whispering. This, in my view, is a kind of allusion, as is not hidden. It has been said otherwise as well.

The verb is transitive to the first two by the preposition of origin (min), because from those two (directions) it comes toward them, and to the other two by the preposition of passing beyond (ʿan), because the one who comes from those two is like one who deviates from them, passing by their side. A parallel to this is the saying: "I sat on his right side (ʿan yamīnihi)."

Al-Qutb, in explaining the reason for this, built it on what some of the wise men of Islam said: that "min" indicates connection and "ʿan" indicates separation. The effect of the Devil on the two powers of the brain is the acquisition of false beliefs such as polytheism, anthropomorphism and negation (of divine attributes), which are imprinted upon the human soul and connected to it; and in appetite and anger is the acquisition of evil deeds of appetite and anger, which separate from the soul and cease to exist. For this reason, in the first two directions he used "min," which is connective, and in the other two "ʿan," which is separative. It has also been said that he specified right and left with "ʿan" because there are two angels who require passing beyond these. There is an examination of this that is not hidden. Some claimed that the verse is like evidence that the accursed one cannot enter the body of the son of Adam and mix with it, for if that were possible he would have mentioned it in the section of exaggeration. The hadith "Indeed the Devil runs through the son of Adam as the blood runs" is of the type of representation, and so it requires that it not be mentioned. So reflect.

﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ (17). That is, obedient. He said this by supposition, as is narrated from al-Hasan and Abu Muslim, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Iblis did indeed confirm his assumption about them﴾ (Surah Saba': 20), when he saw that the soul has nineteen powers: the outer and inner senses, appetite and anger, and the seven vegetative powers—the attractive, the retentive, the digestive, the expulsive, the nutritive, the growth-producing, and the generative—and that all of them together call the soul to the world of the body, and that there is nothing calling to the world of spirits except a single power, which is the intellect; and one does not accomplish anything against many.

"I see a thousand builders who cannot be erected by a single demolisher; how then with a building behind which stand a thousand demolishers?"

It is also narrated from al-Jubba'i that he heard this from the angels and said it as a certainty. It has been said that he saw it before the Preserved Tablet.

The word "wajada" (found) is either in the sense of "ṣādafa" (came upon), in which case it takes one object, which is ﴿aktharahum﴾, and "shakirin" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); or it is in the sense of "ʿalima" (knew), in which case it takes two objects, the second of which is ﴿shakirin﴾. The sentence is either conjoined to the thing sworn to (al-muqsam ʿalayhi), or it is independent (mustanaffah). The reason it was not made a consequence of what preceded is that its content, by the requirement of natural disposition (al-jibillah), is also not merely by his seduction. The reason for the expression "most" is clear.

"He said" (﴿قالَ﴾) is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as has passed more than once. ﴿Get out of it﴾ means out of Paradise, or out of the company of the angels, or out of the heavens; the disagreement mentioned earlier applies. ﴿Disgraced﴾ (مَذْءُومًا, madh'um) means blamed, as related from Ibn Zayd, or humiliated and cursed, as related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Its verb is dhaa'a. Al-Zuhri read it as "madhum" (مَذُومًا), with a dammah on the dhal and a silent waw. There are two possibilities for this. The first is that it is a lightened form of the hamzated word, with the vowel of the hamza moved to the silent letter and then the hamza dropped. The second is that it comes from dhaam, with an alif, like "baa'a". By analogy its form would have been "madhim", like "mabi'" (sold), but the waw has replaced the ya', following the pattern of their saying "makul" for "makil" (measured), even though it comes from kayl (measure). Its accusative case is that of a circumstantial state (haal). The same applies to His saying ﴿mardhuran﴾ (مَدْحُورًا), which comes from al-dahr, meaning expulsion and banishment. It is also permitted that this word be a descriptive adjective (sifah). The lam in His saying ﴿for whoever follows you among them﴾ (لَمَن تَبِعَكَ مِنهُمْ), according to ad-Durr al-Masun (ad-Durr al-Masun, a grammatical commentary by al-Samin al-Halabi), is a lam introducing an oath (muwatti'ah lil-qasam), and "man" is a conditional noun in the nominative position as a subject. His saying ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾ (لأمْلأنَّ جَهَنَّمَ مِنكم أجْمَعِينَ) is the answer to the oath, and it stands in place of the answer to the condition. The disagreement concerning the predicate of the subject in such constructions is well known. It is also permitted that the lam be the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') and "man" a relative pronoun (mawsulah) subject, whose relative clause is "tabi'aka" (followed you), and the oath clause is the predicate. 'Ismah, from 'Asim, read "liman" with a kasrah on the lam. It is said that it is connected to "disgraced" and "banished" by the grammatical principle of tanazu' (competition between two verbs), with the second one operative, meaning: "Get out with these two qualities, because of your following." It is also said that the prepositional phrase is the predicate of an omitted subject, to be understood as postponed, meaning: "This threat is for whoever follows you," and His saying ﴿I will surely fill﴾ indicates it. Perhaps this is what az-Zamakhshari meant when he said that ﴿la-amla'anna﴾ is in the position of the subject and ﴿liman tabi'aka﴾ is its predicate, as the explanation of the meaning indicates. ﴿From you﴾ (مِنكم) means from you and from them, and the addressee is given precedence, as in His saying: ﴿You are a people who are ignorant﴾. Then, the apparent meaning is that these addresses to Iblis, may God's curse be upon him, came from God, Glorified and Exalted, directly, without an intermediary. The purpose of them was not honour and dignity, but punishment and rebuke. al-Jubba'i held that they came through some of the angels, because God Most High does not speak to the disbeliever. But this is open to examination.

* * *

This is from the allusive (ishari) interpretation of the verses. ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad﴾ (المص): the alif indicates the Unique Essence (al-dhat al-ahadiyyah); the lam indicates the Essence together with the attribute of knowledge; the mim indicates the meaning of Muhammad, which is his reality; and the sad indicates his form, upon him be blessings and peace. It may also be said: the alif indicates Unity (tawhid), the mim indicates Sovereignty (mulk), and the lam lies between them as an intermediary, to be a link between them. The sad, because it is a letter of a round shape, receptive to all shapes, as the Shaykh al-Akbar, may God sanctify his secret, said: In it is an indication that the matter, though it appears in different forms and multiple images, its beginning and end are other than it (the essence). The subtlety of opening this surah with these letters is not hidden, based on what the Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, mentioned in his Futuhat (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyyah) that each of them, apart from the alif, is the "a'raf" (the heights). As for the alif, he has mentioned, may God benefit us through the blessings of his knowledge, that it is not among the letters according to whoever has perceived a fragrance of the realities. But the common people have called it a letter. So when the realizer (muhaqqiq) says this, it is only by way of metaphorical usage (tajawwuz) in the terminology, and God Most High knows best the true state of affairs. ﴿A Book sent down to you, so let there be no constriction in your breast because of it﴾, meaning, a tightness from bearing it, so that you cannot contain it because of its greatness, and you would dissolve in annihilation (fana'), unity (wahdah) and absorption (istighraq) in the Unity of the Gathering ('ayn al-jam'). ﴿That you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers﴾, meaning, so that warning and reminding may be possible for you, for in absorption you see only the Truth, and so this is not possible from you. ﴿How many a town﴾ — of the towns of the hearts — ﴿We have destroyed﴾, meaning, We have corrupted its readiness. ﴿Our punishment came upon it by night﴾, meaning, while they were sleeping on the bed of heedlessness during the night of youth. ﴿Or they were resting at midday﴾, meaning, under the shade of hope during the day of old age. ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the Truth﴾: according to many of the Sufis, it is the reckoning of deeds. They mentioned that the tongue of the scale of Truth is the attribute of justice, one of its two pans is the world of the senses, and the other pan is the world of the intellect. Whoever's acquisitions are from enduring intelligibles, noble characters, and good deeds joined with a sincere intention, his scale becomes heavy, that is, he has worth, and he prospers, that is, he wins everlasting bliss. And whoever's possessions are from perishable sensible things, pleasures and corrupt desires, and base characters, his scale becomes light, is not regarded, and he loses himself, by being deprived of bliss and destroyed. ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾, meaning, when We made you vicegerents (khulafa') upon it. ﴿And We have made for you therein means of livelihood﴾, numerous, not for others, for they have one livelihood only. That is because the human being has an angelic aspect, an animal aspect and a satanic aspect. So the livelihood of his spirit is the livelihood of the angel, the livelihood of his body is the livelihood of the animal, and the livelihood of his commanding soul (nafs ammarah) is the livelihood of the devil. He has other livelihoods besides these, namely the livelihood of the heart through witnessing (shuhud), the livelihood of the secret (sirr) through unveilings (kashf), and the livelihood of the secret of the secret (sirr al-sirr) through union (wisal). ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾. If you had given thanks, you would not have been content with the lowly.

﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾, that is, We began that with the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, and his fashioning. ﴿Then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam﴾, for he is the greatest manifestation. In a report: God created Adam in His form, and in another narration, in the form of the Merciful. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ and submitted to the Truth ﴿except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾, because of the deficiency of his insight. ﴿He said: I am better than him; You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾. The accursed one meant that he is from the spiritual presence, and that Adam, peace be upon him, is not like that. ﴿He said: Then get down from it﴾, meaning from that presence. ﴿It is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾, because arrogance is incompatible with it. ﴿So get out, for you are among the humbled﴾, the abased, by inclining towards the demands of the self.
﴿He said: Because You have led me astray﴾ — an oath by what is among the attributes of the acts, and he was not veiled from them, but he was veiled from the Unique Essence. ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, and it is the path of Unity. ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left﴾, meaning: I will certainly strive to mislead them. What the philosophers of Islam have said about this has been mentioned before, and al-Nisaburi's interpretations contain much discussion about it, and what some have said is the best in this area. Some have mentioned, for not mentioning the directions of above and below, a reason: that the approach from the first direction is not possible for him, because the upper direction is the one that is adjacent to the spirit, and from it come the true inspirations and angelic inspirations and the like. And the lower direction is where sensory judgments and particular arrangements in matters of worldly interests arise, and that does not necessarily cause misguidance; rather, it may even benefit one in the natural and mathematical sciences. But this is open to examination.

﴿And you will not find most of them thankful﴾, using what He created for them for what it was created for. ﴿He said: Get out of it, disgraced﴾, despised, ﴿banished﴾, expelled, ﴿for whoever follows you among them﴾ through self-conceit, seeing other than God Most High, and committing sins, ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾, so you will remain imprisoned in the prison of nature, tormented by the fire of deprivation from the desired, and that is the most severe punishment; everything short of separation from the beloved is easy. He, Glorified is He, is our sufficiency, and the best Disposer of affairs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 19:

﴿And, O Adam, dwell﴾ That is, "And We said," as occurred in Surat al-Baqarah. This story in its entirety is conjoined to a similar one, namely His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿We said to the angels, "Prostrate"﴾, according to what was held by a number of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun). They did not conjoin it to what comes after because He said, "He said," meaning: "He said, 'O Iblis, get out,' and 'O Adam, dwell,'" since that occurs in the context of resumption (isti'naf) and recompense for what the accursed one swore to, and this is part of the completion of the favour bestowed upon the children of Adam and the honouring of their father. And [they did not conjoin it] to what comes after ("We said"), because it reverts to "We said to the angels, O Adam."

Some have claimed that what the arrangement requires is conjunction to what comes after "He said," and they supported this with reasoning that has a basis, but it contradicts the apparent meaning. The opening of the speech with the vocative is to alert to the importance of the thing commanded. Singling out Adam, peace be upon him, for the address is to signal his primacy in receiving and undertaking the command. ﴿Dwell﴾ is from al-sukna (dwelling), which means residing, abiding and settling, not the stillness that is the opposite of motion; this has already been discussed, as has His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿you and your spouse, the Garden﴾. The address is directed to both of them in His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿So eat from wherever you wish, both of you﴾ to generalise the honouring and to signal that they are equal in undertaking the command, for Eve is an example for him, peace be upon him, regarding eating, unlike dwelling, for in that she follows him. And [the address is directed to both] to tie the prohibition that follows to both of them explicitly. The meaning is: "So eat from it wherever you wish, as in al-Baqarah," and the word "plenteously" (raghadan) is not mentioned here, trusting in what was mentioned there.

His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ is an intensification in the prohibition against eating from it. It has been read as ﴿hadhi﴾, which is the original form, except that the yā' was deleted and the hā' was substituted for it, so it is the hā' of compensation (iwad), not the hā' of pause (sakt). Ibn Jinni said: "What indicates that the original is the yā' is their saying of the masculine, dhā, with the alif being a substitute for the yā', since the original is dhiyy with a shadda, as evidenced by its diminutive dhiyyā. The triliteral is diminutived but not the biliteral, as with mā and man. One of the two yā's was deleted for lightness, then the other was replaced by an alif, out of dislike that its last letter resemble the last letter of kay."

﴿So you would be﴾, that is, "so you would become" ﴿among the wrongdoers﴾ (19), that is, those who wronged themselves. ((takūnā)) may be read in the jussive by conjunction to "approach" (taqrabā), or in the accusative as an answer to the prohibition.

[Page 99]

﴿فَوَسْوَسَ لَهُما الشَّيْطانُ﴾ *Fa-waswasa lahuma al-shaytan* (So Satan whispered to them). That is, he performed the whispering (waswasa) on their account, or he cast it into them.

Waswasa, in its original sense, is a hidden sound that is repeated. From this, the sound of ornaments is called *waswasa*. Forms of the *fa'lala* pattern are common for sounds, such as *haynama* (a faint sound), *hamhama* (a murmur), and *khashkhasha* (a rustling). The word is also applied to the soul's inner talk. Its verb is *waswasa*, which is intransitive. One says *rajul muwaswis* (a man who is prone to whispering) with the *wa* vowelled with a kasra, by way of elision and transitivity. The discussion of how the accursed one whispers has already been referred to in the commentary on Surat al-Baqara.

﴿لِيُبْدِيَ لَهُما﴾ *Li-yubdiya lahuma* (to expose to them). That is, so that it would appear to them. The *lam* here is either the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqiba*), because Satan did not intend this by his whispering and it did not occur to him, but the matter ended up leading to it; or it is the *lam* of causation, which is its original function. It is not unlikely that he intended by his whispering to distress them by the exposure of their private parts, and for this reason the text refers to them as *saw'a* (private parts). This would be based on conjecture, or on knowledge gained by hearing from the angels, or on looking at the Preserved Tablet. It has been said: this is evidence that exposing the private parts in seclusion, or before one's spouse without need, is ugly and abhorrent to natural disposition.

﴿ما وُورِيَ عَنْهُما مِن سَوْآتِهِما﴾ *Ma wuriya 'anhuma min sawatihima* (what was concealed from them of their private parts). That is, what was covered and hidden from them of their private parts. They did not see them in themselves, nor did either of them see them in the other. They were concealed by light, according to what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and others reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, or by a garment like a nail, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi. The word *sawat* is in the plural in the manner of *sagat qulubukuma* (your hearts inclined), and considering the parts (as plural) is remote. The apparent meaning of this statement is its literal sense. It has been said that it is a metaphor for the removal of sanctity and the loss of standing. The word *wuriya* is with two *wa*s; it is the past tense of *wara* (to conceal), like *darib* and *duriba*, whose first *alif* has been changed to *wa*. So the first *wa* is the first radical of the word, and the second *wa* is augmentary.

Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read *uriya* with a *hamza*. The rule is that when two *wa*s come together at the beginning of a word, if the second is vowelled, it has a vowelled counterpart, and the first must be changed to a *hamza* for lightening. An example of the first case is *uwaysil* and *uwasil* in the diminutive of *wasil* and its diminutive. An example of the second is *ula*, whose original form is *wula*; the first was changed when the second was vowelled in the plural, and the plural is *'ulun*. If the second is not vowelled, either in act or in potential, changing the first is permitted or not, as here. This is what al-Shihab stated, quoting the grammarians.

*Sau'atihima* (their private parts) was also read in the singular, with the *hamza* in its original form. It was also read as *sawatahuma*, with the *hamza* changed to *waw* and the *waw* assimilated into the *waw*. It was read as *siwatihima* in the plural, with the vowel of the *hamza* dropped onto the preceding letter and the *hamza* deleted. And it was read as *suw'atihima*, with the vowel dropped and the *hamza* changed to *waw* and assimilated.

﴿وقالَ﴾ *Wa-qala* (and he said). This is conjoined to *waswasa* as an explanation (*'ala tariq al-bayan*). ﴿ما نَهاكُما رَبُّكُما عَنْ هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةِ﴾ *Ma nahakuma rabbukuma 'an hadhihi al-shajara* (Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree), that is, from eating of it. ﴿إلا أنْ تَكُونا مَلَكَيْنِ﴾ *Illa an takuna malakayn* (except that you become two angels). This is an exceptive construction (*istithna' mufarragh*) from the object of purpose, with an omitted noun or the deletion of the negative particle, so that it becomes a cause; that is, out of dislike that you become two angels, or lest you become two angels. ﴿أوْ تَكُونا مِنَ الخالِدِينَ﴾ *Aw takuna min al-khalidin* (or that you become among the immortals). That is, those who never die at all, or those who will be made to abide in Paradise.

Ibn 'Abbas and Yahya ibn Kathir read *malikayn* with a kasra on the *lam*. Al-Zajjaj said: the words of the Exalted, quoting the accursed one, support this reading: ﴿هَلْ أدُلُّكَ عَلى شَجَرَةِ الخُلْدِ ومُلْكٍ لا يَبْلى﴾ (Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?).

The verse has been used as evidence for the superiority of the angels, since the accursed one said this and it was not rejected, and Adam, peace be upon him, committed what was forbidden, hoping for what Satan had indicated of becoming an angel. Had the angels not been superior, he would not have committed it. It is answered that their desire was only that they should acquire the attributes of the angels in innate perfections, and independence from foods and drinks and the like. We do not deny the superiority of the angels in these respects; what we deny is their superiority in every respect, and the verse does not indicate that. It may also be said that their desire was only for immortality, and the verse of Ta-Ha indicates this, since in it the call to immortality is followed by eating. It has been objected that desire for immortality entails disbelief, because of what that entails of denying resurrection and the Last Day. For this reason al-Hasan said to Amr ibn Ubayd, when he said to him that Adam and Eve believed the words of Satan: "God forbid! If they had believed them, they would have been among the disbelievers." It is answered that by immortality is meant a long duration of stay, and belief in it is not disbelief. And even if it is granted that the meaning is eternal perpetuity, we do not grant that believing this at that time was disbelief, because knowledge of death and of resurrection after it depends on textual evidence, and perhaps it had not reached them at that time.

Some have claimed that by immortality is meant the immortality that comes after death through entering Paradise, and then there is no difficulty. But this is contrary to the apparent meaning. It is reported from al-Sayyid al-Murtada, regarding the meaning of the verse, that he said: the accursed one led them to think that what was forbidden regarding taking from the tree was for the angels and the immortals only, and not for them, just as one of us says to another: "You were not forbidden from such-and-such except that you should be so-and-so," meaning that the one forbidden is so-and-so and not you. And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 7, verse 21:

﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisors."﴾ (21) He swore to them. The verb is expressed in the *mufa'alah* form (the form implying mutual action, here *qasama*, "to swear with someone"), for emphasis (*mubalaghah*), because whoever competes with someone in an action exerts himself in it. So the form is used for its implication. It has also been said that the *mufa'alah* is on its usual pattern and that the oath came from both sides, but its object differed. He swore to them regarding the sincere advice, and they swore to him regarding acceptance.

This has been criticized: this interpretation holds only if the mutual swearing is accompanied by mention of what is sworn to, which is the advice. Where it is mentioned, it does not hold unless one says that the acceptance of the advice was called "advice" by way of *mushakalah* (figurative correspondence) and *muqabalah* (antithetical pairing), as was said regarding the verse ﴿And We made an appointment with Moses﴾, that He called Moses's commitment to fulfilment and attendance at the appointment an "appointment," and so attributed the *mufa'alah* form to it. It has also been said: they said to him, "Do you swear by Allah, the Exalted, that you are among the sincere advisors?" and he swore to them, and so He made that a mutual swearing. On this view, as Ibn al-Munir said, the speech contains *lafh* (a figure of wrapping, in which two parts are presented together and then distinguished). This is because Adam and Hawwa' (peace be upon them) did not swear in the first-person form of speech but in the second-person form of address. It has also been said that this reading is closer to *taghlib* (the grammatical precedence given to one gender or form over another), and it has been said that there is no need for it: the meaning is an oath to them that he says to them, "Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisors."

﴿So he brought them down﴾, that is, he lowered them from their position and removed them from the rank of obedience to the rank of disobedience. It is from *dalla al-dalw fi al-bi'r* (he lowered the bucket into the well), as Abu 'Ubaydah and others said. From al-Azhari: its meaning is that he made them covet, and its origin is from lowering a thirsty man something into a well so that he finds nothing to quench his thirst. It has also been said that it is from *al-dalalah*, which is boldness, so that *fajarra'uhuma* (he emboldened them), as the poet said:

*I think forbearance has emboldened my people, and a forbearing man is sometimes treated as ignorant.*

Here one of the two doubled letters was changed to a *ya'*.

﴿With deception﴾, that is, with what he deceived them into by means of the oath, or while they were engaged in it. So the *ba'* is for accompaniment or association, and the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring either to the doer or to the object. Some have made "deception" a metaphor for the oath, because it is its cause, but there is no need for this.

The cause of their being deceived, as many have said, is that they thought no one swears falsely by Allah, the Exalted, and they related a report about this. The apparent meaning of this is that they believed what he said and so proceeded to do what they had been forbidden.

However, many of the verifying scholars (*al-muhaqqiqun*) held that they did not believe him at all, neither with certainty nor with conjecture. They proceeded to do what was forbidden only because their desire overpowered them, just as we find in ourselves that we act when another person makes what we desire seem attractive, even though we do not believe that the matter is as he claimed. Perhaps the speech of the accursed one, on this view, belongs to the category of rhetorical premises (*al-muqaddimat al-shi'riyyah*): it stirred up desire until it prevailed, and they forgot the prohibition with it, so the act occurred without deliberation.

Al-Qutb said: It is possible to say that when the accursed one whispered to them with his words, ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree...﴾ and so on, and they did not accept from him, he turned to the oath, as Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And he swore to them﴾, and they did not believe him either. So after that he turned to something else, and perhaps Allah, glorified is He, alluded to it with His words, the Exalted:

[Page 101]

﴿So he lured them with deception﴾: that is, he occupied them with enjoying pleasures until they became wholly absorbed in them, so they forgot the prohibition, as His words indicate: ﴿and he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾. He made the reproach that follows concern their failure to guard themselves, so reflect on this. ﴿When they tasted the tree﴾, meaning they ate from it, eating only a little. ﴿Their private parts became exposed to them﴾. Al-Kalbi said: their clothing fell away from them, so each of them saw the private part of the other and felt shame. ﴿And they began﴾, meaning they took up and started to do so. It belongs to the verbs of beginning (af'al al-shuru'), and the kasra on its fa' is more eloquent than the fatha. Abu al-Sammal recited it this way, ( يَخْصِفانِ ) meaning they patch and stick one leaf upon another. The original meaning of khasf is sewing together the seams of sandals and the like, by joining one part to another. It has also been said that its original meaning is gathering and joining together. ﴿Over themselves﴾, meaning over their private parts, or over their bodies; so there is an implied elided noun in the sentence. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to their private parts.

﴿From the leaves of the Garden﴾. It was some of the leaves of the fig tree, according to what is narrated from Qatada. It has also been said that it was the banana. Al-Zuhri recited ( يَخْصِفانِ ) from akhsafa, and its origin is khasafa, but, as al-Jarbardi said, it was transferred to akhsafa for transitivity, and the verb was given, for this purpose, the meaning of "making", so that the subject became in meaning an object of "making", the basic verb being retained. The sense is therefore: they sew themselves, meaning they make themselves sewers over themselves from the leaves of the Garden, so the object of "making" is omitted. Some scholars allowed that khasafa and akhsafa have the same meaning. Al-Hasan recited ( يَخْصِفانِ ) with a fatha on the ya', a kasra on the kha', and a shadda on the sad, from the ifti'al form, its original being yakhtasifan; the ta' was made sukun and assimilated, then the kha' was given a kasra because of the meeting of two sukuns. Ya'qub recited it with a fatha on the kha'. It was also read ( يُخَصِّفانِ ) from khassafa in the intensive form, with a fatha on the kha', and it was given a damma by assimilation to the ya'; this reading is difficult to pronounce.

﴿And their Lord called out to them﴾ in a manner of reproach and rebuke. ﴿Did I not forbid you﴾: this is an explanation of the calling out, so it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis); or it is governed by an omitted saying, meaning: he said, or saying: ﴿Did I not forbid you﴾. ﴿From that tree﴾: a reference to the tree from which they were forbidden to approach, and the dual form is for the dual of the addressees.

﴿And did I not tell you﴾: coordinated with ( أنهكما ), meaning: did I not say to you ﴿that Satan is an manifest enemy to you﴾ (22), meaning clearly hostile. According to what has been said, this is a reproach and rebuke for being deceived by the words of the enemy, just as the first was a reproach for opposing the prohibition. This statement is not related here, but it is related in Surah Ta-Ha in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife﴾, and so on. ( لَكُما ) is connected to ( عَدُوٌّ ) because of the verbal meaning it contains, or to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial qualifier of it.

Some scholars cited this verse as evidence that an absolute prohibition signifies forbiddance (tahrim), because of the severe blame it contains, together with the remorse and seeking of forgiveness that is understood from what follows. Most scholars hold that the prohibition here is for disapproval (tanzih), and their remorse and seeking of forgiveness were for leaving the better course, which in their view was great, and whose doer may be blamed most severely if he is one of those brought near.

﴿They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves"﴾. That is, we harmed ourselves through disobedience. It was also said: we diminished their share (of good) by exposing ourselves to expulsion from the Garden. The particle of address (the vocative "yā") is omitted to emphasize their reverence, since the phrase carries something of the sense of a command.

﴿And if You do not forgive us﴾ that is, by not punishing us for it, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ by being pleased with us. It was also said: the meaning is, "And if You do not conceal our faults by preserving us from what would cause a loss of our share (of good), and have mercy on us by bestowing favour upon us with what would compensate for what we have missed," ﴿we will surely be among the losers﴾ (23). The clause is the answer to an implied oath, and it indicates the answer to the preceding conditional clause, according to what has been said. The verse has been cited as evidence that minor sins (ṣaghā'ir) are punished even when major sins (kabā'ir) are avoided, if God Most High does not forgive them. The Mu'tazilah held that avoiding major sins necessitates the expiation of minor sins even if the servant does not repent of them. They explained what is mentioned here as conforming to the habit of the saints and righteous people, who magnify minor misdeeds and belittle great good deeds. Thus it does not contradict their being forgiven. Many of the People of the Sunnah took it as an instance of self-abasement, based on the view that what occurred was out of forgetfulness, and that there is neither a major nor a minor sin with forgetfulness. The Imam claimed that this act was a minor sin and that it occurred before Adam's prophethood, peace be upon him, since prophets, peace be upon them, may not commit either a major or a minor sin after receiving prophethood. The discussion of this question is well known.

[p. 102]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 24:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as has been noted many times before. ﴿Go down﴾. It is related from many of the early generation (salaf) that this is addressed to Adam, Eve, and Iblis, may the curse be upon him. He repeated the command to Iblis by following the two of them, indicating that he would not be separated from their kind in this world. Or the command was given in parts, and this has been transmitted in meaning, and it is a summary of it, as in His saying, ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. It is also said that the command with respect to the accursed one is other than what preceded it, for it is a command to him to go down from the place where he whispered (waswasa).

Al-Farra' chose that it is addressed to the two of them and to their offspring, and in this there is the address of one who does not yet exist (khitab al-ma'dum). It is also said that it is addressed to the two of them alone, due to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you"﴾, and the story is one, and the plural pronoun is because they are the origin of humankind, so they are as if they were humankind. Some people said that al-Farra's choice is this. It is also said that it is addressed to them, to Iblis, and to the serpent. This was objected to and answered with what was mentioned in surah al-Baqarah. The apparent meaning of the noble composition is that his Lord, glorified is He, hastened to rebuke and reproach Adam, peace be upon him, for his action, and nothing intervened there.

Al-Ajhuri related from Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali that when he, peace be upon him, ate from the tree, his stomach moved to expel the waste, and that this was not placed in Paradise in any of its foods except in that tree, and therefore he was forbidden to eat from it. So he began to wander about in Paradise, and God, exalted is He, commanded an angel to address him. The angel said to him, "What do you want, O Adam?" He said, "I want to expel what is in my belly of filth." The angel said to him, "Where will you put it? On the carpets, or on the couches, or in the rivers, or under the shade of the trees? Do you see any place here suitable for that?" Then he commanded him to go down. I do not see any soundness in this report. Similar to it is what was narrated from Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: when he, peace be upon him, ate from the tree, his Lord called out to him, "O Adam, why did you eat from it when I had forbidden you?" He said, "Eve gave me to eat." He, glorified is He, said, "O Eve, why did you make him eat it?" She said, "The serpent commanded me." He said to the serpent, "Why did you command her?" It said, "Iblis commanded me." God, exalted is He, said, "As for you, O Eve, I will make you bleed every month as you made the tree bleed. As for you, O serpent, I will cut off your legs, so you will walk upon your face, and everyone who meets you will crush your face. As for you, O Iblis, you are accursed."

﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿Go down﴾, and it is either a concomitant circumstance or a anticipated one. Some grammarians (al-mu'rabin) chose that the sentence is resumptive, as if, when they were commanded to go down, they asked how their state would be, and they were answered that some of them are enemies to others. The matter of enmity is apparent on the assumption that Satan is included in the address. As for the assumption that it is restricted to Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, it has been said that it is in view of the intention that their descendants are meant by the two of them, either by metaphor, like the use of Tamim for all of his children, or by suffice with mentioning the two of them instead of them. Some chose that enmity here means injustice, that is, some of you wrong others because of the misguidance of Satan. So let this be understood.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾, that is, a settling, or a place of settling. It is either a mimi verbal noun or a noun of place. It is also permitted that it be a noun of the passive participle, meaning that your sovereignty over it is established and your disposal of it is permitted. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it needs deletion and connection. The word in itself may be a noun of time, but this is not admissible here, because it would be repeated with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and provision﴾, that is, sustenance, ﴿for a time﴾ (24). He means by it the time of death. It is also said the Resurrection. Dwelling in the grave may be made a form of enjoyment on the earth. Or it may be said that the meaning of "for you" is for your kind and for your totality. The adverbial phrase has been said to be connected to "provision," or to both it and "dwelling place" by way of dispute (tanazu'), if the latter is a verbal noun. It has also been said that it is connected to a deleted element that functions as an adjective of "provision."

Page 103

"He said": it is repeated for resumption (isti'naf), either to signal that what follows is not connected to what precedes, or to show special concern for what follows, namely His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿In it you will live, and in it you will die, and from it you will be brought forth﴾ (25) at the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment. The people of Kufa, other than ʿĀṣim, read ﴿takhrujūn﴾ with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and a ḍamma on the rāʾ, in the active voice (binā' lil-fā'il), meaning "you will come forth."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 26:

﴿O children of Adam﴾ is an address to all of mankind. It has been used as evidence that the descendants of descendants enter under the term "children" in a bequest (waqf) made for "children," and the secret of this form of address in this context is not hidden.

﴿We have sent down to you clothing﴾ means: We created that for you by means of causes sent down from the sky, such as the rain by which cotton grows, which is made into clothing. This was said by al-Hasan. It is also reported from Abu Muslim that the meaning is: We gave you that and bestowed it upon you. Everything that Allah the Exalted gives to His servant is said to have been sent down to him, without there being any height or lowness involved; rather, it is used as a form of honoring, as when you say: "I raised my need to so-and-so" and "my case to the amir," and there is no transfer from a low place to a high place. It has also been said that the intended meaning is: We decreed it for you and apportioned it, and the decrees and apportionments of Allah the Exalted are described as descending from the sky, inasmuch as they are written in the Preserved Tablet. In any case, the statement is not free of metaphor. It may be in the predicate (musnad), which is the apparent reading, and it may be in the clothing or in the attribution (isnad).

As for His words, glory be to Him: ﴿that conceals﴾, meaning covers, is a supporting element (tarshih) on some of the possible interpretations. It is reported from al-Jubba'i that the statement is to be taken literally, claiming that this clothing descended together with Adam and Eve from the Garden when they were commanded to descend to the earth. But we have not come across any report on this that is sound enough to establish it as clothing. Yes, Ibn 'Asakir reported with a weak chain from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, were sent down together, both naked, and upon them were leaves of the Garden. Adam was afflicted by the heat until he sat down weeping and said to her: 'O Eve, the heat has harmed me.' Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him with cotton and commanded her to spin it and taught her, and taught Adam and commanded him to weave, and taught him."

Another report states that when he, peace be upon him, was sent down, he had seeds with him, and Iblis placed his hand upon them, and whatever his hand touched lost its benefit.

In another report narrated by Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Jurayj, he, peace be upon him, was sent down with him eight pairs of camels, cattle, sheep and goats, and with a sanah, and al-'Ala and al-Kalbatan, and a vine-cutting, and basil. All of this, in the form in which it is stated, does not indicate the claim, although some of what it contains could be a starting point for that which conceals ﴿your private parts﴾, meaning those which Iblis, may the curse be upon him, intended to expose of your two parents, until they were compelled to stick leaves together. And you are free of that. Many have related that the Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked, saying: "We circumambulate in garments in which we have disobeyed Allah the Exalted," so this verse was revealed. It has also been said that they used to circumambulate in that manner as an omen of being stripped of sins and transgressions. Perhaps the mention of the story of Adam, peace be upon him, at that point is to announce that the exposure of the private parts was the first evil that befell humanity from the side of Satan, and that he misled them in that matter just as he did to their two parents.

In the Kashshaf it is said that this verse comes in a digressive manner (istitrad) after the mention of the beginning of the private parts and the leaves stuck over them, to display the favor in what was created of clothing, and because of the humiliation and disgrace in nakedness and the exposure of the private parts, and to indicate that concealment is a great door among the doors of piety.

﴿And as adornment (riš)﴾, meaning as ornament, taken from the feathers of birds, because they are an adornment for the bird. Its conjunction with this is a conjunction of attributes, so the clothing is described as having two things: covering the private parts and adornment. It may also be a conjunction of one thing with another, meaning: We sent down two garments, a garment of covering and a garment of adornment. In that case it is among those where the described noun is omitted, meaning: clothing with feathers (riš), i.e., possessing feathers.

Interpreting riš as adornment is reported from Ibn Zayd. Some verifiers have mentioned that it is a homograph shared between the noun and the verbal noun. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi that the intended meaning is wealth, and from it comes the expression tarayyasha al-rajul, meaning he became wealthy. It is reported from al-Akhfash that it means abundance and livelihood. Al-Tabarsi said: it is everything that is needed.

'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, read (wa-riyashan), and it is either a verbal noun like libas, or the plural of riš like sha'b and sha'ab.

﴿And the garment of piety﴾, meaning righteous action, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas; or the fear of Allah the Exalted, as reported from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr; or modesty, as reported from al-Hasan; or faith, as reported from Qatada and al-Suddi; or that which covers the private parts, which is the first clothing, as reported from Ibn Zayd; or the garment of war, the coat of mail, the helmet and the implements by which one guards against the enemy, as reported from Zayd ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, and chosen by Abu Muslim; or the garments of devotion and humility, such as wool and coarse garments, as chosen by al-Jubba'i. So the wording is either a figure by association (mushakala), or a metaphor, or literal. Its nominative is by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate is the clause ﴿that is better﴾. The linking element is the demonstrative, since it serves as a link like a pronoun.

It is permitted that the predicate be ﴿better﴾, with ﴿that﴾ as an attribute of "garment." This was the view of al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Anbari and others.
