It was objected that demonstrative nouns are more definite than what is defined by the article (al-) and what is annexed, and an attribute must either equal the described noun in degree of definiteness or be less definite than it, and it cannot be more definite than it; hence it was said that ﴿that﴾ is an apposition (badal) or an explanatory element (bayan), not an attribute. It was answered that this is not agreed upon, for the definiteness of the demonstrative, since it is by sensory pointing outside the convention, has been said to be less than that of the article, and it has been said that they are of one rank. And it is reported from Abu 'Ali, and this is rare, that ﴿that﴾ has no place in grammatical case and is a separator (fasl) like a pronoun.

It has been read (wa-libasa al-taqwa) in the accusative, as a conjunction with (libasan). Some verifiers said: then the garment sent down would be three, or (libas al-taqwa) is interpreted as the garment of war, or the sending down is made a figure by association. It was mentioned on the well-known reading that if ﴿that﴾ refers to the covering garment, then "garment of piety" is literal and the annexation is by the slightest connection; and if it refers to the garment of piety, then it is a implicit metaphorical metaphor (isti'ara makniyya takhyiliyya) or of the type of "the silver of the water." In either case the demonstrative is used with the distant form to express exaltation, by treating distance in rank as distance in the senses. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

﴿That﴾, meaning the sending down of the garment mentioned, all of it or the last of it, ﴿is among the signs of Allah﴾ indicating His great bounty and His all-encompassing mercy, ﴿that perhaps they may take heed﴾ (26), so that they recognize His blessing, or are admonished and thus refrain from ugly deeds.

"O children of Adam" — the repetition of the address signals the complete attentiveness to the content introduced by it. ﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾, i.e., let him not bring you into temptation (fitnah) and trial (mihnah) by whispering to you what would keep you from entering Paradise, so that you obey him. It has been read as *yuftinannakum* (with a *ḍammah* on the initial letter of the imperfect, from *aftanahu*, "he caused him to fall into temptation"), and as *yaftinukum* without emphasis (*tawkid*). This is grammatically a prohibition addressed to Satan, but the real intent is the prohibition of the addressees from following and doing what leads to temptation. ﴿As he drove your parents out of the Garden﴾, i.e., as he tempted your parents and tried them by driving them out of it. The cause has been placed in the position of the effect. It is also permissible that the sense be: "Let him not tempt you with a temptation like the temptation of the expulsion of your parents," or "Let him not drive you out through his temptation with an expulsion like his expulsion of your parents." The expulsion is attributed to him because it occurred as a result of his seduction. Likewise, the stripping is attributed to him in His words, glorified is He: ﴿stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts﴾. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) either from "your parents" or from the subject of "drove out." The imperfect verb form here, according to what al-Qutb (al-Qutb) said, is for narrating a past situation (*hikayat al-hal al-madiyah*), because the stripping (*nazʿ*) is the removal, and it is past relative to the expulsion, even though the nakedness remained.

As for the words of Him, majestic is His glory: ﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you do not see them﴾, this is a justification for the prohibition, as is well known in sentences introduced by *inna* of this kind, and an emphasis of the warning, because an enemy who comes from where he cannot be seen is more severe and more frightening. The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refers to Satan.

It has been permitted that it be the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamir al-shan*), and it is then an emphasis of the concealed pronoun in *yarakum*, and "his tribe" is a conjunction upon it, not upon the explicit pronoun, because the latter is not suitable for emphasis. It has also been permitted that it be the subject of a omitted predicate, with *min* indicating the starting point of the end, and *haythu* being an adverb for the place where sight is negated, and the clause ﴿lā tarawnahum﴾ is in the position of a genitive by addition. From Abu Ishaq it is reported that *haythu* is a relative word and what follows it is its relative clause; but his intent is probably that this is like a relative word, since otherwise no one else holds this view, as Abu 'Ali al-Fārisī said. The *qabīl* is the group; if they are from one father they are a tribe (*qabilah*), and what is meant by them here is his armies from among the jinn.

Al-Yazidi read *wa-qabīlahu* with the accusative, and it is a conjunction upon the noun of *inna*. In this case it is necessary that the pronoun refers to Satan, and it cannot refer to the matter, contrary to those who erred in this respect, because conjunction upon it is not valid, nor is it followed by a follower.

The proposition is unrestricted (*muṭlaqah*), not perpetual (*dā'imah*), so it does not indicate what the Mu'tazilah maintain, that the jinn are not seen and do not appear to humans at all, nor do they take on forms.

What supports what we have said is what is authentically reported of the Prophet's (ﷺ) seeing their chieftain when he (the chieftain) intended to distract him from his prayer, so God Most High enabled him over him, and he wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque for the children of Medina to play with him, but he remembered the supplication of Solomon (peace be upon him) and left him. Also the seeing of Ibn Mas'ud of the jinn of Nusaybin; and what is reported from al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) that whoever claims that he saw them, his testimony is rejected and he is disciplined for opposing the Qur'an, understood, as some have said, as referring to one who claims seeing them in the forms in which they were created, since seeing them after the transformation which God Most High has empowered them to do is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah, and he (al-Shafi'i), may God be pleased with him, is among their masters. As for what has been disputed regarding the claim of their ability to transform, it is that it entails removing trust from anything, for whoever sees even his own child may be supposed to have seen a jinn who took his form. This is rejected by the fact that God Most High has guaranteed this community protection from what would lead to such a thing, which would result in doubt in religion and the removal of trust in scholars and others; thus the mentioned entailment is impossible by the law.

As for the statement of the scholar al-Bayḍawi, after defining the jinn in their chapter with what has been defined, "and in it is evidence that he (ﷺ) did not see them and did not recite to them, but their presence coincidentally occurred at some times of his recitation, so they heard it, and God Most High informed of that," it arises from lack of awareness of the many authentic hadiths explicitly stating his seeing of them, his reciting to them, and their requesting provisions from him for themselves and their animals in various manners. In my view, there is no impediment to his (ﷺ) seeing the jinn in the forms in which they were created, for he saw Gabriel (peace be upon him) in his original form twice, and their seeing is not more remote than his seeing. The seeing of every existing thing with us is within the realm of possibility, and the subtlety which the Mu'tazilah consider to prevent seeing them does not necessitate impossibility nor prevent occurrence as a breach of custom (*kharq al-'adah*). Likewise, the Ash'ariyyah's explanation of the non-seeing, that God Most High did not create in the eyes of humans the power of perception, does not imply impossibility either, since God Most High may create in the eye of His Messenger (peace be upon him), who saw Him, majestic is His glory, with the eyes of his head, according to the more correct view, on the night of the Ascension (*mi'raj*), that power, so he sees them. Indeed, it is not far-fetched to say that the friends of God (may God be pleased with them) may see them in the same way; but I have not found an explicit statement establishing the occurrence of this seeing. As for the seeing of the friends of God, and indeed of all people, of them in transformed forms, the books of this group are full of it, and the registers of historians and storytellers are replete with it. On this basis, the one who claims to see them in their original forms is not declared a sinner if it is a source of honor (karamah). The verse contains nothing more than the negation of seeing them in that manner according to ordinary custom. Moreover, it is possible that the verse is given as an illustration of the subtlety of their deception and the hidden nature of their stratagems, and the purpose of it is not literal negation of sight. From this it is known that the claim that the one who asserts such a sight is a disbeliever is outside of fairness, so reflect.

﴿Indeed, We made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾ (27): i.e., companions to them, empowered over them, enabled to seduce them through the affinity We placed between them, or by sending them upon them and empowering them over them. The sentence is either another justification for the prohibition and an emphasis of the warning following an emphasis, or a summary (*fadhlakah*) of the preceding narrative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 28:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And when they commit an indecency﴾ is a nominal sentence (jumlah mubtada'ah) having no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case analysis). It has also been permitted that it be conjoined (ma'tuf) to the relative clause (silah). The word al-fahishah (indecency) means an ugly deed that has reached the extreme of ugliness. The ta' (feminine marker) is either because it is treated as an attribute of a feminine noun, i.e., fi'lah fahishah (a shameful act), or for transferring it from being an adjective to being a noun. What is meant by it here is the worship of idols, uncovering the private parts during circumambulation (tawaf), and the like.

From al-Farra' it is related that it is restricted to uncovering the private parts. In the verse, according to what al-Tabarsi said, there is an ellipsis (hadhf), meaning: "And when they commit an indecency and they are forbidden from it." ﴿They say﴾ is the reply to those who forbid them: ﴿We found our fathers upon it, and Allah has commanded us with it﴾, arguing with two matters: imitation of the fathers, and attributing falsehood to Allah, the Exalted. The placing first of the premise (taqdim al-muqaddam) indicates that it is what they rely upon, or it is an allusion from them that their fathers used to do it by the command of Allah, the Exalted. Moreover, the pronoun in "amaranā" (He commanded us) may refer, as has been said, to them and to their fathers. In that case the reason for turning away from the first argument in refuting their statement becomes clear, through His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, Allah does not command indecency﴾. For His habit, the Exalted, has been to command good deeds and to urge noble characteristics, and this is what is fitting to wisdom, which requires that it not be contravened. The Imam (al-Razi) said: He, glorified be He, did not mention an answer to their first argument, because it points to mere imitation, and it has been established in intellects that it is a corrupt method, for imitation occurs in contradictory religions; so if imitation were true, it would necessitate the truth of contradictory religions, and that is impossible. Since the corruption of this method is evident, Allah, the Exalted, did not mention an answer to it. Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) have mentioned that the turning away is only from explicitly refuting it; otherwise His saying, glorified be He: "Indeed Allah..." etc., contains a refutation, for when He, glorified be He, commands good deeds, how can His command be abandoned for the mere following of fathers in what is intellectually ugly? What is meant here by intellectual ugliness is the aversion of sound nature and the disapproval of upright reason, not that a thing is subject to blame before the prohibition about it arrives, which is the matter in dispute between us and the Mu'tazilah, not the first, as has been verified in the principles of jurisprudence (usul). So there is no proof in the verse for what they claim.

It has also been said: what is mentioned is an answer to two sequential questions, as if it were said to them: when you did it, why did you do it? They said: "We found our fathers," and it was then said: "From where did your fathers take it?" They said: "Allah commanded us with it." The speech then, in this case, is on the presumption of an omitted noun, meaning: "Allah commanded our fathers." It has also been said: there is no such presumption, and the shift away from the apparent form of their command in that case is to indicate the claim that the command to their fathers is a command to them. On both views, imitation is forbidden when evidence to the contrary has been established; so there is no proof in the verse for the prohibition of imitation in every case.

﴿Do you say against Allah what you do not know?﴾ (28) This is part of the speech that was commanded to be said. The interrogative particle (hamzah) is for denouncing what has occurred and deeming it abominable, and an allusion that it should not be. The denunciation is directed at their saying about Him, the Exalted, what they do not know to have proceeded from Him, may His majesty be exalted, although some of them do say about Him, glorified be He, what they know has not proceeded from Him, as an exaggeration in denouncing that form. There is no proof in the verse for one who negates analogy (qiyas) on the basis that what is established by it is conjectural (maznun) and not known, because that is specified from its generality by the consensus of the Companions and those whose opinion counts, or by another proof. It has also been said that what is meant by knowledge includes conjecture.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 29:

﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice.ⴰ﴾ This explains what is commanded, following the negation of the matters whose commandment was attributed to Him, Exalted is He, among the forbidden things. Al-qist (justice), as stated by more than one scholar, is al-'adl (equity), which is the midpoint of everything, avoiding both extremes of excess and deficiency.

al-Raghib said: It is the portion (nasib) with equity, like al-nisf (half) and al-nasafah (fairness). It is said: al-qist is taking another's portion, and that is injustice; al-iqsat is giving another his portion, and that is fairness. For this reason it is said: qasata al-rajul (the man acted unjustly) when he oppressed, and aqsata when he acted justly. This is more preferable than what al-Tabarsi said, that its origin is inclination: if it is toward the truth, it is justice, and from it is His, Exalted is He, saying: (Indeed, Allah loves the just [al-muqsitin]). If it is toward falsehood, it is wrongdoing, and from it is His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿As for the deviators (al-qasitun), they will be fuel for Hell﴾. What is meant here, as transmitted from Abu Muslim, is all acts of obedience and means of drawing near (to Allah).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak that it is tawhid and the saying "There is no god but Allah." Mujahid, al-Suddi, and most of the exegetes held that it is uprightness and justice in affairs. ﴿And set your faces [toward worship]﴾, i.e., turn toward His worship, Exalted is He, upright, not deviating toward anything else. ﴿At every place of prostration (masjid)﴾, i.e., at the time of every prostration, as al-Jubba'i said, or at its place, as others said. So "ʿinda" means "fi" (in), and "masjid" is a noun of time or place in its linguistic sense. Its basis should have been an open ʿayn (masjid, with fatha in the past form) since the present form takes a damma, but it is among the irregular forms that deviate from the rule. Some claimed it is a mimi verbal noun, with a time understood before it. "Prostration" is a metaphor for prayer. Other scholars said: the meaning is turn toward the direction that Allah, Exalted is He, commanded you to face in your prayers, which is the direction of the Ka'bah. The command, according to both views, is for obligation.

al-Maghribi chose that the meaning is: when you reach the prayer in any mosque, pray and do not delay it until you return to your mosques. According to this, the command is for recommendation, and "masjid" is in its technical sense. The distance of this is not hidden. Similar to it is what was said: the meaning is intend the mosque at the time of every prayer, as a command to congregation, recommended according to some and obligatory according to others. The waw is for conjunction, and what follows it is said to be conjoined to the command into which the verbal noun resolves together with "an" (that), i.e., an aqsitu (that you act justly). A verbal noun resolves into the past, the present, and the imperative. al-Jurjani said it is conjoined to the preceding statement, the one said to "qul" (say), which is a performative in meaning; and if you refuse, then the speech is of the mode of narration.

It is permitted that there is an implied "qul" conjoined to its counterpart, with ﴿aqimu﴾ being its object of speech, and that it is conjoined to an omitted element whose estimate is: say, "Turn [to Him] and set [your faces]." ﴿And call upon Him﴾, i.e., worship Him, ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, i.e., in obedience. Thus the calling is in the sense of worship, because it includes it. "Religion" is in its linguistic sense. It is said: this is a command to supplication and humble petition to Him, Exalted is He, in the manner of sincerity, i.e., beseech Him in supplication after your sincerity to Him in religion. ﴿As He originated you﴾, i.e., created you at first, ﴿you will return﴾ (29) to Him, Exalted is He, and He will recompense you for your deeds. So comply with His commands, or devote worship to Him sincerely. Thus it is connected to the command before it. al-Zajjaj said it is connected to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In it you will live, in it you will die, and from it you will be brought forth﴾. The distance of this is not hidden. He, Exalted is He, did not say "He will restore you," as would be fitting with what precedes it, indicating that restoration is less than origination from non-matter, such that if independence from an agent were imagined, origination would be possible without Him. It is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾, whether restoration is the bringing into existence after complete annihilation, or the gathering of scattered parts. He, Exalted is He, made it similar to initiation only to establish its possibility and His power over it. Qatadah said the meaning is: as He originated you from dust, you will return to it, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you﴾. It was also said the meaning is: as He originated you, you possess nothing; likewise you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection.

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that the meaning is: whoever Allah, Exalted is He, begins to create upon wretchedness, will arrive at it even if he does the deeds of the people of happiness; and whoever He begins to create upon happiness, will arrive at it even if he does the deeds of the people of wretchedness. This is supported by what al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us with two books in his hand. He said: Do you know what these two books are? We said: No, O Messenger of Allah. He said to the one in his right hand: This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, containing the names of the people of Paradise, the names of their fathers and tribes, and then it is summed up at the end of them, so nothing will be added to them or subtracted from them forever. Then he said to the one in his left: This is a book from the Lord of the worlds, containing the names of the people of the Fire, the names of their fathers and tribes, and then it is summed up at the end of them, so nothing will be added to them or subtracted from them forever. His companions said: Then what is the point of deeds, O Messenger of Allah, if the matter has already been decided? He, peace be upon him, said: Be upright and draw near (to the mark), for the companion of Paradise is sealed with the deeds of the people of Paradise, whatever deed he does; and the companion of the people of the Fire is sealed with the deeds of the people of the Fire, whatever deed he does. Then he said, i.e., the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gestured with his hands and threw them away, then said: Your Lord has finished with the servants: a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze."

Close to this is what is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, that the meaning is: as it was written for you, so you will be. It is also narrated from the Habr (Ibn 'Abbas) that the meaning is: as He originated you, believer and disbeliever, He will restore you on the Day of Resurrection. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He it is who created you, and among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾. Upon this, His saying, Exalted is He,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 30:**

﴿A party He has guided, and a party upon whom error has been decreed.﴾ This is an explanation and elaboration of that (verse 29). Its parallel is His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he is.﴾ (3:59), after His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam.﴾ (3:59). It has been said, and this is the most fitting to the context.

Al-Tayyibi mentioned that here there is a subtle point, namely that He, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿As He originated you, you will return.﴾ (7:29), placed the comparison (mushabbah bihi) before the thing compared (mushabbah), to alert the intelligent person that the decree concerning affairs does not at all contradict the divine decree and the eternal knowledge. Just as this subtlety was observed in the text being explained, it was observed in the interpretation (tafsir), and another point was added to it: that He, glorified is He, placed the object of (hada, "guided") first, to indicate exclusivity (ikhtisas), and that He did not intend the guidance of another party. He confirmed this by coordinating with it ﴿and a party upon whom error has been decreed﴾, and presented it in the form of an implied verb, according to the condition of interpretation, meaning: "He led astray a party upon whom error has been decreed." Together with the exclusivity there is emphasis (tawkid), as the author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki) established, so that the doubt of the opponent is cut off and he does not say that the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, has no effect on their error. End of quotation.

It seems that by this he is pointing to the refutation of al-Zamakhshari's view concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, they took the devils as protectors besides Allah﴾ (7:30), meaning: they obeyed them in what they commanded them. He says: this is evidence that the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, has no effect on their error, and that they themselves are the ones who err by their own choice and by their taking the devils as protectors instead of Allah, the Exalted. Thus the clause ﴿Indeed, they took﴾ in this case is an explanation (ta'lil) of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and a party upon whom error has been decreed﴾. This is supported by the reading ﴿أنهم﴾ (annahum, with a fatha), which may be an emphasis of their error and a confirmation of it.

I and the truth deserve more to be followed, along with the one who says that the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, does not affect the known, and that whoever gives the doctrine of compulsion (jabr) as a reason based on it is in error. How could it be otherwise, when the Mutakallimun (scholastic theologians) without exception say that knowledge relates to a thing as it is in itself? The matter at issue is that the power of Allah, the Exalted, has no effect according to the claim of the misguided followers of al-Zamakhshari, and we strongly reject that. There is no objection to giving the taking as a cause according to the Ash'ariyya, since acquisition (kasb) and choice are established, and this causal relevance suffices for the explanation.

Al-Zamakhshari estimated the verb in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and a party, He decreed upon them﴾ as "forsook" (khadhala), and some people agreed with him. What al-Tayyibi did is the preferred view of some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun), because of the evident suitability in it and its freedom from the suspicion of Mu'tazilism.

Its estimation as postponed (mu'akhkharan) was chosen so that the two clauses would be coherent. According to most, they are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿ta'udun﴾ (you return), with the implied qad, or they are two independent clauses (mustanifatan). It has also been permitted that the first ﴿fariqan﴾ (a party) and the second ﴿fariqan﴾ be in the accusative as circumstantial clauses, and the two clauses after them are their qualifiers. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: ﴿you return as two parties, a party He guided and a party...﴾, etc. The accusative in this reading is either an apposition (badal) or an object for an implied verb "I mean" (a'ni). The feminine marker was not attached to (haqqa, "decreed") either because of the separation or because the feminine is not real. According to some, the statement is in the form of an omitted modifier, meaning: "decreed upon them the word of error," which is His saying, glorified is He: (they went astray) ﴿and they think that they are guided﴾ (7:30). It is coordinated with what precedes it and is included with it in the scope of explanation or emphasis.

Perhaps the speech is of the type "the sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so." The first (the guided and the misguided) is, because it stands in opposition to "those whom Allah has guided," inclusive of both the obstinate (mu'anid) and the mistaken (mukhti'). The second is specific to the second, and it applies to the one who falls short in reflection and who exerts the utmost effort in it. There has been disagreement about the justification of blame for the latter and his eternal abiding in the Fire. The view of some is that he is excused. They did not distinguish between one who has no intellect at all and one who has intellect but did not reach the truth by it, after he had left no avenue unexplored in seeking it. Where the former is excused because the proof was not established against him, the latter is excused for the same reason. They do not regard mere ownership (malikiyya) and absolute disposal as a proof, while the proof of Allah is decisive. The commitment that every obstinate disbeliever after the sending of the Messenger and the manifestation of the matter of truth is like a fire upon a mountain, and that there is not in the east and west of the earth today a disbeliever who reasons from what only a Muslim obstinate would undertake, or a Muslim reasoning from what is weaker than the spider's house, and that it is indeed the weakest of houses (cf. 29:41).

Some have claimed that what is meant by the coordinated term is the obstinate one, and what is meant by the coordinated-with is the mistaken one. The apparent meaning is what we have stated. Making the clause circumstantial, in the sense that "they took the devils as protectors while they think that they are guided in that taking," is not without its problems.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 31:

﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment﴾, that is, your clothing, to cover your private parts, because what is understood from the command is obligation, and what is obligatory is only the covering of the private parts. ﴿At every place of worship﴾, that is, at every circumambulation or prayer. This was the view of Mujahid, Abu al-Shaykh and others. According to what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, the occasion of revelation was that some Bedouins used to circumambulate the House naked, to the extent that a woman would circumambulate the House while nude, tying on her rear thongs like those placed on the faces of donkeys to ward off flies, and she would say:

Today some or all of it appears,
And what appears of it, I do not make lawful.

So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. Some scholars understood "adornment" to mean beautiful clothing, since that is what is immediately understood from it. This view is attributed to al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also narrated from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that whenever he stood for prayer he would wear his finest clothing. It was said to him: "O son of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), why do you wear your finest clothing?" He said: "Indeed Allah is Beautiful and loves beauty, so I adorn myself for my Lord, and He says: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship﴾, so I love to wear my most beautiful clothing." It is not hidden that in this case the command cannot be taken to mean obligation, since it is clear that this adornment is recommended, not obligatory. It was also said that according to the first possibility, the verse points to the recommended nature of beautifying oneself, because when it indicates the obligation of taking adornment to cover the private parts at those times, it is understood from it, in general, that it is good to adorn oneself by wearing what is good and beautiful in one's own estimation. The lie-fabricated line was attributed to al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that the taking of adornment means combing the hair, as if it were said: "Comb your hair at every prayer." Perhaps this is by way of restricting the mention to some of the adornment, and it is not intended to confine it to what has been mentioned. Similar to this is what Ibn Adi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: «Take the adornment of prayer.» They said: "What is the adornment of prayer?" He said: «Wear your sandals and pray in them.»

Page 110

Ibn Asakir and others transmitted from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, concerning His words, glorified is He: ﴿Take your adornment﴾ ... etc.: «Pray in your sandals, and eat and drink of what is good for you.» Al-Kalbi said: The people of the Jahiliyyah would not eat any food except the basic staples, and they would not eat fat during the days of their pilgrimage. So the Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have more right to that." So Allah the Exalted revealed the verse. From this appears the reason for mentioning eating and drinking here. ﴿And do not be extravagant﴾, by prohibiting what is lawful, as is suitable in view of the occasion of revelation; or by transgressing into what is unlawful, as narrated from Ibn Zayd; or by excess in food and gluttony, as many scholars held. Abu Nu'aym transmitted from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Beware of overfilling yourselves with food and drink, for it corrupts the body, produces illness, and makes one lazy in prayer. Instead, adhere to moderation in both, for it is better for the body and further from extravagance. Indeed Allah the Exalted detests the fat scholar, and a man will not perish until he prefers his desire over his religion."

It was also said that the intended meaning is extravagance and exceeding the limit in a broader sense than what has been mentioned. Among it is counted a person eating whenever he desires, and eating twice a day. Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: «Among extravagance is that you eat everything you desire.» The second transmitted it and declared it weak, from Aisha, who said: «The Prophet (ﷺ) saw me having eaten twice in one day, and he said: "O Aisha, do you not like to have some concern other than your stomach? Eating twice a day is extravagance."» In my view, this differs according to the individuals, and it is not far-fetched that what has been mentioned refers to excess in food. Among it is counted cooking food with rosewater and adding something like musk to it, for example, without any purpose for it except desire. Some scholars held that the forbidden extravagance also includes what is in clothing. This is narrated from Ikrimah. Ibn Abi Shaybah and others transmitted «from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Eat what you wish and wear what you wish, as long as two things do not reach you: extravagance and arrogance."» Al-Bukhari transmitted it from him as a suspended report. This does not conflict with what al-Tha'alibi and other men of letters mentioned, that a person should eat what he desires and wear what people desire, as it has been said:

I gave him advice that the wise have approved:
Eat what you desire, and wear what people desire.

This is for abandoning what is not regarded as customary among people. And this is for permitting everything they have become accustomed to. In al-Ajaib by al-Kirmani, a Christian physician said to Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid: "There is no knowledge of medicine in your book. Knowledge is of two kinds: knowledge of bodies and knowledge of religions." He replied: "Allah the Exalted has gathered all of medicine in half a verse of His Book." He asked: "And what is it?" He said: (Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant). The Christian said: "Nothing has been transmitted from your Messenger about medicine." He said: "Our Messenger, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, has gathered medicine in brief words." He asked: "And what are they?" He said: his saying (ﷺ): «The stomach is the house of disease, and restraint is the head of every remedy», and «Give every body what it has been accustomed to.» The Christian said: "Neither your Book nor your Prophet has left anything for Galen in medicine." End of quotation. What he attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ) is from the words of al-Harith ibn Kaladah, the physician of the Arabs, and it is not authentic to trace it back to the Prophet (ﷺ). In al-Ihya', it is cited as a raised (prophetic) tradition: "Overfilling is the root of disease, and restraint is the root of cure, and returning to, and eating, what the body has become accustomed to." Al-Iraqi commented on it, saying: "I have not found any source for it."

In Shu'ab al-Iman by al-Bayhaqi and in Luqat al-Manafi' by Ibn al-Jawzi, from Abu Hurairah, also as a raised report: «The stomach is the basin of the body, and the veins flow toward it. When the stomach is sound, the veins become sound, and when the stomach is corrupt, the veins become diseased.»

Page 111

Al-Daraqutni commented on it, saying: "We know this from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), but it is actually from the words of Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Abjar."

In al-Durr al-Manthur: Muhammad ibn Khallal transmitted from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that «the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her while she was complaining of illness, and he said to her: "O Aisha, restraint is a remedy, and the stomach is the house of ailments. Accustom the body to what it has become used to."» I have not seen anyone who commented on it. Yes, I have seen in al-Nihayah by Ibn al-Athir: "Amr asked al-Harith ibn Kaladah, 'What is the remedy?' He said: 'Al-azm, that is restraint (dieting), and holding the teeth together, one upon another.'" Yes, the authentic traditions are abundant in condemning satiety and excessive eating, and in this there is guidance for the community to all wisdom. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ (31), rather He hates them and does not approve of their deeds. The clause is in the position of giving a reason for the prohibition. As has been said, this verse has gathered the foundations of the rulings: command, permission, prohibition, and information.

﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾, from clothing and everything with which one beautifies oneself, ﴿which He has brought forth for His servants﴾, that is, which He created for their benefit, from plants such as cotton and flax, from animals such as silk and wool, and from minerals such as rings and coats of mail, ﴿and the good things of provision﴾, that is, the delicious things. It was also said: the lawful foods and drinks, such as the flesh of sheep, its fat and its milk. The verse has been used as evidence that the basic ruling regarding foods, clothing, and all kinds of adornment is permissibility, because the interrogative in "who" is for denying their prohibition in the most emphatic way. It is related from Ibn al-Furs that he said: "Those who permit men to wear silk and khazz (a fabric of silk and wool) have used it as evidence." It is narrated from Zayn al-Abidin, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to buy a khazz cloak for fifty dinars, and when winter came he would give it in charity, seeing no harm in that, and he would say:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 32:

﴿Say: "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah, which He has brought forth for His servants?"﴾.

It is narrated that al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, was struck while wearing a jubba of khazz (a silk-and-wool garment), and that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, when 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, sent him to the Kharijites, wore his finest clothes, perfumed himself with his best perfume, and rode his finest mounts. He went out to them and met them, and they said: "O Ibn 'Abbas, you are the best of people, yet you have come to us in the clothing and mounts of tyrants." He then recited this verse. However, it is related from Tawus that he recited this verse and said: "Allah, glorified is He, did not command you to wear silk or brocade. Rather, when one of them performed the tawaf wearing his garments, he would be beaten and his garments would be stripped from him." So he (Tawus) denounced them for that. The truth is that everything for which no proof of its prohibition has been established falls within this adornment, and there is no hesitation in using it, so long as it does not involve something like arrogance, as has been indicated earlier.

It is also related that he (ﷺ) went out wearing a cloak worth a thousand dirhams. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, used to wear a cloak worth four hundred dinars, and he would instruct his companions to do likewise. Muhammad (ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani) used to wear fine garments and would say: "I have wives and female slaves, so I adorn myself so that they do not look at anyone other than me." The jurists have explicitly stated that adornment is recommended, based on his saying (ﷺ), "When Allah bestows a blessing upon a servant, He loves to see the trace of His blessing upon him." It was said to one of them: "Did not 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wear a shirt with such-and-such a patch?" He replied: "He did that for a wisdom: he was the Commander of the Believers, and his governors would follow his example, and perhaps they would not have wealth, so they would take from the Muslims." Yes, some imams disliked wearing saffron-dyed and safflower-dyed garments, and they also disliked other things, which are sought in their proper places.

﴿Say: "It is for those who believed in the life of this world."﴾ That is, it is theirs primarily, for the increase of their honor before Allah, the disbelievers sharing in it only secondarily. There is no difficulty regarding the exclusivity derived from the lam. ﴿Purely for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, with no one else sharing it with them. It is related from al-Jubba'i that the meaning is: "It is for those who believed in the life of this world, not purified from worries, sorrows and hardship; and it is purely theirs on the Day of Resurrection, free of all that." The accusative of (خالصة, khalisatan, "purely") is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the concealed pronoun in the prepositional phrase, and its governing element is what it depends on. Nafi' read it in the nominative, considering it a predicate following a predicate, or that it is the predicate, with ﴿for those who believed﴾ depending on it, placed first to emphasize purity and exclusivity. ﴿Thus We detail the signs﴾, that is, just as We have detailed this ruling, We detail all the rulings ﴿for a people who know﴾ (32), [who know] the subtle meanings contained within them.

It is permitted that the comparison be in the manner of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾, and its counterparts, whose verification has been mentioned earlier.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 33:

﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies (al-fawahish), what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾. That is, what has grown in ugliness among the sins; and it is said: what relates to the private parts. ﴿What is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the indecencies﴾, that is, their open and their secret forms. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "what is apparent" is fornication done openly and "what is hidden" is fornication done secretly. They used to dislike the first and practise the second, so they were forbidden from that in every form.

And it is related from Mujahid: "what is apparent" is going naked during the circumambulation (tawaf), and "what is hidden" is fornication. It is said: the first is men circumambulating with women, and the second is women circumambulating at night naked. ﴿And sin (al-ithm)﴾, that is, what makes one deserving of sin. Its basic meaning is blame, so it was applied to what brings it, from the general sense of wrongdoing. It was mentioned for generalization after specification, based on what preceded regarding the meaning of the indecencies. It is also said that al-ithm is wine (al-khamr), as related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan al-Basri, and as mentioned by the lexicographers such as al-Asma'i and others, who cited for it the verse of the poet:

"The Messenger of Allah forbade us to approach fornication, and to drink the ithm, which brings about burden."

And the saying of another:

"I drank the ithm until my intellect went astray, / Thus does ithm take away the intellects."

Ibn al-Anbari claimed that the Arabs did not call wine ithm in the Jahiliyyah or in Islam, and that the poetry is fabricated. The well-known view is that this is by way of metaphor, because wine is the cause of sin. Abu Hayyan and others said: this interpretation is not correct here, because the surah is Meccan, and wine was not prohibited except in Medina after Uhud. Also, it would then require the claim that the restriction is relative (idafi), so reflect.

﴿And transgression (al-baghy)﴾: injustice and domineering over people. It was mentioned separately on the basis of the generality of what precedes it, or its inclusion among the indecencies, for the emphasis in warning against it. ﴿Without right (bi-ghayr al-haqq)﴾ is connected to al-baghy, because transgression is never except in this manner.

It is permitted that it be an emphasizing circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah). It is also said: it was brought so that transgression against another in retaliation for his transgression is excluded, for it is called transgression in a general sense, but it is with right; and this is, as you see, far-fetched. ﴿And that you associate with Allah that for which He has not sent down any authority (sultan)﴾, that is, proof and evidence. The meaning, on the negation of both sending down and authority together, is in the most emphatic form, like the saying of the poet:

"You do not see the dabb lizard entering through it."

And in it is a degree of mockery of the polytheists that is not hidden. ﴿And that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ (33). This refers to atheism regarding His attributes and fabrication against Him, like their saying: ﴿And Allah has commanded us to it﴾. And it is not hidden what there is in directing the prohibition to their saying about Him, glory be to Him, what they know to have occurred, rather than what they know not to have occurred, from the noble secret.

[Page 113]

﴿And for every nation﴾ among the destroyed nations ﴿is a term﴾, meaning a fixed time set for their annihilation, as al-Hasan said, and this is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. As some have said, this is a warning to the people of Makkah of a punishment that descends at a known term with Allah, just as it descended upon the nations before them, and a return to exhorting them to follow (the message) after the digression (istitrad) that some have mentioned.

A subtle point has been observed in its being placed after the prohibition of indecencies, since it is also appropriate to that. Some have interpreted the term (ajal) here as the specified period they were given before the punishment descends. Others have interpreted it as the time of death, and they said the implied meaning is: "And for every individual of a nation (there is a term)." According to the first interpretation, there is no need for this supposition.

﴿So when their term comes﴾: the pronoun, as some of the scholars (muhaqqiqun) have said, refers either to the nations implied by "every nation," or to "every nation." According to the first, the explicit mention of "term" with a pronoun attached to it serves to convey the intended meaning, which is that each nation reaches its own particular term, and its coming to them occurs through the acquisition of the term by means of the plural sense conveyed by the generality of the addition. It is as if it were said: "When their terms come, in such a way that each one of those nations receives its own particular term." According to the second, which is the apparent one, the explicit mention in place of the pronoun is for the increase of confirmation, and the addition serves to convey the most complete distinction.

Ibn Sirin read ﴿آجالهم﴾ (ājāluhum) in the plural form, and Ibn Jinni regarded it as preferable, and took the singular to be intended as a generic noun, the generic noun being of the nature of the verbal noun (masdar). Its suitability lies in its being added to a group. The fa' (in "fa-idha") is said to be a fa' faṣīḥa (an eloquent fa', indicating an implied condition), and it is omitted in the verse of Yunus, for a reason that we will mention there, Allah willing. The intended meaning of "coming" is the approach or completion of the term, i.e., when it arrives and draws near, or when it ends and is completed.

﴿They cannot delay﴾ from it ﴿an hour﴾: a portion of time of the utmost brevity. The word is not meant in the sense of the "hour" in the terminology of the astrologers (munajjimin), which is divided into an equal hour (called "falakiyya," i.e., astronomical), namely the period equal to fifteen degrees always, and a curved hour (called "zamaniyya," i.e., temporal), namely the period equal to one-sixth of a half of the day or the night, always. The first is generally used by the people of computation (ahl al-hisab), and the second by the jurists (fuqaha') and the practitioners of talismans (ahl al-tala-simat) and the like. According to them, the total of the night and day is always twenty-four hours, whether the hour is equal or curved, except that each of the night and the day does not exceed twelve curved hours, always. For this reason they lengthen and shorten, and sometimes they equal the equal hour, and that is when the night and the day are equal. The intended meaning is that they cannot delay at all. The form of the verb "istif'ar" (in "yasta'khirun") is used to indicate their inability and deprivation of that, despite their seeking it.

﴿Nor can they advance﴾ (34): i.e., nor do they go before it.

Apparently it is coordinated with ﴿they cannot delay﴾, as al-Hufi and others gave its i'rab (grammatical analysis). It has been objected that advancing is not conceivable at the time of its coming, so there is no benefit in negating it; rather, it is a case of informing about something necessary, like your saying: "If you stand in the future, your standing will not have preceded your standing in the past." It has also been said that it is coordinated with the conditional clause and not the consequent clause, so it is not restricted by the condition. The meaning of the verse then is: "For every nation there is a term; when their term comes, they cannot delay from it; and for every nation there is a term; they cannot advance before it." Our master, the scholar al-Salkoti, has criticized this by saying: it is not hidden that the benefit of restricting the words of the Exalted, ﴿they cannot delay﴾, alone by the condition is not evident, even if it is valid. Rather, what comes first to the sound understanding is what has preceded. In it there is an indication that just as it is impossible to precede the term even by the briefest period, which is an hour, so it is impossible to delay from it, even though it is rationally possible. For opposing what Allah the Exalted has decreed and known is impossible. The combining of the two matters in what has been mentioned is like combining between one who postpones repentance until the presence of death and one who dies in disbelief, in negating repentance from him in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾, and the verse continues. Perhaps this is the meaning of the one who said it is coordinated with the consequent, on the basis that the meaning of the words of the Exalted, ("They cannot delay. Nor can they advance") is: they cannot change it, in the manner of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Nor is there anything fresh or dry but it is in a clear record﴾, and the saying of them: "I spoke to him and he did not respond to black or white," so he does not respond to what is said. You know, however, that this meaning is attained by mentioning the consequent without mentioning ﴿nor can they advance﴾. The correct view is coordination with the conditional clause. In the commentary on the Miftah (Sharh al-Miftah) it is stated that when a restriction is made a part of the coordinated element (ma'tuf 'alayh), the coordinated element does not share it. It is exemplified by this verse, and on this basis there is no objection to coordination with ﴿they cannot delay﴾, since there is no sharing in the restriction. You know that they have mentioned in this topic that when something is coordinated with something and is preceded by a restriction, the coordinated element necessarily shares that restriction with the element it is coordinated to. As for when it is coordinated with something that is followed by a restriction, sharing is possible. Coordination to what is restricted has two considerations. The first is that the restriction is prior in consideration and the coordination is subsequent to it. The second is that the coordination is prior and the restriction is subsequent. On the first, the two coordinated elements must share the mentioned restriction, since the restriction is part of the components of the coordinated element. On the second, sharing is required, since it is one of the rulings of the first, in which sharing is required. Some have founded the coordination here on the basis that the intended meaning of "coming" is approaching to a degree such that advancing is possible in general, like the coming of the day that was appointed for their destruction, an hour of it. This is not the case. The presentation of the negation of delay first, as has been said, is because the primary aim is to show that they cannot escape the punishment. As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay﴾, the precedence of "precedes" is due to its being mentioned first, because the intended meaning here is to show the secret of the delay of their destruction despite their deserving it, as His saying, glorified is He, indicates: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope divert them; but they will soon know﴾. Therefore, the more important matter there is to show the negation of precedence.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 35:

﴿O children of Adam﴾ is an address to all of mankind, and the concern it shows for what lies within its scope is not hidden. Ibn Jarir reported from Abu Yasar al-Sulami, who said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, placed Adam and his offspring in His palm and said: ﴿O children of Adam, if messengers come to you﴾ until [He said] ﴿so fear Me﴾. Then He scattered them." The view taken by some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin) is that this is a narration of what occurred with every people. It has been said that the intended "children of Adam" is the community of our Prophet (ﷺ), but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it is made remote by the plural "messengers" in His words, glorified is He: ﴿if messengers from among you come to you﴾, meaning, of your own kind. The prepositional phrase "from among you" is connected to an omitted element that functions as an attribute of "messengers." ﴿Imma﴾ (إمّا) is the conditional particle "in" (إنِ) to which "ma" has been joined to emphasize the meaning of the condition. It is therefore merely an emphatic addition. It has also been said that it conveys generality as well, so that the meaning of, for example, "imma taf'alanna" (إمّا تَفْعَلَنَّ) is "if an act occurs from you in any way whatsoever."

After this addition ("ma"), the verb is necessarily followed by the emphatic nun (نُونُ التَّوْكِيدِ, the nun of emphasis), and it is not elided, according to the view of al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and those who followed them, except in cases of necessity (ḍarūrah). Among the examples of this is the poet's saying:

"Then if you see me, and I have a lock of hair,
Indeed the calamities have worn it away."

It has been refuted by the argument that the frequency with which the elision is heard makes the claim of necessity remote. The reason for this obligation, according to some, is to avoid lowering the rank of the conditional verb below its particle. It has also been said that the emphatic nun does not enter a pure future verb unless something indicating emphasis has first entered before the verb, such as the oath formula or the extra "ma," so that this serves as a preparation for the entry of emphasis. On this view, the matter of the consequent (al-istitba') is the reverse of what was previously stated. In the use of ﴿in﴾ (إنْ) there is an indication that sending messengers is something permissible, not obligatory. This is the view held by Ahl al-Sunnah. The Mu'tazilah said that it is obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted, because, according to their claim, it is obligatory upon Him to do what is best (al-aslah).

His words, glorified is He: ﴿who relate to you My signs﴾ are an attribute of "messengers." It is also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either from "messengers" or from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, meaning: they present to you My rulings and My laws, inform you of them, and make them clear to you. His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever fears [Allah] and makes amends, there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾ (35) — the answer to the condition. "Man" (مَن) is either conditional or relative. "Minkum" (مِنكم, "from among you") is understood in the structure of the sentence so that the answer is linked to the condition, and the meaning is: whoever among you fears [Allah] by avoiding denial and makes amends in his deeds, ﴿then there is no fear for them﴾, etc. The singular and plural forms of the pronoun are used in accordance with the wording and meaning of "man."

Page 115

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 36:

﴿And those who denied﴾ from among you ﴿Our signs﴾ which relate (the news of the unseen) ﴿and were arrogant towards them﴾ and did not accept them, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ (36) Because of their denial and their arrogance.

This sentence is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the preceding sentence. The mention of piety (ittiqa') in it is to make known that the basis of success is not merely the absence of denial, but rather piety (ittiqa') and avoidance of it (ijtinab), and the insertion of the fa' (fa, "so") in the promise (wa'd) but not in the threat (wa'id) is for emphasis in the former and leniency in the latter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 37:

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah, or denies His signs?﴾ That is, one who deliberately lies about Him, glorified is He, and attributes to Him what He did not say, or denies what He has said, exalted is His majesty. The interrogative is for denunciation (inkar), and its verification has already been discussed. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative clause, and the plural is used in view of the meaning, just as the singular is used in the concealed pronoun in the two verbs, in view of the wording. The sense of distance is included to indicate their persistence in an evil state. That is, ﴿those﴾ are the ones described with what was mentioned of fabrication and denial. ﴿Their portion from the Book will reach them﴾, that is, what is decreed for them will befall them: ﴿their portion﴾ of what was written for them and decreed of provisions and terms of life. Despite their injustice and fabrication, they will not be deprived of what has been decreed for them until the end of their term. Thus "the Book" means "what is written," and restricting it to what was mentioned is related from a group of exegetes, and from Ibn 'Abbas that the intended meaning is what was decreed for them of good or evil, and similarly from Mujahid.

And from Abu Salih: what was decreed of punishment, and from al-Hasan the same. Some exegetes interpreted "the Book" as "what is written in it," namely the Preserved Tablet. "Min" is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghaya), and it has been permitted for it to be explanatory (tabyin) or partitive (tab'id). The prepositional phrase is related to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "their portion," meaning: being from the Book. ﴿Until, when Our messengers come to them﴾, that is, the Angel of Death and his assistants, ﴿causing them to die﴾, that is, while they are taking their souls. "Until" marks the limit of their receiving their portion. It is a particle of beginning, not a preposition, but rather it enters upon sentences, as in the verse:

*And even the horses, they are not led by reins.*

It has been said that it is a preposition, and it has been said that it has no indication of a limit, but this is nothing. It is related from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is: until, when the angels come to them to gather them to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and what prompted him to this was the words of the Exalted: ﴿They will say﴾, that is, the messengers will say to them: ﴿Where is what you used to call upon besides Allah?﴾, that is, where are the deities you used to worship in the world and seek help from in matters of importance? ﴿They will say: They have strayed from us﴾, that is, they have vanished, ﴿and we do not know where they are﴾. This question and answer, and what follows from them that will come later, will only occur on the Day of Resurrection without doubt. Perhaps, according to the apparent meaning, the time of the coming of the messengers and the state of causing death refers to the extended period from the beginning of the coming and causing death until the end of the Day of Recompense, based on the realization of the coming and causing death in that time as a continuity, even if their occurrence is only at its beginning. Or it is intended to show the extreme speed with which resurrection and recompense occur, as though both were present at the beginning of causing death. The fact that "where" is joined in the Uthmanic codex is contrary to its proper form of separation, for it is a separate word; had it been a conjunction, it would have been joined.

﴿And they will bear witness against themselves﴾, that is, they will acknowledge against themselves. There is nothing in the composition indicating that their acknowledgment was with the word "testimony," so "testimony" is a metaphor for acknowledgment. ﴿That they were﴾ in the world ﴿disbelievers﴾ (37), worshipping what does not deserve worship at all, since its condition became clear to them. The sentence may be a resumed statement from Allah, the Exalted, about their acknowledgment against themselves of disbelief, and it may be a conjunction with "they will say"; its conjunction with what is said is not free from difficulty. The interrogative, according to what many have held, is not genuine but is for rebuke and reproach; and according to this there is no answer, and what has been mentioned is only for lamentation and acknowledgment of the loss and ruin they are in.

Page 116

There is no contradiction between what is in this verse and the words of the Exalted: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, because the groups differ, or the standing-places are many, or the states are various.

[p. 117 appears within the text]

﴿He says﴾, that is, Allah, mighty and majestic, says to those liars who denied Him on the Day of Resurrection, either directly or through an angel: ﴿Enter among nations﴾, that is, along with nations. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning that you will be accompanying nations, ﴿who have passed away﴾, that is, who have gone, ﴿before you, of jinn and humankind﴾. This means the disbelieving nations of both kinds. The jinn are mentioned first because of the greater extent of their evil. ﴿Into the Fire﴾ is connected to "enter." It is also permissible for ﴿among nations﴾ to be connected to it, and for ﴿into the Fire﴾ to be taken as a substitute (badal) or as a description of ﴿nations﴾. Some exegetes permitted that this is a report that Allah has placed them among those [others] without there being any statement at all, that is, that He, exalted is He, made them such, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden. ﴿Every time a nation enters﴾, from among the nations, whether as followers or as leaders, ﴿into the Fire﴾, ﴿it curses its sister﴾, that is, it calls down curses upon its counterpart in religion. Thus the follower curses the leader who misled it, and the leader curses the follower who added to his error. According to Abu Muslim, the followers curse the leaders, saying: "You brought us to these places, so may Allah curse you."

﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another therein﴾: this is an end point (ghāyah) for what precedes it, meaning that they enter group after group, cursing one another, until they catch up with one another and are gathered together in the Fire. The original form of "ādāraku" is "tadārakū," and the tā' was assimilated into the dāl after being changed into a dāl and made quiescent. Then a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) was added.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAmr that he read ﴿adārakū﴾ with a hamza of cutting (qaṭʿ) in place of the connecting alif. It is said that this is based on treating it as a pause, similar to the pause of one who is recalling, and then starting afresh and cutting. Otherwise, there is no acceptable basis for this in the words of the Exalted Lord.

He also read ﴿idhā addārakū﴾ with a single quiescent alif, followed by a doubled dāl. This involves the juncture of two quiescent letters, and it was permitted because the second is assimilated. There is no difference between the connected and the separated forms.

﴿The last of them, in rank﴾, who are the followers and the lowly, say ﴿to the first of them, in rank﴾, who are the leaders and the chiefs. Or it may mean: "The last of them in entering says of the first of them in entering the same thing." That one of the two groups precedes the other in entering is transmitted from Muqatil.

The lām in ﴿li-ūlāhum﴾ is for causation (taʿlīl), not for conveying a message (tablīgh), as in your saying: "I said to Zayd, do such-and-such." This is because their address is with Allah, exalted is He, not with them, as is indicated by His statement, exalted is He, reporting about them: ﴿Our Lord, these led us astray﴾, that is, they called us to error and commanded us to it, since they established it as a way, so we followed them. ﴿So give them a double punishment﴾, that is, a multiplied one, as is narrated from Mujahid. ﴿Of the Fire﴾. The term "ḍiʿf" (double) according to what Abu ʿUbayd said, and what al-Shafiʿi explicitly stated in the chapter on bequests, is the like of a thing once. But according to al-Azhari, this is a customary meaning, while "ḍiʿf" in the speech of the Arabs, and to which the words of Allah, exalted is He, are returned, means "the like" extended to more, not restricted to two; rather, it is unlimited. Several have chosen this meaning here.

Al-Raghib said: "ḍaʿf" with a fatḥah is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and with a kasrah is a noun (ism), like "thanyy" and "thinyy," which is that which doubles something. When it is attributed to a number, that number requires its like, as when one says "double ten" or "double a hundred," which is twenty or two hundred, without disagreement. Upon this is the poet's verse:

Your recompense is double the affection for what you complained of,
and no one before me gave you double of it.

If one says "give him double of one," it requires the one and its like, because its meaning is the one and the two that pair with it. This is when ḍiʿf is attributed. When it is not attributed, and you say "ḍiʿfayn," it is said that it functions like the pair (zawjayn), in that each one pairs with the other, so this requires two, because each of them doubles the other and they do not depart from them. End of quotation.

﴿Ḍiʿf﴾ is put in the accusative as a description of ʿadhāb (punishment), and it is permitted that it be a substitute for it. ﴿Of the Fire﴾ is a description of the punishment or of the doubling.

﴿He says﴾, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿for each﴾ of you and of them there is a punishment, ﴿double﴾ ﴿of the Fire﴾. As for the leaders, it is for their error and their misleading others, and that is the cause of the preceding supplication. As for the followers, it is also for that according to some. Their being astray is evident, and as for their misleading others, it is because their taking those leaders, who issue commands to them, increases their rebellion, as He, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿And that there were men from humankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn, so they increased them in rebellion﴾. It has been objected that this is not consistently true, for the followership of many followers is not known to the leaders, unless it is said that it applies to some of them specifically. It has also been said: "The better view is that the doubling for the followers is because of their turning away from the manifest truth and their following of the leaders in order to obtain the goods of this world, following their desires." This is indicated by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed: Did we turn you away from guidance after it came to you? Rather, you were criminals﴾. There is more to be said about this. The better view is that this applies to the followers because of their disbelief and their imitation. There is no doubt that imitation in matters of guidance is error, and its practitioner deserves punishment.

Al-Raghib transmitted from some of them regarding the verse that the meaning is: for each of you and of them is a double of what the other sees, for there is a punishment that is apparent and one that is hidden, and each perceives from the other only the apparent, not the hidden, so he supposes that the hidden punishment does not apply to him. He chose that the meaning is: "But for them is double of what you have of punishment." The apparent meaning is what we have relied upon.

﴿But you do not know﴾ (38). What is for you, or what is for each group? For this reason you spoke in a way that indicates your belief that the leaders deserve the doubling and you do not. Thus the address, under both interpretations, is to the followers, as is the apparent meaning.

It has been said that under the first interpretation the address is to the followers, and under the second it is to both groups, by giving precedence to the addressed, who are the followers, over the absent, who are the leaders. Ghalb (the grammatical device of giving precedence to one group in address) is the device of giving precedence to one of the two parts. ʿĀṣim read ﴿lā yaʿlamūn﴾ with the yā' (third person), so that this statement is separated from what precedes it, being a concluding remark (tadhyīl) not intended to be included in the answer. Whoever claims that the address is to both groups by way of ghalb said: this reading places the leaders apart from the followers, for on this reading it is not possible to say ghalb, since the absent is not given precedence over the addressed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 39:

﴿And the first of them said to the last of them﴾ when they heard God the Exalted's answer to them. The lam here (lam) may be for conveying (al-tabligh), because their speech to them is indicated by His words, glorified is He: ﴿So you had no advantage over us﴾, meaning: we and you are equal in deserving the punishment and in its cause. This is arranged upon the words of God the Exalted in the manner of causation, because His announcement, glorified is He, with His words, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿For each is double [punishment]﴾ is a cause for their knowledge of equality. So the fa' is responsive (jawabiyya) to a presumed condition, meaning: if it is so, then it is established that you have no advantage over us. It was also said that it is coordinating (ataifa) upon a presumed clause, meaning: you called upon God the Exalted, so He made equal between us and you, ﴿So you had no advantage over us﴾ ... etc. And this is nothing.

Whatever the case, they meant by "advantage" the lightening of the punishment and the unity of the cause. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: you had no advantage over us in opinion and intellect, and the punishment that befell us has reached you, so why did you follow us? Then, as you see, it is as such. And it was said: the meaning is: you had no advantage over us in the world through your following us; rather, your following and your not following are alike to us. Your following us was by your own choice, not by our compelling you to it. On this basis it is not arranged upon the words of God the Exalted, and its answer is as in the first aspect. ﴿So taste the punishment﴾, the doubled [punishment], ﴿for what you used to earn﴾ (39). That is, because of your earning, or what you were earning. The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of the leaders, which they said to them by way of gloating (tashaffi). Its arrangement upon what precedes it, according to the last opinion on the meaning of the verse, is most evident. It is also permitted that it is from God the Exalted's speech to both groups, by way of rebuke, and that the pause is on ﴿fadl﴾. It was also said: it is from the speech of both groups, meaning: each group said to the other "taste..." etc. And this is very contrary to the apparent meaning.
