Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs﴾, meaning the signs that point to the foundations of the religion and the rulings of the Sharia, such as the proofs that indicate the existence of the Creator and His oneness, the proofs that indicate prophethood and the return (ma'ad), and the like. ﴿And were arrogant towards them﴾, meaning they went to great lengths to belittle them and to disregard them, did not give them any attention, turned their eyes away from them, cast them behind their backs, did not adorn themselves with the garments that their requirements call for, and did not act upon them. ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾, meaning for their souls when they die, ﴿as they are opened for the souls of the believers﴾. Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dying person is attended by the angels. If the man is righteous, [they] say: 'Come out, O good soul that was in the good body; come out praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest, sweet fragrance and a Lord who is pleased and not angry.' This continues to be said to it until it comes out. Then it is raised up to the heaven, and the gate is requested to be opened for it, and it is asked, 'Who is this?' They say, 'So-and-so son of so-and-so.' It is said, 'Welcome to the good soul that was in the good body. Enter, praiseworthy, and rejoice in rest, sweet fragrance and a Lord who is pleased and not angry.' This continues to be said to it until it reaches the seventh heaven. And if the man was evil, [they] say: 'Come out, O evil soul that was in the evil body; come out blameworthy, and rejoice in boiling water, dark liquid and other torments of similar kind.' This continues to be said to it until it comes out. Then it is raised up to the heaven, and the gate is requested to be opened for it, and it is asked, 'Who is this?' They say, 'So-and-so son of so-and-so.' It is said, 'No welcome to the evil soul that was in the evil body. Return blameworthy; the gates of heaven will not be opened for you.' Then it is sent down from the heaven and then it goes into the grave." The reports on this are numerous. It has also been said: the gates of heaven will not be opened for their deeds or their supplications. This was narrated from al-Hasan and Mujahid. It has been said: the gates will not be opened for their souls nor for their deeds, and this was narrated from Ibn Jurayj. It has been said: the meaning is that no deed of theirs ascends and no blessing descends upon them. That heaven has gates which are opened for righteous deeds and good souls, and that the gates of acceptance are opened for the one about whom the texts were revealed, is a matter that is possible, reported by the Truthful One, so there is no need to interpret it otherwise. That heaven is spherical and does not accept rending or joining is something for which we have no complete proof. The apparent meaning of the words of the people of the New Astronomy is the permissibility of rending and joining in the celestial spheres. Some claimed that saying there are gates does not contradict saying that rending and joining are impossible, but there is scrutiny in this, as is not hidden. The "ta'" in ﴿tuftahu﴾ is for the feminine gender of "al-abwab" (the gates), and the doubling (tashdid) is for the frequency of the action, since it does not suit the context. Abu 'Amr read it with the single letter (takhfif), and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with that and with the yaa' (third person masculine). This was narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because the feminine is not real and the verb is placed first with a separator present.

It was also read in the active voice with "al-abwab" in the accusative, with the ta' above (tu-), on the basis that the verb is attributed to the signs metaphorically, since they are the cause of that; and with the yaa' (yu-), on the basis that it is attributed to Allah, exalted is He. ﴿Nor will they enter the Garden﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿until the camel passes through﴾, meaning enters ﴿the eye of the needle﴾. The "jamal" is the camel when it has reached maturity, its plural being "jimal" and "ajmal", and the latter is pluralized as "jimalat". It was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about the "jamal" and he said: it is the mate of the she-camel.

And it was narrated from al-Hasan that he said: it is the son of the she-camel that stands in the pen on four legs. In this there is a rebuke to the questioner and an indication that seeking another meaning is an affectation. The Arabs use it as a proverb for great bulk of body, so it is as if it were said: "until there enters what is a proverb for great bulk of body." ﴿Into the eye of the needle﴾, meaning the hole of the needle, and this is also a proverb among them for narrowness of passage. This is among things that do not happen, so likewise what depends upon it, nay, power is not related to it since it is impossible while the large remains large and the narrow remains narrow. Power relates only to possibilities in themselves, and passage is possible only by diminishing the large or widening the narrow. Such a limit is common in their speech; they say "I will not do such-and-such until the crow turns white," "until the pitch becomes white," and "until the two evening-returners return," meaning "I will never do such-and-such." Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi read ﴿al-Jumma[l]﴾ with a damma on the jim and a shadda on the mim, like "al-qumml". 'Abd al-Karim, Hanzalah, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr in another narration read "al-Jumal" with a damma and a fatha with lightening, like "nughar". In a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he read "al-Juml" with a damma on the jim and sukun on the mim, like "al-qufl", and "al-Jumul" with two dammas, like "al-nusub". Abu al-Sammal read "al-Jaml" with a fatha on the jim and sukun on the mim, like "al-habl". In all of these it was interpreted as a thick rope made of hemp; and it has been said it is the rope of the ship. It was read "fi summ" with a damma and a kasra on the sin, both being dialects for it, and the fatha is most well known. Its meaning is a small hole in general; and it has been said its origin is what is in an organ such as the nose or ear. 'Abd Allah read "fi sam al-mikhyat" with a kasra and fatha on the mim; and it and "al-khiyat" are that with which one sews, such as a belt, a girdle, a covering, and a cover. ﴿And thus﴾, meaning like that dreadful recompense, ﴿We recompense the criminals﴾ (40), meaning their kind, and those are included in it by primary inclusion. The root of "jirm" is cutting fruit from a tree, and it is said "ajrama" meaning he became one with a jirm, like "atmara" and "athmara." It is used in their speech for acquiring what is disliked, and is hardly ever said of praiseworthy gain.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 41:**

﴿For them there will be a bed of Hell beneath them﴾, meaning a bedding beneath them, and it is an emphatic expression of grandeur. The phrase ﴿مِن جَهَنَّمَ﴾ serves as the subject of the adverbial complement (*zarf*, a term for a time or place adverbial), or it is a subject (*mubtada'*) and the sentence is either a resumptive sentence (*mustaanifa*) or a circumstantial clause (*hali*). The *min* in ﴿مِن جَهَنَّمَ﴾ is *tajridiyya* (a *min* that abstracts a part from a whole, or that specifies the source). The prepositional phrase is linked to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of ﴿مِهادٌ﴾, because it has been placed before it. ﴿And above them are coverings (ghawashin)﴾, meaning coverings, the plural of *ghashiya*. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that they are blankets. The verse, as it has been said, is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿For them there will be canopies of fire above them, and beneath them canopies﴾. The intended meaning is that the Fire surrounds them from all directions. Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and then said: "They are layers above him and layers beneath him, and he does not know whether what is above him is more or what is beneath him. However, the lower layers lift him up, and the upper layers press him down, and it narrows between them until it is like the rod in the cup."

The tanwin on ﴿ghawashin﴾ is a substitute for the omitted letter or its vowel, and the kasra is not an inflection marker (*i'rab*, the grammatical case ending). It is not declinable (*ghayr munsarif*), because it follows the pattern of the final plural forms (*muntaha al-jumuu'*, the plural pattern that does not take tanwin). Some Arabs inflect it with visible vowels on the letter before the *ya'*, treating the *ya'* as omitted, as in ﴿nasyan mansiyyan﴾. For this reason it was read as *ghawashun* in the nominative, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And His are the ships raised high (al-jawari al-munsha'at)﴾, in the reading of 'Abdullah.

﴿And thus﴾, meaning and like that severe recompense, ﴿We recompense the wrongdoers﴾. He refers to them once as "the criminals" and once as "the wrongdoers", to draw attention to the fact that by their denial of the signs and their arrogance toward them, they combined both attributes. He mentioned the crime together with being deprived of Paradise, and the wrongdoing together with the punishment of the Fire, to alert the reader that it is the greatest of crimes. Nor is it hidden from one who reflects on the subtleties of the Mighty Qur'an what is contained in preparing the bedding and coverings for these arrogant ones toward the signs, and in preventing them from ascending to the realm of the heavens, and in restricting their non-entry into Paradise to the passage of a camel through the eye of a needle, which is the height of subtlety. So let him reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 42:

﴿Those who believed﴾, i.e., in Our signs, and did not deny them, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, and did not act arrogantly toward them, ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, i.e., what it is able to do with ease, not what constricts it.

صفحة 120

The sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) placed between the subject, which is the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), and the predicate, which is the clause ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise﴾, to encourage the pursuit of what leads to everlasting bliss, by showing how easily it is attained and how readily it can be obtained. It has also been said that the meaning is: "We do not burden any soul except with what yields for it expansiveness," i.e., a Paradise whose breadth is the heavens and the earth. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, although the verse under this reading is still not free of encouragement. It is also permitted that the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) be a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun, with what follows being the predicate of the subject; and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the distance of their rank in virtue and nobility.

It is also permitted that the clause "We do not burden..." etc. be the predicate of the subject, with a returning pronoun (al-'a'id) understood, i.e., "from among them." His words, glorified is He: ﴿They therein abide forever﴾ (42), are a circumstantial clause (hal) from "companions of Paradise." It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from "Paradise," since it contains a pronoun referring to it, and the operative element in it is the sense of the annexation (idafah) or the implied lam. It has also been said that it is a predicate of "those" according to the opinion of one who permits this, and "therein" is connected to "abide forever," placed before it for the sake of the closing rhyme (fasilah).

And We removed whatever resentment (ghill) was in their breasts. That is, We uprooted from their hearts the hidden hatred and enmity that were, by the nature of human disposition, caused by matters that had occurred between them in the world. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi that he said: When the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and reach it, they find at its gate a tree, at the root of whose trunk are two springs. They drink from one of them, and whatever resentment is in their breasts is removed; this is the "pure drink" (al-sharab al-tahur). They wash themselves in the other, and the radiance of bliss flows over them, so that their hair will never become disheveled and their faces will never become discolored after that, ever.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: "It has reached me that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: The people of Paradise will be detained after they have crossed the Sirat (the bridge over Hell), until the wrongs (zalamat) they committed against one another in the world are settled. Then they will enter Paradise, and there will be no resentment in the heart of any one of them toward another." It has also been said that the meaning is: We purified their hearts and protected them from envy, regarding the ranks of Paradise and the degrees of nearness, such that the holder of a lower rank does not envy the holder of a higher rank. This is in contrast to what He, glory be to Him, mentioned about the people of the Fire cursing one another.

Whichever of these is the case, the intended meaning is "We will remove," because it is in the Hereafter; however, the past tense is used to indicate that it is certain to occur.

It has also been said that this removal took place in the world, and the meaning is that they did not possess such resentment from the outset, but that He expressed the absence of this quality, despite the presence of what human nature sometimes calls for, by the term "removal," metaphorically. This is perhaps with regard to the perfect believers, such as the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for they are "merciful among themselves" (cf. Qur'an 48:29), each loving the other as he loves himself. Or the meaning is its removal by Allah's grace before death, after it had been present according to the requirements of human natures.

It is possible that both of these interpretations include what was related by more than one narrator from Ali, may Allah honour his face, that he said regarding this verse: "I truly hope that I, Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr will be among them." And it is said, according to the second interpretation, regarding what occurred among them that outwardly indicates resentment: it was only out of ijtihad (independent reasoning), to elevate the word of Allah. But the remoteness of this meaning is not hidden, even if the apparent form of the expression supports it.

The phrase "from resentment" (min ghill), according to all the other possibilities, is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to "what" (ma). His, glory be to Him, statement "Rivers flow beneath them" (tajri min tahtihimu al-anhar) is also a circumstantial clause, either referring to the pronoun in "their breasts" (suduriham), because the genitive-annexed noun is a part of the noun it is annexed to, and the operating element is the sense of annexation; or the operating element is in the annexed noun; or it refers to the pronoun in "We removed" (nazana), according to what has been said, and the operating element is the verb. Some have chosen that the clause is a new, resumed sentence (mustani'ah), giving information about the description of their condition; the meaning being that the waters of the rivers flow beneath their mansions, as an increase in their pleasure and happiness.

﴿And they say: "Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this"﴾: that is, to this great success and enduring bliss. The meaning of "guidance" here is guidance to what leads to the actions of the heart and of the body, metaphorically; and that is by granting success in them and turning away the obstacles to their performance.

[Page 121]

It has also been said that the meaning of the guidance is to what they are in of bliss, namely, crossing the Sirat until they reached it. Some have taken the reference to be to the removal of resentment from the breasts, but I do not consider that anything.

﴿And we would not have been guided﴾: that is, to this, or to some other of the matters of which this is one, ﴿had it not been that Allah had guided us﴾, that is, granted us success in it. The lam here is for emphasizing the negation, and it is what is called lam al-juhud (the lam of denial). The answer to "lawla" (had it not been) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it; it is not the same as it, because the response cannot precede the conditional particle according to the correct view. The object of "to be guided" (nahtadi) and the second object of "guided us" (hadana) are omitted, either because the intended meaning is clear, or for the sake of generality, as has been pointed out. The clause is either circumstantial (hali) or resumed (isti'nafiyyah). In the codices of the people of Syria the reading is "ma kunna" without a waw, and this is the reading of Ibn Amir; so the clause is then like an explanation of the first.

As you see, whoever is granted good in this world speaks in such terms, and cannot restrain himself from saying it, out of joy and out of devotion.

His, glory be to Him, statement: ﴿Indeed, the messengers of our Lord came with the truth﴾ is a clause of oath (qasamiyyah), which is also not intended to draw nearness; and it is an explanation of the truthfulness of the promise of the messengers, peace be upon them, to them of Paradise, as some of the eminent scholars have affirmed. It has also been said that it is a justification (ta'lil) for their guidance.

The bi' (in "bil-haqq") is either for transitivity (ta'diyah), in which case it is connected to "came" (ja'at); or for accompaniment (mulabasah), in which case it is connected to an implied element that occurs as a circumstantial clause of "the messengers." And there is no hiding what this verse contains of clear refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination in human actions), who claim that every guided person created guidance for himself, and that Allah, exalted is He, did not create that for him. Consider, then, the statement of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), who say in the world that the guided one is the one who guided himself, in contrast to the words of Allah, exalted is He, quoting the words of the monotheists in "a seat of truth" (Qur'an 54:55): ﴿And we would not have been guided had it not been that Allah had guided us﴾. Choose for yourself which of the two groups you will follow. I do not see you, O intelligent one, exchanging what Allah, exalted is He, has made noble for the saying of a misguided person who vacillates with his desire and his partisanship. When al-Zamakhshari saw that this verse was directly confronting his people, he interpreted guidance as the grace (lutf) by means of which the servant creates guidance for himself. By my life, this is the speech of one who has been deprived of grace. We ask Allah, exalted is He, for pardon and well-being.

﴿And they will be called﴾: that is, the angels will call out to them. Some have permitted the possibility that the caller is Allah Himself, but the reports support the first.

﴿That is the Paradise⁠—﴾: that is, "that," with "an" (an) being explanatory of what is in the call of a meaning of saying. It is also permissible that "an" be the lightened form of "anna," with an implied preposition, and its noun being an implied pronoun of matter (damir sha'n); the meaning being "that it" or "that he," (is) "that." Some have made the second obligatory, on the basis that the pronoun of matter must be feminine when the predicate in the explanatory clause is feminine; but the correct view is that it is not obligatory, as Ibn al-Hajib and Ibn Malik have explicitly stated. The sense of distance in the demonstrative may be either to raise its rank and the remoteness of its station, or because they were called upon at the moment of seeing it from a distant place, or to indicate that it is the very Paradise that they were promised in the world. To this last meaning al-Zajjaj's statement points.

The apparent reading is that "that is the Paradise" is a subject and predicate. The statement "you have inherited it" (uwrithtumuha) is a circumstantial clause of "the Paradise," and the operating element in it is the sense of the demonstrative. It is also permissible for "the Paradise" to be an adjective of "that," or an apposition, with "you have inherited it" as the predicate. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause of the subject or of "kum," as Abu al-Baqa' said, and that is clear. Some, in order to justify the distance, have committed to the view that "that" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "this is that Paradise promised to you before"; or that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "that Paradise which you were informed of or promised in the world is this one." But there is no need for this.

The thing for which the call is made primarily and directly is their being given it as an inheritance; and what precedes it is a preparation for it. Inheritance is a metaphor for giving: that is, you have been given it ﴿for what you used to do﴾ (Qur'an 7:43) in the world of righteous deeds. The bi' is causal, and by it is meant, metaphorically, giving, indicating that the cause in it is not a necessitating one, even if it is a cause in outward appearance, just as inheritance is ownership without earning, even if kinship, for example, is a cause of it.

[Page 122]

The bi' in his (ﷺ) statement, as is in some books: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds," and likewise in his statement, peace be upon him, as in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Jabir: "None of you will be saved by his deeds," is causal in the sense of a complete cause, so there is no contradiction. It is also permissible that the bi' in what we are discussing is for exchange, meaning in return for your deeds. It has been said that the reference "that" is to dwellings in Paradise which were for the people of the Fire had they obeyed; Allah made them an inheritance for the believers. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi that he said: "There is not a believer or a disbeliever but he has in Paradise and in the Fire a designated dwelling. When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, and they enter their dwellings, Paradise is raised up for the people of the Fire, and they look at their dwellings in it. It is said: 'These are your dwellings, had you worked in obedience to Allah, exalted is He.' Then it is said: 'O people of Paradise, inherit them from them for what you used to do.' So the people of Paradise divide their dwellings." And you know that the claim of this strange inheritance does not dispense with the need for metaphor.

The Mu'tazilah claimed that entry into Paradise is by means of deeds and not by bounty, on the basis of this verse. But it is not hidden that there is no escape for a believer from the bounty of Allah, exalted is He, because to say that deeds in themselves necessitate entry into Paradise, or that Allah, exalted is He, causing their doers to enter it, is something that can hardly be conceived. What can be conceived at most is that Allah, exalted is He, out of bounty, ordained entry into Paradise as a consequence of them; so, were it not for His bounty, that would not have occurred. And I do not see anyone more audacious than the Mu'tazilah in this domain, as in many other domains. For the upshot of their speech on it is that Paradise and its endless bliss is a grant to them by right, owed to them by Allah, exalted is He, who neither benefits from anything nor is harmed by anything; so there is no bounty from Him to them in that, but rather it is like a debt paid back to its owner. Glory be to You; this is a great calumny and a lie against no sound report.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 44:

﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out﴾ after settling in it, as is the apparent meaning, and the use of the past tense (ṣīghat al-māḍī) is to affirm that the event will certainly occur; the meaning is "they will call out," and it is necessary that each group of the people of the Garden [calls out] ﴿to the companions of the Fire﴾, that is, to whoever they knew in the world among its people, out of boasting over their condition, gloating over their enemies, and causing them grief, not merely for the sake of informing or inquiring. ﴿Indeed we have found what our Lord promised us﴾ through the tongues of His messengers, peace be upon them, of bliss and honour ﴿truly﴾, since we have attained that. ﴿So have you found what your Lord promised you﴾, that is, what He promised you of disgrace, humiliation and punishment ﴿truly?﴾ The object is omitted for brevity, conciseness and sufficiency by the first. It has also been said that what displeased them of the promises was not entirely specific to them, such as the promise of resurrection, reckoning, and the bliss of the people of the Garden, for they have found all of that to be true, even though the promise was not specific to them.

It has been objected that there is no doubt that the companions of the Garden believe in everything, and everything gives them joy, so their promise ought to be stated as well. Therefore the proper reading is to take it according to what preceded. ( ḥaqqan ) is in the accusative in both places as a circumstantial (ḥāl) accusative, and it has been permitted that it be a second object, with ( wajada ) meaning ( ʿalima ) "to know." The expression "promise" has been said to be for the sake of mushākala (matching), and it has been said to be for mockery (tahakkum). Some people permitted that the omitted object of ( waʿada ) be ( nā ), and then there is neither mushākala nor mockery. In any case, this call there is not improbable, even if the distance between the Garden and the Fire is great, as is not hidden.

﴿They will say﴾ in answer to the companions of the Garden: ﴿Yes﴾, indeed we have found that to be true. al-Kisā'ī read ( naʿim ) with a kasra on the ʿayn, and it is a dialect of it, attributed to Kinānah and Hudhayl. No heed is to be paid to one who denies it, given that it is read with it, and given the affirmation of the lexicographers of it by sound transmission.

Yes, as for what is narrated that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked a people about something and they said: "naʿim," ʿUmar said: "As for an-naʿam, it is camels; say: naʿam." I do not consider this sound, because it opposes the most correct eloquent usage. ﴿Then a caller will call out﴾ — it is, according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, the angel of the Trumpet, peace be upon him. It has been said: Mālik, the keeper of the Fire; and it has been said: an angel other than these two whom Allah commands with that. The narration of the Imamiyyah from al-Riḍā and Ibn ʿAbbās that he is ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, is among what has not been established through the people of Sunnah, and it is far from this Imam to be a caller while he is then in the enclosures of holiness. ﴿Between them﴾, that is, between the two groups, not between those who said "yes," as has been said. It is not objected that the apparent wording would be "between them both," since "other" here is definite. ﴿That the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ (44). With ( bi-anna ) the light (mukhaffafah) or explanatory form. The intent is to announce the curse of Allah upon them, as an increase in the joy of the companions of the Garden and the grief of the companions of the Fire; or it is the beginning of a curse.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ( anna laʿnata Allāh ) with shadda and the accusative. al-Aʿmash read with a kasra on the hamza, on the basis of intending the act of saying through implicit inclusion or estimation, or on the basis of direct speech after ( adhdhana ), because it carries the sense of saying, so it takes its position.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 45:**

﴿Those who turn away from the way of Allah﴾. That is, they turn away from His religion, glorified is He, by their own selves (*yaṣuddūna bi-anfusihim*), and they disregard it. The relative clause (*al-mawṣūl*, the relative pronoun construction) is a clarifying qualifier (*ṣifah muqarrirah*, a descriptive attribute that restates an implied sense) for "the wrongdoers," because this turning away is necessary for every wrongdoer. It is also permitted to treat it as a disconnected clause (*qaṭʿ*, grammatical severance from the preceding noun) in the nominative (*rafʿ*) or the accusative (*naṣb*), and both are for censure (*dhamm*). The matter of the pause (*waqf*) is clear. The Imam al-Nasafi interpreted *al-ṣadd* (turning away, barring) here as preventing others (*manʿ al-ghayr*), and according to this there is no clarifying qualifier. The meaning is that they prevent people from the religion of Allah, the Exalted, by forbidding it and introducing doubts into its proofs.

﴿And they seek to make it crooked﴾. That is, they seek its crookedness (*iʿwijājahā*) and they disparage it, so they do not believe in it; or they seek for it a distorted interpretation (*taʾwīlan*) and an inclination toward falsehood. The word *ʿiwaj* is either in its original sense, which is inclination (*al-mayl*), or in the sense of bending and tilting (*al-taʿwīj wa-al-imālah*). Its accusative form (*naṣb*) is said to be a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāliyyah*, expressing a state), and it is said to be an object (*mafʿūliyyah*). Al-Tabarsi permitted that it be an accusative of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), like *rajaʿa al-qahqarā* (he returned backwards) and *ishtamala al-ṣammāʾ* (he wrapped himself in the single garment). He mentioned that *ʿiwaj* with a kasra (*ʿiwaj*, pronounced with an i-vowel) is used for religion and the path, while with a fatha (*ʿawaj*) it is used for physical form, so one says *fī sāqihi ʿawaj* (in his leg there is a bend) with a fatha, and *fī dīnihi ʿiwaj* (in his religion there is a crookedness) with a kasra. Al-Raghib said: *al-ʿiwaj* is used for what is perceived by sight, such as an upright piece of wood and the like, while *al-ʿawaj* is used for what is perceived by thought and insight, as it occurs in an uneven land (*arḍ basīṭ*, a level or flat surface) and in religion and livelihood. There will be a continuation of this, if Allah the Exalted wills.

﴿And they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers﴾ (45). That is, they do not acknowledge the Resurrection and what is in it. The prepositional phrase (*al-jārr wa-al-majrūr*) is connected to what follows it. The fronting (*taqdīm*) is for the sake of the verse endings (*fawāṣil*, the rhyming ends of verses). The shift from the verbal sentence to the nominal sentence is to indicate permanence and stability, as an indication of the firm entrenchment of disbelief in them.

[Cont.] Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 7, verse 46:

﴿And between them is a barrier﴾, i.e., between the two groups, as in His saying: ﴿So a wall with a gate will be struck between them﴾ (57:13). Or, between Paradise and the Fire there is a great barrier, so that the effect of one of them is prevented from reaching the other, although the calls are not prevented from reaching. The matters of the Hereafter cannot be measured by the matters of this world.

﴿And upon the heights﴾, i.e., the heights of the barrier, meaning its upper parts, and it is the wall struck between them. *A'raf* is the plural of *'urf* (ridge, crest), a term borrowed from the *'urf* (crest) of an animal or a rooster. It was also said: the *'urf* is what is raised above a thing, that is, its highest point, because it is the most noble and the most prominent part of it, the part that stands above what is lower. It was also said that this refers to Mount Uhud.

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Uhud loves us and we love it." It is also said that on the Day of Resurrection it will stand between Paradise and the Fire, and that some people will be held back at it, and they recognize each one by their mark, and they, if Allah wills, are among the people of Paradise. It was also said that it is the *Sirat* (the bridge over Hell). This was narrated from al-Hasan ibn al-Mufaddal, and it is reported from some people that they did not interpret *al-A'raf* as a place, and that they said: the meaning is "and upon the knowledge of the people of Paradise and Hell are men." The truth is that it is a place, and the men are a group of the monotheists whose bad deeds fell short of bringing them into Paradise and whose good deeds carried them past the Fire. They are kept there until Allah judges between the people. While they are in this state, their Lord looks upon them and says to them: "Stand up and enter Paradise, for I have forgiven you." Abu al-Shaykh, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated this from Hudhayfah. In another narration from him: Allah gathers the people, then says to the companions of the *A'raf*: "What are you waiting for?" They say: "We are waiting for Your command." It is then said: "Your good deeds have carried you past the Fire so that you will not enter it, and your sins have stood between you and Paradise. So enter it by My forgiveness and My mercy." A group of the Companions and the Successors held this view. It was also said that they are the Prophets, peace be upon them all, whom Allah seated upon the heights of that wall to distinguish them from the rest of the people of the Resurrection and to show their nobility and the elevation of their rank.

al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they are al-'Abbas, Hamzah, 'Ali and Ja'far Dhu al-Janahayn, may Allah be pleased with them all. They sit at a place on the *Sirat*, and they recognize their lovers by the whiteness of their faces and their enemies by the blackness of theirs. It was also said that they are the just witnesses of the Resurrection who testify against the people concerning their deeds, and that they are from every nation. This was related by al-Zuhri. Al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Tabarani and others narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the companions of the *A'raf*, and he said: "They are people who were killed in the cause of Allah while their parents were disobedient. The disobedience of their parents prevented them from entering Paradise, and their being killed in the cause of Allah prevented them from entering the Fire." It was also said that they are people whose one parent was pleased with them and the other was not.

al-Hasan al-Basri said: they are a people in whom there was *'ujb* (self-admiration). Muslim ibn Yasar said: they are a people who had debts. It was also said: they are the people of the *fatrah* (the period between Prophets). It was said: they are the children of polytheists. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that they are the children of fornication. And from him also: they are the poor among the people of Paradise.

It is narrated from Abu Muslim that they are angels who appear in the form of men, not that they are really men, because angels are not described as male or female. It has been said, and it has been said, and the most preferred of these opinions, as al-Qurtubi said, is the first. Some scholars reconciled them by saying that it is possible that all of those who were described as companions of the *A'raf* sit there together despite their differing ranks. Yet among these opinions some are clearly overlapping.

Some people preferred the view that the companions of the *A'raf* are a people whose ranks are high, because the statements that follow, and what branches from them, do not fit anyone else. ﴿They recognize each of them﴾, from among the people of Paradise and the Fire, ﴿by their marks﴾, by their sign with which Allah has informed them, such as the whiteness of faces in the case of the people of Paradise, and their blackness in the case of the people of the Fire.

Its form is *fa'la* (فَعْلى), from *sawama* (سام) his camel, when he sent it out to pasture marked, or from *wasama* (وسم) with metathesis, like *jah* from *wajh*. Its form would then be *'afla* (عَقْلى). It is said *sima'* (سِيماءُ) with a long vowel and *simiya'* (سِيمِياءُ) like *kibriya'*. The poet said:

*He has a mark that does not hide from the sight.*

Their knowledge that this is the sign of Paradise and that is the sign of the Fire is by inspiration or by the teaching of the angels. This is what was narrated from Abu Mijlaz, may Allah be pleased with him, before the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire. Some scholars preferred this, since after entering there is no need for a sign. The statements of others suggest that it is after entry. The *ba'* (بِ) here is for *mulabasah* (association, accompaniment).

﴿And they call out﴾, i.e., the men of the *A'raf*, ﴿to the companions of Paradise﴾, when they see them and recognize them: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, either as a supplication and greeting, or as a statement of their deliverance from hardships. ﴿They have not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the subject of ﴿they call out﴾ or to its object.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿while they hope﴾ (46) is a circumstantial clause referring to the subject of ﴿they enter it﴾, meaning: they called out to them while they had not entered it, in a state in which they were hoping to enter it, looking forward to it. That is, they had not entered it, and at the time of not entering it they were hopeful. This was stated by some scholars.

Al-Hasan and Abu 'Ali interpreted *tama'* (hope) as *yaqin* (certainty), and it was interpreted this way in His saying, quoting Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin﴾ (26:82). In *al-Kashshaf* it is stated that the clause ﴿they have not entered it﴾ ... etc. has no place in the i'rab, because it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*), as if a questioner asked about the condition of the companions of the *A'raf*, so it was said: ﴿they have not entered it while they hope﴾. It was also permitted that it be in the position of a nominative as an attribute of *rijal* (men), but this was considered weak because of the separation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 47:

﴿And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire﴾ — i.e., toward their direction. It is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), and there is no other maṣdar in the forms on the pattern tiʿāl with a kasra on the taʾ, apart from tibyān (clarification) and zilzāl (earthquake). Then it was used as an adverb of place (ẓarf makān) in the sense of the direction of encounter and facing. According to the Seven (al-Sabʿa, the seven canonical readers), it is permissible to retain its hamza and the hamza of ﴿aṣḥāb﴾, or to drop the first and retain the second. Not addressing the attachment of their gazes to the companions of Paradise, while expressing the attachment of their gazes to the companions of the Fire by "turned" (ṣurifat), indicates, as many have said, that the first attachment is by way of desire and inclination, and the second is the opposite. Whoever claims that there is an elided conditional clause in the first statement has not come up with anything.

They said, seeking refuge in God, glorified is He, from the evil of what they saw of their own state: ﴿Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people.﴾ (47) I.e., do not gather us and them together in the Fire. Describing them as wrongdoers, rather than by what they are in at that time of punishment and evil condition, which is what calls for the supplication, indicates that what they fear is not the punishment itself alone, but also what leads to it of wrongdoing. In this verse there is, as has been said, an indication that God, glorified is He, is under no obligation to anyone. Some have claimed that the intended meaning here is not supplication, but merely the magnifying of the state of the wrongdoers. Al-A'mash recited ﴿And when their eyes are turned away (qullibat)﴾, and it is related from Ibn Mas'ud and Salim something similar to that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 48:

﴿And the companions of the heights called out⟩ He repeated their mention, although the pronoun would have sufficed, to add emphasis (taqrir). It was said: he did not rely on the pronoun, in order to distinguish between who is meant by them here and who is meant by them in what preceded, for the one calling out there is all of them, while here it is some of them. And the application of "companions of the heights" to those men, on the basis that their final destination is Paradise, is evidence that the title of companionship (suhbah) to a thing does not require constant attachment to it, as some have claimed. ﴿men⟩ from among the chiefs of the disbelievers, such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and al-As ibn Wa'il, until they saw them among the companions of the Fire. ﴿They recognise them by their marks⟩ by their sign with which Allah Most High informed them, namely blackness of the face, disfigurement of form and blueness of the eye, as al-Jubba'i said; or by their forms by which they used to recognise them in the world, as Abu Muslim said; or by their sign indicating the evil of their state on that day and their leadership in the world, as has been said, and this is perhaps the better view. In any case, the prepositional phrase is connected to what precedes it. It is understood from the words of some of them, though it is far-fetched, that it is connected to "called out," and the meaning would be: they called out to men whom they knew in the world by their names, their kunyas, and the attributes by which they were addressed.

﴿They said⟩ is an explanation of "called out," or a substitute for it. ﴿What availed you⟩ is an interrogative for rebuke and reproach. It is permissible that a negation is intended, meaning: what you were in did not suffice you. ﴿your gathering⟩ your followers and partisans, or your gathering of wealth, in which case it is a verbal noun whose object is implied. ﴿and what you used to be arrogant about⟩ (48). That is, your constant arrogance in refusing to accept the truth, or towards creation, and this is more fitting with what follows.

It was read as ﴿tastakthirun⟩ from abundance (al-kathrah), and "what" (ma) under this reading may be a relative pronoun, meaning: what your followers availed you, and what you used to amass of wealth.

In my view it is also possible that in the canonical (Sab'iyyah) reading it is so, and the intended meaning then is the idols, and the sense of their being arrogant towards them is their belief in their greatness and magnitude, i.e. what your gathering and your idols, whose greatness and magnitude you used to believe in, did not avail you.

Are these the ones about whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy?" This is part of what they said to the men, and so it is also in the accusative position (*maḥall naṣb*) as the object of the verb of saying. That is, they said what was mentioned. They said, "Are these the ones...?" The demonstrative refers to the weak (*ḍu'afā'*) among the people of Paradise, whom the disbelievers used to despise in the world, and whom they swore that Allah would not grant mercy or good, nor admit to Paradise, such as Salman, Suhayb, and Bilal, may Allah be pleased with them. Alternatively, the swearing is inferred from their conduct that indicates it, as was said regarding the verse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Did you not swear before this that you would have no decline?﴾

﴿Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve.﴾ (49) This is also part of the speech of the people of the Heights (*A'rāf*). That is, they turned to those mentioned from among the people of Paradise and said to them: remain in Paradise, neither fearful nor grieving, in the most complete joy and the most perfect honour.

It was also said: this is a command to the act of entering at all, on the basis that their being on the Heights and their saying this occurred before some of the people of Paradise entered Paradise.

Many have said: the words of Allah, glorified is He, "Are these the ones...?" etc., form a new sentence (*isti'nāf*) and are not part of the speech of the people of the Heights. The ones pointed to are the people of Paradise, the speaker is Allah, the Exalted, or some of the angels, and the one addressed is the people of the Fire, according to one view. It was also said: the ones pointed to are the people of the Heights, who are also the speakers, and the ones addressed are the people of the Fire. "Enter Paradise" is also part of the speech of the people of the Heights, meaning that they return and address one another, saying: enter Paradise. Its remoteness is not hidden.

It was also said: when the people of the Heights reproached the people of the Fire, the people of the Fire swore that the people of the Heights would not enter Paradise. Then Allah, the Exalted, or some of the angels, said, addressing the people of the Fire: "Are these the ones about whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy?", pointing to the people of the Heights. Then the address was directed to them, and it was said: "Enter Paradise..." etc.

It was also read (*quri'a*, a canonical recitation) as *udkhulū* and *dakhalū*, in the derived form passive and the unaugmented form active. In both cases it is necessary that "no fear shall be upon you..." etc. be a statement (*maqūl*) introduced by an omitted verb of saying, which occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), so that the address is coherent and the speech is connected. That is, "enter" or "they entered Paradise" is said to them: "no fear...", etc.

It was also read *adkhilū* (in the derived imperative form), addressed to the angels. The apparent sense is that this reading requires an additional supplied element.

﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾, after both groups have settled into their abodes and the place has come to rest with them: ﴿Pour out upon us﴾, that is, pour down on us, ﴿some water﴾, ﴿or some of what Allah has provided for you﴾. That is, or from what Allah the Exalted has provided for you of the other drinks, so that it fits with pouring; or from the foods, as was related from al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. For the conjoined element (ma'tuf) a fitting governing verb may be supplied; or the first governing verb may be interpreted (ta'wil) in a way that suits both conjoined elements; or the meaning of the verb that governs the second element may be included (tadmin) in the first; or this may be taken as a figure of speech based on assimilation (mushakalah). The verse indicates the extreme of their thirst and the severity of their hunger, and that the torment they are in does not prevent them from seeking food and drink. On this basis, it is reported that Musa al-Kazim, may Allah be pleased with him, refuted Harun al-Rashid's denial that the people of the gathering eat, arguing that what they are in is the strongest barrier preventing them from that.

The scholars differed over whether this request was made while hoping for it to be granted or in despair of it, since they knew that what they were in would last forever. Some held each view.

﴿They will say﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon the question, as if it were said, "Then what did they say?" So it is said: they replied, ﴿Indeed, Allah has forbidden both of them to the disbelievers﴾ (50). That is, He has prevented each of them, or He has prevented both of them in the manner of prohibiting something forbidden to a responsible person. So there is no way to that, decisively. And the forbidding cannot be understood in its common meaning, because the abode is not an abode of obligation (taklif).

[p. 127]

**﴿Those who took their religion﴾** means the religion that God, exalted is He, commanded them to follow, or the religion they were obliged to adopt. **﴿as diversion and play﴾**: they did not practice it, or they forbade what they wished and permitted what they wished. *Lahw* (diversion), as has been said, is diverting one's concern to what it is not proper to direct it toward. *La'ib* (play) is seeking joy in what is not proper to seek. Their detailed discussion has already been given, so recall it. **﴿and the life of this world deceived them﴾** means it occupied them with its immediate adornments and its false promises. This is its nature with its people: *qatalaha Allahu ta'ala* (God fight it), it deceives, harms, and passes away.

**﴿So today We will forget them﴾** means We will treat them as one who forgets treats the forgotten: disregarding them and leaving them in the Fire entirely. The statement is therefore given in the form of a figurative illustration (*tamthil*). *Nisyan* (forgetting) has frequently come to mean *tark* (abandonment), and it may be interpreted that way here, making it a metaphor (*isti'ara*) or a *majaz mursal* (metonymy). It is related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning is "We will delay them in the Fire." On this reading, the more apparent sense of *nansahum* is that it derives from *nas'* (postponement) and not from *nisyan* (forgetting). The *fa'* in His words ﴿fa-al-yawma﴾ is *fasiha* (an expressive particle, introducing an implied condition).

His words, exalted and majestic is He, **﴿as they forgot the meeting of this day of theirs﴾**: it has been said that it is in the accusative position as an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "We will forget them with a forgetting like their forgetting the meeting of this great day, which should not be forgotten." The statement is also not literal, because they were not remembering that day so as to forget it. Rather, the non-occurrence of that day to their minds and their failure to prepare for it is likened to the state of one who knew something and then forgot it.

From Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan: the meaning is "as they forgot working for the meeting of this day of theirs." This interpretation is not necessary, as is not hidden. Others have held that the *kaf* here is *kaf al-ta'lil* (causal), connected to what precedes it, not *kaf al-tashbih* (comparative), since the comparative reading is blocked by His words, **﴿and they used to deny Our signs﴾** (51), because it is coordinated (*'atf*) with *ma nasu* (what they forgot), which requires that the thing being compared to (*mushabbah bihi*) be forgetting like it.

The likening of forgetting to denying is not evident, and whoever claims it says: the intended meaning is "We will leave them in the Fire in a continuous abandonment, just as they were continuously denying that the signs were from God, exalted is He, in a continuous denial." Al-Qutb said: *al-juhud* (denial) has the meaning of forgetting. The apparent sense of the speech of many exegetes is that the words from ﴿and the life of this world deceived them﴾ are the speech of the people of Paradise, and not that God forbade these two things to the disbelievers alone. Others have said that it is only the latter. On this view, ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who) may be a *mubtada'* (subject), and the clause ﴿today We will forget them﴾ its *khabar* (predicate), and the *fa'* in it is like it in your saying: "Whoever comes to me, then for him is a dirham," as has been said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 52:

﴿And indeed We brought them a Book which We have detailed⦆ We have explained its meanings, concerning the creeds, the rulings, and the admonitions, in detail. The pronoun (the "them") refers to the disbelievers in general, and it was said: it refers to them and to the believers. The intended meaning of "Book" is the genus, and it was said: it refers to the contemporaries among the disbelievers, or among them and the believers. The Book is the Qur'an, and its tanwin (indefiniteness) is for glorification. Some scholars have versified the types of content it includes in the words:

Permitted, forbidden, clear (muhkam), ambiguous (mutashabih), bearer of glad tidings, warner, narrative, admonition, parable.

The intended meaning is the negation of emptiness, as is not hidden. ﴿With knowledge﴾ from Us regarding the manner of its detailing. It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (fassalnahu, "We have detailed it"). Its indefiniteness is for magnification, i.e., knowing in the most perfect manner about it, so that it came wise and firmly established. In this, as has been said, is evidence that He, glory be to Him, knows by an attribute additional to the essence, which is the attribute of knowledge, and that His knowledge is not the very essence of His Being, as the philosophers and those who resemble them claim; and there is room for debate on this. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the object, i.e., containing much knowledge. Ibn Muhaysin read (fadalnahu) with the dotted dad (ḍād), and the apparent sense of some scholars' words is that the prepositional phrase in this reading is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the subject, and is not made a circumstantial clause from the object: i.e., We preferred it over the rest of the Books, knowing that it is worthy of that. Some scholars permitted making it a circumstantial clause from the object, in the manner already mentioned. It has also been said that (ʿalā) here denotes causation, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and that you may magnify God for having guided you﴾, and it is connected to (fadalnahu), i.e., We preferred it over the rest of the Books for the sake of knowledge within it, i.e., because it includes a knowledge that the others among them did not include. It has also been said that (ʿalā) in both readings is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿We brought them﴾, i.e., We brought them with that while they were among those possessing knowledge
صفحة 128
capable of understanding what We brought them with; so reflect.

﴿A guidance and a mercy﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the object of (fassalnahu). It is permitted that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and that it be a circumstantial clause from the Book, since it is specified by the description. The discussion of such a construction serving as a circumstantial clause is well known. It has also been read in the genitive by way of apposition to (ʿilm), and in the nominative by supposing an omitted subject, i.e., it is a great guidance and a mercy likewise. ﴿For a people who believe﴾ (52), because they are the ones who draw light from its lights and benefit from its radiance.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 53 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Do they await anything but its ta'wil (its ultimate outcome)?﴾ That is, what do these disbelievers await, since they do not believe in it, other than its ta'wil, meaning its final outcome and what its matter comes to, namely the manifestation of its truth through the appearance of what it reported of promise and threat? The meaning is that they are like those who await, and they are in the same position, in that what was mentioned will certainly come to them. In that case, it cannot be asked: how can they await it when they deny it and do not expect it?

It has also been said: among them are groups who doubt and expect it. So the statement is of the type of "the sons of so-and-so killed Zayd" (where the killing is attributed to the group, though only some did it). ﴿On the day its ta'wil comes﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection, and it has been said it is the Day of Badr. ﴿Those who had forgotten it will say﴾ means: those who abandoned it as one abandons what is forgotten, turning away from it and not acting by it, ﴿before﴾, that is, before the coming of its ta'wil, ﴿"The messengers of our Lord came with the truth."﴾ That is, it became clear that they had indeed come with the truth. It was interpreted in this way because that is what occurs there, and because it is what requires the request for intercession understood from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"Have we any intercessors that they may intercede for us?"﴾ today, and that they might ward off from us what we are in. ﴿Or are we returned?﴾ This is coordinated with the sentence before it, and it falls under the same interrogative force, with (min) being superfluous in the subject position.

It has been permitted that (min) be superfluous in the agent position with the adverbial phrase, as if it were said: "Have we any intercessors, or are we returned to the world?" Its nominative status comes from its occurring in a position where a noun could stand, as you say: "A beginning: is Zayd beaten?" and no other verb is required for it to be coordinated with, so one does not supply "Will any intercessor intercede for us, or are we returned?" This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and he meant, as in al-Kashf, the wording, because the adverbial phrase is implicitly a clause. (Hal) is among the particles specific to the verb, and the shift (to the noun) indicates that the wish for an intercessor is primary and the wish for return is secondary, because leaving the verb for the noun while (hal) calls for a verb conveys that. So if it were supplied, the subtle point of the shift would be lost in meaning, despite being dispensed with in wording.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿or are we returned﴾ in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿that they may intercede for us﴾ which is in the accusative after the interrogative, or because (aw) means "until" (ila an) or "until that" (hatta an), according to what al-Zamakhshari chose, to make the causal sense explicit. Al-Qadi said: "With the nominative, what is asked is one of two matters: the intercession or the return to the world. With the accusative, what is asked is that they have intercessors, either for one of two matters, intercession for their pardon and return, if (aw) is coordinating, or for a single matter, if it means 'until', since its meaning then is: they intercede until there is a return; likewise if it means 'until that', that is, they intercede until the return occurs."

﴿Then we would do﴾ in the accusative is the answer to the second interrogative, or it is coordinated with (nuradda) and is its consequence, according to the reading of Ibn Abi Ishaq.

Al-Hasan read (nuradda) in the accusative and (na'malu) in the nominative, meaning: "then we do." ﴿Other than what we used to do﴾, that is, in the world, of shirk and disobedience. ﴿They have lost their souls﴾ by directing their lifespans, which are their capital, toward shirk and sins. ﴿And what they used to invent has strayed from them﴾ (53), that is, that which they used to invent of idols as partners to God, glorified is He, and as their intercessors on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that its falsehood became evident and it benefited them nothing.

(From the door of allusion in the verses) ﴿And O Adam, dwell, you and your spouse﴾: that is, the soul (nafs). It was named Hawwa' (Eve) because of its constant companionship with the dark body, since al-hawwa is the color that is dominated by blackness. Some of them make Adam an allusion to the heart, because it is from al-udma, which is the brownness, and it was named thus because of its attachment to the body rather than the soul. The address was directed to him because of Adam's honour, peace be upon him, and his spouse is a follower of him in dwelling. The Garden, according to them, is an allusion to the heaven of the world of spirits, which is the garden of holiness (rawdat al-qudus). ﴿Then eat from wherever you wish﴾: it is a restriction upon you both in receiving the meanings, the knowledge and the wisdoms, which are the spiritual nourishments and the spiritual fruits. ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, that is, the tree of nature and desire that is in your presence. ﴿Lest you be among the wrongdoers﴾, those who place light in the place of darkness, or who diminish the light of your readiness. Some interpreted the tree as the tree of love, bearing leaves of various kinds of trial, meaning: do not approach it lest you wrong yourselves, because in it is the burning of the lover's selfhood and the annihilation of his identity in the identity of the Beloved. Then he said: this tree was planted by the Merciful with His own hand for Adam, peace be upon him, just as He kneaded his clay with His hand for it:

"It was not fit except for him, and he was not fit except for it."

And the prohibition was an incitement to partake of it, for a person is eager for what is forbidden. Al-Nayshaburi chose this, and he strained in the rest of the verse in the way he strained, so if you wish it, return to him.

﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them what was hidden from them of their private parts﴾, that is, so that there would appear to them, through their inclination toward the tree of nature, what had been veiled from them at the time of their stripping from the base matters, which are nakednesses in the sight of the intellect. ﴿And he said: "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortals."﴾ He caused them to imagine that in being characterized by corporeal nature there are angelic pleasures and immortality in it, or kingship and dominion over the faculties without cessation, if (malikayn) is read with a kasra on the lam.

﴿So he brought them down﴾, that is, he lowered them from the chambers of holiness to attachment to it and inclination toward it. ﴿By deception﴾, by what deceived them from the cup of oaths, filled with the wine of the remembrance of the Beloved. ﴿And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾, and the little of it was, relative to them, much. ﴿And they began to fasten over themselves from the leaves of the Garden﴾, that is, they began to conceal those nakednesses and the natural indecencies with good manners and beautiful customs, which are among the ramifications of intellectual opinions and the deductions of the scientific intellectual faculty, and they conceal them with practical stratagems.

﴿And their Lord called to them: "Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a manifest enemy?"﴾ By what I placed in your intellects of the inclination toward detachment and the apprehension of intelligibles. And that saying is by what the intellect was inspired with, of the contradiction to the judgments of the illusory faculty and its opposition to its perceptions, and the awareness of its violations and its obstinacies against it. ﴿They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves"﴾ by inclining toward the side of nature and the extinguishing of its light and the breaking of its power. ﴿And if You do not forgive us﴾ by clothing us with spiritual lights and pouring them upon us, ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾ by pouring upon us true knowledge, ﴿we will surely be among the losers﴾, those who have destroyed the readiness which is the material of felicity, and who have been deprived of detached perfection by the constant companionship of natural deficiency.

﴿He said: "Go down"﴾ to the lower direction, which is the corporeal world, ﴿some of you to others an enemy﴾, because the aims of the lower direction are partial and do not admit partnership, so whenever one of them obtains something, another is deprived of it, and hostility and hatred arise between them, unlike universal aims.

He used the plural form of address because it carries the force of an address to the whole species. ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you a garment﴾, which is the garment of the Sharia. ﴿It conceals your private parts﴾, it covers the ugly qualities of your attributes and the indecencies of your actions with its emblem and its covering. ﴿And as adornment﴾, beauty and grace in the outward and the inward, by which you are distinguished from the rest of the animals. ﴿But the garment of piety﴾, that is, the quality of scrupulousness and caution, is among the qualities of the soul. ﴿That is better﴾ than the rest of the pillars of the laws; abstention is the head of the cure. It is also said: the garment of piety is the garment of the heart, the spirit, the secret, and the hidden. The garment of the first

of these is sincerity in seeking the Master, by which the shame of greed and what it contains is concealed. The garment of the second is love of the Lord of the highest glory, by which the shame of attachment to other than Him is concealed. ﴿That﴾, that is, the garment of piety, ﴿is among the signs of God﴾, that is, among the lights of His attributes, glorified is He, since guarding oneself is a quality of the soul which cannot be achieved except by the manifestation of the theophanies of the attributes of the Truth; or by the sending down of the Sharia and the Reality, which indicate God, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿Perhaps you will remember﴾ upon the manifestation of those lights, your original luminous garment; or you will remember your knowledge of Him when the covenant was taken, so that you may cling to its skirts today.

﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you﴾ by stripping you of the garment of the Sharia and piety, so that you are deprived of entering the Garden, ﴿as he removed your parents from the Garden, stripping them of their garment﴾, the natural luminous garment, ﴿Indeed he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them﴾, and that is by the requirement of humanness; though they may be seen through the medium of the divine light.

﴿Say: "My Lord has commanded justice"﴾, that is, equity, and it is the straight path. ﴿And set your faces [toward Him]﴾, that is, your selves, by restraining them from inclining toward either extreme of excess or deficiency. ﴿At every place of prostration﴾, that is, a place of prostration or its time. Prostration, according to them, as some of them said, is of four kinds: the prostration of submission and obedience, which is setting the face toward Him with sincerity, leaving aside the turning to other than Him, observing conformity to the command, sincerity of intention, and abstaining from opposition in all matters; the prostration of annihilation in actions, which is setting the face toward Him by not seeing any agent other than God, the Exalted, at all; the prostration of annihilation in attributes, which is setting the face toward Him by not disliking anything, without inclining to excess by abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil, nor to deficiency by scolding and reproaching the opponent, belittling him; and the prostration of annihilation in the Essence, which is setting the face toward Him by being absent from the remainder, being completely effaced, and refraining from affirming selfhood and duality.
