It may also be said: the needle is an indication of the needle of the Sharia and the Path, and its mark is what obliges one to act in accordance with it. The passage of that camel is not possible with arrogance; rather, submission, obedience, and abandoning the carnal appetites are necessary. At that point the camel becomes smaller than a gnat, indeed finer than a hair, and then it passes through that eye.

﴿For them from Gehenna﴾: deprivation. ﴿is a bed﴾ and ﴿above them are coverings﴾: that is, deprivation has encompassed them. It was said: for them from Gehenna is the struggle (mujahada) and discipline (riyada) as a bed, and above them, from the oppositions of the self and the severing of desire, a blanket; so it melts them and burns their egoism.

﴿The companions of Paradise will call out﴾: the beloved ones (al-marhumun) ﴿to the companions of the Fire﴾: the deprived (al-muharramun) ﴿that we have found what our Lord promised us﴾: of nearness ﴿to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised﴾: of distance ﴿to be true?﴾ ﴿Then a caller will call out among them﴾: the caller of might and majesty ﴿that the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾: those who place a thing in other than its place, ﴿who bar﴾: the travellers ﴿from the way of God﴾: that is, the path that leads to Him, the Glorified. It was said: they bar the heart and the spirit from that.

﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾: by describing it with what repels the traveller from it, of deviation and inclination away from the Truth. It was said: they seek to turn their faces toward the world and what is in it. ﴿And they, of the Hereafter﴾: that is, of annihilation in God, the Exalted, or of the Great Resurrection; ﴿are disbelievers﴾: because of the great increase of their veiling by what they are in.

﴿And between them﴾: that is, between the people of Paradise, which is the Paradise of the reward of deeds, of the worshippers and ascetics, and the people of the Fire; ﴿is a veil﴾: so each of them is veiled from his companion. ﴿And upon the heights (al-a'raf)﴾: that is, the heights of that veil, which is the veil of the heart; ﴿are men﴾: and what men! They are the gnostics (al-'urafa'), the people of God, the Glorified, and His elect. It was said: they were called men because they exercise authority, by God's permission, over what is other than Him, the Mighty and Majestic, in the manner of men's authority over women, and no such authority is exercised over them. ﴿They recognize each by his mark﴾: because of the light of physiognomic insight (firasa) that they have been given. ﴿And they call out to the companions of Paradise﴾: that is, the Paradise of the reward of deeds: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾: by what God the Exalted has bestowed upon you of deliverance from the Fire. It was said: their peace upon the people of Paradise is by supplying them with the means of purification (tazkiya), emptying (takhliya), heart-lights, and the outpouring of goodness and blessings upon them.

﴿They have not entered it﴾: that is, those men have not entered Paradise, because they have no need of it. ﴿though they hope﴾: at every moment, for what is higher and more precious. It was said: the people of Paradise hope to enter [the company of] those men, so that they may kindle from their light, be illumined by the rays of their faces, and find companionship in their presence.

﴿And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire﴾: so that they may take warning, ﴿they say: "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing folk"﴾: by keeping our hearts from deviation.

﴿And the companions of the heights call out to men﴾: from the leaders of the people of the Fire. The application of the word "men" to them and to the companions of the heights is like the application of "al-Masih" to the accursed Dajjal and to Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿"Are these they?"﴾: an indication to the people of Paradise.

﴿And the companions of the Fire call out to the companions of Paradise: "Pour upon us some water"﴾: that is, of the life in which you are; ﴿or some of what God has provided you﴾: that is, of the bounty which God has bestowed upon you. Or: "Pour upon us some knowledge or action, so that we may attain what you have attained."

﴿They say: "God has forbidden them﴾: from eternity ﴿to the disbelievers"﴾: because of the evil of their predisposition. It was said: when the disbelievers were slaves to their bellies, eager for food and drink, they died as they had lived, and were gathered and admitted to the Fire as they had died; so they asked for water or food.

﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book﴾: which is the Prophet ﷺ, comprehensive of everything and the greatest manifestation of Us. ﴿We have detailed it﴾: that is, We have made manifest of it what We made manifest; ﴿with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾: because they are the ones who benefit from it, though in another respect it is a mercy to all the worlds.

﴿Do they await anything but its interpretation (ta'wil)﴾: that is, what its matter will ultimately come to in its outcome. It was said: the Book which was detailed "with knowledge" is an indication of the human body, detailed into organs, limbs, instruments, and senses, fit for perfection in accordance with what divine knowledge requires. Its interpretation is what its matter comes to in the end, by transformation, except what is not fit for that; at the resurrection, [it becomes] forms, figures, and shapes that correspond to their attributes and beliefs, in accordance with the words of the Glorified: ﴿He will recompense them for their description﴾. As the Glorified said: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb, and deaf﴾. End of quotation.

It is also possible that the Book mentioned refers to the horizons and the selves, and to what every outward thing comes to. And God, the Exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.

[Page 133]

**﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾** This begins an account of the origin of creation (*fitrah*), following the account of the return of the disbelievers. It is also possible that when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the disbelievers and their worship of other than Him, He argued against them through His power and His creation, exalted is His majesty, and thereby indicated that there is no deity besides Him. So He said, addressing them with a general address: **﴿Indeed your Lord﴾**, that is, your Creator and Owner, **﴿who created the heavens﴾**, the seven, **﴿and the earth﴾** along with what is in them, as indicated by what is in Surah al-Sajdah, which, God willing, will be verified as it comes, **﴿in six periods﴾**, as in His saying, exalted is He: **﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾** (8:16). Or it means **﴿in the measure of six days﴾**, as in His saying, glory be to Him: **﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾** (19:62).

For the common usage is that the day is from sunrise to sunset, and the sun did not exist at that time, nor did the Throne (*al-ʿArsh*), which is the outermost sphere according to the well-known view, exist at that time, as some verses indicate. And it is not eternal, as is claimed by one who has strayed from the straight path. But that does not help in establishing the conventional day. Therefore a group of scholars went to interpreting "day" according to its common usage and supplying an omitted noun (*taqdir al-muḍaf*), and they asserted this. It is the view of ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Kaʿb al-Ahbar, al-Dahhak and Mujahid, and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari preferred it: that the beginning of creation was on Sunday (*al-Ahad*), and nothing was created on Saturday (*al-Sabt*). It is taken from *al-sabt* in the sense of "cutting," because creation ceased on it, and the completion of creation occurred on Friday (*al-Jumʿah*), and it is named so because creation was gathered (*ijtimaʿ*) on it. Ibn Abi Hatim and others transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he named those days: Abu Jad, Hawaz, Huttiy, Kalamun, Saʿfas, and Qiriyashat.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others said: The beginning of creation was on Saturday, and it was named *sabt* because some of the creation of the earth was cut off on it, according to what Ibn al-Anbari said, or because the matter was, as it were, cut off and begun on it, according to what has been said. This view is supported by what Muslim transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of my hand and said: 'Allah, exalted is He, created the clay on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the trees on Monday, created the disliked things on Tuesday, created the light on Wednesday, created the animals in it on Thursday, and created Adam after the afternoon prayer on Friday, at the last of creation, in the last hour of the hours of Friday, between the afternoon prayer and the night.'"

It is not hidden that this report contradicts the noble verse. So it is either not authentic, even though Muslim transmitted it, or it requires interpretation. I myself hold that the first day on which creation occurred is called Sunday, the second day Monday, and so on, and the day on which creation was gathered is called Friday. Understand this. Others went to interpreting it in its linguistic sense without supplying an omitted noun, and they said: The measure of each day was a thousand years. This is narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam. In it, His creating things gradually, as is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, is an instruction for creatures in deliberation and patience in affairs, as in the hadith: "Patience is from Allah, exalted is He, and haste is from Satan." Many others said: In creating them gradually, along with His power, glory be to Him, to originate them all at once, there is evidence of choice (*ikhtiyar*) and a lesson for those who reflect (*nuzzar*). This was objected to on the ground that the agent might be a necessitating cause (*mujib*), and the existence of the effect might be conditioned on conditions that come into being one after another. Also, that would depend on establishing that the creation of the angels preceded the creation of the heavens and the earth, and that is not established.

It was answered that the first objection is based on neglecting His words "with the power to originate them all at once." Its explanation is that if the agent is one who chooses, as the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*) say, the existence of the effect depends on the attachment of will to it. So the will is then part of the complete cause, and therefore the effect may be delayed from the agent because the attachment of will is absent. Thus it does not follow from its eternity that the effect is eternal. But if the agent is a necessitating cause, bringing about existence by its essence once its receptivity (*istiʿdad*) is complete, then if the effect is complete in its receptivity in its own essence, like sulfur in relation to fire, its existence is necessary and its delay is impossible, otherwise delay from the complete cause would follow. Then from the eternity of the agent its eternity follows. The celestial bodies are of this kind according to the philosophers (*falasifah*). If the completion of its receptivity depends on a newly occurring matter, then as long as that has not occurred, its origination is impossible, like wet wood, for as long as it has not dried, fire does not burn it. Daily occurrences are of this kind according to them. For this reason they posited an intermediate realm (*barzakh*) between the realm of eternity and the realm of origination, so that the linking of occurrences to eternal principles might be possible.

So in the case where the agent is a necessitating cause whose effect's existence is conditioned on successive conditions, the origination all at once is impossible. The possibility of the existence of these things, which indicates that they depend on nothing else at all, all at once, together with gradual creation, which requires the delay of the effect's existence from the existence of the agent, does not combine with necessity, which requires the impossibility of delay at that point. Choice, which justifies that delay, is required, as you have learned. And it was answered that gradual origination of things is an expression of acts of origination each of which is attached to a thing, and this indicates the attachment of knowledge, will and power to each of them in detail. This is unlike the single origination of them all, which is one act attached to the whole, and this indicates the attachment of the aforementioned to the whole insofar as it is a whole, in summary. This is clarified by the difference between stamping a seal on paper and writing those words. For in the second case you imagine them word by word, even letter by letter, and you intend them that way, and you set them down on the page. This is unlike the first case, and it is evident. So the theologians (*nuzzar*) derive from gradual creation and understand the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, glory be to Him, and His will and power over things in detail, saying: "Glory be to Him from whose knowledge not an atom's weight escapes, in the earth or in the heaven."

Also they said: "We did something that we first conceived, then we believed it had a benefit, then a desiring state arose in us, then a psychic inclination, which is the will, then the motivating power was stirred toward the motive power that moves the limbs toward producing it, so that thing comes to be. Thus each of these matters has a role in the existence of that thing." Then they said: "Just as in the acts of choice in us these matters must be present, so too must acts of choice proceed from the Necessary Being (*al-Wajib*) of a similar kind, which is not impossible for Him, glory be to Him." So they affirmed for Him, exalted is He, knowledge, will, power, and a purpose for His acts. And they argued for that from His being one who chooses. So since gradual creation indicates choice, which indicates what has been mentioned, it is true that in it there is a lesson for the theologians.

The summary of this is that the "theologians" are people of reflection and insight among the rational. The aforementioned does not depend on the creation of the angels having preceded [the heavens and earth], and whoever says that the creation of the Throne and the Footstool preceded the creation of the earth and heavens is also saying that the creation of the angels preceded. Indeed, it has been said that some people held that a kind of angels was created before the Throne and the Footstool, and they called them "the Overwhelmed" (*al-Muhayminun*).

You know that this does not help us, because the Overwhelmed, according to this speaker, are not aware of any heaven or earth, but are wholly absorbed in Him, glory be to Him. Moreover, that is not established, as the objector also says. It has also been said: When a thing comes into being all at once, it may occur to the mind that that thing happened by chance. But if it comes into being gradually, by way of benefit and wisdom, that is more eloquent in power and stronger in indication. It has also been said: Haste in creation is more eloquent in power, and deliberation is more eloquent in wisdom. So God, exalted is He, willed to manifest His wisdom in creating things through deliberation, just as He manifested His power in creating things by "Be!"

**﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾**. It is, according to the well-known view, the body that encompasses all other bodies, and it is the sphere of spheres. It was named *ʿarsh* either because of its height, or by analogy with the throne of a kingdom, for it is called *ʿarsh*. From this is His saying, exalted is He: **﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾** (12:100), because affairs and governances descend from it. It is used as a metonym for honor, authority and dominion, so one says: "So-and-so's throne has been severed," meaning his honor and dominion have gone. And they recited his saying:

*When the sons of Marwan's thrones are severed,*
*and they perish as Iyad and Himyar perished.*

And his saying:

*If they kill you, their thrones are already severed,*
*by ʿUyaynah ibn al-Harith ibn Shihab.*

Al-Raghib mentioned that the Throne is among the things that human beings know only by name, and that it is not what the notions of the common folk imagine, for if it were so, it would be carrying Him, exalted is He above that. And it is not as some people said, that it is the highest sphere, and the Footstool is the sphere of the stars. There is room for debate about this.

People differ in discussing this verse and similar ones. Some explained the Throne by its well-known meaning and explained *istiwaʾ* (establishment) as *istiqrar* (settling). This is narrated from al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Al-Bayhaqi transmitted it in his book *al-Asmaʾ wa al-Sifat* with many narrations from a group of the *Salaf* (early generations), and he weakened all of them. As for what is narrated from Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was asked, "How did He establish Himself?" and he lowered his head for a long time until sweat (*ruhaʾ*, the perspiration of heat) overcame him. Then he raised his head and said: "The establishment is not unknown, the modality is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation (*bidʿah*)." Then he said to the questioner: "I do not think you are anything but misguided," and then he ordered that he be taken out. This is not explicit in this doctrine, since it is possible that his words "not unknown" mean that it is established and its establishment is known, not that its meaning, which is settling, is not unknown. And from his words "the modality is not conceivable" [it may mean] that everything that is an attribute of Allah, exalted is He, the intellect would perceive a modality for Him, and He is exalted above that. So the withholding of modality from Him is an obligation.

This is supported by what came in another narration from ʿAbd Allah ibn Wahb, that Malik was asked about the establishment, so he lowered his head, and sweat overcame him, then he said: **﴿The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne﴾** (20:5), as He described Himself. And it is not said to Him, "How?" and "how" is removed from Him. Up to the end of what he said. Then, if this is together with the negation of the implications (*lawazim*), the matter is easy. But if it is together with affirming them, and we seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, then it is misguidance, and what misguidance, and ignorance, and what ignorance regarding the King, the Exalted.

I do not know what one of the knowers said, one of those who were immersed in the currents of gnosis, speaking in the tongue of the state of the Throne, addressing the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the Ascension, when his sun rose upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, in the highest assembly, so that every light and lamp paled before it, as al-Imam al-Qastallani transmitted, alluding to the misguidance of people like the adherents of the second view. His wording, with omission, is: "When he ﷺ reached the Throne, it clung to his skirts and called out to him with the tongue of its state: 'O Muhammad, you are in the purity of your time, safe from His anger.'" Until he said: "O Muhammad, you are the one sent as a mercy to the worlds, and I must have a share of this mercy. My share, O my beloved, is that you bear witness to the innocence of what the people of falsehood have attributed to me and what the people of delusion have fabricated against me. They claim that I am wider than the One who has no likeness, and that I encompass the One who has no modality. O Muhammad, He whose essence has no limit and whose attributes have no count, how could He be in need of me and carried by me, when the Merciful is His name, the establishment is His attribute, and His attribute is joined to His essence? How could it join with me or separate from me? O Muhammad, by His might, I am not near to Him in union, nor far from Him in separation, nor able to bear Him. He created me from Him out of mercy and grace, and if He had annihilated me, that would have been a truth and a justice from Him. O Muhammad, I am carried by His power and made by His wisdom. Alas!"

The Mu'tazilah (*al-Muʿtazilah*, the "Separatists" who held rationalist doctrines) and a group of the theologians (*mutakallimun*) went to the view that the Throne is in its literal meaning, and that "established" means "took dominion" (*istawla*). They argued for this by His saying:

قَدِ اسْتَوى بِشْرٌ عَلى العِراقِ
مِن غَيْرِ سَيْفٍ ودَمٍ مِهْراقِ

Bishr has risen over Iraq
without sword or spilled blood.

Only the Throne was singled out for the report that God "istawa" over it, meaning that He took possession of it (istila', "seizure of dominion"), because it is the greatest of the created things. This view has been refuted on the grounds that the Arabs do not know "istawa" to mean "istawla" (to take possession). Rather, one says "istawla fulan 'ala kadha" (so-and-so took possession of such-and-such) only when it was not already in his ownership. God Most High has always been the owner of all things and in possession of them. This view is attributed to the Ash'ariyya (the followers of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari). Ibn al-Qayyim went to great lengths in refuting them, and then said: "The lam of al-Ash'ariyya is like the nun of al-Yahudiyya (the 'Jewish' suffix), and in my view it is not part of the upright religion." Al-Farra' and al-Qadi chose the view that the meaning is "then He intended the creation of the Throne." This is made unlikely by the fact that "istawa" is transitive through "'ala" (on). There is also an opinion that the creation of the Throne came after the creation of the heavens and the earth, and this, as you see, is weak. Al-Qaffal held that what is meant is the penetration of power, the flow of will, and the soundness of dominion, but he expressed this in the manner that people are accustomed to from their kings and that has become fixed in their hearts. It is said that evidence for the correctness of this is the saying of God, Glorified is He, in Surat Yunus: ﴿Then He istawa over the Throne, directing the affair﴾. The phrase ﴿directing the affair﴾ serves as an explanation of ﴿istawa over the Throne﴾. The discussion of this will come, God willing. It is mentioned that al-Qaffal explains the Throne as dominion, and says what he says. It has been objected that God has always been of upright dominion and "istawa" over it before the creation of the heavens and the earth, and this implies that He, Glorified is He, was not so before. Exalted is God far above that, greatly exalted. It was answered that God was the owner of the heavens and the earth before their creation, but it is not correct to say "Zayd became satisfied" except after he has eaten food. So when the Throne is explained as dominion, it is correct to say that His dominion became established (istawa) only after the creation of the heavens and the earth. Some hold that the attribution is metaphorical and supply an agent in the sentence, meaning "His command became established." The omission of the agent does no harm when what is attributed to it takes its place. On this view, istawa is not an attribute of Him, Exalted is He, but this is not correct. As for whoever explains it as "istila'," he returns it to the attribute of power.

Al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari that God, Exalted is He, performed an act upon the Throne which He called "istawa," just as He performed acts upon other things which He called provision, blessing, and others of His acts, Glorified is He. This is because "thumma" (then) denotes sequence, and that occurs only in acts. Al-Ustadh [Page 136] Abu Bakr ibn Furak transmitted from some of them that "istawa" means "'ala" (to be high, to rise above), not in the sense of elevation by distance, spatial location, or being situated in a place, but in the sense of a meaning which may be rightly attributed to Him, Glorified is He. On this view it is one of the attributes of the Essence. The word "thumma" is connected to the one upon whom He is established, not to the istawa itself, or it denotes a difference in rank. This is a sound opinion.

You know that the well-known position of the early generations (salaf) regarding such matters is to delegate (tafwid) the intended meaning to God, Exalted is He. They say: "He istawa over the Throne in the manner that He intended, transcending settling and occupying." They consider the explanation of istawa as istila' to be a rejected interpretation, since whoever holds it cannot say "like our seizure." Rather, he must say: "It is a seizure befitting Him, Mighty and Majestic," so he should say from the outset: "It is an istawa befitting Him, Exalted is He." The Sufi masters, may God sanctify their secrets, have chosen this, and it is the most knowledgeable, the safest, and the most judicious, though some disagree. Perhaps we will return to this topic, God willing.

﴿He covers the night over the day﴾, that is, Glorified is He covers the day with the night. Since the one covering is found together with the one covered in existence, and that cannot be imagined here, they said: the meaning is that He clothes it in its place, so the atmosphere becomes dark after it had been bright. The metaphor is then in the attribution, attributing to the thing what belongs to its place, and its place is the atmosphere, in the sense that it is a place for the light which is its necessary accompaniment, not that it is a place for the day itself, since time has no place. It was also allowed that there is a metaphor here, by making the covering and darkening of the place of the day equivalent to the covering of the day itself, so that it is as if it wraps around it with the wrapping of a covering. Or it resembles making it disappear by its descent upon it, like covering with a garment, by way of close association. It was also allowed that the meaning is: Glorified is He covers the night with the day.

The first aspect is preferred for two reasons: the covering (taghshiya) means concealment, and this is more suitable for the night than the day. And because according to the second, the night would have to be the second object and the day the first object. Abu Hayyan mentioned that when a verb transitively reaches two objects and one of them is the agent in meaning, it must be the first of them according to them, just as this is required in malaktu Zaydan 'Amran (I possessed Zayd, 'Amr). The order of precedence is what clarifies it, because it is the agent in meaning, just as this is required in darab Musa 'Isa (Musa struck 'Isa). By contrast, in a' tu Zaydan dirhaman (I gave Zayd a dirham), the determination of the first object depends on the order.

The second was preferred on the ground that Hamid ibn Qays read ﴿yaghshi al-layla al-nahara﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and the accusative on al-layla and nominative on al-nahar, and according to this reading the day would be the seeker, and the night is attached to it. And the agreement of the two readings is preferable to their divergence.

And because the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip off from it the day﴾, from which it is known, according to al-Marzuqi, that the night precedes the day, since the thing stripped off from precedes the thing stripped; so the day is more suited to being the one that overtakes. And because the saying of God, Glorified is He: ﴿seeking it urgently﴾, meaning carried swiftly, so fa'il in the sense of maf'ul is more suited to this aspect, for this seeking is more evident from the day. They have said: the light of the day is the one that falls upon the darkness of the night. And some have recited:

As if we, and the light of dawn hastens the darkness,
we are scattering a crow with black wing-feathers.

And one of the later scholars has some lines:

And as if the East were a gate for the darkness, which has nothing
but the fear of the assault of dawn, so it was opened.

As for the claim that covering is more suited to the night, it is said to be accepted only if covering were taken in its literal sense. But that is not what is meant. Rather, what is meant is reaching and overtaking, and this is more suited to the day, as you have understood. The stated rule is not free of discussion. Moreover, according to what we establish, it is not far-fetched that the statement is of the type of a' tu Zaydan dirhaman. As for the view that the meaning of the verse is that He makes the night [Page 137] ashgha (whitened) with the day, that is, whitened by the light of dawn, based on what is in al-Sihah that al-ashgha among horses and others is that whose head is entirely white while the rest of its body is not, like the Arkham (a bird) which is hardly approached: God mentioned one of the two matters and did not mention both together, as in His saying: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, because the other is known from what is mentioned, since it points to it, or because the wording admits it, as it is said.

Some of the verifiers said: "night" and "day" here mean every night and every day, and it is by the succession of similar ones that the exchange is continuous, so it indicates the change of each of them by the other, in the briefest expression, without strain and without contradicting what is well known of the rules of Arabic grammar.

The clause ﴿yughshi﴾, according to what Ibn Jinni said, on the reading of Hamid, is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿then He istawa﴾, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: He covers the night over the day by His command or by His permission. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿seeking it urgently﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿yughshi﴾ ... and so on, for emphasis. On the reading of the majority, it is a circumstantial clause of ﴿al-layl﴾, meaning: He covers the night over the day, seeking it urgently, and ﴿urgently﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in ﴿yatlubuhu﴾. Another allowed that the clause could be a circumstantial clause of the day, on the basis of Hamid's reading as well.

Abu al-Baqa' allowed the clause to be taken as a new sentence (isti'naf) in the first clause. Some said: ﴿hathithan﴾ may be a circumstantial clause of the subject, in the sense of "urging," or of the object, meaning "urged," and it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "an urgent seeking." The seeking was described in this way because the succession of night and day, as the Imam and others said, occurs only through the motion of the greatest sphere, and it is the swiftest of motions, for when a person is at his fastest run, in the time it takes to lift his foot and set it down, the sphere moves three thousand miles, which is a thousand farsakh.

It was objected that if the greatest sphere is the Throne, as they say, then its motion is not granted by the majority of the scholars of hadith. Rather, they do not grant the motion of any of the other spheres either, namely the Kursi and the seven heavens. They even claimed that the stars are in the hands of angels who move them wherever God wills and however He wills. Al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, said: "They run through the thickness of the spheres as fish run through water," [cf. ﴿each in a sphere swimming﴾]. And it is transmitted from him that he explained the saying of God, Glorified is He: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾ as "making it a coverer of it, the coverage of a man of a woman," and he said: "God mentioned the covering here and the entering in another verse, and this is the spiritual intercourse, and He made it pervasive in all existents." If this is correct, then how correct is the saying of people: "The night is pregnant," and how subtle it is! The urging toward it is clear to whoever has tasted the sweetness of intercourse. The outcome of this covering, according to those who hold it, is what exists in this world of minerals, plants, and animals, which are the three generated kinds, or of events in general. Close to this is his saying:

It has whitened the young and worn out the old,
the returning of morning and the passing of evening.

You know that there is no influence in existence in truth except God, Exalted is He. The reason for His mentioning this after mentioning the istawa, according to what is transmitted from al-Qaffal, is that when He, Majestic is His affair, informed the servants of His istawa, He informed them about the continuity of the affairs of the creatures in accordance with His will, and He showed them this in what they witness, so that sight would be joined to report and doubt would vanish from every direction. It is not hidden that this may be a fine reason for mentioning that and what follows it, the mention of istawa. But as for mentioning it specifically there, rather than the subjugation of the sun and moon, there is no such reason. The author of al-Kashf mentioned, in explaining the choice of the author of al-Kashshaf here, that the one who covers is the day, while in al-Ra'd it is the night; and his explanation of covering there as clothing and here as joining, in view of what is understood from the essence, is the reason for presenting covering before the subjugation mentioned in this verse, and the reverse in the verse of al-Ra'd. He said: "The point in that is that the subjugation of the sun and moon was mentioned there earlier, in enumerating the signs; when He finished, He mentioned the entering of the night into the day, to match it. Also because it is more manifest in the verse, and because the sun is subjugated and commanded. Here He brought it in another style, as a preparation for His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, that is, from this power and His signs regarding your affairs." So the wording was preferred over the original, and also to combine the two readings. End of quotation. So reflect upon this, and do not be heedless.

(Qur'an-quoting and mid-argument passage; translating as given.)

"And it is He who covers the night with the day, which seeks it urgently" — no. Here is the translation of the passage:

It is also read as "yughashshi" with shaddah, to indicate repetition. ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars [are] subjected by His command﴾, meaning: He created them while they are made subservient, following the direction of His disposal of them, as He wills, not resisting Him, exalted is His affair, as if they were discerning beings who were commanded and so obeyed. Thus calling that a "command" is by way of simile and metaphor. It is also valid to take "command" as "will", as has been said: these great bodies and wondrous creatures are submissive to His will. Others took "command" to mean the verbal command, and said: Glory be to Him, He commanded these bodies to move constantly, in continual motion in a specific manner, wherever He wills; and there is nothing preventing Allah the Exalted from giving them perception and understanding of that. Indeed, some claimed that they are perceptive absolutely, and some reports indicate that some of them have a perception of other than what has been mentioned.

The mention of the sun and the moon specifically, despite their being included among the stars, is to show their excellence over them, because of the greater brightness and light in them, and because by their movement through the mansions the times are known; and the sun's precedence over the moon; and in observance of the correspondence with what preceded, which is of the figurative kind (al-badi'). And because the sun is more noble than the moon and higher in rank and place, based on what has been said, that the sun is in the fourth heaven and the moon is in the first heaven. This is not accepted by the scholars of hadith, as is the saying that its light is derived from its light, because its various forms vary in different ways according to its position relative to the sun in nearness and distance from it, along with the eclipse that affects it, not because of the variation of forms alone. For variation of forms alone does not necessarily entail the definite judgment that the light of the moon is derived from the sun, since it is possible that half of it is luminous in itself and half is dark, and it revolves on its axis with a motion equal to the motion of its orbit; so when it moves slightly after the conjunction, we see it as a crescent, and it increases until we see it as full, then its dark half gradually inclines until it returns to conjunction. In their being "subjected" there is an indication that they have no influence of their own whatsoever.

Ibn 'Amir read all of them in the nominative, as a beginning and predicate, and in the accusative by conjunction with "the heavens" and the circumstantial sense, as we have indicated. It is also permitted to assume "made" (ja'ala) and "made" with the sun as the first object and "subjected" as the second object.

﴿Certainly, to Him belong creation and command﴾ is like a concluding statement to the preceding speech, meaning: He, the Exalted, is the One who created things, and the heavens and the earth are included in that primarily; He is the One who manages them and directs them according to His will, and included in that is what He indicated by His words, glory be to Him: ﴿subjected by His command﴾, none other than Him, as the fronting of the adverbial phrase indicates.

Some also interpreted "command" here as "will", and others interpreted "command" as the opposite of prohibition, and "creation" as "the created": that is, to Him the Exalted belong the created beings because He created them, and to Him belongs the right to command them with what He wills. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna drew from this that the speech of Allah, exalted is His affair, is not created, saying: Indeed Allah the Exalted distinguished between creation and command, so whoever combines them has disbelieved, meaning whoever makes the command, which is His speech, glory be to Him, part of what He created, has disbelieved, because a created thing subsists only in a created thing like itself. Thus it is in the tafsir of al-Khazin; but it is nothing, as is not hidden. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan that "creation" is what is below the Throne and "command" is what is above that. The expression "the world of command" became common among some for the world of immaterial beings.

﴿Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (54): that is, He is sanctified and exalted above every deficiency, and included in that is His exaltation above deficiency in creation or in command, primarily.

In that there is an indication that both are according to wisdom and in the utmost perfection, and this is not said of other than Him, the Exalted; rather it is a quality specific to Him, glory be to Him, as in the Qamus. And the Imam said: "Barakah" has two interpretations: one is permanence and stability, and the second is abundance of excellent effects. If you take it in the first sense, then the one who is lasting and enduring is Allah the Exalted; and if you take it in the second sense, then all good and perfections are from Allah the Exalted, so this praise befits none but His presence, majestic and exalted. Al-Zajjaj chose that it is from "barakah" in the sense of abundance of every good; and no present-tense form, imperative, or active participle of it has come, for example. Al-Baydawi said: the meaning is that He is exalted in unity and divinity, and glorified in singularity and lordship. On this, it is a conclusion in which its opening is taken into account; then he verified the verse in a way that is not free from confusion and contradiction with what the early generations of the Ummah held.

Then, after He, may He be exalted, had explained the oneness of God (tawhid) and informed that He alone creates and commands, He instructed His servants to call upon Him with sincerity and humility. So the Mighty One who speaks said: ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, the One whose glorious attributes you have come to know. The meaning of "du'a" (supplication), as many have said, is asking and requesting, and it is the essence of worship (mukh al-'ibadah). This is because the one who supplicates does not approach supplication unless he recognizes within himself his need for that which he seeks and his inability to attain it, and he knows that his Lord, blessed and exalted, hears supplication, knows the need, and is able to bring it to him. Undoubtedly, the servant's knowledge of his own helplessness and deficiency, and his knowledge of his Lord's power and perfection, are among the greatest acts of worship.

It has also been said that what is meant here is worship, because He followed it with: ﴿call upon Him in fear and hope﴾, and the conjoined element must be different from the element it is conjoined to. But this is open to question. Firstly, because difference is sufficient by way of its objects, as you say: "I struck Zayd" and "I struck 'Amr." Secondly, because this does not require interpreting du'a here as worship; rather, interpreting it that way is either here or there. Thirdly, because it contradicts the transmitted tafsir (tafsir ma'thur, interpretation based on transmitted reports), as you will learn, God willing.

﴿Tadarru'an﴾ means "with humility" or "those who are humbly submissive," so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject, by implicit or interpreted estimation. Its accusative use as an infinitive (masdar) has also been allowed, and the same applies to what follows. It derives from ad-dara'ah (submissiveness and lowliness). It is said: "Fulan dara'a li-fulan" when he humbled himself and submitted to him. Al-Zajjaj said: tadarru' is flattery (tamallug), which is close to what they said, i.e., call upon Him humbly. It has also been said that tadarru' is the opposite of secrecy (khufyah), and Abu Muslim preferred this, meaning: call upon Him openly. ﴿And in secret﴾, i.e., privately.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan, who said: "The Muslims would strive in supplication, and no voice of theirs was heard except a whisper between them and their Lord. That is because He, exalted, says: ﴿Call upon your Lord with humility and in secret﴾, and because He, glorified, mentioned a righteous servant and approved of his act, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾." In another narration from him, he said: "Between the supplication in secret and the supplication openly is seventy times."

There has also come a hadith from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to a people who were raising their voices: "O people, ease up on yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing, All-Seeing, and He is with you, and He is nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount." The meaning is: be gentle and refrain from shouting in supplication.

From here, a group said that raising the voice in supplication is disliked. In al-Intisaf, it is said: "It is sufficient to establish the secrecy of it that it is paired in the verse with humility, so neglecting it is like neglecting humble submission to God, the Exalted. A supplication without humility and reverence is of little benefit; likewise a supplication without secrecy or accompanying dignity." You will see many people of your time relying on shouting in supplication, especially in congregational mosques, until the clamor grows great, the ears are deafened and stunned, and they do not realize that they have combined two innovations: raising the voice in supplication and doing so in the mosque.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jurayj that raising the voice in supplication is among the transgression (i'tida') referred to by His words, glorified be He: ﴿Indeed, He does not like transgressors﴾ (55). Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted the same from Zayd ibn Aslam. Some scholars held that it is something not objectionable. The supplication of transgressors, which God does not love, is seeking what is not fitting for the supplicant, such as the rank of the prophets, peace be upon them, and ascending to heaven. Among it is what a group held to be disbelief (kufr), such as seeking the entry of Iblis, Abu Jahl and their like into Paradise, and seeking the descent of revelation or prophethood, and similar impossibilities, because that involves seeking to make God Himself a liar.

Ahmad in his Musnad and Abu Dawud transmitted from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'There will be a people who transgress in supplication. It is enough for a person to say: O God, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings closer to it of speech and deed, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings closer to it of speech and deed.'" Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, He does not like transgressors﴾.

Others made distinctions and said: secrecy is better when there is fear of showing off (riya', ostentation), and openness is better when there is no such fear. Better than this is the view that secrecy is preferred over openness when showing off is feared, or when raising the voice would disturb one who is praying, sleeping, reciting, or occupied with religious knowledge; and that openness is preferred over secrecy when none of that is present and there is intent to teach an ignorant person, or to remove loneliness from a lonely person, or to drive away drowsiness or laziness from the supplicant himself, or to bring joy to a believer's heart, or to deter an innovator from an innovation, or similar purposes. Among this is loudly invoking God's pleasure with the Companions and supplicating before the Muslims in the khutbah (sermon). The Shafi'is have prescribed saying "Amin" aloud after al-Fatihah, and it is a supplication; the imam and the follower both say it aloud according to them.

Some distinguished between raising the voice very loudly, as the muezzins do on minarets when supplicating for relief, and raising it so that those nearby hear it. He said: there is no harm in the second, generally, but the first is not so.

The apparent meaning of "transgressors" is those who exceed what they were commanded in every matter, and it includes those who transgress in supplication by way of primary inclusion. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Jubayr that the meaning of the verse is: call upon your Lord in all your needs, of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, and do not transgress by calling down evil upon a believing man or woman, such as disgrace or curse. The scholars have differed regarding the disbelief of one who supplicates against another that he be stripped of faith or die as a disbeliever, and that is among the gravest kinds of transgression; the legal opinion adopted is that it is not disbelief.

They mentioned many etiquettes (adab) for supplication, among them: being in a state of purity, facing the qibla, emptying the heart of distractions, beginning and ending it with blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), raising the hands toward the sky, including the believers in it, and seeking the times of answer. Among these times, according to many, is the hour of the Friday sermon, during which one supplicates silently in the heart, as the most excellent of the later scholars of his land, al-Fadil al-Tahtawi, stated in his glosses on al-Durr al-Mukhtar, as transmitted from him by the most learned of the contemporary scholars, Ibn 'Abidin al-Dimashqi. Also at the time of rain falling, at the time of breaking the fast, in the last third of the night, after completing the Qur'an, and other times, all of which are expounded in their proper place.

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾: a prohibition against all kinds of corruption, such as corrupting lives, property, lineages, minds, and religions, ﴿after its reform﴾, meaning after God Most High has reformed it, created it in the form suited to the benefits of creation and the welfare of the responsible beings, and sent prophets into it with the rulings He legislated. ﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾: that is, fearful of being rejected because of your shortcomings in being fit for response, and hopeful of His response out of His bounty. It has also been said: fearful of His punishment and hopeful of His abundant reward.

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning is fear of justice and hope for grace. From Ata: fear of the scale and hope for the Gardens. The root of fear is the unsettling of the heart due to the lack of security from harm. It has been said: fear is the anticipation of something disliked that will occur later, and hope is the anticipation of something loved that will occur to one. Both are in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl), as has been indicated.

It is also permissible that they be accusative as objects of purpose (maf‘ūl li-ajlih). It has been said: since calling upon God has a great status, He repeated it and restricted it first with the outward attributes and last with the inward attributes. It has also been said: the earlier command is in the category of stating the condition of supplication, and the second is in the category of stating its benefit. It has been said: there is no repetition, for what came before commanded calling upon Him in the sense of asking, and this command is calling upon Him in the sense of worship. The meaning is:
[p. 141 continues]
worship Him while combining in yourselves fear and hope in your inward and outward worship. And this, as you see, is so. Some people kept the supplication in its apparent sense and generalized the object of fear and hope, and their meaning is: call upon Him while you combine in yourselves fear and hope in all your actions. But this is nothing. The preferred view among the majority of exegetes is what has preceded.

﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the good-doers﴾ (56): their deeds. And among goodness in supplication is that it be accompanied by fear and hope. Much has been said about the justification for the masculine form of ﻗﺮﻳﺐ (qarīb, "near") though it is an attribute predicated of a feminine noun. Ibn Hisham transmitted several explanations for this, mentioning what each has in its favor and against it. The first: that "mercy" is in the sense of an addition, and the Arabs sometimes add to the genitive construct. The Exalted said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, meaning: glorify your Lord. Do you not see that one says in glorification "Glory be to my Lord," not "Glory be to the name of my Lord"? The sense is: indeed God Most High is near, so the predicate is in reality about the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a‘ẓam). He objected to this: it is not valid according to the scholars of Basrah, because in their view nouns are not added, only particles are added. The meaning of the verse according to them is: exalt the names of your Lord from what does not befit them, so do not attribute to Him, glory be to Him, a name that does not befit His perfection or a name not permitted for Him. So there is no addition.

The second: that it is by omitting a noun, meaning: the place of God's mercy is near. The predication is then about the place, which is masculine. A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), pointing to gold and silver: "Indeed these two are forbidden," where the predicate is singular because the sense is: indeed the use of these two is forbidden. And the verse of Hassan:

"They give to drink to whoever comes to al-Barīṣ, while over them the Barada flows, mixing with pure wine."

Here the sense is: water of the Barada, which is why he said "yuṣaffiqu" (flows) in the masculine, though Barada is feminine. It was objected that this omitted noun is very remote, not near, and the default is no omission, and the meaning without omission is better than with it. The third: that it is by omitting the qualified noun, meaning: a thing that is near, as the poet said:

"She stood weeping over his grave: who will I have after you, O ʿĀmir?
You left me in the house as one in exile, and he who has no helper is humbled."

That is, a person who is in exile. On this basis is explained the saying of Sibawayh: "a menstruating woman" (ḥāʾiḍ), meaning a person who is in menstruation, and the saying of the poet also:

"If you, in the day of ease, asked me for your divorce, I would not withhold it, though you are a friend."

It was objected that this is weaker than the previous, because making the attribute of a feminine noun masculine by taking it as predicated of an omitted masculine noun is anomalous, and the speech of God Most High is too exalted for it. Moreover, there is no eloquence in saying "the mercy of God is a near thing," nor any elegance; rather, to one of taste it is an objectionable expression. Attributes like ḥāʾiḍ, which are specific, do not need a marker, because the marker serves to remove ambiguity, and there is no ambiguity with specificity. Sibawayh, although he is a skilled rider in this field, a skilled rider may stumble, and everyone's words are taken and left. Do you not see how he permitted, in the category of the attributive adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha), "I passed by a man beautiful of face," by annexing "beautiful" to "face" and annexing "face" to the pronoun of the man? All the Basrans and Kufans disagreed with him in this, because he annexed a thing to itself. You also know that the default is no omission. The fourth: that the Arabs give the genitive construct (muḍāf) the grammatical gender of the second term (muḍāf ilayhi) when it is valid to dispense with the first, and this is a well-known matter. Mercy, by being annexed to the glorious Name, has acquired what validates predicating the masculine of it. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi objected to this in his glosses on the Book (of Sibawayh): this estimation and interpretation in the Qur'an is
[p. 142 begins]
remote and corrupt; it is permitted only in the necessity of poetry. Al-Rawdharawari said: the acquisition of the feminine by the feminine has been established by the speech of a trustworthy source, but the reverse requires evidence, and whoever claims its permissibility must provide proof. The fifth: that faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl is common to masculine and feminine, like "a wounded man" (rajul jarīḥ) and "a wounded woman" (imraʾa jarīḥ). It was objected that this is a gross error, because faʿīl here is in the sense of fāʿil. It was also objected that this is not a regular pattern, especially outside the second. The sixth: that faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil may be likened to faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, and so it is withheld from the feminine marker; just as they liken faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl to faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, and so attach the feminine marker to it. The first is like His saying: ﴿Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?﴾, and the noble verse is of this kind. The second is like their saying "a blameworthy trait" (khaṣla dhamīma) and "a praiseworthy quality" (ṣifa ḥamīda), by analogy with their saying "ugly" (qabīḥa) and "beautiful" (jamīla). This was not answered by anything. Al-Rawdharawari objected to it: it is a mere claim without proof, even if the grammarians said it. It may be countered that one of the two verbs is derived from an intransitive and the other from a transitive, so if the ruling of one were applied to the other, the distinction between transitive and intransitive would be void, if it is in general; and if in particular, where is the proof for it? There is room for consideration. The seventh: that the Arabs sometimes predicate of the second term of the genitive construct and omit the first term, like His saying: ﴿So their necks remained humbly subject to it﴾. Here ﴿subject﴾ (khāḍiʿīn) is a predicate about the pronoun annexed to "necks," not about "necks." Do you not see that if you say "the necks are subject" it is not permitted, because the masculine sound plural is only for rational beings, so one does not say "hands long" (aydin ṭawīlūn) or "dogs barking" (kilāb nābiḥūn)? It was objected that this perhaps goes back to the view of addition, and you know what is in that. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "necks" is the chiefs and the honored ones, and it has been said: the group, as one says "Zayd came in a neck of the people," meaning in a group. Al-Rawdharawari said: if it were permissible to disregard the genitive construct and rule on the second term, it would be permissible to say "the owner of the coat of mail was a fully-covering one" and "the owner of the house was spacious," and there is no such thing. The eighth: that "mercy" (raḥma) and "womb" (raḥim) are close in wording, which is evident, and in meaning, by the evidence of transmission from the imams of the language. So one gave one the ruling of the other. It was objected that this is nothing, because "admonition" (waʿẓ) and "exhortation" (mawʿiẓa) are also close, so this proponent should permit saying "a beneficial exhortation (mawʿiẓa nāfiʿ)" and "a good admonition (waʿẓa ḥasan)"; and likewise "remembrance" (dhikr) and "reminder" (dhikrā), so it should be said "a beneficial reminder (dhikrā nāfiʿ)" as one says "a beneficial remembrance (dhikr nāfiʿ)." The ninth: that faʿīl here is in the sense of a relational adjective (nasab), so its meaning "near" is "possessing nearness," as al-Khalil says of ḥāʾiḍ that it means "possessing menstruation." It was objected that this is false, because the attributes indicating the relational sense are restricted to specific patterns: faʿāl, faʿl, and fāʿil.

The tenth: what al-Rawdharawari said, that faʿīl in general is common to feminine and masculine. It was objected that this is among the most corrupt things said, because it contradicts what is actually found in Arabic speech, for they say "a clever woman (imraʾa ẓarīfa)," "a knowing woman (ʿalīma)," "a forbearing woman (ḥalīma)," and "a merciful woman (raḥīma)," and it is not permitted to use the masculine in any of these. For this reason Abu ʿUthman al-Mazini said, regarding His saying: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste (baghiyyan)﴾, that baghiyyan is faʿūl, and the original is baghawī, then the waw was changed to yāʾ and the ḍamma to kasra, and the yāʾ was assimilated into the yāʾ. As for his saying:

"Languid of standing, cutting off speech, when she smiles her teeth show pearls, and the front teeth are spaced."

The answer to it is in several respects. One: that it is rare. Two: that the original is qaṭīʿa, then the tāʾ was dropped for annexation, as in His saying: ﴿and establishing the prayer﴾; annexation permits dropping the tāʾ just as it requires dropping the nūn and the tanwīn, and this has been stated explicitly by more than one of the Qur'an readers. Three: that this was permitted only for the sake of harmony with fatūr, because it is faʿūl, which is common to masculine and feminine. Eleventh: they say in relationship-kinship "qarīb" (near), even when applied to a feminine, as in "so-and-so is qarīb to me," and they distinguish between it and nearness of distance. It was objected that this is based on saying in kinship-nearness "so-and-so is my qarāba," and a group has stated explicitly that this is an error, and that the correct form is "so-and-so is dhū qarābatī (a kinsman of mine)," as he said:

"The stranger weeps over him, though he does not know him, while his close kinsman in the tribe is glad."

The twelfth: of the interpretation of the feminine by a masculine agreeing with it in meaning. Those who hold this differ: some estimate that the kindness of God is near, and some estimate that the subtle kindness (luṭf) of God is near. Among this is his saying:

"I see a man among them, distressed, as if he were pressing to his flanks a hand dyed (with henna)."

Here "hand" (kaff) was interpreted as meaning "limb." It was objected that this is false, because that happens only in poetry, and it has been established that one does not say "admonition (mawʿiẓa) good (ḥasan)," although "admonition" is equivalent to "exhortation" in meaning and close to it in wording too. As for the line of verse, the grammarians stated explicitly that it is a necessity of poetry, and what is of this nature is not to be applied to the speech of God the Exalted. Moreover, some said: "hand" may be masculine.

The thirteenth: that what is meant by "mercy" here is rain. This was transmitted from al-Akhfash, and rain is masculine. It was supported by the fact that "mercy" in what comes after means rain. It was objected to this in several respects. One: if the second "mercy" were the first "mercy," it would not be mentioned as an explicit noun, as is the apparent case, since the place calls for a pronoun. Two: if the general meaning is possible, one should not turn to the specific, and there is no necessity here for that, as is not hidden. Three: rain, which is mercy, is not specific to the good-doers, because God the Exalted provides for the obedient and the disobedient alike; what is specific in the usage of the Sharia is the mercy that is forgiveness, pardon, and reward. The answer to this is that just as the address about mercy in the legal sense may be specified to the good-doers as an encouragement, likewise it is permissible to specify rain, which is the cause of provisions, to them as an encouragement to goodness. This is nothing in my view. Fourth: if you said "the rain of God is near," you would find this annexation something that ears reject and natures recoil from, unlike "indeed the mercy of God," which shows that it does not have the same status in meaning.

وأُجِيبَ عَنْهُ بِأنَّ مَجْمُوعَ (رَحْمَةَ اللَّهِ) اسْتُعْمِلَ مُرادًا بِهِ المَطَرُ، وبِأنَّ الإضافَةَ في (مَطَرِ اللَّهِ) إنَّما لَمْ تَحْسُنْ لِلْعِلْمِ بِالِاخْتِصاصِ، ولا كَذَلِكَ (رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ تَعالى). وهَذا كَما يَحْسُنُ أنْ يُقالَ: (كَلامُ اللَّهِ تَعالى)، ولا يَحْسُنُ أنْ يُقالَ: (قُرْآنُ اللَّهِ سُبْحانَهُ). والإنْصافُ أنَّ هَذا القَوْلَ لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ، كَما لا يَخْفى عَلى ذِي ذِهْنٍ طَرِيٍّ. وقالَ ابْنُ هِشامٍ: لا بُعْدَ في أنْ يُقالَ: إنَّ التَّذْكِيرَ في الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ لِمَجْمُوعِ أُمُورٍ مِنَ الأُمُورِ المَذْكُورَةِ، واخْتارَ أنَّهُ لَمّا كانَ المُضافُ يَكْتَسِبُ مِنَ المُضافِ إلَيْهِ التَّذْكِيرَ، وكانَتِ الرَّحْمَةُ مُقارِبَةً لِلرَّحِمِ في اللَّفْظِ، وكانَ (قَرِيبٌ) عَلى صِيغَةِ (فَعِيلٍ)، وفَعِيلٌ الَّذِي بِمَعْنى فاعِلٍ قَدْ يُحْمَلُ عَلى فَعِيلٍ بِمَعْنى مَفْعُولٍ، جاءَ التَّذْكِيرُ، وادَّعى أنَّهُ لا يُناقِضُ ما قَدِمَهُ مِنَ الِاعْتِراضاتِ، لِأنَّهُ لا يَلْزَمُ مِنَ انْتِفاءِ اعْتِبارِ شَيْءٍ مِن هَذِهِ الأُمُورِ مُسْتَقِلًّا انْتِفاءُ اعْتِبارِهِ مَعَ غَيْرِهِ. اهـ. ولا يَخْلُو عَنْ حُسْنٍ، سِوى أنَّهُ إذا أُخِذَ في المَجْمُوعِ كَوْنُ الرَّحْمَةِ بِمَعْنى المَطَرِ، يُفْسِدُ الزَّرْعَ. وقَدْ جَرى في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ بَحْثٌ طَوِيلٌ بَيْنَ ابْنِ مالِكٍ والرَّوَذَراوَرِيِّ، وفي كَلامِ كُلٍّ حَقٌّ وصَوابٌ، وفي نَقْلِ ذَلِكَ ما يُورِثُ السَّآمَةَ. وأجابَ الجَوْهَرِيُّ بِأنَّ الرَّحْمَةَ مَصْدَرٌ، والمَصادِرُ لا تُجْمَعُ ولا تُؤَنَّثُ، وهو كَما تَرى.

وقِيلَ: التَّذْكِيرُ لِأنَّ تَأْنِيثَ الرَّحْمَةِ غَيْرُ حَقِيقِيٍّ. ولا يَخْفى بُعْدُهُ، لِأنَّ المُتَضَمِّنَ لِضَمِيرِ المُؤَنَّثِ، ولَوْ كانَ غَيْرَ حَقِيقِيٍّ، لَمْ يَحْسُنْ تَذْكِيرُهُ عَلى المَشْهُورِ. وقِيلَ: إنَّ (فَعِيلًا) هُنا مَحْمُولٌ عَلى (فَعِيلٍ) الوارِدِ في المَصادِرِ، فَإنَّهُ لِلْمُؤَنَّثِ والمُذَكَّرِ، كَ(فَعِيلٍ) بِمَعْنى مَفْعُولٍ، كالنَّقِيضِ بِالنُّونِ والقافِ والضّادِ المُعْجَمَةِ، وهو صَوْتُ الرَّحْلِ ونَحْوِهِ، والضَّغِيبِ بِالضّادِ والغَيْنِ المُعْجَمَةِ والياءِ المُثَنّاةِ مِن تَحْتُ والباءِ المُوَحَّدَةِ، صَوْتُ الأرْنَبِ. وأنْتَ تَعْلَمُ أنَّ حَمْلَهُ عَلى (فَعِيلٍ)
[صفحة 144]
بِمَعْنى مَفْعُولٍ أوْلى مِن هَذا الحَمْلِ، وهو الَّذِي أمِيلُ إلَيْهِ. نَعَمْ رُبَّما يُدَّعى أنَّ في ذَلِكَ إشارَةً ما إلى مَزِيدِ قُرْبِ الرَّحْمَةِ، لَكِنَّهُ بَعِيدٌ جِدًّا، وقَدْ لا يَسْلَمُ. والَّذِي أخْتارُهُ أنَّ (فَعِيلًا) هُنا بِمَعْنى فاعِلٍ، لا بِمَعْنى مَفْعُولٍ، كَما زَعَمَ الكَرْمانِيُّ، لِما مَرَّتِ الإشارَةُ إلَيْهِ، ولِأنَّ الرَّحْمَةَ صِفَةُ ذاتٍ عِنْدَ جَمْعٍ، وصِفاتُ الذّاتِ (وهي الصِّفاتُ اللازِمَةُ لِذاتِ اللَّهِ تَعالى) سَواءٌ قُلْنا بِعَيْنِيَّتِها، أوْ بِغَيْرِيَّتِها، أوْ بِأنَّها لا (هِيَ هُوَ ولا غَيْرُهُ)، ولا يَحْسُنُ الإخْبارُ عَنْها بِأنَّها مُقَرَّبَةٌ، وذَلِكَ عَلى القَوْلَيْنِ الأخِيرَيْنِ ظاهِرٌ، وعَلى الأوَّلِ أظْهَرُ. والقَوْلُ بِأنَّ في ذَلِكَ تَرْغِيبًا في الإحْسانِ، حَيْثُ أُشِيرَ إلى أنَّهُ كالفاعِلِ، وقَدْ أثَّرَ فِيما لا يَقْبَلُ التَّأثُّرَ، مِمّا لا يَكادُ يَسْلَمُ، وأنَّهُ قَدْ حُمِلَ عَلى (فَعِيلٍ) بِمَعْنى مَفْعُولٍ، كَما حُمِلَ عَلى ذَلِكَ في خُصُوصِيَّةِ (قَرِيبٍ) في قَوْلِ جَرِيرٍ:

أتَنْفَعُكَ الحَياةُ وأُمُّ عَمْرٍو ∗∗∗ قَرِيبٌ تَزُورُ ولا تُزارُ

وإنَّما لَمْ يَقُلْ (قَرِيبَةٌ) عَلى الأصْلِ، لِلْإشارَةِ لِأرْبابِ الأذْهانِ السَّلِيمَةِ إلى أنَّها قَرِيبَةٌ جِدًّا مِنَ المُحْسِنِينَ، كَما لا يَخْفى عَلى المُتَأمِّلِ. واخْتارَ بَعْضُهم تَفْسِيرَ الرَّحْمَةِ هُنا بِالإحْسانِ، لِمَكانِ المُحْسِنِينَ، وهَلْ جَزاءُ الإحْسانِ إلّا الإحْسانُ؟ ولَعَلَّهُ يُعْتَبَرُ شامِلًا لِلْإحْسانِ الدُّنْيَوِيِّ والأُخْرَوِيِّ. ووَجْهُ القُرْبِ عَلى ما قِيلَ: وُجُودُ الأهْلِيَّةِ بِحَسَبِ الحِكْمَةِ مَعَ ارْتِفاعِ المَوانِعِ بِالكُلِّيَّةِ. وفَسَّرَها ابْنُ جُبَيْرٍ بِالثَّوابِ، والمُتَبادَرُ مِنهُ الإحْسانُ الأُخْرَوِيُّ.

ووَجْهُ القُرْبِ عَلَيْهِ: أنَّ الإنْسانَ في كُلِّ ساعَةٍ مِنَ السّاعاتِ في إدْبارٍ عَنِ الدُّنْيا وإقْبالٍ عَلى الآخِرَةِ، وإذا كانَ كَذَلِكَ كانَ المَوْتُ أقْرَبَ إلَيْهِ مِنَ الحَياةِ، فَلا يَكُونُ بَيْنَ المُحْسِنِ والثَّوابِ في الآخِرَةِ إلّا المَوْتُ، وكُلُّ آتٍ قَرِيبٌ.

وجَعَلَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ الآيَةَ مِن قَبِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ﴾ .. إلَخْ. أيْ عَلَّقَ فِيها الرَّحْمَةَ بِإحْسانِ الأعْمالِ، كَما عَلَّقَ الغُفْرانَ فِيهِ بِالتَّوْبَةِ والإيمانِ والعَمَلِ الصّالِحِ، فَكَأنَّ (مَن تابَ وآمَنَ) .. إلَخْ. تَفْسِيرٌ لِلْمُحْسِنِينَ. وهو إشارَةٌ إلى ما يَزْعُمُهُ قَوْمُهُ مِن أنَّ الآيَةَ تَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّ صاحِبَ الكَبِيرَةِ (أي الذَّنْبَ العَظِيمَ) لا يَخْلُصُ مِنَ النّارِ، لِأنَّهُ لَيْسَ مِنَ المُحْسِنِينَ، والتَّخْلِيصُ مِنَ النّارِ بَعْدَ الدُّخُولِ فِيها رَحْمَةٌ.

وأُجِيبَ بِأنَّ صاحِبَ الكَبِيرَةِ مُؤْمِنٌ بِاللَّهِ تَعالى ورَسُولِهِ ﷺ، ومَن يَكُونُ كَذَلِكَ فَهو مُحْسِنٌ، بِدَلِيلِ أنَّ الصَّبِيَّ إذا بَلَغَ ضُحًى وآمَنَ ومات قَبْلَ الظُّهْرِ، فَقَدِ اجْتَمَعَتِ الأُمَّةُ عَلى أنَّهُ داخِلٌ تَحْتَ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أحْسَنُوا الحُسْنى﴾، فَهو مُحْسِنٌ بِمُجَرَّدِ الإيمانِ. والقَوْلُ بِأنَّ المُحْسِنِينَ هُمُ الَّذِينَ أتَوْا بِجَمِيعِ أنْواعِ الإحْسانِ، عَلى ما يُؤْذِنُ بِهِ الآيَةُ المُمَثَّلُ بِها أوَّلَ البَحْثِ أوَّلَ المَسْألَةِ، وأخْرَجَ أبُو الشَّيْخِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أنَّهُ فَسَّرَ (المُحْسِنِينَ) بِالمُؤْمِنِينَ.

وعَنْ بَعْضِهِمْ تَفْسِيرُهُ بِالدّاعِينَ (خَوْفًا وطَمَعًا)، لِقَرِينَةِ السِّياقِ عَلى ذَلِكَ، ونُظِرَ فِيهِ.

﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ is coordinated with the preceding sentence, or with the account of the creation of the heavens and the earth. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿الرِّيحَ﴾ (*al-rih*, "the wind") in the singular. It carries the sense of a collective noun, so it can be applied to many winds. The report of the supplication, "O Allah, make them winds and do not make them a single wind," is related according to the reading of the majority.

﴿بُشْرًا﴾ (*bushran*, "as good news"), with a dammah on the *ba'* and a sukun on the *shin*, is a lightened form of ﴿بُشُرًا﴾ (*bushuran*), the plural of *bashir* (bearer of good news), like *nudhur* and *nadhir*. That is, "bearers of good tidings." This is the reading of 'Asim, and it is also related from him as ﴿بُشُرًا﴾ in its original form. It has also been read with a fatha on the *ba'*, as a verbal noun of *bashara* in the lightened form, meaning *bashsharah* in the intensive form. The meaning is "bearers of good tidings," or "for the sake of good tidings." It has also been read ﴿بُشْرى﴾ (*bushra*), on the pattern of *hubla*, which is likewise a verbal noun from *bisharah* (good tidings).

The people of Madinah and Basra read ﴿نُشُرًا﴾ (*nushuran*, "scattering"), with a dammah on the *nun* and the *shin*, the plural of *nashur* (with a fatha on the *nun*), meaning *nashir* (one who spreads). The pattern *fa'ul* in the sense of *fa'il* has a regular plural, like *sabur* and *subur*. Its plural was not taken to be like *nashir*'s plural *buzl* (as in *bazil* and *bazl*), because the plural of *fa'il* in the form *fa'l* is anomalous.

The meaning of *nashir* has been disputed. The *Hawashi al-Shihabiyyah* states: it has been said that it is in the relative form, either relating to *nashr* (spreading), the opposite of *tayy* (folding), or relating to *nushur* in the sense of giving life, because the wind is described as dying and living, as in the saying of the poet:

*Inni la-arju an tamuta al-rihu fa-aq'udu al-yawma wa-astarihu*
"Indeed I hope that the wind will die, so I may sit today and rest."

Just as the later scholars describe it with illness and sickness. Among the things that the breeze is said to suffer from is the saying of one of them in the intense heat:

*Azunnu nasima al-rawdi mata li-annahu* ∗∗∗ *lahu zamanun fi al-rawdi wa-huwa 'alilu*
"I think the breeze of the meadow has died, because it has a season in the meadow, and it is sick."

It has also been said that it is a *fa'ul* from *nashara*, the intransitive counterpart of *anshara*. Allah the Exalted revives the dead, so he is *nushira*, and he is *nashir*, as in the saying of the poet:

*Hatta yaquluna an-nasu mimma ra'aw* ∗∗∗ *ya 'ajaban lil-mayyiti an-nashiri*
"Until people say, from what they have seen: 'How wondrous is the dead one who was raised!'"

It has been said that *nashir* means *munshir*, that is, one who gives life. It has also been said that *fa'ul* here means *maf'ul*, as in *rasul* and *rusul*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted this, but it is rare in both its singular and plural forms.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿نُشْرًا﴾ (*nushran*) with a dammah on the *nun* and a sukun on the *shin* wherever it occurs. The lightened form is regular for the pattern *fi'l*. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿نَشْرًا﴾ (*nashran*) with a fatha on the *nun* wherever it occurs. It is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning "spreading ones," or it is an absolute object, since sending and spreading are close in meaning.

﴿بَيْنَ يَدَيْ رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ means "before his mercy," that is, in front of his mercy. This is a metaphor, as reported from Abu Bakr al-Anbari. By "mercy," as most of the commentators have held, is meant rain. It is called mercy because of the benefits that follow from it according to the customary course of events. It should not be overlooked that mercy in its established usage is general. So applying it to this particular thing: if that is taken in terms of its particularity, it is a metaphor, because the word is used for something other than what it was coined for, since the word was not coined for that particular sense in its specificity. But if its application to it is not in its particularity but in terms of its generality and its being one of the individual instances of that general category, then it is literal, because it is the use of the word for what it was coined for, as explained in the commentary on the *Talkhis* and elsewhere.

Al-Shihab claimed that some lexicographers established that rain is among the meanings of mercy. But Ibn Hisham's statement in his treatise written to explain the reason for the masculine form of ﴿قَرِيبٌ﴾ (*qarib*), mentioned above, is: "We do not find the lexicographers, when they speak about mercy, saying that among its meanings is rain. Had it been coined for it, they would have mentioned it." At most this shows non-finding, and non-finding does not require non-existence. It is well known that affirmation takes precedence over negation, and whoever has memorized a proof is a proof against whoever has not memorized it. The context clearly points to this meaning.

As for showing that the winds are sent before that, it has been said: the *saba* (east wind) stirs the clouds, the *shimal* (north wind) gathers them, the *janub* (south wind) makes them pour, and the *dabur* (west wind) scatters them. These are among the well-known types of wind among the Arabs. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the winds are eight, four of which are punishment: the *qasif*, the *'asif*, the *sarsar* and the *'aqim*; and four of which are mercy: the *nashirat*, the *mubashshirat*, the *mursalat* and the *dhariyat*.

The wind is among the greatest of the bounties of Allah the Exalted upon his servants. It is reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar that if Allah the Exalted withheld the wind from his servants for three days, most of the people of the earth would stink. In some reports it is said that Allah the Exalted created the world and filled it with air, and if he withheld the air for a moment, what is between the heaven and the earth would stink. Many scholars have mentioned that it is disliked to revile the wind. Al-Shafi'i related on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "A wind struck the people on the road to Makkah while 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was on the pilgrimage, and it became strong. 'Umar said to those around him: 'What has reached you about the wind?' They did not answer him with anything. I had heard what 'Umar had asked about regarding the wind, so I urged my mount until I caught up with 'Umar, for I was at the back of the people. I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, I have been informed that you asked about the wind. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: The wind is from the spirit of Allah, the Exalted. It brings mercy and it brings punishment. So when you see it, do not revile it, and ask Allah the Exalted for its good and seek refuge in Allah, glory be to Him, from its evil.'"

There is no contradiction between the verse and this report, for the verse does not say that he, glory be to him, sends it only before mercy. Even if that were granted, it would be outside the usual course, since punishment by wind is rare. It has also been said that what is in the report is only the bringing of mercy and the bringing of punishment, not the sending before each.

﴿حَتَّى إِذَا أَقَلَّتْ﴾ (*hatta idha aqallat*, "until when they have carried") is a limit (*ghayah*) for his saying, glory be to him, ﴿يُرْسِلُ﴾ (*yursilu*, "sends"). *Iqlal*, as in *Jami' al-Bayan*, is carrying a thing in its entirety. Its derivation is from *qillah* (fewness). The literal sense of *aqallahu*, as some verifiers said, is that he made it little, or found it little. The intended meaning is that he thought it so, as in *akdhabahu*, when he made him a liar in his claim. It was then used in the sense of carrying, because the one who carries regards what he carries as small, that is, considers it little. From this is the saying: "the effort of the one who carries" (*juhd al-muqill*), that is, the carrier.

﴿سَحَابًا﴾ (*sahaban*, "clouds") means a cloud, named so for its drawing (*insihab*) through the air. It is a collective noun (*ism jins jam'i*) that is distinguished from its singular by the *ta'* marker, like *tamr* and *tamrah*. It may be masculine or feminine, its adjective may be singular, and it may be pluralized. Lexicographers like al-Jawhari and others call it a plural, so both considerations are observed in its adjective and its pronoun. In the plural it is also *suhub* and *sahaib*.

﴿ثِقَالًا﴾ (*thiqalan*, "heavy") is from *thiql*, on the pattern of *'inab*, the opposite of lightness. It is said *thaqula*, like *karuma*, *thiqalan* and *thaqalah*, so he is *thaqil*. The heaviness of the clouds is due to the water in them.

﴿سُقْنَاهُ لِبَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ﴾ (*suqnahu li-baladin mayyitin*, "We drove it to a dead land") means for its sake and its benefit, or for giving it life, or for watering it, as has been said. In *al-Bahr* it is stated that the *lam* is for communication, as in "I said to you." A distinction is made between *suqtu laka mal* (I conveyed wealth to you) and *suqtu li-ajlika mal* (I drove wealth for your sake). The first means "I delivered that to you and conveyed it to you," while the second does not necessarily imply that it reached him.

*Baladun*, as al-Layth said, is every place on the earth, whether inhabited or uninhabited, desolate or populated. A part of it is a *baldah*, and the plural is *bilad*. *Baldah* is also used for a desert (*mafazah*). From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*Wa-baldatun mithla zahri al-turs muwhishatun* ∗∗∗ *lil-jinni bil-layli fi hafatiha zajalu*
"And a town like the back of a shield, desolate, where at night the jinn make a sound at its edges."

﴿فَأَنْزَلْنَا بِهِ الْمَاءَ﴾ (*fa-anzalna bihi al-ma'*, "then We sent down water by it") means by the land, or by the cloud, as al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said, or by the driving, or by the winds, as has been said. The masculine form is by way of interpreting the thing mentioned. Likewise is his saying, exalted is he: ﴿فَأَخْرَجْنَا بِهِ﴾ (*fa-akhrajna bihi*, "then We brought forth by it"). It is possible that the pronoun refers to the water, which is the most apparent, because of its nearness both verbally and in meaning. The matching of parallel expressions and the separation of pronouns is not objectionable when there is evidence for it and good coherence.

If the pronoun refers to the land, then the *ba'* is for location in the second case, and for attachment in the first, because sending down is not in the land but the thing sent down is. It has also been permitted that it is for location, as in "I shot the game in the sanctuary" (*ramaytu al-sayd fi al-haram*), as you know from what has passed. If the pronoun refers to something else, then it is for causation, and it includes what is near and what is far.

﴿مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ﴾ (*min kulli al-thamarat*, "of every kind of fruit") means of all its kinds, because totality is neither intended nor actual here. This is more eloquent in showing the intended power. It has been said that the totality is customary, but the apparent meaning is that it is for abundance. Some have allowed that *min* is partitive, and some that it explains the genus.

﴿كَذَلِكَ نُخْرِجُ الْمَوْتَى﴾ (*kadhalika nukhriju al-mawta*, "Thus We bring forth the dead") is a reference either to the bringing forth of fruits or to the giving of life to the dead land, meaning: as We give it life by producing the growing powers in it and by filling it with varieties of plants and fruits, We bring forth the dead from the earth, and We give them life by returning souls to the substance of their bodies after gathering them and filling them with powers and senses. This is what they said. It is, as has been said, a reference to the two ways of those who hold to bodily resurrection: the creation of the body after its non-existence and then its revival, and the joining of some of its parts to others in the same pattern as before after they have been scattered, and then its revival.

The first is preferred, because what is immediately understood from the verse is that the comparison is between the two bringings forth from the hiding of non-existence. The second needs the strained supposition of a revival and the consideration of gathering parts, even though that is not considered on the side of the thing compared. It has been permitted that what is in the second part, the revival by returning souls ... etc., refers back to the first. But you know that there is no barrier to bringing forth from the hiding of non-existence, and the proofs of its impossibility are not something that stands on one leg.
