However, the transmitted proofs for each of the two ways are in tension. When the doctrine of bodily resurrection is valid, there is no harm in holding either of them. That the bringing forth of fruits is from the hiding of non-existence may not be granted, for they have some origin in a general sense. Furthermore, the bringing forth of the dead according to the first way is a re-creation, and the bringing forth of fruits is not like that, since they had no existence before. Yes, the more apparent view is that the comparison between the two bringings forth is undoubtedly so.

In *al-Khazin* they differed about the aspect of the comparison. It was said: just as Allah creates plants through the sending down of rain, so He gives life to the dead through the sending down of rain as well. It is reported from Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both, that when people die at the first blast, water from beneath the Throne is rained down upon them, called the water of life, for forty years, and they sprout as plants sprout from water. In another report it is forty days. They sprout in their graves like the growth of crops. When their bodies are complete, the spirit is breathed into them. Then sleep is cast upon them, and they sleep in their graves. When the trumpet is blown the second blast, they are revived and then gathered from their graves, finding the taste of sleep in their heads and eyes as one who wakes from sleep finds it. At that they say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?" Then the caller calls to them: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truly﴾.

Many have reported from Mujahid that when Allah the Exalted wishes to bring forth the dead, He sends rain from the sky until the earth splits open over them. Then glory be to Him sends the spirits, and each spirit returns to its body. So Allah the Exalted gives life to the dead by rain, as He gives life to the earth.

It has been said: the comparison was made only with the basic fact of giving life, without considering its manner. Therefore it is obligatory to believe it, and we are not required to investigate the manner, for Allah, glory be to Him, does what He wills. ﴿So that you may remember﴾ (57): that you may know that whoever has power over that has power over this without doubt. The original is ﴿تَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ (*tatadhakkarun*), and one of the two *ta'*s was dropped. The address has been said to be to the reflecting people in general, and it has been said to be to those who deny the resurrection.

[p. 148]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 58:

﴿And the good land﴾: that is, the land of noble soil, which has neither *sabakhah* (salt-flat, saline ground) nor *harrah* (rocky lava-field). The use of *al-balad* (the land, town) to mean *al-qaryah* (the village) is a widespread usage, and among its examples is its application to the Noble Makkah. ﴿Its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾: by His will and His facilitation. The phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). What is meant is that it is good, abundant, and of great benefit, since it stands in contrast to His words: ﴿And that which is bad﴾ of the lands, such as the salt-flat and the lava-field, ﴿comes forth only as meagre﴾, that is, scanty, with no good in it. From this is the verse of the poet:

Do not fail to fulfil a promise if you promise, and if you give, give a trifle, a meagre gift.

*Nakidan* is in the accusative either as a circumstantial clause or as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun. The original sentence is *lā yakhruju nabātuhu* (its vegetation does not come forth), so the genitive pronoun was deleted and the noun it modified was put in its place, so it became nominative and concealed (*mustatir*). It is also permissible that the original be *wa-nabātu alladhī khabuth* (and the vegetation of that which is bad). The expression first with *al-ṭayyib* (the good) and second with *alladhī khabuth* (that which is bad), rather than *al-khabīth* (the bad), indicates that the basic state of land is to be good and productive, and its opposite is a passing, accidental condition.

It was also read *yukhraju nabātuhu* with the passive *yukhraja* (the passive form, for the unnamed agent) and the nominative *nabāt* as a substitute for the agent. And *yukhriju nabātahu* with the active *yukhriju* from the causative form, and the accusative *nabātahu* as the object; the agent is the pronoun referring to *al-balad* (the land). It has been said that the pronoun refers to God the Exalted, or to the water. It was similarly read with *yukhriju* in the negated clause, and *nakidan* is then accusative as an object. Abu Ja'far read *nakadan* with two fatḥas, on the pattern of the verbal noun, and it is accusative either as a circumstantial clause or as a verbal noun, meaning *dhā nakadin* (possessing meagreness) or *khurūjan nakadan* (a meagre emergence). He also read *nakdan* with sukun for lightening, like *nazhun* in the words of the poet:

So he said to me the words of one of judgment and capability, experienced, sensible, free from doubt.

﴿Thus﴾: like that wondrous variation. ﴿We vary the signs﴾: that is, We repeat and reiterate the signs that point to the overwhelming power, and We repeat them. The basic meaning of *tasrif* (variation) is the change of one state into another, and from it comes the turning of the winds (*tasrif al-riyah*). ﴿For a people who give thanks﴾ (58) for the blessings of Allah the Exalted; and among them is the variation of the signs, and the thanks for it is reflecting upon them and taking lessons from them. He specified the thankful because they are the ones who benefit from this.

Al-Tayyibi said: the mention of ﴿for a people who give thanks﴾ after ﴿so that you may remember﴾ is by way of progression (*tarraqi*), because whoever remembers the favours of Allah the Exalted knows the right of the blessing and gives thanks. This, as more than one has said, is an example for one in whom admonition and warning take effect among the responsible, and for one in whom nothing of that has any effect.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Ibn Abbas that His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And the good land﴾ ... etc., are an example that Allah struck for the believers: he is good and his deed is good; and ﴿and that which is bad﴾ ... etc., is an example for the disbeliever: he is bad and his deed is bad.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid that this is an example that Allah struck for Adam, peace be upon him, and all his offspring, since they were all created from a single soul; so among them is one who believed in Allah the Exalted and His Book and became good, and among them is one who disbelieved in Allah the Exalted and His Book and became bad.

Ahmad, al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The example of the guidance and knowledge with which Allah the Exalted has sent me is like the example of a rain that fell upon a land; a portion of it was good, received the water, and produced grass and abundant herbage. And there were among it hard patches (*ajadib*) that held the water, and Allah the Exalted benefited people by them, so they drank from them, gave drink, and planted. And it fell upon another portion which were mere flat barren expanses (*qi'an*) that hold no water and produce no herbage. That is the example of one who comprehends the religion of Allah the Exalted and benefits from what Allah the Exalted has sent me with, so he knows and teaches. And the example of one who does not lift his head to that and does not accept the guidance of Allah the Exalted with which I have been sent." 

The specific choice of the example of the good and bad land is a digression (*istitrad*) following the mention of the rain and its descent upon the town, and a balancing between the two mercies, as in *al-Kashshaf*. And because of its closeness to parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*), the conjunction *wa* (and) was used in His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And the good land﴾. In this there is an indication of the meaning of what is recorded in Sahih Muslim from Iyad al-Mujashi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in his sermon, concerning Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "I created My servants as *hunafa'* (upright in monotheism), all of them, and the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Every child is born upon the *fitrah* (natural disposition), then his parents make him a Jew or a Christian." The point of the indication has already passed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 59:

Then, glory be to Him, He followed that with what confirms and establishes it: the stories of the earlier nations and the past generations. This also serves as consolation for His Messenger (ﷺ). So He, exalted is His majesty, said: ﴿Indeed We sent Noah to his people﴾. This is the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, indeed We sent..." etc. The use of this lam with qad in the past tense is consistent, as al-Zamakhshari said, and it is rare to use the lam alone, as in his saying:

I swore to her by Allah an oath of a sinner: "We slept, and there was neither talk nor one warming himself (by the fire)."

The secret behind this is that the oath clause is only brought as emphasis for the clause sworn to, which is its answer. Thus it was a context for the listener to expect the occurrence of what is sworn to, because the oath indicates emphasis, so it was appropriate to introduce qad. It is transmitted from the grammarians that they said: if the answer to an oath is a affirmative past verb that is inflected, then either it is close to the present, so it is introduced with qad, or otherwise the lam alone is used. So they permitted both forms according to two considerations.

No conjunction is used here, but it is used in Hud and al-Mu'minun, according to what al-Kirmani said, because the mention of Noah precedes explicitly in Hud and implicitly in al-Mu'minun, where He mentioned earlier ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾. He (peace be upon him) was the first to build it, unlike here.

Nuh ibn Lamak (with two fatahs; it is said: with one fatha and then a sukun; it is said: Malkan, with a fatha on the mim, a sukun on the lam, and a nun at the end; it is said: Lamak, like Hajir, son of Mutawashlakh, with a damma on the mim, a fatha on the taa' with two dots, a waw, a sukun on the shin with a dot, on the pattern of maf'ul, as more than one scholar recorded it; it is said with a fatha on the mim, a damma on the doubled taa' with two dots, a sukun on the waw, a fatha on the lam, and a kha' with a dot, son of Akhnukh, with a hamza with a fatha at its beginning, a sukun on the kha' with a dot, a damma on the nun, a sukun on the waw, and also a kha'; its meaning in that language, as it is said, is "the readers"; and it is said: Khunukh, with the hamza dropped, and he is Idris (peace be upon him)). Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Asakir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Noah (peace be upon him) was sent in the second millennium, and Adam (peace be upon him) did not die until Noah was born to him at the end of the first millennium. Both transmitted from Muqatil and Juwaybir that when Adam (peace be upon him) grew old and his bones became fragile, he said: "O Lord, until when shall I strain and strive?" He said: "O Adam, until a child is born to you who is circumcised." So Noah was born to him after ten generations, and at that time he was a thousand years minus sixty years old. He was sent, as is narrated from Ibn Abbas, at the completion of four hundred years. Muqatil said: he was a hundred years old. It is said: he was fifty years old. It is said: he was two hundred and fifty years old. He remained calling his people for nine hundred and fifty years, and he lived after the flood two hundred and fifty years, so his lifespan was one thousand four hundred and fifty years.

He was sent from al-Jazirah, as Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir narrated from Qatadah. He was the first prophet whom Allah punished his people, and he met from them what no other prophet among the prophets, peace be upon them, had met.

Scholars differed about the universality of his mission at its inception, while there is agreement on its universality at its end, since after the flood none remained except those who were with him in the ship. The view of universality does not detract from the fact that this is among the special features of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because what is among his special features (peace be upon him) is the universality of the mission to all of the two species, jinn and humankind. This is agreed upon and known by necessity from the religion, so whoever denies it is a disbeliever. Indeed, the angels as well, as was preferred by a group of verifiers such as al-Subki and those who followed him, and they refuted whoever opposed that, citing the explicit verse ﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾, since "the worlds" are all that is other than Allah, Exalted. The report in Muslim, "I have been sent to all creation," supports this. Indeed, al-Barizi said that he (ﷺ) was sent even to inanimate objects after they were made perceptive.

The benefit of sending to the infallible and to the non-accountable is seeking their submission, due to his nobility, their entry under his call, and their following him, as an honour above the rest of the messengers. This is not the case with the mission of Noah (peace be upon him), and the difference is as clear as the morning. He, as al-Qamus said, is a non-Arabic name that is made diptote due to its lightness. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Juwaybir and Muqatil reported that he (peace be upon him) was only named Noah because of how much he wailed (naha) over himself. The cause of this has been disputed: it is said that it was his supplication against his people for destruction; it is said that it was his returning to his Lord regarding his son Kan'an; it is said that he passed by a mangy dog and said to it, "Begone, O ugly one," so Allah revealed to him, "Did you find fault with Me, or with the dog?" It is also said that it was the persistence of his people in disbelief, so whenever he called them and they turned away, he wept and wailed over them. It is said that his name before was al-Sakan, for people's inclination toward him after Adam (peace be upon him); and it is said: Abd al-Jabbar. I do not rely on any of these reports. What I rely on is what is apparent: that it is a name given to him when he was born, and it is not derived from lamentation, and that, as the author of al-Qamus said,

﴿So he said: "O my people, worship Allah"﴾, meaning Him alone, and the restriction to Him was left out to indicate that this is worship in its true sense; as for worship alongside association, there is no worship at all. And by the indication of His words, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾, meaning one deserving of worship. ﴿Other than Him﴾ is a resumptive clause given to justify the mentioned worship or the command to it. "Min" is an extra particle, and "ghayr" in the nominative, which is the reading of the majority, is an adjective of "ilah," or a substitute for it in view of its position, which is the nominative, either as subject or as agent.

Al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive, in view of its form. It was read irregularly in the accusative as an exception. The rule of "ghayr," as in al-Mufassal, is the rule of the noun following "illa," which is the well-known view, meaning: "You have no god except Him," like your saying, "There is no one in the house except Zayd, other than Zayd." If "ilah" is made the subject, then "lakum" is its predicate; or its predicate is omitted, and "lakum" serves for specification and clarification, meaning: "You have, in existence or in the world, no god other than Allah, exalted." ﴿Indeed I fear for you﴾ if you do not worship as I have been commanded. The estimate "if you do not believe" is given because His worship, glory be to Him and exalted, entails belief in Him, which is its most important kind. He (peace be upon him) said "I fear" and did not state it definitively, out of tenderness toward them and to win them over gently.

﴿the punishment of a great day﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection, or the Day of the Flood, since he knows best its occurrence if they do not comply. The clause, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is a justification for the worship by explaining what deters from abandoning it, following the justification by explaining what motivates it. Describing the day as great is to show the magnitude of what happens in it and to complete the warning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 60:

﴿The chiefs of his people said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the narration of his words, peace be upon him, and his counsel to his people, as if it were said: "What did they say after that was said to them?" So it was answered: "[The chiefs] said..." etc. The mala' (chiefs, the assembly of notables), according to al-Farra', are the group of men specifically, and many have interpreted it as "the nobles who fill hearts with their dignity, eyes with their beauty, and gatherings with their followers." It was also said: they were called mala' because they are capable (mali'un) and able to fulfill what is required of them in managing affairs. ﴿Indeed, we see you in error﴾ meaning: in going astray from the path of truth. The seeing here is of the heart (qalbiyyah), and its two objects are the pronoun and the adverbial phrase. It was also said that it is visual (basariyyah), in which case the adverbial phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿Clear﴾ (60), meaning: manifest in its being error.

(qala) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) in the same style as its predecessor:

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 7, verse 61]**

﴿O my people﴾: he addressed them by attributing them to himself, to win them over towards the truth. ﴿There is no error in me﴾: this is a negation of error from his noble self in the most emphatic form. The *ta'* here is for the single instance (*al-marrah*), because the context of emphasis in the reply to their foolish statement requires it. The unity (*al-wahdah*) understood from it is taken in terms of the smallest amount that can be applied, so the meaning returns to: "There is in me not even the least trace of error, let alone manifest error." As for what may occur to the mind, that negating the quiddity (*al-mahiyyah*) is more emphatic, since negating a thing together with the qualifier of unity may be achieved by the absence of unity in favour of plurality, this is dispelled by the fact that unity is not a restricting attribute. Rather, the word is applied to the smallest part, which is the single one that exists together with plurality and without it. Moreover, considering the qualifier of unity in a general term within a context of negation is also rejected. Consider "*lā rajula shāhidan*" (there is no man as a witness), for it is applied to the single one of the genus, and on this basis he distinguished between it and "*Usāmah*". When it occurs as a general term, that is not considered. Even if it were granted that one may say "*laysa bihi ḍalālatun wāḥidah*" (there is in him not one error), but rather various errors at the outset, it is not permissible in a context of contrast, as in our case. This is what he said in *al-Kashf*, and with it is answered what was raised against *al-Kashshaf* in this place.

In *al-Mathal al-Sa'ir* (of Ibn al-Athir): singular nouns that denote a genus, and between them and one of their units there is the feminine *tā'* (*tā' al-ta'nith*), when negation is intended, the use of the singular is more emphatic, and when affirmation is intended, the use of the form with the *tā'* is more emphatic, as in this verse. It should not be thought that, since *ḍalāl* and *ḍalālah* are both verbal nouns from your saying *ḍalla yaḍillu ḍalālan wa ḍalālah*, the two statements are equal, because *ḍalālah* here is not an expression for the verbal noun but for the single instance and the negation, as you have come to know. He, peace be upon him, emphasised the negation only because of their emphasis in affirming, since they made him, and far be it from him, to be fixed in manifest error, the fact of its being error being clear.

And His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿But I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾ (61). This is a corrective (*istidrāk*) following what precedes it, removing what might be imagined from it. This is, as is said, because when the people attributed error to him, they meant by it his abandoning the religion of the forefathers and his claim to prophethood. So when he negated error, it was imagined from it that he was upon the religion of his forefathers and had abandoned the claim to prophethood. Therefore the information came that he is a Messenger and firm upon the straight path, as a corrective to that. It has also been said: it is a corrective following what precedes it in terms of what it entails, namely that he is at the furthest stage of guidance, for his being a messenger from the Lord of the worlds necessarily entails this. It is as if it were said: "There is in me nothing of error, but I am at the utmost extreme of guidance." The summary of this, according to what al-Ṭībī established, is that *lākinna* ought to come between two statements that differ in negation and affirmation, and the difference here is established in terms of meaning, as in your saying: "Zayd came to me, but ʿAmr was absent." The purpose of turning away from the apparent form is to intend emphasis in affirming guidance to the utmost possible, just as he negated error entirely. He also took the path of elaboration (*iṭnāb*), because this corrective is an addition beyond the answer, since his saying "There is no error in me" was sufficient in it. Therefore it is from the wise method (*al-uslūb al-ḥakīm*), which comes to make a transition (*takhallus*) to the call, in the manner of moral return (*al-tarjīʿ al-maʿnawī*), because he began with calling to affirm monotheism and sincere worship of God, the Exalted. When he wished to affirm prophethood, he could not do so when they objected to him with their saying ﴿Indeed, we see you in manifest error﴾. So he seized the opportunity and incorporated his purpose into the reply in the best manner, bringing it out in the form of gentleness and even-handed speech. That is, "Leave off attributing error to me, and consider what is more important for you: following your counsellor and trustworthy one, the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds. Do you not see that Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him, when they did not object to him, followed the affirmation of prophethood with the affirmation of monotheism?" So in this verse there are five kinds of *badīʿ* (rhetorical embellishment). When the context requires this elaboration, limiting oneself to the concise expression is a shortcoming. End.

It is not hidden that this corrective is not the corrective in the well-known sense. Many scholars of Arabic have stated that the corrective in *lākinna* is that it attributes to what follows it a ruling that is contrary to what precedes it, whether the two differ in affirmation and negation or not. Ṣāḥib *al-Basīṭ* and a group explained it as removing what is supposed to be established. The full discussion of this is in *al-Mughnī*. Taking the implied meaning to achieve the corrective in the second sense is hardly acceptable, because no mind goes to the thought, from the negation of error from himself, that the addressee might suppose that the prophethood is also negated just as error is negated, so that he corrects it with *lākinna*, as in your saying: "Zayd is not a jurist, but he is a physician." And you know that this, if it does not return to what was established first, is nothing. It has also been said: when one of two opposites is negated, the mind immediately goes to the negation of the other opposite, not to the negation of things unrelated to it. For this reason, what occurs in the context of the corrective is interpreted as what is opposed to error, for example, one says: "Zayd is not standing, but he is sitting." One does not say "but he is drinking" except after interpretation, that the drinker is sitting.

Some of the excellent scholars of the Romans said: the correct view on this corrective is that it is like his saying:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords*
*are notched by the clashing of the battalions."*

And his saying:

*"He is the full moon, except that he is the surging sea;*
*other than that he is the lion, but he is the rain-cloud."*

It is as if it were said: "There is in me no error, and no fault, except that I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds." And you know that this kind is called by them *ta'kīd al-madḥ bi-mā yushbihu al-dhamm* (affirming praise through what resembles blame). It has two types: one in which, from a negated blameworthy attribute of a thing, an exception is made by an attribute of praise for that thing, on the supposition that it is included in the negated attribute of blame; and one in which an attribute of praise is established for a thing, and this is followed by an exceptive particle, after which comes another attribute of praise for it. The apparent view is that what is in the verse is of the first type, except that it is not free of interpretation, so consider this.

And *min* in it is for the beginning of the extent (*ibtidāʾ al-ghāyah*) in a metaphorical sense, and it is connected to an omitted element which occurs as a qualifier of "Messenger", confirming what the nunation (*tanwīn*) indicates of grandeur in essence. It is as if it were said: "I am a messenger originating from the Lord of the worlds."

The verse ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that continues the discourse without grammatical attachment), brought to affirm his prophethood and to detail its rulings and conditions. Abu al-Baqa' and others allowed that it could be another qualifier (*sifa*) of a messenger, taking the sense of the pronoun in "Indeed I," since it is an expression for that pronoun. This is like the words of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, when he came out against Marhab the Jew on the day of Khaybar:

I am the one whom my mother named Haydara,
like a lion of the thickets, fearsome in appearance.

I give them full measure with the *sa'* (a dry measure),
the measure of *al-sandara*.

He did not say "named him" (*sammathu*) but treated the word in terms of its sense, since there is no ambiguity. Some scholars held that it must be taken as a resumptive clause, claiming that what was mentioned is ugly, to the point that al-Mazini said: "Were it not for its fame, I would have rejected it." Al-Shihab responded to this by saying that what al-Mazini mentioned concerns the relative clause (*sila*) of a relative pronoun, not the qualifying of an indefinite noun (*nakira*), for it occurs in the Qur'an, as in ﴿Rather you are a people who are ignorant﴾. Its goodness has been stated in books of grammar and rhetoric. Its being in the relative clause too, as he mentioned, is rejected by the scholars of verification (*muhaqqiqun*), even though Ibn Jinni followed him in this, to the point that he deemed the saying of al-Mutanabbi contemptible:

I am the one whom the blind man looked upon with my refinement.

In *al-Intisaf* it is stated that it is good in usage, and the generosity of Abu al-Hasan is the most truthful witness to what he said, and to the goodness of the speech of Ibn al-Husayn. This, as al-Shihab said, applies when the pronoun is not postponed, as in *alladhi qara al-duyuf ana* ("the one who hosted the guests, I"), or when it is used for comparison, as in *ana fi al-shaja'a alladhi qatala Marhaba* ("I am, in courage, the one who killed Marhab").

Abu 'Amr read *Ublighukum* with a sukun on the *ba'* and a light *lam*, from *al-iblagh* (conveying). The plural *al-risalat* (messages) is used although the message of each prophet is one, and it is a verbal noun (*masdar*). The basic principle is that it should not be pluralized, out of regard for the differences in its times, or for the variety of the meanings with which he, peace be upon him, was sent. Or he intended his own message and the messages of others before him among the prophets, such as Idris, peace be upon him, to whom thirty scrolls were revealed, and Shith, peace be upon him. After the statement of its generality to "the worlds," this is to indicate the reason for the ruling, which is conveying His message to them. His lordship (*rububiyya*) over them is one of the requirements of obeying His command to convey His message.

﴿And I give you sincere advice﴾: that is, I seek out what is good for you, on the basis that sincere advice (*nusḥ*) is the pursuit of that, whether by word or deed. It has also been said that it is making known the aspect of benefit together with purity of intention from any trace of harm. The meaning here is: I convey to you the commands and prohibitions of Allah, I encourage you to accept them, and I warn you of His punishment if you disobey Him.

The basic meaning of *nusḥ* in the language is purity. It is said: "I purified the honey" (*nasahtu al-'asal*) when I separated it from the wax. It is also said that it is derived from "a man's *nusḥ* of his garment," when he sewed it. They likened the act of the advisor, in what he seeks of the welfare of the one advised, to the act of the tailor in mending a gap in a garment. It is also used to mean purity of love for the one advised, and diligence in what his right requires. On this basis is understood what Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Tamim al-Dari, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the religion is sincere advice." We said: "For whom, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "For Allah, for His Book, for His Messenger, for the leaders of the Muslims and their common people."

It is said: *nasahtuhu* and *nasahtu lahu*, just as one says *shakartuhu* and *shakartu lahu*. It has been said that the *lam* is brought here so that the speech indicates that the purpose is nothing other than advice, and that the advice is not for their benefit in the sense that its benefit returns to them and not to him, peace be upon him, as in His saying: ﴿I do not ask you any reward for it﴾. This is based on the *lam* being for specification (*ikhtisas*), not an extra (*za'ida*) particle. The apparent sense of some scholars' statements indicates that it is nonetheless extra, but there is ambiguity in this.

Page 153

The use of the present tense indicates the renewal of his giving advice to them, peace be upon him, as made clear by His saying: ﴿My Lord, I have called my people night and day﴾. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ (62) is coordinated (*'atf*) with what precedes it and affirms his prophethood, peace be upon him. That is: I know, from Him, may He be exalted, through revelation, things you have no knowledge of, from the matters that are to come. Thus *min* is for the beginning of the end (*ibtida' al-ghaya*) figuratively, or it means: I know, from His affairs, may He be mighty and majestic, His overpowering might and His severe seizing of those who do not believe in Him and do not accept His messengers, what you do not know. Thus *min* is either partitive (*lil-tab'id*) or explanatory (*bayaniyya*) of *ma* (what), and in both cases an omitted noun must be supposed.

It has been said: they had not heard of a people upon whom punishment had descended before them, so they were secure and heedless, not knowing what Noah, peace be upon him, knew. Thus they were the first people to be punished for their disbelief.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 63:

﴿Or do you wonder that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord﴾. This is a rebuttal of what gave rise to their saying: ﴿Indeed, we see you in manifest error﴾. The interrogation (istifham) is for denial, meaning: why should that be, when there is no cause for it? The wāw is the conjunctive wāw (wāw al-'atf) coordinating with an implied element that the discourse extends over. According to al-Zamakhshari and his followers, something is understood between the hamzah (the interrogative particle) and the conjunctive wāw, as if it were said: "Do you consider it unlikely, and do you wonder?" According to Sibawayh and the majority, the hamzah is part of the conjoined element itself, but it has been placed before the conjunctive particle to draw attention to its original position at the head of the sentence. The view of the first group has been regarded as weak because of the artificiality it involves, in that it claims the omission of a clause. If it is objected that this is matched by the fronting of part of the conjoined element, it may be said that this is easier than that, because the figurative extension in it is smaller in wording, and it draws attention to the originality of one thing within another. Also, this practice is not consistent, as in ﴿Then is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾. Its full verification belongs in its proper place. ﴿That there has come to you﴾ is construed with an implied "bi-anna" (that), because the preceding verb is transitive with it. By "the reminder" is meant what was sent down with him, just as the Qur'an is called a reminder. It may be interpreted as admonition. The min is for origin (ibtida'), and the prepositional phrase is either related to "jā'a" (came) or to an implied element which occurs as a qualifier of "dhikr", meaning: a reminder issuing from the Master of your affairs and your Sustainer.

﴿upon a man from among you﴾: that is, from among your number, whose birth and upbringing you know; or from your kind. In the latter case, min is partitive (tab'īḍiyyah) or explanatory (bayāniyyah), as has been said. ʿAlā (upon) is related to "jā'a" with an implied noun, meaning: upon the hand or tongue of a man from among you, that is, through him. It has also been said that ʿalā is in the sense of maʿa (with), so no implied element is needed. It has been said that it is related to "unzila" (was sent down), since its meaning is that, as the words of Abu al-Baqa' indicate, or because its meaning is implied in the verb. It is also permitted that it be related to an implied element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "dhikr", meaning: descending upon a man from among you. ﴿That he may warn you﴾ is the cause (ʿillah) of the coming, meaning: that he may caution you against the punishment and the retribution for disbelief and sins. ﴿And that you may fear God﴾ is conjoined to ﴿that he may warn you﴾, and likewise His words, exalted is He: ﴿and that perhaps you may receive mercy﴾ (63), according to what is apparent. Thus the coming is motivated by three things, and this is not the disallowed convergence of multiple causes upon one effect. Between them there is a sequence in reality, for warning is a cause of piety, and piety is a cause of the attachment of mercy to them. The sentence does not indicate that each of the three is the cause of what follows it; had causation been intended, the particle fa' (so) would have been used. Some have regarded the conjunction of "that you may fear God" to "that he may warn you", and of "and that perhaps you may receive mercy" to "that you may fear God", while observing the sequence, meaning: that you may fear God because of the warning, and that perhaps you may receive mercy because of piety. This should be considered carefully.

The particle of hope (ḥarf al-tarajjī) was used in accordance with the custom of great persons in their promises, or to draw attention to the rarity of the aim, and that mercy is dependent upon the bounty of God, exalted is He, so there is no reliance except upon Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 64:

﴿So they denied him﴾ i.e., they persisted in denying him and insisted (on their disbelief) after he had said to them what he said and called them to God, the Exalted, night and day. ﴿Then We saved him﴾ from the drowning. The word "invoking salvation" (al-inja') in the Surah of the Poets (al-Shu'ara') refers to deliverance from the intent of God's enemies and from the evil of what they had plotted against him, peace be upon him. ﴿And those who were with him﴾ of the believers, who, as has been said, were forty men and forty women; and it has been said that they were ten: his three sons and six others who believed in him, peace be upon him. The fa' (then) here indicates causation, with reference to the drowning, and is not the fa' of fasiha (the fa' that implies an omitted condition). His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿in the ship﴾, i.e., the ark, is connected to what the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) that serves as the relative clause (silah) is connected to, i.e., "they settled with him in the ship."

It is also permitted that the ship itself be the relative clause, with "with him" (ma'ahu) connected to what it is connected to, and that it be connected to "We saved him," with the sense of location (zarfiyyah) or causation (sababiyyah). It is also permitted that it be connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial state (hal) of "those who" (alladhina) itself or of their pronoun. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾, i.e., they persisted in denying them. What is meant by this includes those chieftains and others among the obstinate deniers. The mention of salvation before drowning is for the sake of hastening to report it and to signal that mercy precedes wrath. ﴿Indeed they were a blind people﴾ (64), i.e., blind of heart as to knowledge of monotheism, prophethood and the Resurrection, as related from Ibn 'Abbas; or blind to the descent of punishment upon them, as transmitted from Muqatil. It is also read as ('amin) "blinded" (a variant reading). The first meaning is more eloquent, because it is a descriptive adjective (sifah mushabbahah), which indicates permanence. Its original form is 'amiyyin, which was lightened. Some have distinguished between 'amin and 'amin, holding that the first is for blindness of insight and the second for blindness of sight, and they recited the verse of Zuhayr:

"I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it, but concerning the knowledge of what is in tomorrow I am blind."

It has also been said that both are the same in meaning.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 65:**

﴿And to ʿĀd﴾ is attached to an implied verb, coordinated with ﴿We sent﴾ earlier. That implied verb is what governs the phrase ﴿their brother﴾, meaning: "And We sent to ʿĀd their brother." It has also been said that there is no implied verb, and that the whole phrase is coordinated with the preceding phrase, with the governing verb being the one already mentioned. The construction was changed for the sake of the pronoun in ﴿their brother﴾, because if it had been stated in the same pattern as the first, the pronoun would have referred to something coming after it, both in wording and in rank. ʿĀd was originally the name of the tribe's ancestor (ab al-qabilah), and then the tribe or group (al-hayy) was named after him. Therefore it may be treated as diptote (ṣarf) or as not diptote (ʿadam al-ṣarf), as Sibawayh mentioned.

The phrase ﴿Hud﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿their brother﴾ or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it. It is well known that it is an Arabic name, but the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's statement is that it is foreign (aʿjamī). This view is supported by what has been said: that the first of the Arabs was Yaʿrub, who was Hud ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also held this view. Some who hold this opinion said that Nuh was the paternal cousin of the father of ʿĀd. It has also been said that he was the son of ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and it has been said that he was the son of ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabah ibn al-Khulud ibn ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him.

The meaning of his, peace be upon him, being their brother is that he was of their lineage (nasaban). This is the view of most of the genealogists (al-nassabin). Those who do not hold this view say that what is meant is that he was their companion and one of them, as one would say, "O brother of the Arabs." The wisdom in a prophet being sent to a people from among themselves is that they understand his speech better than the speech of others, and they know his circumstances better, including his truthfulness, his trustworthiness, and the nobility of his lineage.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf bayani), as if it were asked: "What did he say to them when he was sent to them?" So it was answered: "He said..." etc. The particle fa (then) was not used here as it was in the story of Nuh, because Nuh was persistent in calling his people, not delaying in responding to their doubts for a single moment. Hud, peace be upon him, did not go to this extreme, so the sequential connection (taʿqib) appears in Nuh's speech but does not appear here.

The author of al-Fara'id, in distinguishing between the two stories, mentioned that the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, is a beginning of speech, so the question is not required by the context. But the story of Hud was coordinated with the story of Nuh, so it may occur to the listener: "Did Hud say what Nuh said, or did he say something else?" Thus it was likely to be asked, "What did he say to his people?" So it was answered: "He said..." etc.

It has also been said that the disjunction (fasl) was chosen here to indicate that each of the sentences is independent in meaning, since the disbelief of these people was greater than the disbelief of the people of Nuh, in that they knew what Allah, exalted is He, had done to the disbelievers and yet persisted. The people of Nuh did not know this. What indicates their knowledge of this is what will come within the verses. However, this needs examination.

Page 155

﴿O my people, worship Allah﴾ alone, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ indicates. This is a resumptive clause functioning as an explanation (bayan) of the worship commanded and as a reason (taʿlil) for it, or as a reason for the command. It is as if it were said: "Devote worship to Him, and do not associate anything with Him, for you have no god besides Him."

The word (ghayru) has been recited with all three vowel-endings, as in the previous (ghayru) case. ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ is a rebuke and an expression of surprise at their not being wary of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, despite their not having known what befell the people of Nuh, peace be upon him. As Shaykh al-Islam said, he addressed them with each of the two (phrases), and he suffices with recounting each of them in one place rather than recounting it in another place. Likewise, he did not mention here what he mentioned there, such as His saying ﴿You are nothing but fabricators﴾. Apply the same to the condition of the rest of what was mentioned, and of the parts of the story not mentioned. Indeed, the condition of their counterparts in the other stories applies, especially in the exchanges that took place at multiple times.

Others have said: the reason ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ is said here, whereas in the earlier address of Nuh, peace be upon him, to his people, it was said ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾, is that these people had already known what had befallen their likes, and there had been no event before the event of the people of Nuh, peace be upon him. It has also been said: because these people were closer to the truth and to answering the call than the people of Nuh, peace be upon him. This is less than ﴿Indeed I fear for you﴾ etc. in terms of warning, and what guides to this is what preceded together with His saying, exalted is He:

﴿The chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said﴾. Here the obstinate chiefs are specified as "those who disbelieved," whereas elsewhere the term is left unqualified. They have stated that this description was given because not all of them were disbelievers. Among the nobles there were some who believed in him, peace be upon him, such as Marthad ibn Sa'd, who used to conceal his faith. This was not the case with the people of Noah. Those among them who believed in him, peace be upon him, were not of the nobles, as is generally the case with those who follow the messengers, peace be upon them. It has also been said that at the time Noah, peace be upon him, addressed his people, they had not yet believed, unlike the people of Hud. Al-Shihab said that a similar view requires transmission (from authorities). Mawla Baha' al-Din objected to this distinction between the two peoples, saying that in Surat al-Mu'minun the people of Noah are described with the same description that is applied to the people of Hud here, so how can this distinction not hold? It was answered that the description there is to be understood as expressing blame, not as distinguishing, and that the reason it does not blame them here is to indicate the distinction.

Al-Tibi said: It may be said that the description here also expresses blame, and the context requires their blame because of the intensity of their obstinacy, as is indicated by their reply, which Allah the Exalted related: ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾, meaning, firmly established in a lightness of mind, in that you have abandoned the religion of your fathers, ﴿and indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾ (66), in that you have claimed prophethood. And this is more emphatic than "liar" (kadhiban), as the indication of this has already passed. The word "think" (zann) is either in its literal sense, as al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj said, or in the sense of "know," as has been said. That is because they said what they said while he, peace be upon him, was known among them for the opposite of that. This does not entail blaming the people of Noah, peace be upon him. Where blame is entailed in Surat al-Mu'minun, it is because they said, as Allah the Exalted related there: ﴿This is only a man like yourselves who wishes to make himself superior to you. Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our earliest fathers﴾, and ﴿He is only a man possessed by madness, so wait for him for a time﴾.

Some of them said: The apparent meaning is that what is related here about the people of Noah, peace be upon him, was their statement in one gathering, or the statement of some of them, while what is related in Surat al-Mu'minun was their statement in another gathering, or the statement of others. So the requirement of each of the two statements was observed in its own setting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 67:

﴿Qāla﴾ (he said), peace be upon him, seeking their goodwill or winning their hearts: ﴿"O my people, there is no folly in me"﴾, not even a trace of it, let alone my being mired in it as you claimed,
Page 156
﴿"but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾

(67) Messengership from Him, exalted is He, necessarily entails possessing the utmost degree of right guidance and truthfulness. The Prophet, peace be upon him, did not explicitly deny lying, being content with what is implied within the context of the contrastive particle (istidrak). It has also been said: lying is a type of folly, so negating folly necessarily entails negating it. The preposition ﴿min﴾ (from) indicates the starting point of the source, used figuratively, and it is related to an omitted element that occurs as a descriptor of "messenger," emphasizing what the nunation (tanwin) conveyed of intrinsic grandeur with the grandeur of the annexation (idafah).

And His saying, ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord﴾, is in the same manner as what is in the story of Noah, peace be upon him.

Abu 'Amr recited "ubligukum" (أُبْلِغُكم) with the lightened form from the verb of the form if'āl (al-if'āl, the causative form). ﴿And I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you﴾ (68). He is known for sincere counsel and trustworthiness, and famous among people for that; so how could I be accused of any of the things you have mentioned? On this reading, no complement is supposed for the two attributes. It is also possible to supply a complement for them, meaning: a sincere adviser to you in what I call you to, and trustworthy regarding what I tell you, not lying in it. On the first reading, as al-Tibi said, the sentence is a fresh (resumptive) clause that falls in as a parenthetical insertion; on the second reading it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah). The shift from the verbal to the nominal sentence has its own significance, which is not hidden. Perhaps the use of the nominal form here, and the verbal form in what preceded, is to indicate the renewal (tajaddud) of the counsel coming from Noah, rather than Hud, peace be upon them both.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 69:

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you?﴾ The discussion here is like the discussion of the previous verse. The prophets, peace be upon them, when the disbelievers address them with foolish words, such as what is reported of them, and when they turn away from answering them in kind, show complete sincere counsel, compassion, self-abasement and fine argumentation. Relating this contains instruction for the servants on how to address the foolish and how to overlook them and let their own skirts trail over what they do. The verse also indicates that it is permissible to praise a person when there is a need for it.

﴿And remember when He made you successors﴾ This begins an explanation of the ordering of the rulings on sincere counsel, trustworthiness and warning, and their details. The word *idh* (when), as some have understood and others have stated explicitly, is an adverbial complement (*zarf*, of time or place) in the accusative, governed by a verb implied here (*ala'*, "blessings" or "favours"), as indicated by what follows it, because it carries the meaning of a verb. Many scholars, following al-Zamakhshari, have chosen that it is the object of *udhkuru* (remember), meaning: remember this time which contains these great favours. The directing of the command to remember toward the time rather than toward what occurred in it, although what is intended in essence is the latter, is for emphasis on the obligation of remembering it, and because when the time is brought to mind, it is present with all its details. This is based on a broad use of the adverbial complement, or on the view that it is not necessarily locative, contrary to what is well known among the grammarians. The *wa* (and) is conjunctive. It has been said that what follows it is coordinated with the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿worship Allah﴾, but its remoteness is clear.

Shaykh al-Islam said: Perhaps it is coordinated with an implied element, as if it were said: Do not wonder at that, or reflect, so that He may command you, and remember when He made you successors ﴿after the people of Nuh﴾, that is, in their dwellings or in the land, by making you kings, for Shaddad ibn 'Ad was among those who ruled the inhabited parts of the earth. The attribution on this view is figurative. In the mention of Nuh, it has been said, there is an indication of removing the wonder, meaning: what I have brought is not an innovation. So remember Nuh and his being sent to his people, and the threat and warning, that is, remember the destruction of his people for their denial of the Messenger of their Lord. ﴿And He increased you in creation﴾, that is, in creating and shaping, or in the number of created beings, meaning He increased you among people above your like ﴿in stature﴾, meaning strength and increase of body. Al-Kalbi said: the height of the tallest of them was one hundred cubits, and the height of the shortest was sixty cubits.

Ibn 'Asakir reported from Wahb that he said: the head of a man among them was like a great dome, and his eye would have wild beasts nesting in it. 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada that he said: It was mentioned to us that they were twelve cubits tall. And from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him: they were as if they were tall palm trees, and a man among them would come to a mountain and break off with his hand a great piece of it.

(Page 157)

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayra: If one of them took a door-leaf of stone, even if five hundred of this community gathered around it, they would not be able to lift it. And if one of them put his foot into the ground, it would sink into it.

And from some of them: one of them was taller than the rest of creation by the measure of a person stretching his hand up over his head. So the height of each of them was a stature and a stature-plus-spread. This is closer, to those of short intellect, to grasping the length of the hand of power.

Ishaq ibn Bishr and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that Hud, upon him be peace, was the most handsome of them in face, and he was of a physique like theirs, white, with straight hair, his beard visible at the lower lip and his beard long, (may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him).

*Basta tan* (stature/expansion) is in the accusative as the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*) of the verb before it. It has been said that it is a specifier (*tamyiz*). *Fi al-khalq* (in creation) is connected to the verb. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be connected to an implied element which stands as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of *basta tan*.

﴿So remember the favours of Allah﴾, that is, His blessings, glory be to Him and exalted is He. They are the plural of *ili* (with kasra, then sukun, like *himl* and *ahmal*), or *ulu* (with damma, then sukun, like *qufl* and *aqfal*), or *ila* (with kasra, then fatha, as a defective noun, like *mi'an* and *am'a'*), or with two fathas as a defective noun, like *qafa* and *aqfa'*. Both forms are used in the verse of al-A'sha:

"White, who strikes fear into hunger, does not cut ties of kinship, and does not break a pledge."

It has been said that the *ma* in the line is *illa* with the shadda, but it was lightened, and its meaning is covenant. This is remote.

This repetition is a reminder for the sake of greater affirmation, and a generalization after a specification, meaning: remember the favours of which the aforementioned are a part. ﴿That perhaps you may prosper﴾ (69). That is, so that the mention of the blessings may lead you to thank Him, of which the practice of the limbs and obedience is a part, leading to deliverance from distress and attainment of the sought goal. This is because prosperity is not merely the result of remembrance. Some of the people have interpreted the mention of the favours as their thanking, and the order of consequence upon it is evident.

**Qāla** [They said], answering those great admonitions, which contained a warning, as has been pointed out: **"Have you come to us that we should worship Allah alone** [wahdahu]**"**, meaning, that we should single Him out for worship, **"and abandon** [wa-nadhara] **what our fathers used to worship"**, meaning, the idols. This is a denial and a dismissal of his (ʿalayhi al-salām) coming with this message. Its source is their absorption in imitation (taqlīd) and their love for what they had become accustomed to, and what they had found their forefathers upon. As for the meaning of "coming" (al-majī'), it may mean his coming from a place where he used to seclude himself for worship (yataḥannath fīhi), as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to do at Ḥirāʾ before the mission. Or it may mean his coming from the sky, i.e., "you were sent down to us from the sky." Their intention in this is mockery and derision, and this comes from their assumption that a messenger sent by Allah Exalted can only be an angel from the sky. Or it is a metaphor for intending something and beginning it, since *jāʾa*, *qāma*, *qaʿada* and *dhahaba* are, as a number of scholars have said, used by the Arabs for this purpose, to depict the state. So they say *qaʿada yafʿalu kadhā* [he sat down to do such-and-such], *qāma yashtumunī* [he got up to insult me], *qaʿada yaqraʾu* [he sat down to read], and *dhahaba yasubbunī* [he went off to abuse me].

**Waḥdahu** is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative). According to the majority of grammarians, including al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, it is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning *īḥādan* [singling out] the object, placed in the position of the ḥāl, meaning *muwaḥḥidan* [singling out]. These scholars differed regarding the case when you say, for example, *raʾaytu Zaydan waḥdahu* [I saw Zayd alone]. Most of them estimate it as being in the state of singling him out by the seeing, so they make it a ḥāl of the agent (fāʿil). Al-Mubarrad estimates it as being in the state of him being singled out (mufradan) by the seeing, so he makes it a ḥāl of the object (mafʿūl).

Abū Bakr ibn Ṭalḥa prohibited making it a ḥāl of the agent and made it obligatorily a ḥāl of the object only, because when they intend a ḥāl of the agent they say *raʾaytuhu waḥdī* [I saw him by myself] and *marartu bihi waḥdī* [I passed by him by myself], as the poet said:

*"The wolf I fear if I pass by it alone,
and I fear the winds and the rain."*

What he said in the verse is correct, and the two preceding possibilities in *raʾaytu Zaydan waḥdahu* do not thereby become impossible, since the meaning remains valid with both of them. Some say that it is a verbal noun placed in the position of the ḥāl, and according to some, no verb was established for it.

Al-Aṣmaʿī related *waḥdayḥid*. Yūnus and Hishām, in one of his two opinions, went to the view that it is in the accusative in the manner of adverbs of place and time (ẓurūf). So *jāʾa Zaydun waḥdahu* [Zayd came alone] is understood as *jāʾa ʿalā waḥdihi* [came on his own], then the preposition was deleted and it became accusative as an adverb. The preposition *ʿalā* has been explicitly stated in the speech of some Arabs. When it is said *Zaydun waḥdahu*, the estimate is "Zayd is in a place of being alone." Perhaps the one who holds what has been mentioned says it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adverb. And it is said of some that in this usage it is accusative by a hidden verb, as one says *Zaydun iqbālan wa-idbāran* [Zayd (came) advancing and retreating].

This is the essence of their discussion on this topic. Once you have grasped it, know that *naʿbudu Allāha waḥdahu* [we worship Allah alone] is, according to Sībawayh, estimated as *muwaḥḥidīna iyyāhu bil-ʿibādah* [singling Him out in worship], being a ḥāl of the agent, and the *ḥāʾ* in *muwaḥḥidīn* is kasra-vowelled. According to the view of Ibn Ṭalḥa, it is *muwaḥḥadan* [singled out], with the *ḥāʾ* fatḥa-vowelled, and it derives from the quadriliteral *awḥada*. The estimate according to Hishām's view is "we worship Allah Exalted in isolation," and it derives from the triliteral *waḥada*. The meaning does not differ in the three estimates except slightly. The statement in which it occurs contains both affirmation and negation, and it has possibilities both of negation and of affirmation. The detailed treatment of this is in the treatise of our master Taqī al-Dīn al-Subkī entitled *al-Rifda fī maʿnā waḥdahu* [The Gift regarding the meaning of "alone"], and in it al-Ṣafadī says:

*"Leave aside your sleep and wake up to the gift;
you will gather from it knowledge that surpasses the taste of honey."*

By what is in His saying Exalted: **"Then bring us what you promise us"** he meant the punishment indicated by His saying Exalted: **"Will you not then fear (Allah)?"** **"If you are among the truthful"** (70), by informing of its descent. It was also said: by informing that you are a messenger of Allah Exalted to us. The answer to *in* (if) is omitted, being indicated by what has been mentioned, meaning: *fa-</br>*

[Page 158]

*fa-'ti* [then bring it].

﴿He said, "Abomination and wrath have already fallen upon you from your Lord."﴾ That is, it became obligatory and established. The original use of *wuqu'* (falling) is for the descent of physical bodies, and its use here for what has been mentioned is figurative (*majaz*), through the mention of the cause for the effect (*itlaq al-sabab 'ala al-musabbab*). It is also possible that the speech contains a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*), and the meaning is "it has descended upon you." Some have chosen that *waqa'a* here means "decreed and determined," because decreed matters are attributed to the heaven, and the particle of elevation (*harf al-isti'la'*) is clear on that reading. In *al-Kashf* [of Zamakhshari] it is said that *wuqu'* means "establishment," and the particle of elevation is either because it is a strong establishment, the most emphatic and most certain, or because it is a perceptible establishment of a thing descending from above, and the punishment of Allah the Exalted is described as descending from the heaven. So reflect upon this. The expression in the past tense is to present what is anticipated as if it had already occurred, as in His saying, ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾.

﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, from the One who owns your affairs, glorified and exalted is He. The prepositional phrase is said to be connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial (*hal*) for what follows it, but the apparent view is that it is connected to the verb before it. The fronting of the first adverbial phrase over it, although the origin (*mabda'*) precedes the end (*muntaha*), is, as Shaykh al-Islam said, for the sake of hastening to clarify that what is disliked will strike them. Likewise its fronting over the subject, which is His saying, ﴿abomination﴾, together with what that carries of suspense for the delayed element, and because there is a kind of length in what is conjoined to it, His saying, ﴿and wrath﴾. So fronting both of them might disturb the harmony of the noble composition.

*Rijs* (abomination) means punishment, and in this sense it is used throughout the Qur'an according to Ibn Zayd, from *al-irtijas*, and it and *al-irtijaz* have the same meaning, to the extent that it has been said that its origin is that, and the *zay* was changed to *sin*, just as the *sin* was changed to *ta'* in the poet's saying:

"Surely Allah has cursed the sons of al-Sa'alat,
'Amr ibn Yarbu', the worst of the nations.
They are neither chaste nor shrewd."

He meant *al-nas* (people) and *akyas* (the shrewd). Its original meaning is agitation, and then it became common for what is mentioned, because of the agitation of whoever is struck by it. On this basis, the conjunction in His saying:

[p. 159]
"When a drought was spreading over Najd,
and upon them was its abomination and its punishment."

is explanatory. Wrath, according to many, means the intention of retribution. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he explained *rijs* as curse and *ghadab* as punishment, and he recited the verse cited above as evidence, but there is obscurity in this. Those who follow the earlier view explain it as punishment only so that it does not repeat what comes before it. It is not far-fetched to explain *rijs* as punishment and *ghadab* as cursing and expulsion, the reverse of what is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. In that case the speech would contain an allusion to their state in both the first and the second. It is possible to bring what many exegetes have mentioned back to this. Otherwise, the apparent meaning is that there is no subtlety in your saying, "Punishment has descended upon them," and the intention of retribution is in the apparent sense of their speech. Whatever the case, the tanwin (indefiniteness) is for magnification and dread.

﴿Do you dispute with me over names that you have named, you and your fathers?﴾ This is a denunciation and a condemnation of their denial of his coming, peace be upon him, calling them to the worship of Allah alone and to abandoning what their fathers used to worship of idols.

"Names" is an expression for those false idols, and this is like the saying: "It is nothing but a mere name" for what is not fitting. The meaning is: Do you dispute with me over referents for which you have set names that do not suit them? You named them gods, though there is in them no trace whatsoever of the reality of divinity, because the one deserving of worship is none but the one who brought all things into existence, while they have no part in creating even an atom. And if they deserved it, that would be by the appointment of Him, the Exalted, either through sending down a revelation or establishing a proof, and both of these are impossible. This is His saying, ﴿for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾, that is, no proof or evidence. Since that was not within the realm of possibility, the falsity of what they held was established. The blame that the speech conveys is directed at the naming that is empty of meaning, filled with greater error, misguidance, and great fabrication. It has also been said that they named them "creators," "providers," and "sending down rain," and similar things. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿you named them﴾ refers to "names." According to what has been said, it is the first object, and the second object is omitted as indicated. It has also been said that the first object is omitted and the pronoun is the second object, and the meaning is "you named your idols with them."

It has also been said that what is meant by "you named them" is "you described them," so there is no need for it to take two objects. Reading the verse according to what was first mentioned in its explanation is what a group has chosen. Some have permitted that the speech is by omission of a modifier, that is, "Do you dispute with me concerning possessors of names?"

Others have claimed that it is permissible that it contains the rhetorical device of *istikhdam* (a term used for a word bearing two meanings). Those who say that the name is the same as the named have taken evidence from this verse, and so have those who say that languages are *tawqifiyyah* (divinely instituted), for if they were not so, the denial and nullification would not be directed at them as "invented names which Allah has not sent down any authority for." What is wrong with this is not hidden from you.

﴿So wait﴾ for the descent of the punishment that you requested by your saying, ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with﴾, since the truth has become clear while you persist in obstinacy and ignorance. ﴿Indeed, I am with you among those who wait﴾ (71) for its descent upon you. The *fa'* in "so wait" is for sequence following what has preceded.

In the words of His saying, ﴿So We rescued him﴾, the particle *fa* is an *fa-faṣīḥa* (the "eloquent" *fa*, which indicates an implied clause). The meaning is: what happened happened, so We rescued him. ﴿And those who were with him﴾ means those who followed him in the religion. ﴿By a mercy﴾ means a great mercy whose extent cannot be measured. ﴿From Us﴾ means from Our side. The prepositional phrase is related to an omitted verb and functions as an attributive adjective (*naʿt*) of "mercy," emphasizing its magnitude, as has been mentioned more than once before. ﴿And We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs﴾ is a *kināyah* (metonymy) for total annihilation. *Al-dābir* means "the last" or "the end," so the meaning is: We destroyed them completely and obliterated them to the last one. Some scholars have used this verse as evidence that they had no descendants.

﴿And they were not believers﴾ (72). This is coordinated with ﴿denied﴾ and is included with it in the relative clause. The meaning is that they persisted in disbelief and denial and did not refrain from that at all. According to al-Zamakhsharī, the benefit of this negation is *taʿrīḍ* (implicit allusion) toward those among them who did believe. Its explanation, as al-Ṭībī stated, is that when a believer hears that destruction was specific to the deniers, and knows that the cause of salvation is faith, his desire for faith increases and its worth becomes greater in his eyes. A parallel to this, in showing the nobility of faith, is ﴿Those who bear the Throne﴾, and so on. Others have said that the benefit of this is to make clear that, according to what was known of their condition, had God not destroyed them, they would never have believed. As He, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿And We had destroyed generations before you when they wronged, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they would not have believed﴾. So this is like an excuse for not granting them respite and for not being patient with them.

As for the secret of placing the account of the rescue before the account of the destruction, it is known from what has preceded. Their story, as mentioned by al-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and others, is that ʿĀd were a people who lived in al-Aḥqāf, which are sand dunes between ʿUmān and Ḥaḍramawt. They had spread throughout the earth and subjugated its people. They had idols that they worshipped: Ṣudāʾ, Ṣumūd and al-Habāʾ. God, exalted is He, sent to them Hūd, peace be upon him, as a prophet. He was among the most central of them in lineage and the most noble of them in ancestry. He commanded them to monotheism and to refrain from wrongdoing, but they denied him and increased in arrogance and tyranny, saying: "Who is stronger than us in power?" So God withheld rain from them for three years, until this affliction exhausted them. At that time, when a calamity befell people, they would seek its removal from God at His Sacred House, both the Muslim and the polytheist among them. The people of Mecca at that time were the ʿAmālaqa, the descendants of ʿAmlīq ibn Lāwadh ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ, and their chief was Muʿāwiyah ibn Bakr, whose mother was Kahlada from ʿĀd. So ʿĀd dispatched to the Sacred Precinct seventy men from their notables, among them Qīl ibn ʿAnz, Liqīmu ibn Hizāl, Luqmān ibn ʿĀd the Younger, Marthad ibn Saʿd, who used to conceal his Islam, and Jalhama, the maternal uncle of Muʿāwiyah ibn Bakr. When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Muʿāwiyah, who was outside the Sacred Precinct. He lodged and honored them, since they were his maternal uncles and in-laws. They stayed with him for a month, drinking wine, while two singing slave-girls belonging to Muʿāwiyah entertained them. The name of one was Warda and the other Jarāda, and they are called "the two Jarādas" by way of *taghlīb* (naming by the predominant one). When he saw how long they stayed and how absorbed they were in amusement, forgetting what they had come for, it grieved him. He said: "My in-laws and maternal uncles are destroyed, and these are as they are." He was too shy to speak to them, fearing they would think he found their stay burdensome. So he complained of this to his two slave-girls, and they said: "Say a poem that we may sing to them, and they will not know who said it. Perhaps that will move them." So he said:

Ah, O Qīl, woe to you! Rise and hasten, perhaps God will give us rain as a cloud,

So that the land of ʿĀd may be watered, if ʿĀd... ∗∗∗ they have become such that they cannot even speak,

From the severe thirst. There is no one for whom we hope, ∗∗∗ neither the old man nor the boy.

Their women were once in good state, ∗∗∗ but now their women have become sheep without shepherds,

And the wild beasts come to them openly, ∗∗∗ and do not fear the arrows of the people of ʿĀd.

And you are here, in what you desire, ∗∗∗ your day and your night in continual pleasure,

Shameful is your delegation, a delegation of a people ∗∗∗ who did not receive greeting or peace.

When the two girls sang this, some of them said to others: "O people, your people only sent you to seek relief from you from the affliction that has befallen them, and you have been slow to come to them. So enter this Sacred Precinct and ask for rain for your people." Marthad ibn Saʿd said: "By God, you will not be given rain by your supplication, but if you obey your prophet and turn in repentance to your Lord, you will be given rain." At that, he openly declared his Islam and said:

ʿĀd disobeyed their messenger, so they became ∗∗∗ thirsty, and the sky does not moisten them.

For them is an idol called Ṣumūd, ∗∗∗ facing it are Ṣudāʾ and al-Habāʾ.

The Messenger has shown us the path of right guidance, ∗∗∗ so we have seen the guidance, and the blindness has departed.

And that the god of Hūd ∗∗∗ is my God; upon God is reliance and hope.

They said to Muʿāwiyah: "Hold Marthad back from us, so that he does not come with us to Mecca, for he has followed the religion of Hūd and abandoned our religion." Then they entered Mecca to seek rain. Marthad went out from the dwelling of Muʿāwiyah and reached them before they had asked for anything of what they had come for. When he reached them, he stood up and called upon God, exalted is He, saying: "O God, let my request be for myself alone, and do not include me in anything for which the delegation of ʿĀd asks You." Qīl was the head of the delegation. So he prayed and said: "O God, give ʿĀd rain as You used to give them." The people said: "O God, give Qīl what he asks of You, and make our request together with his request." Then God, exalted is He, produced three clouds: a white one, a red one and a black one. Then a caller called out from the sky: "O Qīl, choose for yourself and for your people from these clouds whichever you wish." Qīl said: and God acts in this way toward whoever calls upon Him at that time. Qīl said: "I choose the black one, for it has the most water." The caller called out to him: "You have chosen a fine ash that leaves nothing of the family of ʿĀd alive." God, exalted is He, drove that cloud with what it contained toward ʿĀd, until it came out upon them from a valley called al-Mughīth. When they saw it, they rejoiced and said: "This is a cloud bringing rain to us." But from it there came a barren wind upon them. The first to see it was a woman among them called Muhdar. When she saw it, she clapped her hands. When she regained consciousness, they said: "What did you see?" She said: "I saw a wind in which were sparks like shooting stars, with men in front of it leading it." So God, exalted is He, subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, continuous, and it left no one among them without destroying him. Hūd, peace be upon him, and those with him withdrew into an enclosure, where the wind reached them only in a way that softened their skins and gave pleasure to their souls. Then he, peace be upon him, went with those with him to Mecca, and they worshipped God there until they died. His grave, peace be upon him, is said to be there in the area between the Corner and the Station and Zamzam. In it, as Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sābiṭ, are the graves of seventy-nine prophets, among them Noah, Shuʿayb, Ṣāliḥ and Ismāʿīl, peace be upon them all. Al-Bukhārī in his *Tārīkh*, Ibn Jarīr and others narrated from ʿAlī, may God honor his face, that his grave, peace be upon him, is in Ḥaḍramawt, in a red sand dune, with a lote tree at its head. Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Ibn Abī al-ʿĀtikah who said: "The direction of the mosque of Damascus is the grave of Hūd, peace be upon him." He lived as Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, four hundred and seventy-two years. And God knows best.

* * *

(As for the allusive interpretation of the verses) according to what those people, may God be pleased with them, have said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is God, who created the heavens﴾, meaning the heavens of the spirits, ﴿and the earth﴾, meaning the earth of the bodies, ﴿in six days﴾, which are six thousand years. And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count. These are from the time Adam, peace be upon him, was created until the time of the Prophet ﷺ. In reality, they are from the beginning of the period of the caliphs until the beginning of the manifestation, which is the time of the seal of prophethood and the manifestation of sainthood. ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾, which is the Muḥammadan heart, by complete self-disclosure, which is the disclosure through His all-comprehensive name, which encompasses all attributes. The Sufis have several thrones, which we have pointed out in our book *al-Ṭirāz al-Mudhahhab fī Sharḥ Qaṣīdat al-Bāz al-Ashhab*, and the complete discussion of them is in *Shams al-Maʿārif* by the Imam al-Būnī, may his secret be sanctified. ﴿He covers the night﴾, meaning the night of the body, ﴿with the day﴾, meaning the day of the spirit, ﴿seeking it﴾ through readiness and preparation to receive it, by the balance of its temperament, ﴿swiftly﴾, meaning quickly. ﴿And the sun﴾, meaning the sun of the spirit, ﴿and the moon﴾, meaning the moon of the heart, ﴿and the stars﴾, meaning the stars of the senses, ﴿subjected﴾ by His command, which is the matter mentioned in His saying: ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾. ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, meaning worship Him, ﴿humbly and secretly﴾, which is an indication of the path of manifestation and seclusion. Or it means call upon Him with the limbs and the heart, or by fulfilling the right of servanthood and the demands of the right of lordship. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, those who exceed what they were commanded by abandoning obedience, or those who seek from Him other than Him. ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾,
[Page 162]
