meaning the earth of the body, ﴿after its reformation﴾ through readiness. ﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope﴾, so that there is no neglect of one of the two attributes of majesty and beauty. ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾, meaning the winds of care, ﴿before His mercy﴾, meaning His self-disclosures, ﴿until when they carry﴾, meaning bear, ﴿heavy clouds﴾ with the rains of love, ﴿We drive it to a dead land﴾, meaning a dead heart, ﴿and We send down water therewith﴾, the water of love, ﴿and We bring forth with it of all fruits﴾, meaning of witnessings and unveilings. ﴿Thus We bring out the dead﴾, the dead hearts from the graves of breasts, ﴿that you may remember﴾ the days of your life in the world of spirits, when you were in the gardens of holiness and the pools of intimacy. ﴿And the good land﴾, which is the one whose readiness is good, ﴿its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾, good and abundant in benefit. ﴿And that which is corrupt﴾, which is the one whose readiness is bad, ﴿does not come forth except scantily﴾, with no good in it. ﴿Indeed We sent Noah﴾, meaning the Noah of the spirit, ﴿to his people﴾, from the heart and its helpers, and the soul and its helpers. ﴿So they denied him, and We rescued him and those with him﴾, such as the heart and its helpers, ﴿in the ship﴾, which is the ship of following. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs﴾ in the seas of this world and the waters of desires. ﴿Indeed they were a blind people﴾, blind to the path of arrival and to the vision of God, exalted is He. In this same manner the discourse is woven through the rest of the verses.

Our master, the Greatest Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, has a discourse about these people and others like them, before which thoughts stand bewildered. Whoever wishes it, let him return to the *Fuṣūṣ* and he will see wonders and marvels. And God, exalted is He, is the Guide to the path of right direction.

**[Page 163]**

﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih﴾ is a conjunction with what preceded it, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾. It matches it in fronting the prepositional phrase over the object. (*Thamud*) is a tribe of the Arabs. Their dwellings were al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham, extending to Wadi al-Qura. They were named after their eldest forefather, Thamud ibn 'Amir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. It was also said that he was the son of 'Ad ibn 'Ws ibn Iram, etc. This is what is related from al-Tha'labi.

'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: They were named so because of the scarcity of their water. It comes from *thamad al-ma'* (the water became scant), and *al-thamad* is scant water. It is reported that the word is treated both as diptote (with no *tanwin*, *munsarif* excluded) and as triptote. As for the first case, it is considered with respect to the tribe. Or, because it was originally a name for an ancestor or for a small amount of water, it is inflected as *munsarif* because it is a masculine proper noun or a common noun; after being transferred to a proper name, its original form is retained. As for the second case, it is considered as the name of a tribe, so it has the features of proper-name status and feminine gender.

Salih, upon him be peace, was from Thamud, so the brotherhood is one of lineage. According to what Muhyi al-Sunnah al-Baghawi said, he was the son of 'Ubayd ibn Asaf ibn Mashih ibn 'Ubayd ibn Hadhir ibn Thamud, and he was the brother of Sasm and Judays, as it is said. Wahb said: He was the son of 'Ubayd ibn Jabir ibn Thamud ibn Jabir ibn Sam ibn Nuh. He was sent to his people when he approached puberty. He was a man reddish-white in complexion with straight hair. He remained among them for forty years. Al-Shami said: He was sent as a young man and kept calling his people until his hair turned grey and he grew old. al-Nawawi reported that he remained among them for twenty years, and died in Mecca at the age of fifty-eight.

﴿He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him."﴾ The discussion of its parallels has already passed. ﴿There has certainly come to you a clear sign﴾, i.e., a sign and a miracle, clear in its indication, testifying to my prophethood. It is among the words that function like *al-abtah* and *al-abraq* in being used without mention of the things they describe, in the singular and plural, and with *tanwin* for magnification. That is, a great clear sign from your Lord. The phrase *min rabbikum* is connected to a deleted element that occurs as an attribute of *bayyinah*, as has been stated more than once, or it is connected to *ja'atkum*. Here *min* denotes the starting point, metaphorically, or partition if it is taken as *min bayyinat rabbikum* (some of the clear signs of your Lord). The intended meaning of this clear sign is the she-camel. There is nothing in this speech of his, upon him be peace, that was the first thing he addressed them with, nor the impact of the call to monotheism. Rather, he said it only after advising them and reminding them of the blessings of Allah, exalted is He, but they did not accept his speech and denied him, as the account in Surat Hud indicates.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ is a grammatical resumption (*istinaf nahwi*), used to explain the clear sign and miracle. It is also permitted that it be an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*), an answer to an implied question, whose assumed form is: "what is it?" In both cases the sentence has no place in i'rab. It is also permitted that it be a substitute for *bayyinah*, a substitution of a sentence for a singular noun for explanation, but its remoteness is not hidden.

The attribution of the she-camel to the Name of Majesty is for its magnification, just as one says *Bayt Allah* (the House of Allah) for the mosque, except that the attribution there is for a minimal connection, whereas it is not so in our case. Or, because it was not the product of ordinary gestation and familiar causes, as will become clear to you, if Allah wills. For this reason it was a sign, and what a sign it was. It was also said: because no one owns it but Him, glorified is He. It was also said: because it was the proof of Allah against the people of Salih. The accusative of *ayatan* (as a sign) is as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from *naqatu*, and the governing element in it is the meaning of the demonstrative; the grammarians call this the implicit governing element (*al-'amil al-ma'nawi*). *Lakum* is an explanation of for whom it is a sign, as in *suqya laka* (watering for you), so it is connected to a deleted element. It is also permitted that *naqatun* be a substitute for *hadhihi*, or an explanatory apposition to it, or a second subject, with *lakum* as the predicate. In that case *ayatun* is a circumstantial state from the pronoun concealed in it, and its governing element is either the predicate or its complement.

﴿So leave her﴾ is a branch derived from her being a sign of the signs of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: derived from her being the camel of Allah, glorified is He, for that is something that requires not interfering with her, i.e., so leave her ﴿to eat in the land of Allah﴾, the herbage, and it is omitted because it is known. The verb is in the jussive mood because it is the answer to the imperative.

Abu Ja'far, in one transmission from him, read *ta'kulu* with the nominative. Then the clause is circumstantial, i.e., eating. The prepositional phrase is connected to what is with him, or to the preceding imperative, and so the two are in dispute (*mutanazi'an*). The land is attributed to Allah, glorified is He, to cut off their excuse for interfering with her, as if it were said: the land is the land of Allah, exalted is He, and the camel is the camel of Allah, exalted is He. So leave the camel of Allah to eat in His land. Thus the land is not yours, nor is the vegetation in it from your growing. So what excuse do you have for preventing her? Drinking is not mentioned because eating suffices for it. It was also said that it is for its generality, including drinking, as in his saying:

*"I fed her straw and cold water."*

This was mentioned by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿For her is a share of drinking, and for you is a share on a known day﴾.

﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾ is a prohibition against touching, which is the prelude to striking with evil, encompassing types of harm, as an exaggeration in deterrence. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. The prepositional phrase is connected to the verb, and the indefiniteness is for generality, i.e., do not interfere with her with anything that would harm her at all, such as driving her away, hamstringing her, and other such things. It was also said: the prepositional phrase is connected to a deleted element that occurs as a circumstantial state from the subject of the verb, and the meaning is: do not touch her intending harm to her, let alone striking her. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾.

﴿Lest a painful punishment seize you﴾ (73). It is in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition. The meaning is: do not combine touching her with the seizing of punishment upon you. The latter, although it is not, in literal fact, their doing, is as if it were their doing because they engage in its causes.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 74:

﴿And remember when He made you successors (khulafa) after ʿĀd.﴾ That is, successors in the land, or successors to them. It was said "successors after ʿĀd" rather than "successors of ʿĀd," even though the latter is shorter, to indicate that a long period of time lay between them. ﴿And settled you﴾ means He caused you to dwell and gave you a dwelling place ﴿in the land﴾, that is, the land of al-Hijr between the Hijaz and al-Sham. ﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾ means you build, in its plains, lofty dwellings. Here "min" (from) carries the sense of "fi" (in), as in His saying: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾. It may also be initial (ibtidaʾiyya, indicating origin) or partitive (tabʿidiyya, indicating part), meaning: you make the palaces from material taken from the plain, such as mud bricks and baked bricks made of clay. The prepositional phrase, as Abu al-Baqa said, may be connected to an elided verb that serves as a circumstantial clause (hal) describing what follows; it may be a second object of ﴿you take﴾; or it may be connected to the verb itself, which is transitive to one object. The word "al-sahl" (plain) is the opposite of "al-hazn" (rough, stony ground), which is the place of stones and mountains. The clause is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) explaining how the settling took place, since this taking was by His power, glorified is He. ﴿And you hew out the mountains﴾ means you carve them out. Al-nahṭ (hewing) is well known in every hard substance, and its present-tense form has a kasra on the ḥāʾ.

Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the ḥāʾ, because of a guttural letter. In the Qamus, it is reported from him that he read "tanḥātūna" with a prolonged vowel, like "yanbāʿu." The accusative of "al-jibal" (mountains) is as a direct object. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿houses﴾ is accusative as a prospective circumstantial clause (ḥal muqaddara), because the houses were not yet houses at the time of hewing, just as in "I sewed the garment into a robe" (khiṭtu al-thawba jubbatan). The circumstantial sense, as al-Shihab said, is in terms of the houses being inhabited, if the derivation of the word is held to apply to them. It was also said that the accusative of "al-jibal" is by eliding the preposition, meaning "from the mountains," and this is supported by its occurrence in this form in another verse. "Buyutan" (houses) is accusative as a direct object. It is also permissible that hewing be treated as implying the sense of taking, so that both words are direct objects.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they took the palaces in the plains to spend summer in them, and they hewed houses out of the mountains to spend winter in them. It was also said that they hewed the mountains into houses because of the length of their lifespans, and their buildings would decay before their lives did.

﴿So remember the bounties of Allah﴾, that is, His blessings which He bestowed upon you, of what has been mentioned, or all of His blessings, of which what has been mentioned is included in the first instance. The intent is not mere remembrance by the tongue, as you have come to know.

﴿And do not go about in the land causing corruption﴾ (74). Since His bounties deserve to be thanked and not neglected, how much more so is disbelief. Al-ʿathy means corruption (al-ifsad). So ﴿causing corruption﴾ (mufsidin) is a confirmatory circumstantial clause, as in "(they turned back retreating)" (wallaw mudbirin).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 75:**

﴿The eminent ones (al-mala') of his people who were arrogant said﴾: that is, the nobles who transgressed and grew proud. The sentence is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as has been explained more than once. Ibn 'Amir read *qala* with a *waw* (*wa-qala*), as a conjunction linking it to what precedes it, namely the words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "O my people..."﴾, and so on.

The *lam* in His words, glorified is He, ﴿to those who were deemed weak﴾, means that they were considered weak and abased, and it is the *lam* of delivery (li-l-tabligh), as in *alam aqul lakum* ("Did I not tell you?"). His words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿to those among them who believed﴾, are a substitution (badal) from the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), by repeating the governing particle, the substitution of the whole from the whole (badal al-kull min al-kull), like your saying *marartu bi-Zaydin bi-akhika* ("I passed by Zayd, your brother"). The pronoun in the genitive refers to "his people." It has also been permitted that it be a substitution of part from whole (badal ba'd min kull), on the basis that the pronoun refers to "those who were deemed weak," so that the weakened ones would be of two kinds, believers and disbelievers. Its remoteness is not hidden.

The interrogation in His words, exalted is His majesty, ﴿Do you know that Salih is one sent from his Lord?﴾ is for mockery (istihza'), because they know that they themselves know this. For this reason they did not answer them according to the apparent requirement, as He, glorified is He, related of them in His words: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are believers in that with which he was sent."﴾ (75). For the answer that corresponds to their question would have been "Yes," or "We know that he is sent from Him, exalted is He." From this, more than one scholar said that it is from the wise mode of address (al-uslub al-hakim), so it is as if they said: knowledge of his being sent and of what he was sent with is something about which there is no dispute and no doubt that enters it, because of its clarity and brilliance. The dispute is only about the obligation of believing in it, so we inform you that we are believers in it.

Al-Alusi says that Ibn al-Munir, in *al-Intisaf*, chose that this is not a report about the obligation of believing in it, but about carrying out the obligation, for that is more eloquent than that. So it is as if they said: knowledge of his being sent and of the obligation of believing in it is not what we are asked about; rather, the matter is in carrying out the obligation and acting upon it, and we have already carried it out.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 76:

﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ It is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), as previously mentioned, and the relative pronoun is repeated together with its relative clause, even though a pronoun would have sufficed, to indicate that they said what they said in the manner of insolence and arrogance. ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed﴾ (76). This is also a departure from what the apparent wording requires, which would have been: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which he was sent." Its purpose, as they stated, is to reject what the believers had taken as known and accepted as established; it is as if they said: "What you have made known and established is not of that kind." Al-Alusi (al-Alusi cites al-Intisaf, by Ibn al-Munayyir) said in al-Intisaf: they departed from that wording out of caution regarding what its apparent sense implies, namely their affirmation of his prophethood, while they were denying it. This is not a context of mockery (tahakkum) such that it would resemble the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾, for the aim here is to inform each of the believers and the deniers about his own state. Therefore the disbelievers purified their statement of any implication of acknowledging the message, out of caution for disbelief, and they went to extremes in obstinacy.

**﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾**: that is, they slaughtered her. Al-Azhari said: In the usage of the Arabs, the original meaning of *'aqr* (hamstringing) is cutting the hamstring (*'urqub*) of a camel, and then it was used for slaughtering, because the one who slaughters a camel first hamstrings it and then slaughters it. Attributing the act to all of them, though only some of them actually did it, is a metaphor (*majaz*), because all of them were involved in that act, since it took place among them, and they were in agreement on error and disbelief; or because all of them approved of it; or because they had all ordered it, as indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿Then they called their companion, and he took it up and hamstrung her﴾. It has also been said that *'aqr* is a linguistic metaphor (*majaz lughawi*) for approval, in reference to someone other than the doer, but this is not correct.

**﴿And they rebelled against the command of their Lord﴾**: that is, they were arrogant toward obeying it, namely what Salih, upon him be peace, had conveyed to them of the earlier command. Here *al-amr* is the singular of *al-awamir* (commands). It is also permitted that it be the singular of *al-umur* (affairs), meaning they were arrogant toward the affair of God Most High and His religion; but this is far-fetched.

Some scholars, according to the first reading, held that *'ataw* (rebelled) must be taken to imply the meaning of *tawalla* (turned away), that is, they turned away from obeying His command while being insolent, or the meaning of *al-isdar* (proceeding from), that is, their insolence proceeded from the command of their Lord and because of it. This is because, when God Most High commanded them by His words ﴿leave her alone﴾, and so on, He tested them, and they did not comply, so they became insolent because of it. Had it not been for the command, the hamstringing would not have followed. The reason for interpreting it as *tawalla* or *sadar* is that *'ata* is not transitive with *'an* (from); its transitivity with *'an* here is for this reason, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿and I did not do it of my own accord﴾. Some scholars, however, say that it implies a meaning, based on the view that *'ata* means *istakbara* (was arrogant), as in the *al-Qamus*, and that it is transitive with *'an*. So understand this.

**﴿And they said, addressing him, upon him be peace, in a manner of challenge and confounding, according to their corrupt assumption: "O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with"﴾** of the punishment, **﴿and specify its time for us, if you are among the messengers﴾** (77). For your being one of them requires the truth of what you say of promise and warning.

**Al-Farra'** and **al-Zajjaj** said: *al-rajfah* (the violent tremor) means *al-zalzalah al-shadidah* (a severe earthquake).

**Mujahid** and **al-Suddi** said: it is *al-sayhah* (the mighty cry). The two statements are reconciled by saying that it is possible that the earthquake seized them from beneath them and the cry from above them. Some said: *al-rajfah* is the pounding and agitation of the heart until it stops. In another place the cry is mentioned, and in yet another place *al-taghiyah* (the overwhelming one). There is no contradiction between these, as some heretics (*al-malahidah*) claimed. For a great cry that breaks the normal course of things produces a trembling in their hearts, and because of its greatness and its going beyond the usual limit, it is called *al-taghiyah*, since *al-tughyan* is exceeding the limit. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you﴾. Or it may be said that the destruction by it was caused by their transgression, which is the meaning of *al-taghiyah*. This seizing was not the immediate result of what they said, but came after what had befallen them of the beginnings of the punishment during the three days, as you will know, God willing. The *fa'* (so) does not reject this.

﴿So they became in their home, prostrate﴾ (78). *Hamidin* (lifeless), dead, with no movement in them. The root of *al-judhum* is kneeling on the knees.

**Abu Ubaydah** said: *al-judhum* for people and birds is like *al-buruk* (kneeling) for camels. So the *judhum* of birds is their settling flat on the ground while at rest at night. *Asbaha* may be used as a complete verb, in which case *jathimin* is a circumstantial state (*hal*), or as an incomplete (linking) verb, in which case *jathimin* is its predicate (*khabar*), and the adverbial phrase in both cases is related to it. It was also said that it is a predicate, and *jathimin* is a state, but this is not correct, since it leads to the information about their being in their home becoming the main intended point. The intended meaning of *al-dar* (home) is the land, as in your saying "the House of War" and "the House of Islam." In another verse it appears in the plural, intending the particular dwelling of each one. Al-Naysaburi mentioned that wherever *al-rajfah* is mentioned, *al-dar* is singular, and wherever *al-sayhah* is mentioned, it is plural, because the cry came from the sky, as in most reports, and not from the earth, as some said. Its reach is therefore greater and more far-reaching than the earthquake, so each of them is paired with what is most fitting to it. So reflect upon this.

[Page 166]

﴿So he turned away from them﴾ after what had befallen them, as is the apparent meaning, grieved and regretful over what they had missed of faith, [and] sorrowful over them. ﴿And he said: "O my people, I had indeed conveyed to you the message of my Lord, and I advised you sincerely"﴾ through encouragement and warning, and I spared no effort, but it brought no benefit, and you did not accept from me. The use of the present tense in His words, glorified is He: ﴿but you do not love sincere advisers﴾ (79) is a narration of a past state, meaning: your condition has been continuous hostility toward and hatred of sincere advisers. His address (peace be upon him) to them is like the address of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the slain of the polytheists when they were thrown into the well of Badr, when he called out: "O so-and-so, O so-and-so, by their names: We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?" This is based on the premise that Allah, exalted is He, returns their souls to them so that they hear; and this is among what was specific to the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. It is also possible that he (peace be upon him) mentioned this by way of sorrow and regret, as one addresses abandoned dwellings and ruins.

It has been permitted to take ﴿So he turned away﴾ as coordinated with ﴿then the quake seized them﴾, in which case the address would be to them at the moment they were on the verge of destruction; but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Even more remote is what has been said, that the verse is in inverted order (taqdim and ta'khir), so that its sense is: "So he turned away from them and said: 'O my people, I had indeed conveyed to you the message of my Lord, and I advised you sincerely, but you do not love sincere advisers,' then the quake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes."

The story of Thamud, as Ishaq and others have mentioned, is that when 'Ad were destroyed, Thamud were allowed to live on after them, were made successors in the land, and were given long lives, until one of them would build a dwelling of clay which would collapse while the man was still alive. When they saw this, they took dwellings out of the mountains, and they were in ease regarding their livelihood. But they transgressed in the land and worshipped other than Allah, the Exalted. So Allah, the Exalted, sent to them Salih. They were an Arab people, and Salih (peace be upon him) was among the most noble of them in lineage. He was sent to them while he was young, and he called them to Allah, the Exalted, until his hair turned grey and he grew old, and only a few followed him from among them, and they were the weak. When he persisted with them in calling and warning, they asked him to show them a sign that would confirm what he said. He said to them: "What sign do you want?" They said: "Come out with us tomorrow to our festival." They had a festival on which they would go out with their idols. [They said:] "You call on your God and we call on our gods; if your call is answered, we will follow you, and if ours is answered, you will follow us." Salih said to them: "Yes." So they went out, and he went out with them. They called on their idols and asked them that Salih's supplication should not be answered in anything he asked for. Then Jundu' ibn 'Amr ibn Hiraysh, who at that time was the chief of Thamud, said: "O Salih, bring forth for us from this rock, from a solitary rock beside al-Hijr called al-Kathibah, a she-camel, mukhtarijah (that is, resembling the Bukht camel), or mukhrajah in the form of a camel, hollow-bellied and hairless. If you do this, we will confirm you and believe in you." So Salih took from them their solemn pledges: "If I do it, will you truly confirm me and truly believe in me?" They said: "Yes." So he prayed two rak'ahs and supplicated his Lord, and the rock quivered like a woman in labour with her child, and it split open, and out came a she-camel, pregnant, hollow-bellied and hairless, just as they had described, of which no one knows the extent between her sides except Allah, the Exalted, in size, while they were watching. Then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundu' and a group of his people believed in him, and their nobles wished to believe, but Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr ibn Labid, al-Habab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Su'ar, their soothsayer, prevented them. When the she-camel came out, he said to them: "This is the she-camel of Allah; she has a share of water, and you have a share on a known day." So the she-camel remained, with her young one, in their land, grazing the trees and drinking water. She used to come down to drink on alternate days; on her day she would put her head into the well of al-Hijr, which is now called the Well of the She-Camel, and she would not raise her head until she had drunk all that was in it. Then she would raise her head and spread her legs apart for them, and they would milk what they wished of the milk, and they would drink and store it. Then she would leave by a passage other than the one by which she had come, for she could not leave by the way she had entered because it was too narrow for her. When the next day came, it was their day, and they would drink what they wished and store what they wished for the day of the she-camel. They continued in ease and plenty. The she-camel used to pasture in the summer, when the heat was intense, on the upper part of the valley, so their livestock would flee from her and descend to the bottom of the valley in its heat and dryness; and she used to pasture in winter in the bottom of the valley, so their livestock would flee to its upper part in cold and dryness. This harmed their livestock, because of the matter Allah, the Exalted, intended for them: trial and test.

[Page 167]

That grew heavy upon them, so they transgressed against the command of their Lord and agreed unanimously to hamstring her. There were two women of Thamud, one of whom was called 'Unayzah, daughter of Ghunaym ibn Mijlaz, and was known as Umm Ghanm; she was the wife of Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr; she was an old, aged woman, with beautiful daughters, and possessed wealth in camels, cattle and sheep. The other was called Sadu, daughter of al-Mukhtar; she was beautiful and wealthy, with many livestock, and she was among the most hostile people to Salih (peace be upon him). Both of them loved the hamstringing of the she-camel, because she had harmed their livestock. So Sadu called a man called al-Habab to hamstring the she-camel, and offered herself to him if he did it, but he refused. Then she called a cousin of hers called Mus'da' ibn Muhrij, and promised herself to him if he did it, and he agreed to that. 'Unayzah, Umm Ghanm, called Qidar ibn Salif, who was a red, blue-eyed, short man; they claimed that he was the son of an illegitimate union, though he was not the son of Salif, but was born on his bed. She said to him: "I will give you whichever of my daughters you wish, on condition that you hamstring the she-camel." He was powerful and invulnerable among his people. He agreed, and he and Mus'da' set out, and they seduced the foolish ones of Thamud, and seven followed them, so they were nine men. They set out and lay in wait for the she-camel until she came back from the water, and Qidar had hidden for her at the base of a rock on her path, and Mus'da' had hidden at the base of another. She passed by Mus'da', who shot her with an arrow, which struck the muscle of her leg. Then Umm Ghanm came out and ordered one of her daughters, who was among the most beautiful of people, to uncover her face so that Qidar would see her. Then she urged him to hamstring the she-camel. So he struck at the she-camel with the sword and cut her hamstring, and she fell and let out a single cry. Her young one ran down from the mountain. Then Qidar stabbed her in the base of the neck and slaughtered her. The people of the town came out and divided her meat. When her young one saw that, he ran away until he reached an inaccessible mountain called Qara, and he cried out three times. Salih (peace be upon him) had said to them: "Pursue the young camel; perhaps it will ward off the punishment from you." So they went out after him and saw him on the mountain and chased him, but they could not catch him, and the rock split open after his cry, and he entered it.

Salih said to them: "For every cry there is a term: you will enjoy your abodes for three days. That is a promise that will not be denied."

It is related from Ibn Ishaq that of the nine, four followed the young camel, among them Mus'da', who shot him in the heart with an arrow, then dragged him by his leg and brought him down, and they threw his flesh together with the flesh of his mother. Salih said to them: "You have violated the sanctity of Allah, the Exalted; so rejoice in His punishment and vengeance." They used to mock him and say: "When is it, and what is its sign?" He said: "You will rise tomorrow with your faces yellow; the day after tomorrow your faces will be red; and the third day your faces will be black; then the punishment will strike you at morning." That group of men resolved to kill him, so they came to him at night, but the angels struck them with stones and killed them. When they were slow in returning to their companions, they came to Salih's dwelling and found them crushed by stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them." Then they intended to attack him, but his tribe protected him. Then when they saw the signs, they sought him to kill him, but he fled and joined a tribe of Thamud called Banu Ghunm. He stayed with their chief, whose name was Nufayl and who was called Abu Hudb. They sought him from him, but he said: "You have no way to him." So they left him, and what had befallen them occupied them. Then Salih (peace be upon him) and those with him went out to Syria and settled at Ramlah in Palestine. When the fourth day came and the forenoon had risen, they embalmed themselves with aloes and wrapped themselves in leather shrouds. Then a cry came to them from the sky, their hearts were torn apart, and they all perished, except for a paralysed girl called Dhari'ah, daughter of Silf, who was an unbeliever and extremely hostile to Salih (peace be upon him). Allah, the Exalted, freed her legs after she had witnessed the punishment, and she went out quickly until she came to the Valley of al-Qura, and she told them the news. Then she asked for water, and was given some; when she drank it, she died. There was a man among them called Abu Righal, who was the father of Thaqif, and he was in the sanctuary of Allah, the Exalted, so the sanctuary protected him from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted. But when he left it, what had befallen them befell him, and he was buried, and with him was a branch of gold. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by his grave and was informed of its story, so the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, hastened to it with their swords; they dug around it and extracted that branch.

It is also related that he (peace be upon him) went out with a hundred and twenty of the Muslims, weeping. He turned and saw the smoke rising, and he knew that they had perished, and they had been one thousand five hundred dwellings. It is related that he returned with those who were with him, and they settled in their homes.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Wahb, who said: When Salih and those who were with him were saved, he said: "O my people, this is a dwelling upon which Allah has become wrathful, and upon its people. So depart, and join the sanctuary of Allah and His safety." So they assumed the state of ihram for Hajj at that very moment and set out until they came to Mecca, and they remained there until they died. Those are their graves on the west side of the Ka'bah.

Ibn al-Zubayr related from Jabir that "when our Prophet (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr during the Battle of Tabuk, he said to his Companions: 'None of you should enter the town, nor drink of its water, nor enter upon these punished people, unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them.'"

Muhyi al-Sunnah al-Baghawi mentioned that the believers who were with Salih numbered four thousand, and that he went out with them to Hadramawt. When he entered it, he (peace be upon him) died, and so it was named Hadramawt for that reason. Then the four thousand built a city called Hadhuraa. Then it was reported from some people of knowledge that he died in Mecca at the age of fifty-eight; and perhaps this is the one relied upon. It has come that the most wretched of the first (generations) was the slaughterer of the she-camel, and the most wretched of the last (generations) is the slayer of Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed Ali (may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face) of this. In my view, the most wretched of the last is more wretched than the most wretched of the first, and the difference between them is like the difference between Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and the she-camel. The reports have indicated, rather have clearly stated, that the slayer of the Commander (of the Faithful) considered it lawful to kill him, indeed believed he would be rewarded for it, and his companions praised him for that. 'Imran ibn Hittan said, may Allah be angry with him:

O blow from one pious man, he intended by it only to attain the good pleasure of the Lord of the Throne.

Indeed I remember him one day, and I reckon him to be the one with the greatest balance of merit before Allah among all created beings.

And by Allah, how well said is the one who said:

O blow from a wretched man, which the Blaze has brought to its end, and so he will meet the Merciful with His wrath.

As if he did not intend anything by his blow except to roast in the fires on the Day of Gathering.

Indeed I remember him one day, and I curse him, as I curse 'Imran ibn Hittan.

As for the claim that his act was based on a doubt that saves him from what is not doubtful as to its being a form of raving: if such a doubt were a means of rescue from the punishment for such a sin, then every person would do whatever he wished. Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander. The she-camel's slaughterer has been struck as an example, and how elegant is the saying of 'Imarah al-Yamani:

Do not be amazed at Qidar, the slaughterer of Salih's she-camel, for every age has a she-camel and a Qidar.

In this story there are other reports which we have left out for brevity, since what has preceded is the more famous.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 80:

﴿And Lot⦆ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, i.e., "We sent," and it is coordinated with what preceded it, or it is governed by that same verb, without any need for an estimated term. The reason the recipients are not mentioned in the manner of what came before and after is that his people, as it is said, were not known by a well-known name that the context would require to be mentioned with him, peace be upon him, as an addition to them, as in the stories before and after. He is the son of Haran, son of Tarakh, and the son of Ishaq. Ishaq mentioned Mazar in place of Tarakh. Most genealogists hold that he, peace be upon him, was the son of the brother of Ibrahim (ﷺ). Al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Sulayman ibn Surad that the father of Lut, peace be upon him, was the paternal uncle of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. It is also said that Lut was the maternal cousin of Ibrahim, and that Sarah, his wife, was the sister of Lut. He was in the land of Babil (Babylon) in Iraq with Ibrahim, and he emigrated
[p. 169]
to al-Sham (Greater Syria) and settled in Filastin (Palestine), and he settled Lut in al-Urdunn (the Jordan), which is a district in al-Sham. Then Allah the Exalted sent him to the people of Sadum (Sodom), which is a town in Hims.

Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Lut was sent to the Mu'tafikat (the overturned cities). The villages of Lut were four cities: Sadum, Umur, Amura, and Sabuwayr. In each village there were one hundred thousand fighting men. The greatest of their cities was Sadum, and Lut dwelt in it. It is in the lands of al-Sham and in Filastin, a day and a night's journey away.

This word, according to what al-Zajjaj said, is a non-Arabic proper noun, not derived from the root L-W-T, from "latta al-hawd" (I plastered the basin) when one smears clay upon it. It is also said: "hadha alwat bi qalbi min dhalika," meaning "this is more clinging to my heart than that," i.e., more attached to it. And "lata al-shay'" means he concealed the thing.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿when he said to his people⦆, form an adverbial clause of time (zarf) governed by "We sent," as many have said. It has been objected that the sending occurred before the time of the saying, not during it, as this temporal adverb implies. This was answered by the consideration that the time-adverb is taken to be extended, as one says "Zayd is in the land of the Romans," so it is a non-literal time-adverb, in which it suffices that the thing contained occurs within some part of it, as al-Qutb (al-Shirazi) established. It is also permissible that "Lut" be in the accusative governed by an omitted "udhkur" (mention), so that it becomes a coordination of one narrative upon another, and ﴿when⦆ is a substitute for Lut, a substitute of inclusion, on the basis that it entails temporal meaning. Abu al-Baqa' said that it is the time-adverb of the message, with an omitted "message," i.e., "and mention the message of Lut when he said: ﴿Do you commit the abomination⦆, an interrogation in the manner of rebuke and reproach, i.e., do you do that deed which has reached the utmost of ugliness and its extreme? ﴿that no one among the worlds has preceded you in⦆ (80), i.e., no one has done it at any time before you. The "bi" here is for transitivity, as in the Kashshaf in the saying: "sabaqtuhu bi'l-kurah" when you strike the ball before him. From this is what is authentically related from his words, may (ﷺ) said: "'Ukkasha has preceded you with it." Abu Hayyan objected that the meaning of transitivity here is very strained, because the transitive "bi" in a verb transitive to one object makes the first object perform that action on what the "bi" governs, so it is like the hamza (causative). Thus when you say "sakaktu al-hajar bi'l-hajar," its meaning is "asukku al-hajar al-hajar," i.e., I made the stone strike the stone. Likewise "dafa'tu Zaydan bi-'Amrin 'an Khalid" means "adfa'tu Zaydan 'Amran 'an Khalid," i.e., I made Zayd repel 'Amr from Khalid. So the first object has an effect on the second, and this meaning does not hold in what is mentioned except with artificiality. Therefore the apparent view is that the "bi" is for accompaniment, i.e., no one has preceded you being accompanied by it and engaged in it. It was answered that the meaning according to transitivity is: "sabaqtuhu bi'l-kurah" means "asbaqtu kurati kurathu" (I made my ball precede his ball), because the precedence is between the two balls, not between the two persons or the two strikes. The same applies in the verse, and this is understood without artificiality. Al-Qutb al-Razi said that the meaning is: "I made my striking of the ball precede his striking of the ball by my striking of the ball," i.e., I made my striking of the ball precede his striking of the ball. Then he inclined toward making the "bi" a temporal indicator (zarfiyya), because it does not need what its transitive reading requires, i.e., no one preceded you in committing the abomination. Perhaps the matter is as he said. The first ﴿min⦆ is an added particle for emphasizing the negation and conveying the meaning of comprehensiveness, and the second is partitive. The sentence is a resumptive grammatical resumption (istinaf nahwi), brought to emphasize the denunciation and intensify the reproach and rebuke. It is also permissible that it be an explanatory resumption, as if it were said: "Why do we not come to it?" So he said: ﴿No one has preceded you in it⦆, so do not do what you have not been preceded in of the evil deeds, for that is more severe. It should not be supposed that the reason for denouncing the abomination is that it was invented, and that without this it would not have been denounced, since there is no room for that once it is an abomination. The reason this sentence emphasizes the denunciation is that it indicates the invention of evil, and there is no doubt that inventing it is worse, since there is no room for excusing it, just as they excused their worship of idols, for example, by saying: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers⦆.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the sentence be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object or the subject. Al-Nisaburi permitted that it be a qualifier of the abomination,
[p. 170]
on the pattern of the poet's verse:

"And indeed I pass by the base man who reviles me."

It was rejected on the grounds that "the abomination" here is specific, unlike "the base man." In any case, the meaning of the negation of anyone preceding them in it is that they were preceding every other person among the worlds in it, not that they equaled others in it. Al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "No male ever mounted a male until the people of Lut did." What led them to that, as Ibn 'Asakir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that they had fruit trees in their dwellings and their gardens, and fruit trees outside on the side of the road. They were afflicted with drought and scarcity of fruit. Some of them said to others: "If you prevent travelers from taking these outward fruits, you will have a livelihood from them." They said: "By what means shall we prevent them?" They said: "Make your custom that whenever you find a stranger in your lands, you marry him and impose on him a fine of four dirhams, for people will not travel through your lands if you do that." So they did it, and it became entrenched among them. In some narrations it is said that Iblis, may the curse of Allah be upon him, came to them when they were mentioning what they had mentioned, in the form of a boy, the most beautiful boy the people had seen, and he invited them to himself, so they had intercourse with him. Then they became bold in this. In a narration of Ibn Abi al-Dunya from Tawus, it is related that the people of Lut only had intercourse with women in their anuses, then they turned to men. In His words, ﴿among the worlds⦆ rather than ﴿among the people⦆, there is an exaggeration that is not hidden.

Almighty God says: ﴿Indeed, you approach men⁠﴾. This may be taken as a resumptive (istiʼnaf) clause of explanation (bayan) and grammatical analysis (nahw), and it clarifies that indecency (fahisha). Here "approach" (ityan) means sexual intercourse (jima').

Ibn ʻAmir and a group of readers recited (ʼa-innakum) with two clear hamzas. Among them are those who softened the second hamza without elongation, and among them are those who elongated it. In that case it is an emphasis of the earlier denunciation (inkar) and an intensification of the reproach (tawbikh). The use of "inna" (indeed) and the lam of emphasis (lam al-tawkid) is an addition expressing condemnation and rebuke, as if that act were something that could not be imagined to proceed from anyone, so it is emphasized strongly. As for the wording "the men" (al-rijal) rather than "the youths" (al-ghilman), "the beardless youths" (al-murdan) and the like, this is, as Shaykh al-Islam said, an exaggeration in rebuke, as if he had said: "you approach your own kind."

﴿Desire⁠﴾ (shahwa) is in the accusative. It is a object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning for the sake of appetite alone. Or it is in the accusative of circumstance (hal), with the sense of "desiring." It is also permitted that it be an infinitive of manner (masdar), with its governing verb being "you approach," since it carries the sense of "you desire."

Restricting intercourse, which is never separate from desire, to desire is an indication of describing them with pure animality, and that their aim is nothing but satisfying appetite. It is also permitted that the purpose is denunciation of them and rebuke for their desire for that filthy, foul act, as his words, Exalted is He, indicate: ﴿Other than women⁠﴾, that is, transgressing beyond women, who are the object of desire according to people of sound natures, as His words, Glorified is He, indicate: ﴿Rather, you are a people who exceed⁠﴾ (81). So the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the pronoun in "you approach." It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause relative to "the men," according to what Abu al-Baqa' said, meaning you approach them isolated from women. And it may be in the position of a qualifier (sifa) of "desire," as has been said, though its being connected to it has been deemed unlikely.

"Bal" (rather) is for a turning away (idrab), a transitional turning away from the mentioned denunciation to an informing of what led to it, which is the habit of excess in everything, or to a clarification that they combine all defects.

It is also possible that it is a turning away from something unmentioned, namely what they imagined as an excuse for that, meaning: there is no excuse for you in it; rather, you are a people whose habit is excess and going beyond limits. This carries the meaning of censuring them for ignorance, as in Surat al-Naml, except that here he expressed it with a noun and there with a verb, for the sake of conformity with the preceding verse-endings in each case. And God, Exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His speech.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 82:

﴿And the answer of his people was not but that they said﴾ — that is, of the arrogant among them, those who took it upon themselves to bind and loosen (al-'aqd wa'l-hall, i.e., to decide and command). ﴿Expel them﴾ — that is, Lot and those with him — ﴿from your town﴾ — that is, your city in which you have gathered and in which you dwell. The noble composition is of the kind of:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

The purpose of this is to negate the answer in the most emphatic manner, because what is mentioned falls within the scope of the exception and has no connection with his peace be upon him words of denouncing the abomination, magnifying its matter, and branding them with that which is the root of all evil. Had it been said, "And they said: Expel them," it would not have had this degree of effect.

As for His, glorified is He, words: ﴿Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾ (82) — this is a reason for the command to expulsion. The intent of the wretched ones by this description is mockery of Lot and those with him, and of their purity from the abominations, their distance from them, and their being pure from what is in the private parts, and boasting of the filth they were in, as the rogues among the immoral say to some of the righteous when they admonish them: "Get this ascetic away from us, and relieve us of this self-denier."

It has been read with the nominative ( jawab ) as the subject of kāna, and ﴿except that they said﴾ ... etc. as the predicate. It has been said: this is more apparent, although the first is stronger in grammatical construction, because the more definite is more deserving of being the subject. What benefits you here has already been mentioned, so recall it.

In any case, the meaning is not that nothing proceeded from them in response to the words of Lot, peace be upon him, and his admonitions except this false statement, as is understood by the mind; rather, nothing proceeded from them in the last of the exchanges that took place between him, peace be upon him, and them except this shameful word. Otherwise, many nonsensical things had proceeded from them before that, as is related of them in more than one place in the Noble Book. The same is said of its counterparts.

It has been said: the particle wa (and) has been used in ﴿And it was not﴾ ... etc., rather than fa (then), as in an-Naml and al-'Ankabut, because the noun occurs before it here and the verb occurs there, and following a verb with a verb is good, whereas following it with a noun is not. Yet there is room for reflection on this.

Perhaps the mention of ﴿Expel them﴾ here and ﴿Expel the family of Lot﴾ in an-Naml is an indication that they said this on one occasion and that on another; or that some said this and another said that. Al-Naysaburi said: "What came in an-Naml as ﴿Expel the family of Lot﴾ was so that it would be an explanation of this metonymy." It has also been said: that surah was revealed before al-A'raf, and the first explicitly stated the matter while the second used a metonym. End of quotation. Perhaps what we have mentioned is more preferable, so reflect.

So We saved him and his family, meaning whoever was specific to him and followed him among the believers, whether of his own kin, peace be upon him, or not. It was said that his two daughters were Raytha and Yaghuth. The word "family" (ahl) has several meanings, and every context has its own speech. According to the Imam al-A'zam, may Allah be pleased with him, in the chapter on bequest (wasiyya), the wife is included by custom. This is supported by His words, "He said to his family, 'Stay here'" and "and he set out with his family." Accordingly, the bequest is given to her, whether she is a People of the Book or a Muslim, provided the heirs permit it. According to the two Imams, Ahl al-Zajal, everyone who is in his care and maintenance is included, other than his slaves and his heirs. Their view, as in the commentary on al-Takmila, is a juristic preference (istihsan). Ibn al-Kamal supported it with this verse, since the word cannot in any way mean "wife" here, because of His words, "except his wife," which is an exception from "his family." If that were so, the exception would not be valid. You know that the discussion concerns the general term in light of the indication, not "family" in an unrestricted sense. The name of his wife, peace be upon him, was Waahila, and it was said Waaliha. "She was among those who remained behind" means, that is, she was one of them. The masculine form is used by way of predominance, and to show that she deserves what those who committed the indecency deserve. She used to conceal her disbelief and befriend his people, so she perished as they perished.

It is also permissible that the meaning be: she was with the people who remained behind, so there is no predominance. Here "ghabir" means "remaining," and from it comes the line of the Hudhali:

"So she remained after them in a life of toil."

It also comes in the meaning of "past" and "gone," and from it comes the line of al-A'sha: "In the bygone time." Therefore it is one of the words with opposite meanings, as in al-Sihah and elsewhere. It may also mean "destroyed." Regarding whether his wife remained with those people, there are two reports. The second is that he, peace be upon him, took her out with his family and forbade them to look back, but she looked back, and a stone struck her, and she perished. The verse here allows both meanings.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said that "remaining" here means remaining in the punishment of Allah, the Exalted. What follows, if Allah wills, will complete this discussion. The sentence is a resumption, arising as an answer after the exception, as if it were said: "What then was her state?" So it is said, "she was among those who remained behind."

[Page 173 begins mid-passage]

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾ means a kind of rain that was extraordinary. Allah's statement, ﴿And We rained upon them a rain of stones of sijjil﴾ clarifies it. In al-Khazin (Lubab al-Ta'wil fi Ma'ani al-Tanzil) it is reported that those stones were mixed with sulfur and fire. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the rain fell upon all of them. However, some reports state that those who were residing among them were swallowed up by the earth, and the stones rained down upon those who were traveling and their camel drivers, to the extent that a merchant among them was in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and a stone stood over him for forty days until he finished his trade. When he left the Sacred Precinct, it fell upon him.

A distinction is made between *muTira* and *umTira*. According to Abu 'Ubayda, the triliteral form (*muTira*) is used for mercy, and the quadriliteral form (*umTira*) for punishment. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) has a similar view. In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari), it is related from some people that *umTirat al-sama'* and *amTarat* have the same meaning. In al-Qamus, it is said: "Allah the Exalted does not 'amTarahum' (rain upon them) except in the case of punishment." The apparent statement of al-Kashshaf in Surat al-Anfal indicates synonymy, as in al-Sihah, but it says: "The use of *al-imtar* in the sense of punishment has become frequent." It is mentioned here that it is said: *maTarat-hum al-sama'* (the sky rained on them) and *wadin mamTur* (a valley that has been rained upon), and it is said: *amTarat 'alayhim kadha*, meaning it sent it down in the manner of rain.

The essence of the distinction, as in al-Kashf, is considering the meaning of striking/reaching in the first and sending down in the second; for this reason it is followed by *'ala* (upon). Ibn al-Munir mentioned that al-Zamakhshari's intent was to refute those who say that *muTirat* is used for good and *umTirat* for evil, and it is assumed that this is a linguistic distinction. He clarified that *umTirat* means "it sent something in the manner of rain, even if it was not rain itself." Thus, if Allah the Exalted sent down from the sky kinds of good, it would be permissible to say concerning it, "The sky rained good," meaning it sent it down in the manner of rain. So there is no particular connotation of evil in this quadriliteral form. However, it so happens that the sky has not sent down anything except rain, and that was a punishment, so it is assumed that the coincidental occurrence is intended in the linguistic formation, but this is not the case. End of quote.

From this, as in al-Shihab, it is understood that the statement of Abu 'Ubayda and his like is to be interpreted, even though it was rejected by His statement, ﴿A cloud bringing us rain﴾, since he meant by it mercy. It is not hidden that if it were said that the linguistic distinction is only between the two verbs and not their derivatives, this rejection would not stand. However, their statements are not explicit on this, and perhaps some have stated what contradicts it.

Then, ﴿maTaran﴾ is either a direct object or an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*).

﴿So look at how was the end of the criminals﴾ means: what was the final outcome of those disbelievers who committed that shameful deed. This is an address to everyone who is capable of reflecting and contemplating, out of wonder at their condition and as a warning against their actions.

Lut (peace be upon him) remained among them, according to some reports, for thirty years, calling them to what would bring them good, but they did not respond to him. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used to ride his donkey and come to them and advise them, but they refused to accept. He would come after having despaired of them, look at Sodom, and say, "Sodom, what a day for you from Allah the Exalted!" until the Decree reached its term. What Allah the Exalted related to His Prophet (ﷺ) occurred, and the detail of that will come, Allah willing.

Then, Lut (peace be upon him), as Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from al-Zuhri, when his people were punished, joined Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and remained with him until Allah the Exalted took him to Himself. In these verses there is evidence that *liwat* (sodomy) is among the greatest of the grave sins.

It has come in a report that al-Bayhaqi narrated in Shu'ab al-Iman from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), and al-Hakim authenticated it, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah the Exalted cursed seven of His creation above the seven heavens. He repeated the curse upon one of them three times, and cursed each one after that with a curse, a curse. He said: 'Cursed, cursed, cursed is the one who does the deed of the people of Lut.'" The hadith continues. It has also come: "Four people wake up in the anger of Allah the Exalted and go to sleep in the displeasure of Allah the Exalted," and he counted among them "the one who has intercourse with a man."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and others narrated from Mujahid (may Allah be pleased with him) that the one who does that deed, even if he washes himself with every drop from the sky and every drop from the earth, will remain impure. That is, water does not remove from him that great sin which distances him from his Lord. The intent is to magnify the matter of that immorality.

Some scholars have also attached *sihaq* (female-female intercourse) to it. It also began among the people of Lut (peace be upon him), as women would come to women. Regarding this, Hudhayfa (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The decree against the people of Lut (peace be upon him) only came when women became content with women and men with men."

And from Abu Hamza (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I said to Muhammad ibn 'Ali, "Did Allah the Exalted punish the women of the people of Lut for the deed of their men?" He said: "Allah the Exalted is more just than that. Men were content with men, and women with women."

Others (argued about) having intercourse with a woman in her buttocks ('ajiza), and they relied on what many narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said on the pulpit, "Ask me!" Ibn al-Kawwa' said, "(Do they) have intercourse with women in their buttocks?" He, may Allah ennoble his face, said: "You are lowly! May Allah lower you! Did you not hear His statement, ﴿Do you commit the immorality...﴾ [the verse]?" It is not hidden that this is not complete except through analogy, since otherwise, the immorality in the verse is clarified by what you know. Yes, many reports have come that indicate the prohibition of having intercourse with a wife in her buttocks, and the matter, as was previously mentioned, is disputed, and the relied-upon position regarding it is that it is prohibited.

There is no difference in *liwat* whether it is done with a slave (*mamluk*) or with someone else. They differed concerning the disbelief (kufr) of one who considers it lawful to have intercourse with a menstruating woman and with the anus. In al-Tatarkhaniyya, quoting al-Sirajiyya, it is stated: "*Liwat* with one's male slave, female slave, or wife is forbidden, except that if one considers it lawful, he does not become a disbeliever." This is in contrast to *liwat* with a stranger, for one who considers it lawful becomes a disbeliever by unanimous opinion. And what is mentioned among what is known and not known, as in al-Sharanbulaliyya, is that the wicked dare to commit it because they assume it is lawful.

The legal punishment (hadd) for *liwat* has been disputed. Imam (Abu Hanifa) said: there is no hadd for anal intercourse in any case, and there is ta'zir (discretionary punishment). According to the relied-upon position, whoever repeats it is to be executed. The apparent position, as al-Biri said, is that he is executed on the second occasion, because the term "repetition" applies to it. The two Imams said: if one does it with strangers, he is punished with the hadd of fornication (zina). If it is with his slave, female slave, or wife through a valid or invalid marriage, there is no hadd by consensus, as in al-Kafi and others. Rather, he is subject to ta'zir in all of those cases, and whoever habitually does it is executed. In al-Hawi al-Qudsi, it is stated: "The scholars discussed this ta'zir, including flogging, throwing one from a high place, imprisoning him in the most foul place, and other things, apart from castration and cutting off (the organ). Flogging is most correct." In al-Fath it is stated: he is subjected to ta'zir and imprisoned until he dies or repents.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the hadd for *liwat* is execution, for both the active and passive partners, and he narrated it as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report. In another report from him, he was asked, "What is the penalty for the one who commits *liwat*?" He said: "He is looked at from the highest building in the town and thrown down upside down, then pelted with stones." Al-Fath said: It seems that the basis for this is that the people of Lut were destroyed in this manner, when their towns were lifted and overturned upon them, and there is no doubt about following the demolition with them while they were still in it.

It is also narrated from 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) that he threw a practitioner of *liwat* from a height and then stoned him, and this is most similar to what Allah related about the destruction of the people of Lut (peace be upon him) by a rain of stones upon them.

They have affirmed that it does not exist in Paradise, because He, the Glorified, found it repugnant and named it *fahisha* (immorality), and Paradise is free of that. In al-Ashbah, it is stated that its prohibition is rational, so it does not exist in Paradise. It has also been said that its prohibition is based on revelation (sam'iyya), so it may exist there, meaning it is possible for it to exist. It seems that by "prohibition" here he meant "ugliness," using the name of the cause for the effect; that is, its ugliness is rational, in the sense that it is perceived by reason even if the Law has not come with it. This is not the position of the Mu'tazila, as is not hidden.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti quoted from Ibn 'Aqil al-Hanbali, who said: This matter took place between Abu 'Ali ibn al-Walid the Mu'tazili and Abu Yusuf al-Qazwini. Ibn al-Walid said: "There is nothing preventing it from being included among the pleasures of Paradise, since the corruption is removed. It was only forbidden in this world because of what it entails of cutting off offspring and being a place of harm, and there is none of that in Paradise. For this reason, drinking wine was permitted (in Paradise), because there is no intoxication, quarreling, and loss of intellect in it, but rather pure pleasure." Abu Yusuf (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Inclination toward males is a defect, and it is repugnant in itself, because it is a place not created for intercourse. For this reason it was not permitted in any religious law, unlike wine." Ibn al-Walid said: "It is repugnant and a defect, because of the soiling with filth, and there is no filth in Paradise, so nothing remains but mere enjoyment." End of quote.

[Page 174]

I see that denying the rational repugnance of *liwat* is obstinacy. For this reason, the pre-Islamic Arabs used to reproach it, and they would say in disparagement, "So-and-so has a yellowed behind." I do not know whether Ibn al-Walid would be pleased for himself to be penetrated in Paradise or not. If he is pleased today to be penetrated tomorrow, then the most likely assumption is that the man is a catamite or has become accustomed to it. If he is not pleased, he is obliged to acknowledge rational repugnance. And if he claims that his lack of pleasure is because people have become accustomed to reproaching him for it, and that this is absent in Paradise, we say to him: it is required of you to be pleased with it in this world when you are not reproached and no one sees you. If he commits to that, then it is as you see, and his claim of a distinction between the active and passive partner does not benefit him, as is not hidden from the free-minded.

They explicitly stated that the prohibition of *liwat* is more severe than the prohibition of fornication, because it is repugnant by reason, nature, and law, whereas fornication is not prohibited in this way, and its prohibition is removed by marriage or purchase, unlike *liwat*. The absence of the hadd according to the Imam is not due to its lightness, but rather for the sake of severity, because according to many scholars it purifies the one who is punished, although this is contrary to our school. Some of the wicked people today, may Allah destroy them, make light of its matter, long for it, and boast of practicing it frequently. Some of them commit it seeking revenge, but how can that be? And some of them praise Allah, the Glorified, for it, in the passive voice, because they have attained leadership through their behinds. We ask Allah the Exalted for pardon and well-being in religion, this world, and the Hereafter.

Know that *liwat* has other rulings. They have said that no dower (mahr) is obligatory because of it, nor is a waiting period ('idda) in an invalid marriage, nor in the case of one who was penetrated by it due to a doubt (shubha). It does not establish a *tahlil* (legal restoration) for the first husband, nor does it establish the revocation of divorce (raj'a), nor the prohibition of affinity (musaharah) according to the majority, nor expiation (kaffara) in Ramadan according to one report. If one accuses someone of it, he is not subject to the hadd, nor is there *li'an* (mutual oath-cursing), contrary to the two (Imams) in both matters, as in al-Bahr, taken from al-Mujtaba. In al-Sharanbulaliyya, quoting al-Siraj, it is stated: two just witnesses suffice for testimony regarding it, not four, contrary to the two (Imams) again.

This is all. I have not come across the Sufi masters, may Allah sanctify their secrets, on what is of the nature of allusion (isharah) in the story of the people of Lut (peace be upon him). Some of them mentioned in the story of the people of Salih (peace be upon him), after belief in the outward meaning, that the she-camel is the vehicle of the human soul for Salih (peace be upon him), and its attribution to Him, the Glorified, is because it was commanded by His command, Mighty and Majestic, and was specific to Him in obedience and nearness to Him. As for what is said: that the water was divided between her and them, one day for her drinking and one day for them, this is an allusion that their drinking is from the practical rational faculty, and his drinking is from the theoretical rational faculty. And what is related: that on her day of drinking she would spread her legs and milk would be drawn from her until the vessels were filled, is an allusion that his soul extracts through thought from its innate universal knowledge the knowledge beneficial to those deficient in the sciences of ethics and religious law. And her coming out of the mountain is her coming out from the body of Salih (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 84 (part 2 of 2):

Others said: The she-camel was the miracle of Salih, peace be upon him. This is because they asked him to bring forth for them, from the stone of the heart, the she-camel of the innermost secret (*naqat al-sirr*). It came forth and was given to drink the secret of the secret, and it gave to the land of the mould, that is, the faculties and the senses, the milk of the Divine outpourings (*al-waridat al-ilahiyya*). Then he said to them: "Leave her to graze in the gardens of holiness and the pools of intimacy. ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾ through violations of the Sharia or opposition to the Path, ﴿lest a painful punishment seize you﴾, which is the punishment of being cut off from reaching the Truth. ﴿And remember when He made you successors﴾, meaning, prepared for the vicegerency, ﴿and settled you in the land﴾, meaning the land of the heart, ﴿taking for yourselves palaces from its plains﴾, which are dealings in truthfulness, ﴿and hewing out the mountains﴾, which are the mountains of the heart's states, ﴿as houses﴾, which are the stations (*maqamat*) of those who travel to God, exalted is He."

﴿The eminent ones among his people who were arrogant said to those who were deemed weak﴾, meaning the human attributes and the blameworthy traits, ﴿to those who were deemed weak﴾, meaning the attributes of the heart and the spirit: ﴿"Do you know that Salih is a messenger from his Lord?"﴾, to call to the luminous attributes. ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾ with the knives of opposition, ﴿and the earthquake seized them﴾ because of the weakness of their hearts and the lack of strength in their knowledge, ﴿and they became prostrate in their homes﴾, dead, unable to move toward the presence of holiness.

Some have mentioned that the she-camel and the young camel are images of faith in God, exalted is He, and faith in His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Both appeared, directly and through an intermediary, from the stone to which the hearts of that people are similar. Their hamstringing of the she-camel is of the same kind as the slaughter of Yahya, peace be upon him, for the death that appeared in the ram on the Day of Resurrection. This indicates that they were the worst of people in readiness and the most complete in deprivation. That the Greatest Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, did not include them in the *Fusus al-Hikam* in the line of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, where he judged them to be saved in the manner he mentioned, also shows their wretched condition. Likewise, the people of Lot, peace be upon him, were not included in that line. It seems that this is because of their excessive ignorance, their remoteness from wisdom, their coming to houses other than through their doors, their filthiness, and the baseness of their souls. What the followers of the Sharia hold is that all those peoples are fuel for Hell, and none of them will be saved. And God, exalted is He, is the Most Judicious of judges.

[Page 175]

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾: this is conjoined with what came before. The meaning is "We sent [to] Madyan…" and so on. Madyan, and it is also heard as Madyan, was originally a proper name of the son of Abraham the Friend, peace be upon him. It is not declined (mamnu' min al-sarf, diptotic) because of its status as a proper name (ʿalamiyya) and its foreignness (ʿujma, non-Arabic origin). The tribe was then named after him. It is also said that it is Arabic, the name of a water source they were beside. It is also said that it is the name of a town, and it is not declined because of its status as a proper name and its feminine form. In that case a genitive noun must be supplied, meaning "the people of Madyan" for example, or it is a figurative usage. According to this view, the yā' is, for some, extra (zā'ida). According to Ibn Barrī, the mīm is extra, since there is no fa'īl in their speech but there is maf'al.

Others said that it is anomalous (shādhdh), like Maryam, since by analogy its treatment should be like maqām. According to al-Mubarrad it is not anomalous. It is said that this is the correct view, because it follows the pattern of a verb.

As for Shu'ayb, it is said to be the diminutive of shi'b (with a fatḥa then a sukūn), the name of a mountain, or of shi'b (with a kasra then a sukūn), meaning the path in a mountain. It is preferred that it was coined as a原 non-derived name (murtajal) in this form. The claim that the name is a diminutive is false, because the names of the prophets, peace be upon them, may not be diminutized. There is room for consideration in this, because what is prohibited is diminutizing after the naming, not what accompanies it. The one who makes this claim may claim this, and this is according to what was found in the handwriting of al-Nawawī in his Tahdhīb: Ibn Mīkīl ibn Yashjur ibn Madyan ibn Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him. It is also said: Ibn Mīkīl ibn Yashjur ibn Lāwī ibn Yaʿqūb. Some say Mīkā'īl instead of Mīkīl, and this was reported from the handwriting of al-Dhahabī in his Ikhtiṣār al-Mustadrak. Another says Malkānī instead of it.

It is mentioned that the mother of Mīkīl was a daughter of Lūṭ, peace be upon him. Ibn ʿAsākir reported through the chain of Isḥāq ibn Bishr from al-Sharqī ibn al-Qaṭāmī, who was an expert in genealogy, that Shu'ayb is Yathrūb in Hebrew, and that he is the son of ʿAyfā ibn Yawbab (with a letter yā' with two dots below at its beginning, and a wāw and two bā's), on the pattern of Jaʿfar, son of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him. It is also said that his lineage is other than this. The Prophet (ﷺ), as Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, whenever Shu'ayb was mentioned, would say: "That is the orator of the prophets," because of his fine argumentation with his people, that is, his dialogue with them. It seems, as has been said, that he (ﷺ) meant what is mentioned in this sūrah, as is known upon reflection on it. He was sent as a messenger to two communities: Madyan and the People of the Thicket. Al-Suddī and ʿIkrima, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Allah did not send a prophet twice except Shu'ayb: once to Madyan, and Allah seized them with the Blast, and once to the People of the Thicket, and Allah seized them with the punishment of the Day of the Canopy."

Ibn ʿAsākir in his History reported from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that the people of Madyan and the People of the Thicket are two communities to whom Allah sent Shu'ayb. Ibn Kathīr said this is gharīb (a weak, isolated report), and there is room for consideration regarding its being traced to the Prophet. He chose that they are one community, and he argued for this by saying that each of them was admonished about fulfilling the scale and the measure, which indicates that they are one. There is in this what is not hidden. Among the people is one who claimed that he, peace be upon him, was sent to three communities, and the third is the People of the Rass. The claim that he, peace be upon him, was blind with no staff to lean on is not sound. Rather, scholars of insight have affirmed that a messenger must be free of anything repellent, and they gave as examples blindness, leprosy, and elephantiasis. The trials of Job and the blindness of Jacob do not refute this, on the basis that it is literal, since it occurred after the prophetic mission; the discussion concerns what accompanies it. The difference is that the former is repellent, unlike the latter, for one whose prophethood is established. It may be said: if that is reported, then it is of this kind.

﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), based on a question that arose from the report of his being sent to them, as if it was said: "What did he say to them?" It was answered: he said, ﴿O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾, whose explanation has already passed. ﴿There has certainly come to you a clear proof from your Lord﴾, that is, a great and manifest miracle from the Master of your affairs. His miracle, peace be upon him, is not mentioned in the Mighty Qur'an, just as most of the miracles of our Prophet (ﷺ) and of the prophets, peace be upon them, are not mentioned in it.

The statement that he, peace be upon him, had no miracle is an error, because the fā' in His, the Glorified's, statement ﴿So fulfill the measure and the scale﴾ is for the arrangement of the command upon the arrival of the proof. The possibility that it is conjunctive to ﴿worship﴾ is remote, even though the worship of Allah, the Exalted, necessitates avoiding the prohibitions, most of which come after disbelief, the defrauding. So it is as if it was said: "A miracle has come to you bearing witness to the validity of my prophethood, which makes it obligatory upon you to believe in it and to act upon what I have commanded you. ﴿So fulfill…﴾" and so on. If a claimant claimed prophethood without a miracle, it would not be accepted from him, because it is a claim about a matter that is not manifest, and it imposes an obligation on others, and such a thing is not accepted without proof. Some people claimed that the proof is Shu'ayb himself, and some claimed that the intended proof is the admonition, and that it is the statement ﴿So fulfill…﴾ and so on. This is nothing, as is not hidden. Al-Zamakhsharī said: among his miracles, peace be upon him, is what was reported about the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, fighting the dragon when he gave him his flock; and the sheep giving birth to the speckled ones exclusively when he promised him that the speckled ones among their offspring would be his; and the staff of Adam, peace be upon him, falling into his hand in the seven times; and other signs, because all of these occurred before Moses, peace be upon him, was made a prophet, so they were miracles for Shu'ayb. End of quotation.

There is room for consideration in this, because that is later than the dialogue, so it is not correct to base the command on it.
