Also, it is possible that it was a karāma (miracle granted to a righteous servant) for Moses, peace be upon him, or an irhāṣ (a precursor miracle announcing a prophet) for his prophethood. Rather, in al-Kashf it is held that this is definite, because Moses met Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, after the destruction of his people, and because that was not the occasion of challenge.

Al-Imām claimed that the irhāṣ is not permissible according to the Muʿtazila, and therefore he made that a miracle for Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. Al-Ṭībī objected to this, saying that al-Zamakhsharī said in Āl ʿImrān, regarding the angels speaking to Maryam, peace be upon her, that it is a miracle for Zakariyyā or an irhāṣ for the prophethood of ʿĪsā, peace be upon them both.

By ﴿the measure﴾ is meant that by which it is measured, metaphorically, like "livelihood" meaning that by which one lives. This is supported by the fact that al-Mikyāl (the measuring vessel) occurs in Sūrat Hūd, and likewise the conjunction of al-Mīzān (the scale) to it here, since what is understood from it is the instrument, although it is permissible that it be a verbal noun meaning weighing, like al-Mīʿād meaning the promise. It is also said that the measure and what is conjoined to it are both verbal nouns, and the speech involves an ellipsis, meaning: fulfill the instrument of measuring and weighing. ﴿And do not defraud the people﴾, that is, do not diminish them. It is said: "He defrauded him of his right" if he diminished it for him. From this comes the saying that the tax is called "bakhs." In their proverbs: "You think her a fool, but she is one who defrauds (bākhis)," meaning one with fraud. It transitively takes two objects, the first being ﴿the people﴾ and the second ﴿their things﴾, those existing in the transactions, of the price and the thing sold. The benefit of explicitly forbidding diminution after commanding fulfillment is to emphasize that command and to explain the ugliness of its opposite. Sometimes "things" is intended to mean rights in general, because they used to be tax collectors who left nothing without taxing it.

It has come from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they were a people, tyrannical and oppressive, who sat on the road and defrauded the people of their wealth. Whenever a stranger came to them, they would take his good dirhams and say, "These dirhams of yours are counterfeit," then they would cut them and buy them from him at a low price. It is also reported that they would give him counterfeit ones in exchange. So, as if, when they were forbidden to defraud in measuring and weighing, they were forbidden from defrauding and taxing in everything. It has been said: this includes a man defrauding another of his right of good dealing and of the honor befitting him, and of explaining his excellence, as is due, to the one who asks about him. Many of those who have attributed themselves to the people of knowledge today are afflicted with this fraud. Would that they were content with it, but they have gathered [bad] dates and bad measuring. ﴿To Allah we belong, and to Him we return﴾.

He, peace be upon him, began by mentioning this incident, according to al-Imām, because it is the custom of the prophets, peace be upon them, that when they see their people turning toward one kind of corruption with more eagerness than their turning toward the other kinds, they begin by forbidding them from that kind. His people were occupied with defrauding and short-measuring more than with anything else. By "the people" is meant what includes them and others: that is, do not defraud others, and do not let some of you defraud others. ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ by oppression, or by it and by disbelief, ﴿after its reformation﴾, that is, after the reformation of its affairs or its people through the sacred laws. So the genitive is from the genitive of the verbal noun to its object, with the omission of the governing noun, and the agent is the prophets and their followers.

It is permitted that no genitive noun be supplied, and that figurative usage be considered in the causative attribution, because the reformation of those on the earth is a reformation of it; and that the genitive be from the verbal noun to its agent, by way of figurative attribution to the place; and that it be in the sense of "in," meaning: after the prophets' reformation in it. Taking it literally is rejected, because reformation relates to the earth itself, such as its settlement and the reform of its roads. ﴿Do not cause corruption on the earth﴾. ﴿That is better for you﴾: a reference to what has been mentioned, of fulfilling the measure and scale, and abandoning fraud and corruption; or a reference to acting upon what he commanded them and forbade them from. Whichever it is, the singular demonstrative and its masculine form are clear.

The meaning of betterness is either increase in general, or in humanity, and good repute, and what they seek of gain and profit, because when people know them for trustworthiness, they desire to deal with them and trade with them. It has been said: what is meant here by "better" is not the meaning of increase, because it is not comparative; rather the meaning is: that is beneficial for you. ﴿If you are believers﴾ (85). It is said that by faith is meant its linguistic meaning, and the betterness is restricted to the affair of this world, meaning: if you are affirming me in what I say. According to al-Ṭībī, such a condition is only brought at the end of a statement for emphasis. From this it is known that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was well known among them for truthfulness and trustworthiness, just as our Prophet (ﷺ) was well known among his people as "the Trustworthy." Some who followed what was mentioned said: the conditioning of betterness on this affirmation is by way of interpreting it as knowledge of it; otherwise it is better absolutely.

Al-Quṭb al-Rāzī said: that is not a condition for the betterness itself, but for their action, as if it was said: "So bring it, if you are affirming me." Thus it is not objected that the betterness of humanity does not depend on their affirmation of it. It has been said: what is meant by it is the opposite of disbelief, and by betterness what includes the affair of this world and the Hereafter, meaning: that is better for you in both abodes, on condition that you believe; and the condition of belief is because the benefit of obtaining reward along with safety from punishment is evident with belief, and hidden with its absence, due to immersion in the depths of disbelief. Some built the benefit of abandoning fraud and the like in the Hereafter on the basis that disbelievers are punished for sins just as they are punished for disbelief, so abandoning them would be better for them without doubt. But it is not hidden that if corruption on the earth is explained as corruption in it through disbelief, then this conditioning on belief has no meaning, as is not hidden; and removing it from the scope of the demonstrative is very remote.

Al-Khayālī claimed that it is more apparent that ﴿That is better for you﴾ is a parenthetical clause, and the condition is connected to the commands and prohibitions that preceded it. It seems he was compelled to this because the conditional aspect was hidden for him. He fled from a cat and fell into a lion, ran from the drizzle and stood under the gutter. So take heed, O people of understanding.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 86:

﴿And do not sit on every path,﴾ meaning every road of the sensible roads, ﴿threatening﴾ meaning frightening those who believe with killing, as is reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that their land was narrow, and people used to obtain provisions from them, so they would sit on the road and frighten people from going to Shu'ayb, saying to them that he is a liar, so that he would not tempt you away from your religion.

It is permissible that sitting on the path be meant figuratively (tamthil), as in what is related of the words of Satan: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾. The meaning then is: do not sit on every road of the religions, like Satan, and to this points what is also reported from Mujahid. The word "every" (kulliyyah) is used although the religion of God is one and true, in view of its division into knowledge, limits and rulings. Whenever they saw someone beginning on any of these, they would prevent him by every possible trick. It was also said: they used to cut the road (highway robbery), so they were forbidden from that, and this is reported from Abu Hurayrah and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd. Perhaps what is meant by it is what returns to one of the first two opinions, otherwise there is obscurity in it. And if it is said that in the verse, on this reading, there is exaggeration in the warning and an intensification of what they intended of cutting off the way, that is also said.

﴿and bar from the way of God﴾, meaning the road leading to Him, which is faith, or the way upon which they sat. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun as an explanation of every path, indicating the magnitude of what it applies to and a reproach of what they were upon. The words of the Glorified: ﴿whoever believes in Him﴾ are the object of "you bar" by the principle of the nearer verb operating (i'mal al-aqrab), not "you threaten", contrary to what the speech of al-Zamakhshari seems to imply, since according to the majority in such a case the second pronoun must then be expressed, and it is not permissible to omit it except in poetic necessity; so it would have to be said: "you bar them." And if "you bar" is taken to mean "you turn away," it becomes intransitive and is not of what we are discussing. The pronoun in (bihi) refers to God the Exalted, or to every path, or to the way of God the Exalted, because the word "sabil" (way) is masculine and feminine, as has been said. The clause ﴿you threaten﴾ and what is conjoined to it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿you sit﴾, meaning threatening and barring. It was said: on the first interpretation it is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), and the more evident is what we have mentioned.

﴿and seek for it crookedness﴾, meaning you seek for the way of God the Exalted crookedness by casting doubts, or by describing it to people with what diminishes it, and it is further from any trace of crookedness. This is a statement carrying the meaning of reproach, and it may be mockery of them, since they sought what is impossible, for the path of truth does not become crooked. In the speech there is a progression, as if it were said: Is it not enough for you that you threaten people for following the truth and bar them from the way of God the Exalted, until you describe it as crooked, so that the barring is by proof and evidence? And according to what is reported from Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Zayd, it is permissible that by "seek for it crookedness" be meant their living on the earth, and the crookedness of the road is an expression for the loss of its safety.

al-Tibi mentioned that the meaning of this seeking then is the meaning of the lam in the words of the Glorified: ﴿so that it might be to them an enemy and a sorrow﴾, and in all other aspects of the speech there is ellipsis and transitivization.

﴿And remember when you were few﴾ in number, ﴿so He multiplied you﴾, increasing your number through blessing in offspring, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It is related that Madyan ibn Ibrahim married the daughter of Lot, and she bore children, and God cast blessing and increase into their offspring, so they multiplied and spread.

al-Zajjaj permitted that the meaning be: when you were poor and needy, so He made you wealthy and affluent; or: you were few and humbled, so He strengthened you with abundance of number and equipment. "When" (idh) is the object of "remember," or an adverb of an implied element such as the event or the blessings, meaning: remember that time or what was in it. ﴿And look how was the end of the corrupters﴾ (86), meaning the final outcome of those who corrupted before you among the nations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and take warning from them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 87:

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ of the laws (shara'i') and rulings (ahkam), ﴿and a group who have not believed﴾ in it, or who have not performed belief, ﴿then be patient until Allah judges between us.﴾ This is an address to the disbelievers and a warning to them, meaning: wait, so that you may see the judgment of Allah the Exalted between us and you, for He, glorified is He, will surely grant victory to the one in the right (al-muhiqq) over the one in falsehood (al-mubtil) and make him prevail over him. Or it is an address to the believers and an admonition to them and an exhortation to patience and to bearing the harm that the polytheists were inflicting upon them, until Allah the Exalted judges between them and takes vengeance on their behalf against them. It is also possible that it is an address to both parties, meaning: let the believers be patient over the harm of the disbelievers, and let the disbelievers be patient over what grieves them of the belief of those among them who have believed, until He judges, distinguishing the wicked from the good. The apparent reading is the first possibility, and it seems that the intended meaning is that the belief of some of you benefits you in averting the trial of Allah the Exalted and His punishment. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾ (87), since there is no one to reverse His judgment and no injustice in it, so He is in the utmost rectitude.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), built upon a question that the discourse brings along with it, as if it had been said: "What did they say to him, peace be upon him, after they had heard from him these admonitions?" So it was said: the nobles of his people, who were arrogant and overbearing towards him, peace be upon him, not content with mere disobedience but reaching a great degree of insolence, said: ﴿"We will surely drive you out, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town."﴾ Out of hatred for you and to repel your corruption (fitnah) that results from living together and being neighbours. The oath-form of emphasis (ta'kid qasami) is for intensification and to give importance to the ruling. The phrase (ma'aka, "with you") is connected to the expulsion, not to the belief. The attribution of the expulsion to him, peace be upon him, first, and then to the believers, second, is to draw attention to his primacy in that matter and their following him in it. The placing of the address by his exalted name between the two conjoined items serves to increase the affirmation and the threat, arising from the utmost impudence and transgression. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Or you will return to our religion"﴾ is conjoined to the response of the oath, meaning: by Allah, one of the two matters will definitely occur, either the expulsion or the return, though the more important purpose is the return. The first was mentioned merely for compulsion and coercion, as is revealed by his, peace be upon him, not addressing the answer concerning the expulsion. The customary meaning of "return" is going back to the former state, and this is not possible in the case of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, because the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from everything short of disbelief by degrees. Yes, it is possible in the case of one who has believed in him, so attributing it to him, peace be upon him, is by way of predominance (taghlib). It was said: the believers have here become predominant, just as he became predominant over them in the address; so in the verse there are then two instances of predominance. Many scholars said: "to return" (an ta'ud) means "to become" (tasir), as some grammarians and lexicographers have affirmed, so it does not require return to a previous state. On this basis is his saying:

"If the days do not treat me kindly once, then indeed their sins have returned to them."

Thus it is as if they said: "We will surely drive you out, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will become like us." Then there is no difficulty and no predominance. The same is said concerning what follows, and it is good and not rejected. ﴿"After Allah had delivered us from it"﴾: this admits that the predominance is applied here too, or it may be said that deliverance does not necessarily have to occur after falling into what is disliked; do you not see His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿"So We delivered him and his family"﴾ and similar verses.

Ibn al-Munir said: Granting the use of "return" in the sense of going back to a previous matter, it may be answered that it follows the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their guardians are the Taghut, who bring them out of light into darkness."﴾ For expulsion requires a prior entry into that from which one is expelled, and this is not realised in the case of the original believer and the original disbeliever. But since belief and disbelief are among the voluntary acts which Allah, exalted is He, created the servant able to perform, each of them facilitated for him and empowered to do if he wills, He expressed the believer's being empowered to disbelieve, then his turning away from it to belief by choice, as "bringing out of darkness into light," as a grace and guidance from Allah, exalted is He, to him; and the reverse regarding the disbeliever. A parallel to this occurs in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance."﴾ This is a metaphor in which the cause is expressed by the effect. The benefit of choosing this expression in these places is to establish the empowerment and the choice, to set up the proof of Allah, exalted is He, against His servants.

It was also said: this statement was in accordance with their assumption that he, peace be upon him, was in their religion, because he had remained silent before the prophethood, not denouncing them; or that it was issued by their leaders to deceive the people and give the impression that he was of their religion. What proceeded from him, peace be upon him, during the course of the dialogue occurred by way of mushakalah (matching in form). Al-Shihab mentioned another possibility in the answer: namely, that the apparent meaning is that "return" is the counterpart of "going out" to that from which one went out, which is the town, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: let there be from you either the going out from our town or the return to it while being in our religion. Thus the difficulty is resolved without need for what was previously mentioned. But its remoteness is not hidden. They did not say "or we will restore you" in the manner of what precedes it, because their intention was that they would return in the form of obedience, fearing expulsion from the homeland, by choosing the lesser of two evils, since they would be returned by all kinds of compulsion and torture. Some people claimed that "you will return" (ta'udunna) is not suitable to be the answer to the oath, because it is not the verb of the one swearing; and they made what we pointed to as better for explaining the meaning, as a way out of this. But this is false, for it implies that an oath may not be made on the act of another, and no one has said this; indeed such usage as "By Allah, Zayd shall surely be beaten" is widespread without objection. The verb "to return" is transitive with "fi" (in), indicating that their religion is for them like a container encompassing them.

﴿He said﴾: a resumptive sentence like its counterparts, meaning: Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said, in rejection of their false saying and denial of their wicked oaths: ﴿"Even though we were unwilling?"﴾ The hamzah is for denying the occurrence and negating it, and the waw is for conjunction with an omitted element. It may also be said that in such a position it is the waw of circumstance (hal) as well. The "law" (lau) here is the one used to clarify what the preceding statement implies, directly or indirectly, of the affirmed or negated ruling, in every hypothetical state among the states accompanying it, in general, by placing it upon the most distant and most contrary of them, so that by its affirmation or negation, together with the affirmation or negation in the other states, it becomes evident by way of priority. The discourse here is in the sense of: "Shall we return to it if we were not unwilling, and even if we were unwilling, not caring about compulsion?" So the clause is in the position of a circumstance from the implied verb, and the outcome is: "Shall we return to it in a state of not being unwilling and in a state of being unwilling," as a denial of what their outrageous word implies by its generality, of return in any state. He was content with mentioning the state that is most contrary to return and furthest from it, as an alert that it is the one which actually obtains, and trusting that its mention suffices clearly in place of the other. For the return which was the subject of the denial, once it is realised together with unwillingness according to what their speech entails, then its realisation together with unwillingness being absent is more fitting. This is part of what Shaykh al-Islam mentioned in this place; he expanded upon it extensively and presented objection and resolution, so refer to it. It is also permitted that the interrogation remains in its original state. Some made the hamzah mean "how," directing the wonder towards the return: "How could we return to it while we are unwilling of it?" The assumption of the verb of return, because the meaning of the discourse strongly indicates it, is better than assuming the verb of restoration, as al-Zamakhshari did. In al-Taysir, the verb of expulsion is assumed: "You would drive us out without fault while we are unwilling, because of leaving our homelands." This was explained by saying that return is something taken for granted, which no sane person could conceive, so only expulsion can be meant. The weakness of this assumption is not hidden.

Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that "law" here means "an" (that), since it is for the future, and he permitted that it remain in its own meaning. What Shaykh al-Islam indicated in this place has a more far-reaching significance, so let it be considered.

[Page 4]

﴿We would have indeed invented a great lie against God﴾, a lie so great that its magnitude cannot be measured.

﴿If we return to your religion﴾, which is polytheism (shirk), and we claim, as you claim, that God, glorified be He, has a rival (nidd), exalted is He above that by a great exaltation.

﴿After God has delivered us from it﴾, and we know its falsehood and that there is no god but God, alone, with no partner. The apodosis (jawab al-shart) of the conditional is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. That is: if we return to your religion, then we have indeed invented a lie. This has been raised as an objection: the apparent rule, when the apodosis is like what has been mentioned, is that its occurrence and its being known depend on the condition, as in: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has indeed stolen before﴾ and ﴿If you do not help him, God has already helped him﴾, and: "If you honour me today, I have honoured you yesterday." Here, however, the intended meaning is to restrict the act of invention itself by the return, while the particle qad and the perfect form prevent this. The answer is what al-Zamakhshari indicated: that it belongs to the category of ikhraj (a departure from the expected pattern), not in accordance with the apparent requirement. The use of qad and the perfect, which indicate emphasis, is either because it is the answer to an implied oath, or because it is an expression of wonder, meaning: "How great a liar we would be if we returned, etc." The point of the wonder is that the apostate is more eloquent in invention than the unbeliever, because the unbeliever invents a lie against God, exalted is He, in claiming that God has a rival, though He has no rival; and the apostate is like him in this, and goes beyond him in claiming that what was hidden from him of the distinction between truth and falsehood has become clear to him. Taking the sentence as an expression of wonder is preferable, as stated in al-Kashf, because the deletion of the lam (of the answer) is weak. Abu Hayyan, following Ibn 'Atiyya, also permitted that the verb mentioned is an oath, as one says: "I am free from God, exalted is He, if I do such and such," and like the saying of Malik ibn al-Ashtar al-Nakha'i:

*I have preserved my wealth and turned away from glory,*
*and I have met my guests with a stern face.*

*If I do not raid the son of Hind,*
*a day will not pass without the departure of souls.*

This is a kind of the rhetorical embellishment (al-badi'), and many authors of the works on badi' have mentioned it. Izz al-Din al-Mawsili illustrated it with his saying:

*I am free from my predecessors, and lofty aspiration is from my resolve,*
*if I do not draw near with a piety whose oath is accepted.*

And al-Baghunniyya with her saying:

*Let not lofty aims grant me their lordship,*
*if I am not among their servants.*

﴿It is not for us﴾, meaning: it is not right for us, nor does it occur (for us). So the verb is complete (tammah), and it may also come in the sense of: "it is not fitting nor becoming."

﴿That we return to it﴾, in any state or at any time.

﴿Unless God, our Lord, wills﴾, meaning: except in a state or at a time when God wills our return. Mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyya) is to make explicit that He is the Owner, who is not questioned about what He does.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. So He, glorified be He, knows every wisdom and benefit, and His will follows the requirement of wisdom; therefore everything that occurs contains it. This is an indication of not feeling secure from the plotting of God, glorified be He, for none feels secure from the plotting of God except the people who are disbelievers. There is in this a clear reliance upon God, exalted is He. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿In God we have put our trust﴾, for trusting in Him, glorified be He, is a manifestation of helplessness and reliance upon Him, majestic is His glory. The use of the noble Name is for emphasis, and the fronting of the object is for the purpose of restriction. In the verse there is evidence that it is possible for God, exalted is He, to will disbelief.

Shaykh al-Islam claimed that the intended meaning is the impossibility of this occurring, as if it were said: "It is not for us to return to it, except that God, exalted is He, wills the return, and far is that, and it hardly could be," as indicated by the mention of the title of Lordship, and by their saying: ﴿After God has delivered us﴾, for His delivering them from it is among the proofs that He, glorified be He, does not will their return to it. And this was made a consequence of His saying ﴿He has encompassed﴾, etc., after he interpreted it by what he interpreted, namely the impossibility of His willing the return. But this is a subtle point and an aspect of the verse, and perhaps what I have gone to in it is preferable. It is not objected, on the assumption that the return is the object of the will, that the mention of the breadth of knowledge after that has no great meaning; rather the appropriate thing would be the mention of the comprehensiveness of the Will and that all events are by the will of God, exalted is He, as is not hidden. It need not be said that this is a response from Him, peace be upon him, to the claim of restriction, by the possibility of a third case. Al-Zamakhshari built his exegesis upon his corrupt creed, that it is obligatory to observe what is good and what is best, and that God, exalted is He, cannot will disbelief in any way because it departs from wisdom. He cited His saying, glorified be He: ﴿He has encompassed﴾, etc. Ibn al-Munir refuted him by saying that the context of what is mentioned is the acknowledgment of falling short of knowing the outcome and of being informed of unseen matters. A parallel to this is the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him, except that my Lord wills anything. My Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. For when he (peace be upon him) referred the matter to the Will, which is unseen, he glorified God, exalted is He, by singling Him out with the knowledge of unseen things. End of quotation. And to the view that the intended meaning of the exception is perpetuity went Ja'far ibn al-Harith and also al-Zajjaj, and they made it like the saying of the poet:

*When the crow turns white, I shall come to my family,*
*and pitch becomes like milk, fresh and sweet.*

You know well that this contradicts the textual (naqliyya) and rational (aqliyya) proofs, and both the explicit and implicit meanings of the text. Al-Jubba'i and the Qadi said: the intended meaning of "millah" is the sacred law (shari'a), and in it there are things that do not relate to belief, and it is possible that God, exalted is He, may make His servants worship by it. The object of the will is the return to that, meaning: it is not for us to return to your religion, except that God wills it, by commanding us to worship by it, and transferring us, and abrogating what we are in of the law. It has also been said: the intended meaning is, except that God, exalted is He, wills that He enable you over us by compelling us, and leave you and Him, so that we return to the manifestation of your religion under compulsion. This is strengthened by the preceding: ﴿Even though we were unwilling?﴾

It has also been said: the pronoun in His saying, glorified be He, ("in it") refers to the town (qarya), not to the religion (millah). So the meaning is: "We shall leave your town and not return to it, except that God wills, by what He fulfils for us of the promise of manifestation over you and victory against you, and we shall return to it." And it has been said: the estimated sense is: except that God wills that He return you to the truth, so that we all are of one religion. But it is not hidden that all of this is of what makes the bereaved woman laugh. In sum: the verse is clearly in favour of what the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) hold, and glory be to Him who closed the door of right guidance to the Mu'tazila.

﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾. This is a turning away from disputing with them, following what has appeared of their insolence and obstinacy, and a turning toward God, exalted is He, in supplication. The word "fath" here means judgement and decision, a dialect of Himyar or of Murad. Al-fattah among them means the judge, and al-futaha, with a ḍamma, means arbitration.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that he said: "al-fath" means the judgement, a Yemeni dialect. al-Bayhaqi and a group related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I did not know what His saying ﴿Our Lord, decide﴾ meant until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan, when a dispute had occurred between me and her, and she said: 'I will fatih you (fātiḥuka),' meaning: 'I will judge between you and me.'" The word "baynana" is in the accusative as an adverb of place. The restriction by "with truth" is to show fairness. It is also permitted that it be a metaphor for clarification and manifestation, and al-Zajjaj went to this, and from it is "fath" of a difficult matter, meaning its clarification and solution, likening it to opening a door and removing the bolt so that one can reach what is behind it. "Baynana" is, as has been said, an object, with the estimated sense "what is between us." ﴿And You are the best of those who decide﴾, meaning the best of judges, because Your judgement is free from injustice and partiality, or the best of those who make manifest, by Your great knowledge and vast power. This sentence is a concluding remark that confirms the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 90:

﴿وقالَ المَلأُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِن قَوْمِهِ﴾ "And the chiefs who disbelieved among his people said" is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to ﴿قالَ المَلأُ﴾ "the chiefs said", and so on. The meaning of "these chiefs" may be those arrogant ones (al-mustakbirin), and the change of the relative clause is because the basis of their previous statement was arrogance (al-istikbar). This would be a narration of their misguidance (iḍlāl) after the narration of their own straying (ḍalāl), as has been said. It may also be that they were others, lower in rank, whose role was to act as intermediaries between them and the common people and to manage their affairs as the arrogant ones saw fit. That is, they said to the people of their religion, to make them flee from and be discouraged from faith, after they had witnessed the steadfastness of Shu'ayb (ﷺ)... [the text here reads "عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ", so: Shu'ayb, peace be upon him,] and of those believers with him in it, and feared that they would leave them: ﴿لَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتُمْ شُعَيْبًا﴾ "If you follow Shu'ayb"

ودَخَلْتُمْ في مِلَّتِهِ وفارَقْتُمْ مِلَّةَ آبائِكم ﴿إنَّكم إذًا لَخاسِرُونَ﴾ "and enter his religion and abandon the religion of your fathers, then indeed you would be losers" — that is, defrauded (maghbūnūn), since you would be exchanging error for guidance and losing what you gain through cheating and short-measuring (al-takhsīs wal-taṭfīf). So the "loss" (khusran) is a metaphor (isti'āra) according to the first view and literal (ḥaqīqa) according to the second. Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) went to interpreting "the losers" as "the defrauded," while ʿAṭā' interpreted it as "the ignorant," and al-Ḍaḥḥāk interpreted it as "the sinners" (al-fajara). And idhā (إذا) is a particle of response and consequence, parenthetical (muʿtariḍ), as more than one scholar said, between the noun of inna (ism inna) and its predicate (khabar).

It has been said: it is the temporal, future-referring idhā (idhā al-ẓarfiyya al-istiqbāliyya), and the sentence it is attached to has been omitted and replaced by tanwin. Abu Ḥayyan rejected this, saying that none of the grammarians has said it. The sentence is the answer to the oath (qasam) which the lam (اللام) preceded, as evidenced by the absence of the fa' (الفاء) and by its serving in place of the answer to the condition (sādda masadda jawāb al-sharṭ). It is not an answer to both of them together, as some of their statements seem to imply, because that, as has been said, besides contradicting the grammatical rules, would require it to be one sentence having a place in i'rab, while it has no place, though it may be permissible from two perspectives.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 91:**

﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾, that is, the quaking (al-zalzala), as al-Kalbi said. In Surah Hud it says: ﴿And the Cry seized those who did wrong﴾, that is, the Cry of Jibril, peace be upon him. Perhaps the Cry was among the beginnings of the earthquake, so their destruction was attributed at times to the immediate cause and at other times to the remote cause. Some scholars said: the story is not one story, for Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent to two communities, the people of Madyan and the people of al-Ayka. One of them was destroyed by the earthquake and the other by the Cry. But this holds only if the people of Madyan were not destroyed by the Cry. What is narrated from Qatada is that the people who were destroyed by the Cry were the people of Madyan, and that the people of al-Ayka were destroyed by the overshadowing cloud (al-zulla).

In some reports it has come that the people of Madyan were destroyed by the cloud and the earthquake. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others, regarding this verse, that God Most High opened for them a gate of Hell, and sent upon them a fierce heat that seized their breaths. Neither shade nor water benefited them. So they entered the caves (al-asrab), but found them hotter than the outside, and they went out into the open desert. Then God Most High sent a cloud containing a pleasant wind, which overshadowed them, and they found coolness in it. They called to one another until they gathered beneath it, their men, their women and their children. Then it set fire to them, and the earth quaked beneath them, and they burned as locusts burn when they are fried, and became ash.

What makes their total destruction, men and women alike, difficult to accept is what is related from 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, who said: Abu Jad, Hawaz, Hutti, Kalaman, Sa'fas and Qarashat were the kings of Madyan. Their king in the time of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was Kalaman. When he perished on the day of the cloud, his daughter lamented him with her words:

Kalaman has broken my pillar, his destruction in the midst of the encampment,
The lord of the people, there came to him the cry, fire beneath the cloud.
Fire was set upon them, their abode became like something dissolved.

Unless it is said that she was a believer and was saved. It may also be said that this report is one for which there is no chain of transmission (sanad) on which one can rely.

﴿So they were found in their homes, prostrate﴾: its parallel has already been mentioned. ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining their being afflicted by the evil consequence of their words:

﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town."﴾ The relative clause is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is God Most High's words: ﴿as though they had never flourished therein﴾, that is, they had not dwelt in their homes. Qatada said: the meaning is "as though they had never lived therein in prosperity." Many have mentioned that one says: "ghaniya bi-l-makan yaghna ghina wa ghayanan" when one stays in a place for a long time. Some restricted it to dwelling in a comfortable life. Ibn al-Anbari, like others, said: it is from richness (al-ghina), the opposite of poverty, as in the words of Hatim:

We were rich for a time through poverty and wealth, until time gave each of us to drink from its cup.
Our wealth did not increase us in insolence over any kinsman, nor did poverty diminish our honour.

This is also the interpretation of Qatada. Al-Raghib refuted the meaning "stayed" in favour of this sense, saying: "ghaniya bi-l-makan" means that his stay there was prolonged while he was independent of other places. The saying of some who explain the verse, that they were utterly uprooted, is a statement of the resultant meaning. Building the predicate upon the relative clause indicates that the cause of the judgment is the relative clause itself. It is as if it were said: those who denied Shu'ayb perished, for their denial of him, with an everlasting perishing. This suggests here that those who believed in him, peace be upon him, were saved with an everlasting salvation. This is what those who speak of restriction (ikhtisas) in the verse mean. It has also been said that this construction, like one that yields affirmation (taqwiya), may also yield restriction, as in: ("God extends provision"). The indication here is that God, glory be to Him, mentioned earlier the believers and the disbelievers, but here He mentions only the destruction of the deniers. The final meaning returns to this: they were punished for their earlier threat of expulsion, and they became the ones expelled from the town, an expulsion after which there is no return, while Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and those with him were not.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 92:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—they were the losers﴾ is another resumptive clause (isti'naf) to explain their being afflicted with the punishment of their final statement. The restrictive sense (hasr) is clearer here than it was in what preceded it. That is: those who denied him, peace be upon him, were punished for their statement: ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb, indeed you will then be losers﴾. So they became the losers, in this world and the next, because of their denial, not those who followed him, peace be upon him, those who affirmed him, peace be upon him. With this restriction, one is spared an explicit mention of the rescue, as occurred in Surah Hud in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him﴾, and so on.

In the Kashshaf, it is stated that in this resumptive clause and the repetition of the relative pronoun and its clause there is emphasis in rejecting the claim of the chiefs made to their followers, a mockery of their opinion, a ridicule of their advice to their people, and an expression of the magnitude of what befell them. You know that deriving all of that from this very verse is obscure, while the apparent sense is that the two resumptive clauses together indicate it. Al-Tibi explained this as follows: when He, exalted is He, ordered the punishment by the seizure of the earthquake, leaving them prostrate and motionless upon denial and obstinacy, there arose for a questioner the question: What became of their affair after they lay prostrate?

So it was said: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—as if they had never dwelt therein﴾; that is, they were uprooted and their bodies were annihilated, as if they had never lived there. Then he asked: Was the destruction restricted to them, or did it extend to others? So it was said: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—they were the losers﴾; that is, the destruction was restricted to them. The first relative clause was thus made a means to establishing the report, as in his saying:

Indeed she who struck a tent, emigrating, in the city of the army-camp, the ghoul devoured her love.

Likewise, the report concerning the destruction of the people was emphasized, and the judgment and restriction were brought in with force. The second relative clause was made the cause for the existence of the report. The rebuke of their opinion came from the reply to them using the very words they had uttered in advising their people, and the mockery came from the indication that what they had regarded as counsel became disgrace, and the condition they had claimed was reversed. The magnitude of the loss is derived from defining the predicate with the definite article of genus (lam al-jins). As for the expression of the magnitude of what occurred, it comes from His saying, exalted is He: (as if they had never) etc. And likewise from the whole discourse. It is not hidden that the view that this is a resumptive clause without a conjunction (ʿatf) accords with the custom of the Arabs in such a context, for their custom is to use the resumptive form in this way in blame and reproach, saying:

Your brother, who plundered our wealth; your brother, who tore away our veil; your brother, who wronged us.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the second relative clause be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in (yaghnaw), and that it be in the accusative position by an implied "I mean" (a'ni), and that the first be a subject (mubtada') with the predicate ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—they were﴾, and (as if they had never dwelt) a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (denied); and that the first be an attribute (sifah) of "those who disbelieved" or a substitute from it. On both of these possibilities, (as if they had never) etc. is a circumstantial clause. What we have chosen is the better, as is apparent, so let it be pondered.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 93:

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you, but how can I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾ the discussion of its counterpart has already passed, except that this statement may be understood as a rebuke and reproach directed at them. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿how can I grieve over a disbelieving people?﴾ is a denial of its content, meaning: I had certainly given you every excuse in conveying, advising, and warning you of what has befallen you, but you did not hear my words and did not believe me. ﴿So how can I grieve﴾, meaning: I do not grieve over you, because you are not deserving of grief, which is sorrow (al-asa, "grief"), as in al-Sihah and al-Qamus, or intense sorrow, as in al-Kashshaf and Majma' al-Bayan. It may also be that it is an expression of regret over them because of his intense sorrow for them. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿how⁠ ﴾ etc. is a denial addressed to himself for that. In it there is tajrid (abstraction) and iltifat (turning of address), as has been said, since he, peace be upon him, abstracted from himself a separate person and denied to him his sorrow over a people who do not deserve it, and the address turned from second person to first person. Some verifiers have stated that apparently it is not part of iltifat or tajrid at all, for it requires the first-person form, which contradicts tajrid. Rather, it is a type of badi' called ar-ruju' (retraction), which is returning to a previous statement by negating it; because when he said "I had certainly conveyed to you" was an expression of regret that contradicts what follows, it is as if it occurred to him and he retracted the regret, denying his earlier action. This occurs frequently in their speech, and among it is the saying of Zuhayr:

Stop at the abodes that the ages have not effaced, / yes, but the winds and the rains have changed them.

The point in it is the indication of bewilderment and distraction from intense perplexity at the greatness of the matter, such that one does not distinguish between what is like a contradiction in speech and other things. Ibn Hijjah did not distinguish between this type and the type of negation and affirmation, and perhaps the source of that is his reliance, for the latter type, on the definition of Abu Hilal al-Askari; had he relied on the definition of the master of the craft, Ibn Abi al-Isba', the distinction would not have been confused for him. And on the two possibilities in His saying, glorified is He: (over a people) etc., placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun indicates that they do not deserve regret over them because of their disbelief. Yahya ibn Thabit read: (fakayfa iysa), with a kasra on the hamza and the alif converted to ya', according to the dialect of those who vowel the prefix letter of the imperfect with kasra, as in the saying:

Your companion is that you do not make me hear blame, / nor reopen the wound of the heart so that it aches.

and imalah of the second alif. Then, Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, after the destruction of those to whom he was sent, descended with the believers in him to Makkah, until they died there; and their graves, as narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, are on the western side of the Ka'bah between Dar al-Nadwah and Bab Sahm.

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: In the Masjid al-Haram there are two graves in which there is nothing else: the grave of Isma'il and the grave of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both. As for the grave of Isma'il, it is in al-Hijr, and as for the grave of Shu'ayb, it is opposite the Black Stone.

It is also narrated from him that he, peace be upon him, used to read the scriptures which Allah, exalted is He, had sent down to Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Among the strange things is what al-Shihab reported, that Shu'ayb is two persons, and that the in-law of Musa, upon them both be blessings and peace, was from a tribe of the Arabs called 'Anazah, and 'Anazah ibn Asad ibn Rabi'ah ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd ibn 'Adnan; and between him and those who preceded there is a long age, so reflect. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 7, verse 94:

﴿Wa-ma arsalna fi qaryatin min nabiyyin﴾ is a general indication, explained in detail elsewhere, of the conditions of all the nations mentioned. It contains a warning and a caution to the Quraysh. "Min" (*min*) is here, "sayfu khatib," brought in to emphasize the negation. In the sentence the qualifier of "nabiyy" is omitted, meaning: he was denied, or his people denied him.

﴿Illa akhadhna ahlaha﴾ is an exception with no stated antecedent (*istithna' mufarragh*) from the most general of states. "Akhadhna" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "arsalna." In al-Radi's (*al-Radi*) work it is stated that when a past-tense verb serving as a circumstantial clause follows "illa," it is sufficient with the pronoun without the "wa" (conjunction), and this is common, as in: *ma laqituhu illa wa-akramani* ("I did not meet him except that he honored me"). This is because "illa" most often precedes a noun, so the clause is interpreted as: *illa mukriman li* ("except honoring me"), and so it becomes like a present-tense affirmative verb. What is in this verse is of this kind. It may also come with "wa" and "qad," as in: *ma laqituhu illa wa-qad akramani*, and with "wa" alone, as in:
[p. 9]
*ma laqituhu illa akramani*, because the "wa" with "illa" enters into the predicate of the subject, so how much more so the circumstantial clause, though "qad" without "wa" has not been heard in this construction. Al-Murradi said in his commentary on the *Alfiyya*: a circumstantial clause introduced by an affirmative past-tense verb, when it follows "illa," requires the pronoun and the absence of "wa," and the entry of "qad" is prohibited. His saying:

*Mata ya'ti hadha al-mawtu lam talfa hajatan li-nafsi illa qad qadaytu qada'aha*
("When this death comes, you will not find a need of mine unless I have already fulfilled it.")

is rare, and al-Ashmuni and others also state this explicitly. The apparent meaning is that the prohibition of "qad" after "illa" in the cases mentioned applies when the past verb is a circumstantial clause, not absolutely. Otherwise, al-Shihab has mentioned that a past-tense verb does not occur after "illa" except under one of two conditions: either a verb has preceded it, as here, or it is accompanied by "qad," as in: *ma Zaydun illa qad qama* ("Zayd only stood up"). It is not permitted to say: *ma Zaydun illa duriba* ("Zayd was only struck"). From what we have mentioned it is known that what occurs in most copies of the commentary of our master Shaykh al-Islam, that a past-tense verb does not occur after "illa" except under one of two conditions, either the implied presence of "qad" as in this verse, or the accompaniment of "qad" as in your saying *ma Zaydun illa qad qama*, is not as it should be; rather it is a manifest error, as is not hidden.

The meaning in what we are discussing: "We did not send to any town of the destroyed towns a prophet from among the prophets, peace be upon them, in any state, except that We were seizing its people ﴿with adversity﴾, that is, with hardship and poverty, ﴿and affliction﴾, that is, with harm and sickness." Ibn Mas'ud explained them thus, and this is the meaning of the saying of one who said: "adversity" is in wealth and "affliction" is in the self. It is not meant that the beginning of the sending coincides with the seizing mentioned, but rather that it entails it and is inseparable from it. ﴿So that they may humble themselves﴾, that is, that they may humble themselves, submit, repent of their sins, and comply with the command of God, exalted is He.

﴿Then We replaced﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿We seized﴾, and falls within its ruling. ﴿In place of the evil﴾ that had befallen them, because of what preceded, ﴿the good﴾, which is abundance and safety. The word ﴿مَكانَ﴾ (makān, "in place of") is in the accusative, as has been said, as an adverb of place (ẓarf). The verb ﴿بَدَّلْنا﴾ (baddalnā, "We replaced") is taken to include the meaning of أعطى (aʿṭā, "to give"), which takes two objects. Here they are the omitted pronoun and ﴿الحَسَنَةَ﴾ (al-ḥasanah, "the good"). The sense is: We gave them the good in place of the evil. That the good is "in the place" of the evil means that it is a replacement for it.

Some of the verifiers (al-muḥaqqiqīn) said: "The more apparent view is that ﴿مَكانَ﴾ is a direct object of ﴿بَدَّلْنا﴾, not an adverb of place. The meaning is: We replaced the evil state with the good state. So ﴿الحَسَنَةُ﴾ is the thing taken, which came to be in the place of the evil thing left behind, and the thing left behind is the one accompanied by the preposition (bāʾ) as in the phrase: بَدَّلْتُ زَيْدًا بِعَمْرٍو (I replaced Zayd with ʿAmr)."

﴿حَتّى عَفَوْا﴾ means they increased and multiplied in their persons and their wealth. Ibn ʿAbbas and others interpreted it this way, from عفا النبات (ʿafā al-nabāt, "the plant grew abundantly") and عفا الشحم والوبر (ʿafā al-shaḥm wal-wabar, "the fat and the wool increased") when they became plentiful. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Trim the moustaches and let the beards grow (aḥfū al-shawārib wa-ʿfū al-liḥā)."

The verse of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

"By a lush thicket of dense trees whose plants have grown abundant, the saddle knocks me off with the sound of a hoopoe."

And his saying:

"But we strike the sword with it against riders with fat, abundant (ʿāfiyāt al-shaḥm) flanks, sturdy."

The interpretation of Abu Muslim, that it means turning away from gratitude, is not an explanation of the lexical meaning, as is not hidden.

This ﴿حَتّى﴾ (ḥattā, "until") that governs a past verb is inceptive (ibtidāʾiyyah), not terminal (ghāyiyyah), according to the majority (al-jumhūr), and the clause following it has no grammatical position (lā maḥalla lahā), as al-Jalal al-Suyuti related in his commentary on Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ, from some of his teachers. As for the claim of Ibn Malik that it is a terminal preposition (jārrah ghāyiyyah) with a hidden ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) after it, on the reasoning of the verbal noun (taʾwīl al-maṣdar), Abu Hayyan declared this an error, and Ibn Hisham followed him, saying: "I know of no predecessor for him in this." It also involves an unnecessary assumption of an omitted element. Nor is there a problem for him, or for those who say that the sense of terminus is inherent in ﴿حَتّى﴾, even if it is inceptive: a past verb, because it is past, cannot serve as the terminus of what precedes it, since the terminus would come after the thing it terminates. For although the verb is past, it is future relative to what has become its terminus. Understand this.

[Page 10]

﴿And they said﴾, not pausing to consider that what befell them of the two conditions was a trial from Him, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed the harm and the ease have touched our fathers﴾ just as they have touched us.

﴿The harm and the ease﴾. This is nothing but the custom of time (ʿādat al-dahr), which alternates among people between harm and ease, and rotates them among them without there being any motive for them or consequence that follows from them. This is not like the saying of the poet:

"Eight things have overtaken creation through their causes, and every person must meet the eight:
Joy, sorrow, union, separation, hardship, ease, then sickness and health."

As is not hidden. Perhaps the delay of ﴿السَّرّاء﴾ (al-sarrāʾ, "the ease") is to indicate that it follows the harm, so there is no harm in it. ﴿Then We seized them﴾ is conjoined either to the whole of ﴿they pardoned (ʿafaw)﴾ and ﴿they said﴾, or to ﴿they said﴾ alone, because it is the cause of it. That is: We seized them immediately after that. ﴿Suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly.

﴿While they did not perceive﴾ any of that, and did not imagine any of the calamities in their minds. The clause is a circumstantial (ḥāl) emphasizing the meaning of suddenness. This is the most severe kind of seizing, as has been said: "The most painful thing that strikes you is the sudden calamity (al-baghtu)." It has also been said: the intended meaning of not perceiving is their not believing the reports of the messengers, peace be upon them, about this, not that their minds were empty of it or of its time, due to His saying: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were unaware﴾. And what is in this of neglect of the meaning of neglect, and of the place of the clause, is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 96:**

﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God﴾, that is, the towns that were destroyed, indicated by His words, glorified is He: ﴿in a town﴾. The definite article is for the *ʿahd dhikrī* (anaphoric reference to something already mentioned). Although *qaryah* (town) is singular, it occurs in a negative context and so is equivalent to the plural. It has also been permitted that the article be for the *ʿahd khārijī* (reference to something external to the text), pointing to Makkah and its surroundings. This has been criticised on the grounds that it is not evident from the context. It has been justified on the grounds that, when God, exalted is He, informed about the destroyed towns through the denial of the messengers, and that had they believed they would have been safe and prosperous, He moved on to warn the people of Makkah and its surroundings about what befell the earlier nations and towns.

Al-Zamakhshari, in *al-Kashshaf*, permitted that the article be for the *jins* (the class or genus), and the apparent meaning then is that what is intended includes the towns to whose people a messenger was sent, from among those mentioned and others, not only those to which a prophet was sent and whose people were seized as they were seized, and others, as it has been said, because of the clear rejection of what falls under the subsequent *istidrāk* (contrastive clause) that follows it. ﴿Had believed﴾, that is, in what was sent down to their prophets; ﴿and been mindful﴾, that is, of what God, exalted is He, forbade them, as Qatadah said. This includes what they intended by their earlier word.

﴿We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾: that is, We would have made goodness easily available to them from every direction. It has been said that the intended "heavenly blessings" are rain, and the "earthly blessings" are vegetation. Whichever it is, *fatahna* (We opened) contains a *istiʿārah tabiʿiyyah* (derivative metaphor). The point of resemblance between the borrowed-from and the borrowed-for, which we have pointed out, is the ease of obtaining. It is also possible that there is a *majāz mursal* (metonymy), with the relation being that of necessity, and it is possible to construe an *istiʿārah tamthīliyyah* (metaphor of image). There is, as has been said, a difficulty in the verse: it is understood from its apparent meaning that blessings from the heaven and the earth were not opened to them. In al-Anʿam (6:44) occurs: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of all things﴾, and this indicates that He opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth. This is the meaning of His words, glorified is He: ﴿the gates of all things﴾, because what is meant by them is abundance, prosperity, health and well-being, in contrast to "We seized them with misfortune and adversity". To take the opening of blessings as their continuation or increase is a departure from the apparent meaning and is not suitable to their interpretation of *fatḥ* (opening) as the facilitation of goodness, nor to rain and vegetation. Al-Khayali answered this by saying that it is proper to intend by "blessings" something other than good, or to intend that they believed from the beginning and so were saved from misfortune and adversity, as is the apparent meaning; and what is intended by *fatḥ* in al-Anʿam is what is intended by *ḥasanah* (good) here, so no difficulty is imagined. End.

You know that the intention that they believed from the beginning until the end is not evident. Rather, the apparent meaning is that if they had believed after being tested, We would have made easy for them what We made easy in place of what befell them of the varieties of punishment, some of which come from the heaven, such as the raining down of stones, and some from the earth, such as the earthquake. With this the difficulty is resolved, because the verse of al-Anʿam does not indicate that He opened this opening for them, as is clear from what follows it. As for what has been mentioned, that what is meant by *fatḥ* there is what is meant by *ḥasanah* here: if it means that the opening there occurred in the place of the giving of *ḥasanah* instead of *sayyiʾah* (evil) here, since the mention of each of them came after the mention of seizing with misfortune and adversity, and after it seizing suddenly, then perhaps it has a point, but this alone is of no benefit. If it means that the meaning of that general term, intended for abundance, is the meaning of *ḥasanah*, then what is in it is not hidden. So reflect. It has also been said that the intended heavenly and earthly blessings are the things whose outcomes are praised and by which their possessor is happy in both abodes. The word *barakah* has come in their speech with the meaning of happiness, so it should be taken here as the complete form of that kind. This opening is granted only to the believer, unlike rain, vegetation, health and well-being, which are granted to the believer and also to the unbeliever as a respite and a deception. This interpretation is required according to what has been said, if what is meant by "towns" includes towns to which a prophet was sent and whose people were seized as they were seized, and others. It has also been said that the heavenly blessings are the answering of supplication, and the earthly ones the fulfilling of needs. So let this be understood.

Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿*la-fattaḥnā*﴾ with the doubled letter (intensive form). ﴿But they denied﴾: that is, but they did not believe and were not mindful. He was content with mentioning the first, because it implies the second, and to point out that it is the greater of the two matters. ﴿So We seized them for what they were earning﴾ of kinds of unbelief and sins, of which their earlier word is one. The apparent meaning is that this seizing and the one preceding it in His words, glorified is He: ﴿So We seized them suddenly while they were not aware﴾ are one and the same, and it is not an expression for drought and famine as has been said, because these two have ceased with the replacement of good in the place of evil. Taking one of the two seizings as the otherworldly seizing and the other as the worldly one is far-fetched. And whoever holds that the article is for the *jins* in the last sense must consequently take "they denied, so We seized them" as referring to denial and seizing that occurred among them, and the remoteness of this is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 97:

﴿Then are the people of the towns secure﴾? The interrogative hamza (the question particle *al-hamza*) is for denouncing what has occurred and deeming it abhorrent. It was said that it is for denouncing the occurrence and negating it. This was objected to on the grounds that ﴿So they feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾ etc. contradicts it, and the *fa'* (*al-fa'*) is for sequence with causation. As for the intended "people of the towns": it was said they are the people of the towns mentioned, the apparent noun being used in place of the pronoun to indicate that the basis of the rebuke is the security of each group from the punishment that came upon it, not the security of all the nations together. It was also said they are the people of Makkah and its surroundings, to whom our Prophet ﷺ was sent, and this is preferable in my view. Muhyi al-Sunnah (the Reviver of the Sunnah) went to this view. The conjunction, according to both views, is upon ﴿We seized them suddenly﴾, not upon an omitted element, and the omitted element is to be supplied as suits the context, as occurs similarly in the Qur'an many times. The matter of the interrogative's priority is easy.

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah﴾ etc. is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*) placed between the two, for the sake of hastening to explain that the seizure mentioned is among what their hands had earned, with regard to the first. It also supports what was mentioned, that the seizing suddenly was consequent upon belief and piety. Had it been reversed, the matter would be reversed with regard to the second. If you make the *lam* in what preceded generic (*li-l-jins*), it emphasizes this parenthetical clause, the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to alike, and encompasses them both equally, according to what is in al-Kashshaf. The conjunction upon ﴿So We seized them﴾ was not made the nearer one, because it was not brought forth intentionally to explain the towns and the story of their destruction as the preceding one was. So conjunction upon the preceding one rather than upon it is more fitting. This is when the towns intended are the towns indicated by what preceded. As for when they are intended to be Makkah and its surroundings, the reasoning is clearer, because the source of the denunciation is what befell the earlier nations, not what befell the people of Makkah and those around them of famine and hardship. It may be said: if the intended "people of the towns" in both places are the people of Makkah and its surroundings, then the conjunction upon the nearer is more fitting. The meaning is: after that seizure of those who were arrogant, grew mighty, and opposed the Messengers, peace be upon them, and after its becoming widespread and known, do the people of the towns who share with them in that feel secure ﴿from Our punishment coming upon them﴾, that is, Our chastisement, ﴿by night﴾, that is, at the time of *bayat* (a nightly attack), which is what is meant by those who said "at night." It is a verbal noun of *bata* (to spend the night), and its accusative is in the adverbial sense (*zarfiyya*) with an implied noun. It may also be a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) of the object, meaning "while they were spending the night." It was also permitted that it be a verbal noun of *bayyata*, its accusative being an absolute object (*maf'ul muṭlaq*) of ﴿comes upon them﴾ from a root other than its own verb, meaning "a night-attack," or a circumstantial state of the subject in the sense of "attacking" (with *kasra*), or of the object in the sense of "being attacked" (with *fatḥa*). More than one scholar preferred the adverbial sense to match what follows. ﴿While they are asleep﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of their pronoun, whether the explicit or the implicit one in *bayatan*, since it is treated as a descriptive, as you have heard. It is then a multiple-layered circumstantial clause (*ḥāl mutadākhila*).

Page 12

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 98:

﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾ This is a denial following upon a denial, for the sake of intensifying the rebuke and emphasis; the sequence between the two is not intended, which is why the particle fa' (then) is not used.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read (aw) with a sukun on the waw, and it denotes one of two things. The intended meaning is an alternation between the punishment coming upon them by night (bayatan) and what is indicated by His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿that Our might comes upon them in the forenoon﴾, that is, at the time of the late morning (duha), which in origin is the rising of the sun, or its shining at the time of its rising. Then it was used for the time in which that occurs, and it is one of the hours of the day in their reckoning. These are: al-dhurur, al-buzugh, al-duha, al-ghazalah, al-hajirah, al-zawal, al-dulug, al-asr, al-asil, al-sanut, al-hudur, and al-ghurub. Some of them call them: al-bukur, al-shuruq, al-ishraq, al-radd, al-duha, al-munawwa', al-hajirah, al-asil, al-asr, al-tifl, al-hudur, and al-ghurub. As al-Shihab said, it is mutasarrif (declinable) if it is not meant as a specific time of a particular day, and ghayr mutasarrif (indeclinable) if it is meant as the forenoon of a specific day, in which case it requires the accusative as an adverb of time and is maqsur (with a short final alif); if its initial letter is given a fatha, it is mamdud (with a long alif). They have also counted the word duha among those words that are used both as masculine and feminine.

﴿while they are at play﴾ That is, they amuse themselves out of excessive heedlessness. This is a metonymy (majaz mursal) in that sense, and it is possible that there is a metaphor (isti'arah) there, meaning they occupy themselves with what has no benefit in it, as if they were playing.

﴿Did they then feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾ This is a repetition of both preceding denunciations combined together, separated in purpose, with the aim of increasing warning and admonition. A group of the leading verifiers (muhaqqiqun) mentioned that if it were made a repetition of this and also of the heedlessness of the people of the earlier towns, on the meaning that all of it is a result of feeling secure from the plan of Allah the Exalted, it would be permissible. However, since it has been made a threat to those present, it is more appropriate to restrict it, though this requires consideration. Makr (plan) originally means deception, and it is also used for concealment. One says: "The night schemed (makara al-layl)," meaning it concealed what is in it with its darkness. When it is attributed to Him, glory be to Him, the intended meaning is His leading the disobedient servant on gradually (istidraj) until He destroys him in his heedlessness, likening that to deception. This attribution to Him, glory be to Him, is permissible without mushakala (the convention of using the same word for an attributed act), contrary to some scholars. Here it means the coming of the punishment (al-ba's) in the two times and the two states mentioned. Was the replacement of the evil with the good mentioned before a plan and gradual leading, or a gentle treatment and alternation? There is disagreement about this, and all of it is possible. ﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾, that is, those who lost their own souls, so they wasted the innate nature of Allah upon which He created people, and the near readiness acquired from reflecting on the signs. The fa' here is, as al-Qutb al-Razi and others said, connected to an implied element, as if it were said: "When they felt secure, they lost; so none feels secure." Etc.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is for alerting to the punishment's following upon feeling secure from the plan of Allah the Exalted. It may be said that it is to give the reason for what the statement implies of blaming security and deeming it repugnant. Or it may be said that it is a fasiha (eloquent elliptical) fa', and what is understood from the speech is supposed as a condition, meaning: if security is in the utmost ugliness, then none commits it except one who has lost himself. The Hanafiyya used the verse as evidence that feeling secure from the plan of Allah the Exalted, which, as in Jami' al-Jawami' (a legal-theological compendium), is persisting in sins relying on Allah's pardon, is kufr (disbelief). Similar to it is despair of the mercy of Allah the Exalted, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾. The Shafi'iyya held that both are major sins (kaba'ir), due to the explicit statement of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) to that effect. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bazzar narrated from Ibn Abbas that: "He (ﷺ) was asked: What are the major sins? He said: (Associating partners with Allah, despair of the mercy of Allah, and feeling secure from the plan of Allah, and this is the greatest of the major sins)."

They said: what has been reported that this is kufr is understood as an intensification (taghlid), and the verse "None despairs..." etc. is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿The adulterous woman is not married except by an adulterer﴾ and ﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger﴾, according to one opinion. Some verifiers said: if feeling secure includes the belief that Allah the Exalted cannot take retribution from him, and likewise if despair includes the belief that He is unable to show mercy and kindness or the like, then that is undoubtedly kufr. If it is free of such belief and there is no laxity or lack of concern for Allah the Exalted, then it is a major sin. This is like weighing between the two statements.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 100:

﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the earth after its (former) people?﴾ That is, they succeed those nations who passed away before them. What is meant by them, as narrated from al-Suddi, is the polytheists. Others have explained them as the people of Makkah and its surroundings. On this reading, there is nothing unlikely in the verse using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun, if what was meant earlier by "the people of the towns" was the people of Makkah and those around it. The verb of guidance (yahdi) takes the preposition lam because, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, it carries the sense of "making clear" (al-tabyin). It is said that this is either by way of metaphor (majaz), or by way of implicit meaning (tadmin, where one verb is understood to carry the sense of another), or by treating it as an intransitive verb, as if it were said: "they were heedless, and He did not make guidance clear to them." ﴿That if We willed, We would strike them for their sins﴾, that is, for the requital of their sins, just as We struck those before them. If "strike" (asabna) is taken to imply "destroy" (ahlakna), there is no need to posit an omitted noun. "That" (an) is the light form of the heavy form (an mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), its noun is an unexpressed pronoun of the matter (damir sha'n), and its predicate is the conditional clause. The verbal noun formed with it (al-masdar al-mu'awwal) is the subject of yahdi, and its object, on the reading that takes tadmin, is omitted. That is: "Has it not become clear to them what the outcome of their affair will be, or something similar?" It is also permitted that the subject be God Most High, or a pronoun referring to what is understood from the preceding context, that is: "Has what befell the earlier nations not made itself clear to them?" 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Qatadah, and Ya'qub, and it is also narrated from Mujahid, read (nahdi) with the letter nun. In that case the verbal noun is the object. Some scholars have restricted the consideration of tadmin or metaphor to this reading, and the consideration of treating the verb as intransitive to the reading with the letter ya'. There is discussion on this.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We seal over their hearts﴾, this is a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah) serving as a concluding statement (tadhyili). That is: it is part of Our way and custom that We seal the heart of whoever We do not intend to have faith, so that he does not take warning from the conditions of those before him and does not heed the proofs. If by "the people of the towns" earlier one means the people of Makkah, then this is an emphasis on what He had censured in them of heedlessness, false security, and loss. That is: "And We seal over their hearts; therefore they followed the traces of those before them, did not take lessons from the signs, and felt secure from being overtaken by night raids, as those who succeed them follow exactly in their footsteps." It is also permitted that it be coordinated (ataf) with an omitted element indicated by His saying ﴿Has it not become clear﴾, and that it be coordinated with that phrase itself. Although that phrase is in the form of a request (insha'), its intended meaning is to report their heedlessness and their failure to be guided, that is: "they are not guided, or they are heedless of guidance or of reflection and contemplation, and We seal over their hearts," and so on.

It is also permitted that it be coordinated with "inherit" (yarithun). This has been objected to on the grounds that it is a relative clause (silah), and a coordinated element of a relative clause is itself part of the relative clause, so this would separate parts of the relative clause with a foreign element, namely ﴿that if We willed﴾, whether it is the subject or the object. Abu Hayyan transmitted from al-Anbari that he said: it is permitted that it be coordinated with ("asabna"), since it carries the sense of ("nusibu"), and so the past tense is placed in the position of the future when the future sense is clear, as in His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, shall give you better than that﴾, that is, if He wills, indicated by ﴿and will give you palaces﴾. So "law" here is treated as conditional, meaning "in" (in), and not as the "law" that indicates that something would have happened because something else happened. "Asabna" is taken to mean "nusibu." Sometimes the interpretation is applied to the coordinated element, so that "nathba'u" is interpreted as "taba'na" (we sealed). Al-Zamakhshari rejected this coordination on the grounds that the meaning does not support it, because these people were already sealed over in their hearts, described with the attribute of those before them in committing sins and being struck by them, and that would lead to their being free of this attribute, and that God, had He willed, would have made them possess it. Ibn al-Munir objected to this by saying that it does not necessarily follow that those addressed must be described as sealed, and they, even though they were disbelievers and committers of sins, sealing is by no means a necessary consequence of committing sins. Sealing is persistence in disbelief, insistence on it, and extreme firmness in it, to the point that the one described by it is despaired of accepting the truth. It does not follow that every disbeliever is in this state. Rather, the disbeliever is threatened, for his persistence in disbelief, that God Most High will seal over his heart, so that he never believes. This is what the coordination with ("asabna") requires, so the verse threatens them with two things: being struck for their sins and being sealed over in their hearts. The second is more severe than the first, and it is also a type of striking for sins and a punishment for them, but it is the most painful kind of torment and the most complete form of punishment. God Most High often punishes sins by causing a person to fall into a greater sin, and punishes disbelief by increasing its firmness and extremity, as He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿So it added to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾, just as He increased the believers in faith upon their faith.
