This kind of reward and punishment is fitting for what was its cause and what it is recompense for: the reward of faith is faith, and the reward of disbelief is disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari, however, is only wary of this view because it brings the sealing within God's will, and that, in his view, is impossible, since he claims it is ugly, and God is exalted above it. In al-Taqrib there is something similar to this. He examined what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that what is mentioned is their being sinners and not the sealing, and also that it may be meant: "If We willed, We would increase the sealing in their hearts, or We would have made them secure." The truth, as many verifying scholars have said, is that his objection to this coordination is not only because it does not agree with his opinion. Rather, the composition of the verse does not require it. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿so they do not hear﴾, that is, hearing with understanding and taking heed, indicates that they are sealed over in their hearts, because what is meant is the continuation of this state, not that it falls under the ruling of the will. The non-hearing was already present, and if it were so, it would have to be negated. Also, verification does not suit the purpose. His saying ﴿Thus does God seal over the hearts of the disbelievers﴾ clearly indicates that both the inheritors and those inherited from are of the people of sealing. Likewise His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿and they were not such as to believe﴾ indicates that their state is incompatible with faith and that faith never comes from it at all. Also, the persistence or increase of sealing is not suitable as a punishment for disbelievers. Rather, it may be the punishment for a believer's sin, as occurs in the authentic (hadith) collection. What is raised as an objection to this is not worth considering.

[p. 15]

﴿Those cities—We relate to you some of their news.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustanʾafa*, a clause that begins a new sentence), serving as a summation (*fadhlaka*) of what precedes it, and it indicates the extreme of the misguidance of the nations mentioned. *Tilka* ("those") is a demonstrative referring to the cities of the nations recounted: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud and their likes. The *lam* in *al-qurā* ("the cities") is for prior reference (*li-l-ʿahd*). It has also been permitted that it be for the genus (*li-l-jins*), in which case *tilka* is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), *al-qurā* is its attribute (*ṣifa*), and the clause after it is the predicate (*khabar*).

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that *tilka* be the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), *al-qurā* the predicate (*khabar*), and the clause a second predicate following the first, according to the view of those who permit the second predicate to be a clause. He also permitted that the clause be a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), and that the utility of the statement lies in its restriction by it. Al-Taqrib objected to this, saying that he made the condition for the utility of the statement to be restriction by the circumstantial state, and on the supposition that this is a predicate following a predicate, the condition is void, unless he means: *those cities* whose state or attribute is known, on the basis that the *lam* is for prior reference. But this necessitates dispensing with the requirement that its utility be by way of the state. [Al-Taqrib's objection] ends. In it there is the point that the discussion of dispensing [with the condition] is disputed; for the meaning, as in *al-Kashf*, differs under both suppositions. For when it is made a state, the intended purpose is to restrict it by the state, as al-Zajjaj mentioned in examples like: *this is Zayd standing* (*hādhā Zaydun qāʾiman*). When it is made a restriction of the predicate, the speech is only with one who knows that it is Zayd; otherwise there arises reference to the unknown (*al-iḥāla*), because Zayd would be standing whether or not [he is]. And when it is made a predicate following a predicate—*(fa-tilka al-qurā)* according to the style of that book, on one of the views—*(naqussu)* is a second predicate, for magnification upon magnification, since it draws attention to the fact that these [cities] have stories and other conditions which are hidden.

Al-Tibi said: Since the circumstantial state is a superfluous element (*faḍla*), the difficulty arises regarding the non-utility of the predicate. It is answered that it is not a superfluous element in every respect. As for the predicate, there is no wonder in its being like a part of the first, as in your saying: *this is sweet sour* (*hādhā ḥulwun ḥāmiḍun*), and it is in that position. In it there is the point that counting what we are discussing among that kind—*sour* and dispensable beside *sweet*—and its like, indeed more grievous and more bitter. The answer is that since the two sweets share the same subject, the utility of one suffices, and the form of the present tense (*al-muḍāriʿ*, *naqussu*) is to signify that the story has not yet ended. And *min* (*from*) is partitive (*li-l-tabʿīḍ*), i.e., some of their reports which contain admonition and reminder. The opening of the speech with the mention of the cities, and the attribution of *al-anbāʾ* (the news)—i.e., the great reports—to them, although the intended meaning is the news of their people and the explanation of their conditions, is as indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And there came to them their messengers with the clear proofs﴾. This is because Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that the narration of their total destruction in the manner of annihilation, in a way that includes their dwellings too, by sinking and by the quake, and their remaining desolate and abandoned, is more terrifying and more horrible. The *bāʾ* in His saying, exalted is He: *(bi-l-bayyināt)* ("with the clear proofs") is related either to the verb mentioned, on the basis that it is transitive (*li-l-taʿdiya*), or to an omitted element which occurs as a circumstantial state of its subject, i.e., *while clothed in the clear proofs*, meaning that the messenger of each of the destroyed nations, specific to them, came to them with abundant clear miracles—not that each messenger came with one single proof. As for what they mentioned, that the correspondence of a plural with a plural requires the distribution of the individual units over the individual units, this does not require, as the scholar al-Mawla al-Mudaqqiq Abu al-Qasim al-Samarqandi said in his glosses on *al-Mutawwal*, that in every correspondence there must be a matching of one with one; for the distribution of individuals over individuals may be equal, and it may be unequal. For example, if it is said: *the people sold their animals* (*bāʿa al-qawmu dawābbahum*), it is understood that each of them sold what he had of an animal, and it is permissible that some have multiple animals. For this reason it has been said regarding His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So wash your faces and your hands﴾ that the washing of each person's two hands is established by the Book. The context here requires what we have mentioned: the sentence is resumptive, explaining the perfection of their rebelliousness and obstinacy.

As for His saying, exalted be His majesty: ﴿So they were not to believe﴾, it is an explanation of the continuation of their non-belief in the past time, not of the discontinuation of their belief. A parallel to this is: ﴿So no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾. And the ordering of their condition here upon the coming of the messengers with the clear proofs by the particle *fa* (so) is because continuing upon an act after the arrival of what necessitates abandoning it is considered, according to the heading, a new act and a fresh deed, as in: *I admonished him but he did not desist*, and *I called him but he did not answer*. The *lam* is for emphasizing the negation, i.e., it was not valid nor fitting for a people of those nations at any time *to believe*. Rather, that was impossible for them until they met what they met, owing to the extreme of their rebelliousness and the severity of their stubbornness in disbelief and transgression. Then, if the narrated [case] is the last state of each people among them, then what is meant by their non-belief is their persistence in that after the repeated admonitions; and by what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿because of what they had denied before﴾ is their denial from the time of the coming of the messengers, peace be upon them, until the time of persistence and obstinacy. This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement: *So they were not to believe after seeing those miracles because of what they had denied before seeing them*, meaning: when they first came to them, they came with denial; then they were given miracles, and they persisted in denial. Al-Hasan also went to this view. And it was not made the primary intended meaning in the way the first was, but was made a relative clause (*ṣila*) of the omitted relative pronoun (*al-mawṣūl al-maḥdhūf ʿāʾiduhu*), i.e., *that which they denied*, as a signal that it is clear in itself. What requires explanation is their non-belief after the successive, striking proofs and the manifest miracles which would have compelled them to accept, had they been people of intellect. The relative pronoun to which belief and denial are attached, affirmatively and negatively, is an expression for all the laws which every messenger brought, their roots and their branches. And if the narrated [case] is the states of each people among them, then what is meant, according to what has been said, is what was mentioned first: their continuous disbelief from the time of the coming of the messengers, peace be upon them, until the end of their affair; and by what was indicated last is their denial before the coming of the messengers. So the relative pronoun must be taken as an expression for the roots of the laws which do not accept alteration or change, upon which all the messengers agreed and to which they called the nations: the word of monotheism (*kalimat al-tawḥīd*) and its necessary implications. And the meaning of their denial of them before the coming of the messengers is that they used to hear them from the remnants of those before them, and they denied them—not that reason guides to them and judges by them while they opposed it. Then their state after the coming of the messengers to them was like their state before, as if no one had been sent to them. The restriction of the denial and non-belief to the mentioned roots is because the state of the remainder is evident by the indication of the text (*dalālat al-naṣṣ*); for when they did not believe in what all the messengers agreed upon, then it is more fitting that they not believe in what only some of them held exclusively. The non-making of this denial the primary intended meaning is because it is not the axis of the punishment; rather its axis is denial after the sending, as His saying, exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿And We never punish until We send a messenger﴾. The matter that occurred before it was mentioned only as an explanation of their deep-rootedness in disbelief and denial. It has also been said: what is meant by what was indicated last is their denial which they concealed on the Day of the Covenant. This was narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi and Muqatil, and al-Tabari chose it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have transmitted from Mujahid that the verse is on the pattern of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾. So the meaning is: *they would not have believed, even if We had destroyed them and then revived them, in what they had denied before their destruction*. On this view, what is meant by the relative pronoun is all the laws, their roots and their branches. There is in this from the exaggeration regarding their persistence and rebelliousness what is not hidden, except that it is in the utmost obscurity. In any case, the three pronouns agree in their referent. It has been said: the pronoun in *(kadhdhabū)* ("they denied") refers to their forefathers, and the meaning is: *the sons would not believe in what the fathers denied*. The strained nature of this is not hidden. Al-Akhfash went to the view that the *yāʾ* (in *bi-mā*) is causal (*sababiyya*) and *mā* is verbal-nominal (*maṣdariyya*). Upon it, the meaning, as has been said, is: *so they were not to believe now*, i.e., at the coming of the messengers, because of the denial that had preceded in them, which they had become accustomed to and trained in before their coming; or they never believed at all and persisted in their denial because of the denial that arose in them at the coming of the messengers.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that firm and strong sealing (*ṭabʿ*), ﴿God seals upon the hearts of the disbelievers﴾, i.e., their hearts. He placed the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun to show that the sealing is due to disbelief. To this the statement of al-Zajjaj points, and some have stated it explicitly. It is permissible—and perhaps this is the better—that by *the disbelievers* be meant what includes those mentioned and others, and in that there is a warning to the listeners that is not hidden. The display of the majestic Name by way of *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical address) is to cultivate awe and to bring in dread.

[p. 16]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 102:

﴿We did not find in most of them﴾, i.e., most of the nations mentioned. "Wajada" (found) here is transitive to one object, and the lam is attached to it, as in your saying: "I did not find wealth for Zayd" (ma wajadtu li-Zayd malan), i.e., I did not come upon wealth for him, nor did I meet with him. Or the lam is attached to something omitted, as Abu al-Baqa' said: it occurs as a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the words of the Exalted: ﴿of covenant﴾, because it was originally an attribute of the indefinite noun, and when it was placed before it, it became accusative as a circumstantial phrase. The min is extra (mazidah) for generality (istighraq). It is also permitted that "wajada" be cognitive (ilmiyyah), but the first is more apparent. The speech is according to an omitted genitive construction, i.e., we did not find the fulfilment of a covenant belonging to most of them, for they broke what they had pledged to God the Exalted when adversity and hardship touched them, saying: "If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful." Qatadah went to this view. The specification of this matter to most of them is not because some of them used to fulfil the covenant, but because some of them neither made covenants nor fulfilled them. It was said: the intended covenant is what occurred on the day of the taking of the covenant (mithaq), and this was narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-'Aliyah. It was also said: the intended meaning is what God the Exalted enjoined upon them of faith and piety, by establishing proofs and arguments and sending down signs. Ibn Mas'ud explained it as faith, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. It was also said: it has the meaning of remaining, i.e., we did not find for them any remaining upon their natural disposition (fitrah). The "most" is taken in all cases to mean all. Many people went to the view that the pronoun in "akthariham" refers to mankind, which is known due to its fame, and the sentence ﴿Indeed, most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, since it is not specific to what precedes it, but by its generality it emphasizes it. According to the first view, it is a completion (tatmim), as stated by al-Tibi and others. ﴿And indeed We found most of them﴾, i.e., most of the nations or most of mankind, meaning: we knew them, as in your saying: "I found Zayd virtuous." Between this "wajada" and the preceding "wajada" in the first sense there is a perfect paronomasia (jinas tamm) of identical type. "In" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy, its pronoun of the matter is omitted, and it has no governing effect on it, because it is cancelled (mulghah) according to the well-known view. The explanation of "wajada" as "'alima" (knew) which governs the subject and predicate is determined, because it enters upon both of them. The majority have stated that it enters only upon the subject or upon the abrogating verbs, but al-Akhfash disagreed in this and does not hold that view. He permitted its entering upon other than these two.

The Kufans held that "in" is negative, and the lam in the words of the Exalted ﴿certainly defiantly disobedient﴾ is the lam of distinction (al-lam al-farigah). According to the Kufans, "in" is negative and the lam has the meaning of "illa" (except), i.e., we did not find most of them except as those who went out of obedience, and breaking the covenant enters into that. Al-Tibi mentioned that when "the defiantly disobedient" is interpreted as "the covenant-breakers," the verse contains the device of tard and 'aks, which is that two statements are given, the first confirming by its explicit meaning the implication of the second and vice versa. It is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission﴾ up to His saying: ﴿there is no sin upon you or upon them after these﴾. The explicit command of asking permission at the three times specifically confirms the implication of lifting blame at other times, and vice versa. Likewise the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾ This type of expansion (itnab) is matched in conciseness by the type called ihtibak,

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 7, verse 103:

﴿Then after them We sent Moses﴾. That is: We sent him, peace be upon him, after the messengers or after the nations. The first reading is antecedent in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And there had certainly come to them their messengers﴾. The second is indicated by (*bi-tilka al-qura*, "those towns"). The first possibility is preferable. The explicit statement of sequence, together with *thumma* (then), which indicates it, is said to be for the emphatic specification that the sequence is one of temporal distance, since *thumma* is frequently used in other senses. It is also said that it is to signal that his sending, peace be upon him, followed the established pattern of Divine practice in sending messengers one after another. *Min* (from) indicates the starting point. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is, as has been noted many times, for the sake of giving attention to what is fronted and creating anticipation for what is delayed.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿with Our signs﴾, are connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object of *ba'athna* (We sent), or as a qualifier of its verbal noun. That is: We sent him, peace be upon him, accompanied by them, or We sent him in a sending accompanied by them. By "them" is meant the nine signs, which are detailed. ﴿To Pharaoh﴾: it is a proper name (*'alam*) of a person, which then became a title (*laqab*) for every king who ruled Egypt from among the Amalekites, just as Khosrow is the title of whoever ruled Persia, Caesar the title of whoever ruled the Romans, Najashi the title of whoever ruled Abyssinia, and Tubba' the title of whoever ruled Yemen. It is also said that from the outset it was a title for the one mentioned. His name is al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan. It is said: Qabus, and his kunya is Abu al-'Abbas. It is said: Abu Murra. It is said: Abu al-Walid. And it is reported from a group that Qabus and al-Walid are two names for two persons, one of them being Pharaoh of Moses and the other Pharaoh of Joseph, peace be upon them both. It is reported from al-Naqqash and Taj al-Qurra' that the Pharaoh of Moses was the father of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, and it is said he was his son. This is quite strange. The title is applied to every tyrant. It is pronounced *fir'awn* as *zunbur* (with the same pattern), and Ibn Khalawayh reported from al-Farra' the pronunciation with the *f* vowelled with *damma* and the *'ayn* with *fatha*, which is a rare dialect form. It is also said *fur'ay'* on the pattern of *zubayr*, and on this is the verse of Umayya ibn al-Salt:

"Greet David son of 'Ad and Moses,
and Fur'ay', whose building is at al-Thiqal."

It is said that this is a poetic necessity. It is treated as not taking nunation because it is non-Arabic. Abu al-Khattab ibn Dihya, in *Muruj al-Bahrayn*, reported from Abu al-Nasr al-Qushayri in *al-Taysir* that in the Coptic language it is the name for the crocodile. The view that it is not declined because it has no namesake, like Iblis according to those who derive it from *ablasa*, is worthless. It is said that it and its similar predecessors are proper names of individuals and are not generic proper names (*'alam al-jins*), because they are pluralized as *fara'ina*, *qayasira* and *akasira*, and a generic proper name is not pluralized. Therefore one must hold that each one to whom it is applied has a specific imposition. This has been criticized as worthless, because what misled him is the statement of al-Radi that a generic proper name is not pluralized because it is like an indefinite noun, encompassing the few and the many, since it is imposed for the quiddity, so there is no need to pluralize it. The grammarians have explicitly stated otherwise, and among those who mentioned its plural is al-Suhayli in *al-Rawd al-Unuf*. So the intent of al-Radi is that its pluralization is not regular. What he mentioned is far-fetched, and we are in no need of it.

﴿And his chiefs﴾: that is, the nobles of his people. Their being singled out for mention, despite the generality of his mission, peace be upon him, to his people as a whole, is because they are the principal ones in managing affairs, and others follow them in what they bring and what they send out.

﴿So they wronged them﴾: that is, wronged by means of them, i.e. the signs. The basic meaning of *zulm* (wrong) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. It transitively takes its object directly, not with *bi* (by/with). However, since it and disbelief (*kufr*) are of one kind, it is given the same construction as disbelief, or it has the meaning of disbelief figuratively (*majaz*), or by implicit meaning (*tadmin*), or it implicitly contains the meaning of denial (*takdhib*). That is: they wronged by disbelieving in them, or by denying them. As for the view of some that the meaning is: they disbelieved in them in place of belief, which is their due because of their clarity, it is clearly an instance of implicit meaning, as if it were said: they disbelieved in them, placing disbelief in other than its proper place, since belief was what befitted them.

It is also said: the *ba'* is causal, and the object of *zalamu* is omitted, meaning: they wronged the people by preventing them from belief, or they wronged themselves, as al-Hasan said, and al-Jubba'i said: by means of them. Its intent is persistence in disbelief in them until they met the punishment they met.

﴿So look, how was the outcome of the corrupters﴾: that is, the final end of their affair. He placed "the corrupters" in the position of their pronoun to indicate that wrongdoing entails corruption. The *fa'* (so) is because, just as their wronging by the signs entails that awful outcome, so the narration of it entails the command to look upon it. The address is either to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, or to everyone who is capable of looking. *Kayfa* (how), as Abu al-Baqa' and others said, is the predicate of *kana* (was), fronted before its subject because it requires initial position. The clause, according to what has been said, is in the place of accusative by removal of the preposition: that is, look with the eye of your intellect at the manner of what We did to them.

﴿And Moses said﴾: This is a new sentence, brought to elaborate what was summarized in the preceding verses.

﴿O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger﴾: That is, to you, as is indicated by what follows. (I have come to you) to the Eternal. The meaning is that what had been decreed of destroying their enemy and making them inherit the land passed and continued upon them. (Al-husna), the feminine of al-ahsan (the best), is an attribute of the word (kalima). It was described as such because it contains a promise of what they love and find good. It is related from al-Hasan that by the word is meant the promise of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, to them of Paradise. It is not hidden that the preceding context (al-sibaq) and the immediate context (al-siyaq) reject this. The discourse shifts from the first person to the second person, (or to you) as is indicated by "so send" ﴿so send﴾, ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾: that is, their master and the owner of their affairs. ﴿Worthy of me is that I should not say about Allah except the truth﴾: this is an answer to his (peace be upon him) being denied, which is implied by His saying, glorified be He: ﴿but they wronged themselves by them﴾. "Worthy" (haqiq) is an attribute of "messenger," or a predicate following another predicate.

It has been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "I am worthy," and it means "deserving." "Upon" (ala) is in the sense of "bi" (with), as al-Farra' said, or in the sense of "eager" (haris), and "upon" retains its literal meaning. Abu 'Ubayda said: or it means "obligatory." This was raised as an objection: that saying the truth is obligatory upon Moses (peace be upon him), not the reverse, and the wording is apparent in that. It is answered that its original form...

﴿Bound to﴾ with the yāʾ doubled (shaddah), as in the reading of Nāfiʿ and Mujāhid: (that I should not say) etc. The letter is then changed (qalb) to avoid confusion, as in the verse of Khirāsh ibn Zuhayr:

"You have lied, by the House of God, until you treat the forelocks of a war that does not soften or grow gentle."

And horses will charge, with no leniency among them, and the spears will be broken by the red, stubborn ones.

It has been held weak, because whether the transposition concerns the words, through prefixing and postfixing, like "the cloth pierced the nail," or only the meaning, as here, it is eloquent only when it contains a subtle point (nukta), as in the verse, where the point is the indication of the intensity of the stabbing, so that the spears were broken on them through their breaking because of it. Al-Mutanabbi made this explicit in his saying:

"The sword suffers as the ribs suffer from it, and swords have their appointed times as people do."

It has also been argued that there is a constant connection between the obligated party and the one who is obligated, so he expressed his necessary bond to the obligation by his being obligated toward the obligation, as the reverse is also well known. This is not an allusive metonymy (kināyah īmāʾiyyah, a suggestive indirect expression), like the saying of al-Buḥturī:

"Did you not see that generosity has placed its saddle in the house of Ṭalḥah, and has not moved on?"

And the saying of Ibn Hāniʾ:

"Generosity has not surpassed him, nor has it stood before him, but generosity travels wherever he travels."

Rather, it is a figurative usage (tajawwuz, metaphor) containing fine hyperbole (mubālaghah), and this is clear from the extreme description of truthfulness, in that the saying of the truth has been placed in the position of a man upon whom something is obligatory. Then he made himself, that is, his readiness for the saying of the truth and his standing by it, to be in the position of the one obligated toward the saying of the truth. Thus it is a concealed metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah) and an imaginative metaphor (istiʿārah takhyīliyyah). The meaning is: "I am obligated toward the Truth to strive that I be its sayer and its speaker, so how can lying be conceived of from me?" Al-Quṭb al-Rāzī and others objected to this, saying that it would only hold if he were bound upon the saying of the Truth, whereas in fact he is bound upon his saying the Truth, and his saying the Truth has been made such that it is obligatory for him to strive that he be its sayer, which has no meaning.

It has been answered that this rests on the premise that the infinitive clause (maṣdar muʾawwal, the verbal noun formed by "that" plus the verb) must be annexed to what was its subject, and this is not granted, for it may disregard that. Some grammarians have stated that it may be indefinite, as in ﴿It was not for this Qur'an to be invented﴾, meaning: invention. Here, the consideration of the agent has been set aside, since the meaning is: "The saying of the Truth is incumbent upon me," and this is the sum of the whole utterance, so there is no difficulty.

Ibn Miqsam, in explaining the verse according to the reading of the majority, claimed that it is preferable that "upon me that I should not say" be connected to "a messenger," if we hold that a modifier (ṣifah, adjective) may govern when it is qualified. If we do not hold this, which is the well-known view, then it is connected to a verb implied by it, meaning: "I was sent on the condition that I should not say," etc. In my view, it is preferable that "ʿalā" carries the sense of "bāʾ" (with), and this is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "with that I should not say."

ʿAbd Allah read: "that I should not say," with the preposition omitted, and it is either ʿalā or bāʾ. The earlier mentioned ʿalā is read with a doubled yāʾ. His glorious saying: ﴿I have indeed come to you with a clear sign from your Lord﴾ is a resumptive statement confirming what precedes it. This and what follows it were not part of Pharaoh's reply immediately after what is mentioned here, but after the exchanges that took place between them, which God related in more than one place, and their mention has been omitted here for brevity. The word "from" (min) is connected either to "I have come to you," in the sense of the starting point of the action in a figurative manner, or to an implied word that serves as an attribute of "a sign," conveying its grandeur through the added phrase, and emphasizing its intrinsic grandeur, derived from the magnifying indefiniteness, as has been mentioned more than once. The addition of the name "the Lord" to the pronoun of the addressees, after it had earlier been added to "the worlds," serves to emphasize the obligation of believing in it. The all-encompassing, majestic name was mentioned to show that he is worthy of the saying of the Truth upon Him, glorifying the matter of inventing lies against Him, exalted is His majesty, together with an indication of the cause, the reason beyond which there is no further reason.

﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾: that is, release them so that they may go with me to the Holy Land, which is the homeland of their forefathers. The enemy of God and the Copts had enslaved them after the passing of the tribes (asbāṭ), making them serve and imposing on them arduous labours such as building and carrying water. So God rescued them through Moses, peace be upon him. Between the day Joseph, peace be upon him, entered Egypt and the day Moses, peace be upon him, entered it, there were, according to what is related from Wahb, four hundred years. The use of "sending" in the sense indicated here, as appears from the words of al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī), is literal. It has also been said that it is a metaphor drawn from releasing a bird from its cage, either as an allegorical metaphor (tamthīliyyah) or a subordinate metaphor (tabaʿiyyah). It is not hidden that this has fallen away from the nest of acceptance. The particle "fa" (so) indicates that the sending, or the command to send, follows from what precedes it: his messengership and his coming with the clear sign.

Pharaoh said: [This is] a rhetorical resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if it were asked: "What did Pharaoh say?" So it was answered: "He said:"

﴿If you have come with a sign﴾ from the One who sent you, as you claim, ﴿then produce it﴾, i.e., bring it forward before me so that your truthfulness in your claim may be established by it. The difference between the conditional clause (al-shart) and the response (al-jaza') is therefore beyond dispute. Perhaps the matter does not require this stipulation, since it is attained by what, I suppose, is not hidden from you, ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in your claim, for your being among those known for truthfulness necessarily requires that the sign be displayed without any doubt.

So he cast down his staff. It was, as Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, of ʿawsaj (wild jujube) wood.

It is also reported from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, that it was of almond wood.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah that he said: "It was mentioned to us that it was the staff of Adam, peace be upon him. An angel gave it to Musa when he set out for Madyan. It would shine for him at night, and when he struck the earth with it by day, his provision would come forth for him, and he would herd his sheep with it." The well-known view, however, is that it was of the myrtle of Paradise and belonged to Adam, peace be upon him, and then came to Shuʿayb, who gave it to him. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that its name was Mashaa.

﴿And behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, that is, a huge, long snake. From al-Farraʾ it is reported that the thuʿban is the large male of the snakes. Others said that it is the snake in general.

In Majmaʿ al-Bayan it is stated that the word is derived from thaʿaba al-maʾu (the water gushed forth), so it was named thuʿban because it moves like a gushing stream of water. ﴿Manifest﴾, that is, its matter is clear, with no doubt that it was a serpent. This indicates that the transformation was real and not imaginary (takhyili). The use of the nominal sentence serves to show the complete speed of the change and the permanence of the quality of being a serpent, as though it was originally so.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi that when he cast it down, it became a yellow, hairy snake, its mouth wide open, with a distance of eighty cubits between its jaws. It rose from the ground to the height of a mile, stood upright on its tail, placed its lower jaw on the earth and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace, and turned toward Firʿawn to seize him. He leapt from his throne fleeing and voided his bowels. In some reports it is said that he voided his bowels four hundred times that day, and in another that the stomach ailment remained with him until he drowned. It was also said that it took hold of Firʿawn's dome between its fangs, and that it charged at the people, so they fled in a crush, and twenty-five thousand of them died. Then Firʿawn cried out: "O Musa, I beseech you by the One who sent you to take it, and I will believe in you and send the Children of Israel with you." So he took it, and it returned to being a staff as it had been.

It is reported from Maʿmar that it was as large as a city. It was also said that its length was eighty cubits. And from Wahb ibn Munabbih that the distance between its jaws was twelve cubits. With all these reports, there is no contradiction between what is mentioned here and His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿as if it were a jinn﴾, on the basis that the jinn here is a small snake; because they said the story occurred more than once; or that the purpose of that is to liken it to the jinn in the lightness of its movement, not to describe its bulk; or because it was said that it turned into a jinn and then into a serpent, so the two states were related in two verses. This will be verified, Allah willing, later.

[p. 21]

The verse is among the strongest evidences that a thing may change from its reality, as copper into gold. For if that were imaginary, the miracle (iʿjaz) would be void, and the word ﴿manifest﴾ would have no clear meaning, and resorting to what is not apparent is itself not apparent. This is also supported by the fact that there is no impediment, in terms of power, to the creative command being directed to what has been mentioned and the will being specified for it. As for the claim that reversing realities is impossible and power does not relate to it, so that copper cannot become gold, but only a deceptive lead-like metal, the correct view is that transformation is permissible, either in the sense that God creates gold in place of the copper, according to the opinion of the investigating scholars, or by stripping the particles of the copper of the attribute by which it became copper and creating in it the attribute by which it becomes gold, according to the view of some theologians regarding the homogeneity of substances and their equal readiness to receive attributes. What is impossible is only that it becomes gold while remaining copper, since it is impossible for a thing to be both copper and gold at the same time. And upon one of these two considerations, the leaders of tafsir relied regarding the matter of the staff,

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, i.e., he brought it out from his collar, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And put your hand into your bosom﴾. Or [he drew it out] from under his armpit, in accordance with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And draw your hand to your side﴾. Both can be done at the same time. The hand was the right one, as stated in some reports. ﴿Then behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾, i.e., white with a luminous whiteness beyond the ordinary, such that the spectators gathered around it.

It is related that its light illuminated everything between the heavens and the earth. In another narration, he showed his hand to Pharaoh, and [Pharaoh] said: "What is this?" He said: "Your hand." Then he put it back into his collar, while he was wearing a woolen garment, and drew it out, and behold, it was white with a luminous whiteness whose radiance overpowered the rays of the sun.

It was also said: the meaning is "white for the sake of the onlookers," not that it was white in its original creation, because he (peace be upon him) was very dark-skinned.

Al-Bukhari related from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "As for Musa, he was dark-skinned, tall, with straight hair, as if he were one of the men of al-Zutt."

By "al-Zutt," the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) meant a people of the Sudanese and the Indians. Some scholars stated that this whiteness was only in the palm, and that applying the term "hand" to it is literal usage.

In the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit): "The hand (yad) is the palm, or from the tips of the fingers to the palm. Its original form is yady, as shown by its plural being aydi. The word yad is not found when attached to a pronoun, for reasons established in its proper place. In their speech, yaddun with doubling (tashdid) also occurs, and it is a dialectal variant of it."

The Chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: ﴿The chiefs from among his people said﴾, i.e., the nobles among them, who are the people of his counsel and the leaders of his state.

﴿Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer﴾, i.e., one who has excelled in the knowledge of magic and is adept in it. ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾, i.e., out of the land of Egypt.

﴿So what do you advise?﴾ i.e., what do you counsel regarding his affair, as Ibn 'Abbas explained it. So it is from amr (command) in the sense of mushawarah (consultation): one says "amartuhu fa-amarani", meaning, I consulted him and he advised me. It has also been said that it is from the well-known sense of amr (command). The word "madha" (what) is in the accusative position as the object of ta'murun with the preposition omitted, i.e., "with what do you command?" It has also been said that "ma" is a predicate placed before its subject, and "dha" is a relative pronoun serving as a postponed subject, i.e., "what is it that you command with?"

The Chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: ﴿The chiefs from among his people said﴾, i.e., the nobles among them, who are the people of his counsel and the leaders of his state.

﴿Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer﴾, i.e., one who has excelled in the knowledge of magic and is adept in it. ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾, i.e., out of the land of Egypt.

﴿So what do you advise?﴾ i.e., what do you counsel regarding his affair, as Ibn 'Abbas explained it. So it is from amr (command) in the sense of mushawarah (consultation): one says "amartuhu fa-amarani", meaning, I consulted him and he advised me. It has also been said that it is from the well-known sense of amr (command). The word "madha" (what) is in the accusative position as the object of ta'murun with the preposition omitted, i.e., "with what do you command?" It has also been said that "ma" is a predicate placed before its subject, and "dha" is a relative pronoun serving as a postponed subject, i.e., "what is it that you command with?"

﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother, and send out to the cities"﴾, meaning: delay their matter and dismiss them from your presence, and do not hasten regarding their affair until you see your opinion about them. It was also said: "Detain them." This was objected to on the grounds that detention from him has not been established.

It was answered that the command to do something does not necessitate that it occurs. It was also said against this: he was no longer able to detain them after he had seen what he had seen. And his statement, ﴿I will surely make you among those imprisoned﴾, in ash-Shu'ara' was before this. It was answered that those who spoke perhaps did not know of that from him. Abu Mansur said: the command to delay indicates that another command had preceded it from him, namely, the intention to kill him (Moses). So they said: "Delay him, so that his condition may become clear to the people." But this is not necessary, as is not hidden.

The original form of *arjih* (أرْجِهْ) is *arji'hu* (أرْجِئْهُ), with a silent hamza and a damma on the ha', without a waw. Then the hamza was dropped and the ha' was made silent, to make the separated resemble the connected, and *arjih* was treated like *ibil* (إبِلْ) in the silencing of its middle. Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr, and Ya'qub recited it this way, considering it to be from *arjaat* (أرْجَأتُ). Likewise is the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Hisham, and Ibn 'Amir: *arji'huw* (أرْجِئْهُو), with a silent hamza and a ha' connected to a waw of vowel-lengthening (ishba').

Nafi', in the transmission of Warsh, Isma'il, and al-Kisa'i recited *arjihi* (أرْجِهِي) with a kasra on the ha' followed by a ya', from *arjaytu* (أرْجَيْتُ). In the transmission of Qalun it is *an arjihi* (أنْ أرْجِهِ), with the ya' omitted, being sufficient with the kasra. Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, recited *arji'hi* (أرْجِئْهِ) with the hamza and a kasra on the ha'. Some have mentioned that the damma and kasra on the ha', and the presence or absence of the hamza, are two well-known dialects (lughatan). And is the root of the two forms distinct, or is the ya' a substitute for the hamza, as in *tawadda'tu* and *tawadda'ytu*? There are two opinions.

The recitation in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan was criticized. al-Hufi said: it is not a good recitation. al-Farisi said: the damma on the ha' with the hamza is the only permissible form, and the kasra is an error, because the ha' is not given a kasra except after a silent ya' or a kasra. It was answered, as al-Shihab stated, in two ways. The first: the hamza is silent, and a silent letter is a weak barrier; so it is as if the ha' came directly after the kasra on the jim, and therefore it was given a kasra. The second: the hamza is liable to considerable change, by deletion and by being replaced with a ya' when it is silent after a kasra; so it is as if the ha' came after a silent ya', and therefore it was given a kasra. Abu Shamah objected to this that the hamza is counted as a barrier, and that if the hamza were a ya', the preferred form would be the damma, in view of its original root. This is not a valid objection, after they have said that the recitation is mutawatir (widely transmitted) and what has been mentioned is an established dialect from the Arabs.

Here the combination of what is here and what is in ash-Shu'ara' is problematic. For in it (ash-Shu'ara') there is: ﴿He said to the chiefs around him: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer"﴾ ﴿"He wants to drive you out of your land by his sorcery; so what do you advise?"﴾ And this is explicit that ﴿Indeed, this is a sorcerer﴾ up to ﴿so what do you advise?﴾ is the speech of Pharaoh. And what is here is explicit in attributing the saying of this to the chiefs. The story is one, so how can the speaker differ in the two places? Is this not a contradiction? It was answered that there is no contradiction, because of two possibilities. The first: this statement was said by Pharaoh and the chiefs of his people, and it is like the striking of a hoof upon a hoof; so his speech is reported in ash-Shu'ara' and their speech here. The second: this statement was said by Pharaoh first, then the chiefs said it, either by way of relating it to their children and others, or by way of conveying it to the rest of the people. So what is in ash-Shu'ara' is Pharaoh's speech originally, and what is here is the chiefs' speech, transmitted from him.

al-Zamakhshari preferred that what is here is the saying of the chiefs, transmitted from Pharaoh by way of conveying it, and nothing else. For when the people heard it, they addressed Pharaoh with their saying: "Put him off," etc. And if that had been the speech of the chiefs from the start, the fitting reply would have been "Put them off" (arji'u). And there is no way it was a transmission by way of relating, for in that case it would not have been a consultation or deliberation with the people, and so their reply would not have been relevant at all. Thus it is necessarily a conveying; therefore they answered him. What remains is to say: this answer with delay in ash-Shu'ara' is the speech of the chiefs to Pharaoh, and here is the speech of the rest of the people. But there is no contradiction, since it is permissible for the two replies to coincide. The statement of Shaykh al-Islam, that the fact that this was the reply of the common people is refuted by the fact that the address is to Pharaoh, and that consultation is not among their functions, is not valid. For a great matter whose consequence reaches the people of the land, a wise king consults his common people and his elite in it, and he may gather them for that and say to them: "What do you see?" For this is a matter that does not afflict me alone, and a good opinion may come from one who was not suspected of it. Moreover, in that there is a gathering of their hearts upon it and upon attending to its importance. We have witnessed that great events are referred to the common people. And the matter of Moses (peace be upon him) was among the greatest events for Pharaoh, after he had witnessed what he witnessed from him.

Then they differed about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾. It was said that it is part of the chiefs' speech, and many have considered this more likely, because it is joined with their speech without any separation; so the more fitting view is that it is part of their speech. al-Farra' and al-Jubba'i said that the speech of the chiefs was complete at His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾
[Page 23]
Then Pharaoh said: "So what do you advise?" They said: "Put him off." And in that case it may be understood, as al-Qutb said, that the speech of the chiefs is addressed to Pharaoh, and the plural address in ﴿to drive you out﴾ is either for magnifying his station, or for considering him together with his servants and helpers. It may also be understood that it is with the people of Pharaoh, and the consultation is from him. Then he said: They adopted this strained interpretation only so that it would agree with what is in ash-Shu'ara', in that His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ is from Pharaoh's speech, and His saying ﴿Put him off and his brother﴾ is the speech of the chiefs. But the contradiction is not entirely removed, because His saying ﴿Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer﴾ and ﴿He wants to drive you out﴾ is Pharaoh's speech to the chiefs. And in this surah, according to what they have interpreted, it is the speech of the chiefs to Pharaoh; perhaps they would say that he said it to them once, and they said it to him another time. End of quotation.

It is possible to say: when the chiefs saw what they saw from Moses (peace be upon him), some of them said to others: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer; he wants to drive you out of your land. So what do you point out, and what do you find good regarding his matter?" And when Pharaoh saw that they were concerned about this, he said to them, to encourage them and to affirm what they were upon, before they replied to one another with what he had, similar to what they had said among themselves. So they turned to him and said: "Put him off and his brother." Thus He, exalted is He, here relates the consultation of some of them with others, and the presentation of what they had to Pharaoh at the first moment, before mentioning it among themselves. And in ash-Shu'ara' He relates his speech to them and his consultation with them, which is the exact counterpart of the consultation of some of them with others related here, and their reply to him after that consultation. On this view, the common people do not enter into the consultation, and here it is more eloquent in blaming the chiefs. So let it be pondered. And God, exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His speech.

﴿And send to the cities﴾, i.e., the lands. It is the plural of *madinah* (مَدِينَةٌ), which is from *madana bihi* (مَدَنَ بِالمَكانِ), like *nasara*, when he dwelt in it. Because the ya' is extra, as many have said, it is changed to a hamza in the plural. It is intended by it the cities in general. It was also said: the cities of Upper Egypt.

﴿Gatherers﴾, i.e., men who gather the sorcerers. Some explained it as the police (shurtah), who are the helpers of the rulers, because they make a sign for them. One individual is called *shurti* (شُرْطِيٌّ), with a silent ra', in relation to *shurtah*. al-Qamus also reports its vowelling with a fatha, but in al-Asas it is said that this is an error, because it is a relative form to *shurat*, which is a plural. The descriptive is put in the accusative because it is an attribute of an omitted noun, and its object is also omitted, as has been indicated. Al-Jawhari explicitly stated this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 112:

﴿Bring to you every learned sorcerer.﴾ That is: skilled in sorcery. The verb is in the jussive mood as the answer to an imperative (ṭalab).

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī recited (saḥḥār) [i.e., "sahhar"]. In it there is both imālah (the vowel-leaning of the ā sound toward i) and its absence. It is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah, the form expressing emphasis or intensity). Some of the scholars explained it as meaning one who constantly practices sorcery, whereas the sāḥir (sorcerer) is one who has practiced sorcery at some times and not at others. It has also been said: the sāḥir is the one who begins in the craft of sorcery, while the saḥḥār is the one who has reached completion, from whom that art is learned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 113:

﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾ after he had sent to the summoners (al-hashirin) to them. The reason it was not stated explicitly is to signal Pharaoh's haste in sending for them and the eagerness of the summoners and the sorcerers to comply.

Their number has been disputed. From Ka'b, they were twelve thousand; from Ibn Ishaq, fifteen thousand; from Abu Thumama, seventeen thousand, and in another report, nineteen thousand; from al-Suddi, some thirty thousand; from Abu Bazza, they were seventy thousand; and from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, eighty thousand. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Jarir, who said: "The sorcerers were three hundred from his own people, three hundred from al-'Arish, and they doubted about three hundred from Alexandria."

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, they were seventy sorcerers, and they had learned sorcery from two Magian men from the people of Nineveh, the city of Yunus (peace be upon him). Something similar is related from al-Kalbi. The apparent view is that this is not sound, because Magianism appeared in the time of Zoroaster according to the well-known view, and he came after Musa (peace be upon him). The name of their leader, as Muqatil said, was Shim'un; Ibn Jurayj said it was Yuhanna. Ibn al-Jawzi, quoting the scholars of biographical histories, said: their chiefs were Sabur, 'Azur, Hutahut and Musafa.

﴿They said﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani); therefore it is not conjoined, as if it were said: "What did they say to him when they came to him?" And it was answered: "They said, etc." This is better than the view that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "came", meaning: they came saying: ﴿Indeed for us there will surely be a reward﴾, i.e., a recompense and a great payment.

﴿If we are the victors﴾. The purpose of the statement is to make the reward obligatory and conditional, as if they said: "On condition that you make a reward for us if we overcome." It is possible that the sentence is in the form of an omitted interrogative particle, which is common; and that Ibn 'Amir and others read (a'inna) with the hamza retained supports this, and agreement between the two readings is better than their disagreement. For this reason al-Wahidi preferred this possibility. The conditional is mentioned merely to specify the basis on which the reward is established, not because they were doubtful about victory. It has been said that the phrase is "lahu" (to him). The placing of the pronoun and the definite article on the predicate are for restriction (qasr), meaning: "We are the victors, not Musa (peace be upon him)."

ۤ﴿He said, "Yes, indeed, [you will receive a reward]."﴾ Indeed, for you there is a reward.

﴿And indeed you will be among those brought near.﴾ This is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to an implied clause, which is exactly the preceding statement, indicated by the affirmative particle (naʿam, "yes"). Such a construction is called ʿaṭf al-talqīn (the conjunction of prompting/suggestion). Whoever says that it is conjoined to what precedes means the same thing we have mentioned. The meaning is: indeed, for you there is a reward, and indeed, along with that, you will be among those brought near. That is, I do not limit my bestowal to you to the gift alone; rather, there is with it something greater than it, namely closeness (al-taqrīb) and honour (al-taʿẓīm). For whoever is given something is only gratified by it and rejoices when he attains with it dignity and elevation. In this there is an extent of emphasis on encouragement and exhortation that is not hidden. It is also reported from al-Kalbī that he said to them: "You will be the first to enter my assembly and the last to leave it."

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new clause that follows on from what precedes it), like its counterpart earlier. ﴿O Musa, either you throw﴾ what you throw first, ﴿or we are the throwers﴾ of what we throw first, or the ones who perform the throwing first. He, peace be upon him, was given the choice of initiating the throwing out of consideration for good manners (adab); and for this reason, as has been said, God Most High bestowed favour upon them with what He bestowed. Or it was to show boldness, and that the situation for them would not differ whether the order was put first or last. But their desire was for going first, as their altering of the arrangement indicates: by making the predicate definite, by placing the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl, the pronoun of separation) in the middle, and by emphasising the concealed pronoun. The apparent meaning is that the same occurred in the reported speech, with something equivalent to it.

As for the statement of Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti: the detached pronoun is either a separating pronoun (fasl) or an emphatic one (ta'kid), and the two cannot be combined, because on the first view it has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), and on the second it has a place like the word it emphasises. This is an error (wahm), as is not hidden.

Al-Tibi distinguished between the pronoun being a separator and its being an emphasis, on the ground that emphasis removes the figurative use of the subject, so that it requires restriction derived from the definiteness of the predicate, meaning: "We, we alone throw, not anyone else." A separator restricts the throwing to them by restricting the predicate to the subject, and so it is free of emphasis. The verification of this is sought from its proper place.

[Page 25]

﴿He said﴾, i.e., Musa, peace be upon him, confident in his own matter, belittling them, and indifferent to them: ﴿Throw﴾, you (all), what you are going to throw first. From what we have mentioned, the answer to what is said becomes known: that their throwing is an opposition to the miracle through magic, which is disbelief, and commanding it would be like it. So how could he command them, while he is who he is? The essence of the answer is that he, peace be upon him, knew that they would have to do that, and the choice was only in advancing and delaying, as he clarified in His words, glorified is He, in another verse: ﴿The first to throw﴾. So he permitted them to go first, not to make their act lawful, but to belittle them. There is no indication in that of approval of this opposition. It may also be said: he, peace be upon him, only permitted them so that he would nullify their magic. Thus it is a nullification of disbelief in the Hereafter and a confirmation of his miracle, peace be upon him. In accordance with this is understood what has come in some reports, that when they said, Musa, peace be upon him, heard a caller saying: "Rather, you throw, O friends of Allah, the Exalted," so he felt fear within himself because of that, until he was commanded, peace be upon him. The verification of that will come, God willing, the Exalted. ﴿So when they threw﴾ what they threw, and each of them had with him a rope and a staff, ﴿they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, by imagining to them what the reality was contrary to. For this reason He, glorified is He, did not say "they bewitched the people." The verse is in the manner of His saying, majestic is His affair: ﴿It was imagined to him, because of their magic, that they were moving﴾. ﴿And they frightened them﴾, i.e., they terrified them with severe terror, as if they had sought to terrify them. ﴿And they came with great magic﴾ in its kind.

It is related that they threw thick ropes and long sticks, and then there were serpents like mountains, filling the valley, some of them mounting others.

In some reports it is said that the land's extent was a mile by a mile and was filled with serpents and vipers. It is also said that they coated those ropes with mercury, colored them, and placed mercury inside the staffs as well, and threw them onto the ground. When the heat of the sun affected them, they moved and twisted over one another, until it appeared to the people that they were serpents. Those who said, like the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology), that magic has no reality but is merely imagination, used this verse as evidence. In response: if they mean that the magic that occurred in the story was like that, this is granted, and the verse indicates it; but if they mean that every magic is imagination, this is rejected, and the verse does not indicate it. What the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah (the followers of the Sunnah, the mainstream Sunni community) have adopted is that magic has types: some of it has no reality, and some of it has a reality, as the sorcery of the accursed Labid ibn al-A'sam, the Jew, against the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, testifies to this, and the sorcery of the Jews of Khaybar against Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, when he went to estimate their dates.

They also mentioned that magic may reach the point of walking on water, flying in the air, and the like, and that the result of this from it is like the result of satiety from eating, quenching from drinking, and burning from fire, while the true agent in all of that is Allah, the Exalted. Indeed, al-Qurtubi said: The Muslims have agreed that what Allah, the Exalted, does at the sending of locusts, lice, and frogs, the splitting of the stone, the turning of the staff, the reviving of the dead, the making of the dumb animal speak, and similar signs of the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, is not part of magic. As for whoever denies its reality, he argues from the necessity of confusion with the miracle, and it is objected that the difference is as clear as the dawn.

And We revealed to Moses (through the angel, as is apparent), "Throw down your staff," the staff whose nature you know well. The *an* here is *tafsiriyya* (explanatory, an *an* that introduces an explanation of a preceding idea), since what precedes it contains the sense of speech without its letters. It has also been permitted that it be *masdariyya* (the verbal *an* that forms a verbal noun), in which case the verbal noun is the object of *al-Iha'* (revelation).

As for the *fa'* in His words, ﴿and behold, it swallows up what they fabricate﴾, it is *fa sayha* (the "eloquent" *fa*, which indicates an implied omitted clause). The meaning is: so he threw it, and it became a serpent, and behold, it swallowed..., etc. It was omitted to signal Moses's (peace be upon him) haste in throwing, and the extreme speed of the transformation, as if its swallowing of what they fabricated had occurred immediately upon the command to throw.

The present-tense form *talqafu* (it swallows up) is used to bring the strange scene vividly before the mind. *Al-laqf* is like *al-laqfan* (both meaning) the taking up quickly, and al-Hasan [al-Basri] interpreted it here as *al-sarṭ* (gulping down) and *al-bal'* (swallowing).

*Al-ifk* is the turning of a thing and its diversion from its customary direction. It is also applied to lying, and Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid interpreted it in this sense, because the lie is turned away from its true face. This usage became so common in it that it became a real (established) meaning.

The *ma* in ﴿what they fabricate﴾ is either a relative pronoun (*mawsula*) or a descriptive (*mawsufa*), and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: what they fabricate and lie about. Or it is *masdariyya* (verbal), and it with the verb has the sense of the passive participle, i.e., *al-ma'fuk* (that which is fabricated), because it is what is swallowed.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read *talaqqafu* (with the *shadda* and the omission of one of the two *ta'*s).

﴿So the truth came to pass﴾, i.e., it became manifest and clear, as said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Farra'.

﴿the truth﴾, which is the command of Musa, peace be upon him. Some of them explained وقع (waqa'a) as ثبت (thabata, "was established"), on the basis that وقع has been used figuratively (isti'arah, metaphor) for being established and taking place, or for stability and permanence, because it stands in opposition to بطل (batala, "was nullified"), and falsehood is transient. The benefit of the metaphor, as has been said, is to indicate effect, because وقع is used for physical bodies. It was also said that what is meant by "the truth fell" is the staff's actual transformation into a serpent, but this is not significant. ﴿And what they had been doing was nullified﴾, i.e., the nullity of what they had been persistently engaged in doing became manifest.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verses 119–120:**

﴿فَغُلِبُوا﴾ means: Pharaoh and his people.

﴿هُنالِكَ﴾ means: at that great assembly.

﴿وانْقَلَبُوا صاغِرِينَ﴾ means: they became humiliated, or they returned to the city in that state. Thus, *inqilab* (turning back, reverting) is either a metaphor for *sayrurah* (becoming), and the connection is evident, or it carries its literal meaning of returning, in which case *saghirin* (humbled) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The first interpretation is preferred because of His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿And the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾, since that took place in the presence of Pharaoh, certainly. It is also permissible that the pronoun in *ghulibu* (they were overcome) and *inqalabu* (they returned), according to the first possibility, refers to the magicians as well. However, this has been objected to on the grounds that they had no humiliation, and interpreting it as fear of Pharaoh or as referring to the state before their faith does not escape its difficulties.

What is meant by "the magicians were thrown down" etc. is that they fell down prostrate. He expressed it with this wording rather than another to indicate that the truth overwhelmed them and compelled them to prostrate, to the extent that they had no self-control left, as if someone had pushed them and thrown them down. Or it means that God Most High inspired them with this and moved them to it, so the one who threw them down is God Most High through His inspiration to them, so that Pharaoh would be broken by those with whom he intended to break Moses, peace be upon him, and the matter would turn against him. It is also possible that the speech is in the manner of a figurative image (*tamthil*), an exaggeration of the speed and intensity of their falling, and al-Akhfash's statement points to this. It is also permissible that the expression with this wording is by way of *mushakalah* (figurative correspondence) with the casting (*ilqa'*) that accompanied it, though it is inferior to what was mentioned earlier.

It is related that the gathering of the people took place in Alexandria, and that the tail of the serpent reached from beyond the sea, and that it opened its mouth eighty cubits wide and swallowed what they had made, one after another. It then turned toward the people, who panicked, and crowding occurred, and twenty-five thousand of them died as a result. Then Moses, peace be upon him, took it, and it returned in his hand as a staff as it had been. God Most High, by His power, annihilated those great bodies. It is also possible that He, glorified be He, divided them into fine particles. When the magicians saw that, they knew that it was from the affair of the heavens and not from magic at all. At that point they fell down prostrate. The apparent meaning of prostration is its literal sense, and it is not far-fetched that they knew its manner. It was also said that Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, prostrated in thanks to God Most High for the manifestation of the truth, so the magicians followed them and prostrated with them. Prostration has also been interpreted as humble submission, meaning that they submitted when they saw what they saw, contrary to the apparent reality which the reports affirm, without any reason to adopt it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 121–122:

﴿Qālū﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in inqalabū, but this is nothing (laysa bi-shay'). It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause relating to the magicians, or to the pronoun in them that is implicit in ﴿sājidīn﴾ (prostrating), meaning that they were thrown down prostrating while they were saying: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾, i.e., the Owner of their affairs and the One who disposes of them.

﴿The Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ is a substitution (badal) for what precedes. They substituted it so that it would not be imagined that they meant Pharaoh and did not restrict themselves to Musa, peace be upon him, since a trace of that imagination might remain. For Musa, peace be upon him, was raised by him (Pharaoh) in his childhood. That is why Harun was placed first in another passage, since that is more effective in removing the imagination, or for the sake of the fasila (verse-ending rhyme). Or because he was older than him. Musa is placed first here for his nobility, or for the sake of the fasila. As for the fawasil (verse-endings) being in the speech of God Most High and not in their speech, it has been said that this does no harm. It is related that when they said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds," Pharaoh said, "I am the Lord of the worlds." So they said in response to him, "The Lord of Musa and Harun." The attribution of Lordship to them is like its attribution to the worlds. It was also said that this attribution is in the sense of belief, i.e., the Lord whose lordship Musa and Harun believe in, and that its non-applicability to Pharaoh by his own claim as well is very evident. However, that is contrary to the apparent sense of the attribution. What was mentioned above makes clear the secret of placing prostration before this statement.

Al-Khazin said regarding this: when God Most High cast faith into their hearts, they fell down prostrating to God Most High, for what He had guided them to and inspired them with of faith. Then they manifested their faith by that. It was also said that they hastened to prostrate, glorifying His majesty, because of the great power they saw, and then they manifested faith. Whoever makes the sentence a circumstantial clause says it is concurrent; so understand. The first to hasten to faith, as related from Ibn Ishaq, were the four leaders whom Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned; then the magicians all followed them,

However, that is contrary to the apparent sense of the attribution. What was mentioned above makes clear the secret of placing prostration before this statement.

Then they manifested their faith by that. It was also said that they hastened to prostrate, glorifying His majesty, because of the great power they saw, and then they manifested faith. Whoever makes the sentence a circumstantial clause says it is concurrent; so understand. The first to hasten to faith, as related from Ibn Ishaq, were the four leaders whom Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned; then the magicians all followed them,

﴿Pharaoh said﴾, rebuking the magicians and reproaching them for what they had done: ﴿Have you believed in Him?﴾ That is, in the Lord of Moses and Aaron, or in God Most High, since this implies that, or in Moses, peace be upon him. It was said that this is because of His words in another verse: ﴿Have you believed in him?﴾ where the pronoun refers to him, peace be upon him, on account of His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾, and so on. The purpose of this declarative sentence is reproach. When a declarative statement is not intended for its usual benefit or its implication, what suits the context arises from it. Here, when the tyrant addressed them about what they had done, informing them of it while it was clear that he did not intend to convey either of the two matters, and the situation was the same, it conveyed reproach and rebuke. It is also permissible to posit an interrogative hamzah here, on the basis that this is common usage, and the question is for denial, meaning that such a thing is not fitting. This is supported by the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim, and Rawh on the authority of Yaʿqub: (ʾa-āmantum), with two clearly articulated hamzahs. The first may be made clear and the second softened to a sound between (bayna bayna, an intermediate sound between a hamzah and the vowel it carries), which is also among the readings transmitted.

﴿Before I give you permission﴾, that is, before I command you to do so myself. This is in the manner of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Were the sea to be ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted﴾, not that permission from him would be possible in this matter. The original form of (ādhana) is (ʾa-ʾdhana) with two hamzahs, the first for the speaker and the second part of the root itself. The second was changed to an alif because it came as a quiescent letter after a hamzah. ﴿Indeed, this﴾ act ﴿is a plot you have plotted﴾, a stratagem you have devised, you and Moses, and it is not something the situation required of you, given the strength of the proof and the manifestness of the miracle. This is a deception on his part toward the Copts, showing them that they were not defeated and that their proof had not been cut off. It was said that his words ﴿before I give you permission﴾ are likewise. ﴿In the city﴾, that is, in Egypt, before you go out to the appointed meeting.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud and a number of the Companions, who said: Moses, peace be upon him, met the chief of the magicians, and Moses said to him: "Tell me, if I defeat you, will you believe in me and bear witness that what I have brought is true?" The magician said: "I will surely bring tomorrow a magic that no magic can overcome. By God, if you defeat me, I will surely believe in you and surely bear witness that you are true." Pharaoh was watching them, and this statement arose from him. ﴿So that you may expel its people from it﴾, that is, the Copts, and so that it may be cleared for you and the Children of Israel.

﴿Then you will soon know﴾ the outcome of what you have done. This is a threat he delivered in summary form, for the sake of frightening them.

Then he followed it with the detail, saying: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, i.e., from every side a limb different from the other, such as the hand from one side and the foot from the other. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "differing." The view that (min) is causal (ta'līliyyah), attached to the verb, meaning "because of your opposition," is far-fetched.

﴿Then I will surely crucify you all﴾, as a disgrace to you and an exemplary punishment for those like you. Crucifixion (taṣlīb) is derived from ṣalb, which means binding someone to a piece of wood or something else. It has become common for it to refer to hanging a person by a rope around the neck until he dies, which is the familiar meaning today. I have seen in some books that the crucifixion meant by the Tyrant is binding the person beneath the armpits and hanging him until he perishes. This, like the cutting of hands and feet, was first instituted by Pharaoh, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir and others from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Allah the Exalted prescribed it for highway robbers (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq) to magnify their crime, and for this reason
صفحة 28
He, glory be to Him, called it "war against Allah and His Messenger."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 125:

﴿Qālū﴾ is an explanatory resumption (isti'nāf bayānī). ﴿Indā ilā rabbinā munqalibūn﴾ means: we will return to His mercy and reward, glorified is He, if You do that to us. How wonderful that would be!

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Jubayr that when the sorcerers fell down prostrating, they saw their dwellings being built for them. He also narrated from al-Awza'i that Paradise was raised up for them until they looked at it. It is also possible that they meant: "Indeed we are surely going to die, so there is no harm in what you threaten us with, and the appointed term is decreed and does not come later than its time":

"Whoever does not die by the sword dies by something else; the causes are many, but death is one."

It is also possible that the meaning is: indeed we all will return to Allah the Exalted, and He will judge between us:

"To the Judge of the Day of Religion we go, and before Allah all adversaries gather."

The pronoun of the plural (in "munqalibūn") on the first interpretation refers to the sorcerers only, and on the second to them and to Pharaoh. On the second interpretation it may carry both meanings.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 7, verse 126:**

﴿And you do not resent﴾ means: you do not hate. In the past tense it comes as *naqama* and *naqima* on the pattern of *daraba* and *alima*.

﴿from us﴾, the group of those who believed, ﴿except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us﴾. This is the root of boasts and the greatest of virtues. The exception is *mufarragh* (an exceptive construction whose stated object is absent, so the sense depends on the context). The verbal noun (*al-masdar*) is in the position of the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*). The statement follows the pattern of his saying:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their guests are blamed for forgetting the beloved and the homeland."*

It has also been said that *tanqimu* is the present form of *naqima* meaning "to punish." It is said: *naqama minhu naqaman wa tinqaman*, and *intaqama* when he punished him. This is what is indicated by what is reported from 'Ata'. On this view, ﴿that we believed﴾ is in the position of the object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). In both interpretations, the aim is to cut off Pharaoh's hope of achieving his purpose through his threats against them. It is possible that, on the second interpretation, the statement confirms what they had earlier pointed to: mercy and reward. Then they turned away from addressing him, fled to God, the Exalted, and said: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾. That is, pour upon us patience that overwhelms us, as water is poured out, or pour upon us that which purifies us from sins, which is patience in the face of Pharaoh's threat. In the first interpretation, *fa-afrigh* (pour) is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*), explicit (*tasrihiyyah*), and *sabran* (patience) is its indicator (*qarinah*).

The meaning is: grant us complete and abundant patience. On the second interpretation, *sabran* is an original metaphor (*isti'arah asliyyah*) that is implicit (*makniyyah*), and *afrigh* is imaginative (*takhyiliyyah*). It has also been said that the statement on the first interpretation is like the statement on the second, except that the common element there is overwhelming, while here it is purification. But this is not so, although its speaker is great.

﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾, that is: steadfast upon what You have granted us of Islam, not swayed by the threat. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and al-Suddi that he did to them what he had threatened them with. It has been said that he was not able to do so, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿They shall not reach you by Our signs; you two and those who follow you are the victors﴾.

The earlier scholars answered this by saying that the intended victory is victory through proof, or victory at the end and conclusion of the matter. This does not preclude the killing of some of them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 127:
