﴿And the chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said﴾, addressing him after they had witnessed what had happened from the affair of Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿Will you leave Musa﴾, that is, will you abandon him, ﴿and his people to cause corruption in the land﴾, that is, in the land of Egypt.

By corruption (ifsad) is meant what includes both the religious and the worldly. The object of the verb is omitted for generality. Alternatively, the verb is treated as intransitive, or it is taken as implying aticket: they corrupt people by calling them to their religion and by rebelling against you. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When the magicians believed, Musa, peace be upon him, was followed by six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel."

﴿and abandon you﴾ is conjoined to the verb ﴿yufsidu﴾ in the mansub (accusative) form governed by "an" (that). Or it is in the accusative as the answer to the interrogative, as the accusative is used after the fa' (so). On this basis is the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

"Did I not use to be your neighbour, and between me and you there was affection and brotherhood?"

The meaning is: how can it be that you leave Musa, peace be upon him, and his people corrupting the land, while they leave you alone, and so on? That is, such a thing cannot occur.

al-Hasan and Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read ﴿wayadharaka﴾ in the nominative (raf'). This is either coordinated with the verb ﴿tadharu﴾, or it is a new (resumptive) sentence, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) with the subject omitted, that is, ﴿wa-huwa yadharuka﴾ (while he abandons you). This is because the verbal (present-tense) clause is not conjoined with the waw in the eloquent usage. The clause, under the assumption of a resumptive sentence, is a parenthetical clause that emphasises the meaning of what precedes it: "you abandon him, and his habit is to abandon you." It is necessary to supply huwa (he), as al-Tibi said, as in the possibility of the circumstantial reading, to indicate continuity. Under the circumstantial reading, it serves to fix the aspect of the difficulty.

It is narrated from al-Ashhab that he read it with a sukun on the letter ra'. Ibn Jinni explained this as the dammah having been dropped for lightness, as in the reading of Abu 'Amr: ﴿ya'murukum﴾ with sukun on the ra', the sukun being used for the dammah when vowels succeed one another. Abu al-Baqa' preferred this. It is also said that it is coordinated with what precedes according to the meaning, and this is called ʿaṭf al-tawahhum (coordination by supposition) outside the Qur'an. It is as if it were said: ﴿yufsidu﴾ and ﴿yadharaka﴾, like the words of the Exalted: ﴿fa-asaddaqa wa-akun mina al-salihin﴾ (so that I may give charity and be among the righteous).

﴿and your gods﴾, that is, your objects of worship. It is related that he used to worship the stars, so they were his gods, and he believed that they governed the lower world absolutely, and that he was the lord of the human species. It is narrated from al-Suddi that Pharaoh had taken idols for his people and commanded them to worship them as a means of drawing near to him, and for this reason he said: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾. It is also said that he had a cow which he worshipped, and whenever he saw a beautiful cow he commanded his people to worship it. For this reason the Samiri produced a calf for the Children of Israel. This is a weak narration from Ibn 'Abbas. Sulayman al-Taymi said: "It has reached me that he used to put on his neck something which he worshipped." The plural form in this regard requires further consideration.

Ibn Mas'ud, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and al-Sha'bi read ﴿wa-ilahataka﴾ (and your worship), like ﴿ibadatika﴾ (your worship) in form and meaning, so it is a verbal noun (masdar).

Ibn 'Abbas, and others narrating from him, used to reject reading the plural with the plural and would read it as the verbal noun, saying: "Pharaoh was worshipped and did not worship. Do you not see his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾?" From this some have said: "The more likely view is that he was a materialist who denied a Creator." It is also said that ilaha is a name for the sun, and that he worshipped it. Abu 'Ali recited:

"And the ilaha (sun) hastened us that it should return."

He replied to them: ﴿We will kill their sons and keep alive their women﴾, as we used to do to them before, so that it may be known that we are still in the same state of subjugation and dominance. One should not imagine that this refers to the boy whom the astrologers and soothsayers had judged would bring an end to our kingdom at his hand.

Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read ﴿sanaqtulu﴾ (we will kill) with light and doubled forms, as in mutta't al-ibil (the camels died).

﴿And indeed we are above them, dominant﴾, that is, victorious, just as we were; our condition has not changed, and they are subdued under our hands. Pharaoh had abandoned hope of killing Musa, peace be upon him, so he did not promise the chiefs to kill him, because of what he saw of the exaltedness of his affair and the greatness of his station. It seems that for this reason he did not promise to kill his people either. The apparent meaning, as is said, is that this statement from Pharaoh is an explanation, since they are not able to cause corruption in the land, and an indication that he does not care about them, and that their affair henceforth is like their affair before, and that killing them is futile and bears no fruit. al-Tibi mentioned that it is of the wise (hakim) style, even though it came from a fool, and that the nominal clause (al-jumla al-ismiyya) is like a concluding summary (tadhyil) for what precedes it. So understand.

[Page 29]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 128:

﴿Mūsā said to his people﴾ as consolation for them when they were vexed by what they had heard, with wise discourse: ﴿Seek help in God and be patient.﴾ Be patient over what you have heard of the false sayings, ﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to God﴾, meaning the land of Egypt or the earth in general, and it is included in it by primary inclusion.
Page 30
﴿He bequeaths it to whomever He wills of His servants, and the final outcome is for the God-fearing.﴾ Those of whom you are. Its summary is that the matter is not as Pharaoh said: ﴿And indeed we are dominant over them.﴾ For domination and victory belong to whoever is patient and seeks help in God, and to whom God Most High has promised the inheritance of the earth. I am that promised one, whom God Most High promised you victory through, the subjugation of enemies, and the inheritance of their land. His saying "and the final outcome" (etc.) is a confirmation of what preceded.

And Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read (wal-'āqibata) in the accusative, as a conjunction with the noun of inna (ism inna).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 129:

﴿They said﴾, that is, the people of Moses said to him, peace be upon him: ﴿We were harmed﴾ by the side of Pharaoh.

﴿Before you came to us﴾ with the message. By this they meant the tyrant's killing of their sons, both before his birth and after it, when it was said to him: "A boy will be born among the Children of Israel who will strip you of your kingdom, and your destruction will be at his hands."

﴿And after you had come to us﴾, that is, as a messenger. By this they meant what he had threatened them with, namely the renewed killing of the sons and the various kinds of oppression and torment he used to inflict on them out of enmity toward Moses, peace be upon him. It was also said that the threat itself is a form of harm, and it was also said that his threatening was treated as the same as his deed, because he was a tyrant.

It was also said that they meant the harm of killing the sons both before the birth of Moses, peace be upon him, and after his birth. It was also said that what is meant is the servitude and humiliation they suffered, in the various kinds of labour and menial work. This has been criticised on the grounds that such things do not befall them through Moses, peace be upon him, so mentioning him here is not very fitting to the context. The apparent meaning is that there is no difference between *al-ityan* (coming) and *al-majī'* (arrival), and that combining them is for variety of expression and to avoid verbal repetition, since human nature is inclined to dislike repeated words. For this reason *an* (the masdariyyah particle, which turns the following clause into a verbal noun) was used first, and *ma* (its sister) second.

Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti mentioned, in distinguishing between the two, that *al-ityan* is used for meanings and times, while *al-majī'* is used for substances and concrete things. This is not evident here unless it is forced. It is related from al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), in distinguishing between them, that *al-ityan* is coming with ease, so it is more specific than general coming. Here too it is like the preceding usage. This complaint from them is in the manner of lamentation, because they were not satisfied with what he, peace be upon him, had alluded to them, owing to the extent of what had afflicted them and the severity of what had befallen them. The situation requires expansion (*itnab*), for the way of one who grieves and complains is to lengthen his speech, hoping that by this some of the burning will be quenched. It was also said that it is a request from them for what he, peace be upon him, had promised them of deliverance and victory, and the first view is more preferable. The words of the Exalted: ﴿He said: It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾, who did to you what he did and threatened you with what he threatened.

﴿And will make you successors﴾, that is, will make you caliphs (khulafa') ﴿in the land﴾. That is, the land of Egypt. This is an explicit statement of what he had alluded to, and an emphasis to console them in the most eloquent way. Within it is the incorporation of the meaning that whoever opposes the friends of God, the Exalted, has openly challenged Him to war, and deserves ruin and loss. *Asa* (it may be) in such a context signifies certainty in the fulfilment of the promise and in attaining what is sought. More than one scholar has stated that the use of it here follows the custom of generous people.

It was also said that this is out of courtesy toward God, the Exalted, even though the matter was decided by revelation and information from Him, glorified and exalted be He. It was also said that this is because Moses, peace be upon him, was not certain that they themselves or their children would be the ones made successors. It is related that Egypt was conquered in the time of David, peace be upon him.

This has been criticised on the grounds that the words of the Exalted do not support it: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾. The obvious meaning of making the oppressed successors is that the oppressed themselves are made successors, not that their children are, and metaphor is contrary to the original sense. Indeed, it is well known that the Children of Israel, after they went out of Egypt with Moses, peace be upon him, did not return to it during his lifetime. And in the words of the Glorified: ﴿So He will see﴾, that is, He will observe or know.

﴿How you act﴾, whether well or badly, and He will recompense you according to the deeds that appear from you. This is guidance for them to give thanks, and a warning against falling into the pits of disbelief. It was also said that in it there is an allusion to what happened from them after that.

[Page 31]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 130:**

﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾. This begins the detailing of the early stages of the destruction that was promised, and it signals that they were not granted respite to pass from one state to another until the punishment of annihilation ('adhab al-isti'sal) descended upon them. The sentence opens with an oath (qasam) to show concern for its content. By "the people of Pharaoh" (al, "family/followers") is meant his followers from the Copts. The word al (family) is attached to Pharaoh, though it is only attached to nobles, because of the apparent worldly honour it carries, even if in reality it is base. It is reported from al-Khatib that the intended meaning is Pharaoh and his household. "Al-sinin" is the plural of sanah (year), and by it is meant the year of famine. The term became so dominant in this sense that it became almost like a proper name for it, because it is so often mentioned and used for dating, whereas a fertile year is not like this. Its final radical is either waw or ha'. They derived from it, saying asnata al-qawm ("the people entered a year of drought") when they suffered famine, and they changed the lam into ta' to distinguish this from their saying asna al-qawm ("the people remained in one place for a year"). Al-Mazini said: this is anomalous (shadhdh) and cannot be analogized upon. Al-Farra' said: they supposed that the ha' was original, since they found it to be original, so they changed it into ta'. And there is the expression: asabatna sunniyyah hamra' ("a red drought struck us"), i.e., a severe barrenness. The diminutive here (sunniyyah) is for magnification (lil-ta'zim), i.e., al-tasghir (the diminutive form). The treatment of the plural as the other sound plurals that are inflected by letters (al-jam' al-salim al-mu'rab bi'l-huruf) is the well-known dialect. The other dialect is to inflect the nun itself, but only with the ya' specifically, so it is treated in the manner of the three vowel-inflections (al-i'rab bi'l-harakat al-thalath) with tanwin according to the Banu 'Amir, while the Banu Tamim do not use tanwin for lightness, and in that case the nun is not dropped for the idafah (genitive construction). Upon this the poet's saying goes:

*"He called me from Najd, for its years have played with us, making us grey-haired, and have made us, while young, to grow grey."*

And from it is his (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, make them years like the years of Yusuf (peace be upon him)." And in another narration: "O Allah, help me against them with years like the years of Yusuf (peace be upon him)." And this is according to the well-known dialect.

﴿And a loss of fruits﴾: by the great prevalence of blights on fruits and the emergence of little from them, to the extent that the palm would not bear except a single unripe date (busrah), as is reported from Rija' ibn Haywah. The famine, as 'Abd ibn Humayd and others reported from Qatadah, affected their desert dwellers and the people of their livestock, while the loss affected their cities and villages. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and Ibn Abi Hatim, reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: When Allah seized the people of Pharaoh with years, everything belonging to them dried up, and their livestock perished, until the Nile of Egypt dried up. They gathered before Pharaoh and said to him: "If you are as you claim, then bring us water into the Nile of Egypt." He said: "By morning the water will reach you." When they left his presence, he said: "What have I done? I am not able to do that, and tomorrow they will call me a liar." When it was the middle of the night, he rose, performed ghusl, put on a woollen cloak, and went out barefoot until he came to the Nile and stood in its bed and said: "O Allah, You know that I know that You are able to fill the Nile of Egypt with water, so fill it with water." Then he heard nothing but the sound of water coming, so he went out, and the Nile came flowing full of water, for what Allah, exalted is He, intended for them of destruction. And this, if sound, indicates that the man was not a dahri (materialist) denying the Creator, as some have said.

﴿So that they might be mindful﴾: that is, in order that they might take warning and abandon what they are upon; or in order that they might remember Allah, exalted is He, and humble themselves before Him and seek refuge in Him, desiring what is with Him. It is also said: in order that they might recall that if Pharaoh were a god he would have repelled that harm.

It is reported from al-Zajjaj that they were only seized with adversity because states of hardship soften hearts and incline them towards what is with Allah, exalted is He. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing﴾... [the verse continues in the source as: ﴿and when harm touches him, he is one of abundant supplication﴾].

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 131:**

﴿Then when good came to them﴾, etc. This explains their failure to take heed and their persistence in error. By "good" (al-hasanah), as the apparent sense of some scholars' words implies, is meant fertility and prosperity. Mujahid explained it as ease and well-being, and some scholars took it in a broader sense than that. That is: when there came to them what they found pleasing, ﴿they said, "This is ours"﴾, meaning that we deserve it by virtue of our own blessedness. ﴿And if evil afflicted them﴾, meaning hardship,
Page 32
drought, or drought together with sickness, or punishment and affliction, ﴿they ascribed their misfortune to Moses and those with him﴾, meaning they regarded them as an omen of ill and said: "This has befallen us only because of their ill omen." The original application of the term tatayyur (augury, taking omens from birds) to the sense of taking an ill omen is, as al-Azhari said, that the Arabs used to scare birds away and take an ill omen from the barih (a bird passing from right to left, considered inauspicious) while taking a good omen from the sanih (a bird passing from left to right, considered auspicious). There is a proverb: "Who will give me the sanih after the barih?" Abu 'Ubaydah said: Yunus asked Ru'bah, while I was present, about the sanih and the barih. He replied: "The sanih is that which passes you on your right, and the barih is that which passes you on your left." It was also said: the barih is that which comes from the direction of the north, and the sanih is that which comes from the direction of the right. They recited:

I drove away for her the bird of the left, so if your desire is what you desire, avoiding it will befall you.

Then they named ill omen "bird" (ṭayr) and "a flying thing" (ṭa'ir), and taking an ill omen "tatayyur". They also used the word "bird" for one's share or portion, whether good or bad, to the point that it was said that the original meaning of tatayyur is the division and dispersal of property among people, so that each person's share of good or evil "flies" to him, and then the term came to be predominantly used for evil. In the verse there is an exaggeration in describing them as dull-witted and hard-hearted, for hardships soften hearts, humble stubborn spirits, and dispel obstinacy, especially after witnessing the signs. Yet they were such that nothing of these had any effect on them; rather, they only increased in insolence and obstinacy. As many scholars have said, the definite article on "good" and its mention with the particle of certainty (inna / qad-type affirmation) is due to its frequent occurrence and to the fact that the divine will is directed at its occurrence essentially, since divine providence required that mercy precede and that favour be general before deeds take place. The indefiniteness of "evil" and its mention with the particle of doubt is due to its rarity and to the fact that the divine will is directed at its occurrence only incidentally, since retribution, in accordance with that providence, is merited only by deeds.

Al-Zamakhshari explained "good" as fertility and prosperity, and then said, in explaining what was mentioned: because the category of good occurs as if it were obligatory, owing to its abundance and breadth, whereas evil does not occur except rarely, and only some of it occurs. The author of al-Kashshaf said: this indicates that the definite article is for the external, affirmed reference (al-'ahd al-khariji al-taqriri), as evidenced by the fact that it is mentioned in contrast to His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿And We had seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾, and his saying "because the category…" etc., meaning the category of fertility and prosperity. There is an emphasis in this: that because of the frequency of occurrence, it is as if the entire category were necessarily occurring, and for this reason it keeps multiplying until it encompasses the whole category. His saying "as for evil…" etc., in contrast to that, is clear proof of the intention of this meaning, so there is no contradiction between his words. He did not intend by "the category" the mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni), and this is the intention of the author of al-Miftah, and with it what the author of al-Idah imagined is refuted. End of quotation.

In it there is an indirect criticism of his teacher al-Tibi, in that he took "the category" to be the mental reference and said what he said. The discussion is lengthy, so it should be sought in the commentaries on al-Miftah and the commentary on al-Talkhis by al-'Allamah al-Qazwini and its glosses. His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿Indeed, their omen is with Allah﴾ is a resumptive statement from Him, glorified be He, to refute their false claim and to establish the truth in this matter. Its introduction with the particle of alerting is to show the utmost concern with its content, meaning: their ill omen is only with Allah, that is, from Him and by His judgment, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that the ill omen that befalls them is only that which they were promised of punishment with Him, not what they encounter in this world. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that what they took as an omen is recorded against them until Allah requites them for it on the Day of Resurrection. Some scholars explained "omen" (ṭa'ir) here as "portion", meaning: their portion and what has flown to them of decree and destiny is due to their ill omen with Allah. Al-Hasan recited: "Indeed, their bird (ṭayruhum)," which is a collective noun for ṭa'ir according to the correct view, since it follows the patterns of singular nouns. Al-Akhfash said it is a plural of it. It is related from Qutrub that ṭayr may be singular or plural, and likewise ṭa'ir. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

As if it were the drizzle of a rainy day, upon heads like the heads of birds.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ this, so they say what they say. Attributing lack of knowledge to most of them is to indicate
Page 33
that some of them do know, but do not act in accordance with their knowledge.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 132:**

﴿And they said﴾ This begins an account of another part of the punishments with which they were seized, which are in themselves clear signs, and of their refusal to desist from the disbelief and obstinacy in which they were. That is: they said after they had seen what they saw of the staff, the years of drought, and the loss of fruits.

﴿Whatever sign you bring us﴾ The word *mahma* (whatever) is one on which opinions differ. It is said that it is a single word coined to intensify generality. It is also said that it is composed of *mah*, a verb-noun (*ism fi'l*, a noun functioning as a verb) meaning "stop," which either retains that meaning or is stripped of it, plus *ma*, the conditional particle. Al-Khalil said its origin is *ma ma*, with the first *ma* being conditional and the second an indefinite particle attached to it for added generality; then the alif of the first *ma* was changed to a *ha'* to avoid the harshness of repetition. The most sound of these views, as many have said, is the view of simplicity (that it is a single word). In the margin of Ibn Hisham's *al-Tashil* (Hashiyat al-Tashil), it is stated that whoever holds the view of simplicity should write *mahma* with a *ya'*, and whoever holds that its origin is *ma ma* should write it with an alif. In the commentary (*al-Sharh*), it is stated that the same applies if it is said its origin is *mah ma*. Al-Shumunni objected to this, saying that those who hold the two origins mentioned are agreed that *mahma* has another origin, so what should be written at its end according to the first view should also be written according to the second. There is room for consideration in this.

It is a conditional noun (*ism shart*), not a particle, according to the correct view. Its position here is nominative (*raf'*) as a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is either the condition (*al-shart*), or the response (*al-jaza'*), or both, according to the difference of opinion. Or it is in the accusative (*nasb*), as a direct object of a verb that is explained by what follows *ay* (whatever): "whatever sign you bring us, bring it to us [*tuhdiruhu ladayna*]." Some people permitted its occurrence in an accusative position as an adverb of time (*zarfiyya*), and al-Zamakhshari strongly denounced this in *al-Kashshaf*. Ibn al-Munir noted that the reason those who held this view were misled was the statement of al-Khalil, or its resemblance to *mata ma* (whenever). Ibn Malik disagreed with this and said that it is attested from the Arabs, as in the verse:

*"Indeed, whenever you give your belly its desire,*
*and your private parts, they will attain the furthest end of blame, all of them."*

Al-Shihab said that it is in harmony with this the use of it by the logicians with the meaning of *kullama* (whenever), and their making it the quantifier of the universal proposition (*sur al-kulliyya*), since it conveys generality, as they have stated explicitly. It is not one of their inventions, as is supposed. You know that its being an adverb here is something one should not venture into in any way, because of the statement of Allah the Exalted that refutes it:

﴿from a sign﴾ This is an explanation of *mahma*, and not a time. Their calling it a sign is by way of going along with Musa, peace be upon him, and mocking him, with an indication that this title does not affect them. Otherwise they deny that it is a sign in reality and claim that it is magic, as their statement indicates: ﴿to bewitch us with it﴾. The two pronouns in the genitive (*majrurān*) refer back to *mahma*. The masculine form of the first is for the sake of the wording, since it is indefinite, and the feminine form of the second is to preserve the sense, since it refers back to it only after it has been clarified by "a sign." Ibn Hisham claimed that it is better for the second pronoun to refer back to "sign" (*ayah*). Perhaps he took into account proximity. Whoever goes to the first view took into account that "sign" is brought as an explanation, so it is better for the pronoun to return to the intended explained element in itself, though the outcome is one. That is: ﴿to bewitch us with that sign and make us confused﴾, ﴿so we will not believe you﴾, that is: we will not accept you as truthful, nor believe in your prophethood at all.

﴿So We sent upon them﴾ as a punishment for their crimes, especially this statement of theirs, ﴿the flood﴾, that is, what overwhelmed them and covered their dwellings and tilled land, from rain or torrent. It is an ism jins (a generic noun) from the root of tawaf (circumambulation/encompassing). It was said that it is originally a masdar (verbal noun) like nuqsan (decrease), and that it is a name for every sudden calamity that encompasses from all directions and spreads, such as abundant water, widespread killing, or a sweeping death. It has become well known for the flood of water. Its interpretation here as that has come in several narrations from Ibn 'Abbas. From 'Ata' and Mujahid, it is interpreted as death, and Ibn Jarir and others transmitted this from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) report. From Wahb ibn Munabbih, it is the plague in the language of Yemen, and from Abu Qilaba, it is smallpox. They were the first people to be punished with it. These two opinions lead back to a marfu' report.

﴿And the locusts﴾ is well known. Its singular is jaradah, and it is named so because it strips (jarada) whatever is on the earth. It is one of the soldiers of Allah the Exalted, whom He sends against whomever of His servants He wills. Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, and others transmitted from Abu Zuhayr al-Numayri, as a marfu' report, a prohibition against fighting it, giving the reason mentioned. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned that if this is authentic, it refers to the case when it does not attack the farms; but if it attacks them, it is permissible to repel it by whatever repels it, such as fighting and killing. Or it may be intended to indicate the impossibility of resisting it by that means.

Abu Dawud and those with him transmitted from Salman, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about locusts, and he said: 'The greatest of the soldiers of Allah the Exalted—I do not eat it, nor do I forbid it.'"

As for the claim that it was created from the sins of the children of Adam, it is to be interpreted figuratively.

﴿And the lice﴾, with a damma on the qaf and a shadda on the mim (qummal). It was said that it is al-da'a, which are the young locusts, and they are not called locusts until their wings grow. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Suddi. It was also said that it is the qirdan (ticks), the plural of the well-known qurad (tick). It was said that it is the small ants. From Habib ibn Abi Thabit, it is the ju'lan (dung beetles). From Ibn Zayd, he said: "Some people claim that they are fleas." From Sa'id ibn Jubayr, they are the weevils, which is the insect found in wheat and other grains. It is also called qaml with a fatha and then a sukun, and al-Hasan recited it this way.

﴿And the frogs﴾, the plural of difdi' (frog), like zibrij, Ja'far, Jundab, and dirham. This is a weaker opinion or a rejected one. It is the well-known aquatic creature.

﴿And the blood﴾ is well known, and a shadda on its dal is a dialectal variant.

It is reported that when Musa, peace be upon him, saw from Pharaoh and his people stubbornness and persistence, he supplicated and said: "O my Lord, Pharaoh has exalted himself in the land, and his people have broken the covenant. My Lord, seize them with a punishment that You make a vengeance upon them, an admonition for my people, and a sign and lesson for those after them." So Allah the Exalted sent upon them rain for eight days, in a severe darkness, so that no one could leave his house. The water entered their houses until they stood in it up to their necks, and not a drop of it entered the houses of the Children of Israel. It became entangled in their houses, and the water overflowed onto their land and stagnated, preventing them from farming and from managing their affairs. This water remained upon them for seven days, from Saturday to Saturday. They said: "O Musa, pray to your Lord for us, that He may lift this from us, and we will believe in you and send the Children of Israel with you." So he prayed to his Lord, and He removed it from them, and grass and herbage grew of a kind never seen before. They said: "This water was only a blessing upon us," and they did not believe.

So Allah the Exalted sent the locusts upon them, and they ate their crops, fruits, doors, roofs, clothes, and goods, until they even ate the iron nails in the doors. Nothing of that befell the Children of Israel. They cried out and wailed to Musa, peace be upon him, and said to him what they had said at first. So he went out, peace be upon him, into the open desert and pointed with his staff toward the east and the west, and the locusts returned to the regions from which they had come.

It was also said: a wind came and cast them into the sea, but they did not believe. So Allah the Exalted sent the lice upon them, and they ate what the locusts had left. It would enter between a man's garment and his skin and suck at him, and when one wanted to eat food, it would fill with lice. Ibn al-Musayyab said: "They were afflicted with weevils; a man would go out to the mill with ten sacks, and would return with only three qafiz of flour from them." It took their eyebrows, their eyelashes, and all their hair, and it did to their skins what smallpox does. It also prevented them from sleeping and from rest. So they fled to Musa, peace be upon him, and it was lifted from them. They said: "Now we are certain that you are a sorcerer."

So Allah the Exalted sent the frogs upon them, and their houses, courtyards, goods, and vessels were filled with them. No one uncovered a vessel without finding them in it. A man would sit among the frogs, and they would reach his throat; when he wanted to speak, a frog would leap and enter his mouth. They would leap into their pots, spoiling their food and extinguishing their fires. When one of them lay down, they would pile upon him until they were a heap over him, and he could not turn over. When one wanted to eat, they would outrun him to his mouth, and whenever one kneaded dough, it would fill with them. So they fled to him, peace be upon him, and implored him humbly. He took from them covenants and pledges and prayed, and Allah the Exalted removed that from them. But they broke the covenant. So Allah the Exalted sent blood upon them, and the Nile flowed over them with fresh blood, and their waters became blood. Pharaoh would gather a Copt and an Israelite in one vessel, and the part nearest the Israelite would be water while the part nearest the Copt would be blood. When they both went to a jar containing water, blood would come out for the Copt and water for the Israelite. Even a woman of the family of Pharaoh would come to a woman of the Children of Israel and say: "Give me water to drink," and she would pour for her from her waterskin, and it would become blood in the vessel, until she said: "Put it in your mouth and then spit it into mine," and she would do so, and it would become blood.

Ibn Aslam said: the blood that was sent upon them was nosebleeds.

﴿Signs﴾ is a hal (circumstantial accusative) of the things mentioned earlier.

﴿Distinct﴾, clarified, such that no sensible person doubts that they are divine signs and not sorcery as they claim. Or, some of them are distinguished from others, separated by time to test their conditions, and there was a month between every two of them, and each one lasted a month, as Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The nine signs were over nine years, one sign each year." Ahmad in al-Zuhd and others transmitted from Nawf al-Shami, who said: "Musa, peace be upon him, remained among the family of Pharaoh after he overcame the sorcerers for twenty years, showing them the signs: the locusts, the lice, etc., ... but they refused to submit."

In a narration of Abu al-Shaykh from Ibn 'Abbas: he remained, peace be upon him, after he had overcome them, for forty years, showing them what has been mentioned. I saw in the Musamarat of Shaykh Ibn al-'Arabi, may his secret be sanctified, that Musa, peace be upon him, remained warning the family of Pharaoh for sixteen months until they were drowned, then they were entered into fire, and they did not benefit from the signs they saw. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾ toward believing in them.

﴿And they were a criminal people﴾ is a parenthetical clause affirming the content of what precedes it.

[p. 35]

﴿So when the punishment fell upon them﴾, that is, the punishment mentioned in detail, as reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid. The particle (lamma) does not contradict the detail or the repetition, as is not hidden.

And from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, that a red hail fell upon them, which they had never seen before, and many of them perished.

And from Ibn Jubayr that it was the plague (ta'un). Its application to it has occurred in the marfu' hadith of Usamah ibn Zayd: "It is a punishment (rijz) sent upon a group of the Children of Israel, or upon those who were before you. So when you hear of it in a land, do not enter upon it, and when it befalls a land while you are in it, do not leave fleeing from it."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Musa (peace be upon him) commanded the Children of Israel, saying: "Let each of you slaughter a ram, then let him dip his palm in its blood, then let him strike it upon his door." They did so. The Copts said to them: "Why do you put this blood on your doors?" They said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted intends to send a punishment upon you, so we will be safe and you will perish." The Copts said: "Does Allah the Exalted recognize you only by this sign?" They said: "Thus our Prophet commanded us." So they woke up, and seventy thousand of the people of Pharaoh had been stabbed (to death). Then in the evening they had no one to bury them.

The meaning according to the first view is that whenever one of the mentioned punishments fell upon them, each time, [they said: "O Musa"]; according to the view that the intended rijz is other than what was mentioned earlier, that when the destroying hail or the sweeping plague fell upon them, [they said: "O Musa, pray for us to your Lord by what He has covenanted with you"], that is, by His covenant (subhanahu) with you, which is prophethood, as Abu Muslim said. (Ma) is a masdariyyah.

Prophethood was called a covenant (ahd), as the second 'Allamah said, because Allah the Exalted covenanted to honour the prophets (peace be upon them) with it, and they covenanted with Him to bear its burdens; or because it has rights that are preserved as covenants are preserved; or because it is in the position of a covenant and a decree from Him, exalted is He; or it means by that which was covenanted to you, that you should call upon Him by it, and He would answer you as He answered you in your signs. (Ma) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the prepositional phrase is a complement to "ud'u" (pray); or it is a circumstantial element (hal) from the pronoun in it, meaning: pray to Allah the Exalted, seeking intercession through what is covenanted with you. It is possible that the ba' is for the entreating oath (al-qasam al-istita'ifi), as one says: "By your life, do such and such," so the intent is to appeal to him, peace be upon him, that he should pray. And that it may be for the true oath, whose answer is: ﴿If you remove from us the punishment﴾ which has fallen upon us, ﴿we will surely believe in you and surely send with you the Children of Israel﴾, that is, we swear by the covenant of Allah the Exalted with you, ﴿if you remove﴾, etc. The summary of what they mentioned regarding the ba' here is that it is either for attachment (ilsaq), or for causation (sababiyyah), or for oath in its two kinds.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 135:

﴿So when We removed from them the punishment until a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾ That is: until a limit of time which they were certainly going to reach, whereupon they would be punished or destroyed therein. This is the time of drowning, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, or death, as related from al-Hasan. The meaning is that We saved them from the punishment until that time. From here it is valid for the end-point (ghayah) to be connected to the removing (kashf), and there is no need to make the prepositional phrase connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the punishment (rijz), contrary to the one who claimed that.

It has been said: the intended "term" (ajal) is what they had set for their faith, ﴿behold, they broke their word﴾, that is, they breached the covenant. The original meaning of nakth (breaking) is the untwisting of the strands of spun wool so that it may be spun again; it is then used figuratively for breaking a covenant after it has been confirmed. The answer of (lamma) is a verb that is omitted, indicated by the sudden-surprise particle (idha al-fuja'iyyah), not the clause that accompanies it; and if this is said, it is a loose usage. That is: when We removed that from them, they suddenly broke the covenant without pause or reflection, so it is said. According to this, both nouns, i.e. lamma and idha, are objects of that verb, with the first being its adverbial complement of time and the second its object, as stated by al-'Allamah. The motive for this is to preserve what they held, namely that the verb following the word lamma must be past, either in form or in meaning. However, what they stated implies that idh and idha of sudden surprise, in the position of the object of the two verbs they contain, means that the implied sense is: they suddenly came upon the time or place of breaking.

It may also be said: positing a verb is an artificial supposition that is dispensable, since they have explicitly stated that lamma is answered by the sudden-surprise idha followed by a nominal clause. Yes, they mention what gives the impression of such an omitted verb, but it is not so; rather it is a clarification of the resulting meaning and an explanation of it, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 136:

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾ i.e., We intended to take vengeance upon them. This was interpreted in this way so that His words, glorified is He, ﴿so We drowned them﴾ may follow from it as a consequence; otherwise, drowning is itself the very vengeance, so it would not be correct to make it a consequence of it.

It has been permitted that the fa' (the fa' of "fa-") be explanatory (tafsiriyyah), and some have affirmed this, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord..."﴾ etc. In that case there is no need for interpretation. ﴿In the sea (yamm)﴾, i.e., the sea (al-bahr), as was related from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi, may Allah be pleased with them. The word (yamm) applies to salty water, to a great river of sweet water, and it is not broken into a plural nor made into a sound masculine plural. Al-Layth said: it is the sea whose bottom cannot be reached. It was also said: it is the deep part of the sea (lujjat al-bahr). It is Arabic according to the well-known view, while Ibn Qutaybah said: it is Syriac, and its original form, as it has been said, was yamma, then it was Arabized to what you see. The view that it is the name of the sea in which Pharaoh drowned is a drowning in the sea of weakness.

﴿Because they denied Our signs﴾ is a causal explanation for the drowning. The meaning is that the cause of the drowning, and what made that punishment deserved, is denial of the great signs, and this is what required that Allah's will be connected to it in an immediate (tanjizi) manner. This does not contradict the consequence of the will upon the breaking of the covenant, because denial is the final cause and the nearest cause, and there is no barrier to multiple causes and some of them following upon others. So said al-Shihab, and the light of truth shines from it. Shaykh al-Islam said: although the fa' indicates that the drowning follows what preceded it of breaking the covenant, he has nevertheless stated the cause explicitly, signaling that the axis of all of that is denial of the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and what is joined to it, so that it would be a deterrent for the listeners from denying the manifest signs at the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. End of quote. In this there is a discussion that is not hidden.

﴿And they were heedless of them﴾: the pronoun in (anha, "of them") refers to the signs, and heedlessness is a metaphor for not remembering and not caring, i.e., because of their denial of the signs and their not caring for them and their not reflecting upon them, to the point that they became as those entirely heedless of them. Otherwise, one who denies a matter is not heedless of it, due to the contradiction between the two matters. In this there is an indication that whoever has witnessed the like of them should not deny them while knowing them. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the pronoun refers to the vengeance, meaning the drowning, as what precedes it indicates. On this view, the clause may be circumstantial with a implied qad, and there is no metaphor in heedlessness then. The first view is preferable, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 137 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We caused the people who were oppressed to inherit﴾ by enslavement and the slaughter of their sons. The combination of the past and future verb forms is to indicate the continuation and renewal of the oppression. By them is meant the Children of Israel, and they are mentioned with this description to show the complete kindness towards them and the great favour done to them, in that they were raised from the depths of humiliation to the summit of honour. Perhaps there is in this an indication that God, glory be to Him, is near to broken hearts. The word "the people" is in the accusative because it is the first object of awrathna (We caused to inherit), and the second object is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿the eastern and western parts of the land﴾, meaning all its regions and quarters. What is meant by it, according to what is related from al-Hasan, Qatadah and Zayd ibn Aslam, is the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Al-Baghawi, the Reviver of the Sunnah (Muhyi al-Sunnah), mentioned that it is the land of al-Sham and Egypt. In one report it is the land of Egypt which was in the hands of the oppressed, and al-Jubba'i went to this view. Abu al-Shaykh related it from al-Layth ibn Sa'd. That is: We caused the oppressed to inherit the land of their oppressors and their dominion. The meaning of making them inherit it, on the view that they had not entered it after they left it with Musa, peace be upon him, is bringing it under their control and there being no obstacle preventing them from disposing of it, or the enabling of their descendants in it; and that was in the time of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both. It is not hidden that this is contrary to what is apparent, as the reference to it has already passed. Moreover, after Egypt was conquered in the time of Dawud, peace be upon him, the Children of Israel did not have firm establishment and settlement there; rather there was only possession and disposal, while the (true) establishment was in the Holy Land. The context, it is said, requires mention of what they were established in, not what they owned. I say: It may be said that what is meant by "the land" here and in His earlier saying, glory be to Him: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land﴾, is the Holy Land to which Musa, peace be upon him, asked Pharaoh to let the Children of Israel go so that he might take them to it, for it was the homeland of their forefathers. Thus Musa, peace be upon him, had promised them the destruction of their enemy who prevented them from going there, and God, exalted is He, made them successors in it after their forefathers and ancestors, or after whoever was in possession of it at that time, namely the Amalekites. Then He, glory be to Him, informs here that the promise has been fulfilled, and We have destroyed the enemies of those who were promised and caused them to inherit the land from which they had been prevented and in which We had established them, and in this is the attainment of the aim of Musa, peace be upon him. How gracious is the inheritance by the sons of the dwellings of their fathers ﴿which We had blessed﴾ with fertility and abundance of provision, or with that and with its being the dwelling of the prophets and the righteous, peace be upon them. This is evident on the assumption that what is meant by the eastern and western parts of the land is al-Sham and its regions. Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that he said: "The thunder, the lightning and the blessings will surely migrate to al-Sham."
Page 38
Ibn Asakir related from Damrah ibn Rabi'ah that he said: "I heard that no prophet was sent except from al-Sham, and if he was not from it, he was taken by night journey to it."
Ahmad related: "From Abdullah ibn Hawalah al-Azdi that he said: 'O Messenger of God, choose for me a land in which I may dwell.' He said: 'Keep to al-Sham, for it is the chosen one of God among His lands; God draws to it His chosen ones from among His servants.'"
Ibn Asakir related from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' that he said: "I heard the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, say: 'Keep to al-Sham, for it is the purest of the lands of God, and His chosen servants dwell in it.'"
al-Hakim related and authenticated it from Abdullah ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "A time will come upon the people when no believer will remain except that he joins al-Sham."
It has come from the hadith of Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban and also al-Hakim, who authenticated it, from Zayd ibn Thabit that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Blessed is al-Sham." It was said to him: "And why?" He said: "The angels of the Most Merciful spread their wings over it."
The hadiths on the virtue of al-Sham are numerous, and more than one scholar has collected them, but many of them have weaknesses in their chains, though the cause of their fabrication was strong. Al-Sham is the name of one of the conventional regions. In the Qamus it is said that it is a land on the left side of the qiblah, and it was so named because a people of the sons of Kan'an went leftward to it, that is, they turned to the left; or it was named after Sam ibn Nuh, for his name in Syriac is with a shin; or because its land has white, red and black moles, and on this view it is not hamzated.
Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Aghbash, who had met companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he was asked about what has been blessed in al-Sham, where its boundary ends. He said: "Its first boundary is the 'Arish of Egypt, the other boundary is the edge of the al-Thaniyyah, the other boundary is the Euphrates, and the other boundary is where the tomb of the Prophet Hud, peace be upon him, was placed." What is meant by it is not what people commonly understand today, namely Damascus. Yes, Damascus is included in it, and we have discussed its boundaries in more detail in our glosses on the commentary of the Samarqandiyyah abridged by Ibn 'Isam. People have been fanatical about Damascus in praise and blame, and some have said:
Avoid Damascus and do not go to it, even if the crowded congregation desires you;
For the transgression of transgressions there is a sinner, and the dawn of debauchery there is rising.
Another said:
Damascus has become a paradise for mankind, its radiance and the life in its shade are pure;
In it is whatever the soul desires, and there is no fault in it except its people.
Another said about al-Sham, and perhaps he meant the common usage of people:
I was asked what one says about al-Sham, the scholar of Sham, from the lightning of felicity, what Sham is.
I said: what shall I say in describing a land which is in the cheek of beauties, a mole?
As for me, I say: if the hadith is authentic, then it is my doctrine, and we seek refuge in God, exalted is He, from following desire. The relative pronoun (al-lati) is an attribute of "the eastern and western parts"; it was said to be an attribute of "the land." Abu al-Baqa' declared this weak, because it involves the coordination of the described before the attribute, and it is like your saying: "Umm Hind's father and she the sensible one came." It is also permitted that it be the second object of awrathna, i.e., "the land which"; on this view the accusative of "the eastern and western parts" and what is coordinated with it is by yastad'afuna (were oppressed), in the sense of "were oppressed therein," and it is permitted that "the eastern and western parts" be accusative by yastad'afuna, and alladhi (which) is an attribute as in the first view; and the second object of awrathna is omitted, i.e., "the land" or "the dominion." Its remoteness is not hidden, and the more apparent is the first.
﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., it passed over them and continued, from the saying "he persisted in the matter" when it continued. By the word is meant His promise to them of victory and establishment through the tongue of their prophet, peace be upon him, which is His earlier saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾, etc. Many have held that it is the promise indicated by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors﴾.
Page 39
It was also said that what is meant by it is His eternal knowledge, and the meaning is: there passed and continued over them what had been decreed of the destruction of their enemy and the making of them inherit the land. "The good" is the feminine of "the best," an attribute of "the word," and it is described thus because of what it contains of promise of what they love and find pleasing. It is related from al-Hasan that by the word is meant His promise, glory be to Him, to them of Paradise. It is not hidden that the preceding and the context reject this. The shift from first person to second in His saying, glory be to Him: "your (Lord)" is, according to al-Tibi, because what preceded of the narratives was not known to him, peace be upon him. As for His being, majestic is His glory, the one who fulfils what He promised and carries out what He decreed and determined, this is known to him, peace be upon him. In al-Kashshaf it is mentioned that he included in this shift that the word of your Lord would also be fulfilled concerning your affair. Asim, in one narration, read "kalimat" (words) in the plural, because they are promises, and the description as "good" is for the interpretation of them as a group. It has been mentioned that it is permitted to describe any plural with a feminine singular adjective, but the common practice with such is feminization by the ta' marbutah, and it may be feminized with alif as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿other uses (ma'arib ukhra)﴾. ﴿Because they were patient﴾, i.e., because of their patience with the hardships which they endured from Pharaoh and his people. This is sufficient as an incitement to patience and an indication that whoever meets affliction with impatience, God leaves him to it, and whoever meets it with patience, God, exalted is He, guarantees him relief.
Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from al-Hasan that he said: "If people, when they are afflicted by their ruler with something, were patient and called upon God, God, exalted is He, would not delay to remove that from them; but they flee to the sword, and so they are left to it." Then he recited this verse. In another report from him he said: "The Children of Israel were given what they were given only by their patience, and this community has never fled to the sword and come to good."
I say: We have witnessed people in the year 1248 who fled to the sword, and it did them no good; nor was any aim of theirs achieved, nor was any matter of theirs praised; rather they fell into the stony tract of Rahilah, the valley of Khidbat, and Umm Hubukar, and by the Lord's oath they were struck by the third of the three stones, and the forward and rear feathers of their wing of might were clipped, and they did not know that the life of the harmed is sweet yet bitter and bitter in its persistence, and that relief is only caught with the nets of patience. How excellent is the saying of al-Hasan: "I wonder at one who grows light, how he became light, when he has heard His saying, glory be to Him, and recited the verse." From it we know that grief does not contradict patience, for God, glory be to Him, described the Children of Israel with it, along with their earlier saying to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾.
﴿And We destroyed﴾, i.e., We ruined and annihilated: ﴿what Pharaoh and his people had been making﴾ in the land of Egypt of buildings and palaces. That is: We destroyed what Pharaoh had been making, with "ma" as a relative pronoun, the subject of "kana" being a pronoun referring back to it, and the clause "Pharaoh makes" consisting of verb and subject is the predicate of "kana," and the clause is the relative clause of "ma," with its returning pronoun omitted. It is also permitted that Pharaoh be the subject of "kana," with "makes" as a fronted predicate, and the existential clause is the relative clause of "ma," with its returning pronoun also omitted. Abu al-Baqa' objected that "yasna'u" can govern "Fir'awn," so there is no need to posit a fronting, just as the verb is not posited to be fronted in your saying "Zayd stood." This is heedless of the difference between the example and what we are discussing, and it is clearly so. It was said: "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), and "kana" is the verb of a preacher's sermon, the meaning being "what Pharaoh makes," etc. It was also said: "kana" is as mentioned, and "ma" is a nominal relative, with its returning pronoun omitted, the meaning being: "We destroyed what Pharaoh makes," etc., i.e., made. The shift to the present form on these two views is to bring the image vividly before the mind.
﴿And what they had been erecting﴾ of gardens, or what they had been content with of structures, such as the palace of Haman. The first is indicated by the saying of al-Hasan, and the second by the saying of Mujahid.
Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read here and in al-Nahl "ya'rushun" with a dammah on the ra', while the rest read it with a kasrah. These are two eloquent dialects, and the kasrah, as mentioned by al-Yazidi and Abu 'Ubaydah, is more eloquent. There was also read in the irregular readings "yaghrisun" (they plant), from the planting of trees; but al-Kashshaf says that it is a scribal error and is not so.
* * *

(This is) also from the category of allusion (al-ishara) in the verses. As for what I have found attributed to some of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) among the gnostics (al-'arifin): the staff is an allusion to his own soul (nafs), upon which he leans (yatawakka'u). That is: he relies on it in the animal movements and actions, and drives with it the sheep of the sound animal faculty (quwwa bahimiyya) and the tender shoots of the virtuous qualities (malakat) and praiseworthy habits from the tree of thought. Because of its sanctity, it was obedient to his commands and restrained from its animal actions except by his permission, like the staff. When he sends it forth in confronting opponents, it becomes like the serpent that swallows what they fabricate of falsehoods and display of the ropes of doubts (shubahat) and the staffs of sophistries (mughalatat), so it overcomes them and subdues them. And the drawing out of the hand is an allusion to manifesting the dazzling power from which the lights of truth shine. Some have made Pharaoh an allusion to the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammara), his people an allusion to its qualities, and likewise the magicians; and Moses an allusion to the spirit (al-ruh), and his people, the Children of Israel, to the intellect ('aql), the heart (qalb) and the innermost secret (sirr). And on this analogy. Al-Nisaburi interpreted the flood as abundant knowledge, the locusts as incoming spiritual states (al-waridat), the lice as inspirations (al-ilhamat), the frogs as passing thoughts (al-khawatir), and the blood as the various kinds of spiritual striving and discipline (al-mujahadat wa'l-riyadat). And it is, as you see, (far-fetched).

And a number of scholars have mentioned that magic was prevalent in the time of Moses (peace be upon him); therefore his miracle was what it was. And medicine was prevalent in the time of Jesus (peace be upon him); therefore his miracle was of the kind of medicine. And eloquence was prevalent in the time of our Prophet (ﷺ), and boasting by it was more famous than (qifa nabki); therefore his miracle was the Qur'an. The miracle of every prophet is only of the kind of what prevailed in his time, so that this would be more conducive to the acceptance of his claim.

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾. This begins after the account of Pharaoh has ended, and turns to the story of the Children of Israel. It explains what they did after God had bestowed on them His favours and shown them the signs He showed them. This serves to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he encountered from the Jews in Medina, for they treated him in the same way as their forefathers treated his brother Moses (peace be upon him). It also serves to awaken the believers so that they do not neglect to hold themselves accountable and to watch over God's blessings upon them, for the Children of Israel fell into what they fell into because they were heedless of what God had bestowed upon them. Jawaza is used in the sense of jaza (to pass through), and it is also read as jawwazna with the doubled letter, which likewise means jaza, and so it takes the preposition bi. The meaning is: We crossed the sea with them. By "the sea" is meant the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea).

In Majma' al-Bayan it is said that it is the Nile of Egypt, and this, as in the sea, is an error. It is reported from al-Kalbi that Moses (peace be upon him) brought them across on the day of 'Ashura' after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, and so they fasted on it out of gratitude to God, may He be exalted.

﴿Then they came﴾, meaning they passed by after the crossing.

﴿upon a people﴾. Qatada said: they were from Lakhm, the name of a tribe, and they were called after Lakhm ibn 'Adi ibn 'Amr ibn Saba', as Ibn 'Abd al-Barr confirmed. It was also said that they were from the Canaanite Amalekites, whom Moses (peace be upon him) had been commanded to fight.

﴿who were devoted to their idols﴾, meaning they persisted in worshipping them and kept constantly to them. As Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Ibn Jurayj, these were images of cows made of copper, and this was the beginning of the affair of the calf. It was also said that they were made of stone, and it was said that they were actual cows. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (ya'kifun) with a kasra on the kaf. When they saw this, they said: ﴿O Moses, make for us a god﴾, a likeness that we may worship, ﴿just as they have gods﴾. The kaf is connected to an omitted element that stands as an attribute of (ilahan), and (ma) is a relative pronoun, (lahum) is its complement, and (alihah) is a substitute for the concealed pronoun within it. The implied meaning is: make for us a god existing like the one that they themselves possess.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ma be a particle that makes the kaf restricted (kaffah), which is why a nominal clause follows it, and that it be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). Lahum is connected to a verb, meaning: as it is established for them.

﴿He said: Indeed you are a people who act in ignorance﴾. He (peace be upon him) marvelled at their saying this after they had witnessed the greatest sign and the mightiest proof. He described them as ignorant in the most complete manner, in that he did not mention any object or complement for it, either to make it stand in the position of an intransitive verb, or because its omission indicates its generality, meaning you are ignorant of everything, and so ignorance of lordship is included in this by way of priority. He emphasised this with inna, with the placing of qawm (people) in between, and with making what is the intended content of the report into a description of it, so that it would be as the Allamah said, like something verified and known. This, as al-Shihab (al-Alusi himself) mentioned, is a subtle nuance in the predicate that prepares for the claim that the predicate is so evident and the proof for it so established that it is as though it were known and verified, so it conveys its affirmation and confirmation. Without this, there would be no rhetorical reason for placing the described element in between.

[p. 41]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 139:

﴿Indeed, these people﴾ meaning: the people who are devoted (ya'kufun) to these idols.

﴿Are doomed (mutabbar)﴾ meaning: destroyed and ruined, as Ibn 'Abbas said.

﴿What they are engaged in﴾ of religion, meaning: Allah the Exalted will destroy their religion, which they follow, at my hands, and will ruin their idols and reduce them to dust.

﴿And what they have been doing is in vain﴾ meaning: completely nullified. This is more eloquent than taking it to mean "contrary to the truth."

﴿What they used to do﴾ meaning: what they persisted in doing of worshipping them, even though they intended thereby to draw near to Allah the Exalted. And the intended meaning is that this does not benefit them at all. Taking "what they used to do" to refer to the idols, on the grounds that the idols are made by them (ma'mulah lahum), is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning. The sentence is a justification for establishing the emphatic ignorance of the people. The placement of the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) as the subject of inna, as in al-Kashshaf, and the fronting of the predicate of the subject within the clause that serves as the predicate of inna, is a marking of the idol-worshippers as those who are exposed to ruin, that it definitely does not pass beyond them, and that it is for them a binding decree (darbat lazib), in order to warn them of the outcome of what they sought and to make hateful to them what they loved. The reasoning behind this, according to al-Kashf, is that the demonstrative, after conveying presence and the fullest distinction, indicates that they deserve what is reported about them through what preceded of their devotion. The fronting indicates that the state of what they are engaged in is nothing other than ruin, and the state of their action is nothing but futility; so they do not exceed these two, and these two are for them a binding decree.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "what they are engaged in" (ma hum fihi) be the subject (fa'il) of "doomed" (mutabbar), since it relies on the element to which it is attributed; in itself this is equal to the possibility that ma hum fihi is a subject (mubtada') with mutabbar as its predicate, or it is more likely than that. However, the context, as al-Qutb and others said, required this. So let it be understood.

"He said: Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, when He has preferred you above the worlds?"

It is said: this is the answer, and what preceded it is an introduction and preparation for it; perhaps for this reason the word "قال" (he said) was repeated.

Shaykh al-Islam said: it is the beginning of an explanation of the affairs of Allah the Exalted which necessitate restricting worship to Him, glorified is He, after the explanation that what they asked to be worshipped is something whose seeking is impossible at all, because it is entirely destroyed and false; and for this reason "قال" was placed between the two. Each of them is the speech of Musa, peace be upon him. Al-Shihab said: the word "قال" was repeated although the speakers are the same, because this is a rhetorical argument (dalil khitabi) by their being preferred over the worlds, and the argument from rational mutual exclusion (al-tamanu' al-'aqli) was not used, because they were common folk ('awamm). End of quotation.

As for establishing the proof of mutual exclusion against the idolaters who say, "We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah in nearness," and who, when asked, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", answer, "Allah created them," there is no obscurity; yet the apparent sense is that it is established upon the drawing of attention, as is well known. The interrogative is for denial, and the accusative of "غَيْرَ" (ghayra, "other than") is as the object of "أبْغِيكُمْ" (abghikum, "I seek for you"), and it is on the basis of omission and conveyance (al-hadhf wal-iysal), the original being "أبْغِي لَكُمْ" (abghi lakum, "I seek for you"). On this is the statement of al-Jawhari explained, although its apparent meaning is that the verb is transitive to two objects and the pronoun "ه" is a specifier (tamyiz). It is also permitted that "al-baqa'" (the remainder) be an object of "أبْغِي", and "غَيْرَ" be an adjective of it that was placed first and thus became a circumstantial (hal). In any case, the intended meaning here is the restriction of the denial to other than Him, the Exalted, not the denial of restriction. The meaning: "Shall I seek for you a deity other than the One deserving of worship?"

"وهُوَ فَضَّلَكم عَلى العالَمِينَ" — "And He has preferred you above the worlds": that is, above the worlds of your time, or above all the worlds. On this basis, the intended meaning is their being preferred by those signs, not absolutely, so that it would not follow that they are preferred over the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the prophets and the angels, peace be upon them, they do not enter among those preferred over them in any way; rather they are excluded from that by a rational indication. The clause is circumstantial (hali), confirming the aspect of denial, meaning: while the state is that He, the Exalted, specified the preference for you, giving you blessings He did not give to others. In this is an admonition concerning what they did of bad conduct, in that they met favour with its opposite by intending to associate with Him the most base of His creatures. This specification is drawn from the meaning of the speech itself; otherwise there is nothing in it that conveys that. The placing of the pronoun before the predicate does not convey it, although it is another form of specification according to what has been said; that is, He is the one specified as having preferred you over whoever else. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the clause be a resumptive (mustaanifa) sentence.

﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ by destroying them and rescuing you from them. "Idh" (when) is either the object of the omitted verb "udhkurū" (remember), on the view that it has gone beyond its temporal sense, meaning "remember that time," and this would be a figurative way of saying "remember what happened in it." Or it is an adverb of time modifying the omitted object of "udhkurū," meaning "remember Our deed with you at that time." This is a reminder from God, the Exalted, of His great blessing. It is read as ﴿najjaynākum﴾ (from "tanjiyah," deliverance). Ibn ʿĀmir reads ﴿anjākum﴾, in which case it is part of Moses' speech, peace be upon him. Some have said that even according to the majority reading it is likewise part of Moses' speech, with the pronoun in "anjaynā" referring to Moses and his brother, peace be upon them both, or to the two of them and those with them, or to Moses alone, peace be upon him, the plural being used to magnify the matter of the deliverance. This goes against the apparent meaning. It has also been said that it is part of God's own speech, completing Moses' speech, as in His saying ﴿and We brought forth thereby pairs﴾ after His saying ﴿Who made the earth a cradle for you﴾, and it serves as an explanation of His saying ﴿and that He preferred you﴾.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿they subjected you to the worst torment﴾, meaning they inflicted that upon you and imposed it on you. It is either a explanatory resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf bayānī*), as though it were said: "What was done to them, or from what were they saved?" and so it was answered with what was mentioned. Or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to the pronoun of the addressees, or to the people of Pharaoh, or to both together, since it includes a pronoun referring to both of them.

His saying, Mighty is His name: ﴿slaughtering your sons and sparing your women﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿they subjected you﴾, explaining it. It may also be read as a resumptive sentence. ﴿And in that﴾, that is, in the deliverance or in the worst torment, ﴿there was a trial﴾, meaning a blessing or an affliction. It has been said that what is meant is something that includes both.

﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the Owner of your affairs, ﴿great﴾, whose greatness cannot be measured. In the verse there is a shift (*iltifāt*) in address relative to what came before. Moreover, this request was not, as Muhyi al-Sunnah al-Baghawi said, from doubt about the oneness of God, the Exalted. Rather, their aim was a god whom they could venerate, and through venerating it they would draw near to God, the Exalted. They thought that this would not harm their religion, and this was due to the intensity of their ignorance, as the verses indicate. It has also been said that their aim was literally to worship the idol, and in that case it would be an apostasy on their part. In either case, the one who said it was some of them, not all of them. Something similar has occurred in this community. Al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Abu Waqid al-Laythi: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, went out on the expedition of Ḥunayn and passed by a tree of the polytheists upon which they used to hang their weapons and around which they used to sit in devotion. It was called Dhat Anwat. They said: 'O Messenger of God, make for us a Dhat Anwat just as they have a Dhat Anwat.' The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Glory be to God!'" In another narration: "God is greatest." This is just as the Children of Israel said to Moses, peace be upon him: "Make for us a god just as they have gods." By the One in whose hand is my soul, you will surely follow the ways of those before you.

Al-Ṭabarānī and others narrated through the route of Kathīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "We campaigned with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, in the year of the Conquest, and we were a thousand and a few more. God, the Exalted, conquered Mecca and Ḥunayn. When we were between Ḥunayn and al-Ṭāʾif, in a land where there was a great lote tree on which weapons used to be hung, it was called Dhat Anwat, and it was worshipped besides God. When the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, saw it, he turned away from it on a scorching day to a shade nearer than it. A man said to him: 'O Messenger of God, make for us a Dhat Anwat just as they have a Dhat Anwat.' The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'These are the ways! You have said—by the One in whose hand is Muhammad's soul—just as the Children of Israel said: Make for us a god just as they have gods.'"

In this report there is an explicit statement that the one who spoke was a single man. Perhaps that was from an ignorance for which he is excused and by which he did not become a disbeliever; otherwise the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, would have commanded him to renew his Islam. This is not transmitted, as far as I have found. People today have adopted many things of the kind of Dhat Anwat that no enumeration can encompass. The one who enjoins good is rarer than the egg of the female vulture, and the carrying out of the command to act rightly depends on the Pleiades. The command belongs to God, the One, the Subduer.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 7, verse 142:**

﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights﴾. It is related that Moses, peace be upon him, promised the Children of Israel, while they were in Egypt, that if God destroyed their enemy he would bring them a Book containing an explanation of what they should do and what they should refrain from. When Pharaoh was destroyed, Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord for the Book, and He commanded him to fast thirty days, and this was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. When he completed the thirty, he noticed a change in the odour of his mouth, so he used the *siwak* (tooth-stick). The angels said: "We used to smell the scent of musk from your mouth, and you have spoiled it with the siwak." God then commanded him to add to it ten days from Dhu al-Hijjah.

Al-Daylami related from Ibn 'Abbas, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ): "When Moses, peace be upon him, came to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and wished to speak with Him after the thirty days, during which he had fasted their nights and days, he disliked speaking to his Lord, Glorified is He, with the breath of a fasting person. So he took some of the plants of the earth and chewed them. His Lord said to him: 'Why have you broken your fast?' and He knows best what had happened. He said: 'O my Lord, I disliked speaking to You except with a pleasant-smelling mouth.' He said: 'Do you not know, O Moses, that the breath of a fasting person is more fragrant to Me than the scent of musk? Return and fast ten days, then come to Me.' So Moses, peace be upon him, did what his Lord commanded him. This is His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿and We completed it with ten﴾." The expression of these days as "nights" is, as has been said, because they are the beginnings of the months.

It has also been said that God commanded him, peace be upon him, to fast thirty days and to perform in them what would bring him near to God, Exalted is He; then the Torah was sent down to him and he was spoken to in it. The mention of the forty has been stated in summary in *al-Baqarah* and is detailed here.

﴿Wa'adna﴾ means "We appointed". Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it this way. It is also permissible for the form to remain on its original pattern (of mutual promise), on the basis of treating Moses' acceptance as occupying the position of a promise; this has been previously investigated.

And ﴿thalathin﴾ (thirty), as Abu al-Baqa said, is the second object of *wa'adna*, with an omitted noun (*mudaf*); that is, "the completion of thirty nights" or "their coming".

﴿So the appointment of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾. This is in the manner of *fadhlakah* (a summing-up, i.e. a conclusive recapitulation) of what came before. The likely purpose of this is that completing the thirty with ten may bear the apparent meaning, namely adding ten to thirty so that they become forty; and it may also bear the meaning that they had been twenty and were completed with ten to become thirty, as one says: "I completed the ten with two dirhams," meaning that without the two dirhams it would not have become ten. So, to remove the suspicion of this second possibility, this phrase was used. It has also been said that the completion with ten is unrestricted and may be determined either by God's determination or by Moses' own choice, so this was stated to indicate that the first is intended. It has also been said that it was stated as a symbol that nothing occurred in those ten days that would require making up for a deficiency. The word *miqat* means "time", but a group distinguished between them, saying that *waqt* (time) is unrestricted, whereas *miqat* is a time set aside for performing some action, as in the *mawaqit* (appointed times) of the Hajj.

As for ﴿arba'in﴾ (forty) being in the accusative, it has been said that it is the circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning "reaching forty".
