Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that on this view it would be a complement of the omitted circumstantial element, not a circumstantial element itself. It was answered that the grammarians apply the ruling of the governing word to its substitute which stands in its place; thus they say in "Zayd is in the house" that the prepositional phrase is the predicate, although the predicate is really what it implies. It was objected that what the grammarians stated concerns the adverbial accusative (*zarf*) alone and not others; so the better view is that it is a circumstantial element, with the implied sense "counted as forty". It was replied that the claim that the mention is restricted to the adverbial accusative contradicts what actually occurs, as is clear to anyone who examines it; and that what he claimed is better than what came before, though it is subject to the same objection. It has also been said that it is a specifier (*tamyiz*). It has been said that it is a direct object, with *tamma* implicitly carrying the sense of "reached" (*balagha*). It has been said that *tamma* is one of the defective verbs (*af'al naqisah*), and this is its predicate; this is a strange view. It has been said that it is in the adverbial (*zarfiyyah*) accusative. It was objected to this: how can the forty be the time-frame of the completion, when completion occurs only at its end, unless the expression is understood figuratively?

﴿And Moses said﴾, when he set out for the private conversation with God, as he had been commanded.

﴿to his brother Aaron﴾. The name is a non-Arabic Hebrew name which does not occur in the language of the Arabs as an original word. It is written without an *alif*. Here the *nun* is vowelled with a *fatha*, on the basis that it is in the genitive as an apposition or explanatory element to "his brother", or in the accusative as a direct object of an implied verb, meaning "I mean, I mean". It was read anomalously with a *damma*, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, namely "he is", or a vocative from which the vocative particle has been removed, meaning "O Aaron". ﴿Take my place﴾, that is: be my successor among my people and watch over them in what they do and what they refrain from. Moses' appointment of his brother as successor, although he, peace be upon him, was himself a prophet and messenger like him, has been explained as follows: the leadership belonged to Aaron and not to Moses. It has been said that the combination of leadership with messengerhood and prophethood is not a necessary matter, as the survey of the stories of the prophets of the Children of Israel indicates. The Shaykh al-Akbar (may God sanctify his secret) mentioned in his *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyyah* that it was told to Aaron that he was a prophet by original status and a messenger by way of following, so perhaps this succession was one of the effects of that following. It has also been said that this is like what one of two men entrusted with a matter for the other says when he wants to go away for some affair: "Be a substitute for me", meaning: exert the utmost of your ability and the limit of your effort, such that your action is the action of two persons. ﴿And set things right﴾, meaning: put right what needs correcting in the affairs of their religion; or be a reformer, understanding the verb as intransitive without an implied object.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he meant kindness towards them and treating them well. It has also been said that the meaning is: bring them to obedience and righteousness.

﴿And do not follow the way of those who spread corruption﴾, that is: do not follow the way of those who take up corruption, whether by calling to it or not calling to it. This is of the nature of emphasis, as is not hidden.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 143 (part 1 of 4)]

﴿When Moses came at Our appointed time﴾, i.e., at the time We had appointed for him, namely at the completion of the forty (nights). The *lam* here denotes specification, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾ (17:78). It is in the sense of *'inda* ("at"), according to some grammarians. ﴿And his Lord spoke to him﴾ without an intermediary of letters or sound. Nevertheless, this is not like the speech of created beings, and there is no impediment in that, as we have clarified in the Fourth Benefit. The righteous early generations (al-Salaf al-Salih) adopted what he has mentioned.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah, the Exalted, spoke to Moses on the day of the Tur, He spoke to him in other than the speech with which He had spoken to him on the day He called him. Moses said: 'O my Lord, is this Your speech with which You spoke to me?' He said: 'O Moses, I spoke to you with the power of ten thousand tongues, and Mine is the power of all tongues and more than that.' When Moses returned to the Children of Israel, they said: 'O Moses, describe for us the speech of the All-Merciful.' He said: 'You cannot bear it. Did you not see the sound of the thunderbolts that comes with the sweetest sweetness you have heard? That is close to it, but it is not it.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Abu al-Huwayrith Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, who said: "Allah, the Exalted, spoke to Moses only to the extent of what he could bear of His speech. Had He spoken to him with all of His speech, nothing could have borne it."

A group narrated from Ka'b, who said: "When Allah, the Exalted, spoke to Moses, He spoke to him in all the tongues. He began to say: 'O my Lord, I do not understand,' until the last of the tongues spoke to him in his own tongue, in a voice like His voice..." and the report continues.

They also narrated from Ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that it was said to Moses, peace be upon him: "What did you liken the speech of your Lord to, of what He has created?" He, peace be upon him, said: "To the still thunder."

Al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet: "When my brother Moses went out to converse with his Lord, He spoke to him a thousand and two hundred words, the first of which He spoke to him was in the Berber language."

It is related from al-Ash'ari that Moses, peace be upon him, only heard the inner speech (*al-kalam al-nafsi*) subsisting in the Essence of Allah, the Exalted, and that what he heard was not specific to any direction. Interpreting it as hearing in actuality is problematic given the reports that indicate otherwise. Apparently, if this transmission is authentic, it is a position from which he retracted to the doctrine of the early generations, whose belief he made clear in *al-Ibana*.

﴿He said: "My Lord, show me Yourself"﴾, i.e., Your Essence or Your self. The second object is omitted because it is known, and he did not state it out of courtesy.

﴿"that I may look at You"﴾ is jussive in response to the supplication. It has been objected that seeing (*ru'ya*) is caused by looking (*nazar*) and comes after it, as indicated by the common expression: "I looked at him and saw him." It is explained that looking is turning the pupil of the eye toward a thing seeking to see it, while seeing is perception by the sight after the turning. Then how can looking be made the answer to a request for seeing, caused by it, when it is the reverse of the matter?

It is answered that what is meant by "showing" is not producing the seeing, but enabling it, absolutely, or by manifestation and appearance (*tajalli*), which precedes looking and is its cause. So in the speech there is a mention of the necessary (*malzum*) and an intention of the consequence (*lazim*). That is: "Enable me to see You, or manifest Yourself to me, so that I may look at You and see You."

﴿He said﴾ is a clarifying resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), as if it were said: "What did the Lord of Majesty say when Moses, peace be upon him, said that?" So it was said: He said: ﴿"You will not see Me"﴾, i.e., you have no capacity to see Me as you are, and this is a categorical negation of the requested showing in the most complete manner.

﴿"But look at the mountain"﴾ is a corrective (*istidrak*) to show that he, peace be upon him, cannot bear the seeing. The mountain intended is Mount Sinai (*Tur Sina'*), as occurs in more than one report. In *Tafsir al-Khazin* (a tafsir by al-Khazin) and others, its name is given as Zubayr, with a fatha on the *za'*, a kasra on the *ba'* and a *ra'* (unpointed), on the pattern of *Amir*.

﴿"But if it remains firm in its place"﴾, not crumbled by the manifestation, ﴿"then you will see Me"﴾ when I manifest Myself to you.

﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾, i.e., He appeared to it in the manner befitting His exalted Majesty, after He had made it capable of perceiving that.

﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾, i.e., made it pulverized and shattered. *Dakk* and *daqq* are siblings, like *shakk* and *shaqq*. Our shaykh al-Kurani said: The mountain is included among the things that glorify Allah's praise, by the text: ﴿There is nothing but that it exalts Him with His praise﴾ (17:44), understood according to its apparent meaning upon careful examination, which entails that it is alive and perceptive with a life and perception appropriate to its world and its mode of existence. It is also said: This is an illustration of the manifestation of His power, glorified is He, and the reach of His will to what He did to the mountain, not that there was an actual manifestation. This is similar to what has been established in His saying: ﴿that He says to it "Be," and it is﴾ (36:82), that what is meant is that what He decreed and willed to exist enters into existence without delay, not that there is actually a saying. Ṣāḥib al-Farā'id (the author of *al-Fara'id*) criticized this, saying that this meaning is not understood from the verse, because *tajalli* is the reflexive form (*mutawi'*) of *jallaytuhu*, i.e., I made it manifest, and one says: "I made it manifest, so it became manifest."

The manifestation of His power cannot be assumed, because that contradicts the default, and moreover this interpretation is far removed from the intended meaning.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, who authenticated both of them, al-Bayhaqi, and others narrated through various chains from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿When His Lord manifested Himself﴾ etc. He said: "Like this," and he pointed with his two fingers, placing the tip of his thumb on the joint of the little finger, and in one wording, "on the upper joint of the little finger," "and the mountain crumbled."

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Nothing of His, glorified is He, manifested to the mountain except the amount of the little finger, and it turned it to dust." This, as is not hidden, is among the ambiguous matters (*mutashabihat*) in which the way of submission is followed, and that is safer and more sound; or it is interpreted in a manner befitting the majesty of His Essence, exalted is He.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿*dakka'*﴾ with a long vowel, i.e., level ground, and from it comes the expression: a *naqa dakka'* for a she-camel whose hump has not risen. Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿*dukkan*﴾ with a *damma* on the *dal* and tanwin, the plural of *dakka'*, like *humr* and *hamra'*, i.e., in pieces, crumbled. So it is an adjective of a plural. In Abu Hayyan's commentary on *Sharh al-Tas-hil*, it is stated that it was treated as a noun and so was made to agree with the masculine.

﴿And Moses fell down﴾, i.e., he collapsed from the terror of what he saw. Some distinguished between *suqut* (falling) and *khurur* (falling down), saying that the former is general, while the latter is a fall that makes a sound like a rushing.

﴿Unconscious (*sa'qan*)﴾, i.e., struck down and crying out, from *al-sa'qa* (the thunderbolt). The meaning is that he fell unconscious according to Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them, and dead according to Qatada.

It is narrated that he remained in that state for the duration of a week. Ibn Abbas also reported that he, peace be upon him, was overtaken by the swoon from the evening of Thursday, the Day of Arafah, until the evening of Friday. Some storytellers (*al-qussas*) related that the angels would pass by him at that time, kicking him with their feet and saying: "O son of the menstruating women, did you aspire to see the Lord of Majesty?" This is a worthless statement that cannot be relied upon in any way, for the angels, peace be upon them, must be cleared of humiliating Allah's interlocutor by kicking him with the foot and by speaking to him with contempt.

﴿Then when he regained consciousness﴾, i.e., returned to his prior state. This occurred through the return of the spirit to him according to Qatada, or through the return of understanding and sense according to others. It is well known that *ifaqa* is the return of reason and understanding to a person after they had left him due to some cause. One does not say *afaqa* of a dead person when his spirit returns to him; this is said only of one who was unconscious. For this reason, most scholars chose what the scholar (*al-Habr*, i.e., Ibn Abbas) had said.

﴿He said﴾, magnifying the command of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿"Glory be to You"﴾, i.e., exalting You above resemblance to Your creation in anything, or above anyone being able to see You in the state he was in before that, or above my asking You anything without Your permission.

﴿"I have repented to You"﴾, from presuming to ask without permission. It is also said: from seeing my own existence and inclining toward my own will.

﴿"And I am the first of the believers"﴾, in Your greatness and majesty, or in that no one will see You in this world, so it is established as has been said. It is intended, as al-Kurani said, that he was the first of the believers in that with a taste preceded by the eye of certainty in his view. It is also said: he meant the first of the believers that it is not permissible to ask without Your permission.

The Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni people) who permit the vision of Allah, glorified is He, used this verse as evidence for its permissibility in general. The Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who deny it, used the same verse to argue the opposite, and fierce debate raged between them. The essence of the matter is that Ahl al-Sunna said: The verse indicates the possibility of seeing from two aspects.

The first: Moses, peace be upon him, asked for it with his words, "My Lord, show me..." etc. If it were impossible, then if Moses, peace be upon him, knew of its impossibility, a sensible person, let alone a Prophet, and even less one of the Resolute Messengers (*Ulu al-Azm*), would not ask for the impossible or seek it. And if he did not know, it would follow that ordinary Mu'tazilis, and anyone who has acquired a fragment of their knowledge, would know Allah, the Exalted, and what is permissible and impermissible for Him better than the chosen Prophet. Saying this is the utmost ignorance and foolishness. Since the claim of impossibility is refuted, permissibility is established.

The second: the verse makes the seeing conditional upon the mountain remaining firm, and what is conditional upon a possible thing is possible.

The opponents raised several objections to the first aspect:

The first: We do not concede that Moses, peace be upon him, asked for seeing. He only asked for necessary knowledge (*al-'ilm al-darurial*) of Allah, the Exalted, but he expressed it by seeing metaphorically, because of the mutual implication between them. Expressing one of two mutually implicating things by the other is common in their speech. This is the view of Abu al-Hudhayl ibn al-Allaf, followed by al-Jubba'i and most of the Basrans.

The second: We grant that he did not ask for knowledge but asked for actual seeing, but we say that he asked to see one of the signs of the Hour, by way of omitting the modified noun and placing the modifying noun in its position. So the meaning of "Show me, that I may look at You" is: "Show me, that I may look at one of Your signs indicating the Hour." This is the view of al-Ka'bi and the Baghdadis.

The third: We grant that he asked for the actual seeing of Allah, the Exalted, Himself, but it was not for his own sake, peace be upon him, but to repel his people who said: ﴿"Show us Allah plainly"﴾ (4:153). He attributed the seeing to himself rather than to them, so that the refusal would be more forceful in repelling and deterring them from what they asked, by way of alerting the lower through the higher. This is the view of al-Jahiz and his followers.

The fourth: We grant that he asked for himself, but we do not concede that this contradicts knowledge of its impossibility, since the purpose of asking for it is that he would know its impossibility through a scriptural proof added to what he had of rational proof, for the purpose of confirmation. This is permissible, as indicated by Abraham's request, peace be upon him, to be shown how the dead are revived, and by his saying: ﴿"but so that my heart may be at rest"﴾ (2:260). This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Asamm.

The fifth: We grant that the request for seeing contradicts knowledge of its impossibility, but we maintain that he lacked the knowledge, and this does not undermine his prophethood, peace be upon him. Prophethood does not depend on knowledge of all the true doctrines, or of everything that is permissible or impermissible for Allah, the Exalted, but only on what the purpose of the mission and the call to Allah, the Exalted, depends upon. That purpose is His oneness and the imposition on His servants of commands and prohibitions, to encourage them toward everlasting bliss. The impossibility of seeing is not of this kind. This is supported by the fact that he asked for the occurrence of seeing in this world, which does not occur according to us or according to you. This view has been attributed to al-Hasan from among us, and it is strange from him.

The sixth: We grant the knowledge of impossibility, but we do not concede that asking is forbidden. The asking would only be impossible if it were prohibited in his law. Why could it not be that it was not prohibited?

[p. 48 begins at the marked point below]

Seventh: We grant the prohibition, but we do not grant that it is a major sin (kabirah). Why could it not be a minor sin (saghirah), which is not impossible for the prophets, peace be upon them?

They (the scholars) discussed the second aspect in two ways. The first: We do not grant that He made the seeing conditional on something possible, because the condition was not on the mountain's remaining fixed while still; otherwise the seeing would have occurred necessarily upon the existence of the condition, since the mountain while still was stationary. Rather, the condition was on its remaining fixed while it was moving, and that is impossible in itself (muhal li-dhatihi). The third: Even if we grant that the mountain's remaining fixed is possible, we do not grant that what is conditioned upon a possible thing is possible. For it is valid to say: If the effect ceases to exist, the cause ceases to exist. The cause may be impossible not to exist while the effect is possible in itself, like the attributes in relation to the Essence according to the mutakallimun (theologians), and the First Intellect in relation to Him, exalted is He, according to the hukama (philosophers). So it is permissible that the impossible seeing be conditioned upon the possible remaining fixed. The secret of the permissibility of this is that the connection between the conditioner and the conditioned is only in accordance with occurrence, meaning that if the non-existence of the effect occurs, the non-existence of the cause occurs. An essentially possible thing may be essentially impossible to occur, so the conditioning between them is permissible. The connection between them is not in accordance with possibility, so that it would follow that the possibility of the conditioned thing requires the possibility of the conditioner.

Then, even if we grant that what you have mentioned from the two aspects indicates the permissibility of seeing, it is opposed by what indicates impermissibility. For the (lan) in the verse is for the perpetuation and emphasis of negation. Also, Musa's words, peace be upon him: ﴿I have repented to You﴾ are evidence that he was mistaken in his request, and if seeing were permissible he would not have been mistaken. Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah Almighty treat him with His justice, claimed that the verse is the strongest proof of the impossibility of seeing. He mentioned in his Kashshaf what he mentioned and said: "Then I am astonished at those who call themselves Muslims and are named the People of the Sunnah and the Community, how they adopted this grave matter as a doctrine. Let not their concealment behind the bilkafa deceive you, for it is one of the inventions of their shaykhs." And the saying is what one of the 'Adliyya (Mu'tazilites) said about them:

"And a group who named their desire a Sunnah,
A group of donkeys, by my life, saddled!
They likened Him to His creation, and feared
The censure of the people, so they hid behind the bilkafa."

It was answered regarding their statement that he, peace be upon him, only asked for necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-darurri): If seeing meant necessary knowledge, then the mentioned look (naẓar) would also have been after its meaning, and it is not so. For the look connected with ila (to) is explicit in seeing and does not admit anything else, so it is not abandoned for mere possibility. In Sharh al-Mawaqif, it is said that seeking necessary knowledge of one who addresses and converses with you is unreasonable. And it was objected to this: [p. 49]
that what is meant is knowledge of His particular identity, and address requires only knowledge in some respect, like one who addresses us from behind a wall. What is meant by knowledge of the particular identity is the unveiling of His identity, exalted is He, in a particular manner such that the intellect cannot consider it true of many, as in what is seen by the faculty of sight. There is no doubt that it is possible for Him, since He is able to create in the servant necessary knowledge of His particular identity in the particular manner without the use of the eyesight, just as He creates it afterward. As for its not necessitating address: address only requires knowledge of the one addressed by universal matters which the intellect can consider true of many, even if in external reality they are confined to one person. So this is of the type of conception (ta'aqqul). By this clarification the soundness of the objection and the removal of what was objected to become known, and it becomes clear from it the feebleness of what al-Amidi said: that taking seeing to mean knowledge necessitates that Musa, peace be upon him, was not knowing of his Lord, lest the obtaining of what is already obtained follow. Attributing this to the Interlocutor (Kalim) is among the greatest ignorances. For we say: Knowledge of the particular identity, as we have mentioned, is not among the necessities of prophethood or of conversation, as is not hidden. Yes, the transitivity (ta'diyah, with ila) prevents this taking, as you know, and the answer with ﴿You will not see Me, but look at the mountain﴾ makes it distant, as is apparent, even if al-Zamakhshari strained to justify it with what the ears reject.

And it was said: If this interpretation were valid, its like would be valid in ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾, since the indication is equal, and this is impossible by consensus; and "openly" adds nothing beyond the look being connected with ila. It was answered regarding their statement that he only asked that He show him one of the signs of the Hour, that this is not sound for three reasons:

First: It is contrary to the apparent meaning without evidence.

Second: He was answered with ﴿You will not see Me﴾, and if this is taken to negate seeing some of the signs about which the question was asked, it is a contradiction, for He has indeed shown him the greatest of the signs, which is the crumbling of the mountain (tadakdukul-jabal). And if it is taken to negate seeing, then the answer does not correspond to the question.

Third: His, may He be glorified, saying ﴿But if it remains in its place, then you will see Me﴾, if taken to refer to seeing the sign, is impossible, because the sign is not in the mountain's remaining fixed but in its crumbling. And if it is taken to refer to seeing (Him), it is not connected with the question. Therefore it is not fitting to take what is in the verse as referring to seeing a sign.

As for their statement that the seeing occurred to repel his people, that is contrary to the apparent meaning without evidence, and that the evidence was the seizure by the thunderbolt (al-sa'qah) is nothing. Also, it was obligatory for him, peace be upon him, to hasten to rebuke and restrain them from seeking what is not befitting the majesty of Allah, exalted is He, as he said ﴿Indeed you are a people who are ignorant﴾ when they said ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾. And their statement that the aim was to join the transmitted proof to the rational proof is nothing; for that could have been achieved by asking for the manifestation of a transmitted proof to him without requesting seeing while it is impossible. Its story has already been discussed. And what they mentioned as the Fifth Aspect, its rejection is evident from the explanation of the First of the two aspects mentioned by the People of the Sunnah. Its summary is that it would follow for them that the Interlocutor, peace be upon him, is less knowledgeable than the ordinary Mu'tazilites, and less than one who has acquired a portion of speech in knowing what is permissible for Him, exalted is He, and what is not. This is a foolish word and a crooked path, which no one of the intelligent follows. For the prophets, peace be upon them, being more knowing than others of His essence and His exalted attributes is a matter about which two rams should not butt heads. And the non-occurrence of seeing in this world according to both groups, if what is meant is that it is not possible to occur, then this is the very issue in question (awwal al-mas'alah). And if what is meant is that it is possible but does not occur for anyone, then we do not grant that both groups agree on this. As for the Mu'tazilites, it is because they do not affirm its possibility. As for the People of the Sunnah, it is because many of them held that it occurred to our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, and others. And the saying of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "Whoever claims that Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah, exalted is He." This is rejected or interpreted to mean: Whoever claims that Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, [p. 50]
in his light, which is his light, meaning the dazzling light which takes away the eyes, and which is indicated in the hadith: "The veils of His face would have burned away whatever His sight reaches," then he has greatly slandered. From this it is known what is in the possibility that the intended meaning is the non-occurrence, setting aside whether it is possible or not. And their statement that it is permissible that this request was not forbidden in His law, so there is no impediment, is refuted by the fact that the evidence of prohibition is evident, for seeking the impossible, if it were not forbidden in his law, peace be upon him, would not have reached such severity of rebuke upon his people when they sought what they sought. Moreover, even if we grant that it is not forbidden, it is said that there is no benefit in it, and what is like that is exempt from the station of prophethood. From this is known what is in their last statement.

And it was answered regarding their statement that the conditioned thing is the mountain's remaining fixed while moving: If they mean that the condition is remaining fixed while the movement exists together with the movement, then this is an addition of an implicit element and abandoning the apparent meaning of the wording without evidence, so it is not sound. And if they mean that the condition is remaining fixed in the state in which movement existed, instead of the movement, then its permissibility is not hidden. So how can it be claimed that it is impossible in itself? Some of them said in reply: The conditioned thing is the mountain's remaining fixed after the look, by the indication of the fa' (then). When the will of Allah, exalted is He, became attached to its not remaining fixed immediately after the look, its remaining fixed became impossible, even if by another (bi-l-ghayr). So he turned from saying it is impossible in itself to saying it is impossible by another, since the purpose is also accomplished by this. This was criticized by al-Salkuti and others: It is nothing, for the mountain's remaining fixed at the time when Allah's will became attached to its not remaining fixed is also possible, by its being replaced by remaining fixed. What is impossible is its remaining fixed together with the attachment of His, may He be glorified, will to its not remaining fixed. And a certain eminent scholar of the Romans had a discussion here, which al-Shihab transmitted: Do not let its clamor deceive you, for apparent meanings are not abandoned merely for a weak possibility.

And it was answered regarding their statement "We do not grant that what is conditioned upon a possible thing is possible," etc.: The meaning of "possible" here is the conditioned-upon possible, which is purely possible and free from impossibility absolutely. There is no doubt that the possibility of the effect in a case where its cause's non-existence is impossible is not like that. Rather, the conditioning between them is only in accordance with impossibility by another, for the necessitating of the non-existence of the attributes and the non-existence of the First Intellect is the non-existence of the Necessary Existent, insofar as the existence of each of them is necessary and their non-existence is impossible by the existence of the Necessary Existent. But considered in itself, setting aside external matters, there is no necessitation. This is unlike the mountain's remaining fixed, for it is purely possible, not impossible either in itself or by accident, as is not hidden. Moreover, some of them examined the soundness of the example linguistically, although there is in it what there is. As for what was said: The aim in the verse is not to explain the permissibility or impermissibility of seeing, since He was not asked about it, but the aim is only to explain its non-occurrence, and the non-fulfilment of the condition takes care of that, this is a word with no benefit in it. For permissibility and impermissibility are among the consequences of conditioning by the consensus of the leading scholars of both groups. And what they mentioned in the counter-argument, that (lan) indicates the perpetuation of negation, is not granted. And if it were granted, it is possible that this is in relation to this world, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But they will never wish for it, ever﴾, for the indication of perpetuation there is more evident, and they took it to that meaning also, because they wish for it in the Hereafter to escape the punishment. And among what points to this: the seeing sought is only seeing in this world, and the right answer is to correspond to the question. And there has come from him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, what indicates that the negation of seeing is restricted, not absolute. So let his explanation be followed, upon him be blessings and peace.

For al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, recited this verse: ﴿My Lord, show me...﴾ etc., and said: "Allah the Exalted said: O Musa, indeed no living thing sees Me except that it dies, nor any dry thing except that it crumbles, nor any moist thing except that it disperses. The only ones who will see Me are the people of Paradise, whose eyes do not die and whose bodies do not decay."

This is evident that what Musa, peace be upon him, sought was seeing in this world while he remained in his state,
[p. 51 follows]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 143 (part 3 of 4):

...in the state in which he was when asked, without a swoon following it. For His saying, "Verily, he will not see Me, one who is alive," etc., ... negates only the seeing in this world together with life, not seeing absolutely. So the meaning of "You will not see Me" in the verse is: "You will not see Me while you remain in this state," not "You will not see Me in this world absolutely," let alone that the meaning is "You will not see Me absolutely, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter." Yes, this hadith is specified by what is authentically related, both as a marfu' and a mawquf report, that "he (ﷺ) saw his Lord on the night of the Isra'," together with the absence of a swoon. Perhaps the wisdom in his (ﷺ) being specified with this is that his creation was the most perfect creation and the most balanced in form and meaning, due to his (ﷺ) comprehensiveness of the realities in a balanced manner, while they are in tension within him. The requirement of that is steadfastness, by God's permission, and yet the manifestation (tajalli) did not occur to him except in the abode of permanence. Thus the requirement of the station combined with the requirement of the perfect balance of his creation.

It may also be said, by way of hypothetical concession: even if we grant that "lan" (never) indicates perpetuity absolutely, the most that would follow is the negation of the occurrence of the seeing, and this does not necessarily entail the negation of its possibility. The Mu'tazilah, however, maintain that. As for their claim that his (ﷺ) saying, "I have repented to You" (7:143), indicates that he was in error, it is nothing; for repentance may be used in the sense of returning, even if no sin preceded it. On this basis, it is not far-fetched that what is meant by "I have repented to You" is: "I have returned to You from seeking the seeing."

Ibn al-Munir mentioned that Musa's (peace be upon him) glorification (tasbih), when it became clear to him that the knowledge had already preceded that the seeing would not occur in this world, and God, exalted, is sanctified above the occurrence of the opposite of what He knows. As for repentance in regard to the prophets (peace be upon them), it does not necessarily follow that it is from a sin, for their lofty station is protected from everything that lowers the rank of perfection. And it was incumbent upon him (peace be upon him), in view of the exaltedness of his station, to pause before asking for the seeing until he had permission; so when he asked without permission, he was leaving what was more fitting for him.

It has been reported: "The good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near (to God)."

Al-Imam al-Razi mentioned something similar. And al-Amidi said: Although repentance requires the prior existence of a sin, there is nothing that definitively indicates that the sin lay in his request. Rather, it is possible that the repentance was from what came before the request, which he (peace be upon him) regarded as a sin. What prompted this was the great terrors he saw, such as the crumbling of the mountain, in line with the custom of the righteous believers of renewing repentance for what has passed when they see a sign or a terrifying matter.

* * *

He mentioned that his (peace be upon him) saying, "And I am the first of the believers" (7:143), does not mean the beginning of faith in that state; rather, what is meant is the attribution of priority to him, not to faith. Perhaps the purpose of this statement was to seek sympathy for the acceptance of his (peace be upon him) repentance for what he considered a sin. By "the believers" he meant his people, according to what is narrated from Mujahid. What al-Zamakhshari's words indicate, that the verse is the strongest proof of the impossibility of the seeing, is not hidden in its weakness to one who is well acquainted with what we have mentioned. Some of the researchers relied, for the verse's indication of its possibility, on something other than what preceded as well, namely that He, exalted, attributed the negation of the seeing to the incapacity and weakness of the seer in regard to it, when He said to him, "You will not see Me." Had the seeing of Him, exalted, been impermissible, the answer would have been: "I am not visible." Do you not see that if he had said, "Show me, let me look at Your form and place," it would not have been fitting in the answer to say, "You will not see My form or My place"? Rather, al-Hasan's answer would be: "I am not one with form or place." Some of them said, after explaining that the verse is evidence that the seeing is permissible in general by some of what preceded: "For this reason He, glorified be He, refuted him with His saying, 'You will not see Me,' rather than 'I shall not be seen,' 'I shall not show You Myself,' or 'You will not look at Me,' as an alert that he, peace be upon him, was incapable of seeing Him, exalted, because it depends on a preparation in the seer which had not yet been found in him. For 'I shall not be seen' indicates the impossibility of the seeing absolutely; 'I shall not show You Myself' indicates that the obstacle is from Him, exalted; but in 'You will not look at Me' there is no alert to the intended meaning, because looking does not depend on a preparation, whereas what seeing and perception depend upon is the preparation." Al-Nisaburi explained why the answer "You will not look at Me" does not correspond to "Let me look at You" by saying that Musa (peace be upon him) did not request absolute looking, but only the looking which entails perception, as shown by "Show me." Some defenders of the Mu'tazilah argued: They may say that the request to be shown includes a request for the removal of the impediments to seeing and the bringing into being of what seeing depends upon, because the meaning of that is: "Enable me to see." Enabling is only complete with what has been mentioned, namely removal and bringing into being. The apparent answer to this request would have been: "I shall not enable you to see Me," but it was diverted to "You will not see Me," as an indication of the impossibility of seeing and its non-occurrence in any way, as if it were said: "Your seeing Me is a thing impossible in itself, and My enabling you can only be with what is possible." Had the intent not been this, but rather that you have no capacity to see Me, Musa (peace be upon him) could have said: "O Lord, I know that there is no capacity, but I asked You for enablement, and it includes a request to bring that capacity into being, since it is among what seeing depends upon." In that case the answer would not be beneficial or convincing to Musa (peace be upon him), unlike the first interpretation, so that one would then be the one required. If it is objected: capacity and lack of capacity follow from readiness and lack of readiness, and these are not created, we say: this, despite its extensive discussion and lengthy dispute, entails our aim of the impossibility of seeing, as is not hidden from one who has even slight readiness to understand realities.

It was answered: asking for enablement from something only includes asking for the removal of the impediments on the side of the one asked, on the apparent reading, not absolutely in a way that covers what is on the side of the one asked and what is on the side of the asker. What indicates this is that your saying, "Zayd did not enable me to kill 'Amr," for example, apparently means that he prevented you from killing him while you were prepared for it and the impediments on your side had been removed. So when his Lord spoke to Musa, the longing for seeing was stirred in him, as al-Hasan said: because the enemy of God, Iblis, dug into the earth until he emerged between his feet and whispered to him that his Speaker was a devil. At that point he asked for it, as al-Suddi said (and I seek refuge in God from believing that), and he was distracted from himself and the impediments within it, so the only thing that occurred to his mind was asking the Lord, glorified be He, to remove the impediments on that side. So He, exalted in majesty, alerted him with His saying, "You will not see Me" to the presence of an impediment in him regarding seeing, namely weakness in bearing it, and showed him the weakness of one stronger than him in that by the crumbling of the mountain at His manifestation to it. So the benefit of the istidrak (corrective addition) on this reading is that it becomes clear to him, peace be upon him, that he is too weak to stand before the manifestation of the seeing, while he remains as he is. It is possible that his repentance was after he came to from this heedlessness, and then there is no doubt that the answer "but look at the mountain..." etc. is beneficial and convincing.

Moreover, some of the researchers mentioned that the essence of the discussion at this point is that Musa (peace be upon him) knew by reason the possibility of seeing and its occurrence in this world for whomever God, exalted, wills of His servants. The conditions mentioned for it are not rational conditions but customary ones. He did not know the non-occurrence together with the unchanged state until he heard it from the Lord, the Most High. And there is no deficiency in his station (peace be upon him) in not knowing what was mentioned, for it is among matters dependent on revelation, and ignorance of revealed matters is not counted as a deficiency. It is established that the most knowledgeable of creation absolutely, our Prophet (ﷺ), was asked about matters and said, "I will ask Jibril," and Jibril (peace be upon him) was asked and said, "I will ask the Lord of Might," and the angels have said, "Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us" (2:32). And the verse is not fit to be evidence for the impossibility of seeing as the Mu'tazilah claim; rather its indication of its possibility in general is clearer and clearer, indeed it is manifestly so, not as the opponents say. And what Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said in the explanation of "You will not see Me": "It will never be so" — there is no proof for them in it, for it does not fulfil their aim. Moreover, the perpetuity in it is with respect to the non-change of the state, as indicated by the report previously narrated from him. Likewise what Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, for in it: "O Musa, no one sees Me and lives." Musa said: "Lord, if I see You and then die is dearer to me than that I not see You and then live." What al-Zamakhshari mentioned from the masters, that they said: "He, exalted, is seen without modality," is the well-known view.

Al-Munawi transmitted that Kamal ibn al-Humam was asked about what al-Daraqutni and others narrated from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw my Lord in the best of forms," on the basis of understanding the seeing as occurring while awake. He answered that this is the veil of form. End of quote. This is the formal manifestation (tajalli suwari) which is common among the Sufis, and from it, according to them, is God's manifestation in the tree to Musa (peace be upon him), and His manifestation, exalted, to creation on the day when the shin is uncovered. He, glorified be He, though He manifests in form, is not confined to it: "And God is encompassing from behind them" (85:20). The seeing that Musa (peace be upon him) asked for is other than this seeing. Some mentioned that Musa was seeing God, exalted, except that he did not know that what he saw was He—He. On this pattern is to be understood what came in some disputed narrations: "I saw my Lord in the form of a youth." In some of them there is an addition: "he had two golden sandals." Some people understood the seeing in the narration of al-Daraqutni as dream-seeing. The apparent sense of al-Suyuti's words is that the modality in it does no harm, and this is what I have heard from the shaykhs, may God sanctify their secrets. The matter is disputed. If what the shaykhs said is correct, and what al-Suyuti's words imply, then I—and all praise is due to God, exalted—have seen my Lord in dream three times. The third time was in the year 1246 after the Hijra. I saw Him, exalted in majesty, and He had of light what He has, facing the direction of the east, and He spoke to me with words which I was made to forget when I awoke. And I saw once, in a long dream, as if I were in Paradise before Him, exalted, and between me and Him was a curtain woven with pearls of varying colours. He, glorified be He, commanded that I be taken to the station of 'Isa (peace be upon him), then to the station of Muhammad (ﷺ), and I was taken to them both, and I saw what I saw. To God, exalted, belongs grace and favour.

Among them are those who understood the form as that by which distinction occurs, and the intended meaning is His, exalted, particular essence, sanctified above resemblance to anything else among things, reaching the utmost degrees of perfection. As for the two verses which he mentioned by one of the 'Adliyyah, in this regard it is a moth that gnaws at smooth skin. And the statement is what Taj al-Din al-Subki said about them:

"How strange, a people of wrongdoers who named themselves with justice, while among them, by my life, there is no knowledge.
There came to them from a place they do not perceive the nullification of God's essence together with the denial of attributes.
They named themselves 'Adliyyah; we say, yes—they were just with their Lord, so their folly is enough for them."

Ibn al-Munir said:

[Page 53]

The group who denied the vision of their Lord (with) this (argument) and the promise of God, which He will not break.

They named themselves "the Justice-upholders" (Adliyya). We say: yes, indeed, they upheld justice regarding their Lord, so they consider them foolish.

They described the saved ones (with the description), "No! Indeed, they, if they are not in the Blaze, then they are on the brink."

After all this, we say: people have differed over whether Moses, peace be upon him, saw his Lord after this request or not. Most of the scholars held that he, peace be upon him, did not see Him, neither before the swoon nor after it. The Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn al-Arabi), may God sanctify his secret, said that he saw Him after the swoon, and that the swoon was a death. He, may God sanctify his secret, mentioned that he asked Moses about this, and Moses answered him with what has been mentioned. In my view, the verse is not clearly indicative of this.

[Page 54]

Among those who held the view of seeing after the swoon was al-Qutb al-Razi, in his explanation of a statement of al-Zamakhshari. However, that (view) is on the possibility of interpreting it as complete unveiling (inkishaf), which does not occur except when the soul is annihilated (fani), its gaze cut off from its own existence, let alone the existence of others. For he said: when Moses, peace be upon him, requested this rank of unveiling and expressed himself with "I" (anā), it showed that his gaze was still upon himself. And the soul is not like that except when attached to bodily ties and mixed with material impurities. Therefore, He withheld this rank from him. It was indicated that its withholding was only for the sake of the remaining of "I" and "You" in His saying: "Show me (Yourself), that I may look at You," and "You will not see Me." Then, since He did not intend to deprive him of attaining this rank, despite his readiness and fitness for it, He taught him the way of knowledge (ma'rifa) by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿But look at the mountain.﴾ For the mountain, despite its lack of attachment, when it could not bear a single glance of the glances of manifestation (tajalli), then how could Moses, with his attachment, bear that? So when he grasped the signal, he fell down in a swoon, unconscious, stripped of ties, annihilated from himself. Thus he attained the sought-after goal. When he recovered, he knew that his request for the vision in that state he was in was an impropriety, so he repented of it.

Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani went to the view that he, peace be upon him, truly saw his Lord, glory be to Him, before the swoon, and so he swooned at that, just as the mountain was crushed by the manifestation. He supported this with what Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, who said: "When God the Exalted revealed Himself to Moses, peace be upon him, he could see the crawling of an ant on the rock in a dark night from a distance of ten farsakhs."

And with what he narrated from Abu Ma'shar, who said: "Moses, peace be upon him, remained forty nights, no one looked at him except that he died from the light of the Lord of the worlds."

[Page 55]

This was reconciled with the statement of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: "Indeed God the Exalted gave Moses speech, and gave me the vision, and favored me with the Praised Station (al-maqam al-mahmud) and the Abundant Pool (al-hawd al-mawrud)." The reconciliation: the vision that He gave to our Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, is the vision with steadfastness and survival, without swooning, just as the speech He gave Moses was of that kind. This differs from Moses's vision, peace be upon him, for it was not combined for him with survival. On this basis, the meaning of his statement, peace be upon him, in the hadith about the Dajjal: "None of you will see his Lord until he dies," is that no one sees Him in this world while surviving, and that both are not combined for anyone in this world.

He interpreted the verse with what is not free from obscurity.

Those who hold the view of no vision at all respond to what he mentioned from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and the report of Abu Ma'shar: as for the second, it contains nothing more than proving the radiance of God's light upon the face of Moses, peace be upon him, and this does not prove the vision, since it is possible that a light from Him, exalted, shines upon his face, peace be upon him, without vision, for there is no necessary link between vision and the shining of light. As for the first, it is not an explicit text on the establishment of the sought vision for him, peace be upon him, because it is, as many have said, an expression for the essential manifestation (al-tajalli al-dhati), while God the Exalted has various other manifestations. Perhaps the manifestation indicated by the hadith, assuming its authenticity, is one of them. This may be definitively established, for He, glory be to Him, manifested to him, peace be upon him, through His speech, His choosing, and His nearness to him in the special manner befitting Him, the Exalted. It is not far that this may be a cause for that seeing. And this is better than what has been said: that the lam in "li-Musa" is for causation, and the object of "tajalla" is omitted, meaning: when God the Exalted manifested to the mountain for the sake of guiding Moses, he, peace be upon him, saw by means of the radiance of some of His lights upon him at the time of the manifestation to the mountain what he saw.

A verse (of poetry):
It spread the scent of musk, the belly of Nu'man,
when Zaynab walked by in a group of modest women.

So the truth that must not be avoided is that Moses, peace be upon him, did not attain what he asked for in this appointment. What I am certain of is that he attained the station of nearness through supererogatory and obligatory acts, which the Sufis mention, may God the Exalted sanctify their secrets, in the sense they mention, however it may be.

[Page 56]

God forbid that I should prefer any of the saints (awliya') of this nation, even if they are (the best) of them, over any of the prophets of the Children of Israel, let alone their messengers, absolutely, let alone the Messengers of Firm Resolve among them.

* * *

(Some of the gnostics (arifin) mentioned, by way of allusion (ishara), concerning these verses) that God the Exalted promised Moses, peace be upon him, thirty nights for the purpose of freeing himself from the veil of actions, attributes, and essence, each ten (nights) for freeing himself from one veil. Ten was chosen because it is a complete number, as the discussion of it has already passed at His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿These are ten complete.﴾ But a remnant of it remained from which he had not been freed. The use of the miswak in the thirty, which some reports spoke of, is an allusion to that. So he added ten more to the thirty, to free himself from that remnant. It came that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to draw near to Him, glory be to Him, by what one draws near by in thirty (nights), and the Torah was revealed to him in the ten that were added to them, to complete forty. This is an indication that he reached complete essential witnessing (shuhud dhati) in the thirty through traveling to God the Exalted, and nothing remained of him, but he was completely annihilated (fana'). In the fourth ten, his traveling was in God the Exalted until he was granted survival (baqa') after annihilation through recovery. They said: on this basis, the request for vision should have been in the thirty, and the recovery after them. The speaking was in the station of the manifestation of attributes, and the question was about his excessive longing, peace be upon him, for witnessing the Essence in the station of the annihilation of attributes with the remaining of a remnant. And ﴿You will not see Me﴾ is an indication of the impossibility of duality and the survival of selfhood (inniyya) in the station of contemplation. This is the meaning of the saying of the one who said: "I saw my Lord by the eye of my Lord." And His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿But look at the mountain﴾ is an indication of the mountain of existence, i.e., look at the mountain of your existence. ﴿If it remains in its place, then you will see Me.﴾ This is of the kind of suspending (ta'liq) on the impossible according to him.

﴿When His Lord manifested to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust.﴾ That is, dissolved, having no existence.

﴿And Moses fell down﴾ from the degree of ecstasy (wajd).

﴿in a swoon﴾ That is, annihilated.

﴿When he recovered﴾ through the bestowed existence of Truth (al-wujud al-mawhub al-haqqani), ﴿he said: Glory be to You﴾ that You should be seen by other than You.

﴿I repent to You﴾ from the sin of the remnant, or "I return to You" according to knowledge and witnessing, since there is no existence besides You.

﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾ according to rank, that is: I am in the first row of the rows of the ranks of spirits, which is the station of the people of unity (ahl al-wahda). It may be said: Moses here is an allusion to the Moses of the spirit (Musa al-ruh), who trained himself for forty nights so that springs of wisdom might appear from him, and said to his brother Aaron, the heart: ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ from the human attributes.

﴿And reform﴾ their relations according to the Shari'a and the rule of the path.

﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ from the natural powers. When the spirit attained the carpet of nearness after that spiritual discipline, and the cups of love followed one another upon it in the gardens of intimacy, the nightingale of his tongue sang in the cage of the mouth of his existence, and he said: ﴿My Lord, show me (Yourself), that I may look at You.﴾ He was told: far-fetched is that! Where is the Pleiades from the hand of the one who reaches for it? You are still in the distance of duality and the veil of the mountain of egoism. If you wish that, then abandon yourself and come to Me.

Keep away from the court of union, far-fetched it was not;
and here you are alive, if you are truthful, die.
It is love: if you do not fulfill, you do not fulfill a purpose
of love, so choose that or leave my passion.

So annihilation became easy for him in the pursuit of seeing the Beloved, and every thing did not seem precious to him, for he saw the honor of the Sought One.

And he called out:
I said to her: my soul is with you, and its taking
is to you; and who am I to be in your grip?
I am not the one who is faithful to passion,
and faithfulness is my nature, and my disposition refuses anything else.

So he gave up his existence and bestowed his being, and His Lord manifested to the mountain of his egoism, then He favored him with His vision. What happened happened, and the earth shone

[Page 57]

with the light of its Lord, and the lamp went out when the morning rose, and the nightingale of intimacy sang in the gardens of holiness with a melody.

I was alone with the Beloved, and between us
was a secret more delicate than the breeze when it blows.
He permitted my gaze a glance I had hoped for,
so I became known, and I had been unknown.

So I was dazzled between His beauty and His majesty,
and the tongue of state (lisan al-hal) became eloquent on my behalf.

This discussion of the vision is long, and the science of kalam has undertaken to verify it in the most complete manner. What is incumbent upon us is only: the unveiling of the cover from what relates to the verse. What we believe is that we have discharged the duty, and it suffices from the necklace what surrounds the neck. And God the Exalted is the guide to the straight path.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 144:**

﴿He said, "O Musa..."﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence that begins a new point) brought to console him (peace be upon him) for not being granted what he asked for, as wisdom required. It is as if it were said: "If I have withheld vision from you, I have given you great blessings, so seize them and persevere in thanking Me for them." ﴿Indeed, I have chosen you﴾, that is, I have selected you. It is from *iftiʿal* (a derived verbal form) of *safwah* (choice, purity), meaning selection. The emphasis is to draw attention to the importance of the news for the people of your time. This is like His, glorified be He, saying about the Children of Israel, favouring them over the peoples of their own time: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. ﴿With My messages﴾, that is, with the books of the Tawrah (Torah). Ahl al-Hijaz and Ruh read it as (*bi-risalati*, "with My message," in the singular).

﴿And with My speech﴾, that is, by My speaking to you directly, without an intermediary. Or the word "speech" is understood with an omitted modifier, meaning by making My speech heard. The meaning is that I favoured you with the combination of these two matters. Hence Harun (peace be upon him) is not an objection, since he was not a *kalim* (one who was spoken to directly by God), and furthermore his prophethood was also subordinate, and he was commanded to follow Musa (peace be upon him). Likewise the seventy who were with him (peace be upon him) at this appointed time, according to one opinion, are not an objection, because although they heard the address, they had no share in the message, and furthermore the one addressed in the speech was Musa (peace be upon him) alone, not them. By restricting the favour to "the people," as you have understood, the Prophet (ﷺ) is excluded. Therefore it is not objectionable that the combination of prophethood and direct speech was found for him (ﷺ) as well, according to the correct view. Moreover, even if we say that direct speech was specific to him (peace be upon him) among the prophets, it does not follow that he is preferred over others in every respect, such as our Prophet (ﷺ), since what is found in the lesser may not be found in the greater. Direct speech was a cause of honour according to the apparent custom. They have said: "How far apart are the one whom the king has taken for himself as a beloved and brought near to him by his kindness, and the one for whom a veil is set up, and between him and the goal stand gatekeepers and deputies!" Furthermore, whoever has tasted the flavour of love, even by the tip of the tongue, knows what there is in the beloved speaking directly, without an intermediary, of great gentleness and immense kindness. His speech, exalted be His majesty, to Musa (peace be upon him) at that appointed time was abundant, as the reports indicate, and you have already had what points to its quantity from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi (*Nawadir al-Usul*) and al-Bayhaqi related through the route of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed God, exalted be His majesty, conversed secretly with Musa (peace be upon him) with one hundred and forty thousand words in three days. When he heard the speech of the sons of Adam, he hated them because of what fell upon his ears from the speech of the Lord, mighty and majestic. Among what He conversed with him was that He said: 'O Musa, the ostentatious have not pretended by the likeness of renunciation of this world, nor have those who seek nearness to Me drawn near by the likeness of scrupulousness regarding what I have forbidden them, nor have the worshippers worshipped by the likeness of weeping out of My fear.' Musa said: 'O Lord, and God of all creation, O Master of the Day of Judgement, O Possessor of majesty and honour, what have You prepared for them and what have You recompensed them?'"
Page 56
He said: "As for those who renounce the world, I shall permit them My Paradise, so that they may dwell in it wherever they wish. As for those scrupulous regarding what I have forbidden them, when the Day of Resurrection comes, no servant will remain except that I call him to account and examine what is in his hands, except the scrupulous; for I shall honour them, ennoble them and admit them into Paradise without reckoning. As for those who weep out of My fear, they shall have the Highest Companionship (*al-Rafiq al-Aʿla*), in which no one else shares."

Adam ibn Abi Iyas related in *Kitab al-ʿIlm*, from Ibn Masʿud, who said: When God brought Musa near as one with whom He conversed secretly, he saw under the shade of the Throne a man, and he envied him for his station. He asked about him, but He did not tell him his name, but informed him of his knowledge, and said: "This is a man who did not envy people for what God gave them of His bounty, was dutiful to his parents, and did not walk about with tale-bearing." Then God said: "O Musa, what have you come seeking?" He said: "I have come seeking guidance, O Lord." He said: "You have found it, O Musa." He said: "My Lord, forgive me for what has passed of my sins, what remains, what lies between, and what You know of me better than I do. I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of my soul and the evil of my deeds." It was said to him: "You have been sufficed, O Musa." He said: "My Lord, which deed is most beloved to You that I should do?" He said: "Remember Me, O Musa." He said: "My Lord, which of Your servants is most pious?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "My Lord, which of Your servants is richest?" He said: "The one who is content with what is given to him." He said: "My Lord, which of Your servants is most excellent?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow his desire." He said: "My Lord, which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people to his own knowledge, perhaps he will hear a word that guides him to guidance or turns him back from ruin." He said: "My Lord, which of Your servants is most beloved to You in deed?" He said: "The one whose tongue does not lie, whose private parts do not commit fornication, and whose heart does not transgress." He said: "My Lord, then which is next after this?" He said: "A believing heart with good character." He said: "My Lord, which of Your servants is most hateful to You?" He said: "A disbelieving heart with bad character." He said: "My Lord, then which is next after this?" He said: "A corpse at night, idle by day."

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, Abu Yaʿla, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, "from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: Musa said: 'O Lord, teach me something by which I may remember You and call upon You.' He said: 'Say, O Musa: There is no god but God.' He said: 'My Lord, all Your servants say this.' He said: 'Say: There is no god but God.' He said: 'There is no god but You, O Lord, but I want something that is specific to me.' He said: 'O Musa, if the seven heavens and whoever inhabits them besides Me, and the seven earths, were placed in one pan of a scale, and there is no god but God in the other pan, the latter would outweigh them: there is no god but God.'"

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When Musa ascended Mount Sinai, the Compeller saw on his finger a ring, and said: "Is there written on it anything of My names or My speech?" He said: "No." He said: "Then write on it: Every term has a Book."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-ʿAla' ibn Kathir, who said: God, exalted be He, said: "O Musa, do you know why I spoke to you?" He said: "No, O Lord." He said: "Because I have not created a creature that humbled itself to Me as you have humbled yourself."

The storytellers have many reports, fabricated, concerning the questions Musa (peace be upon him) asked his Lord and His answers, exalted be His majesty. It is not fitting for a Muslim to accept them as true.

﴿So take what I have given you﴾, that is, what I have given you of the honour of being chosen.

﴿And be among the thankful﴾, that is, be counted among them, so that you have a complete share among them. Its essence: be eloquent in gratitude, for what I have bestowed upon you is among the greatest of blessings.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ka'b that he said: Musa (peace be upon him) said: "O Lord, guide me to a deed which, if I do it, will be a thanks to You for what You have bestowed upon me." He said: "O Musa, say: There is no god but God alone, without partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is powerful over all things."

He said: It seems Musa wanted a deed more wearying to his body than what he had been commanded, so He said to him: "O Musa, if the seven heavens..." The report... and it has the same meaning as the report of Abu Saʿid.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 145 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything﴾ that they need of the lawful and the unlawful, and of the good and the bad, as al-Razi and others said, and as al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Thaqafi, who said: Qays ibn Kharasha and Ka'b al-Ahbar travelled together, and when they reached Siffin, Ka'b stopped, looked for a while, and then said: "Something will be shed in this place of the blood of the Muslims, such as will not be shed in any other spot on earth." Qays said: "How would you know? This is from the unseen, which Allah the Exalted has kept to Himself." Ka'b said: "There is not a handspan of earth but it is written in the Torah, which Allah the Exalted sent down to Musa, what will happen on it and what will come out of it until the Day of Resurrection." This indicates that "everything" is more general than what has been mentioned, and perhaps the mention of that is by way of symbolism, as we claim in the Qur'an.

﴿an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the prepositional phrase, i.e., We wrote for him all of the admonitions and the detailed explanation of the rulings. This is the view of more than one of the grammarians, and it implies that (min) is extra (mazidah), not partitive. Regarding its being extra in affirmative speech, there is discussion. It was said: it was not made inceptive (ibtida'iyyah) as a circumstantial clause (hal) of (mau'izatan), and (mau'izatan) is a direct object, because that has no great meaning. Nor was (mau'izatan) made an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), even though it fulfils its conditions, because the apparent reading is that (tafsilan) is coordinated with (mau'izatan). And it is clear that there is no sense in your saying: "We wrote for him of every thing for the detailing of every thing." As for making it a coordination with the position of the prepositional phrase, it is far-fetched both in wording and meaning.

Al-Tibi chose this coordination, and that (min) is partitive, and (mau'izatan) alone is a substitute. The meaning: We wrote some of everything on the tablets, such as surahs and verses and other things, as an admonition; and We wrote in them the detailed explanation of everything they need of the lawful and the unlawful and the like. In this, the general and the detailed are specific to the admonition, to indicate that concern with this is more intense and care for it more complete. Because it is so, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was frequently praised as "a bringer of good news and a warner." It also indicates that admonition is something to which one must return in every matter mentioned in it. Do you not see that most of the revealed endings and refutations follow this pattern, such as: "Will you not fear Allah? — Will you not remember?" And consider how Surat al-Rahman repeats what it repeats; this is so that the listener may renew remembrance and admonition, and that alertness may be renewed and awakened. You know that the distance we have pointed to remains as it is.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿for everything﴾ are either related to what is before it or to an elided element, as al-Samin said; it is in the position of an attribute of it. The number of the tablets is disputed, as is their substance, their size and their writer. It was said: they were ten tablets. It was also said: two tablets. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible in the language to call two tablets "tablets" (alwah). It was said that they were of green emerald; the Lord, exalted is He, commanded Jibril, peace be upon him, and he brought them from Aden, and this is reported from Mujahid. Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "I was told that the tablets were of chrysolite (zabarjad)." And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "They used to say: they were of ruby (yaqut)." I say: they were of emerald.

Ibn Abi Hatim and others reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "The tablets that were sent down to Musa were of the lote tree of Paradise; the length of each tablet was twelve cubits."

And from al-Hasan: they were of wood that descended from the heaven, and the length of each was ten cubits. It was also said: Allah the Exalted commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to cut them from a hard rock which He softened for him; he cut it with his hand and shaped it with his fingers. It is not hidden that such matters need a sound transmission; otherwise silence is better, since the verse contains nothing indicating it. My preferred view is that they were of lote wood, if the chain to the golden tie (silsilat al-dhahab) is sound. The well-known report from Ibn Jurayj is that their writer was Jibril, peace be upon him, who wrote them with the pen with which he wrote the Reminder.

What is related from Ali, may Allah honour his face, and from Mujahid, Ata', Ikrimah, and a great many others, is that Allah the Exalted wrote them with His own hand. It has also come that they were written while Musa, peace be upon him, heard the scratching (sarif) of the pens with which they were written. This is what is transmitted from the Amir, may Allah honour his face. And it came from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "Allah created Adam with His hand, created the Garden of Eden with His hand, and wrote the Torah with His hand; then
صفحة 58
He said to things: 'Be,' and they were." Abd ibn Humayd reported from Wardan ibn Khalid, who said: "Allah created Adam with His hand, created Jibril with His hand, created the pen with His hand, created His Throne with His hand, wrote the Book which is with Him, which none other than Him beholds, with His hand, and wrote the Torah with His hand." All of this is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters. In some reports, they were written before the appointed time (miqat), and sent down, as it is said, and they were seventy camel-loads, of which one part is read in a year; only four persons read them: Musa, Yusha', Uzayr and Isa, peace be upon them all. Among what was written in them, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, is the mention of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the mention of his community, what has been stored up for them with Him, what He made easy for them in their religion, and what He widened for them in what He made lawful; so much so that it is related that Musa, peace be upon him, marvelled at the good that Allah gave Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his community, and wished to be among them.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah and others reported from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: "Among what Allah the Exalted gave Musa in the tablets was: 'O Musa, do not associate anything with Me, for the word has come from Me that the fire will surely strike the faces of the polytheists. Be grateful to Me and to your parents, and I will suffice you against the calamities, and I will lengthen your life, and give you a good life, and turn you to something better than it. Do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, lest the earth become narrow for you despite its breadth, and the heaven by its horizons, and you incur My wrath and the fire. Do not swear by My name falsely or sinfully, for I do not purify or sanctify whoever does not glorify Me and magnify My names. Do not envy people for what I have given them of My bounty, and do not begrudge them My blessing and My provision, for the envier is an enemy of My blessing, a rejecter of My decree, and displeased with My division which I divide among My servants; whoever is like that, I am not from him and he is not from Me. Do not bear witness to what your hearing has not heard, your mind has not retained, and your heart has not held firmly to; for I will stand those who bear witnesses before their testimonies on the Day of Resurrection, then I will question them about them with a pressing question. Do not commit adultery or steal, and do not commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour, lest I veil My face from you and the gates of heaven be shut to you. Love for people what you love for yourself. Do not slaughter for other than Me, for I accept of offerings only what is dedicated to My name and is sincere for My face. Devote yourself to Me on the day of Saturday, and empty yourself and all your household for Me.'" Then the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Allah the Exalted made Saturday a festival for Musa, peace be upon him, and chose for us Friday and made it a festival."

﴿So take them with strength﴾ i.e., with earnestness and resolve. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the clause is, by the elision of a verb of saying, coordinated with "We wrote" (kataba-na); and the elision of the verb of saying is frequent and regular. The motive for this estimate, as the second scholar (al-Allamah al-Thani) said, is to observe the correspondence with "We wrote for him," since it came in the third person; had its counterpart been "We wrote for you," no estimate would be needed. As for the objection regarding the coordination of an imperative with informative clauses, there is no harm in it, since it is permissible when introduced by fa'.

It was said: it is a substitute for His words, glorified is He: ﴿take what I have given you﴾. This was judged weak, because it involves separation by a foreign element, namely the clause "We wrote," coordinated with the clause "He said," and it disrupts the arrangement. The object pronoun refers either to the tablets or to "everything," since it carries the sense of "things," and generality does not suffice for the return of a plural pronoun without interpreting it as plural. It was permitted that it refers to the Torah by contextual indication. The one who holds the substitution view took it as referring to the messages. The prepositional phrase is related to an elided element and stands as a circumstantial clause of the subject, i.e., "combined with strength"; it was permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of the object, i.e., "its strength combined with the strength of its proofs," but the first is clearer; and that it be an attribute of an absolute object, i.e., "taking with strength."

﴿And command your people to take the best of them﴾ i.e., its best. The preposition (ba') is then extra, as in his saying:

*Black-eyed ones who do not recite with surahs*

It is also possible that the preposition is original, which is the apparent reading. In that case it is either related to "yakhudhu" (they take) by implying the sense of "they act," or it is from taking in the sense of conduct, whence "he took their course" meaning he walked their way and adopted their characteristics, as we say; or it is related to an elided element that stands as a circumstantial clause, and the object of "yakhudhu" is elided, i.e., "themselves," as it was said. The apparent reading is that it is in the jussive after the imperative, so it requires interpretation, since their being commanded does not necessarily mean their taking; i.e., if you command them and Allah the Exalted grants them success, they will take. It was said: by estimating the imperative lam in it, on the basis that this is permissible after a verb of saying or what has its meaning, as here. The annexation of the superlative here, according to more than one scholar, is like its annexation in "Zayd is the best of people"; and on the well-known view it is a true annexation, in the sense of "of" (lam); it was said that it is a verbal annexation, and the practice of some seems to imply that it is in the sense of "in," but that is not so. The meaning is "with the best of the parts that are in it," and the meaning of its being best is that it comprises the best, such as patience, since it is better than retaliation. That is: command them to take it in the manner of recommendation and urging toward the more excellent, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and follow the best of what has been sent down to you﴾.
