Or the meaning is "with the best of its rulings," and what is meant by this is the obligatory acts, for they are better than the recommended and permissible acts; or they together with the recommended acts, as it was said, for they are better than the permissible acts.

It was also said: "the best" here means the absolutely superlative in goodness, not by annexation, and it is what is commanded, whose opposite is what is forbidden. The words of al-Zajjaj point to this, where he said: "They were commanded with good and forbidden from evil, and they knew what was theirs and what was against them, so it was said: ﴿And command your people...﴾ etc." Do likewise with its counterpart in their saying: "Summer is hotter than winter," for it means: summer in its heat is more intense than winter in its cold, since preferring the heat of summer over the heat of winter is undoubtedly not intended. Here it may be said: what is commanded is more eloquent in goodness than what is forbidden in ugliness.

The Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 145 (part 2 of 2):

And the detail of what is at issue here, as mentioned by al-Damamini (d. 827 AH) in his gloss on al-Misbah, and as quoted from him by al-Shihab, is that *af'al* (the elative form, used for comparison of superiority) has four states.

The first, which is the original state, is that it indicates three matters. The first is that the one to whom it applies is characterized by the action from which it is derived, and for this reason it is a descriptive term (wasf). The second is a shared participation (musharaka) with a companion (masḥūba) in that attribute. The third is an excess (maziyya) attributed (marṣūfa) over a companion in it. By each of these two matters it is distinguished from other descriptive terms.

The second state is that it is stripped of what distinguishes it among descriptive terms, and it is left bare for the descriptive meaning.

The third state is that its three meanings remain upon it, but the restriction of the second meaning is removed and replaced by another restriction. This is because the second meaning, which is participation, was restricted by that attribute which is the first meaning, so it becomes restricted by the excess which is the third meaning. Do you not see that the meaning in the saying "honey is sweeter than vinegar" is that honey has sweetness, that this sweetness has an excess, and that the excess of the sweetness of honey is greater than the excess of the sourness of vinegar? Ibn Hisham said this in his *Hawashi al-Tashil*, and it is most original.

The fourth state is that the second meaning, which is participation, is removed, and the third meaning, which is that the excess is over its companion, is restricted. Thus it indicates the attribution of the action and an excess that is unrestricted, not restricted. This is as in: "Yusuf is the best of his brothers." End of quotation.

There is no doubt that the commanded and the forbidden do not share the goodness intended here, even if goodness in general is shared, as is found in *al-Bahr*. The commanded is better in terms of compliance and the reward that follows from it, while the forbidden is good in terms of pleasure and desire.

Qutrub said, as quoted from him by Muhyi al-Sunnah, the meaning is: "they should take the good of them, and all of them are good." This clearly places *af'al* in the second state. It has also been said that the meaning is: "they should take them, and (it is) better in connection." It has no basis in acceptance.

Al-Jubba'i said: the intended meaning is that they should take the abrogating (*nasikh*) and not the abrogated (*mansukh*). It has also been said that taking the best means that a word which has two or more meanings should be understood in the most likely of its possible senses in accordance with the truth and nearest to correctness. The taking should not be understood as beginning (shuru'), as in your saying "Zayd began (akhadha) speaking," meaning he began to speak. The "best" is regarding the creeds. The meaning would then be that He commanded them to begin by adorning themselves with the correct creeds, which, because they are the roots of religion and the validity of deeds depends on them, are better than other branches of religion. This includes commanding them to all that is in them, as is not hidden. However, taking in the sense intended from verbs of beginning is not the usual usage in their speech, and there is a remoteness in it.

Similar to this is that the pronoun in *ahsanihā* refers to "strength" (quwwa), with the meaning "command them to take them with the best strength and resolve." Then it would be a command from Him, glorified is He, that He command them to take them, just as His Lord commanded him. However, He, exalted is He, in His command dispensed with mentioning "the best" through what the tanwin points to. This is contrary to what is transmitted and what comes to mind, and moreover we have not found in their speech "best strength."

The object of *ya'khudhū* is omitted, as in some of the previous possibilities, but there is a clear difference between what is here and what is there.

﴿I shall show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾. This is an affirmation of the command to the people to take the best, and an incitement to it in the manner of a threat and intimidation, based on what is narrated from Qatada and Atiyya al-Awfi, that by "the abode of the defiantly disobedient" is meant the abode of Pharaoh and his people in Egypt. (The verb) *ra'a* is taken as visual (basariyya), and it is permitted that it be cognitive (ilmiyya), with the third object omitted, meaning: "I shall show you it in ruins, upon its foundations, so that you may take warning and strive, and not be negligent in complying with the command, and not do the deeds of its people, so that what befell them may befall you." In this there is an *iltifat* (shift) from the third person (ghayba) to the second person (khitab). What makes this placement good is the intent of emphasis in urging, and the placement of seeing in the position of taking warning. Also, the cause is put in the place of the effect for emphasis, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals﴾. In placing "the abode of the defiantly disobedient" in the position of "the land of Egypt" there is an indication of causation and an alert that they should guard themselves and not follow their practice of defiance. The *sin* (of *sa-*) is for the future, because that is before the return to Egypt, as in *al-Kashshaf*.

Al-Kalbi said: the intended meaning of "the abode of the defiantly disobedient" is the dwellings of 'Ad, Thamud, and the generations who perished. It is narrated from al-Hasan and Ata' that by it is meant Hell. In any case, the discourse follows the first approach too. It is also possible that it follows the approach of promise and encouragement, based on what is narrated from Qatada, also, that by "the abode of the defiantly disobedient" is meant the land of the tyrants and the giants in Syria, for it is among what was permitted to the Children of Israel and prescribed for them, as His saying, exalted and majestic is He, indicates: ﴿O my people, enter the holy land which God has prescribed for you﴾. The meaning of *ira'a* (showing) here is causing to enter by way of inheritance. This is supported by the reading of some: "*sa-ūrithukum*" (I shall make you inherit). It is also permitted in this case that by "the abode" is meant Egypt. In the discourse, with this reading and with the intent of the land of Egypt by "the abode," there is *taghlib* (a figure in which one term covers another), because the meaning is: "I shall make you and your people inherit the land of Egypt." This does not hold for it if by "the abode" is meant the land of the tyrants, based on the view that Musa, peace be upon him, did not enter it, and that he entered it with the people only after his death, peace be upon him. It holds on the view that Musa, peace be upon him, entered it with Yusha' as his vanguard. Taghlib is also permitted on the familiar reading.

Al-Hasan read: "*sa-ūriykum*" with a damma on the hamza, a silent waw, and a light kasra on the ra', and this is a widespread dialect in the Hijaz. The meaning is: "I shall make that clear to you and illuminate it," taken from *awraytu al-zanda* (I struck the flint so that it produced fire). Ibn Jinni, in explaining this reading, chose, and it is perhaps the most apparent, that it is by *ishba'* (vowel lengthening), as in the verse:

*"Wherever they went, approach and look."*

[Page 60]

﴿سَأصْرِفُ عَنْ آياتِيَ الَّذِينَ يَتَكَبَّرُونَ في الأرْضِ﴾ *(I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth)*. This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that continues the preceding discourse), following what Shaykh al-Islam said. It serves to warn them against arrogance, which makes one unable to reflect upon the signs written on the tablets of the Torah, which contain admonitions and rulings, or upon what encompasses them and other signs of creation, among which is what they were promised to be shown of the abode of the wicked. The meaning of turning them away from these signs is preventing them, through sealing (*tab'*) upon their hearts, so that they scarcely reflect upon them or take lessons from them, because of their persistence in the arrogance and haughtiness they are upon. This is like His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿فَلَمّا زاغُوا أزاغَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ *(So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate)*. That is: I will seal the hearts of those who regard themselves as great, and who see that they have elevation in the lower world and superiority over creation, so they do not benefit from My signs nor seize the benefits of their effects. So do not follow their path, lest you become like them.

It has also been said that this is an answer to an implied question arising from the promise of entering the land of the tyrants and the giants, with the meaning of the signs being what has been recited just now and its like, and turning them away from these being the removal of the arrogant from the position of opposing and obstructing them, through the occurrence of their reports and the manifestation of their rulings and effects, by destroying them at the hand of Musa or Yusha', peace be upon them both. It is as if it were said: How do you see their abode while they are in it? So it was said to them: I will destroy them. The shift to "turning away" was made so that they would increase in confidence in the signs and in tranquility through them. According to these two opinions, the discourse is with Musa, peace be upon him, and the verse is connected either to His saying ﴿سَأُرِيكُمْ﴾ *(I will show you)* or to what precedes it, in the manner indicated just now. Al-Tibi (al-Ṭībī) permitted its connection to His, exalted be He, saying: (﴿وأْمُرْ﴾ *(and enjoin)*) and so on, in the sense of the command being thus. As for the will, I will turn away from taking My signs those of the sealed nature and wretchedness.

It has also been said that the discourse is with the disbelievers of Makkah, and the verse is connected to His, exalted be His majesty, saying: ﴿أوَلَمْ يَهْدِ لِلَّذِينَ يَرِثُونَ الأرْضَ مِن بَعْدِ أهْلِها﴾ *(Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people…)* and so on. The mention of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, and Fir'awn is for taking lessons, that is: I will turn away the arrogant from nullifying the signs, however hard they strive, as Fir'awn did, and his deed returned upon him in the opposite of what he intended. It has also been said that, if the discourse is with the saying of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, the verse is an interjection in the midst of what is brought for taking lessons, and it is due to the one who relates a story to him that he indicate its place whenever he finds an opportunity to do so. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is to show concern for what is placed first and to create anticipation for what is postponed, though the postponed element has a certain length, which placing it earlier would disrupt the harmonious correspondence of the parts of the sublime composition. Some of our scholars cited this verse as evidence that Allah, exalted be He, may prevent [people] from faith and hinder them from it. This is evident if the turning away is taken to mean preventing from faith, but it is not definite, as you have come to know. The Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilites) have engaged in interpreting it, and they explained it in various ways, which al-Tabarsi (al-Ṭabarsī) mentioned.

﴿بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ﴾ *(without right)*: it is either an adjunct (*silah*, a complement of the verb) to "arrogance," meaning they are arrogant and exalt themselves with what is not true, namely their false religion and their excessive wrongdoing; or it is connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from its subject, meaning: they are arrogant while involved in what is not right and its outcome, they are arrogant without being entitled, because arrogance that is rightful belongs only to Allah, exalted be He, as in the sacred hadith (ḥadīth qudsī) which Abu Dawud related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Pride is My cloak and greatness is My garment; whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will cast him into the Fire."

It has also been said that the meaning is that they are arrogant toward one who is not arrogant, such as the prophets, peace be upon them, because that is what is "without right." As for being arrogant toward one who is arrogant, it is a charity. You know that this is the form of arrogance and not arrogance in reality, so perhaps the intent of this speaker is that the restriction with what was mentioned is to show that they are arrogant in reality.

﴿وإنْ يَرَوْا كُلَّ آيَةٍ لا يُؤْمِنُوا بِها﴾ *(And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it)*: it is conjoined to "they are arrogant," sharing with it the same status within the relative clause (*silah*). The word "sign" here may mean a station (*manzilah*), so seeing it means witnessing it and perceiving it by hearing it; or it may encompass it and other miracles, so seeing them means witnessing in general, comprising hearing and sight. Some explained the signs mentioned earlier as those set up in the horizons and in the souls, and the sign here is either the station or the miracle, lest the circularity (*dawr*) be assumed, as has been said; so let this be understood. It was also permitted that it be conjoined to "I will turn away," as a causal clause (*li-l-ta'līl*), in the manner of His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿ولَقَدْ آتَيْنا داوُدَ وسُلَيْمانَ عِلْمًا وقالا الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ *(And We gave David and Solomon knowledge, and they said, "All praise is for Allah")*, according to the view of the author of al-Miftah. In any case, the meaning is the generality of negation, not the negation of generality; that is: they disbelieved in every single sign.

﴿وإنْ يَرَوْا سَبِيلَ الرُّشْدِ﴾ *(And if they see the way of right guidance)*: that is, the path of guidance and rectitude.

﴿لا يَتَّخِذُوهُ سَبِيلا﴾ *(They will not take it as a way)*: that is, they do not turn toward it nor follow it at all, because Satanic influence (*shaṭnah*) has taken hold of them.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (الرَّشَدِ) *(al-rashad)* with two fatḥahs, and it was read (الرَّشادِ) *(al-rashād)*; all three vowelings are dialects, as are (السَّقَمِ) and (السُّقْمِ) and (السَّقامِ). Abu 'Amr, as al-Jubba'i said, distinguished between *al-rushd* (with a ḍammah) as righteousness in a matter, and *al-rashad* (with a fatḥah) as uprightness in religion; but the well-known view is that there is no distinction.

﴿وإنْ يَرَوْا سَبِيلَ الغَيِّ﴾ *(And if they see the way of error)*: that is, the path of misguidance.

﴿يَتَّخِذُوهُ سَبِيلا﴾ *(They will take it as a way)*: that is, they choose it for themselves as a continuous course, from which they scarcely turn aside, because it agrees with their desires and leads them to their appetites.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ *(That)*: that is, the aforementioned arrogance, not believing in any of the signs, their turning away from the path of guidance and their complete devotion to the path of error, is established; ﴿بِأنَّهُمْ﴾ *(because they)*: that is, because ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا﴾ *(denied Our signs)*, which indicate the falsity of the vices they are characterized by and the truth of their opposites.

﴿وكانُوا عَنْها غافِلِينَ﴾ *(And they were heedless of them)*: not regarding them as significant; so they do not reflect upon them, for otherwise they would not have done what they did of falsehoods. Many have permitted that this refers to the turning away, and what is at issue there is resolved with minimal care, as is not hidden from one whom care has extended its means to. In any case, the demonstrative is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that occupies the predicate (*khabar*) about it, as we have indicated.

It has also been said that the place of the demonstrative is the accusative, as an absolute object (*maṣdar*), meaning: I will turn them away with that turning because of their denial of Our signs and their heedlessness of them. There is no obstacle to the governing element being "I will turn away" placed before it, because the intervening element is not foreign.

﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾. That is, their meeting the Hereafter abode. This is taken as an idafa (genitive construction) of the verbal noun (masdar) to its object, with the agent omitted. Or it means their meeting what Allah the Exalted promised in the Hereafter of recompense. Here the idafa is to a time/place adverb (zarf) in a broadened sense (tawassu'). The object is understood, as is the agent. The relative clause (al-mawsul) has the position of a nominative in both interpretations, as the subject (mubtada'). His saying, the Exalted, ﴿their deeds have come to nothing﴾ is its predicate. That is: the invalidity of the deeds they did has become apparent, such as maintaining family ties and relieving the distressed, after they had been hoped to benefit them on the assumption of their faith in them. The upshot is that they gain no benefit from their deeds. Otherwise, these are accidents (a'rad) which do not literally come to nothing.

﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ That is: they will not be recompensed on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿except for what they used to do﴾. That is: except the recompense for what they persisted in doing of disbelief and sins. The omission of this genitive term (mudaf) is due to the obvious fact that what is recompensed is not the deed itself. It was said: their deeds will appear in the forms of what they are recompensed with, so there is no need for the supposition. This sentence is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf). It was said: it is the predicate. The preceding sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with qad implied.

The Ash'ariyya argued, for what was said, with this verse against the view of Abu Hashim that one who abandons an obligatory duty deserves punishment even if the opposite act did not proceed from him, because it indicates that there is no recompense except for an action, and abandoning an obligatory duty is not an action.

Abu Hashim replied that he does not call that punishment a recompense. It was rejected: recompense (jaza') is that which suffices (yujzi), that is, it is sufficient in preventing what is forbidden and in urging what is commanded. Punishment for abandoning an obligatory duty is sufficient for deterring from that abandonment, so it is a recompense.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 148:**

﴿The people of Musa took, after him﴾, i.e., after his departure to the mountain to commune with his Lord, glorified is He: ﴿from their ornaments﴾. *Hali* is the plural of *hilyy*, like *thady* and *thudiyy*, and it denotes what is made for adornment and is decorated with, of gold and silver. The prepositional phrase (*al-jarr wa-al-majrur*) is connected to *ittakhadha* ("took"), as in *min ba'dihi* ("after him"), *min qablihi* ("before him"). There is no problem in this, since the two prepositions differ in meaning: the first is for the starting point (*ibtida'*) and the second is for partitive meaning (*tab'id*). It has also been said that it is for the starting point too, and its connection to the verb comes after the connection of the first preposition to it and its being considered together with it. It has also been said: the second prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to what follows it, since if it had come after, it would have been a qualifier (*sifa*) of it. The attribution of the ornaments to the pronoun of the people is for the slightest association, since they belonged to the Copts, and they borrowed them from them shortly before the drowning, so they remained in their hands.
Page 63
It has also been said: [the ornaments belonged to them] in the sense that is understood from them, on the basis that the people owned them after the sea had cast them onto the shore after the drowning of the Copts, or after they had borrowed them from them and perished. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: It is narrated that when God, exalted is He, wished to drown Pharaoh and his people, knowing that none of them would believe, He commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to command the Children of Israel to borrow the ornaments of the Copts so that they might leave after them, for the sake of the wealth, or so that their wealth would remain in their hands.

This has been objected to on the ground that it amounts to an order to take the property of another without right, and that it would only become spoils of war after destruction, while spoils were not lawful for them, as the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I have been given five things that none before me was given: spoils of war have been made lawful for me," and the hadith continues.

Moreover, what is related about the people in surah Ta-Ha, their saying: ﴿We were burdened with loads of the ornaments of the people﴾, also implies that it was not lawful.

It has been answered that this is to say: when they enslaved them without right, and made them serve, and took their property, and killed their sons, God, exalted is He, gave them their land and what is in it as an inheritance. The earth belongs to God, and He bequeaths it to whomever of His servants He wills. This happened by revelation from God, exalted is He, not by way of spoils. This is contrary to analogy, and there are many such things in the laws. As for the saying that is reported, its discussion will come, God willing. This sentence, as al-Tibi said, is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon His words, glorified is He: ﴿And We appointed for Musa﴾, a conjunction of one narrative upon another narrative.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *Hilyihim* with a kasra on the ha', in imitation of the kasra on the lam, like *dilyy*. Some read *Halyahum* in the singular.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿a calf﴾ is the object of *ittakhadha* in the sense of "fashioning" and "making", and it is placed after the prepositional phrase for the reason already mentioned. It has also been said: *ittakhadha* is transitive to two objects and is in the sense of "making", and the second object is omitted, i.e., "a god". *'Ijl* is specifically the young of a cow. This is like how the young of a she-camel is called *hiwar*, the young of a horse *muhr*, the young of a donkey *jahsh*, the young of a sheep *hamal*, the young of a she-goat *jady*, the young of a lion *shibl*, the young of an elephant *daghfal*, the young of a dog *jarw*, the young of a gazelle *khashf*, the young of an antelope *ghafr*, the young of a hyena *farghal*, the young of a bear *daysam*, the young of a pig *khinnawsh*, the young of a snake *harbash*, the young of an ostrich *ra'l*, the young of a hen *farrouj*, the young of a mouse *darṣ*, the young of a lizard *hasl*, and so on. The intended meaning here is that which has the form of a calf.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿a body﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for *'ijlan*, or an appositive (*'atf bayan*), or a qualifier to it by way of interpreting it as "embodied". It has been explained as a body having flesh and blood. Al-Raghib said: *al-jasad* is like *al-jism* but more specific than it. It has been said that it is applied to what is not human, of the creation of the earth and the like, and it is also applied to what has a color, whereas *al-jism* is applied to what has no visible color, such as air. From this, it has been said, comes the name *al-jassad* for saffron, and for garments that have been thoroughly dyed, *mujassad*. The word *mujassad* also came in the sense of "red", and some explained *jasad* here as this, saying: i.e., red, of gold.

﴿It had a lowing﴾. *Khuwar* is specifically the sound of a cow, as *thugha'* is for sheep, *ya'ar* for goats, *nabib* for a male goat, *nubah* for a dog, *zi'ir* for a lion, *'uwa'* and *wa'wa'ah* for a wolf, *diba'* for a fox, *qubā'* for a pig, *mu'a'* for a cat, *nahiq* and *sahil* for a donkey, *sahil*, *dabh*, *qan'*, and *hamhamah* for a horse, *rughā'* for a she-camel, *sanā* for an elephant, *bataghm* for a gazelle, *dagheeb* for a rabbit, *'arar* for an ostrich, *sarsarah* for a falcon, *'aqa'ah* for a hawk, *ṣafir* for an eagle, *hadir* for pigeons, *saj'* for a turtledove, *saqsaqah* for a sparrow, *na'iq* and *na'ib* for a crow, *ṣiqā'* and *zuqā'* for a rooster, *qawqā'* and *naqīqah* for a hen, *faḥīḥ* for a snake, *naqīq* for a frog, *ṣa'iyy* for a scorpion and a mouse, *ṣarīr* for a locust, and so on.

It is reported from Ali, may God ennoble his face, that he read *Ju'ar* with a damma on the jim and a hamza, and it means a very loud sound. Similar to it are *siyah* and *suraakh*.
Page 64
The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a predicate placed first, and *khuwar* is the subject, and the sentence is in the position of a qualifier to *'ijlan*.

It is reported that when al-Samiri had fashioned the calf, he threw into its mouth some dust from the hoofprint of the horse of Jibril, peace be upon him, and it became alive.

Some have mentioned regarding the secret of this that Jibril, peace be upon him, being the Greatest Spirit, a power flowed from him into that dust that produced this effect by the permission of God, exalted is He, for a matter that He willed. It does not follow from this that whatever he, peace be upon him, trod upon would come alive by itself, because the matter is bound to permission, and that happens according to wisdoms that none knows but the All-Wise, the All-Aware. So reflect. Many of the exegetes went to the view of life, and it has been supported by the argument that lowing is only for a cow, not for its image, and by the argument that what will come, God willing, in surah Ta-Ha is clear in what the report indicates. But a group of the Mu'tazilah exegetes said: the calf had no spirit; al-Samiri had fashioned it hollow and placed in its hollow pipes in a particular shape, and placed it in the path of the wind, so the wind would enter those pipes and a sound resembling the lowing of a calf would be heard; that is why it was called *khuwar*. What is in Ta-Ha will come, God willing, with discussion. There has been disagreement about this lowing: it has been said that it happened only once, and it has been said that it happened many times, and whenever it lowed they prostrated to it, and when it was silent they raised their heads. It is reported from al-Suddi that it used to low and walk. It is reported from Wahb the denial of movement, and the verse is silent about affirming it, and there is nothing in the reports to rely upon, so refraining from affirming walking is preferable. This matter is not one of the important ones. The attribution of the taking to the people of Musa, peace be upon him, although it was the act of al-Samiri, is because they were content with it, and it is often attributed to a people when the act was done by one of them, as one says: "the sons of so-and-so killed a slain man," while the killer was one of them. It has also been said: because what is meant is their taking it as a god, so the meaning is that they made it a god and worshipped it, and in this case there is no metaphor in the speech, because the worship of it was done by all of them.

Al-Hasan said: all of them worshipped the calf except Harun, peace be upon him. Others excepted, along with him, others besides him. According to this view, it has been said: it is necessary to supply "so they worshipped it", so that this becomes the target of the denunciation; because the prohibition of making images came into being in our law according to the well-known view, and because the intention is to denounce its worship.

﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them, nor guide them to a way?﴾ This is a rebuke to them and a reproach for the extreme of their error and their neglect of reflection. That is: Did they not see that it cannot do what ordinary human beings can do, of speech and guiding to a path in any way? How then did they make it equal to the Creator of bodies, powers, and destiny? Some have made this an allusion to the true God, His speech which never ends, and His clear guidance which cannot be denied. It has also been said that it is an allusion to God, exalted is He, and His speech with Musa, peace be upon him, and His guidance of his people.

﴿They took it﴾ is a repetition of all that preceded of taking, in the particular manner that includes blame. It is of the type of metonymy (*kinayah*), in the style of: "a seer sees and an attentive listener hears," that is: they went ahead with what they went ahead with of the abominable matter.

﴿And they were wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ tadhyili*), that is: their habit before that was wrongdoing and placing things in other than their proper places, so this great abomination was not something novel from them. He repeated the verb in order to build this upon it. It has also been said: the sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause, that is: they took it in this continuing state for them.

Page 65

﴿And when they were overcome with remorse (lit. "when it fell into their hands")﴾ means: they regretted, as is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Many scholars took it as a kinayah (figurative expression) for the intensity and extreme degree of regret, because when a regretful person's remorse becomes intense, he bites his hand out of distress, so his hand becomes "that into which something has fallen." Its original form is *saqata fūhu* or *ʿaḍḍahu fī yadihi*, meaning "he fell (into regret)," then the subject was deleted and the verb was put in the passive form with the object as its subject, so it became *suqita fī yadihi*, like your saying *murra bi-Zaydin* ("Zayd was passed by"). Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read *saqata* in the active voice, according to the original form, and the "hand" is literal as mentioned. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that remorse fell into their souls. Al-Qutb considered this to be from the allegorical metaphor (*al-istiʿārah al-tamthīliyyah*), where he likened the state of regret in the soul to the state of a thing in the hand in terms of certainty and visibility, then expressed it with *al-suqūṭ fī al-yad* ("falling into the hand"). There is no subtlety in an explicit metaphor (*al-istiʿārah al-taṣrīḥiyyah*) here. Al-Wahidi said: it is said of what occurs even if it is not in the hand: "a disliked matter fell into his hand" (*waqaʿa fī yadihi*) and "a disliked matter occurred in his hand" (*ḥaṣala fī yadihi makrūh*). So what occurs in the soul and heart is likened to what is seen with the eye. The hand was singled out because affairs are carried out by it, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿That is because of what your hands have sent forward﴾. Or because the effect of regret appears in the hand after it occurs in the heart, through biting it, striking it against its counterpart, and similar things. Indeed, He, glorified is He, said about the regretful one: ﴿So he began to turn over his palms﴾ and ﴿On the Day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾.

It has been said: it is the habit of the regretful person to lower his head and place his chin on his hand, such that if he removed it he would fall on his face. So it is as if the hand is that onto which he has fallen, and *fī* here means *ʿalā* ("on"). It has also been said: it is from *al-siqāṭ*, which means frequent error. It has been said: it is from *al-saqīṭ*, which is what covers the ground in the mornings, resembling snow, having no permanence. So it is a proverb for one who lost in his outcome and gained nothing of value from his effort. Some scholars counted *saqaṭa* among the verbs that do not inflect, like *niʿma* and *biʾsa*.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read *ūsqiṭa*, as a quadrilateral verb in the passive voice. This is a dialect transmitted by al-Farra and al-Zajjaj. Some scholars mentioned that this construction was not heard before the revelation of the Qur'an, that the Arabs did not know it, and that it was not found in their poetry and speech. Therefore it was hidden from many, and they made errors in its usage, such as Abu Hatim and Abu Nuwas, who was a learned and skilled scholar. They did not know this, and had they known it, they would have been overcome with remorse (*la-suqita fī aydīhim*).

﴿And they saw that they had gone astray﴾ means: they clearly recognized their misguidance in taking the calf and worshipping it, a recognition as though they had seen it with their own eyes. It has been said: the mention of their remorse before this sight, although it came later, was for the sake of hastening to clarify it and indicating the extreme speed of it, as if it preceded the sight.

Al-Qutb, explaining why the recognition of error came after remorse although it preceded it, said: the transition from certainty about a thing to recognition of certainty in its opposite does not usually happen suddenly, but rather to doubt, then to suspicion of the opposite, then to certainty in it, then to its clarification. The people were certain that what they were upon was correct, and regret over it may have occurred to them in a state of doubt about it. So the recognition of error came after it. End of quote. So understand this and do not be heedless.

﴿They said: "If our Lord does not have mercy on us﴾ by sending down a repentance that expiates, ﴿and forgive us﴾ by overlooking our sin, "we will surely be among the losers." The placement of mercy before forgiveness, although clearing (*al-takhliyah*) should precede adornment (*al-taḥliyah*), was said to be either for hastening to what is the primary aim, or because the intended meaning of mercy is the general will for good for them, which is the beginning of sending down the repentance that expiates their sins. The lam in *la-in* is a preparatory lam for an oath, meaning: "By Allah, if..." etc. And His, glorified is He, saying ﴿we will surely be among the losers﴾ is the answer to the oath, as is well known.

Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi read *tarḥamnā* and *taghfir lanā* with the upper *tā'* (second person), and *rabbanā* in the accusative as a vocative. What is related of them regarding the remorse, the sight, and the saying occurred after Musa, peace be upon him, returned from the appointed time (*al-mīqāt*), as is indicated by what will come, Allah willing, in Surah Ta-Ha. It was placed here so that what they said would be connected to what they did.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 150 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾ at what had happened among them.

﴿Angry (asifan)﴾: that is, extremely wrathful, as said by Abu al-Darda', Muhammad al-Qurazi, 'Ata' and al-Zajjaj. Or, grieved, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with them all. Abu Muslim said: anger and grief (asaf) have the same meaning, and the repetition is for emphasis.

Page 66

Al-Wahidi said: they are close in meaning. When something you dislike comes to you from one who is below you, you become angry; and when it comes from one who is above you, you become grieved. Accordingly, Moses, peace be upon him, was angry with his people for taking the calf, and grieved because Allah had tried them, and He, glory be to Him, had informed him of this before his return. The two descriptions are in the accusative as two synonymous or overlapping circumstantial clauses (hal), such that the second is a circumstance of the implied pronoun in the first. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for the first circumstance, and it is a substitution of the whole (badal kull) not of a part (badal ba'd), as is wrongly imagined.

﴿He said: "Evil is what you have done as my successors after me"﴾: the address is either to the worshippers of the calf, or to Harun, peace be upon him, and those believers with him. That is: evil is what you did after my absence, when you worshipped the calf after you had seen from me the affirmation of Allah's oneness, the negation of partners from Him, glory be to Him, and sincere worship of Him, majestic is His majesty. Or: evil is what you did in standing in my place, when you did not observe my covenant and did not restrain the worshippers from what they did, after you had seen from me their being guided to monotheism and their being restrained from what their eyes had reached out toward, the worship of the cow, when they said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾.

It is also permitted that the address be to both groups, on the basis that the meaning of "successorship" (khilafah) is successorship in what encompasses both matters that were indicated. There is no repetition in mentioning ﴿after me﴾ after ﴿you have succeeded me﴾, because the intended meaning is "after my guardianship and my standing in what I used to uphold"; for true "afterness" of him is, as some have said, only after his death. It was also said that "after me" is an emphasis of the type "I saw it with my own eye," and its benefit is depicting the deputy's representation and his carrying on of the conduct, just as there the depiction of the seeing and what is connected with it is present. "Ma" is an indefinite qualifying noun explaining the hidden subject of "bi'sa," and the object of blame is omitted; that is: evil is the successorship you have succeeded me in after me, your successorship. The blame, if the address is to Harun, peace be upon him, and those believers with him, is not to the successorship itself but to not acting according to its requirements. As for if it is to the Samiri and his followers, the matter is clear.

﴿Have you hastened the command of your Lord?﴾: that is, have you hastened beyond what your Lord commanded you, which was waiting for Moses, peace be upon him, while you were keeping his covenant and what he enjoined upon you. Yet you built the matter on the presumption that the appointed term had reached its end and I had not returned to you, so you spoke to yourselves about my death and changed. It is narrated that the Samiri said to them when he brought out the calf for them: "This is your god and the god of Moses; Moses will not return, and he has died."

It is also narrated that they counted twenty days with their nights, and made them forty, and then did what they did. The well-known usage is that "ajila" takes "'an" and not a direct object, so one says "ajila 'an al-amr" when one leaves it incomplete, its opposite being "tamma 'alayhi," and "a'jalahu 'anhu ghayruhu" (another caused him to abandon it). Here they have made it imply the sense of "preceding," which is a metaphor for "leaving," so it takes its construction, and the meaning of leaving was not implied directly because the relationship between them is obscure and not elegant. Ya'qub held that "preceding" is a literal meaning of it without implication. And "al-amr" is the singular of "al-awamir." It is narrated from al-Hasan that the meaning is: have you hastened the promise of your Lord which He promised you of the forty? Then "al-amr" in this reading is the singular of "al-umur" (matters). The forty meant here, as al-Tibi mentioned, is other than the forty to which Allah pointed in His words: ﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾, and the completion of the discussion on this will come shortly, Allah willing.

﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾: that is, he placed them on the ground like one who casts them down, in order to seize his brother by the head, due to the excess of religious zeal that had overcome him. Peace be upon him was very wrathful for the sake of Allah, glory be to Him. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that when he, peace be upon him, became angry, his skullcap would burst into flame. Qadi Nasir al-Din said: that is, he threw them down out of extreme anger and excessive vexation, as zeal for the religion. Then it is reported that some of them broke when he threw them. The most excellent of the later scholars, our shaykh Sibghat Allah Effendi al-Haydari, objected to this, saying that zeal for the religion requires only respect for the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and protecting it from any defect or disgrace, such that its tablets would not be broken. Then he said: the correct view is that he, peace be upon him, out of excess of religious zeal and intense anger for Allah, the Exalted, could not restrain himself, and the tablets fell from his hand without choice. Thus the failure to be careful was treated as the deliberate casting, and it was expressed with it as a strong rebuke to him, peace be upon him, for the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of the near ones. End.

Al-Allamah Salih Effendi al-Mawsili, may God have mercy on him, rejoined that it is not hidden that this objection arose from taking the Qadi's phrase "zeal for the religion" as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for casting them down, which is not correct. For he stated at the beginning of his commentary on Surah Ta-Ha that a single act does not take two causes, and rather it is: an object of purpose due to the intensity of anger and excess of vexation, by way of the dispute (tanazu'). The interpretation mentioned for the verse is what the Qadi intended, and his explanation of "casting" as "throwing down" does not contradict this, as is not hidden. End. I say: you know that the claim that this interpretation is what the Qadi intended is neither clear nor evident, and that the story that the expression with "casting" was a rebuke to him, peace be upon him, is very far below the level of acceptance; for there is nothing in the context or the wider passage that requires that the situation be a reproach to Moses, peace be upon him, so that this strictness is issued in view of his station, peace be upon him. Rather, the situation clearly shows condemnation of his people, as is not hidden to whoever has even a little share of lofty insight. What this humble writer sees is what we have pointed to at first. The summary is that when Moses, peace be upon him, saw what he saw from his people, he became extremely angry out of zeal for the religion and jealousy against associating partners with the Lord of the worlds, so he hastened to set down the tablets so that his hand would be free to seize his brother by the head. He expressed that setting down as "casting" to denounce the act of his people, since his witnessing it was the cause and the incitement to it, along with the indication of the intensity of his jealousy and the excess of his zeal. There is nothing in that from which one might imagine any kind of insult to the Book of Allah, the Exalted, in any way. The breaking of some of the tablets occurred from an act that was permitted, and it was not Moses' purpose, nor did it come to his mind, nor did he think it would follow from what he did. There was nothing except haste in setting down, arising from zeal for Allah, the Exalted, and perhaps that is of the type: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾. The reports differed concerning the amount that was broken and lifted, and some denied this, since the apparent sense of the Qur'an is contrary to it.

Indeed, Ahmad and others, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Moses; the one who sees is not like the one who is told. His Lord, blessed and exalted, informed him that his people had been tried after him, and he did not cast the tablets; but when he saw them and witnessed them, he cast the tablets, and some of them broke."

So reflect and do not be heedless. As for what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that when Moses, peace be upon him, cast the tablets, six-sevenths of them were lifted and one-seventh remained, and similarly what is narrated from others, is contrary to what was narrated earlier, that the Torah descended as seventy loads, of which a portion was read in a year, and that only four persons read it: Moses, Joshua, 'Uzayr and 'Isa, peace be upon them. Likewise, it conflicts with what is mentioned later in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿He took the tablets﴾, for the apparent meaning of it is the covenant. The answer that the lifting concerned what was on them of writing and not the tablets themselves is contrary to the apparent sense, and Allah, the Exalted, knows best the reality of the matter.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head﴾: that is, by the hair of Harun's head, peace be upon him, because it is what is usually seized and held. This does not contradict his seizing him by the beard, as occurred in Surah Ta-Ha, or it is included in it by way of generalization (taghlib).

﴿Dragging him toward himself﴾: he assumed that Harun had fallen short in restraining them, and he could not contain, due to the intensity of his anger and the excess of his fury, from doing this. Harun was three years older than Moses, peace be upon them both, yet Moses was greater than him in rank, and to him belonged the messengership and leadership independently, while Harun was his minister. Moses, peace be upon him, was very gentle and forbearing. Moses did not intend by this seizing to humiliate him or belittle him, but rather a practical rebuke for the assumed negligence, in accordance with the authority of leadership and the excess of zeal. The claim that he, peace be upon him, seized his brother's head only to speak privately with him and to learn from him the manner of the event, which the taste rejects, as is not hidden to those who possess it; and similar is the claim that it was only to calm Harun because of what he saw in him of distress and anxiety. Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i said: Moses, peace be upon him, treated his brother as he would treat himself, doing to him what a person does to himself at the height of anger. Al-Shaykh al-Mufid of the Shi'a said: this was out of pain at his people's misguidance, and to make known in the most emphatic way the magnitude of what they had done, so that they would desist from the like. It is not hidden that the matter on this view is of the kind of:

"Another committed the offense, and I am the one punished among you, so I am as the pointing finger of one who repents."

Perhaps what we have pointed to is the better view. The clause ﴿dragging him﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of Moses, or from "head," or from "his brother," because the annexed noun is a part of it, and this is one of the things permitted in that regard; Abu al-Baqa' considered it weak.

﴿He said﴾: that is, Harun, addressing Moses, peace be upon him, to remove his suspicion: ﴿O son of my mother﴾, with the vocative particle omitted due to the narrowness of the situation. The specification of "mother" by mention, although they were full brothers according to the more correct view, is for tenderness; and it was said: because she was the one who raised him and endured dangers and hardships in saving him. It was also said: the signs of beauty and mercy were manifest in Harun, peace be upon him, as indicated by His words: ﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Harun as a prophet﴾, and his source and origin were that, and therefore he would constantly mention what indicates mercy. Do you not see how he gently addressed the people when they had committed what they committed, saying: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful." And therefore he mentioned the mother and attributed him to her, because mercy in her is more complete, and had it not been for her, she could not have raised the child or borne its hardships. This is a Sufi tendency, as is not hidden. It was disputed concerning the name of their mother, peace be upon them both: it was said Mihyanah daughter of Yasar son of Levi; it was said Yuhanidh; it was said Yarkha; it was said Yazkhit; and other things were said. Some people claim that her name, may Allah be pleased with her, has a special property for opening locks, and there is a particular exercise for it among practitioners of talismans and letters; but these are nothing but monastic innovations which Allah has not sent down any authority for.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read here and in Ta-Ha: "ibna ummi" with a kasrah, and the original is "ibna ummi" (my mother's son), so the ya' was dropped, being satisfied with the kasrah for lightness, like a vocative annexed to the ya'.

The rest read with a fathah, for additional lightness, or as an analogy with "khamsata 'ashar" (fifteen).

﴿Indeed the people﴾, those who did what they did, ﴿have humbled me﴾, that is, they made me weak and overpowered me, and did not care for me because of the paucity of my helpers.

﴿And they nearly killed me﴾: they came close to killing me when I forbade them from that. The meaning is that I expended my utmost effort in restraining them and spared no effort in preventing them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 150 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾ meaning: do not do what they would gloat over me for, for they do not know the secret of your action. The shamata (gloating) is the enemy's joy at what befalls a person of hardship.
It has been read as: (فَلا تَشْمُتُ بِيَ الأعْداءُ) with a fatha on the letter of present tense and a damma on the mim, and الأعْداءُ in the nominative, "may Allah bring them low." This is also a metonymy (kinaya) for that same meaning, in the manner of: لا أرَيَنَّكَ هاهُنا. The intended meaning of "the enemies" is the people mentioned, except that the apparent noun has been put in place of their pronoun, and its secret is not hidden.
﴿And do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾ meaning: do not count me among them, and do not treat me with their treatment in reproach, or do not regard me as one of the wrongdoers while I am innocent of them and of their wrongdoing. The "placing" (al-ja'l) here is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾.

﴿Qāla﴾ ("He said") is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), arising from the report of the apology. It is as if it were said: "What did Musa, peace be upon him, say when his brother apologized?" It was answered: "He said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me﴾," for what I did to my brother before the situation became clear. The good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near (to God).

﴿And my brother﴾, if he had done something that counts as a sin in relation to him, in the matter of those wrongdoers. In this joining there is consolation for him, peace be upon him, and removal of gloating over him. It has been said that he, peace be upon him, sought forgiveness for himself so as to please his brother and to show the gloaters his contentment, lest their gloating over him be complete, and that he included his brother to signal that he (Harun) too was in need of forgiveness, since he should have fought them. But there is a hesitation in this whose point is not hidden.

﴿And admit us﴾ both together.

﴿into Your mercy﴾, the vast one, by an abundance of favor upon us. This is what the contrast with forgiveness requires, and the shift from "have mercy on us" to what was mentioned. ﴿And You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾. So there is no wonder in our being included in the string of Your vast mercy in this world and the next. The sentence is a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī*, an added closing phrase) that confirms the content of what precedes it. Some have claimed that it contains an indication that He, glorified is He, answered his supplication, but this is obscure.

[Page 69]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 152:

﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ meaning: they persisted in taking it and continued upon it, like al-Samiri and his followers. This is made clear by the fact that the second relative clause refers to those who repented, for that is explicit evidence that the first relative clause refers to the persisters.

﴿will certainly attain﴾ meaning: will overtake and befall them in the Hereafter, as the requital for that. ﴿wrath﴾ great, whose extent cannot be measured, entailing various kinds of punishments because of the magnitude of their crime and the ugliness of their offence.

﴿from their Lord﴾ meaning: their Owner. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur) is attached to "yanaluhum" (will attain them), or to an omitted verb that occurs as an adjective (na't) of "ghadab" (wrath), serving as emphasis (ta'kid) for what the nunation (tanwin) conveys of intrinsic magnificence through the magnificence of attribution: that is, "existing from their Lord." ﴿and humiliation﴾ great.

﴿in the life of this world﴾. According to what I say, this is the humiliation that befell them when their god was burned and scattered into the sea, a scattering, while they were unable to prevent that from happening to it. It has also been said: it is the humiliation of estrangement, by which proverbs are coined, and the wretchedness that encompasses them and their children all together. It is also the humiliation specific to al-Samiri, namely isolation from people and being afflicted with "no touching." It is narrated that their remnants today say this, and that if anyone other than themselves touches one of them, both become feverish at the same moment. What we have mentioned is perhaps preferable, and this narration we have not found any trace of. The use of "sa-" (will) with what befell them is for predominance (taghlib). It has also been said, and Abu al-Aliyah's statement points to it: the intended people are the repentant ones; by "wrath" is meant what they were commanded to do of killing themselves; by "humiliation" is meant their surrendering themselves to that and their admission of error. The use of "sa-" has been excused on the grounds that this is a report of what God Most High informed Musa, peace be upon him, when He informed him of his people's being tempted and their taking the calf, for He said to him: ﴿wrath will attain them﴾, and so on. Thus it precedes the wrath, and the statement has been made as an answer to an assumed question. That is because, when God Most High showed that the people regretted their worship of the calf, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when they were overcome with remorse and saw that they had gone astray﴾, and regret is repentance, they therefore followed it with their saying: ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us﴾. The mention of Musa's reproach of his brother, peace be upon them both, and then his seeking forgiveness, gave rise to a questioner asking: "O Lord, what will become of the affair of the people, their repentance, and the seeking of forgiveness by the Prophet of God Most High? Did God Most High accept their repentance?" So He answered: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will attain wrath﴾, meaning: vengeance, before the repentance of Musa and his brother; and He forgave the two of them specifically. And it was part of the completion of the people's repentance that God, glorified is He, commanded them to kill themselves, and they submitted themselves to being killed. So He placed "those who took the calf" in the position of "the people," to indicate causation (ta'lil). It has been objected that the context of the noble composition, and likewise its preceding context, clearly does not support that, how could it, when His saying, Most High: ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾ calls out against that? For they were martyrs and penitents, so how is it possible to describe them afterwards with fabrication? Moreover, God Most High does not requite all fabricators with this punishment, whose outward aspect is subjugation and whose inward aspect is gentleness and mercy. The response could be: it suffices for the validity of the comparison that the aspect of resemblance exist in general, and it is necessary to uphold that in the manner we have mentioned as well. And what was mentioned in
Page 70
the formulation of the objection and the answer is among the things that the ears of people of understanding recoil from.

ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi said: the intended meaning is: "will attain the children of those who worshipped the calf," and they were those who lived in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). By "wrath" and "humiliation" is meant what befell the Banu al-Nadir and Qurayzah of killing and expulsion, or what befell them of that and of imposing the jizya upon them. According to this interpretation, there is an omitted modifier, namely "the children," and it is possible that it is there, and this is the reproach of the sons for what the fathers did, and similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an. It has also been said: the intended meaning of the relative clause is the actual takers, and by the pronoun in "yanaluhum" are meant their descendants; by "wrath" is meant the wrath of the Hereafter; and by "humiliation" is meant the jizya that Islam imposed upon them, or the more general sense so as to include what Bukhtnassar imposed upon them. This too has been objected to, on the grounds that there is no doubt that placing the condition of these people in the midst of the description of the condition of the takers is like separating the wood from its bark. The intended meaning of "the fabricators" is those who fabricate against God Most High, and the fabrication of those people against Him, glorified is He, is the saying of al-Samiri about the calf: ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa﴾, and their approval of it, and there is no greater fabrication than this, and perhaps no one fabricated the like of it before them or after them. It is reported from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah that he said: "Every possessor of innovation is humiliated," and he recited this verse.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 153:

﴿And those who committed evil deeds﴾ — whatever evil it was — (this is stated) for the generality of forgiveness, and because there is no reason for restriction; ﴿then repented﴾ from them ﴿after them﴾, i.e., after doing them, which is an explicit statement of what is implied; ﴿and believed﴾, i.e., they occupied themselves with faith and what it requires, and its completion through righteous deeds; and they did not persist in what they had done, unlike the first group. This is a conjunction with "repented," and it may be a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied. In any case, according to what has been said, it is the mention of the particular after the general, for the sake of giving it attention, because repentance from disbelief is faith itself, so it is not asked: how did "repentance after faith" come before it?

It has been said: since the intended meaning of faith is that which includes deeds, it comes after repentance. It has also been said: the intended meaning of faith here is affirmation that Allah Most High forgives the one who repents; i.e., "then they repented and affirmed that Allah Most High forgives whoever repents."

﴿Indeed, your Lord, after them﴾, i.e., after the repentance conjoined with what is not accepted without it, which is faith. The pronoun was not made to refer to the evil deeds, because, as some researchers said, there is no need for it after His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿then repented after them﴾, and not because it requires omitting a genitive and a conjunction (namely, "of their deed and repentance from it"), since there is no meaning to its being "after them" except that.

﴿is indeed All-Forgiving﴾ toward their sins, however great and numerous.

﴿Most Merciful﴾, one who abounds in bestowing all kinds of mercy upon them. The relative pronoun is the subject, and the clause "Indeed, your Lord..." etc. is the predicate, and the returning pronoun is omitted; the estimated form, according to Abu al-Baqa', is: "forgiving to them, merciful to them." The mention of the title of Lordship together with the attribution to his pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, is for honour. It has been said: the address is to the one who repents, and the subtlety of this is also evident. In the verse there is an indication that sins, however grave and great, the pardon and generosity of Allah Most High are greater and more sublime. How subtle is the saying of Abu Nuwas, may Allah forgive him:

O my Lord, though my sins are great in number,
I know well that Your pardon is greater.
If none hopes in You but the good, then to whom does the criminal flee and seek refuge?

And among what is attributed to Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him:

When my heart grew hard and my paths constricted, I made hope in my Lord a ladder to Your pardon.
My sin grew great to me, but when I set it beside Your pardon, my Lord, Your pardon was greater.

Page 71
And I am pleased by the saying of one of them, and how fitting this is for the sinner:

I am a sinner, I am one who errs, I am disobedient;
He is the Forgiver, He is the Merciful, He is the Pardoner.
I have set these three against three,
and His attributes will prevail over mine.

﴿When the anger subsided from Moses﴾: this begins the explanation of the rest of the narrative, following the division of the people into those who persisted (in sin) and those who repented, and it indicates in summary what each of the two groups deserved. That is, when his anger was stilled (ﷺ) by his brother's apology and the people's repentance. This explicitly indicates that what is related about his remorse and what follows from it occurred after Moses (peace be upon him) had come. It has been said that the meaning is: when the force of his anger, peace be upon him, was broken and his rage diminished, through his brother's apology alone, because his anger had not wholly disappeared, since the people's repentance was not yet sincere. The original meaning of *sukut* (silence) is the cessation of speech. In the phrase there is a *istiʿara makniyya* (implicit metaphor), in which anger is likened to a commanding and forbidding person, and silence is attributed to it by way of *takhyil* (imaginative representation). Al-Sakkaki said that there is in it an *istiʿara tabiʿiyya* (subsidiary metaphor), in which the subsiding of anger and the cooling of its heat are likened to the silence of one who commands and forbids, with "anger" serving as its indicator. It has also been said that "anger" is a metaphor by implication for the speaking person, and that "silence" is an explicit metaphor for the stilling of its agitation and surging, so that the figure in the phrase is an implicit metaphor whose indicator is explicit rather than imaginative. Whichever of these is the case, the phrase contains exaggeration and eloquence whose elevated status is evident. Al-Zajjaj said: the verbal noun of *sakata al-ghadab* (anger fell silent) is *al-sakta* (a single stilling), and the verbal noun of *sakata al-rajul* (the man fell silent) is *al-sukut*. This implies that *sakata al-ghadab* is an independent verb. It has been said, and attributed to ʿIkrima, that this is an inversion (*qalb*), and that its intended sense is: "when Moses fell silent from the anger." But it is not hidden that *al-sukut* would have been more fitting for this speaker, since what he mentioned has no basis.

Muʿawiya ibn Qurra recited (*sakana*, "was calm"). The meaning on that reading is clear, but the reading of the majority is more excellent in the estimation of everyone with a sound nature and correct taste. It was also read as *suккита* (*sukkita*, in the passive with the verb doubled for transitivity, meaning "was stilled"), and as *ʾuskita* (*uskita*, "was made to fall silent") in the same passive form, on the basis that the one who stilled it is God Most High, or his brother, or the repenting people.

﴿He took the tablets﴾: those which he had cast down.

﴿and in their inscription﴾: that is, in what was copied and written upon them. Thus *nuskha* (copy, inscription) is in the sense of a passive noun, like *khutba* (sermon). *Al-naskh* means writing. The construction is either a specifying genitive (*idafa bayaniyya*) or means "in" (*bi-maʿna fi*). This is the view of al-Jubbaʾi, Abu Muslim, and others. It has been said that the meaning of "inscribed" is what was copied from the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*). It has also been said that *al-naskh* here means transcription, and the meaning is "in what was transcribed from the broken tablets." It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAmr ibn Dinar that when Moses, peace be upon him, cast down the tablets and some of them broke, he fasted for forty days, whereupon there was returned to him what had gone in two tablets, and in them was the same as in the first, as though it had been copied from the first.

﴿guidance﴾: that is, a clear explanation of the truth, of great magnitude.

﴿and mercy﴾: an exalted mercy through guidance to what contains good and righteousness.

﴿for those who fear their Lord﴾: that is, those who dread with the utmost dread. The first *lam* is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of what precedes it, or it is the *lam* of purpose, meaning: guidance and mercy for their sake. The second *lam* serves to strengthen the operation of the verb that comes after it, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿if you can interpret dreams﴾ (12:43). Or it is the *lam* of causation, with an omitted object, meaning: they dread sins for the sake of their Lord, not for display and reputation. The possibility that it is connected to an omitted element, meaning "they fear for their Lord," as Abu al-Baqaʾ held, is remote.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 155 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾. This is a continuation of the explanation of the condition of the Children of Israel. Some have said that it is the beginning of an explanation of how repentance was requested and how it came about. (*ikhtar*, "chose") is transitive to two objects, the second of which is introduced by *min* ("from"), and here it has been omitted, and the verb was made to reach its object directly. The original is *min qawmihi* ("from his people"). Similar to this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*"Among us is the one chosen as men for generosity and munificence, when the stormy winds blow."*

And his other verse:

*"So I said to him: choose from it a fat she-camel, and a stallion that rises above the best of your stallions in the pasture."*

The words of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿seventy men﴾ are the first object of *ikhtar* (chose), the second object being "the chosen." It was postponed after the second object for a reason that has been mentioned many times. It was also said that it is a partitive substitute (*badal ba'd min kull*) for the subject. Most grammarians rejected this, on the basis that the substitute of the subject is considered as if the original was dropped, and choosing requires a chooser and a chosen-from; with the dropping, the second would be lost. Abu al-Baqa permitted it with weakness, and the sense would be: seventy of them. It was also said that it is an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*) for ﴿Our appointed time﴾. Abu Ali, Abu Muslim, and others among the exegetes of the Sunnis and the Shi'is went to the view that it is the first appointed time, which is the appointed time of speech. They said: he (peace be upon him) chose for that purpose from the twelve tribes, six from each tribe, until they completed seventy-two. Then he (peace be upon him) said: let two men remain behind from among you. They disputed over it, so he said: for whoever remains behind from among you is the like of the reward of whoever goes out. So Kalib and Yusha' remained behind. It is narrated that he only found sixty elders, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed that he should choose from the young men ten, so he chose them, and they became elders. It was said: they were sons who were under twenty and had not exceeded forty, so ignorance and youth left them. Then Musa (peace be upon him) commanded them to fast, purify themselves, and purify their garments. Then he went out with them to Mount Sinai. When he drew near the mountain, a column of cloud descended upon it until it covered the whole mountain. Musa approached and entered it, and said to the people: draw near. So they drew near until, when they entered the cloud, they fell down prostrate, and they heard Him, glorified is He, speaking to Musa, commanding him and forbidding him: do, and do not. Then the cloud lifted, and they came to him and asked to see Allah. So he admonished them, and what happened happened. Others went the other way, and this is what is narrated from al-Hasan: that it is other than the first appointed time. They said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded Musa (peace be upon him) to come to Him with some people from the Children of Israel who would apologize to Him for the worship of the calf. So he chose those whom He chose. When they came to the mountain they said what they said. This was narrated from al-Suddi. It is also narrated from Ibn Ishaq that he (peace be upon him) only chose them so that they might repent to Allah, exalted is He, and ask Him for repentance on behalf of those whom they had left behind of their people. Al-Tibi preferred this, claiming that the first contradicts the arrangement of the verses and the sayings of the exegetes. As for the first, when al-Imam said: He, exalted is He, mentioned the story of the appointed time of speech and the request to see Allah, then He followed it with the story of the calf and what is connected with it. The apparent state is that this story is different from the preceding one, since it is not fitting for eloquence to mention part of a story, then move to another, then return to the first; this is an inconsistency from which the speech of Allah is protected. Also, in the first, the falling of Musa (peace be upon him) in a swoon is mentioned, and in the second, His saying after the seizure of the earthquake: ﴿If You had willed, You would have destroyed them before this﴾. Also, if the earthquake had been because of the request to see Him, it would have been said: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?﴾. Al-Tibi added to this that when He mentioned their thunderbolt, He did not mention the swooning of Musa (peace be upon him), and vice versa, which indicates the difference. As for the second, it is based on what was narrated from al-Suddi, which we mentioned just now. Sahib al-Kashf criticized what was mentioned in the first preference, saying: the fair view is that the whole is one story concerning what Allah bestowed upon the Children of Israel after their deliverance, from the fulfilment of the promise to give them the Book, the setting of its appointed time, the worship of the calf, and the request to see Allah, which occurred in those days and in that matter. So some parts are linked with others. The choice of this style remains, and it is clear, because the first is in the context of bestowing favour upon them and preferring them. How, when ﴿We appointed﴾ is conjoined to ﴿We delivered you﴾, and it has been shown that it is an explanation of the preference. The mention of the story of the request to see is a digression to distinguish between the two requests according to us, and in order to put the stone in the mouth of the Mu'tazili. The second concerns their offence after that immense kindness, by taking the calf, quarrelling, and separation, which are necessary consequences of the arrangement. What was mentioned about it second was criticized, saying: the saying of al-Suddi alone is not suitable as a refutation. How, when this contradicts what Muhi al-Sunna narrated in the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿If You had willed, You would have destroyed them﴾, that they were obedient ministers to him, and his loss weighed heavily upon him (peace be upon him), so He had mercy on them and feared for them destruction. And where is: ﴿We will not believe you﴾ from obedience and good ministry? He said: Then the apparent meaning of the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So they said, "Show us Allah openly," and the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing. Then they took the calf﴾ is that taking the calf came later than their saying that, contrary to what was narrated from al-Suddi, and the interpretation of it as a later rank requires some support. How, since it does not contradict a temporal delay, there must be evidence specifying it. This is all, and the exegetes in Surah Ta-Ha have acknowledged that He chose seventy for the appointed time of speech, which they mentioned in the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And what hastened you from your people, O Musa?﴾. As for what al-Tibi excused about it, that the choice of the seventy happened twice, and there is nothing in the transmission that they were with him at the time of the conversation and the request to see, it is evident to the fair-minded that it is untenable. End of quote.

Al-Qutb, in weakening what was narrated from al-Suddi, mentioned: if the going out to apologize was after their killing of themselves and the descent of repentance, then there is no sense in apologizing; and if it was before their killing of themselves, then it is strange that an apology whose fruit is the killing of souls. Then he said: There is no doubt that one story is repeated in the Qur'an, some of it mentioned in one surah and another part in another, and this is only for the repetition of the consideration of those who take lessons from some of that story. So if it is permissible to mention a story in several surahs, with some of it in each surah, why would it not be permissible in various places within one surah, for the repetition of consideration? End of quote. This is evident in preferring what the earlier ones went to. I say: the view that this appointed time is the first appointed time is not devoid of saying, and a group held it, as we have indicated. Our discussion in al-Baqarah is clearly concerned with it. However, the fair view is that the apparent arrangement here requires that it is other than it, and what Sahib al-Kashf mentioned does not require that it is apparent in the opposite. The majority of the exegetes went to the view of otherness.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated, through Abu Sa'd, from Mujahid, that Musa (peace be upon him) went out with the seventy of his people, supplicating Allah, exalted is He, and asking Him to remove the affliction from them, but He did not answer them. So Musa knew that they had incurred of the disobedience what their people had incurred.

Abu Sa'd said: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi narrated to me that He did not answer them because they did not forbid their people from the evil and did not command them with the good.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated, from al-Fadl ibn Isa, the nephew of al-Raqashi, that the Children of Israel said one day to Musa (peace be upon him): Are you not the son of our paternal uncle and one of us? And you claim that you spoke with the Lord of Might? Indeed, ﴿we will not believe you until we see Allah openly﴾. When they refused except that, Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Musa: choose from your people seventy men. So he chose seventy of the best, then said to them: go out. When they emerged, there came upon them what they had no power against. The report...

This is evident that this appointed time is not the first. Yes, it contradicts what was narrated from al-Suddi, but both agree on the view of otherness. Al-Hasan also agrees with al-Suddi in that, so he is not alone in it as Sahib al-Kashf supposed. What he mentioned of the contradiction of al-Suddi's statement with what Muhi al-Sunna narrated is subject to prohibition. As for the saying ﴿we will not believe you﴾ and what follows, its answer becomes apparent from what we mentioned in al-Baqarah at this verse of the possibilities. The view that the choosing happened twice is not far-fetched, and some of them held it. What al-Qutb mentioned about the uncertainty regarding the going out to apologize, the apparent meaning of some narrations from al-Suddi requires determining the first part of it. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: Musa went to his Lord and spoke with Him. When He spoke to him, He said: ﴿And what hastened you from your people, O Musa?﴾ Musa answered Him with what He answered. Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have tested your people﴾ and the verse. So Musa returned to his people angry and grieved. Allah, exalted is He, refused to accept their repentance except in the state they hated, so they did it. Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded Musa (peace be upon him) to come to Him with some people from the Children of Israel who would apologize for the worship of the calf. So He promised them an appointment, and Musa chose seventy men...

[Page 74] ...and so on. This, as you see, is evident in what we have said. As for the saying that there is no sense in apologizing after their killing of themselves and the descent of repentance, it was answered that the meaning may be a request for increased pleasure and for drawing down further mercy; and it may be that they were commanded with that to confirm the announcement of the greatness of the offence and as an increase in it, and as an indication that it reached a level of evil for which the killing of souls is not sufficient for pardon, but rather apologizing along with it is necessary. It is possible to say that it was before their killing of themselves, and the secret in their being commanded with it is that they should also know the greatness of the offence in the most complete way, by its not being accepted. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

﴿So when the earthquake seized them﴾, meaning the thunderbolt or the trembling of the mountain, so they swooned from it. The majority held that they all died, then Allah, exalted is He, revived them. It was said: they fainted, then recovered.
