This is because they said: ﴿we will not believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ according to what is in some narrations, or so that there would be clarified, for those who said that among their people, the increase of His greatness, glorified is He, according to what is in others of them, or for mere discipline according to what is in the report of al-Qurazi. The apparent meaning is that their saying: ﴿we will not believe you﴾ etc. came from them in that place, not after the return, as has been said. We have mentioned this in al-Baqarah. In that case, it is far, according to what has been said, to hold that this appointed time is the first appointed time, because in it there is Musa's request to see after Allah's speech to him without interval, as is apparent. So this request would be after it. And it is unlikely that they would request that after they had seen what happened to Musa (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 155 (part 2 of 2):

What Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir and others related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: When the appointed time of Harun came, Allah the Exalted revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, "Set out, you and Harun and his son, to a cave in the mountain; for We are taking his soul." So they all set out and entered the cave, and there was a bed. Musa lay down on it, then rose from it and said, "How good this place is, O Harun!" So Harun lay down on it, and his soul was taken. Musa and his nephew returned to the Children of Israel, grieving. They said to him, "Where is Harun?" He said, "He died." They said, "Rather, you killed him; you knew that we love him." He said to them, "Woe to you! Would I kill my brother when I asked Allah the Exalted to make him a minister for me? And if I had wished to kill him, would his son have left me alone?" They said, "Yes, you killed him out of envy." He said, "Choose seventy men," and he set out with them. Two men fell ill on the way, so he drew a line around them. Then he and the son of Harun and the Children of Israel went on until they reached Harun, and he said, "O Harun, who killed you?" He said, "No one killed me, but I died." They said, "We will not obey you, O Musa; ask your Lord to make us prophets." Then the thunderbolt seized them and they fainted, and the two men who had been left behind fainted too. Musa, peace be upon him, stood calling upon his Lord, and Allah the Exalted revived them, and they returned to their people as prophets. It is not sound, in my view, because the reports converge against it and the apparent wording of the verses rejects it.

﴿He said, "My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me.﴾ He alluded to the earlier pardon to win the later pardon, meaning: You had the power to destroy them before this, by stirring Pharaoh against them, and by drowning them in the sea and other means, but You showed them mercy and did not destroy them; so have mercy on them now, as You had mercy on them before, in accordance with the requirement of Your generosity. He said "and me" in submission and humility. It was also said: by his words "before" he meant the time when they neglected to forbid the worship of the calf and did not part from its worshippers when they saw their persistence in it; that is, had You willed to destroy them for their sins at that time, and me too, when I asked You to show me Yourself. It was also said: "had You destroyed us when he killed the Copt." It was also said: this is a wish from him, peace be upon him, for the destruction of all of them out of his love that he should not see what he sees of their opposition to him, for example, or for some other reason, and in it there is a delicate hint.

﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ Those of the stubbornness and bad manners, or of the worship of the calf. The interrogative particle (hamza) is either for denying that destruction has occurred, with confidence in the gentleness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as Ibn al-Anbari said, or for seeking compassion, as al-Mubarrad said, meaning: do not destroy us. Whichever it is, it is part of what Musa, peace be upon him, said, like the previous statement. The view of some that this was said by some of them is not evident and there is no reason for it; and the claim that the motive was the impatience in it, which does not befit the station of prophethood, is not hidden from its flaw. Perhaps the intent of the one who said this is that this statement from Musa, peace be upon him, resembles the statement of one of the seventy, so it is as if he said it on their tongues, because they are the ones who were struck with what they were struck with, not he. Understand.

﴿It is only Your trial.﴾ This is a resumptive clause confirming what precedes it and an excuse for what they did. "In" is negating, and it refers to the trial known from the context, meaning: the trial is nothing but Your trial; that is, Your test and affliction, in that You made them hear Your speech, so they desired to see You and followed analogy in a place where it does not apply; or You caused a lowing in the calf, so they deviated by it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Rashid ibn Sa'd, that when Allah said to Musa, peace be upon him, "Your people have taken a calf, a body that has a lowing," he said, "O my Lord, who put the spirit into it?" He said, "I did." He said, "Then You misled them, O my Lord." He said, "O chief of the prophets, O father of the wise, I saw that in their hearts, so I made it easy for them."

Perhaps this is an indication of the eternal predisposition that is not created. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the thunderbolt; that is, it is nothing but Your making worship and hardship heavy upon us by patience in what You sent down upon us. This was related from al-Rabi', Ibn Jubayr and Abu al-'Aliyah. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the request to see, though it was not mentioned.

﴿You lead astray by it whom You will, and guide whom You will.﴾ This is a resumptive clause explaining the ruling of the trial. It was also said: it is a circumstantial clause from the genitive noun or the noun it is attached to. That is: by means of it You lead astray whom You will, by transgressing the limit or by following appearances or the like; and You guide whom You will, so that his faith is strengthened by it. It was also said: the meaning is: by this thunderbolt You strike whom You will and turn it away from whom You will. It was also said: You lead astray, by leaving patience under Your trial and not being content with it, whom You will from attaining Your reward and entering Your Garden, and You guide, by contentment with it and patience under it, whom You will; and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿You are our Protector.﴾ That is: You alone are the one who manages our affairs, worldly and otherworldly, and no other.

﴿So forgive us﴾ what would entail Your punishment.

﴿and have mercy on us﴾ by pouring upon us the effects of worldly and otherworldly mercy. The "fa'" (so) is for the ordering of the supplication upon what precedes it of guardianship, because it is the way of one who manages affairs and takes charge of them to repel harm and bring benefit. Seeking forgiveness is placed before seeking mercy, because clearing away is more important than adorning. His asking forgiveness for himself, peace be upon him, within asking it for those for whom he asked it, is something without harm, even if he did not do what they did, as is not hidden. The claim that his, peace be upon him, daring to say "It is only Your trial" was a great audacity, so he asked Allah the Exalted to forgive it and overlook it, is something the context rejects in the view of the people of taste; and I do not think that Allah the Exalted counted that as a sin of his for which he would seek forgiveness, and his earlier address supports this.

﴿And You are the best of forgivers.﴾ For every forgiver other than You forgives for a self-serving purpose, such as love of praise or repelling harm; but You forgive not seeking any return nor any purpose, but purely out of grace and generosity. The clause is a parenthetical concluding clause confirming what came before, and the mention of forgiveness is singled out because it is the more important.

Some explained what was mentioned as forgiveness of the evil deed and its replacement by a good deed, so that it would be a concluding clause for both "forgive" and "have mercy" together.

And ordain for us ﴿in this world﴾, in which we have been afflicted by what has afflicted us, ﴿a good [thing]﴾: a good life and success in obedience.

It is said: a fine reputation, "and it is not beautiful." From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) it is related that the intent is: accept our coming to You and return us with forgiveness and mercy.

﴿And in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., ordain for us also in the Hereafter a good [thing], which is the good reward and Paradise.

It is said that this is like an emphasis of His saying: "Forgive us and have mercy upon us."

﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾, i.e., we have repented to You, from hada, yahudu, meaning "he returned and repented," as the poet says:

"Indeed I am a man who, for what I have committed, returns (hā'id)."

And from the speech of some of them:

"O rider of sin, return, return, and prostrate as if you were a hoopoe."

It is also said that its meaning is "he inclined" (mala). Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) read (hidna) with a kasra on the ha', from hada, yahidu, when it is moved. Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Abu Wajra al-Sa'di that he denied the damma and said: "By Allah, I do not know it in the speech of any of the Arabs; it is only hidna with a kasra, meaning 'we inclined.'" But this is refuted by mass transmission (tawatur). It is permitted, according to this reading, that the verb be in the active or passive sense, with the meaning "we moved ourselves" or "others moved us." The same applies to the reading of the majority, and the passive form in it follows the dialect of those who say "'ūda al-marīḍu" (the sick man was visited). There is no harm in this if hawd means inclination, except that this dialect is weak. Among those who permitted both options for both readings is al-Zamakhshari. Al-Samin refuted him, saying that whenever there is ambiguity, a vowel must be used that removes it, so one says "'ıqtu" when another has caused you to be harmed (with kasra only), or with ishmam. However, Sibawayh permitted the three vowelings in words like qīla without any reservation.

The sentence is a justification for the request for forgiveness and mercy. Opening it with the particle of affirmation (inna) shows full eagerness and desire for its content.

﴿He said﴾: this is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What did Allah the Exalted say to him after his supplication?" So it is said: He said: ﴿My punishment—I afflict with it whom I will﴾, i.e., My matter is that I afflict with My punishment whom I will to punish, without any interference from anyone else in it.

al-Hasan and 'Amr al-Aswad read (man asa'a) with the unpointed sin (al-sin al-muhmalah), and it is attributed to Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both). Some of them denied its authenticity.

﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾, i.e., its nature is that it is vast, reaching everything. There is no Muslim, nor disbeliever, nor obedient one, nor disobedient one, except that he moves about in this world by My blessing. In attributing affliction to punishment with the imperfect form, and attributing vastness to mercy with the perfect form, there is an indication that mercy is the requirement of the Essence, whereas punishment is the requirement of the sins of the servants. The will (mashi'ah) is also taken into account in the case of mercy. The non-explicit mention of it is said to be a magnification of the matter of mercy; it is also said to be for the sake of making it manifest to the utmost degree. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So I will ordain it﴾? For it is a consequence of considering the will, as is not hidden. It is as if it were said: "If the matter is so, i.e., as mentioned: the affliction of My punishment and the vastness of My mercy for everyone whom I will, then I will ordain it with a specific ordaining for: ﴿those who fear [Allah]﴾, i.e., who fear disbelief and sins, either from the beginning or after being involved in them."

﴿And who give zakat﴾, the obligatory zakat upon them in their wealth. It is also said that the meaning is: they obey Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), but the apparent meaning is other than this. The singling out of giving zakat for mention, although fear of Allah requires it, is an allusion to the people of Musa (peace be upon him), for that was burdensome for them because of their excessive love of this world. Perhaps prayer was not mentioned, despite its superiority over other acts of worship and being the pillar of religion, because it is sufficed by fear of Allah, which is an expression for performing all obligations and abstaining from all prohibitions.

﴿And those who, in Our signs﴾, all of them, as the plural with a possessive suffix indicates, ﴿believe﴾ with a continuous belief without neglecting any of them. The repetition of the relative pronoun, although the intended referent is the same as that of the first relative pronoun, rather than saying "and they believe in Our signs" as a conjunction to what precedes it as he did in the previous one, is said to be because of the restriction indicated by placing the prepositional phrase first, i.e., they believe in all of Our signs, not in some to the exclusion of others. In it there is an allusion to those who believed in some and disbelieved in others, like the people of Musa (peace be upon him).

The interpretation of this answer has been disputed. Shaykh al-Islam said: Perhaps when Allah made the repentance of the worshippers of the calf conditional upon their killing themselves, and the speech that had made the seventy hope to see Allah included in that Musa's supplication for lightness and ease, he said: ﴿And ordain for us in this world a good [thing]﴾, i.e., a good quality free from hardship and severity, for there is in killing an intense punishment that is not hidden. So He answered him, may He be glorified: "My punishment—I afflict with it whom I will," and your people are among those whom My will encompasses; for this reason I made their repentance mixed with worldly punishment. "And My mercy encompasses all things," and your people have received a share of it within the worldly punishment. "And I will ordain mercy pure, unmixed with worldly punishment, as you prayed for those whose attributes are such and such, but not for your people, for they are not like that; so what has been decreed for them of mercy suffices them, even if it is accompanied by punishment." On this basis, Musa (peace be upon him) was not granted his request concerning his people, but Allah the Exalted bestowed upon those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) what he asked for.

In some reports it is related that when he (peace be upon him) was answered with what was mentioned, he said: "I have come to You, my Lord, with a delegation from the Children of Israel, and our delegation has been for others."

And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): Musa asked his Lord, may He be glorified, and made his supplication for those who believed in Muhammad (peace be upon him) and followed him.

In another report, transmitted by a group from him: Musa asked his Lord a request, and He gave him Muhammad (ﷺ), and he recited the verse.

But it is not hidden that what this shaykh has established is remote. The author of al-Kashf said concerning this: It is as if, when Musa (peace be upon him) asked for himself and his people the good of both abodes, he was answered: "My punishment is for those who are not repentant, if I will; and My worldly mercy encompasses the penitent and others. As for combining the two mercies, it is for those who are prepared. So if those for whom you prayed repent and remain steadfast like their predecessors, the special comprehensive mercy will reach them, and your supplication will have its effect on them. But if they persist in what they are in, they will be far from acceptance." The purpose is to encourage them to remain steadfast in repentance and righteous deeds, and to warn them against returning to what has preceded from them, together with a transition to mentioning the Prophet (ﷺ) and urging following him, in the best of transitions and urging, which bewilders minds and reveals to the one who reflects upon it a wondrous marvel. To some of this the words of al-Zamakhshari allude.

Al-'Allamah al-Tibi said in its interpretation: This answer is in the wise manner (al-uslub al-hakim). His saying, may He be glorified, "My punishment," etc., is like a preface to the answer, and the answer is: "So I will ordain it," etc. That is because Musa (peace be upon him) asked for forgiveness, mercy, and good in both abodes for himself and his nation specifically, by His saying: ﴿And ordain for us﴾, and he justified it by His saying: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾. So the Lord, may He be glorified, answered him that your absolute restriction is not from wisdom, for My punishment is by nature subject to My will; so if your nation were exposed to what wisdom requires, the punishment of those who engaged in it, your supplication for them would not benefit them. And My mercy is by nature such that it encompasses creation in this world, the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever. So the worldly good is general and is not specific to your nation, so restricting it would be confining the vast. As for the otherworldly good, it is for those described as such and such. And "So I will ordain it" is placed as if it were a statement in accordance with the implication of the request, for he (peace be upon him) asked for what he asked and made the reason what he made it, so Allah the Exalted combined what He combined, meaning that what requires the specificity of the two goods together is these multiple attributes, not mere repentance. Then he mentioned that the arrangement of this upon what precedes it with "fa" (so) is in the manner of His saying, the Exalted, in answer to the words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿And of my offspring?" He said, "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."﴾

This interpretation is supported by what is related from al-Hasan and Qatadah: His mercy encompassed the righteous and the wicked in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection it is for the God-fearing alone. End of what was intended from it.

What he mentioned about the matter of restriction (tahajjur) in the heart is not from it, for the apparent meaning is that what is in the supplication of Musa (peace be upon him) is not of it. Rather, the restriction is in what Ahmad and Abu Dawud related from Jundub, from 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, who said: "A Bedouin came, made his mount kneel, tied it, and prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he called out: 'O Allah, have mercy on me and on Muhammad, and do not share our mercy with anyone.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'You have restricted a vast mercy. Indeed Allah created one hundred mercies, and He sent down one mercy by which creatures show compassion to one another, jinn, humans and animals, and with Him are ninety-nine.'"

And I say:

It may be said: Musa (peace be upon him) asked, in the most eloquent manner, for forgiveness and worldly and otherworldly mercy for himself and his people, and the justification of that by repentance is undoubtedly correct. Nothing is understood from his words (peace be upon him) that he asked for the people in whatever condition they were, in whatever state they were found, or by whatever path they took, for that is hardly something that would occur from one who has even minimal knowledge of his Lord, let alone from one like him (peace be upon him). Rather, this request for them is on account of their being penitent and returning to Him, glorified is His station. It is not far-fetched to say that his supplication was answered in this manner; indeed, it is a certainty with respect to him (ﷺ). How could one doubt that he was forgiven, shown mercy, and given the good of both abodes, while he is who he is? As for his people, it is apparent that the penitent among them were given the good of the Hereafter, for if this repentance was the repentance by killing, then al-Zuhri related that Allah the Exalted revealed to Musa, after what happened: "What grieves you? As for those among you who were killed, they are alive and provided for with Me; and as for those who remained, I have accepted their repentance." So Musa and the Children of Israel rejoiced at that. And if it was other than that, then it is known that repentance is accepted by virtue of the binding promise, and those whose repentance was accepted in the Hereafter are many. As for the good of this world, the verses have clearly stated that the people were drowned in it, and it suffices in that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾

Given this, it is possible to say in the interpretation of the answer that when He, glorified is He, saw in Musa (peace be upon him) intense anxiety and agitation, and for this reason he exaggerated in supplication, out of fear of the prolonged wrath of Allah the Exalted upon those for whom he feared such things, He, majestic is His glory, calmed his fright and answered his request in a wondrous manner and a marvelous, strange way. So He, glorified is He, said to him: ﴿My punishment﴾, i.e., that which you fear that some of My arrows, which I shoot by the hand of My majesty from the bows of My will, may strike, ﴿I afflict with it whom I will﴾. So your people, about whom you fear what you fear, are not specifically meant to be its target after they have repented of the sin and abandoned committing it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 156 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And My mercy has encompassed all things﴾: whether human or other, obedient or otherwise. There is no thing but that it is within it (My mercy), swimming in its currents or wandering through its wide deserts. Indeed, there is no one punished but that there seeps upon him something of what seeps from it, and not even the lowest of them do I punish with something harsher than what he is in, though I have power over him. So be content in soul and cool of eye. The entry of your people into a mercy that has encompassed all things, and has not been constricted from anything, is a matter about which there is no doubt and no uncertainty that could afflict it. How could it be otherwise, when they have turned back to Me (hādū ilayya) and come to Me as a delegation (wafadū ʿalayya)? Do you think that I would constrict what is broad upon them, and aim the arrows of disappointment at them, and send them back with two hunting-rebuffs (khuffayy Ḥunayn), so that each of them returns with empty hands? No, I do not see Myself doing that. Rather, I will have mercy on them and remove from them what distresses them, and I will write the greatest share of My mercy for their descendants (akhlāf) who come at the end of time, who are characterized by what pleases Me and who bear the burdens of what is required of them. To this the Exalted One's words allude: ﴿So I will write it for those who fear Me﴾, and so on.

Perhaps the mention of the punishment before the mention of the mercy is so that his mind (peace be upon him) might be free of what he fears, although in the reverse of this order there is something that necessitates the spreading out of the noble composition. And the description of their descendants with what they were described with is to rouse their resolve to attain what they are able to attain of it, or to remain steadfast upon it. In the answer he did not state explicitly that the request was granted, by saying, for example: "Your request has been granted, O Moses," choosing instead what is more eloquent in this regard. What we have mentioned, although it is not free from some flaw, is nevertheless preferable to much of what we have come across of the statements of the exegetes, some of which has already passed. I say after all this: the best of the possibilities is what the transmitted reports attest to, and if the hadith is authentic, then it is my doctrine. So reflect.

The sīn in (fa-sa-aktubuhā) may be for emphasis (ta'kīd), and it may be for the future (istiqbāl), as its meaning is not hidden from those of perfection.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 157 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those who follow the Messenger﴾ — the one whom Allah sent for conveying the rulings.
﴿the Prophet﴾
Page 79
That is, the one who informed creation about Allah, the Exalted. The first (Messenger) is considered with respect to its attribution to Allah, the Exalted, and the second (Prophet) is considered with respect to its attribution to creation. The first was placed before the second because of its nobility, and Allah's sending him precedes his conveying. Some scholars went to this view, and they took it as an indication that "Messenger" and "Prophet" here are meant in their linguistic sense, since both are applied to one person, just as they are in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾. In al-Kashshaf, the Messenger is defined as the one to whom a book is revealed, and the Prophet as the one who possesses a miracle, and it points to the difference between the Messenger and the Prophet by saying that the Messenger is one who has a particular book, while the Prophet is more general. Al-Kashf criticized this, saying that most of the messengers were not possessors of an independent book, such as Isma'il, Lot and Elias, peace be upon them, and "how many, how many." Then he said: The verified view is that the Prophet is the one who informs about His Essence, His attributes, and what reason cannot independently comprehend without an intermediary human, while the Messenger is the one who, in addition to that, is commanded to reform the people. So prophethood is considered with regard to informing about Allah, the Exalted, and messengership with regard to those sent to. The second, although more restricted in existence, is nevertheless two concepts that differ; for this reason one does not say "a messenger-prophet" in the manner of "a human animal." End quote.
In this there is a clear contradiction to what was mentioned first, and there is no prohibition on consideration. Yes, what they mentioned is refuted by the fact that the stated distinction, together with the difference of the two concepts, is in every case from the usage of the Sharia and convention; but in the original linguistic meaning and reality, they are general. Both are found in the Qur'an in both usages, so there is no contradiction between them.
It is not objected that mentioning the general Prophet after the specific Messenger is of no benefit, while the known pattern in such cases is the reverse. It is not hidden that what is meant by this Messenger-Prophet is our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him.
﴿the unlettered﴾, that is, the one who neither writes nor reads. According to what al-Zajjaj said, it is a relative noun referring to the nation of the Arabs, because most of them were like that.
Al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not calculate."
Or it refers to Umm al-Qura, because its people were like that. This is attributed to al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him; or to his mother, as if he is in the state in which his mother bore him. He (ﷺ) was described by this to draw attention that the perfection of his knowledge alongside his state is one of his miracles, peace and blessings be upon him. Thus, with respect to him, may my father and mother be his ransom, it is an attribute of praise; but with respect to others, it is not. This is like the attribute of arrogance, which is an attribute of praise for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and an attribute of blame for others.
It has been disputed whether writing ever proceeded from him, peace be upon him: Some said yes, it proceeded from him in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when he wrote the treaty, and this is also a miracle for him (ﷺ); the apparent meaning of the hadith requires it. Others said nothing at all proceeded from him, and that it was only attributed to him in the hadith metaphorically.
It has come from some of the People of the House, may Allah be pleased with them, that when he (ﷺ) looked at written letters, the letters would speak to him.
I have not found a chain that can be relied upon for this, and he (ﷺ) is above that.
Yes, Abu al-Shaykh narrated through Mujahid, who said: Awn ibn Abd Allah ibn Utba told me, from his father, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not die until he had read and written." So I mentioned this hadith to al-Sha'bi, and he said: "He spoke the truth; I heard our companions say that."
It is said: "al-Ummi" is a relative noun referring to umm (mother), with the hamza vowelled with a fatha, meaning "intention," because he is the intended one; and the damma on the hamza is a change of the relative form. Supporting this is the reading of Ya'qub (al-Ummiyyi) with fatha, though it may also be a change of the relative form.
The relative pronoun in the genitive position is a substitute for the first relative pronoun. It is either a substitute of the whole, if what is meant are these specific people, or a substitute of part, if it is general and "of them" is then understood. It is also permitted that it be an adjective for it, and it may be in the accusative position by way of cutting off with an implied governing verb, and it may be in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject. It is said: it is a subject whose predicate is the clause "He commands them" or "those are the successful," and both are contrary to what is immediately understood from the structure.
﴿whom they find written﴾ with his name and his noble attributes, such that they have no doubt that he is he; for this reason it deviated from saying "they find his name or his attribute written."
﴿with them﴾ is an adverbial complement of "written," which is in the position of a circumstantial clause, or of "they find," and it is mentioned for the sake of added confirmation, and that his state (ﷺ) is present with them and never absent from them at all.
﴿in the Torah and the Gospel﴾, which the Children of Israel count among their scriptures, past and future; and perhaps for this reason he restricted to them, otherwise he (ﷺ) is also written in the Psalms.
Ibn Sa'd, al-Darimi in his Musnad, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and Ibn Asakir narrated from Abd Allah ibn Salam who said: "The description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Torah: O Prophet, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news and a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My messenger; I have named you the Trusting. He is not coarse nor harsh, nor one who shouts in the markets, nor does he repay evil with evil, but he pardons and overlooks. Allah will not take him until he establishes through him the crooked community, until they say: There is no god but Allah, and he opens blind eyes, deaf ears and veiled hearts." A similar report is in the narration of al-Bukhari and others from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As.
There has come a report narrated by Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir through the route of Musa ibn Ya'qub al-Rab'i from Sahl, the client of Khaythama, who said: "I read in the Gospel the description of Muhammad (ﷺ): that he is neither short nor tall, white, with two braids, between his shoulders is a seal, he does not accept charity, he rides the donkey and the camel and milks the sheep, and he wears a patched shirt; whoever does that has been cleared of arrogance, and he does that. He is of the offspring of Isma'il, and his name is Ahmad."
There has come a report narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "Indeed Allah revealed in the Psalms: O Dawud, there will come after you a prophet whose name is Ahmad and Muhammad. I will never be angry with him, and he will never disobey Me. I have forgiven him before he disobeys Me, his earlier and later sins. His community is merciful; I have given them supererogatory acts like those I gave the prophets, and I have obligated upon them the duties I obligated upon the prophets and messengers, until they come to Me on the Day of Resurrection with their light like the light of the prophets. That is because I have obligated upon them to purify themselves for each prayer as I obligated it upon the prophets before them, and I commanded them to perform ritual bathing from impurity as I commanded the prophets before them, and I commanded them to pilgrimage as I commanded the prophets before them, and I commanded them to strive as I commanded the messengers before them. O Dawud, I have preferred Muhammad and his community over all the nations. I have given them six qualities that I did not give to other nations: I do not hold them accountable for error and forgetfulness; every sin they committed unintentionally, if they ask Me for forgiveness, I forgive it; whatever good they have sent ahead for their Hereafter, which they gave willingly, I hasten to them manifold, many times over, and they have with Me still more manifold, and better than that; and for calamities, if they are patient and say ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return﴾, I give them blessings, mercy and guidance to the gardens of bliss. If they call upon Me, I respond to them; either they see it quickly, or I turn away evil from them, or I store it for them in the Hereafter. O Dawud, whoever of the community of Muhammad meets Me testifying that there is no god but Allah, alone, without partner, sincere in it, he is with Me in My Paradise and My honour; and whoever meets Me having denied Muhammad, denied what he brought, and mocked My Book, I will pour punishment upon him from his grave, pour upon pour, and the angels will strike his face and back at his resurrection in his grave; then I will place him in the lowest level of the Fire."
Besides this there are other reports stating that he (ﷺ) is written in the divine books. The two adverbial phrases are connected either to "they find" or to "written." The mention of the Gospel before its revelation is of the same kind as what we are dealing with: the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Noble Qur'an before their coming.
﴿He commands them with what is right and forbids them from what is wrong﴾ — a resumed statement, which, it has been said, includes a detailed explanation of some rulings of
Page 81
the mercy that He promised earlier to write in summary; for what the conjunctions indicated are traces of the vast mercy. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative position as a presumed circumstantial clause from the object of "they find" or from the pronoun in "written." It is said: it explains "written," meaning: for what was written. By "what is right" it is said faith is meant; it is said: what is known in the Sharia. By "what is wrong," the opposite of that is meant.
﴿And he makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the wicked things﴾ — the first has been interpreted as things that the nature finds pleasant, like fats, and the second as things that the nature finds repugnant, like blood. Thus the verse indicates that the original rule for everything the soul finds pleasant and the nature enjoys is permissibility, and for everything the soul finds repugnant and the nature dislikes is prohibition, unless there is a separate proof. Some interpreted "the good" as what is good in the judgment of the Sharia, and "the wicked" as what is wicked in it, like usury and bribery.
It has been criticized that the statement then means: he makes lawful what is judged lawful and forbids what is judged unlawful, and there is no benefit in it. They rejected this by saying that it does yield a benefit, and what a benefit: because its meaning is that lawfulness and prohibition are by the judgment of the Sharia, not by reason and opinion. Some allowed that "the wicked" means what is found repugnant by nature, or what is wicked by the Sharia, and said: like blood or usury; and "the good" was exemplified by fat, and this was made to rest on the view that permission presupposes prior prohibition, since fat was forbidden among the Children of Israel; and on the view that prohibition presupposes prior permission, with blood and its like being prohibited by this view, because the original rule for things is permissibility. The verse ﴿Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾ is not an objection, because it is in reply to their saying ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾, or because what is meant is to keep it on its permissibility in contrast with the prohibition of usury. With this he dispelled what was supposed as lack of benefit.
﴿And he relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ — that is, he lightens for them the arduous obligations imposed on them, such as cutting off the place of impurity from a garment or from it and from the body, burning the spoils, the prohibition of the Sabbath, cutting off the erring limbs, and the requirement of retaliation in both intentional and unintentional killing without the legislation of blood money; for although this was not commanded in the tablets, it was legislated afterward as a severity upon them, according to what has been said. The root of "isr" is the heavy weight that binds its bearer from moving. "Aghlal" is the plural of "ghull," with a damma on the ghayn, which, in the original sense, as Ibn al-Athir said, is the iron piece that gathers the captive's hand to his neck, and it is also called "jami'a." Perhaps anything other than iron by which a hand is gathered to a neck is called that too. What is meant by them here is what you have known, and this is what is transmitted from many of the early scholars. And there is no hiding the metaphor in the verse.

Some have considered that there is a figurative sense here. It is reported from ʿAṭāʾ: "The Children of Israel, when they stood to pray, would wear coarse woollen garments and bind their hands to their necks. Often a man would pierce his collarbone, put the end of a chain through it, and tie it to a pillar, restraining himself for worship." On this view, "the shackles" (al-aghlal) may be taken in their literal sense.

Ibn ʿĀmir read *āṣārahum* in the plural. He also read *aṣrahum* with a fatḥah as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and with a ḍammah as a plural.

﴿So those who believed in him﴾, that is, affirmed his message and prophethood.

﴿and honoured him﴾, that is, magnified and revered him, as Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said. Al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said: *taʿzīr* is support together with magnification. The *taʿzīr* that falls short of a prescribed punishment (ḥadd) returns to this meaning, because it is discipline, and discipline is a form of support, since bad character is an enemy. For this reason the Ḥadīth says: "Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed." It was asked: "How can I help him when he is an oppressor?" He (ﷺ) said: "By restraining him from oppression."

According to many scholars, the root meaning of *taʿzīr* is prevention, and the intended sense here is preventing him so that no enemy can overpower him. It was also read *ʿazarūhu* with the lighter form. 

﴿and supported him﴾ against his enemies in religion. Connecting this to what precedes it is clear according to the report from the Ḥabr (Ibn ʿAbbās), and likewise according to what the majority said, since the first (honouring) is, on that reading, of the kind of *dar' al-mafāsid* (averting harms), while this (supporting) is of the kind of *jalb al-maṣāliḥ* (securing benefits). As for one who explained the first as magnification together with strengthening, taking it from al-Rāghib's words, he said here: "They supported him for Me."

Page 82

That is, they intended by supporting him the face of Allah the Exalted and the elevation of His word; so there is no repetition, contrary to those who imagined it.

﴿and followed the light that was sent down with him﴾, which is the Qur'an. It was described as light because it is manifest in itself through its inimitability and because it makes other things manifest, namely the rulings and the truthfulness of the claim. It is therefore most like visible light, which is evident by itself and makes other things evident. Indeed it is light upon light. The adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf*) may be connected to *anzala* (was sent down), and the sentence then contains an omitted modifier: "with his prophethood" or "with his sending (as messenger), upon him be peace", because the light was not sent down with him personally; it was sent down with Jibrīl (upon him be peace). Yes, his being sent or his prophethood was accompanied by the Qur'an, joined to it. Or it may be connected to *ittabaʿū* (followed), in the sense that they shared with him in following it, and then no supposition is needed. It may also be connected to it in the sense that they followed the Qur'an together with their following of the Prophet (ﷺ), as an indication of acting upon the Book and the Sunnah. It is also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *ittabaʿū*, meaning they followed the light while accompanying him in following it; its substance is what was mentioned in the second possibility. And it may be a predicated circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah) from the deputy subject of *unzila* (was sent down).

In *Majmaʿ al-Bayān* it is stated that *maʿa* here means *ʿalā* (upon), and that it is connected to *unzila*, though this usage is not well known. This was narrated, and some said that here it is synonymous with *ʿinda* (with), which is one of its well-known meanings, except that its remoteness is not hidden, even if it is said that the meaning then becomes "it was sent down upon him."

﴿Those﴾, that is, those described with these sublime attributes; ﴿they are the successful﴾, that is, they are the ones who attain the sought goal, not those characterised by the opposites of their qualities. In the demonstrative there is an indication that these qualities are the cause of the ruling. The *kāf* of distance indicates the remoteness of their rank and the height of their degree in excellence and nobility. The relative pronoun about which this sentence is predicated, according to Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), means the Jews who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said that it includes them and others of his community (upon him be peace) who possess this description until the Day of Resurrection. Being characterised by this does not depend on his (ﷺ) having been reached in person, as is not hidden; and this is the better view in my opinion.

Some have claimed that the relative pronoun in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So I will decree it for those who fear (Me)﴾, also has the more general meaning. Ibn al-Khāzin made this the view of the majority of exegetes. There is much to say about it. What is astonishing is that it is claimed the intended group were the Jews who lived in the time of Mūsā (upon him be peace). The sentence is a consequence of what preceded of his (ﷺ) sublime qualities. It was also said that it is based on the decree of mercy for those who passed. Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that it is an instruction on how to follow him (upon him be peace), a demonstration of the lofty rank of his followers, and their gaining the spoils of the vast mercy in both abodes, following the explanation of his sublime qualities, and an indication of his guidance (upon him be peace) and of them through what is contained in ﴿He enjoins them﴾ etc. The restriction indicated by His words, exalted is He, ﴿those are the successful﴾, is taken as relative to other nations. Then he said: "So the people of Mūsā (upon him be peace) enter it by primary inclusion, since they were not spared from the severe hardship of their repentance." This is founded on the method he followed in explaining the verses from the outset, and it is not free of turbidity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 158:

﴿Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all.﴾ When He had related what is in the two Scriptures concerning his attributes, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the nobility of those who follow him, as you have come to know, he was commanded, peace be upon him, to proclaim what contains a rebuke to the Jews who forbade following him, and a warning to the rest of mankind against the fabrication of those among them who claimed that he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was sent only to the Arabs. It has also been said that this is a command to him, peace be upon him, to make clear that the felicity of the two abodes referred to in what preceded is not restricted to those People of the Two Books who followed him, but includes everyone who follows him, whoever he may be. This is by explaining the universality of his mission, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, which is general to both humans and jinn, as the texts affirm, to the extent that scholars have declared the one who denies it to be a disbeliever. What is stated here does not contradict this, and the mafhum (implied meaning by inference) in it
Page 83
is not regarded as valid by the one who holds it, due to the absence of its condition, and this is evident.

﴿The One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is in a position of nasb (accusative) by an implied "I mean" or similar, or of raf' (nominative) by an implied "He is."

It has been permitted that it be in a position of jarr (genitive), as a sifah (qualifier) of the Name of Majesty or a badal (substitute, apposition) from it. Abu al-Baqa' considered this unlikely because of the separation between them. It was answered that it is among what is not foreign, and is in the status of that in which there is no separation. The first possibility was preferred for its grandeur, since it would then be an independent sentence indicating that the one mentioned is known in this regard, i.e., "Mention the One whose status is not hidden from the one who agrees and the one who disagrees." It has also been said that He is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is ﴿There is no god but He﴾. In the earlier possibilities, it is a bayan (explanation) of what precedes it. Al-Zamakhshari, in addition to this, made it a badal from the silah (relative clause). Sibawayh explicitly affirmed the permissibility of this construction, and al-Allamah mentioned that the context of his speech indicates that it is a badal al-isti'mal (substitution in usage). The basis of the explanation is that whoever owns the world, its upper and lower parts, is the God, so there is a mutual implication between them that justifies making the second an explanation of the first. The intended meaning of "explanation" is not proof by evidence, so as to say: the apparent is the reverse, because the proof of His exclusive divinity, may He be glorified, is His ownership of the entire world, though it is also valid to make it a proof of this, saying: the proof that He, majestic is His affair, is the Owner who disposes of that is that divinity is restricted to Him, since if there were another god besides Him, he would have that. Abu Hayyan objected to the view of substitution, saying that the substitution of sentences for sentences not sharing a governing element is not known. It was responded that the scholars of meanings (ma'ani) mentioned it, and that defining the follower as "every second word that takes the i'rab (grammatical case) of its preceding word" is not comprehensive.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is for increasing the affirmation of His divinity, may He be glorified. It has also been said that it is for increasing the specificity of His, exalted is He, being the one who does this, and it has a fine rationale.

The fa' (then) in His saying, may His affair be exalted: ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ is for deducing the command from what has been established of his mission, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. Mentioning his noble self, peace be upon him, with the title of Messenger, by way of iltifat (shift) to the third person, is for emphasis on the necessity of compliance. Describing the Messenger with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Prophet, the unlettered﴾ is for praising him and for increasing the affirmation of his matter and confirming that he is the one written of in the two Scriptures.

﴿Who believes in Allah and His words﴾: these are what was revealed to him and to the rest of the Messengers, peace be upon them, of His books and revelation. It was read as (wa-kalimatihi) (and His word, singular), to intend the genus, or the Qur'an, or Jesus, peace be upon him, as was reported from Mujahid, as an allusion to the Jews and a warning that whoever does not believe in him, peace be upon him, his faith will not be considered. Bringing this description, which urges the People of the Two Books to comply with what they were commanded, and the explicit mention of belief in Allah, exalted is He, is to alert that belief in Him, glorified is He, is never separate from belief in His words and is not realized except through it. The sincerity and the avoidance of tribal partisanship shown in this verse is not hidden, and they considered this a subtle point for the iltifat and the employment of those attributes.

﴿And follow him﴾: that is, in everything he brings and everything he leaves of the matters of the religion.

﴿So that you may be guided﴾: this is a cause (ta'lil) for the two verbs, or a hal (circumstantial clause) from their subjects. That is: in hope of your being guided to the goal, or hoping for it. In linking it to both, there is a notification that whoever affirms him but does not follow him by adhering to his law is still in the wilderness of error.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 159 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And among the people of Musa﴾, meaning the Children of Israel, ﴿there is a community﴾, a great group, ﴿who guide﴾ people ﴿with the truth﴾, i.e., acting justly. The bāʾ (the particle *bi*) here may be for *mulābasa* (accompaniment), so that the prepositional phrase (*al-jārr wa'l-majrūr*) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). Or the bāʾ may be for instrumentality (*āla*), attached to the word *al-ḥaqq*, so that the prepositional phrase is *laghw* (superfluous in terms of grammatical function). ﴿And by it﴾, i.e., by the truth, ﴿they judge justly﴾ in the rulings that apply among them. The use of the present tense in both verbs indicates continuity and renewal. There is disagreement about who is meant. It is said: they were people who were like this during the time of Musa (ﷺ), and the discourse is addressed to remove what the restriction of the writing of mercy, piety and faith in the signs to the followers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) might suggest, namely that the forebears of the people of Musa (peace be upon him) were deprived of all good, and to clarify that not all of them were as their conditions have been described, but among them were those described with such-and-such. The present tense is used to narrate a past state.

Shaykh al-Islam chose this view. It is not far from my opinion that this is an explanation of another group among the people, contrasted with what Musa (peace be upon him) mentioned in his words: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ This is an explicit statement that among the people there were those who did not do it. It is also said: they were people who existed during the time of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and were described with this, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and others like him. Al-Tibi preferred this view, saying it is the closest of the interpretations. That is because when Allah, the Exalted, answered Musa's supplication with His words: ﴿So I will write it﴾, up to His words, glorified is He: ﴿those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered﴾, etc., then He commanded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to declare what contains a rebuke to the Jews and an alert to their fabrications concerning what they claim about his (peace be upon him) matter, while showing fairness. This is by His words, the Exalted: ﴿Say: O mankind﴾, etc., and His words, glorified is He: "So believe" etc. He followed that with His words, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And among the people of Musa﴾, etc. The meaning is that some of those about whom We have related what We related believed and were fair toward themselves, guiding the people to the fact that he (peace be upon him) is the promised Messenger, and telling them: "This is the Prophet, the unlettered Messenger, whom we find written with us in the Torah and the Gospel." They judge justly and do not oppress. But most of them were not fair, confused the truth with falsehood, concealed it, and were unjust in the rulings. Therefore the mention of this group is an allusion to the majority.

It has been objected that those among the people of Musa who believed during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were few, and the word *ummah* indicates multitude. Also, these people have already been mentioned previously. It was answered that the word *ummah* may be applied to a few, especially if they have a distinguished status. It may even be applied to a single individual if he is such, as in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was an ummah﴾. And the mention of them here is for the point that has been indicated, and mentioning them previously for a different purpose does not preclude it. Repeating the same thing for differing purposes is a well-known practice in the Book. Moreover, it has been said: previously they were described with what clearly indicates that they were guided, and here they are described with what clearly indicates that they guide, so from the two mentions it results that they are described with both attributes. Yes, the discussion remains about the wisdom of the separation (*fasl*), and perhaps it is not hidden from the one who reflects.

It is also said: they are a group of the Children of Israel who existed between Musa and our Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon both of them), and they still exist now. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Juraij that he said: "It has reached me that when the Children of Israel killed their prophets and disbelieved, and they were twelve tribes, one tribe disassociated itself from what they did, apologized, and asked Allah to separate them from them. So Allah opened for them a tunnel in the earth, and they travelled through it until they emerged from beyond China. They are there as ḥanīfs, facing our qiblah, and it is to them that the reference is made," as Ibn ʿAbbas said, by His words, the Exalted: ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude﴾. The promise of the Hereafter was interpreted as the descent of ʿIsa (peace be upon him). He said: they traveled in the tunnel for a year and a half.

Muqatil mentioned, as Abu al-Shaykh narrated, that Allah made a river flow for them, and made for them a lamp of light before them, and that their land to which they emerged gathers together vermin, livestock, and predators, mixed together. And that the Prophet (ﷺ) came to them on the night of the Mi'raj with Jibril (peace be upon him), and they believed in him, and he taught them the prayer.

From al-Kalbi, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi': that he (peace be upon him) taught them zakah and ten surahs of the Qur'an that were revealed in Makkah, and commanded them to gather and to abandon the Sabbath. And he conveyed to them the greeting of Musa (peace be upon him), and the Prophet (peace be upon him) returned the greeting.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: "Between you and them is a river of sand that flows." Ibn al-Khazin declared this narration weak, and I do not consider it anything, nor do I think you will find for it a chain of transmission that can be relied upon, even if you sought a tunnel in the earth or a ladder in the sky.

(Furthermore, among the allusive indications in the verses):

﴿He said: O Musa, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech﴾, without seeing Me, according to what those who deny the vision of Allah say.

﴿So take what I have given you﴾ with empowerment.

﴿And be among the grateful﴾ by steadfastness in fulfilling the right of servitude, beyond which there is no higher station:

*Do not call Me except by "O His servant," for it is the most noble of My names.*

And by gratitude favors increase, as this Book has declared.

﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾, i.e., We manifested the engravings of his readiness upon the tablets of the details of his existence, of spirit, heart, intellect, thought and imagination. Thus there appeared in them ﴿of every thing an admonition and a detailed explanation of every thing. So take them with strength﴾, i.e., with resolve, so that you may be among its people.

﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of them﴾, i.e., the most beneficial of them, which are the resolutions.

﴿I will show you the abode of the defiant﴾, i.e., the end of those who do not take up that.

﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾. They are those who are in the station of the self, so their arrogance becomes a veil for them from the signs of Allah, the Exalted. As for those who are arrogant with the truth, who are those whose attributes have passed away and upon whom the attributes of their Lord have appeared, they are not veiled, and their arrogance is not considered blameworthy, because it is not truly arrogance; rather their share of it is that they become a locus of manifestation for it.

﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, since they were veiled by their attributes and their deeds. Their deeds have failed, and they will not bring them closer to anything.

﴿And the people of Musa took, after him, from their ornaments, a calf﴾, which the Samiri made for them. He was from a people who worshipped the calf, or he was one who saw them, and love for it fell into his heart, because of the badness of his readiness, and he concealed its worship. He chose to shape it from their ornaments so that their inclination toward it would be more complete, because the human heart inclines toward what it possesses, especially if it is gold or silver. Many people today are slaves to the dirham and the dinar, and these two are for them the spiritual calf, even if they do not prostrate to it. Most of the sayings are that this calf became possessed of flesh and blood, to which the reference is made by His words, the Exalted: ﴿a body that had a lowing﴾. And in the words of al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, it is that it became possessed of spirit through the dust that the Trusted Spirit (Jibril) trod upon, but he did not explicitly state that it had flesh and blood.

﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾, i.e., he was stunned by the intensity of anger so that he was distracted from them, turned away from the ruling of what is in them, and forgot what is praiseworthy, such as forbearance, for example, in anger, which everyone finds within himself.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself﴾, supposing that he had been negligent in restraining them.

﴿He said: O son of my mother﴾: he addressed him thus because mercy overcame him. The interpretation of this in terms of the inner selves, according to what some interpreters have said, is that the Samiri of desire, after Musa (peace be upon him) went up in spirit for the appointed time of speaking with the Truth, took from the ornaments of worldly adornment and the vanities of human nature, which the Children of Israel had borrowed, the attributes of the heart from the Copts, the attributes of the self, an object of worship toward which they hasten, having a lowing, by which it calls creatures to its own self.

﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾ with what benefits them.

﴿Nor guide them to a way﴾ toward the truth.

﴿They took it, and they were wrong-doers﴾, in that they turned away from the worship of the Truth to the worship of other than Him in their view. ﴿And when they were overcome with regret﴾, i.e., they repented when Musa returned in spirit, and they said: ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy on us﴾ with the pulls of divine care, ﴿and forgive us﴾ by concealing our attributes with His attributes, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿we will certainly be among the losers﴾, having lost the capital of this creation, which is readiness.

﴿And when Musa returned to his people﴾, who are the human attributes, ﴿angry﴾ because the attributes of the heart had worshipped the calf of the world, ﴿grieved﴾ over what was lost to them of the worship of the Truth.

﴿He said: Evil is what you have done in my absence after me﴾ in that you did not follow my path.

﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾ by returning to the perishable without His command, the Exalted.

﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾, i.e., what appeared to him of the divine illuminations at the overpowering of natural anger.

﴿And seized his brother﴾, who is the heart, dragging him toward himself by force. ﴿He said: O son of my mother﴾: he addressed him thus although he was his brother from his father, who is the world of command, and from his mother, who is the world of creation, because they were both in the world of creation. ﴿Indeed the people﴾, i.e., the attributes of humanity, ﴿have oppressed me﴾ during your absence, ﴿and nearly killed me﴾, removing from me the life of my readiness entirely. ﴿So do not let the enemies rejoice at my expense﴾, and they are themselves, and this is what the station of distinction requires. ﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me and my brother﴾, conceal our attributes. ﴿And admit us into Your mercy﴾ by bestowing upon us the true attributes. ﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, because every mercy is a ray of the light of Your mercy.

﴿Indeed those who took the calf﴾, i.e., the calf of the world, as a god, ﴿will be overtaken by wrath from their Lord﴾, which is the punishment of the veil, and humiliation in the life of this world by enslavement to this perishable thing that brings them near.

﴿And thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾, those who fabricate against Allah, the Exalted, thereby affirming an existence for other than Him.

﴿And those who committed evil deeds, then repented﴾, returning to Him, glorified and exalted is He, through striving against their souls and annihilating them. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after them, is Forgiving﴾, so He conceals their attributes; ﴿Merciful﴾, so He bestows upon them from His attributes. When the anger subsided from Musa, he took up the divine tablets, ﴿and in their copy is guidance﴾, direction to the Truth, ﴿and mercy for those who fear their Lord﴾, who are afraid, owing to the goodness of their readiness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 159 (part 2 of 2):

It is said regarding His, glorified and exalted be He, words: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time﴾, that Musa, peace be upon him, chose seventy men from the nobles and choicest of his people, those who were qualified, pure, eager, seeking, and treading the path (sulook). ﴿So when the quaking seized them﴾, that is, the trembling of the body, which is among the beginnings of the swoon of annihilation (fana') upon the flashing of lights and the appearance of the first rays of the manifestations of the Attributes (tajalliyat al-sifat): the shivering and quivering of the body. This movement often comes upon the wayfarers (salikin) at the time of remembrance (dhikr), or the hearing of the Qur'an, or whatever affects them, until their limbs nearly come apart. We have witnessed this in the eternal ones (al-Khalidin) of the Naqshbandi order (al-Tariqa al-Naqshbandiyya), and sometimes a cry (sihah) accompanies it during their prayer. Some of them then repeat their prayer because of it, and some do not repeat it. The objection to them has been great, and I heard some of the objectors saying: "If this state occurs with awareness and intellect, it is bad manners and certainly invalidates the prayer; and if it occurs without awareness and with loss of intellect, it nullifies wudu', and we see them not performing wudu'." It was answered that it is involuntary while intellect and awareness are present, and it is like sneezing and coughing; for this reason wudu' is not nullified, nor is the prayer invalidated. Some Shafi'i scholars have stated explicitly that if laughter overcomes a worshipper during prayer, his prayer is not invalidated and he is excused for it. Therefore it is not far-fetched that what results from the effects of involuntary manifestations is included in what has been mentioned. It does not follow that because something is involuntary it occurs without awareness; for the movement of one who trembles is involuntary while he is aware of it, and this is evident, so there is no point in the objection.

Yes, His Eminence our Master Shaykh Khalid, may his secret be sanctified, used to order those among the disciples who were affected by this to perform wudu' and repeat the prayer, to close the door of objection. The truth is that what affects this group does not nullify wudu', since intellect does not disappear with it, but it invalidates the prayer because of the cry in it, in which two letters become audible, together with matters that prayer does not permit. There is no excuse for one affected by it, unless he is afflicted with it in such a way that no part of the time sufficient for prayer passes without it; in that case he is excused, and there is no obligation to make up (qada') the prayer if that state passes from him, like one who has an itch and cannot bear not scratching.

The Grandfather (al-Jadd), may Allah have mercy on him, stated in his glosses (hawashi) on the commentary of al-Hadramiyya by the scholar Ibn Hajar, regarding a case of one afflicted with chronic coughing of this kind, then said: "Branch: If he is afflicted with this and knows from his habit that the bathhouse calms it for a period sufficient for prayer, it is obligatory for him to enter it, provided he finds the cost of the bathhouse surplus to what is required by natural need (al-fitra), even if he misses congregational prayer and the virtue of the beginning of the time." End of quote.

Yes, he, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, mentioned, regarding the large action that invalidates prayer, which is three acts: that if one is afflicted with an involuntary movement from which a great deal of action results, he is excused. He also said: a sound that does not include the pronunciation of two consecutive letters from the nose or mouth does not harm, even if the lip murmuring of a mute accompanies it, even without need; and even if an intelligent person understands speech, or intends to imitate some animal sounds, provided he does not intend mockery; otherwise it invalidates the prayer. One should investigate the state of these people, for their condition in this varies; but most of what we have witnessed is in the manner we have described. The full discussion of this matter is to be sought in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

﴿He said: My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me﴾. This is from the intensity of the overpowering of longing, and "law" here is for wishing. Will You destroy us with the punishment of veiling and deprivation, because of what the foolish ones did in worshipping the calf? ﴿It is only Your trial﴾, in which no one else has any part. This is required by the station of the manifestation of the Acts (tajalli al-af'al). So forgive us the sins of our attributes and our essences, as You forgave the sins of our acts, and have mercy on us by pouring forth the lights of Your witnessing and lifting the veil of selfhood (inniyya) through Your existence. And ordain for us in this world a good, which is the good of steadfastness through subsistence after annihilation, and in the Hereafter a good, which is the vision. The discussion of the rest of the matter is not hidden from one who has the least taste.

Except that some of them interpreted the punishment in His, glorified and exalted be He, words: ﴿My punishment—I afflict with it whom I will﴾ as the particular punishment of longing that afflicts the elite among the favored ones, which is the mercy whose essence cannot be grasped and whose measure cannot be determined; and indeed it is more precious than red sulphur (al-kibrit al-ahmar). The people of the outward see it as distant, while the people of the Way say: we see it as near. They also said: "al-Ummi" is a relative term derived from "umm" (mother), but in the manner of "ahmari" (red). This was said of the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, because he is the mother of existent things and the origin of hidden things. This term was chosen for what it contains of an indication of mercy and compassion, and he is the one who came as a mercy to the worlds. Indeed he, upon whom be blessings and peace, is more compassionate toward creation than a mother toward her child, since he has the greatest share of morality with the character of Allah, the Exalted, and He, glorified be He, is the Most Merciful of the merciful. They mentioned that his followers, in terms of prophethood, are the elite; in terms of being unlettered, the elite of the elite; and in terms of the message, all those mentioned together with the common folk. We ask Allah, the Exalted, to grant us success in following him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, in all his affairs.

[Page 87]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 160:**

﴿And We divided them﴾, meaning the people of Musa (peace be upon him), not the nation mentioned previously, as proximity might suggest. (*Qatta'a*) is read with shaddah and without shaddah. The first is the mutawatir (widely transmitted) reading. It takes one object, but it may be understood to carry the meaning of *sayyara* (to make), in which case it takes two objects. Thus His statement, exalted is He, ﴿twelve﴾, is either a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) or a second object (*maf'ul thani*). The meaning is: We divided them, counted by this number, or We made them twelve nations, each distinguished from the others. His statement, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿tribes﴾, as Ibn al-Hajib said in his commentary on al-Mufassal, is a *badal* (substitute) for the number, not a *tamyiz* (specifying accusative) for it. Otherwise they would have been thirty-six. Accordingly, the *tamyiz* is omitted, meaning "a group" or something similar. Al-Hufi said: the qualifier of the *tamyiz* has been placed in its position, and the original is "a group of tribes." It is also permissible that it be a *tamyiz*, because it is singular in interpretation. They mentioned that *al-sibt* in the singular means the son of a son, or the son of a daughter or of a son, or a piece of something. These are sayings recorded by Ibn al-Athir. Then the word was used for every community of the Children of Israel, like the tribe among the Arabs. Perhaps this is a naming of them by the name of their ancestor, like Tamim. It may also be applied to each tribe among them as *asbat*, just as the Ansar came to be applied to a specific group. In that case it has the meaning of a clan and a tribe, and for this reason it occurred in the position of a singular in the *tamyiz*. This is like the dual of a plural in the words of Abu al-Najm describing a mare that had become accustomed to war:

*She grazed at the first of the grazing, between the spears of Malik and Nahshal.*

The feminine form of *ithnatay* (two, feminine) is used even though the counted noun is masculine. Numbers below three follow the original masculine and feminine forms, because this is interpreted as a feminine noun, and this is clear from what we have established. Al-A'mash and others read *'ashirata* with a kasrah on the shin. It is also reported from him with a fathah. The kasrah is the dialect of Tamim, and the sukun is the dialect of the Hijaz. His statement, glorified is He, ﴿nations﴾, is a substitute after a substitute from ﴿twelve﴾, not from *asbat*, on the assumption that it is a substitute, because a substitute is not substituted from a substitute. It is also permissible that it be a substitute from it when it is not a substitute and an attribute if it is so, or if it is not.

﴿And We revealed to Musa when his people asked him for water﴾, when thirst overcame them in the wilderness. ﴿Strike the rock with your staff﴾ is an explanation of the act of revelation. (*Fa-an*) here means *ay* (namely). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a verbal particle (*masdariyya*).

﴿Then there gushed forth﴾, meaning it burst forth, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Tabarsi claimed that *al-inbijas* is the emergence of water in small quantity, and *al-infijar* is its emergence in abundance. The expression of this in one way and of the other in another way is in terms of the beginning of the emergence and what it reached. The conjunction is upon an implied element to which the speech extends, meaning: he struck, and there gushed forth. The conjunctive element was omitted because there is no ambiguity, and to indicate speed of compliance, to the point that the revelation and the striking are as though one matter. The gushing forth was by the command of God, to the point that the act of Musa, peace be upon him, seems to have no part in it.

Some of the verifying scholars mentioned that this *fa* is, according to what has been established, an *fasiha* (a particle that indicates an elided condition). Some of them estimate a condition in the speech: "So when you strike, it has gushed forth." This is not fitting to the sublime composition.

﴿Every people knew their drinking place﴾, meaning every tribe. The expression of them by this is to indicate the abundance of each one of the tribes. *Unas* is either a plural or a collective noun. Al-Sa'd mentioned that the people of the language call the collective noun a plural. *'Alima* here means *'arafa* (to know), which takes one object, meaning: he knew.

﴿Their drinking place﴾, meaning their own particular spring. The reason for the plural is clear.

﴿And We shaded them with clouds﴾, meaning We made it such that it cast its shade upon them to protect them from the heat of the sun. It moved with their movement and stood still when they stood still.

﴿And We sent down upon them manna and quail﴾, meaning *al-taranjabin* (a sweet exudate) and *al-sumana* (quail). Each one of them would take what sufficed him of that.

﴿Eat﴾, meaning: We said, or saying to them: eat.

﴿Of the good things We have provided for you﴾, meaning their delicious things. *Ma* is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun, referring to the manna and quail.

﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ is conjoined to an implied element for brevity and to convey that it is an established matter that needs no explicit statement. The meaning is: so they did wrong, by disbelieving in these great blessings.

﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾ by that.

﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ by disbelief, since its harm does not pass beyond them. The fronting of the object conveys the restriction required by the preceding negation. In the speech there is a degree of mockery and an indication of their persistence in what they had, which is not hidden.

[Page 88]

And when it was said to them: ﴿Dwell in this town﴾ is governed by *udhkuru* (remember). The verb is given here in the passive form (*buniya lil-maf'ul*), following the manner of divine majesty (*sunan al-kibriya'*), and with the indication that the agent is too exalted to be named. The meaning is: remember for them the time when We said to their forefathers, ﴿Dwell in this town﴾, the town nearby, which is Bayt al-Maqdis or Jericho (Arihá). The accusative (*al-nasb*) here is either the direct object, as in *sakantu al-dar* (I dwelt in the house), or an adverbial of place used in an extended sense (*ittisa'an*). The use of the word "dwelling" (*al-uskuna*) here indicates that what was commanded in al-Baqarah was entering with the intention of settling; that is, "Settle in this town."

﴿and eat from it﴾, that is, from its foods and fruits, or from the town itself, with *min* being partitive (*tab'idiyya*) or initial (*ibtida'iyya*).

﴿wherever you wish﴾, that is, from its various parts, without anyone competing with you. The conjunction *wa* (and) is used here, whereas *fa* (so) is used in al-Baqarah. The reason is that there the command was "Enter," so the sequence (*ta'qib*) fits with it; here the command is "Dwell," and dwelling is a continuing state, so eating is with it, not after it. It has been said that when the effect (*musabbab*) follows from the cause (*sabab*), both coexist in existence, so either *wa* or *fa* may be used. But this only shows that both expressions are valid, and that is not the question at issue. The word ﴿raghadan﴾ (abundantly) was mentioned there, because eating at the beginning of entering is more pleasant, whereas after dwelling, taking it is not like that.

[Page 89]

It has also been said that he sufficed with the expression "Dwell" and omitted mention of ﴿raghadan﴾, because continuous eating without competition can only be abundant and wide. The first view was taken by the author of *al-Lubab* (Ibn 'Adil). It is objected to both views that He mentioned "abundantly" together with the command to dwell in the story of Adam, peace be upon him, but perhaps the matter there is easy.

﴿And say, "Forgiveness," and enter the gate prostrating﴾. This has been discussed in al-Baqarah, except that the order of the two matters there is the reverse of here in terms of precedence and sequence. There is no harm in that, because what is commanded is the combination of the two commands without considering their order. Al-Qutb (al-Shirazi) said: the benefit of the difference is to draw attention to the goodness of placing each of the two mentioned before the other, since the intent of both is the glorification of God Most High and the manifestation of humility and submission, so the situation does not differ in precedence and sequence.

﴿We will forgive you your misdeeds﴾ is in the jussive after the imperative as its response. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read *tughfar* (be forgiven) with the *ta'* and in the passive voice, and *khatī'atukum* in the nominative and plural, except Ibn 'Amir, who read it in the singular. Abu 'Amr read *khatayakum* as in Surat al-Baqarah. Al-Qutb explained the benefit of the difference between what is there and what is here, according to the well-known reading, as an indication that these sins, whether few or many, are forgiven after the performance of what is commanded.
