The omission of the conjunction *wa* in His words, Glorified and Exalted is He, ﴿We will increase the good-doers﴾, indicates that this increase is pure bounty, not in exchange for what they were commanded, as has been said.

The meaning is that their obedience was rewarded by God Most High with forgiveness, and He added to it, and that addition is pure bounty from Him, Exalted is He. Thus something may enter into the reward in form, since it is consequent upon their action, and it may also go beyond it, since it is an increase over what they deserved. For this reason it is joined with the *sin* (the particle of future), which indicates that it is a promise and a favour. The object of *nazid* (We will increase) is omitted; that is, reward and increase from Him, in His words, may He be exalted in glory:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 162:

﴿So those who did wrong among them substituted⦆ — for the sake of added clarification. That is: those among these people who did wrong substituted for what they were commanded, namely repentance and seeking forgiveness (istighfar), since they turned away from it and put in its place ﴿a different saying﴾ of what has no good in it, ﴿other than what had been said to them﴾ and what they had been commanded to say. The word (ghayr, "other than") is an attribute of the saying, and he stated the difference explicitly, although the substitution already indicates it, in order to confirm the opposition and to specify the difference in every respect.

﴿So We sent upon them﴾ immediately after what they did, without delay.

﴿A plague (rijz) from the heaven﴾: a punishment coming from it, which in one narration was the plague (ta'un).

﴿Because they used to do wrong﴾: that is, because of their continuous wrongdoing, both past and future. This has the same meaning as what is in al-Baqarah, because the pronoun in ʿalayhim refers to those who did wrong, and sending down from above is a kind of sending down (inzal). The explicit statement of this cause is because the ruling here is attached to the pronoun rather than to the relative clause with wrongdoing, as in al-Baqarah. As for the causation by transgression (fisq) after the indication that wrongdoing is the cause there, it is to notify that this is transgression, departure from obedience, and excess in wrongdoing, and that their punishment was for all the abominations they committed, as has been said.

Al-Qutb said regarding the aspect of difference: sending (irsal) implies multiplicity, unlike sending down (inzal), so it is as if He sent down a small punishment which then was made numerous. And the benefit of mentioning wrongdoing and transgression in both places is to indicate that both were present in them together. You have already been given, in the aspects of difference between the verse of al-Baqarah and this verse, what will benefit you to recall, so recall it.

[Page 90]

﴿And ask them﴾ is conjoined with (remember), referred to in what preceded. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the third-person pronoun refers to the Jews of his time who were present with him, peace and blessings be upon him. That is: ask the Jews who were contemporaries of yours a question of reproach and affirmation, given their earlier transgression of the limits of Allah, the Exalted. The purpose is to inform them of this, because they used to conceal it. Knowledge of it, given that he (ﷺ) was not one who had studied their books or learned from their scholars anything that would indicate it came from revelation, would make it a miracle testifying against them. ﴿about the town﴾, that is, about its news, its condition, and what befell its people from the "third of the hearthstones" (the third of the three stones used for cooking pots). Asking about it may be understood to include asking about the people themselves and their families, or the speech is taken with an omitted noun, so that it means the condition of the people of the town. It is also permissible to read the word in a figurative sense. According to Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr, it is Aylah, a town between Madyan and Mount Sinai (al-Ṭūr).

According to Ibn Shihab, it is Tiberias. It was also said to be Madyan, and this is a report from al-Ḥabr (the scholar). According to Ibn Zayd, it is Maqtaʾ, between Madyan and ʿAynūnā.

﴿which was situated by the sea﴾, that is, near it, overlooking its shore.

﴿when they transgressed on the Sabbath﴾, that is, they wronged and exceeded the limits of Allah, the Exalted, by hunting on the Sabbath day, or by (failing to) honor it. The word *idh* (when) is a substitute for the thing asked about, a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion), or it is an adverb of time for the verbal noun (in the phrase "asking about"). It was said that the possibility of it being an adverb of time for *kānat* (was) or *ḥāḍiratan* (situated) is not valid, since there is no benefit in restricting the dwelling or presence to the time of transgression. The pronoun in *yaʿdūna* (they transgress) refers to the people, either understood or implied by the speech. It was also said that it refers to the town, by way of *istikhdam* (a rhetorical device in which one word carries two meanings, here the town and its people). It has been read as *yaʿaddūna* with the meaning of *yaʿtadūna* (they transgress), where the *tāʾ* is assimilated into the *dāl* and its vowel is transferred to the *ʿayn*. It may also be read as *yuʿiddūna* from *iʿdād* (preparing), since they used to prepare hunting equipment on the Sabbath day, although they were forbidden to occupy themselves with anything on it other than worship.

﴿when their fish came to them﴾: this is an adverb of time for *yaʿdūna*, or a substitute after a substitute. Most grammarians took it to be the former, and it is the preferable view, since asking about their transgression is more forceful in reproach. *Ḥītān* is the plural of *ḥūt* (fish), in which the *wāw* was changed to *yāʾ* because it is quiescent and the letter before it is kasra-vowelled, as in *nūn* and *nīnāt* in both form and meaning. Its attribution to them is because the intended fish are those found in the region where they dwelt. It was also said that it indicates that they are specifically theirs, because they have peculiar extraordinary properties not usually found in other members of the species. The distance of this view is not hidden.

﴿on their Sabbath day﴾ is an adverb of time for *taʾtīhim* (came to them). That is, they came to them on the day when they honored the matter of the Sabbath. *Sabt* is a verbal noun from *sabatat al-yahūd*, meaning the Jews honored the Sabbath day by abstaining from work and devoting themselves to worship on it. It was also said that it is a name for the day, and the attribution is due to their being specifically subject to rulings on it. The first view is supported by the reading of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (*yawma isbātihim*), and likewise the negation that follows.

﴿openly⁠﴾, that is, visible on the surface of the water, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: close to the shore. It is the plural of *shāriʿ*, from *sharaʿa ʿalayhi*, meaning he drew near and overlooked. In *sharʿ* (law) there is the sense of manifestation and clarification. It was also said: fish *shurraʿ* (raising their heads), as if this were made a manifestation and clarification. It was also said that the meaning is "successive" (following one another), attributed to al-Ḥaḍḥāk. The apparent meaning is that they were visible, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of *al-ḥītān* (the fish).

﴿and on the day they did not keep the Sabbath﴾, that is, they did not observe the matter of the Sabbath. This is like the saying of the poet: "On a path with no clear track, by whose landmarks no one is guided." The intended meaning is the negation of observing the Sabbath. ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, read *lā yusbitūn* with a *ḍamma* on the imperfect prefix, from *asbata*, meaning he entered the Sabbath, like *aṣbaḥa* (he entered the morning). It is reported from al-Ḥasan that he read *lā yusbatūn* in the passive, meaning they did not enter the Sabbath and were not commanded in it with what they had been commanded on the Sabbath day. It was also read *lā yusbitūn* with a *ḍamma* on the *bāʾ*. The adverbial phrase is related to His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿they did not come to them⁠﴾. That is, they did not come to them on the day they did not keep the Sabbath, as they used to come to them on the Sabbath day, out of fear of their hunting, because the fish had become accustomed to their conditions, and this was by the sheer decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. The arrangement was changed in that the adverb was placed before the verb and not the reverse, because the coming on their Sabbath day suggests the question "so what is their condition on the day they do not keep the Sabbath?" and so it was answered: "on the day they do not keep the Sabbath, it does not come to them."

﴿Thus We test them⁠﴾, that is, We treat them as those who test them, so that what is apparent from them becomes manifest, and We then hold them accountable for it. The present tense is used to narrate a past condition, in order to evoke its image and express wonder at it. The demonstrative refers either to the earlier trial or to the trial mentioned after it, as has been noted more than once. It was also said that it refers to the coming on the Sabbath day, and it is connected to what precedes, meaning: they did not come to them in the same manner as the coming on the Sabbath day. *Al-kāf* (the "like" particle) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state according to al-Ṭabarsī, and it is also permissible that it be attached to an omitted element functioning as an attribute of an implied verbal noun, meaning a coming of such a kind. The clause *nabluhum* (We test them) is a resumptive statement built upon the question about the wisdom behind the difference in the state of the fish, sometimes coming and sometimes not.

﴿because they used to defy⁠﴾, that is, because of their continuous defiance in everything they did and left undone. It is connected to what precedes it. The connection of *idh yaʿdūna* (when they transgressed) to *nablūhum* (We test them) and to *mā yabʿudūna* (what they were distant from) in the sense of "We test them at the time of transgression, with defiance" is something that does not befit the drawing of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, to it.

﴿And when [a group] said﴾ is conjoined to "when they transgressed" (*idh ya'dūn*). It is brought in to show their persistence in transgression and their failure to desist from it after admonitions and warnings.

Al-Tibi and al-Taftazani said: It is not permissible for it to be conjoined to "when there came to them" (*idh ta'tīhim*), even though that is closer in wording, because the clause is either a *badal* (substitute/apposition) or a *zarf* (adverbial of time), which would entail that these speakers are included in the category of the transgressors, and that is not the case. On the view that it is a *zarf*, this is clear. As for the view that it is a *badal*, it is because the *badal* is closer to being independent. It has been argued, in explaining the reason for this, that the time of the saying came after the time of the transgression and was different from it. To regard it as extended, like a year in which all of that occurs, is an unnecessary strain. And the claim that conjoining it to that clause implies or suggests that the speakers were among the transgressors on the Sabbath, and not among the people of the town in general, is problematic.

﴿a community among them﴾, that is, a group of their righteous ones, who spared no effort in admonishing them when they despaired of the acceptance of others, yet did not cease reminding them, hoping for benefit and influence.

﴿Why do you admonish a people whom God is going to destroy﴾, that is, uproot entirely and purge the face of the earth of them,

﴿or punish with a severe punishment﴾, short of total annihilation. It was also said: "destroy them in this world or punish them in the Hereafter," because they did not desist from their corruption and rebellion. The disjunction is not meant to exclude both, on this view. The use of the active participle form in both halves indicates the certainty and firm establishment of each of the destruction and the punishment, as if they were already occurring. They said this to emphasize that admonition does not benefit them, since the intended meaning is: "Do not admonish," or "Do you admonish?" They moved from this to asking about the cause, because of the strangeness of the matter, since the cause of a wondrous matter is not known; or as a question about the wisdom and benefit of admonition. It was also said that this was a dispute that took place among the righteous admonishers, as if some of them said to others: "Why do we occupy ourselves with what is of no benefit?" It is possible on both views that this was said by the speaker in the presence of the people, so it would contain an exhortation to them to take admonition, since the firm declaration of their destruction or punishment casts fear and dread into their hearts. It was also said that those who said this were the transgressors on the Sabbath, who said it mockingly toward the advisers who warned them of destruction and punishment. This view is remote, as you will see shortly, God willing.

﴿They said﴾, that is, those to whom it was said: ﴿an excuse before your Lord﴾, that is, we admonish them as an excuse before Him, exalted is He, taking *ma'dhira* as an object (*maf'ūl*), which is most appropriate to the apparent sense of their words, "Why do you admonish?" Or: we make an excuse, an excuse, taking it as an absolute object (*maf'ūl muṭlaq*) of a deleted verb. It was also said that it is a direct object (*maf'ūl bihi*) of "they said." It is a single word in the sense of a sentence, because it is the speech by which one offers an excuse. *Al-ma'dhira* originally means *al-'udhr*, which is disclaiming a sin. Al-Azhari said it means *al-i'tidhār* (apologizing). It is followed by *ilā* because it implies the sense of informing and conveying. The attribution of the Lord to the pronoun of the addressees contains a kind of allusion to the questioners. This answer is apparent on the first two views. On the last view, it was said that it is from the receiving of the questioner with something other than what he expected, and so it is from the *uslūb al-ḥakīm* (the wise method of response).

Ḥafṣ and al-Mufaḍḍal are the only exceptions; all others read *ma'dhiratun* (with a nominative) as the predicate of a deleted subject, that is, "our admonition is an excuse before Him, exalted is He," so that we are not attributed to any kind of neglect in forbidding wrong.

[Page 92]

﴿and perhaps they will be mindful of God﴾ is conjoined to "an excuse," that is, and in hope that they may become mindful of Him to some degree, since definite despair arises only with destruction. Shaykh al-Islam said: This is explicit that those who said "Why do you admonish…" were not of the doomed group; otherwise the address would have been obligatory. End of quotation.

It may be explained on that view as an *iltifāt* (shift of person) or *mushākalah* (harmonizing of expression), in agreement with their describing themselves in the question as "a people." Or it may be that it is referred to the part other than the group of speakers. But all of this is contrary to the apparent sense.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 165:**

﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾: that is, they abandoned what their righteous men had admonished them with, abandoning it as one abandons a thing that is forgotten, and they turned away from it entirely. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). It has also been permitted that it be a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*), but that is contrary to the apparent sense.

Forgetting (*nisyan*) is a metaphor for abandonment (*tark*). It has been upheld that it is a *isti'arah* (metaphor by analogy), in which abandonment is likened to forgetting through the common quality of non-concern. It has also been permitted that it is a *majaz mursal* (metonymy) based on the relation of causality. It is not taken in its literal sense, as some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) said, for two reasons: because it did not actually occur, and because one is not held accountable for forgetting. Moreover, it is the deliberate abandonment that brings about the rescue of those who forbade evil, as in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿We rescued those who forbade evil﴾, since they did not comply with their command. This is unlike the case where they had forgotten, for then it would have been incumbent upon them to remind them. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the rescue is consequent upon forgetting, whereas in reality it is consequent upon both forgetting and reminding. What is in the conditional clause points to both of them, so it is as if it were said: "When the reminders reminded and the transgressors did not heed," and "they turned away from what they had been reminded of, We rescued the first group and seized the last group." The heading "forbidding evil" encompasses both those who said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy...?" and those to whom that was said. As for its encompassing those to whom it was said, this is clear. As for its encompassing those who said it, this is because they too were forbidden, but they saw that there was no benefit, so they refrained. That does not harm them, for they have explicitly stated that when the one forbidding knows the condition of the one forbidden, and that the prohibition will have no effect on him, the prohibition falls from him. Sometimes abandonment becomes obligatory, as al-Zamakhshari said, because it falls under the category of futility (*'abath*). Do you not see that if you went to the toll-collectors sitting on the road to seize the property of the poor and others unjustly, in order to admonish them and restrain them from what they are doing, that would be futile on your part, and would only be a cause for them to amuse themselves at your expense? Those (who gave admonition) did not turn away as these did, either because they had not reached the same depth of despair as their brethren, or because of their intense eagerness and earnestness in the matter. This is as Allah, exalted is He, described His Messenger (ﷺ) in His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps﴾.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "I do not know what became of the silent group," meaning by them those who had said the admonitions were useless. The basis of this statement of his, as some narrations express, is that he heard His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We rescued those who forbade evil﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We seized those who did wrong﴾, that is, by transgression and violation of the command. Ikrimah, may Allah be pleased with him, did not dive into the matter, although he was the one who plunged deeply into knowledge. So Ikrimah said to him: "May Allah make me your ransom! Do you not see how they denounced and disliked what the people were doing, and said what they said? And if Allah, glorified is He, did not say 'I rescued them,' He would not have said 'I destroyed them.'" Ibn Abbas was pleased with his statement, and ordered that he be given two mantles, and said: "The silent group was saved." Al-Tabarsi attributed to him, may Allah be pleased with him, two other opinions concerning the silent group: one of them is the view of suspension (*tawaqquf*), and the second is the view of their destruction, which Ibn Zayd also held.

It is narrated from Abu Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Then those seized are the silent ones and the wrongdoers."

﴿with a dreadful punishment﴾: that is, severe. The Scholar (al-Habr, i.e., Ibn Abbas) explained it as that which contains no mercy, and this returns to what he mentioned. *Ba'is* is a *fa'il* form, either as an adjective or as a verbal noun, like *nakir*; as an adjective it is used for emphasis. Most scholars hold that it is an adjective derived from *ba'usa, ya'būsu, ba'san*, meaning it became severe.

Al-Raghib said: *al-bu's*, *al-ba's*, and *al-ba'sa'* all mean hardship and what is disliked, except that *al-bu's* is more common in poverty and war, while *al-ba's* and *al-ba'sa'* are more common in affliction. Abu Bakr read *bay'is* on the pattern *fay'al*, like *dayghamun*. This is among the patterns found in adjectives and nouns. When a *ya'* is added to a verbal noun in this way, it turns it into a noun or adjective, like *saql* (polishing) and *sayqal* (polisher). Its middle letter is open (fatha) in the sound form, and kasra in the weak form, like *sayyid*. For this reason it was said that the reading of Asim in one transmission, *bi'is* with a kasra on the hamza, is weak both in transmission and in understanding. What makes it acceptable is that the hamza is the brother of the weak letter. Ibn Amir read *bi's*, with a kasra on the ba' and sukun on the hamza, on the basis that its original form was *ba'isa*, with an open ba' and a kasra on the hamza, like *hadhir*, and it was made sukun for lightness, just as they said *kabid* becomes *kabd* and *kalimah* becomes *kilmah*. Nafi' read *bayyis*, changing the hamza into a *ya'* as it was changed in *dhib*, because it was sukun and the letter before it was kasra. It was also said that these two readings are derived from the principle that the original form of the word is *bi's*, which is the verb of dispraise, made into a noun as in *qil* and *qal*. The meaning would then be: "with a punishment that is blameworthy and disliked." It is also read *bayyis* like *rayyis* and *kayyis*, changing the hamza into a *ya'* and then assimilating it into the *ya'*. It was also said that it is derived from *al-bu's* with a *waw*, and its original form is *bayūs*, like *mayyit*, and it was treated accordingly. *Bays* is read with lightness, like *hayyin*. *Ba'is* is read on the pattern of the active participle, meaning: possessing severity and harshness. Other readings have also been transmitted. Some have brought the readings contained in it to twenty-six. The indefiniteness of *'adhab* (punishment) is for magnification and awe.

﴿because they used to defiantly transgress﴾: this is connected to *akhadhna* (We seized), like the first *ba'* (*bi-'adhabin*), and there is no problem in this because the two differ in meaning. That is: We seized them with what was mentioned of the punishment, because of their persistent defiance. There is no obstacle to this being the cause of the seizing, just as it was the cause of the beginning. Likewise, there is no obstacle to its being given as a reason after the reason given by wrongdoing, which is in the relative clause, for that is also wrongdoing. The first reason was not sufficient by itself, for reasons that are not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 166:

﴿When they exalted themselves⦆ means: they became arrogant.

﴿in defiance of what they had been forbidden﴾ means: in refusing to abandon it. The speech therefore contains an elided noun, since arrogance and refusal in the face of what is forbidden are not blameworthy in themselves.

﴿We said to them, "Be apes, despised"﴾: humiliated, abject, and removed from every good. The command is a command of creation (takwini), not of obligation (taklifi), because it was not within their capacity that they could be charged with it. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾. There is the possibility that there was an actual utterance, and the possibility that the purpose is merely illustrative. The apparent meaning is that God Almighty inflicted on them a punishment in this world other than transformation, but they did not desist from what they were doing, so He transformed them into apes.

It is also permissible that the "wretched punishment" refers to transformation, and that this verse is an elaboration of what precedes it. It is related from Ibn Abbas that the obligation to observe the day that was enjoined upon you (the day of Friday) had been enjoined upon the Jews, but they deviated to Saturday and chose it. Hunting on it was therefore forbidden to them, and they were tested with it. The fish would come to them on Saturday, leaping forth, white and fat, so that the water could not be seen for their abundance. They remained as long as God willed, not hunting. Then Satan came to them and said: "You were only forbidden to take them on Saturday, so make ponds and nets." They would drive the fish into them on that day, then take them on Sunday. In another report, a man among them took a fish, tied it with a thread, drove a stake into the shore, fastened it to it, and left it in the water. When the next day came, he took it and ate it. They blamed him for that. When the punishment did not come upon him, he took two fish on the following Saturday, did the same, and nothing befell him. When they saw that the punishment was not hastening upon them, they became bold, so they took fish, salted them, and sold them. They numbered about twelve thousand, or seventy thousand. The people of the town became three groups, as God Almighty recounted. The righteous said to the transgressors: "We will not dwell with you." They divided the town with a wall: the Muslims had one gate and the transgressors had another gate. This story took place in the time of David, peace be upon him, and he cursed them. One day the righteous awoke and none of the transgressors had come out. They said: "These people have a matter; perhaps wine has overcome them." They climbed over the wall, and behold, the people were apes. They opened the gate and entered upon them. The apes recognised their kin among the humans, but the humans did not recognise their kin among the apes. The apes began to come to their relatives, sniffing their garments and weeping, and the man would say: "Did we not forbid you?" The apes would nod their heads: "Yes." Then they died after three days. It is related from Qatada that the young men became apes and the elders became swine.

It is related from Mujahid that their hearts were transformed, so they were not granted success in understanding the truth. Ibn Jarir and others related from al-Hasan who said: It was a fish which God forbade them on one day, and permitted them on other days. It would come to them on the day God forbade it, as if it were a she-camel in labour, not withdrawing from anyone. They began to be eager and to restrain themselves, and you have rarely seen anyone so preoccupied with a sin without committing it, until they seized it and ate. By God, it was the most ill-omened meal a people ever ate, the heaviest in disgrace in this world and the longest in punishment in the Hereafter. By God, no fish that a people took and ate was greater before God than the killing of a believing man, and the believer is greater in sanctity before God, glory be to Him, than a fish. But God, mighty and majestic, appointed for a people the Hour, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.

Abd ibn Humayd related, from Ikrimah, that on the seashore where they were there were two stone idols, facing the water. One was called Luqaym and the other Luqmanah. God inspired the fish to make pilgrimage on Saturday to the two idols, and inspired the people of the town that He had commanded the fish to make pilgrimage to the two idols on Saturday, so they should not touch them on that day. When it had gone, they were to do as they wished with it and hunt it. The people were tested, and what occurred was that they were transformed into apes. There is some doubt about the soundness of this report, and perhaps it has no soundness, as is not hidden from one who knows the meaning of pilgrimage among those who pray. These two idols resemble the Ayn Haqq, since the island of al-Haditha is near Iraq and close to the shore of the Euphrates. The fish visit it on specific days of the year, to the point that it seems no fish remains in the bed of the Euphrates without being cast there. The people of that region catch from it what God wills and transport it to the islands and nearby villages, such as Alus, Habba, Anat and Hit. Then it ceases, and after those days you do not see a single fish in the spring until its like returns the following year. Glory be to the One who does what He wills.

Some scholars have cited the story of these transgressors as evidence for the prohibition of legal stratagems (hiyal) in religion. This is reinforced by what Ibn Batta related from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not commit what the Jews committed, lest you make lawful the prohibitions of God, Exalted, by the slightest stratagems."

And when your Lord proclaimed ﴿وإذْ تَأذَّنَ رَبُّكَ﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb and conjoined to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and ask them﴾. Ta'adhdhana (تَأذَّنَ) is a form of tafa'ala derived from idhn (إذن, permission/announcement), and it has the sense of adhana (آذَنَ), meaning "he made known." The tafa'ul form can carry the sense of if'al, as in tawa''ada and i'da (threatening and warning). To this reading is interpreted what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that the meaning is "your Lord said." Some commentators explained it as "resolved" (ʿazama, عَزَمَ), which is a kinaya (an indirect expression) or a majaz (a figurative usage) for it, because one who is resolved upon a matter consults himself about doing it or leaving it and then decides firmly; so he seeks permission from himself for it. In al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the Zamakhshari tafsir): if it were taken to mean seeking permission (istidhan) rather than announcing (idhan), as though he asks permission of himself, that would be a valid view. Since it was taken to mean resolve, and the one who resolves is decisive, ʿazama is explained as jazama (جزم, to decide firmly) and qada (قضى, to decree), which gives emphasis. For this reason it is treated as an oath, and it is answered with what answers an oath, which here is ﴿surely He will raise﴾ (ﷺ-less, as stated). The expression "I resolved upon you that you shall do so" (ʿazamtu ʿalayka latafʿalanna) also occurs. This does not imply that attributing resolve to Him, Exalted is He, is permitted, even though this has been explicitly prohibited, because the prohibition is itself refuted, for it has been reported: "a resolve from the resolves of God Most High."

﴿upon them﴾, meaning the Jews, not the transgressors who were transformed into apes, since they did not remain, as you know. It is possible that the pronoun returns to them on the basis of what is narrated from al-Hasan. In that case the intended meaning is them and their descendants. Its return to the Jews and Christians is not correct, though it is narrated from Mujahid. The prepositional phrase is connected to yabʿathanna (يَبْعَثَنَّ, "will raise"), in the sense of "will definitely impose upon them."

﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning until the end of the world. It is connected to yabʿathu (يَبْعَثُ). It was said that it is connected to ta'adhdhana, but that is not the correct view and is not valid, as is not hidden, its connection to the relative clause in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿who will inflict on them﴾, meaning, make them taste and subject them to, ﴿the worst torment﴾, such as humiliation, imposing the jizya (poll tax), the absence of any protection for them, placing them under the rule of others, and other kinds of torment. God Most High raised against them, after Sulayman (peace be upon him), Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar), who destroyed their homes, killed their fighting men, took captive their women and offspring, and imposed the jizya on those who remained of them. They used to pay it to the Magians until the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, and he did what he did, and then he imposed the jizya upon them, so it continues to be imposed until the end of time.

This does not contradict its being lifted at the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him), because that time is attached to the Hereafter due to its proximity to it. Or, the meaning of his (peace be upon him) lifting it from them is that he will accept from them only Islam, and will give them the choice between it and the sword. Thus the people at that time are either Muslims or food for their swords, so there is no difficulty. What they obtain during the time of the Dajjal, despite its being humiliation in itself, is like a summer cloud, and moreover they are not Jews at the time of subordination.

﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾, for whom He wills to punish in this world, and among them these people. It was said: in the Hereafter. It was said: in both.

﴿And indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward whoever repents and believes.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 168:

﴿And We divided them﴾, i.e., We scattered the Children of Israel, or We made them ﴿in the earth﴾, and We placed each group of them in one of its regions, such that no region is nearly free of them, as a completion of their dispersal, so that they would have no power. This is among the unseen matters of the Qur'an, like what the verse before it contains. And His statement, glorified is He: ﴿as communities﴾ (ummaman), is either a second object of qatta'na (We divided), or a circumstantial accusative (hal, a word describing the state of the object) from its object.

﴿Among them are the righteous﴾. As al-Tabari said, they are those who believed in Allah and His Messenger and remained steadfast in their religion before the sending of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It was also said: they are those who reached the Prophet (ﷺ), believed in him, and this was attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It was also said: they are those beyond China, and this is, in my view, "beyond China." The prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted predicate (khabar, the predicate of a nominal sentence) placed first, and "the righteous" is the subject (mubtada', the topic of a nominal sentence). It is permissible that it be the agent of the adverbial phrase (dharaf). The clause, in the position of an accusative, is a qualifier (sifah, an adjective) of ummam (communities) on both possibilities. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial accusative, and it is a substitute (badal, an appositive) for ummam on the second possibility, and that it be a qualifier of an implied noun, which is the substitute on the first, i.e., a people among them who are righteous.

﴿And among them are those other than that﴾, i.e., those who are lower than those righteous ones, not reaching their rank in righteousness. They are those who obeyed some commands and disobeyed others while being believers. It was also said: they are the disbelievers among them, based on the view that righteousness means faith. It was also said: what is meant by them includes disbelievers and sinners. The prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted predicate placed first, and (dūna, "other than/below") according to what al-Tabarsi mentioned is a subject, except that it remained fatha-vowelled because of its full adverbial function together with its being attached to a indeclinable noun. Similar to it, according to the view of Abu al-Hasan, is (baynakum) in His statement, glorified is He: ﴿There has certainly been severed between you﴾. Or the subject is omitted and the adverbial phrase is its qualifier, i.e., and among them are some people or a group other than that. It is well known among the grammarians that the noun described by an adverbial phrase or a clause is regularly omitted when it is part of a noun governed by min (from), or when it precedes it, as in: "Some of us stayed and some of us departed." The point of the statement is the division into two parts: these people are divided into two categories. Some people have burdened themselves with this kind of construction, making the first adverbial phrase a qualifier of an omitted subject and making the second adverbial phrase a predicate for what they thought required this, but this is nothing. The demonstrative refers to the righteous. They have mentioned that the singular demonstrative may be used for the dual and the plural, and the reference to it has already passed. It was also said: it refers to righteousness, as the apparent singular suggests, and in that case a noun is understood, namely "people" (ahl), for example.

﴿And We tested them with good things﴾, i.e., fertility and well-being, ﴿and bad things﴾, i.e., drought and hardship.

﴿So that perhaps they would return﴾, i.e., that they would repent of what they were upon of what they had been forbidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 169:

﴿Then there succeeded them⦅after them⦆﴾ i.e., those mentioned (before them). It was also said: the righteous.

﴿Khalf⦆ i.e., a bad replacement; it is a verbal noun described by it. For this reason it applies to the singular and the plural. It was also said that it is a collective noun (ism jam'), and this is what those who said it is a plural meant. It is common in the sense of evil, and from it comes the saying "he was silent for a thousand years and then spoke a khalf" (a bad utterance). The khalaf, with a fatha on the lam, is used for good. Some claimed that it is coined for this distinction. It was also said that both have the same meaning: one who succeeds another, whether righteous or wicked. Among examples of the sakin form used in praise is the verse of Hassan:

"For us is the first step towards You, and behind us, for our predecessors, is a follower in obedience to God."

Among examples of the mutaharrik form used in blame is the verse of Labid:

"Gone are those among whose flanks one lived, and I remain in a khalf like the hide of a mangy camel."

It is reported from the Basrans that the vocalised and the sukun forms are both permitted for the bad sense, whereas for the good sense only the vocalised form is used. The lexicographers agreed with them, except al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda. Its derivation is either from khilafa (succession) or from khuluf, which means corruption and change, and from it comes khuluf fam al-sa'im (the change in the mouth of the fasting person). Abu Hatim said: khalf with sukun means offspring, and the singular and plural are the same in it; khalaf with fatha means a replacement, whether a son or a stranger. Most scholars hold that those meant by this khalf are those who lived in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and in that case it is not valid to interpret "the righteous" as those who believed in him (peace be upon him). The apparent meaning is that they are from the Jews. It is reported from Mujahid that they are the Christians, but this is not correct.

﴿Who inherited the Book⦆ i.e., the Torah. The inheritance is a metaphor for its being in their hands and for their being the ones who have knowledge of what is in it after their forefathers.

al-Hasan read: (wurrithu), with a damma and shadda, in the passive voice. On both readings the clause is in the position of a description of khalf. His words, glorified be He: ﴿They take the goods of this lower life⦆ is a resumptive clause explaining what they do with the Book after inheriting it. Abu al-Baqa' said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in warithu, and some regarded this as the more probable; it suffices that it coincides with part of the time of inheritance, since that extends. The 'arad is that which has no permanence, and from it the theologians borrowed "accident" ('arad) as the opposite of "substance" (jawhar). In al-Nihaya: 'arad with a fatha is the goods and trappings of this world; Abu 'Ubayda said: it is anything other than gold and silver of its goods, and with sukun it means wealth and property. (al-Adna) is an adjective of an omitted noun, i.e., "the lower thing", and what is meant by it is the world, and it derives from dunuww (nearness) in relation to the Hereafter. That it derives from dana'a (baseness) is contrary to the apparent meaning, although it is apparent in it since it is hamzated. What is meant by this 'arad is what they take as bribes in judgements and in distorting speech.

﴿They say: "It will be forgiven us"⦆ and God will not call us to account for that and will overlook us. The clause is conjoined to what precedes it. The possibility that it is circumstantial requires the assumption of a subject without any apparent need, and the verb is attributed to the prepositional phrase; it was also permitted that it be attributed to the pronoun of "they take".

﴿And if there comes to them goods like it, they will take it⦆ is in the position of a circumstantial clause. It was said: from the pronoun of "they say", and "saying" here means "believing", i.e., they hope for forgiveness while they persist in sin, returning to its like, not repenting of it. It was said: from the pronoun of "for us", and the meaning would be on that basis. The first is more apparent. The claim that restricting the saying to this does not entail restricting the forgiveness to it, and that the second (the restriction) is what the second carries, is not free from consideration.

al-Halabi and al-Saffaqsi preferred that the clause is resumptive, not circumstantial, not because a conditional clause cannot be a circumstantial clause, since its occurrence is beyond doubt, but because in saying it is circumstantial there is a trace of Mu'tazilite tendency. It is not hidden that although the matter is as they say, the circumstantial reading is more eloquent, because their hope of forgiveness in a state contrary to it is more fitting for rebuke against them. Understand.

﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them⦆ i.e., the covenant mentioned in the Torah. The idafa is in the sense of "in". It may also be a possessive idafa in the sense of "for", and the meaning returns to what he mentioned. The (al-) in "the Book" is for previous reference. His words, glorified be He: ﴿that they should not say about God except the truth⦆ is an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to the covenant. It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for it; it was said that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi); and it was said that it is connected to "covenant" with the preposition supplied, i.e., "that they should not say". It was permitted for "that" (an) to be a verbal particle, and to be an explanatory particle for "covenant", since it has the sense of saying. For "la" it was permitted to be prohibitive and to be negative; the consideration of each together with what is valid with it is left to your own understanding. The purpose of the verse is to rebuke those heirs for their categorical claim of forgiveness while persisting in what they are upon. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that they were rebuked for obliging God to forgive their sins, which they constantly returned to and did not repent from. The categorical assertion comes with sin, for it is for emphasis, as the scholars have stated explicitly. Al-Zamakhshari — may God treat him with His justice — alluded in his interpretation of this verse to the People of the Sunna, and claimed that their doctrine is exactly the doctrine of the Jews, in that they permitted forgiveness of sin without repentance. He quoted from the Torah: whoever commits a great sin will not be forgiven by repentance. You know that the Jews emphasised the claim of forgiveness, whereas the People of the Sunna do not affirm forgiveness with certainty for the obedient, let alone for the disobedient in matters that are God's right, and even less for one who disobeys Him in matters that are the rights of people. So those who oblige God, although with respect to the penitent they are closer to it, is what he claimed anything but the proverb: "She struck me with her own ailment and slipped away." If what he quoted from the Torah is an inference from the verse, it indicates nothing beyond what is in al-Kashshaf except their distortion of what the Torah contains concerning the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), the verse of stoning, and similar things from their facilitations for the elite and their relaxations for the common people, who take bribes on that basis. Fabricating against God is a grave matter, even if he read the Torah that was not distorted, and that it is what helps the carrying to shirk with decisive proofs from the Noble Book of God, or that this is for them, while that is for this merciful nation specifically. He himself conceded something similar in His words, glorified be He: ﴿He will forgive you your sins⦆. The People of the Sunna have unanimously condemned the one who wishes for things from God.

They narrated from Shaddad ibn Aws that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The intelligent one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is he who follows his desires and wishes vainly from God, glorified be He."

From here it was said that these people were blamed for their consumption of people's wealth falsely, their following of their own desires, and their wishing vainly from God, glorified be He, and they were rebuked for their fabrication against God concerning the rulings which they altered, and took the goods of this lower life in exchange for altering them. It is as if it were said: Was not the aforementioned covenant taken from them in their Book, that they should not say about God, at any time, except the truth which the Book contains? Why then did they judge contrary to it, and say: "This is from God," when it is not from God, in order to buy with it a small price? In this there is, along with its contradiction to what is reported from the rabbi, a contradiction to the apparent meaning. Al-Jahdari read: (an la taqulu), with the second person, by way of iltifat.

﴿And they studied what is in it⦆ i.e., they read it, so they remember it. It is conjoined to "was not taken" in meaning, although the two differ in being declarative and imperative; the meaning is: the covenant of the Book was taken from them, and they studied... etc. It was permitted for it to be conjoined to "was not taken", with the interrogative of affirmation entering over both, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, or to "they inherited", with the clause "was not taken" being parenthetical and what precedes it circumstantial, or the whole being parenthetical as has been said. There is no objection to this, except that al-Tabarsi reported from some of them an interpretation of "studied" in this manner of conjunction as "abandoned and neglected", and this is far-fetched.

It was said: the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "they say", with "qad" implied, i.e., the covenant was taken from them that they should not say about God except the truth which their Book contains, while they were studying what is in it and remembering it. This, as you see, is far-fetched. al-Sulami read: (idda rasu) with shadda on the dal and an alif after it; its origin is tadarasu, the ta' was assimilated into the dal, and a hamzat al-wasl was brought for it.

﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who are mindful⦆ of God, glorified be He, and fear His punishment, so they do not do what these people did.

﴿Will you not then understand?⦆ so that you learn this, and do not exchange the lower, which leads to punishment, for the enduring bliss. It is an address to those upon whom the covenant was taken, who take the goods of this lower life, and in the iltifat there is an intensification of the rebuke. It was also said that it is an address to the believers, and there is no iltifat in it.

A group read with the ya' in the third person and with the ta' in the second person. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Ja'far, Sahl, Ya'qub, and Hafs read it with the ta'. This verse is clearly a rebuke for taking; some have made His words, glorified be He, "Was not the covenant taken from them..." etc., a rebuke for that saying in the verse, which is of the kind containing the figure of laff and nashr.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 170:

﴿Those who hold fast to the Book﴾ means: they hold fast to it in matters of their religion. It is said: "masaka bi-l-shay'" and "tamassaka bihi" have the same meaning (both mean to hold fast to a thing).

Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: they are those among the People of the Book who believed, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, who held fast to the Book that Musa (peace be upon him) brought, so they did not distort it, did not conceal it, and did not make it a means of gain. ʿAta' said: they are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), and by "the Book" is meant the Qur'an, which is of exalted status.

Abu Bakr and Hammad recited (yumsikūna) with the light form (tashdid omitted) from al-imsak (grasping). Ibn Mas'ud read (istamsakū), and Ubayy read (masakū). In this there is agreement with His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and establish the prayer﴾. Perhaps the change in the well-known reading is to indicate that holding fast is a matter continuing at all times, unlike establishing (the prayer), which is restricted to specific times. Its mention specifically among the other acts of worship, although it is included in holding fast to the Book, is due to its excellence over them, because it is the pillar of the religion.

The place of the relative pronoun may be in the genitive, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "those who are God-fearing" (alladhīna yattaqūn). His saying, ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾, is then a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ) confirming what precedes it. An interjection may be preceded by the fa' particle, as in his saying:

So know, for a person's knowledge benefits him, that everything decreed will certainly come.

Or it may be in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being His, the Glorified's, saying: ﴿Indeed We do not waste the reward of the righteous﴾. The connecting element (rabit) is either the omitted pronoun, as is the view of the majority of the Basran grammarians, meaning: the reward of the righteous among them; or the definite article (alif-lam), as is the view of the Kufans, for it serves as a substitute for the pronoun, so it is as if it were said: "their righteous ones" (muslihīhim). As for the generality in "the righteous" (al-muslihīn), it is, according to the well-known view, one of the connecting elements, and from it (comes) "How excellent a man is Zayd" according to one of the opinions; or the placing of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, on the basis that the original was: "We do not waste their reward," but it was changed for the reason mentioned, to draw attention to the fact that righteousness acts as a deterrent against waste, because linking a judgement to a derived attribute indicates the causative force of the source of the derivation, so it is as if it were said: "We do not waste their reward because of their righteousness."

It is also said: the predicate is omitted, and the estimate is: "Those who hold fast to the Book are rewarded or recompensed." In that case, His, the Glorified's, saying "Indeed We do not waste..." etc. is a parenthetical interjection confirming what precedes it.

﴿And [remember] when We lifted the mountain above them﴾ is joined to what precedes it, with the implied verb "remember." *Naql* means lifting, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn al-A'rabi adopted this view. It is also reported from Muslim that it means pulling, as in "I pulled the bucket (*nataqtu al-gharb*) from the well." From Abu 'Ubayda it is reported to mean uprooting. What is reported from the scholar (*al-Habr*, i.e., Ibn 'Abbas) is more consistent with God's words: ﴿And We raised the Mount above them﴾. On the last two views, the meaning of lifting is implied so that the two verses correspond. The "mountain" is either Mount Sinai (*al-Tur*) or another mountain. It was a farsakh by a farsakh, like the encampment of the people. When they hesitated to accept the Torah, God commanded Gabriel, peace be upon him, because the Torah had come to them as a whole containing what they found burdensome. He uprooted the mountain from its base and raised it over them. ﴿As if it were a canopy﴾, that is, a cloud or a roof. It was described this way even though a *zullah* is anything high that casts shade, because of the particle of comparison (*ka-*). Without it, its presence there would not make sense. ﴿Above (fawqa)﴾ is an adverbial complement of *nataqna* or a circumstantial element (*hal*). ﴿From the mountain﴾ is a specifying element, according to what has been said, to indicate that the lifting was in one of the directions of height. The nominal clause after it is also in a circumstantial position, meaning: resembling that.

﴿And they thought﴾, that is, they were certain, ﴿that it would fall upon them﴾, that is, descend on them if they did not accept. They had been warned of this on this condition. The truthful one does not fail in what He has reported. But since the condition for the event was not met, the thing that was supposed to happen did not occur. It therefore resembled something merely supposed, which may fail to happen, and this is why it was called a *zann* (supposition). 

It has also been said that they were certain of this because a mountain cannot remain suspended in the air. This was objected to: the fact that it does not remain in the air does not require certainty, since that is according to the normal course of custom. But if the custom is broken, then what is established is its staying up, and what is actual is its not falling. That would be like His raising it above them and its standing there until what happened among them occurred. The truth is that what they were certain of was the falling if they did not accept, because that was the conditional consequence. In a report it is said: "The Children of Israel refused to accept the Torah, so the mountain was raised above them. It was said to them: 'Either you accept, or it will certainly fall upon you.' So each of them fell prostrate upon his left eyebrow, looking up with his right eye at the mountain out of fear that it would fall. That is why you never see a Jew prostrate except upon his left eyebrow, and they say: 'It is the prostration by which the punishment was lifted from us.'" They then complied with what they were commanded. The possibility of its staying up through a break in custom does not undermine this, just as the non-occurrence of the fall when they accepted does not undermine it. Do you not see that one is certain that what falls into fire will burn, even though it is possible that it would not, as in the story of the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon him?

Al-Rummani and al-Jubba'i held that *zann* is used in its ordinary sense, and the meaning is that the belief that it would fall grew strong in their hearts. This was chosen by some of the researchers. The sentence is independent (*mustanafah*). It is also permissible that it be conjoined to *nataqna* or be a circumstantial clause with *qad* implied, as Abu al-Baqa' said.

﴿Take﴾, that is, and We said: "Take," or saying: "Take."

﴿what We have given you﴾ of the Book.

﴿with strength﴾, that is, with earnestness and determination to bear its hardships. The prepositional phrase is attached to an implied element functioning as a circumstantial clause from the *waw* (of the verb), and the meaning is: take it while being earnest.

﴿and remember what is in it﴾, that is, act upon it and do not abandon it as one who has forgotten. This is a metaphor or figurative expression for that.

Ibn Mas'ud read: "and be mindful (*wa-tadhakkarū*)," and it has been read as "and remember," with the same meaning as "and be mindful."

﴿so that you may be God-conscious﴾, by means of this, avoiding ugly deeds and base character, or hoping that you will be counted among the God-fearing.

It is also permissible that what is meant by "what We have given you" is the great sign, namely the lifting of the mountain. That is: take this if you are able to bear it, like His words: ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through.﴾ Remember what it contains of overwhelming power and warning. On this view, the lifting of the mountain is meant only to show their inability. The statement is like your saying to someone who claims strength and power after you have defeated him: "Take it from me." Its essence is: if you seek a compelling sign and propose it, then take what We have given you if you are able to bear it. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the reports are against it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 172 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when your Lord took﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb in the same manner as in similar instances preceding it. It is conjoined to what came before it, and is brought to establish the proof against the Jews by means of the general covenant. For among them were some who associated partners with God, saying: "Uzair is the son of God," exalted is His name. This follows the establishing of the proof against them by the particular covenant specific to them, and the argumentation against them by the transmitted and rational proofs, and the prohibition against them of blind imitation (taqlid). Some scholars permitted that it be a *tadhyil* (a concluding clause that generalizes after particularization), and a display of the persistence of these Jews in error after the taking of the particular covenant, which is indicated by His words, glorified is He: ﴿And when We lifted the mountain﴾, in accordance with His words, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount﴾ in Surat al-Baqara. In that case there is no conjunction (*'atf*), and this is more apparent than the *tadhyil* when judged by the apparent wording, and it is preferable to it if the general term is restricted to the polytheists, as has been said. It may also be said that the verse is brought to explain the taking of a prior covenant from all of creation, believers and unbelievers alike,
[Page 100]
before this worldly creation, with that which is most important of matters and the fundamental root of all obligations, in a manner free of anything resembling compulsion. It includes the binding of the polytheists contemporary with him, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the removal of their argument that they were heedless. This follows the indication of the taking of a covenant from particular people in this worldly creation, in a manner most resembling compulsion, with that which apparently is among the deeds. For the people at that time were acknowledging the lordship, indeed they acknowledged it together with the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him. So there was no need for the lifting of the mountain over them for that purpose. Yet if someone were to say that the mention of that amid the verses concerning the Jews is by way of digression (*istitrad*), and the connection in it is evident, it would not be far-fetched. But the first view, which is the one followed by most later exegetes, is: say (to them) or (to) the people: when your Lord took ﴿from the Children of Adam﴾. By them is meant those who were born to them, whether believers or unbelievers, generation after generation, excluding anyone who was not born to him for some reason. Restricting them to the forefathers of the Jews who associated partners with God, the Exalted, on the grounds that they said such things, is something hardly worth considering.

The choice of *akhdh* (taking) over *ikhraj* (bringing forth) serves to announce the status of those taken at that time, because of what it contains of the news of selection and choosing. This is the reason it was attributed to the name of the Lord by way of *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), along with what it contains of preparation for the question that follows. Its attribution to His pronoun, upon him be prayer and peace, is for honor. It has also been said that the choice of *akhdh* over *ikhraj* is for the sake of the connection with the covenant contained in the verse, since what suits it is taking, not bringing forth. The mention of the Lord is because that taking is considered in terms of the effects of lordship that follow it. Some scholars took comfort in the difference of style in this statement, through the *iltifat* it contains, from what precedes it in His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And when We lifted﴾, and from what follows it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them the account of him to whom We gave Our signs﴾, because it is by way of digression.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿from their backs﴾ are a substitute (*badal*) for "Children of Adam," being a *badal al-ba'd* (partial substitution) from the whole, with the repetition of the preposition, as in His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed﴾. It has also been said that it is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution by inclusion), and this is the view of Abu al-Baqa'. Some explained it by saying that *badal al-ishtimal* is that in which there is a connection between it and the substituted noun such that it necessitates attributing to the followed term the attribute of the following term in general, as in: "Zayd impressed me, his knowledge." For it is known at first that Zayd is impressive in respect of his qualities and not in respect of his essence, and the attribution of impressiveness to him includes attributing to him one of his qualities in general. The attribution of the taking, which here means bringing forth, to the Children of Adam is an attribution to their backs in general, because it is known at first that the Children of Adam are not taken in respect of their essences but in respect of their bodies and limbs, and the attribution of taking to them includes its attribution to their limbs in general. It was claimed that this view is preferable to the view of partial substitution, because the attribution to the substituted noun as a whole is complete and the benefit is obtained without mention of the substitute, as in: "I ate the loaf, half of it." For the attribution is complete even if the half is not mentioned. There is no doubt that the attribution here is not complete without mention of the substitute.

Also, the backs are not, strictly speaking, a part of the Children of Adam, but a part of their limbs, and there is no concealing what is questionable in that. The *min* (from) in both places is for origin (*ibtida'iyya*), and in this is further confirmation of its being based on clarification after ambiguity and detail after generality. It has been said: and it is an indication that the covenant was taken from them while they were in the loins of their fathers, and they had not been deposited in the wombs of their mothers. His words, exalted is He: ﴿their offspring﴾ are the object of *akhadha* (took), placed after the object by means of the preposition, because it contains a pronoun referring back to it. If it were placed before, the pronoun would refer to a term that comes later both verbally and in rank, and this is not permitted except in certain places, and this is not one of them. It is also for the sake of observing its originality and origination, and because of the suspense toward the postponed element that has been mentioned more than once. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read: ﴿their offspring (*dhurriyyatihim*)﴾ in the plural, and what is meant is their children in general. Whoever restricted the Children of Adam to the forefathers of the Jews, as has passed, restricted this to their descendants, and there is in that what there is. As for the well-known difficulty, namely that all people are truly called the Children of Adam and his offspring, so that the extracted and that from which it is extracted become one, it is answered by the clear fact that what is meant is the bringing forth
[Page 101]
of branches from roots according to the order of birth. Escape from this does not depend on accepting that restriction.

﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves﴾, that is: He made each one of those offspring, taken from the backs of their fathers, testify concerning themselves and not concerning others, as an affirmation to them of His complete lordship, exalted is He, saying to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾, that is: the Owner of your affairs and your Sustainer in absolute terms, without anyone having any share in any of your matters. ﴿They said﴾ in answer to Him, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Yes, we testify﴾, that is: concerning ourselves, that You are our Lord and that we have no lord other than You. What is meant is: we acknowledged that. It is reported that the judge Shurayh said to a confessor in his presence: "The son of your maternal aunt's sister has testified against you." From here al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: this verse is the basis for confession (*iqrar*). *Bala* (yes) is a particle of answer, and its alif is original according to the majority. A group said: the original is *bal*, and the alif is an added letter. Some of them say it is for the feminine marking of the word, like the *ta'* in *thumma* and *rubba*, because it is pronounced with *imala* (vocalic inclination), and if it were not for the feminine marking it would be an added letter for mere multiplication, like the alif of *qaba'thara*, and that is not pronounced with *imala*. It is specific to negation, so it occurs only as an answer to it, and thus it cancels it, whether the negation is bare or accompanied by an interrogative, whether real or affirmative. They treated negation with affirmative interrogation as bare negation in its answer with *bala*, as in this verse. Accordingly Ibn 'Abbas and others said: if they had said "Yes (*na'am*)" they would have disbelieved. Its justification is that *na'am* is an affirmation of the one who informs with a negation or an affirmation. For this reason a group of jurists said: if someone says, "Do I not have a thousand from you?" and he replies "Bala," he is bound, whereas "Na'am" does not bind him. Others said: he is bound by both, and they followed in this the custom and not the linguistic usage.

Al-Suhayli and a group disputed what is reported from the rabbi and others, relying on the argument that the affirmative interrogative is an affirmation, and for this reason Sibawayh refused to make *am* connected, as is said about His words, exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ and ﴿Am I not better than﴾, for it does not occur after an affirmation. If it is established that it is an affirmation, then *na'am* after an affirmation is an affirmation of it. Ibn Hisham said: what is problematic for them is that *bala* is not used to answer an affirmation, and that is agreed upon. ﴿Yes, My signs have come to you﴾ has preceding it something indicating negation. However, there occurs in a hadith what suggests that it is used to answer a bare interrogative. In Sahih al-Bukhari, he, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to his companions: "Are you pleased that you should be a quarter of the people of Paradise?" They said: "Yes." In Sahih Muslim, he, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Are you the one who met me in Mecca?" The one who was asked said to him: "Yes."

These people cannot argue with this, because it is rare and so the revelation is not to be interpreted in light of it. End. Al-Badr al-Damamini answered that there is no problem in reality, for these people observed the form of the spoken negation, so it is answered with *bala* where the intention is to cancel the negation following the interrogative hamza, and they permitted the answer *na'am* on the basis that it is an affirmation of the whole utterance, the hamza and what it governs, which is an affirmation, as has passed. His claim of consensus is open to dispute. As for the bare affirmation without negation at all, al-Radi reported the disagreement concerning it, and mentioned that some permitted its use after it, relying on the verse:

*"The distance has grown between me and her by separation, Yes, indeed whoever visits the graves will be far off."*

If he meant what is more general, so that it includes the affirmation accompanying negation, then the disagreement about it is present and well known, which he mentioned in the chapter on the letter *nun*. End. It is not hidden that the verse is anomalous, as al-Radi stated. What is mentioned in the discussion of the letter *nun* is that a group of earlier and later scholars, including al-Shalawbin, said: if an interrogative precedes the negation, then if it is in its literal sense its answer is like the answer to a bare negation, and if it is intended as affirmation, then most often it is answered with what is used to answer negation, out of regard for its wording. It is permitted, when there is no ambiguity, to answer it with what is used to answer affirmation, out of regard for its meaning. On this basis is the saying of the Helpers to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, "Na'am," when he had said to them: "Do you not see that this is due to them?" and the saying of Jahdar:

*"Does not the night gather the mother of 'Amr and us, so that this brings us near? Na'am, and I see the crescent as you see it, and the day rises above her as it rises above me."*

On this basis also goes the speech of Sibawayh. Ibn 'Usfur said: the Arabs treated the affirmation in the answer as they treat pure negation, even if it is an affirmation in meaning. So if it is said, "Did I not give you a dirham?" one says in confirming it: "Na'am," and in denying it: "Bala." That is because the one who affirms may agree with what you claim, or may disagree with you. So if he says "Na'am," it is not known whether he meant "Na'am, you did not give me" according to the wording, or "Na'am, you did give me" according to the meaning. For this reason they answered according to the wording and did not turn to the meaning. As for *na'am* in Jahdar's verse, it is an answer to an unmentioned thing, which is what he assumed in his belief that the night gathers him and the mother of 'Amr, and this is permitted because there is no ambiguity, for he knows that everyone knows that the night gathers him with the mother of 'Amr. Or it is an answer to his saying, "And I see the crescent," as if he had come to it. As for the saying of the Helpers, it was permitted because there is no ambiguity, for it is known that they meant "Na'am, that is acknowledged for them." On this basis is to be understood Sibawayh's use of it after affirmation. End.

The best view is that *na'am* in the verse is an answer to his saying: "then that is due to us," and so on. Ibn Hisham then said: from this it becomes clear that if ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ were answered with *na'am*, it would not suffice as confession, because He, glorified and exalted is He, required in confessing what pertains to lordship that it not admit of any meaning other than the one intended by the one who confesses. For this reason one does not enter Islam by saying "There is no god but God" with *ilah* in the nominative, because it admits of the negation of unity. Perhaps Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, only said that if they had said "Na'am" it would not be a full confession. Al-Shalawbin permitted that his meaning, may God be pleased with him, was that if they had said "Na'am" as an answer to the wording, which is the more eloquent form, it would be disbelief, since the basis is that the question and answer correspond in wording. There is room to examine this, for disbelief is not established by possibility. The discourse here, in the context of gathering, is a representation of God's creating all creation at the beginning of the natural disposition, prepared to reason by the signs of the horizons and of the souls, which lead to monotheism, as expressed by His words, may God bless him and grant him peace: "Every child is born upon the fitrah," and the hadith continues.

Based upon the depiction of the abstracted image (tashbih al-hay'a al-muntaza'a, a figure of speech in which a complex scene is drawn from several elements) of His, glorified and exalted be He, presenting them to recognise His lordship and His oneness, after having empowered them with it by what He placed in them of intellects and insight and what He set up for them in the horizons and in themselves of proofs, a complete empowerment. And from their being fully empowered with it, and their strong readiness for it, by the image abstracted from His, exalted be He, bringing them to acknowledge it by way of command, and from their hastening to that without any hesitation at all, without there being any taking, calling to witness, question, or answer. A parallel to this is in the saying of His, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿So He said to it and to the earth, "Come both willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ Among this is all that is related of animals and inanimate things, such as the saying of the poet:

My camel complained to me of the length of the journey:
"Gently, slowly, for both of us are afflicted."

And the saying of another:

The basin filled and said, "Enough for me!"
"Gently, slowly, you have filled my belly."

They have considered His, glorified and exalted be He, saying ﴿lest you say﴾ to be a shift of address (iltifat, a change from one form of address to another) and a turning away from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to his contemporaries among the Jews, for emphasis in the binding of the argument, or to them and to their predecessors by way of prioritisation of one group over another (taghlib). It is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, an accusative noun stating the reason for the action) governing what precedes it, namely the taking and the calling to witness, or a supposed element indicated by that. The meaning, according to what the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra) say: We did what We did out of dislike that you should say. And according to what the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa) say: So that you would not say on the Day of Resurrection, when the matter becomes manifest and the punishment encompasses those who associated others with Allah: ﴿Indeed, we were unaware of this﴾, that is, of the oneness of lordship, ﴿heedless﴾, for we were not alerted to it. But this excuse would not avail them at that time, according to what has been said, because they were alerted by the placing of the proofs and were made fully prepared to verify the truth; and to deny it despite that would be obstinacy. So how could they possibly say that?

Page 103

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 173 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Or [lest] you say﴾ on that Day: ﴿"It was only our fathers who associated partners with God before, and we were offspring after them"﴾. That is, our fathers were the ones who invented association (ishrak) and originated it before our time.
﴿And we were﴾ ourselves ﴿offspring after them﴾, who did not follow the path of monotheism (tawhid).
﴿Will You destroy us﴾, that is: will You punish us and destroy us today with the chastisement ﴿for what the falsifiers did﴾ of our misguiding fathers, [when] we do not see You doing [that]? And "or" (aw) is for preventing the absence of both [the options] but not for combining them; and the verb "say" is coordinated with its counterpart. Abu 'Amr read both with the ya' (third person, ghayba), because the beginning of the speech is in that form; the justification for the reading in the second person (khitab) is what you know. Some said: that is the saying of the Lord, Exalted is He, "your Lord," and this statement was not suitable for the people because what has been mentioned of their preparedness (isti'dad) narrows the routes to it for them; for imitation (taqlid), when the proofs are established and the capacity to infer by them exists, is something that has no way to be accepted at all. This is what the scholars of hadith (muhaddithun) and the Sufis, all of them, hold: that God, Exalted is He, took from the servants in their entirety a covenant spoken (mithaq qawli) before they appeared in this particular structure, and that the bringing forth from the loins (zuhur) was also before [that].

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed God, Exalted is He, took the covenant from the back of Adam at Nu'man on the Day of 'Arafah. He brought forth from his loins every offspring He had created, and scattered them before Him like ants (dharr). Then He spoke to them face to face: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said: 'Yes, we bear witness.'"

Malik in al-Muwatta', Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, and a great many others reported from Muslim ibn Yasar al-Juhani that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, was asked about this verse: ﴿And when your Lord took﴾ etc., and he said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) being asked about it, and he said: 'Indeed God, Exalted is He, created Adam, then passed His right hand over his back and brought forth from it offspring, and said: I have created these for Paradise, and they will act with the deeds of the people of Paradise. Then He passed His hand over his back and brought forth from it offspring, and said: I have created these for the Fire, and they will act with the deeds of the people of the Fire.' A man said: 'O Messenger of God, then what is the point of action?' He said: 'When God creates a servant for Paradise, He employs him in the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of Paradise, and God causes him to enter Paradise. And when He creates a servant for the Fire, He employs him in the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of the Fire, and God causes him to enter the Fire.'"

Al-Baydawi, in his tafsir, took the verse as a figurative expression (tamthil), and likewise in his commentary on al-Masabih, and he mentioned that the apparent meaning of the hadith of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, does not support that, nor does the apparent meaning of the verse, because if He, glorified and exalted, had wished to state that He brought forth the offspring from the loins of Adam in a single act, and not through the generation of some of them from others over the course of time, He would have said: "And when your Lord took from the back of Adam his offspring." The reconciliation between them may be said: the intended meaning of "Children of Adam" in the verse is Adam and his descendants, and it became, as it were, a name for the species, like "human" (insan) and "mankind" (bashar); and the intended meaning of "bringing forth" is the generation of some of them from others over the course of time; and the hadith was limited to mentioning Adam, being content with mentioning the root instead of mentioning the branch.
