Rather, perhaps He, glorified and exalted is He, [knew] that they never direct their choice toward the truth [page 120] ever, but persist in falsehood without any diverting force turning them, nor any inclining factor bending them from the signs and warnings. On this consideration, their creation was made to end in Hell, just as the gathering of the two groups, on account of their perfect natural readiness for worship and their complete capacity for it, was made to have their creation end in worship, as His words, glorified and exalted is He, declare: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾. End quote. But in my view there is no escape from interpretation in this context, so reflect and do not be heedless.

Then, the first prepositional phrase is connected to what is before it (i.e. "for Hell"), and its being placed before the direct object is because its complements contain a kind of length, and placing it between them or after them would lead to disturbing the eloquence of the sublime composition. The second prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted verb that occurs as an attribute of "many." The jinn are mentioned first because they are more fitting than humankind in the attribution of the qualities mentioned, more numerous, and older in creation. There is no difficulty that they were created from fire, so entering it would not be hard for them nor harm them at all. For we say in reply to this, despite its weakness: their creation from fire means that the predominant element in them is the fiery component, which does not preclude their being harmed by it, for humankind were created from clay and are harmed by it. This is clarified by the fact that the reality of fire did not remain in them as it was before they were created from it, just as the reality of clay did not remain in humans as it was before they were created from it. Moreover, what was created from fire is the body, and what is punished is the soul, which was not created from it. The punishment of the soul in a fiery form that is conceived is like its punishment in a clay form.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿they have hearts﴾ are in the accusative position as another attribute of "many." His words, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿with which they do not understand﴾ are in the nominative position as an attribute of "hearts," clarifying that they are not customary, differing from all other members of the category, lacking what they should have. Or it is an emphasis of what their indefiniteness and vagueness indicate of their being thus. By "heart" is meant the human subtle essence, and by "fiqh" is meant understanding, which is its linguistic meaning. It is said: faqiha with a kasra (faqiha) means "he understood," and faquha with a damma (faquha) means "he became a faqih," that is, he became understanding or knowledgeable of fiqh in the technical sense defined in the books of usul al-fiqh. The verb here is transitive, but its object has been omitted for generality. That is: they have hearts which are not such that they understand with them anything that is suitable to be understood, so that there enters into it what is fitting to the context, namely the truth and its proofs, by primary inclusion. The same applies to His words, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿And they have eyes with which they do not see﴾, so it is said: the meaning is that they do not see with them any of the visible things, so the cosmic signs indicating the truth are included in it by primary inclusion. Likewise, it is said of His words, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿And they have ears with which they do not hear﴾, where what is intended is that they do not hear with them any of the audible things, so it encompasses the revealed signs in the manner already mentioned. The case of the servant-girl (wasifa) in the last two is like that of the first. The seeing and hearing that are negated are what is peculiar to rational beings of perception, as is the function of the two species (humans and jinn), not merely the sensing of shape and sound, as is the function of cattle. There occurs in their speech something like: "So-and-so does not hear obscenity," meaning: he does not pay attention to it, does not turn his hearing toward it, and does not accept it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I have made myself deaf to foul speech, though were I to wish, I could hear it.*

In repeating the predicate in the two conjoined clauses, although the speech would be coherent without that, by saying "and eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear," there is something that is not hidden of the affirmation of the bad state of them. Likewise in affirming the three faculties for them and then describing each with what it is described with, rather than first negating them of them, by saying: "They have no hearts with which they understand, nor eyes with which they see, nor ears with which they hear." This is not hidden, according to what has been said, as testimony to the perfection of their firm entrenchment in ignorance and error. The interpretation of the verse in this manner, and taking the omission of the object for the three verbs as we have mentioned, is what some of the researchers (muhaqqiqun) chose, because of what it contains of revealing the true nature of their state, as he indicated. Some of them chose specification, that is: they do not understand the truth and its proofs, they do not see what Allah has created with the sight of consideration, and they do not hear the verses and admonitions with the hearing of reflection and contemplation. Whichever is the case, the meaning is that they did not direct what was created for them toward what it was for, so it is as if they were created thus. Had the literal meaning been intended, blame would not have been directed at them and the proof would not have been established. Whoever claims the literal meaning says: this is due to the bestowal of the Wise according to the eternal readiness that is not created, so the blame for it is because it indicates bad readiness, since it is like an effect of it. In sum, the verse cannot stand as proof for pure compulsion, even if what precedes it is added to it. Moderate compulsion is among what the people of truth have said, and it is "pure milk extracted from between dung and blood." Its essence, according to some shaykhs, is that the servant is free and compelled through his own choice. Perhaps the words of Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, where he said in a long passage: "If you say: I find in myself that if I wish to act, I act, and if I wish to refrain, I refrain, so my act is produced by me and not by other than me. We answer and say: Suppose you found that in yourself. Yet we say: Do you find in yourself that if you wish to will, you will, and if you wish not to will, you do not will? I do not think you would say that, for otherwise the matter would go on to infinity. So neither your will is by you, nor the occurrence of your act after the occurrence of your will is by you. Rather, you are compelled in the form of one who chooses." End quote. This returns to what we have mentioned. We have fully discussed this topic in our book al-Ajwiba al-'Iraqiyya 'an al-As'ila al-Iraniyya (The Iraqi Answers to the Iranian Questions), and by my life it is among the difficult investigations about which the Iranians asked.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those described with the attributes mentioned, ﴿are like cattle﴾, that is, in the absence of awareness in the manner mentioned. It has been said that their faculties are directed toward the means of livelihood and restricted to them, and it seems that the aspect of resemblance is understood from what came before, so the sentence serves as an emphasis of it, which is why it is separated from it.

﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾ than cattle, because cattle perceive what it is in their nature to perceive of benefits and harms, and strive to attract and repel them to the utmost of their ability, whereas these do not do so, since they do not distinguish between benefits and harms, but reverse the matter, abandoning bliss and advancing toward painful punishment. It has also been said: because cattle, when they are restrained, are restrained, and when they are guided to a path, they are guided, whereas these are not guided to any of the good things. It has also been said: because cattle were not given the capacity to acquire virtues, whereas these were given it and did not benefit from what they were given. And because cattle, though not obedient, are not disobedient, whereas these do not know their Lord, do not remember Him, and do not obey Him. In sum, that these are more astray is beyond doubt, and the aspects of this are many, and there is no contradiction between the two statements, as is not hidden.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those described with what has been mentioned of resemblance to cattle and the quality of being worse than them, ﴿they are the heedless﴾, that is, the complete in heedlessness regarding what is good for them. 'Ata' said: heedless of what Allah, exalted is He, has prepared for His friends of reward and for His enemies of punishment. Some made this sentence an explanation of the sentence before it, and therefore it was separated from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 180 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them.﴾ It has been said: this is an admonition to the believers regarding the manner of mentioning Him, exalted is He, and the manner of dealing with those who neglect this and who are heedless of Him, glorified is He, and of what befits His majesty, mighty is His glory. It comes after the statement of their complete heedlessness and complete misguidance. Another aspect of mentioning this will come later, God willing, Exalted is He.

By "names," as the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali and others said, is meant the formed words that indicate different meanings. "Al-husna" is the feminine of "al-ahsan," the superlative (af'al tafdil), and the meaning of this is that they are the most excellent of names and the most glorious, because they inform of the most excellent and most noble meanings.
Page 121
It has also been said: what is meant by "names" is the attributes, and it is from their saying "his name flew in the lands," meaning his fame and his description. The majority hold the first view, because of His words, mighty is His name: ﴿So call upon Him by them.﴾ For it is either from "da'wa" in the sense of naming, as in their saying: "I called him Zayd" or "by Zayd," meaning I named him, or from "du'a'" in the sense of calling out, as in their saying: "I called Zayd," meaning I called to him. Under either reading, it only fits the apparent meaning of the first view, according to what has been said.

﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾ meaning: they incline and turn away from the truth toward falsehood concerning them. It is said "alhada" when one deviates from the aim and the straight path, and from it comes "lahd al-qabr" (the niche in the side of a grave), because it is in its side, unlike the "darih" (the central grave), which is in its middle. Hamza read here and in Fussilat: (yalhadun) with a fatha, from the triliteral form, and the meaning is the same. Abu Ubayda narrated from al-Ahmar that "alhada" means to dispute and argue, while "lahada" means to incline and deviate. Al-Wahidi preferred the reading of the majority and said: "lahid" in the sense of "mulhid" is hardly ever heard. Deviation concerning His names, glorified is He, is to name Him by what has no revelation (tawqif) for it, or by what suggests a corrupt meaning, as in the saying of the Bedouin people: "O father of generosity, O white-faced one, O generous one," and the like. So the leaving commanded means avoiding that. By "His names" is meant what they applied to Him, exalted is He, and named Him by, according to their own supposition, not that His names are such in reality. On this basis the omission of the pronoun is explained, by saying "yulhidun biha" (they deviate by them). What has been said, that "names" here means "namings" (tasmiyat), so that the omission of the pronoun is for this reason, is not worth anything. Whoever explained deviation concerning the names by what has been mentioned went on to hold that the names of God, exalted is He, are tawqifi (fixed by revelation), taking into account the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus. So every name that occurs in these sources may be applied to Him, majestic is His glory, while what does not occur in them may not be applied, even if its meaning is sound. Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri clearly stated this in "Mafatih al-Hujaj wa Masabih al-Nahj," and al-Amidi in "Abkar al-Afkar" said: the basis for permitting the naming by the Most Beautiful Names is not a rational proof nor a verbal analogy, for otherwise it would be permissible to name the Lord, exalted is He, "faqih" (jurist) and "'aqil" (intelligent), since the meanings of these namings are sound regarding Him, namely knowledge and understanding, and these are more fitting than naming Him, glorified is He, with many things whose apparent sense is problematic. Rather the basis for this is only permission and license from the Lawgiver. So whatever permission for it has come from Him, we permit, and whatever prohibition has come from Him, we prohibit, and whatever has no permission or prohibition in it, some of our companions have said it is prohibited. But prohibition in the absence of revelation is no better than permission in the absence of revelation, since prohibition and permission are both rulings, and affirming one of them without evidence is no more preferable than the other. Rather the truth in this is suspension (waqf), namely that we rule neither permission nor prohibition, and what is followed in all of this is the legal indications (al-zawahir al-shar'iyya), as is followed in all other rulings, namely that it be apparent in its indication and in its soundness, and certainty is not required for it, as some companions held, because prohibition and permission are both legal rulings, and distinguishing between one ruling and another by requiring certainty for one but not the other is arbitrary and has no evidence. End of quotation. You know that the well-known position distinguishes between doctrinal (usuli i'tiqadi) rulings and practical (furu'i 'amali) rulings, as we will indicate shortly, God willing. The summary of discussion at this point is that the scholars of Islam agreed on the permissibility of applying names and attributes to the Creator, exalted is He, when permission for them has come from the Lawgiver, and on its prohibition when prohibition has come from Him. They differed where there is neither permission nor prohibition, concerning the permissibility of applying what He, glorified and exalted is He, is described by in meaning, and which is not among the proper names set in all languages, since the permissibility of applying such proper names to Him, exalted is He, is not a point of dispute for anyone, and where its application does not suggest deficiency but rather indicates praise. The majority of the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq) prohibited it absolutely, out of fear of danger. The Mu'tazila permitted it absolutely. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr inclined toward it because of the widespread use of such expressions as "Khuda" and "Takra" without objection, so it was consensus. This was answered by saying that consensus is sufficient for legal permission when it is established.
Page 122
Imam al-Haramayn also objected to it, saying that it is a claim based on analogy, and analogy is a proof in practical matters, and names and attributes are among practical matters. Some narrated from him a suspension of judgment. In the commentary on al-Mawaqif it is mentioned that al-Qadi Abu Bakr held that every expression that indicates a meaning established for God, exalted is He, may be applied to Him, provided it does not suggest what is not fitting to His essence, exalted is He. Then he said: It may be said that, along with the absence of such suggestion, there must be an indication of glorification so that application is valid without hesitation, and making the position of the Mu'tazila other than his is not correct; the well-known view is what we have mentioned.

Al-Ghazali, sanctified be his secret, made a distinction: he permitted applying an attribute (sifa), which is what indicates a meaning additional to the essence, and prohibited applying a name (ism), which is what indicates the very essence itself. He argued by the permissibility of truthfulness and its recommendation, and that the attribute, because it includes a descriptive relation returning to Him, depends only on the realization of its meaning, unlike the name, which does not include a descriptive relation, and which is not used except for parents or those in their position. It was answered that this applies where there is no barrier to using an expression indicating that relation, and the danger remains. How far is dust from the Lord of lords!

A group of later scholars preferred the view of the majority. They said: what has been heard is applied in the manner in which it was heard, and one does not go beyond that except in definiteness and indefiniteness, whether it suggests something, like "al-Sabur" (the Patient), "al-Shakur" (the Grateful), "al-Jabbar" (the Compeller), and "al-Rahim" (the Merciful), or does not suggest something, like "al-Qadir" (the Able) and "al-'Alim" (the Knowing). By what is "heard" (sam'i) is meant what has come in a Book, or a sound Sunnah, or consensus, because it does not lie outside these in verification, unlike weak reports. Analogy too, if we say the question is one of practical matters; but if we say it is one of doctrinal matters, then a weak Sunnah is like a very weak good report, and analogy is like consensus. Some have absolutely prohibited analogy, and this is the apparent view, because of the possibility that one of two synonyms suggests something the other does not.

Some have counted among what is established by analogy synonyms from one language or several languages, but this is not right. Among what is established by consensus they counted "al-Sani'" (the Maker), "al-Mawjud" (the Existent), and "al-Wajib al-Qadim" (the Necessary Eternal). It was said also "al-'Illa" (the Cause). It was said: "al-Sani'" and "al-Qadim" are both heard, like "al-Hannan" and "al-Mannan." Some verifiers stated that the non-annexed form is prohibited when it is a synonym of a heard annexed form, by analogy, just as applying what came in the manner of counterpart (mushakala) or metaphor is prohibited. They also stated that the occurrence of a verb, a verbal noun, or the like is not sufficient for the validity of applying a descriptive name, so one does not apply "al-Harith" (the Sower), "al-Zari'" (the Planter), "al-Rami" (the Thrower), "al-Mustahzi'" (the Mocker), "al-Munzil" (the Sender down), or "al-Makir" (the Schemer) to Him, glorified is He, even though verses come that suggest this.

Furthermore, some people said: the expressions for attributes are of three kinds. The first is what indicates necessary attributes, and it has types: among them is what is valid when applied singly and not in annexation, like "al-Mawjud," "al-Azali," "al-Qadim," and others; among them is what is valid both singly and in annexation to what has no defect, like "al-Malik" (the King), "al-Mawla" (the Master), "al-Rabb" (the Lord), and "al-Khaliq" (the Creator); and among them is what is valid only in annexation and not singly, like "ya munshi' al-rufat" (O Originator of decayed bones) and "muqil al-'atharat" (Remover of stumbles). The second is what indicates impossible attributes, like the hand, the face, descent, and coming; applying these is never valid at all, and if the revelation has come with them, interpretation is necessary. The third is what indicates neither necessary nor impossible attributes, but indicates established meanings, like scheming, deceiving, and the like; applying these is not valid except when revelation has specified it, and one does not say at all "ya Makkar" (O Great Schemer) or "ya Khaddu'" (O Great Deceiver), even if what indicates it is mentioned, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾. End of quotation, and what is in it is not hidden.

Al-Tibi mentioned that the correct position is to rely in application on tawqif, and that whatever the Lawgiver has permitted one to call upon God, mighty and majestic is He, whether derived or not derived, is a name, and whatever is attributed to Him, glorified is He, in another manner, whether interpreted or not interpreted, is a description. He considered "al-Hayy" (the Living) a description and "al-Karim" (the Generous) a name, and he claimed that one says "Ya Karim" but one does not say "Ya Hayy," even though both expressions occur concerning Him, glorified is He, in what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi transmitted,
Page 123
from the hadith of Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, that he said: "Allah, exalted is He, is Shy and Generous; He is shy when a servant raises his hands to Him that He should return them empty, until He places good in them."

He also mentioned that the definite article in "al-asma'" (the names) is for a known reference (al-'ahd), and that there must be a known referent, because He, glorified is He, commanded calling upon Him by them, forbade calling upon Him by other than them, and threatened for that.

Al-Shaykhan and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra that he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "Allah, exalted is He, has ninety-nine names; whoever memorizes them enters Paradise." In another narration: "whoever counts them." And in another: "Allah, exalted is He, has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one."

It was given in a summarizing and emphatic form, lest anything be added to what has been transmitted. In some narrations they are enumerated by his words, upon him be prayers and peace: "He is Allah, there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, the King, the Most Holy, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Majestic, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner, the Ever-Forgiving, the Subduer, the Bestower, the Provider, the Opener, the All-Knowing, the Restrainer, the Expander, the Abaser, the Exalter, the Giver of Honour, the Giver of Dishonour, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the Judge, the Just, the Subtle, the All-Aware, the Forbearing, the Magnificent, the Forgiving, the Appreciative, the Most High, the Great, the Preserver, the Sustainer, the Reckoner, the Majestic, the Generous, the Watchful, the Responsive, the All-Encompassing, the Wise, the Loving, the Glorious, the Resurrector, the Witness, the Truth, the Trustee, the Strong, the Firm, the Protector, the Praiseworthy, the Reckoner of all, the Originator, the Restorer, the Giver of Life, the Giver of Death, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, the Finder, the Glorious, the One, the Eternal Refuge, the Capable, the Powerful, the Expediter, the Delayer, the First, the Last, the Manifest, the Hidden, the Governor, the Exalted, the Good, the Relenting, the Avenger, the Pardoner, the Compassionate, the Owner of Sovereignty, Lord of Majesty and Honour, the Equitable, the Gatherer, the Self-Sufficient, the Enricher, the Preventer, the Harmful, the Beneficial, the Light, the Guide, the Originator, the Everlasting, the Inheritor, the Guide to right, the Patient."

Other lists than this have been transmitted from the People of the House, may Allah be pleased with them, and they took them from the Qur'an. Also there has come to us what differs from this narration in some of the names.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 180 (part 2 of 2):

Many scholars have mentioned that among these names some refer to an active attribute (ṣifah fi'liyyah), some refer to an essential attribute (ṣifah nafsiyyah), and some refer to a negative attribute (ṣifah salbiyyah). Some names are disputed as to whether they refer to any of the attributes mentioned or not, and this is the name Allah. The correct view is that it is a name of the Essence (al-dhāt), and it is the One to whom all affairs are returned. For this reason, most scholars hold that it is the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'ẓam). Another division classifies the names into those whose use is not permitted for anyone other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, such as Allah and al-Raḥmān; those whose use is permitted, such as al-Raḥīm and al-Karīm; and those whose mention alone is permitted for most of them. There are also those whose mention alone is not permitted, such as al-Mumīt (the Causer of Death) and al-Ḍārr (the Harmer). For one does not say, "O Causer of Death, O Harmer," but rather one says, "O Giver of Life, O Causer of Death," and "O Benefactor, O Harmer."

What I hold to be correct is that there is no limit to His names, may His names be exalted, to ninety-nine. This is shown by what al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is afflicted by distress or grief, let him say: O Allah, I am Your servant, the son of Your servant and the son of Your female servant. My forelock is in Your hand. Your judgment over me is binding, and Your decree concerning me is just. I ask You by every name that is Yours, which You named Yourself with, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You, that You make the Qur'an the spring of my heart, the light of my breast, the removal of my distress, and the banisher of my grief." The hadith (continues).

This is explicit in showing that the "or" (aw) does not restrict the count.

Muhyi al-Din al-Nawawi reported a consensus of scholars on this, and that the purpose of the hadith is to inform that whoever counts these ninety-nine names enters Paradise. This does not contradict the fact that He has other names besides them that are not described by this.

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi reported from some scholars that He has one thousand names, and then said: "This is few," and it is as he said. From some others it is reported that they are four thousand, and from some Sufis that they cannot nearly be counted.

In my view, the preferred position is that the use of derived names that refer to a type of essential or active attribute, and likewise negative attributes, for Him, is not dependent on a specific divine stipulation (tawqif khāṣṣ). Rather, the use is valid without it, but only after thorough investigation, and within that capacity, in matters that are explicitly for exalting Him and for guarding in the utmost degree against anything that suggests even the slightest deficiency, God forbid, in respect of Him, glorified is He. This is because we are permitted to exalt Allah, blessed and exalted is He, by statements and actions, and no limit has been set for us in this. So whenever the use contains exaltation of Him, mighty and majestic is He, it is permitted. Obligation is tied to capacity: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. So after exerting one's capacity in exalting Him, the difficulty is removed.

The hadith of danger (ḥadīth al-khaṭar) that they mention requires that only the use of what has been established by mass transmission (tawātur) as applied to Him, exalted is He, or upon which the Muslim community (ummah) has agreed, be valid. This is because establishment beyond that is speculative (ẓannī), while danger in it is certain (yaqīnī). The names mentioned just above are not found in many of the narrations, although they are well known from the hadith of al-Tirmidhi. He said: "A number of narrators related it to us from Safwan ibn Salih, and we do not know it except from his narration, and he is trustworthy according to the scholars of hadith." You know that this degree does not establish certainty, nor even something like it or similar to it. Moreover, the enumeration of some of the People of the House (ahl al-bayt) of the ninety-nine, as in al-Durr al-Manthur, and likewise others, as will not be hidden from one who investigates, differs from this enumeration. The chain of that report, although it is not as strong as the chain of this one, nonetheless gives rise at least to doubt. Unless it is said that there is consensus on what is in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi, to the exclusion of what is in other narrations contrary to it. But I have not come across anyone who reported that.

Furthermore, these names taken from what we have mentioned are not prohibited for supplication with them, or for using them as predicates describing Him, glorified and exalted is He, or as attributes of Him, majestic and mighty is He. All of them are "the most beautiful" (ḥusnā). Their being named thus is because, in the meaning intended by them in relation to Him, exalted is He, they are specific to Him, blessed and exalted is He, with the specificity of a proper name. They are not applied to anyone other than Him in the meaning intended when they are applied to Allah, exalted is He. They are applied to others only in another meaning, between which and that meaning there is nothing but what lies between black and white. For between them is the utmost distance, beyond which no distance can be conceived. Yet they share in accidentality, colouredness, and being perceived by sight, and other things besides that. By this, white is not counted as similar to black, or vice versa, because similarity (mumāthalah) is an expression for sharing in the species and the quiddity (māhiyyah), and that is absent here. Likewise, it is absent between the knower (al-'ālim), for example, which is attributed to Allah, exalted is He, and the knower which is attributed to others besides Him, glorified and exalted is He. No one knows the reality of that and its quiddity except Allah, exalted is He, just as no one knows the reality of Allah, exalted is He, except Allah, exalted is He, in this world and the Hereafter.

Yes, if someone says, "I do not know except Allah, exalted is He," he speaks truly, but from another aspect. The ultimate knowledge of the knowers is inability to know, and their knowledge of the reality is that they do not know Him. So when that is revealed to them, they have known and have reached the furthest point possible for created beings in knowing Him, glorified and exalted is He.

This is what the Greatest Ṣiddīq (Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him) pointed to when he said: "Inability to attain perception is itself perception." Indeed, it is what the Master of mankind (ﷺ) meant by his saying: "I cannot enumerate Your praise; You are as You have praised Yourself."

For peace and blessings be upon him meant: "I do not encompass Your praises and the attributes of Your divinity. Rather, You alone encompass them. It is not that I know from You what I cannot express with my tongue." The variation in the degrees of the prophets, peace be upon them, the angels, and the saints in knowledge is only by standing upon the wonders of His signs in the kingdom (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, and the creation of spirits and bodies. At that point they differ in knowledge of the names and attributes. Knowing that Zayd, for example, is knowledgeable is not like knowing the details of his knowledge, as is not hidden.

What we have mentioned of brevity is not objected to by the division the scholars made of His names into the specific, such as al-Raḥmān, and the non-specific, such as al-Raḥīm. For their meaning of "specific" is that what is taken into its direct conceptual meaning (mafhūm muṭābaqī) includes something that prevents its application to others. Al-Bayḍāwī has stated that the meaning of al-Raḥmān is the true Benefactor who reaches the utmost degree of mercy, and this does not apply to anyone other than Him, exalted is He. Therefore it is not used as a description for anyone else. And "non-specific" means that what does not take that into its conceptual meaning, but rather takes into it a general meaning, so it is applied to Allah, exalted is He, and to others. However, when it is applied to Him, exalted is He, what is intended is the complete individual of that concept, which is not fitting (lā yalīq)

[p. 125]

and cannot be established except for Allah, mighty and majestic is He. It may be said: there is no difference between the derived names whose root of derivation is found in others in general, in that taking account of that existence requires non-specificity, while taking account of existence in its most complete and perfect form requires specificity. There is no distinction between one name and another, except that we have judged them to be specific in some cases and non-specific in others for another reason, such as usage and non-usage, and the permission or non-permission of the Lawgiver. So this does not contradict what we have said either. Indeed, taking the specificity to Allah, exalted is He, in the names mentioned in the verse is not possible on the basis that placing the predicate first (taqdīm al-khabar) also indicates specificity. Then the meaning would be: "To Allah, not to others, belong the names that are specific to Him, exalted is He, and are not applied to anyone else." This amounts to saying that the names specific to Him, glorified is He, are specific to Him, blessed and exalted is He, and that is something without benefit. In that case, it is necessary either to interpret the names as attributes, as some have said, and the meaning of "the most beautiful" (al-ḥusnā) is "perfect in every respect," i.e., for Allah, exalted is He, not for others: the perfect attributes, since the attributes of others, glorified and exalted is He, however imperfect they may be, are at least surrounded on both sides by non-existence.

The meaning of ﴿so call upon Him by them﴾ and what follows is: name Him by what is derived from them, or call upon Him with them. And ﴿leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾ means: those who incline away from the truth regarding His attributes, so they name others by them, or call upon others while believing in association (shirk). Leave them and their deviation. As for using some kind of figurative usage (tajawwuz), and what al-Ṭībī mentioned, that the definite article in "the names" is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and the rest of what he said, which I do not think you are in doubt about its weakness, so reflect.

It has also been permitted that "deviation" (ilḥād) means turning away from naming Him, exalted is He, by some of His noble names, as they said: "And what is al-Raḥmān? We do not know except Raḥmān of Yamamah." In that case, "leaving" means avoiding. Just as "names" was first intended as His names in actuality, the meaning is: name Him, exalted is He, by all His names, and avoid removing some of them from the picture. It has also been permitted that it means applying them to idols and deriving their names from them, such as al-Lāt from Allah, exalted is He, and al-'Uzzā from al-'Azīz. In that case, "names" means His names in actuality. The explicit noun in place of the pronoun, together with stripping it of description in all cases, is to indicate that their deviation lies in the names themselves, without consideration of the description. "Leaving" means turning away and not caring about what they do, anticipating the descent of punishment upon them soon, as His statement, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) which came as an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "Why do we not care?" It was answered: "Because punishment will soon descend upon them, and you will be relieved." The meaning, on the command to avoid, is: avoid their deviation, lest what befalls them befall you, for the punishment for that will soon descend upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 181:

﴿And among those whom We created is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ It has been said: this is a general statement about the condition of all others apart from those mentioned, from among the two categories (al-thaqalan, humankind and jinn) described above with misguidance in its most complete form. According to a group of the muhaqqiqun (verifying scholars), and as appeared to the scholar al-Tibi, it is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿And We have certainly created﴾ and with His statement, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿who guide﴾, and so on. When it is taken in its essence and core, it stands as a counterpart to His statement, exalted is He, ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand … they are the heedless﴾. Both verses are like the unfolding (nashr) of His statement, mighty is His majesty, ﴿Whoever Allah guides is the [rightly] guided, and whoever He sends astray—those are the losers﴾. It also serves as a concluding summation (tadhyil) for the account of the one who was given the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and the great names, and then withdrew from them.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾, is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) owing to the relevance of the account of the names: the account of the great names of Allah, exalted is He, which that one who withdrew was given, as is in some of the narrations. It has also been linked to His statement, mighty is His majesty, ﴿They are the heedless﴾, in the sense that it is like an alert that what necessitates entry into Hell is heedlessness of the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and of His most beautiful names. People of taste (dhawq) and direct witnessing (mushahada) find this in their own spirits, because when the heart becomes heedless of the remembrance of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, and turns toward this world and its desires, it falls into the fire of greed and continues to fall from darkness to darkness until it reaches the depths of deprivation. The opposite is the case when the gate of remembrance is opened to the heart: it then enters the garden of contentment and continues to ascend from light to light until it reaches the highest degrees of excellence (ihsan).

[p. 126]

The particle (min) is either an indefinite noun described by a following clause or it has the meaning of "those who" (alladhi). The intended meaning is: some of those whom We created, or some from among those whom We created, a great and numerous group, who guide people while being connected with the truth, or who guide them with the word of truth and point them to uprightness, and who judge by the truth in the governments that operate among them and do not act unjustly in them.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Juraij that he said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This is my community.'"

And he narrated from Qatada that he said: "It reached us that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say when he recited this verse: 'This is for you, and the people before you have been given the like of it: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among my community there is a people upon the truth until ʿIsa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) descends."

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Muʿawiya and al-Mughira ibn Shuʿba, who both said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There will not cease to be from my community a community standing by the command of Allah, the Exalted. Those who forsake them will not harm them until the command of Allah, the Exalted, comes, and they will be upon that."

Al-Jubba'i used the verse as evidence for the validity of ijma' (scholarly consensus) in every age, whether that be the age of the Prophet (ﷺ), the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), or others. For if it were restricted to one age, its mention would have no benefit, since that is already known. He also used it to argue that no age is free of a mujtahid (a qualified jurist exercising independent judgment) until the Hour is established, because mujtahids are the people of ijma'. It has been said that this contradicts what has been narrated: "The Hour will not be established except upon the most wicked of creation, and the Hour will not be established until it is no longer said on earth: Allah." It is answered that this period is joined to the Day of Resurrection because it is adjacent to it, and the intended meaning is that no age is free of a mujtahid apart from that period. It has also been said that the intended meaning of the two reports is to indicate the predominance of evil, which does not negate the existence of a small number of people of that description, and one of them suffices, and in that case he is the community (ummah). The restriction of their description to guiding people is to indicate that their own guidance is a matter that is established and needs no explicit mention.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 182:

﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, and the guidance of the guiding ones did not benefit them, like the people of Makkah and others. Some restricted it to the earlier ones, but the generality is preferable. The attribution of the signs to the pronoun of majesty is to honour them and to magnify the boldness of denying them. The relative pronoun is in the nominative position, as a subject whose predicate is the clause ﴿We will gradually lead them﴾, meaning: We will certainly bring them closer to destruction step by step. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative position, governed by a verb omitted that the mentioned one explains. Istidraj (gradual leading, a form of istif'al) is from the "daraja" (degree), in the sense of moving someone degree after degree, from low to high, in which case it means ascending, or the reverse, in which case it means descending. al-A'sha used it in his saying:

"Even if you were in a well eighty cubits deep, and you climbed the heavens' ways by a ladder,
The speech would lead you on gradually until you bark at it, and you would know that I am not one who is struck dumb, against you."

in its absolute meaning. Some said: it is istif'al from "daraja", either in the sense of "ascended" which was then extended to be used for every gradual transfer, whether by way of ascent, descent or straightness; or in the sense of "walked a weak walk", from which comes "daraja al-sabi" (the child crawled); or in the sense of "folded", from which comes "adraja al-kitab" (he folded the book), and then it was borrowed for seeking every gradual transfer from one state to another among the states suitable for the one transferred and agreeing with his desire. His leading them by the Exalted, through lavishing blessings upon them while they are immersed in error, is of this kind. Hence it is said: "If you see that God the Exalted has bestowed blessings upon a servant while he persists in his disobedience, know that he is being led on (mustadraj)." This can be understood as ascent, considering their view and their assumption that continuous blessings are a favour from God the Exalted, and this is the apparent meaning. It can also be understood as descent, in terms of reality, for the human nature in its original disposition is sound and prepared to accept the truth, due to the principle: "Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition)." So he is capable of attaining guidance and religion. But when he inclines to the earth, follows desires and commits sins and misdeeds, he descends degree by degree until he becomes the lowest of the lowest. Whatever the case, the aim is nothing but their being led along the path of sins until the word of the otherworldly or worldly punishment becomes due against them, according to what has been said, in the most grievous and dreadful state. The lavishing of blessings is a means to that. ﴿From where they do not know﴾, that it is so; rather, they think it is a favour from God the Exalted. It has also been said: they do not know what is intended for them. The prepositional phrase is connected to an implied element that serves as an adjective to the verbal noun of the mentioned verb, meaning: We will lead them gradually, coming from where they do not know.

And I will grant them respite (﴿وأُمْلِي لَهُمْ﴾), meaning: I will give them time. The conjunction *wa* (and) is for coordination, and what follows it is coordinated with *sanastadriju-hum* (We will gradually lead them on step by step). It is not included in the ruling of the *sin* (the future particle "sa-"), because granting respite is not one of the matters that occur gradually, like the gradual attainment (*istidrak*) that takes place step by step in itself. Rather, granting respite is something that happens all at once, and only its effects and rulings occur gradually. This is indicated by the change of expression to the singular pronoun, along with what it contains of variety (*iftinan*) that points to greater attention to the meaning of the speech, because it is built on renewing the account and the resolve, and on making the one who is not singular included in its ruling. The singularity is not hidden in this case. It has also been said that this is a resumed statement (*kalam mustanaf*), meaning: "And I am granting them respite." The shift from that plural pronoun to the first-person singular pronoun is similar to *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), and it has been argued that it is from *talwin* (variation of style).

As for what has been said, that this is to indicate that the granting of respite is purely by divine decree, and that this is to point out that gradual leading on through the intermediary of the arranging angels (*mudabbarat*) is nothing, because of the statement: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our granting them respite is good for them﴾ and ﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾, this is a confirmation and an emphasis of the threat. *Matin* (firm) derives from *matana* (to be strong), meaning strength and power, and from it comes *al-matn* (the back, or the thick flesh on either side of the spine). Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, interpreted *kayd* (plan) as *makr* (deception). Some interpreters explained it as gradual leading on and granting respite together with their outcome, and it is called *kayd* because its outward appearance is kindness while its inward reality is subjugation. Others explained it as the seizing itself only, and it has been said that it is called so because its preliminaries are of this kind, and it has been said that it is because it descends upon them from where they do not perceive. In any case, the meaning is that My plan is powerful and cannot be repelled by strength or by stratagem. The verse is a proof for the People of the Sunnah regarding the question of divine decree and predestination (*al-qada' wa al-qadar*). Some commentators claimed that it was revealed concerning the mockers among the Quraysh, whom Allah granted respite and then seized on the day of Badr,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 184:

Then, when Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, had intensified the warning to the heretics who turn away and are heedless of His signs and of belief in His Messenger (ﷺ), He followed this, according to what has been said, with a response to their doubt and a denial of their failure to reflect. So the Mighty and Majestic One said: ﴿Do they not reflect? There is no madness in their companion.﴾

The hamza is for denial and reproach, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied clause that the context and the preceding discourse call for. The disagreement over such a construction is well known, and reference to it has already been made.

As for "ma" (what): Abu al-Baqa' said it may be an interrogative of denial in a nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being "bi-sahibihim" (with their companion); it may be a negation, with its noun being "jinnatin" (madness) and its predicate being "bi-sahibihim". It is also permitted that it be a relative pronoun, though this is remote. "Jinnah" is a verbal noun like "jilsah" (a sitting), meaning madness, and it does not mean the jinn, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿from among the jinn and mankind﴾, because that would require supposing an elided noun, i.e., "the touch of a jinn" or "its possession." The indefinite form is for minimisation and belittlement. "Tafakkur" (reflection) is contemplation and the engagement of the mind upon a matter; it is one of the verbs of the heart, so its ruling is their ruling regarding suspension. The position of the clause, on both readings, is accusative by removal of the preposition. The position of the relative clause is accusative on that basis in the last reading, meaning: Have they denied and not reflected upon any madness that exists in their companion, the one who is the greatest of those who guide to the truth and upon whom the verses were sent down? Or [it means]: upon whether there is in their companion any madness, such that reflection would lead them to stand upon his truthfulness and the soundness of his prophethood, so that they would believe in him and in what was revealed to him of the verses? Or [it means]: upon what is in their companion of madness according to their claim, so that they would know that this is not madness in any way and would believe.

Al-Tabarsi preferred that the speech is complete at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Do they not reflect?﴾, meaning: Have they denied and not reflected upon his words and deeds, or: Have they not performed reflection? Then a new sentence begins: "What is in their companion of madness?" in the manner of denial, astonishment and rebuke; or it is said: there is no madness in their companion at all.

By "their companion" is meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The expression of him (ﷺ) by this designation is to emphasise and intensify the denial, since companionship is among the things that let them know of his (ﷺ) purity from any taint of what has been mentioned. The explicit mention of negating madness from him (ﷺ), despite the clear impossibility of its existence in him, is because speaking what is extraordinary proceeds only from one who has a touch of the jinn, speaking in any manner without any basis, or from one who has divine support, informing of the unseen. Since there is none of the first in him (ﷺ), the second is established.

Ibn Jarir and others reported from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) stood upon al-Safa and called the Quraysh clan by clan, saying: "O sons of so-and-so," warning them of the punishment of Allah and its events until the morning, until one of them said: "Your companion this is a madman; he spent the night raving until morning." Then Allah sent down the verse.

Accordingly, the explicit negation of madness is a refutation of their monstrous slander in the eyes of anyone who has the least intelligence, and the expression "their companion" comes in keeping with their own speech, together with the subtle point already mentioned. Some have mentioned regarding the occasion of revelation that when they saw what befell him (ﷺ) of the severity of revelation, they would say: "He has gone mad." Then came: ﴿He is only a clear warner﴾, confirming what preceded it and refuting them in what they claim, since in it the reality of his (ﷺ) condition becomes clear, meaning: he (ﷺ) is none other than one who emphasises warning and manifests it to the utmost degree,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 185 (part 1 of 2):

Then, since the matter of prophethood is built upon tawhid (the oneness of God), He, glorified is He, mentioned what points to it, and said, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿Have they not considered the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth?﴾ This is directed as a rebuke and reproach for their neglect of reflection upon the cosmic signs, following what He had censured them for. The hamza here is like the hamza mentioned before, and the waw is for conjunction with an understood element, as has already been explained, or with the negated sentence introduced by lam. Malakut means the great sovereignty. The meaning is: Did they deny, and not reflect on what has been mentioned, and not look with a contemplative and inferential gaze at what indicates the perfect power of the Creator, the oneness of the Originator, and the great station of the Owner, so that the truth of what that noble Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, calls them to would become clear to them? It seems that the expression "looking" (nazar) is used here rather than "reflecting" (tafakkur), which was used before, to indicate that the evidence here is clearer than what preceded.

His statement, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿and what Allah has created of any thing﴾ may be a conjunction with (malakut), and its specification to the heavens and the earth is because the greatness of sovereignty is most manifest in them. It may also be a conjunction with the genitive-governed element, in which case it applies to all. The generalization is because all share in the greatness of sovereignty in reality. And (min shay') is an explanation of (ma). In this there is an alert that the indication of tawhid is not restricted to the heavens and the earth; rather every atom of the world is a proof of His oneness:
"And in everything there is a sign for Him that points to His being One."
This is a matter agreed upon among the intelligent. Yes, some have made the mode of indication to be contingency (huduth), which is what most of the theologians hold; and some have made its mode to be possibility (imkan), which is what the philosophers hold and some theologians have chosen. The first was preferred by the qutb of his age, Shaykh Khalid al-Mujaddidi, may his secret be sanctified, in his glosses on the marginal notes of 'Abd al-Hakim upon al-Khayali, so refer to them. And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and that perhaps their term has drawn near﴾ is a conjunction with (malakut), so it is an object of (yanzuru) (they consider). But it is not required that the restriction of the conjunctive element be observed in the conjunct, based on what they said: the condition of the conjunctive element need not be taken into account in the conjunct, and this matter has been discussed before. "An" is the light form of the heavy, its noun is the pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is "asa" together with its subject, which is (an yakuna). The predicate of the pronoun of the matter need not be a declarative clause, nor does it require interpretation, as the scholars have explicitly stated, so there is no point in disputing this. The noun of "yakuna" is also the pronoun of the matter, and the predicate is: (qad iqtaraba ajaluhum). They did not make this a case of tanazu' (competition between verbs) because the competition of "kana" and its predicate is not an established pattern, not because that would contradict the norm due to the anaphora before mention that it involves; for that is necessary when the noun is made a pronoun of the matter, and there is no harm in either. The matter of repetition in what we have mentioned is minor, so no departure from what is customary should be undertaken for its sake, in contrast to al-Qutb al-Razi. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a verbal-source particle (masdariyya), and it was objected that it is not joined except to a fully inflected verb, and "asa" is not like that. The meaning is: Have they not considered the approach of their terms and the expectation of their arrival, so that they hasten to seek the truth and turn toward what will save them before the sudden seizing of death and its surprise, and before the descent of punishment? So by "their term" is meant the term of their death. It is also permitted that it refers to the Hour, and the attribution to their pronoun is because they are connected to it through their denial of it and their searching about it. And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ cuts off the possibility of their believing at all, and negates it entirely after the establishing of proof and the guidance to reflection. The ba' is related to "yu'minun" (they believe). The pronoun in "ba'dahu" refers to the Qur'an, according to what most exegetes have held, and it is known from the context. "Hadith" here means speech, so there is no evidence in the verse for those who claim the createdness of the Qur'an. It has been said: even if we grant that it is evidence, what is meant by the Qur'an is its wording, and that is createdness according to the well-known view. The meaning is: if they do not believe in the Qur'an, which is the utmost in clarity, then in what speech will they believe after it? It has been said that the pronoun refers to the signs, with an understood genitive that is implied by "kaddhabu" (they denied), and the masculine form is by considering them as the Qur'an, or by interpreting them as the mentioned matter, or by treating the pronoun as the demonstrative. The meaning: They denied the signs and did not reflect on what necessitates their confirmation, from the states of him, upon him be blessings and peace, and the states of the created things; so in what statement will they believe after denying them? And there is a remoteness in this. It has been said that it refers to the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, with an understood genitive as well, i.e., after his speech they will believe, and he is the most truthful of people. It has been said: what is meant is after this speech. It has been said: after the term; i.e., how will they believe after the expiry of their term? Al-Zamakhshari linked this to His statement: ﴿and that perhaps﴾ etc., as a link of causation from it, and the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, as if it were said: Perhaps their term has drawn near, so why do they not hasten to believe in the Qur'an before death? And what are they waiting for after the clarity of the truth? And in what statement more worthy than it do they wish to believe? The supplying of what was supplied according to the author of al-Kashshaf is not because it must be supplied for the speech to be sound, but to draw attention to the meaning of delay contained within "ayy" (which), and that after this clear explanation there is no awaited matter. And His statement, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him﴾ is a resumptive statement confirming what precedes, based upon the sealing of their hearts. What is meant is the continuity of the negation, not the negation of continuity. And His statement, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿and He leaves them in their transgression﴾ with the ya' and the nominative, as a resumption, i.e., and He leaves them. Several readers read it with the nun of majesty, by way of iltifat (shift of person), i.e., and We leave them. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the ya' and the jussive, as a conjunction with the place of the nominal clause that is the response of the conditional, as if it were said: whoever Allah leads astray, no one will guide him, and He will leave them. It may be that this is a sukun for lightening, as in the reading "yush'irkum" and "yansurkum." The jussive with the nun has also been transmitted from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr among the irregular readings, and its parsing is according to one of the two possibilities. And His statement, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿wandering blindly (ya'mahun)﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the object of "yadharuhum." Al-'Amah means hesitation in error and bewilderment, or not knowing a proof. The singular pronoun in the context of negation is in observance of the wording of (man), and its plural in the context of affirmation is in observance of its meaning, to make explicit that the negation and affirmation apply to all, as has been said.

* * *

(And from the path of allusion in the verses) ﴿And recite to them the news of him to whom We gave Our signs, but he cast them off﴾: an allusion to one who was tested with turning back after advancing, in that he traveled until what appeared to him appeared, then he turned back from the path due to the badness of his preparation and the dominance of wretchedness, and we seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He. In the expression "cast off" (insalakha) there is much that is not hidden.

﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them﴾ to the enclosure of holiness, ﴿but he clung to the earth﴾, i.e., he inclined toward the lower earth of nature, ﴿and followed his desire﴾ in preferring evil, ﴿so his likeness is like the likeness of the dog﴾ in its most base state, ﴿if you drive it away﴾ with rebuke, ﴿it pants﴾ it lolls out its tongue with heavy breathing.

﴿Or if you leave it, it pants﴾ also. The meaning is that it pants constantly, and it seems to be an allusion that this one who has cast off does not cease to let his tongue loose against the people of perfection, whether he is rebuked for that or not.

﴿And We have created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾, and they are the manifestations of wrath.

﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ the secrets.

﴿And they have eyes with which they do not see﴾ the cosmic proofs.

﴿And they have ears with which they do not hear﴾ the revealed signs; so they are deaf, dumb, and blind.

﴿Those are like cattle﴾: they have no concern except eating and drinking.

﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾ than they, because they do not heed when warned and are not guided when shown the way.

Among what is considered improbable by way of reason is what Imam al-Sha'rani transmitted from his shaykh 'Ali al-Khawwas, may his secret be sanctified, that animals are morally responsible, arguing with His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like you﴾, together with His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And there has been no community but a warner has passed among them﴾, and with what was narrated from him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "Verily, retribution will be taken for the hornless sheep from the horned sheep."

Although this concerns sheep, there is no one who makes a distinction. It was also reported from him the saying that everything in existence of animal, plant, and inanimate matter is living and perceptive. Then he said: I said to him: Does the comparison by the Exalted of those of His servants who have gone astray to cattle indicate the deficiency of cattle compared to humans, or their perfection in knowledge of Allah, exalted is He? He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I do not know. But I heard some of them say: their comparison to cattle is not a deficiency; rather it is to show the perfection of their rank in knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted, to the point that they are bewildered in it. So the comparison in reality falls on bewilderment, not on the one bewildered by it. There is no one more bewildered than the scholars of Allah, exalted is He. So the highest that the scholars reach in knowing their Lord, glorified is He, is the starting point of the cattle, which has not moved from its origin, though it moves in its circumstances with the movement of divine circumstances, for it does not remain in one state. Therefore those among these people whom He, glorified and exalted, described were more astray in path than cattle, because they wish to exit bewilderment through their thought and their reasoning, and that is not possible for them. The animals know that and stop at it, and do not seek to exit it, because of the intensity of their knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. It is mentioned that they were only called cattle (bahaim) because their matter is obscured (ubhima) to most creatures, so they do not know it as the people of unveiling know it. End of quotation.

This is a statement that gives the believer who holds it envy of the cattle; may Allah benefit us through them and protect us from envy.

﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ by which every matter is ordered by one of them.

﴿So call on Him by them﴾ according to the degrees, and the highest of them is calling by the tongue of action, which is adorning oneself with their meanings to the extent that is conceivable regarding the servant; and that is the portion of those brought near among them. Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned that their portions from the meanings of His names, exalted is He, are three. The first is knowing them by way of unveiling and witnessing, until their realities become clear to them by a proof that does not admit error, and His being characterized by them is revealed to them with a revelation in which clarity and explanation take the place of the certainty a person has about his inner attributes, which he perceives by inner witnessing and not by the sensation of his outer self. How great is the difference between this and the belief taken from fathers and teachers by imitation, and the insistence upon it, even if it is accompanied by dialectical theological proofs.

The second (point): their awe at the attributes of majesty and perfection revealed to them, in a way that stirs in them a longing to take on as many of those attributes as they can, so that they draw near to the Truth in terms of attributes rather than place, and thereby take on a likeness to the angels brought near to God, exalted is He. Being free of this longing can only result from one of two things: either weakness of knowledge, or the heart being filled with, and absorbed in, another longing.

The third (point): striving to acquire, as far as possible, those attributes, to take on their character and adorn oneself with their excellences. Through this the servant becomes a *rabbani* (one devoted to the Lord), a companion of the Exalted Assembly of the angels, resembling them. At that stage, nearness and distance no longer affect his perception. Indeed, his perception is not confined to what can be conceived in terms of such nearness or distance, and he is made holy above lust and anger. Thus his actions are not driven by them; rather, the motive behind them becomes the seeking of nearness to God, exalted is He.

This does not entail establishing a likeness between God, glorified and exalted is He, and the servant, for He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, because likeness (*mumathalah*) is sharing in kind and essence, not mere sharing (in some quality). A clever horse, however clever it may be, is not a likeness of a human being, because it differs from him in kind, even if it resembles him in cleverness, which is an accident external to the constituents of humanity. And you know, upon the slightest reflection, that no sharing can be conceived between God, the Living, the All-Knowing, the Willing, the Able, the Speaking, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, and the servant who is characterized by life, knowledge, will, power, hearing and sight, except in the mere application of the name. The discussion concerning the tradition: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through supererogatory acts..." and so on, requires plunging into an ocean without shore. So take what We have given you, and leave those who deviate concerning His names (*ilhad*), seeking their meanings from other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, and attributing them to Him. These are among those whom He, glorified and exalted is He, has created for Hell: ﴿They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ of deviation. ﴿And among those We have created is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾; these are the perfect, rightly guided ones. ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, like those who object to this community, ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾, i.e., We will gradually lead them on, ﴿and I give them respite﴾, i.e., I grant them time.

﴿Indeed, My plan﴾, i.e., My seizing, ﴿is firm﴾, i.e., severe. It is the customary practice of God, exalted is He, regarding those who object to His friends, that He seizes them with the most severe seizing. We have witnessed this many times. We seek refuge in God, exalted is He, from His scheming. ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion (*malakut*) of the heavens and the earth, and at what God has created of any thing?﴾ These are the cosmic signs. The meaning of *malakut* has already been mentioned. In the terminology of the Sufis, may God sanctify their secrets, it is an expression for the unseen world specific to spirits and souls, while they interpret *mulk* (dominion) as the world of witnessing, consisting of sensible natural things such as the Throne, the Footstool and others. Every body is composed of its ultimate constituents (*al-istiqsa'at*).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 186:**

﴿Whomever Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him﴾, since there is no guide other than Him, glorified is He:

"To the water he runs, the one choking on a morsel; but where does he run, the one choking on water?"

﴿And He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾: they wander about, because their readiness (isti'dad) requires that, and Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success (al-Muwaffiq).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 187 (part 1 of 2):

Then, since the mention of the approach of their term (ajal) had preceded, the Exalted (subhanahu) followed it with the mention of their questioning about the Hour (al-sa'ah), so He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾. It has also been said that this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain some of their rebellion and misguidance. Al-sa'ah, in its original sense, is a name for a small, indefinite portion of time; according to the astrologers (al-munajjimun), it is one of twenty-four parts of the night and day, and it is divided into "crooked" (mu'wajjah) and "straight" (mustawiyah). In the usage of the Sharia, it is applied to the day of the death of creation and to the day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds. The commentators have explained it as the Day of Resurrection (yawm al-qiyamah). Perhaps what is meant by it is one of those two days, although the well-known meaning is the Last Day. The apparent meaning is that the one asked about is the first day, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj. The term al-sa'ah in that sense is one of the dominant names (min al-asma' al-ghalibah). The reason for applying it to that day, and likewise to the time of the standing (al-qiyam), is clear if what is meant is the time of death or the time of standing, without considering extension, since it is evident that it is a small measure in itself. If what is meant is an extended period of time, its application to it is either because it comes suddenly, as has been said, or because it startles those who encounter it, so it seems little to them, or it makes what preceded it seem little, or because, despite its length, it is a small measure in the sight of God Most High, or because of the swiftness of its reckoning. It is also permissible that calling it by this name is by way of naming a thing by its opposite, for embellishment, as black is called camphor. The ones who asked about this were some people of the Jews.

For Ibn Ishaq and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Himl ibn Abi Qushayr and Sammul ibn Zayd said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Tell us when the Hour is, if you are a prophet as you say; for we know when it is." This was a test from them, while they knew that God had kept its knowledge to Himself. So Allah revealed the verse.

Some have held that the questioners were the Quraysh.

For 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah that the Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, confide to us when the Hour is, because of the kinship between us and you." So it was revealed.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Its time of arrival is when?﴾ — with the hamzah of ayyan pronounced with a fatha. Al-Sulami read it with a kasra, and that is a dialect form of it. It is a temporal adverb (zarf zaman) containing the meaning of interrogation, and it is followed by the subject (mubtada') or the present-tense verb, not the past tense, unlike mata, which may be followed by either. The verified view is that it is simple and primary (basitah murtajalah). It has also been said that its derivation is from ayy, and it is fa'lan from it, because its meaning is "which time" and "which act." Or that ayy is from awaytu, meaning "I returned," because the category of tawaytu and shawaytu is more numerous than the category of hayaytu and wa'aytu, and because of its closeness to it in meaning, since the part returns to the whole and relies upon it. Its original form on this basis is awiyy, then the waw was changed to ya and assimilated into the ya, becoming ayy. It was not made a verb from ayn, because ayyan is a temporal adverb and ayn is a spatial adverb. Some people claimed that its origin is ayya awan or ayya an; but this is nothing.

In al-Kashf, the derivation from ayy was criticized as contrary to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in Surat al-Naml, and that if it were named with it, it would be fa'alan from anna ya'inu, and would not take tanwin. Then he said: "The correct view is what he mentioned there, because derivation in non-inflected words has no basis." Then: "Its derivation from ayy is no more preferable than its derivation from al-ayn in the sense of al-haynunah, because ayyan is a time, and it seems the interrogation changed it; but this is nothing, because it is by implication (tadmin), as in mata and similar words. Likewise, the derivation of ayy from awaytu has no basis, except that the more apparent view is that it is permissible both to take tanwin and not to, as in hima qabban." End quote.

It was answered that what was mentioned is a matter they assumed for the sake of the test, and so that its ruling might be known if it were named with it; so it does not contradict what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, and likewise it does not contradict the verification, so consider this carefully. In any case, it is in the nominative position (mahall al-raf'), being a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and mursaha is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). It is a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi) from arsahu, meaning "when he established it and fixed it," i.e., when is its establishment and fixing? The verb irsa' is hardly used except for a heavy thing, as in His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿and the mountains He set firm﴾, and from it comes mursat al-sufun (the ship's anchor). Its attribution here to the Hour is by way of considering meanings as bodies.

Some have permitted that it be a noun of time, and the objection that it would necessitate that time have a time is not valid; the philosophers differ on its permissibility, since it is interpreted as "when does that occur?" As for the sentence, it has been said that it is in the accusative position as an object of an omitted verb of saying, placed as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in yas'alunaka; i.e., they ask you, saying: "Its time of arrival is when?" It has been said that it is in the genitive position as an apposition (badal) to "the Hour."

The verified view, according to some of the leading verifiers, is that its position is accusative by removal of the preposition, because it is an apposition to the prepositional phrase and not merely to the genitive. In linking the question first to the Hour itself and second to the time of its occurrence, there is an indication that the primary purpose of the question is the Hour itself, in terms of its descent upon its appointed time, with respect to its being a place for it. What is in the answer, namely His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾, is also construed in accordance with that, i.e., its knowledge in the aforementioned respect is with Him, the Exalted, and no other, so there is no need to say: "Only the knowledge of the time of its establishment is with Him, Mighty and Majestic." Some, because they overlooked the subtle point indicated, read the sublime wording as involving an omitted genitive (hadhf al-mudaf), and to this Abu al-Baqa's statement points. The meaning of that being with Him, Mighty and Majestic, specifically, is that He has kept it to Himself, not informing anyone of it, neither an angel brought near nor a sent prophet. The mention of the title of Lordship together with its attachment to His pronoun, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, has been said to be for the purpose of indicating that His granting him success in answering in the aforementioned manner is by way of training and guidance, and this is better than what we will point to, Allah willing. His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿None but He will reveal it at its time﴾ are an explanation of the continuance of its concealment until the moment of its standing, and a complete despair of revealing its matter by way of information. Tajliyah means uncovering and making manifest. The lam is the lam of timing (lam al-tawqit). Opinions differ concerning it: it has been said it means "in" (fi); Ibn Jinni said it means "at" ('inda); al-Radi said it is the lam indicating specification (ikhtisas), which has three kinds: either the act is specific to the time because it occurs in it, as in "I wrote for the first of such-and-such," or because it occurs after it, as in "for five nights having passed," or before it, as in "for a night that remains." With absolute use, the specification is because it occurs in it; otherwise it is according to the context. Many have interpreted it here as "in."

The meaning: none reveals it or makes manifest to people its matter about which you ask except the Lord, Glorified, in His essence, without anyone among the created beings perceiving it so that he would intermediate in making it known to them. Yet this is not in the sense that He does not inform them of its time, as the questioners asked, but rather in that He establishes it, so that they know it in the fullest manner. The prepositional phrase is connected to the tajliyah, and it is a restriction on it after the occurrence of the exception, as if it were said: "None but He will reveal it at its time," except that it was placed first at the outset to draw attention that its revelation is not by way of informing of its time, but by manifesting its very reality at the time about which they ask. His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿It has become heavy in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a resumptive clause, as the preceding one was, confirming what came before. The meaning: it has become great and tremendous for the people of both, since they do not know the time of its occurrence. It is related from al-Suddi that whoever is ignorant of the knowledge of a thing finds it heavy. It is related from Qatadah that the meaning is: it is tremendous to the people of the heavens and the earth, since they fear it and dread its severities; and in another narration from him, the intended meaning is that its knowledge is heavy for them, so they do not know it, and this returns to what was mentioned first.
