It has also been said that the meaning is: it became heavy at the occurrence upon the heavens themselves, until they split and their stars scattered and their sun was folded, and upon the earth itself, until its mountains were moved and its seas were set ablaze, and whatever was in it occurred. To this points what is related from Ibn Jurayj. In that case, there is no need to assume an omitted genitive. The particle "in" in all the other opinions is a metaphor indicating the firm establishment of the act, as is not hidden.

﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾, i.e., except abruptly, in a moment of heedlessness.

Al-Shaykhan related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will certainly arrive when two men have spread out their garment, yet they will not trade it nor fold it. The Hour will certainly arrive when a man has departed with the milk of his she-camel, yet he will not drink it. The Hour will certainly arrive when a man is plastering his cistern, yet he will not water in it. The Hour will certainly arrive when a man has raised his morsel to his mouth, yet he will not eat it."

﴿They ask you as if you were well-versed (hafiyy) concerning it﴾, i.e., knowledgeable of it, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in what Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from him. "Hafiyy" is an intensive form (fa'il) from hafiya 'an al-shay' when one searches to learn its state. Some have mentioned that al-hafawah originally means thoroughness in a matter out of care for it. Al-A'sha said:

"If you ask about me, then many is the questioner, well-versed concerning al-A'sha, by whom he ascended."

From it comes ihfa' al-shari (trimming the moustache). It is also used for goodness and gentleness, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, He was gracious to me﴾. The meaning intended here branches from the first meaning, since whoever searches for a thing and asks about it firmly establishes knowledge of it; so the necessary meaning of the word is intended, metaphorically or by implication.

The verb is construed with 'an in view of its original meaning, which is asking and searching. It has been said that it is because it was implicitly given the meaning of uncovering, and otherwise it would be construed with the bi'. Abu al-Baqa permitted that 'an be in the sense of bi'. It is related from the Learned One (al-Habr, i.e., Ibn 'Abbas) and Ibn Mas'ud that both read it with bi'.

The comparative clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of yas'alunaka; i.e., your state being compared, in their view, to the state of one who is hafiyy. It has been said that 'an-ha is connected to yas'alunaka, and the comparative clause is parenthetical, and the complement of hafiyy is omitted, i.e., with it or with them, based on what has been said: that hafiyy derives from hafawah in the sense of compassion. For Quraysh said to him, upon him be blessings and peace: "There is kinship between us and you, so tell us when the Hour is." This is related from Qatadah and also from the Interpreter of the Qur'an (Turjuman al-Qur'an). The meaning on this view is that they think you have its knowledge but conceal it, so out of your compassion for them they asked you to single them out with it. Connecting 'an on this view with a omitted verb such as "you inform them and uncover for them its matter" is far-fetched. It has been said:

It is from *hafiya* (حَفِيَ) with the sense of being pleased with something, and this is narrated from Mujahid, al-Dahhak and others. The meaning is: as if you are pleased by asking about it, which you love. In this reading, *'an* (عَنْ) is connected to *hafiyy* (حَفِيٌّ), since it implies the meaning of asking, as has been said. According to Shaykh al-Islam, the statement is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) that serves to explain their error in directing the question to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), on the assumption that he knew the thing asked about, or that knowledge of it is one of the requirements of prophethood. It also explains their error in the basic question by informing them of the answer to what was asked.

In *al-Intisaf*, regarding the repetition of *yas'alunaka* (they ask you), it is the established practice in such cases that when a speech is built around a purpose and an incidental matter arises in its course, and one wishes to return to complete the first purpose, after its mention has become distant and has been set aside so that the end connects to the beginning. Here, when He, glorified be He, began the speech with His words, ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it take place?﴾, and then the mention of the answer was interrupted by *qul* (say) into a sudden matter, He intended the completion of their question about it, with a form of rebuke against them. This is contained in His words, ﴿As if you were eager about it﴾, which is intense attachment to the question. Since its mention had become distant, it was renewed so that its completion would follow it. You will never find Him renewing a matter except in a kind of brevity. For this reason He did not mention the thing asked about, which is the Hour, being content with what had preceded. Then, when He, majestic and exalted be He, repeated the question for this benefit, He also repeated the answer in brief, saying, mighty is the One who speaks: ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with God﴾. From this the wisdom of mentioning the Majestic Name here becomes known.

The First Muhaqqiq (*al-Muhaqqiq al-Awwal*) mentioned that the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to repeat the first answer for the sake of affirming the ruling, establishing it, and indicating its cause by the method of proof, through mentioning the Name of the Essence, which points to its entailing the attributes of perfection, of which knowledge is one, and as a preparation for an allusion to their ignorance, through His words, exalted be He: ﴿But most people do not know﴾.

Al-Jubba'i claimed that the first question was about the time of the Hour's occurrence, and that this question was about its manner and the details of the hardships and states within it. It has been said:

It is for this reason that its answer was specified by the Name of the Essence, since it is the greatest of names in awe. This is the view of al-Nisaburi, and it is reported from al-Imam and others. I do not see any sound basis for them in this.

The object of *'ilm* (knowledge), according to what some of them indicate, is omitted: that is, they do not know what has been mentioned concerning the exclusivity of its knowledge to Him, exalted be He. Some of them deny it altogether, so they ask about it only in jest. Some of them know that it will definitely occur and claim that you know the time of its occurrence, so they ask out of ignorance. Some of them claim that knowledge of this is one of the requirements of prophethood, so they take the question as a means to disparage it. And the one who knows the clear state of affairs and asks as a test is counted among the ignorant, because he does not act according to this knowledge of his.

God, glorified be He, concealed the matter of the Hour only because the legislative wisdom requires it, for it is more conducive to obedience and more restraining from disobedience, just as concealing the specific term of a person's life is similar. If it is said that the creative wisdom also requires this, it would not be far-fetched. The apparent meaning of the verses is that the Messenger (ﷺ) did not know the time of its occurrence. Yes, the Messenger (ﷺ) knew in general that it was near, and he was informed of it (ﷺ).

Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and authenticated it, from Anas, traced back to the Prophet (*marfu'*, meaning attributed directly to the Prophet): "I was sent together with the Hour like these two," and he pointed with the index finger and the middle finger.

In the *Sahihayn* (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim), from Ibn 'Umar, also traced back to the Prophet: "Your lifespan, compared to those nations before you, is between the afternoon prayer and the sunset."

It has come in more than one report that the age of this world is seven thousand years, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent at the end of the sixth millennium, and that most of the community (*milla*) falls within the seventh millennium.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti narrated several hadiths that the age of the world is seven thousand years. He mentioned that the duration of this community exceeds one thousand years but does not reach five hundred years beyond that. He based this on reports and narrations that he mentioned in his treatise entitled *al-Kashf 'an Mujawazat Hadhihi al-Ummah al-Alf* (Revealing the Passing of This Community Beyond the Thousand). Some of them named this second millennium *al-mukhadrama* (the mixed one), because half of it is worldly and the other half is otherworldly.

If the Mahdi does not appear at the head of the century we are in, everything he has built collapses, as is not hidden from one who examines it. You would think it has already collapsed.

Al-Saffarini reported from the philosophers that they claimed the management of the world we are in belongs to the spike of wheat (*sunbula*, the Virgo sign). When its cycle is complete, corruption and decay fall upon the world. When the matter returns to the balance (*al-mizan*, the Libra sign), the materials are gathered together and the resurrection is decreed as a return.

Al-Bakri said: their rule of Aries is twelve thousand years, the rule of Taurus is one thousand years less than that, and so on, decreasing by a thousand each time down to Pisces, so its rule is one thousand years. The total of all this is seventy-eight thousand years. When it is completed, the world of generation and corruption ends. This was attributed to Hermes, and he is claimed to have said: "There was no living creature on the earth under the rule of Aries, Taurus and Gemini. When the rule of Cancer came, aquatic creatures were produced, and it is the mother of the earth. When the rule of Leo came, the quadrupeds were produced. When the rule of Virgo came, the two first humans were generated: Adam *Nawas* and Hawwa' *Nawas*."

Some claimed that the duration of the world is the measure of the fixed stars' passage through the degrees of the celestial sphere. According to his claim, each star crosses a sign in three thousand years, so the total is thirty-six thousand years. End of quotation.

It is not hidden from anyone who has examined the books of astronomical observation and the astronomical tables (*zijat*, sing. *zij*) that according to them there are three periods: the greatest, the middle, and the least. They call them *tasyirat* (planetary motions). They are equal across all the signs. The greatest period is that in which each degree is crossed in one hundred years, the middle is that in which each degree is crossed in ten years, and the least is that in which each degree is crossed in one year. They also have a greater period, which they call *al-tasyir al-a'zam* (the greatest motion). In it each degree is crossed in one thousand years. The motion today is in the balance, and four degrees, fifty-six minutes, thirty-one seconds and twelve thirds of it have passed. If the duration of that is reckoned from the point of the head of Aries until now, it amounts to one hundred thousand, eighty-four thousand, nine hundred and forty-three years. The duration of the movement of the fixed stars, according to what is reported from Ptolemy, in each sign is two thousand, one hundred and sixty-two years, eight months, sixteen days and nineteen hours. If that is multiplied by twelve, the number of signs, the result is the duration of their crossing the entire celestial sphere. This is much less than what was mentioned. Perhaps the intended meaning of the cycle of a sign is what is intended by its rule, meaning the ruling of its influence and its ordinary effect, as is understood from some books of these people, by the ruling of its primacy, which is what overflows onto the stars that descend into it. All of this is among the things that God, exalted be He, has not sent down any authority for.

The truth from which one should not turn away is the belief that the world has a temporal origin (*hudūth zamani*), and no one knows its beginning except God, exalted be He. Likewise the age of the world, the beginning of the human creation, the duration of its remaining in this world, and the length of time of its stay in the barzakh, all of this is known only to God, exalted be He. All that has been transmitted on this subject consists of conjectural matters, and most of them lack any sure foundation to rely upon. Beyond this are statements of the people of China and others, which are more calamitous and more bitter than what has preceded. In sum, the remaining age of the world, according to the one who says it will perish, is a very small amount compared to the past portion of it. And God, exalted be He, knows best the reality of what lies beyond.

[p. 135]

[p. 136]

Say: "I have no power to bring about any benefit for myself, nor to ward off any harm," meaning: I have no power, for my own sake, to bring about any benefit or to repel any harm.

The prepositional phrase and what it modifies, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is either attached to ﴿أملك﴾ ("I have power") or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) qualifying ﴿نفعًا﴾ ("benefit"). The intended meaning is that I have no power over that at any time, ﴿except what Allah wills﴾, meaning: except at the time of His will, may He be glorified, by enabling me to do so. Then I would possess it by His will. The exception here is muttaṣil (continuous, i.e., it refers to something within the same category as what precedes it). This indicates, as Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani said, that the power of the servant is effective by the permission of Allah and His will. It has also been said that the exception is munqaṭi' (discontinuous, i.e., it excludes something outside the category), meaning: but what Allah the Exalted wills of that is what will happen. On this reading there is an expression of helplessness that is quite evident. The statement is intended to establish his inability to know the Hour in the most complete manner. The repetition of the command serves to show concern for the importance of the answer and to draw attention to its independence and its difference from the first part.

﴿And if I knew the unseen﴾, that is, that which includes the connections between things, the relations that normally establish causation and its effects, and the oppositions that entail resistance and prevention. ﴿I would have acquired much good﴾, meaning: I would have obtained much of the good that is bound up with arranging causes and removing obstacles. ﴿And harm would not have touched me﴾, meaning: the harm from which one can escape by guarding against its causes and resisting it with its preventatives, even though some harm has no means of escape. It seems that the non-touching of harm is among the consequences of acquiring much good in general. For this reason the second clause does not follow the pattern of the first. The implication in the conditional sentence need not be rational and universal; it is sufficient that it be customary in some cases. Several scholars have ruled that it is of the customary kind in this verse, and with this al-Shihab answered what has been said: that knowledge of a thing does not necessarily entail the ability to act upon it, and its source is heedlessness of the intended meaning.

Interpreting "good" and "harm" as described above is the view taken by the majority of the verifying scholars. Some have explained the first (good) as profit in trade and the attainment of abundance, and the second (harm) as the opposite of that, based on what was reported from al-Kalbi: the people of Makkah said, "O Muhammad, will you not inform us of a cheap price before it rises, so that we may buy and profit, and of a land that is about to become barren, so that we may move from it to one that has become fertile?" Then this verse was revealed.

It is also reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the first means profit in trade and the second means poverty. It has been said that the first is the answer to the question and the second is denial. It has been said that the first is occupation with calling to those for whom happiness has already been decreed, and the second is the weariness resulting from calling those upon whom the word of punishment has become binding.

It has been said, and attributed to Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj, that the unseen means death, the good means increasing righteous deeds, and the harm means what is not of that kind. Other interpretations have been given as well, and all of them, as you see, include some that should not be used as the basis for interpreting the revelation.

The verse mentions good before harm because of the connection with what precedes it, where benefit was mentioned before harm. There, the mention of benefit and harm also followed a pattern of ascending order, as has been said, since warding off harms is more important than bringing about benefits. Al-Naysaburi mentioned that in most places in the Qur'an where harm and benefit are mentioned together, harm is mentioned first before benefit, and this is the original pattern, because the worshipper worships his object of worship first out of fear of its punishment and then worships it out of hope for its reward, as the words of Allah the Exalted indicate: ﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and in hope﴾. Where benefit is mentioned before harm, this is due to the prior occurrence of a word that includes the meaning of benefit, as in this surah, where the word guidance was mentioned just before error in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Whomever Allah guides is the one truly guided, and whomever He leaves astray﴾, and so on. In Surat al-Ra'd, the word willingly was mentioned before in the words of Allah the Glorified: ﴿willingly and unwillingly﴾, and that is a form of benefit. In Surat al-Furqan, the word sweet was mentioned before in the words of Allah the Majestic and Exalted: ﴿This is sweet and palatable﴾, and that is a form of benefit. In Surat Saba', the word expanding was mentioned before in the words of Allah the Blessed: ﴿Allah expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾. Let the rest be measured by this. Ibn Jurayj interprets the benefit here as guidance and the harm as misguidance, and by this the subtle point of the ordering, which this scholar considered in this passage, is strengthened, as is not hidden.

This verse has been raised as a difficulty alongside what is authentically established: that the Prophet (ﷺ) informed of many unseen matters, and things happened as he said, and this is counted among his greatest miracles, peace and blessings be upon him. Scholars have differed concerning the answer. It has been said that what is understood from the verse is the negation of his knowledge, peace and blessings be upon him, at that time, of the unseen that brings about benefits and removes harms that have no connection with rulings and laws. What the Prophet (ﷺ) knew of the hidden matters is not of that kind, and lacking knowledge of such things does not discredit his exalted station, peace and blessings be upon him.

Muslim reported on the authority of Anas and Aisha, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by people who were pollinating palm trees, and he said: "If you did not do this, it would be good." So they did not do it, and the dates came out shriveled (shīṣ). He passed by them again and said: "What did you pollinate?" They said: "You said such and such." He said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life."

In another narration from him: when he was told that it had become shriveled, he said: "If it is a matter of your worldly affairs, then it is up to you; and if it is a matter of your religion, then it is to me."

The Prophet's (ﷺ) lack of knowledge of worldly matters has been regarded as a perfection of his station, since the whole world, in comparison with his Lord, is nothing.

It has also been said that the intended meaning is the negation of the continuous (ongoing) knowledge of the unseen on his part, peace and blessings be upon him, and the use of "kāna" to indicate continuity is common. Continuity is also implied in "increasing much good" and "not being touched by harm." It has been said that the intended meaning of the unseen is the time of the establishment of the Hour, because the question was about it, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, did not know it and was not informed of it at all. In that case, good and harm are interpreted in a way that suits this, such as teaching the questioners and not being subjected to disbelievers' attacks on the matter of the prophetic mission. It has also been said that the article in "al-ghayb" (the unseen) is for comprehensiveness (istighrāq), yet he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, did not know every unseen matter, for among the unseen are things that Allah the Exalted alone has, such as knowing the essence of His own Self, blessed and exalted is He, and knowing the time of the establishment of the Hour, as this verse indicates.

In Lubab al-Ta'wil by al-Khazin, in answer to this, it is said that this statement from him, peace and blessings be upon him, may have been made out of humility and courtesy, and the meaning would be: I do not know the unseen except if Allah informs me of it and decrees it for me. It is also possible that he said this before Allah informed him of the unseen, and then when Allah informed him, he told them about it. Or this statement came out in response to their question, and after that Allah made him aware of some unseen matters so that this would be a miracle for him and a proof of the truth of his prophethood, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. End of quotation. There is room for reflection in it. The words of some verifying scholars point toward preferring the first view.

The meaning of His words, glorified be He: ﴿I am only a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ according to this view is: I am only a messenger sent as a warner and a bringer of good news, and my task is to acquire the knowledge connected with these two functions, not to stand upon the unseen matters that have no connection with them. I have revealed about the matter of the Hour that which is connected with warning, namely that it will certainly come and that it is near. As for specifying its exact time, this is not something that warning requires; rather, it is something that would undermine warning, because, as previously explained, keeping it ambiguous is more conducive to obedience and more restraining from disobedience. The warner is mentioned first because the context is one of warning. ﴿For a people who believe﴾, meaning: who affirm what I have brought. The prepositional phrase may be connected to both descriptions together, and the believers benefit from the warning just as they benefit from the good tidings. Or it may be connected to the latter only, and the object of the first is omitted, meaning: a warner to the disbelievers. It was omitted so that the tongue would be kept clean of it.

Some have intended by the disbelievers those who persist in disbelief, and by their opposites those who believe at any time. In that case, the verse contains encouragement for disbelievers to bring about faith and a warning against persisting in disbelief and transgression.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 189:

﴿He it is who created you﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining what requires the oneness of God (*tawhid*), which is the greatest aim. The relative clause is placed as the predicate (*khabar*) in order to magnify the status of the subject (*mubtada'*). That is: He, glorified is He, is that Great One of exalted status who created you all, alone, without anyone else having any role in that at all. ﴿From a single soul﴾, which is Adam, peace be upon him, according to what the majority explicitly state. ﴿And made from it﴾

[Page 138]

That is, from its kind, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He made for you spouses from your own selves﴾. The *min* here is for origin (*ibtida'iyya*), though the well-known view is that it is partitive (*tab'idiyya*), meaning from its body, because it is narrated that God, glorified is He, created Eve from Adam's left rib. The manner is unknown to us, and nothing can outmatch God, exalted is He. The verb is conjoined to the relative clause (*silat al-mawsul*) and falls under its judgment. There is no objection to its content preceding the content of the first in existence, since the *waw* (conjunction) does not require sequence in it. The verb may mean "made" (*sayyara*), in which case His saying, glorified is He, ﴿its spouse﴾ is its first object, and the second is the prepositional phrase placed before it. Or it may mean "created" (*ansha'a*), in which case the adverbial phrase is connected to it and placed before the explicit object, as has been explained many times. Alternatively, it is connected to an implied element that serves as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object.

﴿So that he might find rest in her﴾ is the final cause (*'illa gha'iyya*) of the making. That is, so that he might find companionship with her and be at peace with her. The concealed pronoun refers to the soul (*nafs*). The apparent form would be feminine, because *nafs* is among the feminine nouns of transmission (*sama'iyya*), and for this reason its adjective is feminine. However, it is masculine because what is meant by it is Adam. If it were made feminine according to the apparent form, the attribution of rest to a female would be understood, while the intended meaning is the opposite. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that the masculine is better in correspondence to the meaning (*tibaq*). In *al-Kashf* he explained this by saying that since rest is explained as inclination, and that includes sexual inclination which is the preliminary to covering (*taghashshi*), especially since it was emphasized with the *fa* in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then when he covered her﴾, and covering is necessarily attributed to the male, the correspondence in its attribution is also to him, even though it is from both sides. In this there is an indication that multiplying the kind is the cause of companionship, just as unity is the cause of loneliness. Also, since the created being was first made the origin, it is fitting that the making of the spouse be for his rest after feeling estranged, not the reverse, for that is not suitable in wording or meaning. However, Ibn al-Shihnah mentioned that when *nafs* is intended to mean the human being himself, it is masculine, even though its wording is feminine, and "three souls" (*thalathat anfus*) came in the sense of three persons. When it is intended to mean the spirit (*ruh*), it is feminine only. Its diminutive is *nufaysa*, so let this be understood. The object pronoun in ﴿covered her﴾ refers to the spouse, which means the wife and is feminine. The covering is a metaphor (*kinaya*) for intercourse. That is: when he had intercourse with her, ﴿she bore a light burden﴾, that is, a burden that was light, which is the fetus when it is a drop of semen, a clot, or a lump of flesh, for there is no heaviness in it compared to what follows of the later stages. Thus *hamlan* is put in the accusative as an object. It is with a *fath* on the *ha'* when it is what is in the belly, or on a tree, and with a *kasr* its opposite. Each of them has been reported with both *kasr* and *fath*. It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun in the accusative as an absolute object, and that the lightness be understood as absence of harm, that is: she bore a burden that was light for her and she did not suffer from it what some pregnant women suffer from their pregnancies of distress and harm.

﴿Then she passed on with it﴾, that is, continued with it, as Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak read it. The meaning is that she remained with it as she was before, moving about, sitting, rising, and lying down, and this is a meaning with no ambiguity. The claim that it is an inversion (*qalb*), meaning that the pregnancy continued with her, is held by the critics to be from inversion. Abu al-Aliyah and others read *marat* with a light *ra'*, and it was said that it is a lightened form of *marrat*, as one says *zalla* for *zallilt*. It was said that it is from *al-mirya*, that is doubt, meaning she doubted the matter of her pregnancy.

Ibn Umar and al-Jahdari read *famarat*, from *mar yamuru*, meaning to come and go. Thus it has the same meaning as the reading of the majority, or it is from *al-mirya* like the reading of Abu al-Aliyah, and its pattern is *fa'alat*, and its final radical was dropped because of two consecutive unvoweled letters.

﴿Then when she became heavy﴾, that is, she became one with heaviness through the greatness of the burden in her belly. The *hamza* in it is for becoming, like their saying *atmar* and *albana*, meaning he became one with dates and milk. It was said that it is for entering into a time of the verb, that is, she entered into the time of heaviness, like *asbaha* meaning he entered the morning. The first is more apparent. What is understood by heaviness is its literal meaning, and the contrast between it and the first meaning of lightness is clear. It may be meant as distress in order to contrast with lightness in the second meaning, but what is understood in both places is the literal meaning. It was read *uthqilat* in the passive voice, with the *hamza* for causation, meaning the burden made her heavy.

﴿They both called upon God﴾, that is, Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both,

[Page 139]

when they feared the consequence of the matter, so they were anxious about it and humbled themselves before Him, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿their Lord﴾, that is, the owner of their affair, deserving that the supplication be specific to Him.

In this there is an indication that they began their supplication with it, which is what is known of them in supplication. The object of the supplication is omitted because the oath-clause indicates it. That is: their claim before Him, exalted is He, that He would grant them a righteous one, and they promised in return to give thanks, as an emphatic oath, and said, or they were speaking: ﴿If You give us a righteous one﴾, that is, offspring of our kind, sound. It was said: a child free from defects in creation, such as lacking some limbs and the like, and a group held this view. From al-Hasan: a male child. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿We will surely be﴾, we or we and our offspring, ﴿among the thankful﴾, those firm in gratitude to You for Your giving. It was said: for Your blessings, of which this blessing is one.

It is also permitted that the pronoun in *ataytana* refers to both of them and to everyone who is born from their descendants, but this is not the case.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 190 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when He gave them a righteous child﴾: that is, what they asked Him for, as offspring in the primary sense, or what they requested, both primarily and by extension, of children, grandchildren and their descendants as they multiply. ﴿They ascribed﴾, that is, the righteous, sound offspring, and he used the dual pronoun in view of the fact that this offspring consists of two kinds, male and female. It has been related that Hawwa' (Eve) would give birth to twins in each delivery in this way. ﴿To Him﴾, that is, to God, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿partners﴾ from among the idols and images ﴿in what He had given them﴾ of children, inasmuch as they attributed that to them. The expression "in what" [using ma] is because this attribution occurs at the time of birth, and the children at that time are counted among what does not reason.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of the relative pronoun is what encompasses all the blessings, for the polytheists attribute that to their gods. The reason for shifting away from the pronoun, by not saying "partners in it," is clear on both views. Attributing the act of ascribing to the offspring is in the manner of: "the Banu Tamim killed so-and-so." ﴿Exalted is God above what they associate with Him﴾: this is a declaration of His transcendence containing the sense of wonder, and the fa' (so) is for the sequence of this after what He detailed of His power, glorified and mighty and majestic be He, and the traces of His blessing which deter from polytheism and call to monotheism. The plural pronoun refers to those descendants who made partners for God, and in it is the predominance of the masculine over the feminine, and an indication of the magnitude of their polytheism. What is meant by that is either the naming or absolute association. The "ma" is either a verbal noun, meaning "above their association," or a relative pronoun, or a qualifying noun, meaning "above what they associate with Him, exalted be He."

This verse, in my opinion, is among the difficult ones, and the scholars have lengthy discussions about it and wide disputes. What we have mentioned is what the words of al-Jubba'i point to, and it is not objectionable, after overlooking its contradiction with the transmitted reports, apart from the dual pronoun at times and the plural at other times while the referent is singular in wording, and we have not found this in eloquent usage.

Many have chosen that in "ja'ala" and "atahuma" afterward there is an elided modifier, and the dual pronoun in them refers to Adam and Eve, in the same style as what came before: that is, their children made [partners] in what He gave their children of offspring. They only estimated it in two places and did not suffice with estimating it in the first, and the pronoun in the second refers to what was estimated first, because the elision lacks any clear indicator, so it is like the non-existent, and the pronoun cannot properly return to it. The meaning of the association in what He gave the children is naming each one of their children with something like Abd al-Uzza and Abd Shams.

It was objected, first, that what has been mentioned, namely the elision of the modifier and placing the modified in its position, is only resorted to where the verb has some connection to the modified as well, by extending to it in reality or in ruling, and includes an attribution to it which shows a distinction required by the context, as in His saying: "And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh" [the verse]. For the deliverance from them, although its connection in reality is only to the forefathers of the Jews, has been attributed to their descendants by virtue of its extension to them, in order to fulfil the requirement of the context of favour. The same is said of its like. Here, however, it is not so, for there is no doubt that Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, are free from any extension of the stated making to them in any way, so there is no basis for attributing it to them in appearance. Second, that the association of their offspring by ascribing them to servitude to their idols is a consequence of taking those idols as gods, and branches from it; it is not a matter that occurred from them that had not been before. So the reproach should be upon this rather than that. Third, that the association of their children did not occur when God gave them a righteous child, but after that by long periods of time. Fourth, that applying "ja'ala" to other than what the first was applied to, and the sequence by fa' would cause disorder in the noble structure.

It was answered regarding the first that the reason for that attribution is to signal their abandoning what was better, since they proceeded to place their children in the same rank as themselves, and committed to thanking them within their own thanks, and swore to that before knowing their circumstances, by showing that their failure in the thanks that He promised them as a firm promise with an oath is like their own failure in the essence, in deserving breach and violation; together with what this implies of the multiplication of their wrongdoing, by showing that by their making [partners] they placed them in the predicament of breach and violation, and made them as if they themselves had committed it directly. Thus they combined the wrong against God, exalted be He, with the wrong against them, peace be upon them. As for the second, the context requires the reproach for this, because when He mentioned the blessings that God, glorified and exalted be He, bestowed upon them and upon them, of creation from a single soul and their multiplication, He reproached them for their ignorance and for attributing those blessings to other than their Giver, and for ascribing them to one who has no power over anything. He had not first mentioned any matter of divinity intentionally, so that they might be reproached for taking gods. As for the third, the word "lamma" is not for a narrow time but an extended one, so it does not follow that the condition and the consequence occur on one day, one month or one year, but that differs according to the matters, as one says: "When Islam appeared, the lands were purified from unbelief and heresy." As for the fourth, [the answer is] by what the author of al-Kashshaf wrote in choosing this view and preferring it over the view that the association refers to Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, and it is not the common usage, but what has been transmitted of naming a child Abd al-Harth. Its matter is that it is apparent that His saying, exalted be He: "It is He who created you from a single soul" is addressed to the people of Makkah, and that after the story of the Jews was concluded in the manner it was concluded, as a consolation and encouragement for the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and as a means of bringing him to steadfastness and patience, following the example of his brethren among the steadfast messengers, peace be upon them all, especially his chosen one and interlocutor Musa, peace be upon him, for what he endured from the Children of Israel was very similar to what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was suffering from the Quraysh. It was concluded with what calls for a connection to the sense for which the discourse was first brought, that is, His saying, exalted be He: "And among those We created is a nation who guide by the truth." There is a transition to mention of the people of Makkah at [the phrase "Those who denied Our signs, We shall draw them on step by step"], and their questioning about what does not concern them is mentioned. When it was intended to show that this is not what concerns you, and that what matters is removing what you are immersed in of the filth of polytheism and sins, it prepared for that with: "It is He who created you," implying the sense of favour and ownership which require monotheism and servitude. Then it was said: "So when He gave them a righteous child, they made partners for Him," meaning: you made, O offspring of them both. There was indeed in your parents an excellent example in their saying: "If You give us a righteous child, we shall surely be among the thankful." It seems that the meaning, and God knows best, is: when He gave them a righteous child and they fulfilled what they promised their Lord of carrying out the requirement of thanks, you, O their offspring, opposed that, so you associated and denied the blessing. In this turning, and in attributing your act to the two parents—in reverse of what was made of the father's creation and formation in the context of favour, connected to them—there is a hint of the extreme of your ingratitude and your persistence in error. Upon this the saying of God, glorified be He, applies: "Exalted is God above what they associate." Then he said: It is evident that the construction of "ja'ala lahu" in a manner other than the first does not cause disorder in the structure, and the sequence by fa' does not cause disorder but rather its harmony. The fair judgment is that the questions and the verse on this view are of the nature of a riddle. From al-Hasan and Qatada it is related that the pronoun in "ja'ala" and "atahuma" refers to the soul and its spouse from among the children of Adam, not to Adam and Eve, peace be upon them. This is the view of al-Asamm, who said: the meaning of His saying, glorified and exalted be He,
صفحة 141
"He created you from a single soul" is that He created each one of you from a single soul, and created for each soul a spouse of its own kind. Then when each soul covered its spouse, it bore a light burden, which is the water of the stallion; then when it became heavy by that water becoming flesh, blood and bone, the man and the woman called on their Lord: "If You give us a righteous child," that is, a male sound one, "we shall surely be among the thankful." Their custom had been to bury daughters alive. So when He gave them what they asked, that is, when God, exalted be He, gave the father and mother what they asked, they made partners for Him, naming them Abd al-Lat, Abd al-Uzza and other such names. Then the reference in His saying, glorified and exalted be He, "Exalted is God above what they associate" returns to all of them. The verse has no connection at all to Adam and Eve, peace be upon them. Yet it is not hidden that what is immediately understood from its beginning is Adam and Eve, and almost nothing else is understood at all. Indeed, Ibn al-Munir chose something that amounts to this in al-Intisaf, and claimed that it is closer and safer than what came before, namely that the intended meaning is the two genders of male and female, with no particular individual meant from among them. Then he said: the meaning, and God knows best, is: He created you as one kind and made your spouses from you also, that you might find rest in them. Then when the kind that is male covered the kind that is female, such and such occurred from these two kinds. He attributed this statement to the kind, although among them are monotheists, because the polytheists are among them, so it is permissible to attribute the speech to the kind, in the manner of: "The Banu Tamim killed so-and-so," when only some of them killed him. Similar is His saying, exalted be He: "And man says, 'When I am dead, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?'" and "Man is killed; how ungrateful he is!" and so on. It has been objected that this involves applying all the words of the verse to remote interpretations.

From Abu Muslim: the beginning of the verse concerns Adam and Eve, as is apparent, except that their narrative is what His saying, glorified and exalted be He, contains: "It is He who created you from a single soul and made from it its spouse," and the narrative ended. Then He singled out the polytheists among the children of Adam by mention. It is permissible to mention the generality and then single out some by mention, but this, as you see, is far-fetched. It has also been said: it is permissible that the pronoun in "ja'ala" refers to Adam and Eve, as is apparent, and the speech comes out in the form of a denying interrogation, and the indication in "fa-ta'ala" and so on is to the polytheists, because they used to say that Adam, peace be upon him, used to worship idols and associate as we associate, so He refuted them with this. The parallel to this is that a man bestows many kinds of favour upon another, and then it is said to that benefactor: the one you have favoured intends to harm you and bring evil upon you, and he replies: I did such and such to him, and I was good to him in such and such ways, and then he repays me with evil and injury; his intent being that he is innocent of that and it is denied of him.

It has been said: it is possible that the address in "khalaqakum" is to the Quraysh, namely the family of Qusayy, for they were created from the soul of Qusayy, and he had a spouse of his kind, an Arab Qurashi woman, and they both asked God, exalted be He, for offspring, so He gave them four sons, whom they named Abd Manaf, Abd Shams, Abd al-Uzza and Abd al-Dar, meaning by that the House of the Assembly (Dar al-Nadwa). The pronoun in "yushrikun" would then refer to the two of them and their descendants who followed them. This is supported by the saying in the story of Umm Ma'bad:

"O Qusayy, what God has withheld from you through him of glory unmatched and lordship..."

This was deemed unlikely in al-Kashshaf, on the grounds that those addressed were not created from the soul of Qusayy, neither all of them nor most of them, but rather the gathering of the Quraysh; and that the claim that his spouse was Qurashi is an error, for she was in fact the daughter of the chief of Makkah from Khuza'a, and the Quraysh at that time were scattered and were not in Makkah. Also, from where is the knowledge that the two of them promised at the time of conception to be grateful to God, blessed and exalted be He, when there is no ingratitude greater than the ingratitude in which they were?

Whoever interprets it in that way is no different from one who builds a palace and thereby destroys a city. As for the House, the sons of Qusayy were singled out in it by mention because they were closest to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace; or because he was their chief and leader, so his mention encompassed all of them, as the mention of Pharaoh encompasses his people, though it is known that not all of them are of Pharaoh's offspring. (It is answered) regarding his saying "from where is the knowledge" and so on, that it is from

صفحة 142

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 190 (part 2 of 2):

...the announcement of Allah, exalted is He, if that is the meaning of the composition (nazm). From it, it is known that his wife not being a Qurashi falls within what is prohibited. Yes, the claim that Qusayy, one of the forefathers of the Prophet (ﷺ), was a polytheist contradicts what a group of scholars held, that all of the Prophet's forefathers, peace be upon him, were not polytheists. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿لَهُ﴾ refers to the child, and the meaning is that the two of them asked Allah, exalted is He, for equals to the righteous child who had been given to them. It was also said that it refers to Iblis, and the meaning is that they made partners for Iblis in his name, when they named their child ʿAbd al-Ḥārith. Both of these opinions were rejected by al-Amidi in Abkar al-Afkar, and by my life, they are weaker than a spider's web. But I have mentioned them for the sake of completeness in presenting the opinions. A group of the early generation (al-salaf), such as Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib and others, held that the pronoun in ﴿جَعَلا﴾ refers to Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both. The meaning of "association" in relation to them is not the usual kind, but rather what we pointed to just above, up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾. It moves on to the story of the Arabs and their association of idols. So it is, as al-Suddi said, of the type that is connected in wording but separated in meaning. What clarifies this, as it has been said, is the change of the pronoun to the plural after the dual. Had the story been one story, it would have said "yushrikani" (they both associate). The same applies to the pronouns after it. This is supported by what Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, and al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, narrated from Samurah ibn Jundub, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Hawwa' gave birth, Iblis circled around her. None of her children used to survive, so he said to her: 'Name him ʿAbd al-Ḥārith, for he will survive.' She named him accordingly and he survived. That was from the inspiration of Satan and his command. He meant by al-Ḥārith himself, for he was called by that name among the angels."

This is not considered association in the true sense, according to al-Qutb, because proper names do not convey their linguistic meanings. However, the term "association" was applied to it as a severe warning and a notice that what those questioners were doing, asking about matters that do not concern them, is a grave matter whose enormity expression can hardly encompass.

In Lubab al-Ta'wil it is said that the attribution of ʿAbd to al-Ḥārith is in the sense that he was the cause of the child's safety. The term ʿabd is sometimes applied to what is not meant to be the slaves of kings, as in his saying:

*"And indeed I am a servant of the guest as long as he remains."*

Perhaps the attribution of the making to both of them, even though the hadith clearly states that the one who made it was Hawwa' and not she and Adam, is because he, peace be upon him, approved of it. In some narrations it is explicitly stated that they both named him so. Some careful scholars have objected to this opinion, saying that the hadith is not suitable as support for it, because it was not transmitted as an explanation of the verse, nor as a denial that this came from them, peace be upon them both, since it is not association. Yes, it would have been better for them both to abstain from such a thing. What is objectionable is interpreting the verse in that way, together with the departure from the apparent meaning it involves, especially according to the reading of the majority, "shurakāʾ" (partners) in the plural form. As for whoever reads ﴿فَتَعالى﴾ and what follows as the beginning of a new statement that returns to the idolaters among the disbelievers, with the fāʾ being a fāʾ faṣīḥa (an eloquent connecting particle), the fact that this view is transmitted from the early generation is countered by the fact that other views are also transmitted from a group of them. End of quotation. It may be said: Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Habr that the verse was revealed concerning Adam and Eve naming their children ʿAbd al-Ḥārith, and such a thing is hardly said from personal opinion. This is clear that the report is an explanation of the verse, and taking the verse in a sense other than its apparent meaning in order to explain it has no escape, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

The reason for the plural "shurakāʾ" is an intensification of the severity, because whoever permits association permits partners. So when they made one partner, it is as if they made partners. The reading ﴿فَتَعالى اللَّهُ﴾ and what follows as the beginning of a statement is what the context (siyaq) and the sequence of the passage (siba'q) require. Many of the pillars of Islam explicitly stated this. Those who went to other than this view are a very small number compared to those who went to it, and they are also inferior to them in knowledge and merit. How far apart are the buzzing of the bee and the melodies of Maʿbad! For this reason, the scholar al-Tibi said: "This opinion is the best of opinions, indeed there is no opinion other than it, and no reliance except upon it, because it is derived from the niche of prophethood and the presence of the message (ﷺ)." You know from me that whenever a hadith is sound, it is my school of thought, and I see that it is sound. Therefore the nib of my pen has refrained from running in the field of interpretation as others have run. And Allah, exalted is He, is the one who grants success to what is correct.

Nafiʿ and Abu Bakr read "shirkan" in the form of a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "sharikah" (partnership), or "dhawī sharikah," meaning those who are partners, and they are the partners.

[Page 143]

﴿Do they associate﴾ with Him, exalted is He, ﴿that which creates nothing﴾. That is, that which is not able to create anything of things at all. It is necessary for the one worshipped that he be a creator of his worshipper without any doubt. By (*bima*, "that which") He means the idols. Referring the pronoun back to them in the singular is in observance of their wording, just as referring the plural pronoun back to them in His statement, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿and they are created﴾, is in observance of their meaning. The use of the pronoun for rational beings (*'uqala'*), although idols are among what does not reason, is only in accordance with their belief about them, their treating them as rational beings, and their naming them gods.

The clause is coordinated (*'atf*) on ﴿does not create﴾. The combining of the two matters serves to show the complete incompatibility of the state of what they associate with Him with what they believe about it, to demonstrate the extreme of their ignorance, and the absence of any mention of the Creator is to announce that He is specified and that His mention is unnecessary, exalted is He.

﴿And they are not able﴾ — that is, the idols — ﴿to help them﴾ — that is, the polytheists who worship them — ﴿any help﴾ — that is, any help whatsoever if their affair grieves them and a grave calamity befalls them. ﴿Nor can they help themselves﴾ if some misfortune of the misfortunes afflicts them — that is, they cannot ward it off from themselves. The mention of "help" here is for the sake of correspondence (al-mushakalah), and it is a metaphor for its necessary implication (majaz fi lazim ma'nahu). This is for emphasizing the inability and need, which are contrary to the entitlement to divinity. They were described earlier as created beings (al-makhluqiyyah) because they are fit for it, but they are not described here as being helped (al-mansuriyyah) because they are not fit for it.

The saying of the Exalted, glorified be He: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you﴾ is an explanation of their inability with regard to what is lower than the help that is negated for them, and easier, namely mere indication of the desired goal and guidance to the path of attaining it, without the seeker actually attaining it. The address is to the polytheists by way of *iltifat* (a shift from third person to second person), as indicated by what follows, and in it there is an announcement of greater concern with the matter of rebuke and reproach. That is: And if you, O polytheists, call the idols to guide you to that by which you attain your aims or are saved from what you dislike, they will not follow you to your purpose, nor will they respond to you, and they are not able to do that. Nafi‘ read (*yatba‘ūkum*) with *takhfif* (the lightened form, without doubling the *ta'*).

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿It is the same for you whether you call them or you are silent﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) that confirms the content of what precedes it and explains the manner of their not following. That is: your calling them and your silence are equal in producing no benefit, for your state does not change in either case, just as their state does not change, by virtue of their being inanimate. The apparent expectation was that the verb would come after (*am*), because what falls within the scope of the *hamzat al-taswiyah* (the interrogative particle of equality) is interpreted as a verbal noun. However, he deviated from that to indicate that the bringing about of the calling is matched by the continuance of silence, and in this there is an exaggeration that is not hidden. It was said that the nominal form has the meaning of the verbal form, and he deviated from it because it is the head of a verse-ending (*ra's fasilah*). In it: if it had said *tasmutūn* (you are silent), the meaning would have been complete.

It was said that the pronoun in *tad‘ū* (you call) refers to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, or to him alone, in the plural for honour (*ta‘ẓīm*), and that the pronoun of the two objects refers to the polytheists. By *al-huda* (guidance) is meant the religion of truth. That is: if you call the polytheists to Islam, they will not follow you, i.e., they did not attain that from you, nor did they become characterized by it. It was criticized: this is something that the context and flow of the noble composition do not support at all. Moreover, if it were so, it would have said *‘alayhim* (upon them) instead of *‘alaykum* (upon you), as in His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾, for the equality of calling and not calling is only in relation to the polytheists, not in relation to the callers, for they are successful by the grace of the call. Perhaps the transmission of that from al-Hasan is not established, and al-Tabarsi is a *hatib layl* (one who gathers firewood at night, i.e., one who speaks without care for what he says).

﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke﴾ confirms what precedes it, namely that they do not follow you. "Invoke" (*al-du'a'*) may mean worship, using the name for the act by one part of it, or it may mean naming, as in "his calling Zayd." Two objects are omitted, meaning: "Indeed, those whom you worship"
Page 144
﴿besides Allah﴾, or whom you name gods besides Him, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿are servants like you﴾, that is, they are similar to you in that they are owned by Allah, exalted, subjected to His command, and unable to benefit or harm, as al-Akhfash said. Their being compared to you in this respect, although their inability in these two matters is more evident and greater than yours, is only because you acknowledge your own inability and suppose that they have power over them, for it is you who call them to worship and seek their help. It was said: It is possible that when they carved the idols in the forms of human beings, He, glorified is He, said to them: At most, their state is that they are living, rational beings like you, so they do not deserve your worship, just as some of you do not deserve worship from others. The likeness in animacy and reason is then by supposition, since they are in the form of living rational beings.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: (*in alladhina tad'una*) with a light *in* and with the accusative *'ibadan amthalakum*. Ibn Jinni explained this on the basis that the light *in* is negative (*nafiyah*) and acts like the Hijazi *ma* (the usage in which *ma* negates and governs the predicate like *laysa*), and this is the view of al-Kisa'i and some of the Kufans. Two objections were raised. First, that such usage is not established. Second, that it implies a negation of their being servants like you, whereas the well-known reading affirms it, so the two readings contradict each other. The answer to the first is that the one who holds this view says it is established in Arabic speech, as in the saying:

*Even if he were in control of anyone,*
*Except the weakest of the madmen.*

The answer to the second is that there is no contradiction, because the well-known reading affirms likeness in some respects, while this reading negates it in every respect, or in another respect: for idols, for example, are inanimate, and those who call upon them are not.

It was said: it is the light form of the heavy *inna*, and it is in the dialect of those who make both of its parts accusative, as in the saying:

*When the darkness of night turns black, then let your coming be,*
*And let your steps be light, for indeed our guards are lions.*

This is one opinion. It is not hidden that governing by the light *in* and making both of its parts accusative is rare and weak. Hence, both are inactive, and the predicate of the subject is omitted; it is the governor of *'ibadan* and *amthalakum*. On both readings, *amthalakum* is also an adjective of *'ibad*.

It was read as *inna* with the heavy form and *'ibadan* in the accusative, as a circumstantial (*hal*) of the omitted returning pronoun, and *amthalukum* in the nominative as the predicate of *inna*. It was also read with the nominative in the light-*in* reading with *'ibadan* in the accusative, and this too was explained as circumstantial and predicative.

﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you﴾: this confirms the content of what precedes it by showing their incapacity and rebuking them. That is, call upon them to remove harm or to bring benefit.

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your claim that they are able to do what you are unable to do.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 195:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ and so on, is a rebuke that follows and emphasizes what the challenge (al-amr al-ta'jizi) implies of non-response, by stating that they entirely lack the organs of that action. It has been said that, according to the first possibility regarding equality (al-mumathalah), this is a reversal of the equality claim by way of refutation, because they are inferior to them, and worshipping one who is equal to oneself is not fitting, so how about one who is inferior to oneself. And according to the second possibility, it returns to the supposition on which the equality was based, by nullifying it. And on the reading with the lightened form and the intention of negation, it is an affirmation of the negation of equality by establishing deficiency and shortcoming. The denial was directed at each of those four organs separately, as a repetition of the rebuke, a doubling of the reproach, and an indication that the absence of each one individually is sufficient to show the impossibility of response. The intent is not that whoever lacks these does not deserve divinity, but that only one who possesses them deserves it, which would entail either the negation of God, exalted is He, deserving them, or the affirmation of that for Him, as some of the anthropomorphists (al-mujassimah) held, and the verse would be replaced as proof for that. Rather, the intent is merely the establishment of incapacity, and from this the negation of deserving divinity is known. His describing the feet as walking with them is to signal that the focus of the denial is the attribute, and it was directed at the feet rather than at the attribute by saying: "Do they walk with their feet?" in order to affirm that, since no sign appears from them of what appears from other feet, they are not feet in reality. The same applies to what follows regarding the remaining three limbs.

The particle (am) in His saying: ﴿Or do they have hands with which they seize?﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the interrogative hamzah in it is for the rebuke mentioned earlier. (Bal) is for transition (al-idrab), which indicates a move from one matter to another after the first is complete, from the same subject matter. (Al-batsh) means seizing with force.

Abu Ja'far read (yabtushun) with a damma on the ta', and this is a dialectal variant of it. The meaning is: "Rather, do they have hands with which they take what they wish, or with which they push away harm from you?" The placement of this after what precedes it, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is because walking is their condition in themselves, while seizing is their condition in relation to others. As for placing this before His saying: ﴿Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ although all are alike in being their conditions in relation to others, it is for the sake of observing the correspondence between hands and feet, and because the negation of walking and seizing is more evident and the rebuke by it is stronger. As for placing the eyes before the ears, it is because they are more well-known than them, more manifest in sight and effect. That seeing is by the eye and hearing by the ear follows the apparent common usage. Those who said that God, exalted is He, placed in some things a power by which they act when God permits them, cited the verse as evidence, contrary to those who said that the effect is with them and not by them. He claimed that this view is close to disbelief, but that is not as he claimed; rather, it is the truth deserving of acceptance.

﴿Say: Call upon your associates⟩ is a command to him, may God bless him and grant him peace, to confront them in argument and to repeat the rebuke upon them after clarifying that their associates are utterly unable to do anything; that is, "Call upon your associates and seek their help against me." ﴿Then plot against me⟩ all of you together, you and your associates, and exert yourselves in arranging whatever scheming and plotting you are capable of.

﴿Then give me no respite⟩ means: do not grant me a moment's delay after arranging the preliminaries of the plot, for I do not care for you at all. The first-person ya' in the two verbs is one that they did not write in the script. Abu 'Amr read with affirming the ya' of (kidunī) when connected and omitting it when pausing, Hisham affirmed it in both states, and the rest omitted it in both. In Hud: ﴿So plot against me, all of you⟩ with the ya' affirmed absolutely according to all. As for the ya' of ﴿give me no respite⟩, al-Ajhuri said: they omitted it only.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 196:

﴿Indeed, my Guardian is God, who has sent down the Book﴾ is a ta'lil (causal justification) for the indifference that is clearly understood from the context of the speech. The definite article in "al-Kitab" (the Book) is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and what is meant by it is the Qur'an. He, glorified is He, described Himself as the One who sent down the Book in order to indicate the proof of guardianship (al-wilayah). It is as if He placed "who sent down the Book" in the position of "who sent me as a messenger." There is no doubt that sending implies guardianship and support.

It has also been said that this contains an indication of another cause for the indifference, as if it were said: "I am not concerned with you and your partners, because my Guardian is God Most High, who sent down the Book that declares that He is my Guardian and my Helper, and that your partners cannot even help themselves, let alone help you."

His statement, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And He takes charge of the righteous﴾ is a tadhyil (concluding addition) that confirms the meaning of what precedes it. That is, it is his custom, may His majesty be glorified, to support His righteous servants and not forsake them.

Al-Tibi said: The name of the Essence (ism al-dhat) was specifically associated with the sending down of the Book, and the verse was made a ta'lil in order to indicate the magnification of the matter of the One who sent it down, and that it is the criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood, that it is the one that unveils the darkness of polytheism, silences the tongues of the masters of eloquence, and is the lasting miracle in every age. It is the clear light and the firm rope. Through it God Most High set right the affairs of His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, for through it He perfected his character, upheld his crookedness, and destroyed the empty falsehoods that nullify. For this reason His saying, glorified and exalted is He: "(And He...)" etc. was brought as a tadhyil and confirmation of what preceded, and as an allusion to those who have lost righteousness through abandonment and ruin.

The meaning is: Indeed my Guardian is the One who sent down the well-known Book, whose reality and examples you recognize, and He takes charge of the righteous and abandons others.

It is not hidden that what was mentioned first regarding the descriptive quality (al-wasfiyyah) is more fitting to the context, while the matter of the tadhyil is undeniable.

This verse is one that I have tested by constant recitation for protection from enemies, and it was the daily litany (wird) of my father, may God have mercy on him, at dawn. Some of the great scholars had commanded him to do so in a dream.

The majority reads the first yaʼ in (wali-yiya) with shaddah and the second with fatha. It is also read with the second yaʼ omitted in pronunciation because it is sukun and what follows it is sukun, and with fatha on the first, without a yaʼ after it, and with the second omitted from pronunciation for lightness.
