Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 197:

﴿And those whom you invoke besides Him﴾ means: whom you worship, or whom you call upon besides Him, glorified and exalted is He, seeking help from them, in accordance with what I have commanded you.

﴿Cannot help you﴾ in any matter whatsoever. The matter mentioned above is included in this by primary inclusion, though it is permissible to restrict the meaning to it. ﴿Nor can they help themselves﴾ when they are struck by some calamity.

**Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, on surah 7, verse 198:**

﴿And if you call them to guidance﴾: that is, to the point that they guide you to that by which you attain your aims in general, or specifically in the matter of the known scheme. ﴿They do not hear﴾: that is, your call, let alone assist or support you. This is more emphatic than negating following (al-ittiba'). Interpreting hearing as acceptance, as in *sami'a Allahu liman hamidah* ("God hears those who praise Him"), as some claim, is worthless. His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And you see them looking at you, while they do not see﴾ explain their inability to see, after explaining their inability to hear. On this basis, as has been said, the causal explanation for their not being concerned is complete, so there is no repetition at all.

Al-Wahidi said: what came before is to distinguish between one who may be worshipped and one who may not. This answer was given to counter their threatening the Prophet (ﷺ) with their gods. The seeing is visual (basariyyah). The clause (*yanzurun*, "they look") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the object that returns to the idols, and the nominal clause is a circumstantial clause from the subject of *yanzurun*. The address is to each individual polytheist, and the meaning is: you see the idols with your own eyes, resembling one who looks at you, and it seems to you that they see, because they have been made with eyes set with gleaming jewels and shaped in the form of a pupil turned toward whatever one looks at, while in fact they are unable to see. Directing the address to each individual polytheist rather than to the whole group, as in the preceding addresses, indicates that seeing the idols in the stated form is not possible for all of them together, but only for each one who faces them.

Some scholars held that the address in (*tarahum*, "you see them") is to everyone who stands before them. It has also been said that it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), with the third-person pronoun remaining as it is, or that it refers to the polytheists, on the basis that the causal explanation was complete at the words of the Exalted, ﴿they do not hear﴾. That is: you see the polytheists looking at you while in fact they do not see you as you are, or they do not see the proof, as al-Suddi and Mujahid said. It is also reported from al-Hasan that the address in ﴿and if you call them﴾ is to the believers, on the basis that the causal explanation was complete at the words of the Exalted, ﴿they are not helped﴾. That is: and if you, O believers, call the polytheists to Islam, they will not turn to you or accept from you. On this reading, interpreting hearing as acceptance is apt. The phrase (*wa tarahum*, "and you see them") is taken as an address to the chief of those addressed, by way of *tajrid* (abstraction, addressing a representative of a group as the group itself). In the passage there is also an indication that the evidences of prophethood and the signs of the message found in the Prophet (may God's blessings and peace be upon him) are so manifest that they are hardly hidden from those who look.

Some scholars allowed that the seeing may be cognitive (*'ilmiyyah*), and that what occupies the place of the circumstantial clause would then occupy the place of the second object, though the first reading is preferable.

﴿Take forgiveness﴾: that is, what is pardoned, easy, and readily available of people's dispositions and conduct. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, 'A'isha, Mujahid, and others, may God be pleased with them all. Ibn Abi al-Dunya related it from Ibrahim ibn Adham as a hadith traced back (marfu') to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

"Taking" (al-akhdh) is used figuratively (majaz) for accepting and being content. The meaning is: be content with people in terms of what is easy and comes readily from their actions and dispositions, without imposing hardship, and do not demand from them effort or what is difficult for them, lest they flee from you. From this is the saying of the poet:

Take forgiveness from me, and your affection will endure,
and do not speak in my fury when I am angry.

It is also permissible that "forgiveness" be understood in its apparent sense, that is: take forgiveness of the wrongdoers, meaning pardon them. In this case there is an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), since forgiveness is likened to a tangible thing that is sought and taken. A group of the early scholars (al-salaf) held this view, and it is supported by what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others related from al-Sha'bi, who said: When God, Exalted is He, revealed ﴿Take forgiveness﴾ to the end of the verse, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What is this, O Jibril?" He said: "I do not know until I ask the one who knows." He went and returned and said: "God, Exalted is He, commands you to pardon those who wrong you, to give to those who deprive you, and to maintain ties with those who cut you off."

Ibn Mardawayh related something similar from Jabir. Perhaps the essence of the hadith explains the essence of the verse; otherwise the application is problematic, as is clear. Al-Qutb undertook to match its wording to the wording of the verse, but there is obscurity in this. From Ibn 'Abbas: the intended meaning of "forgiveness" is what is left over of people's wealth, that is, take whatever they bring you, and this was before the obligation of zakah (obligatory alms). It was also said: "forgiveness" is the surplus of wealth beyond one's expenditure, and al-Jawhari interpreted it this way, as did al-Suddi. Abu al-Shaykh related from him that he said: When this verse was revealed, a man would keep from his wealth what sufficed him and give the surplus in charity, then God, Exalted is He, abrogated it (naskh) with zakah.

﴿And enjoin what is customary﴾: that is, enjoin what is good and approved of actions, for that is closer to people's acceptance without denunciation. In Lubab al-Ta'wil it is said that the intended meaning is: enjoin everything God, Exalted is He, has commanded you and you have come to know through revelation. 'Ata' said: the intended meaning of "what is customary" is the statement "There is no god but God," but this is a specification without a reason.

﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾: that is, do not repay the foolish with the like of their folly, do not dispute with them, be forbearing toward them, and overlook what hurts you from them. From al-Suddi: this is a command to refrain from fighting, and then it was abrogated by its verse (naskh). There is no need to claim abrogation in this verse, as is clear to the one who reflects. Many have also mentioned that there is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of noble character than this verse.

Its essence, as they have said, is: seeking good companionship with people, striving to exert effort in doing good to them, showing patience and tolerance toward them, and overlooking their faults. They considered this similar to the essence of the report (zubdat al-khabar), except that the Qur'an's subject matter is general and its specific subject is particular, and every people knows its own drinking place. The excellence of the placement of this command after what was counted of the falsehoods and ugly deeds of the polytheists, which cannot be borne, is not hidden. And if it is said that "the ignorant" is placed in the position of the pronoun referring to those polytheists, since the discussion is about them, recording against them their lack of restraint and absolutely despairing of them, then the parts of the speech fit together in the utmost cohesion. Furthermore, from Ibn Zayd: when the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ were revealed,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 200:

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'How (should I do), O Lord, when there is anger?' Then there was revealed His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you, then seek refuge in Allah.﴾" Al-nazgh (the prick), al-nasgh and al-nakhs have the same meaning. It is the insertion of a needle, or the tip of a stick, or something similar, into the skin. It is related from Ibn Zayd that one says: "nazaghtu ma bayna al-qawm" (I stirred up discord among the people) when one corrupts the relations between them. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the least movement that occurs. And "from Satan" means his whispering. The first meaning is the well-known one.

Its application to the whispering of Satan is a metaphor, in that his whispering is likened to the urging of people towards sins and the agitation of them by the goad of the driver, who pricks what he drives. The attribution of the verb to the verbal noun is metaphorical, as in "jadda jidduhu" (his effort prevailed). It has also been said that al-nazgh has the meaning of al-nazigh (the one who pricks), so the figurative usage lies in the agent. The first is more eloquent and more appropriate. That is: if an evil suggestion from the direction of Satan carries you away to act contrary to what you have been commanded, such as being seized by anger or the like, ﴿then seek refuge in Allah﴾, seek protection in Him and take shelter with Him, glorified and exalted be He, to repel it from you.

﴿Indeed, He is All-Hearing﴾, who hears your seeking of refuge in the most perfect manner, in words.

﴿All-Knowing﴾, who likewise knows your humble supplication in the heart, whether within speech or without it, so He will protect you from its evil. Or "All-Hearing" means: the One who answers your supplication for refuge; "All-Knowing" means: the One who knows what is good for your affair, so He directs you to it. Or "All-Hearing" means: the One who hears the words of those who harm you, and "All-Knowing" means: the One who knows their deeds, so He will recompense them for them. The verse, as some verifying scholars have stated, is of the type of ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾; so there is no proof in it for one who claims that the prophets, peace be upon them, are not protected from the whispering of Satan and from committing sins.

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but has been assigned a companion from the jinn and a companion from the angels." They said: "And you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "And I, except that Allah has helped me against him, so he submits; so he does not command me except to good."

Others said: the pricking of Satan, with respect to the Prophet (ﷺ), is a metaphor for the arising of anger that disturbs the soul. In the verse, in that case, there is an added emphasis on aversion from anger and an extreme warning against acting upon its dictates. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) repeated the prohibition against it, as came in the hadith. And in the command to seek refuge in Allah the Exalted there is an amplification of this matter and an alert that it is among the calamities from which one is not freed from harm except by taking refuge in the sanctuary of His protection, mighty and majestic be He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 201:

﴿Indeed, those who fear God﴾ is a resumptive clause (istin'af, a new sentence that begins afresh) which confirms what precedes it, the command to seek refuge, by showing that seeking refuge is a practice followed by the God-fearing, and that neglecting it is the habit (shanshana, a characteristic manner) of the misguided. That is: indeed, those who have been characterised by fear of God, the Exalted, ﴿when a visitation from Satan touches them﴾, that is, a passing thought (lamma) from him, as related from Ibn 'Abbas. Its tanwin (nunation) is for diminution, and what is meant is some whispering. It is an active participle (ism fa'il) from "ta'a bi al-shay'" when one circles around it. Calling the whispering a "visitation" (ta'if) signifies that although it touches them, it does not affect them, as if it had circled around them without reaching them.

It is permitted that it be from "taif al-khayal" (the phantom of imagination) when it visits in sleep, so what is meant is a passing thought. Some have held that what is meant by the visitation is anger. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read (ṭayf), either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as a lightened form (takhfif) of (ṭayyif) from the waw-based or ya'-based root, like (hayyin) and (layyin). What is meant by "Satan" is the species, not Iblis alone; for this reason its pronoun is in the plural in what follows.

﴿They remember﴾, that is, what God, the Exalted, has commanded and forbidden, or seeking refuge in Him and turning to Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He, or the enmity of Satan and his scheming.

﴿Then they are seeing clearly﴾, by means of that remembrance, ﴿the places of error and the paths of right guidance﴾, so they guard against what opposes God's command and keep away from what does not please Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He. The apparent meaning is that the relative clause (mawsul) refers to whoever is characterised by the attribute of the relative clause, in general.

Some verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: the address in His words, glory be to Him and exalted is He, ﴿And if an incitement from Satan incites you﴾ etc., is either specific to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, as is apparent. In that case, it is appropriate that the God-fearing mean the resolute messengers (ulu al-'azm). Or it is general, following the manner of the hadith: "Give glad tidings to those who walk to the mosques with perfect light on the Day of Resurrection." Or it is specific in meaning but general in application, like: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾. In that case the God-fearing are the righteous servants of God, the Exalted. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the implication in the first conditional is open to objection, and generality is the more evident on every account. Some claimed that what is meant by the God-fearing, to whom touching is attributed, is other than the prophets, peace be upon them, and that the address in what precedes is specific to the Greatest Master, may God bless him and grant him peace. They asserted that incitement (nazgh) is the first stage of whispering, and touching occurs only after establishment (tamakkun). Then he said: For this reason God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, distinguished between the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the rest of the God-fearing: He expressed incitement with regard to him, peace be upon him, and touching with regard to them. It may be said: Satan's concern with whispering to the perfect one is more complete than his concern with whispering to one below him; therefore he expressed it first with incitement and second with touching.

Wa-ikhwānuhum (﴿وإخْوانُهُمْ﴾): i.e., the brethren of the devils, those who do not fear God. This is the meaning of the brotherhood between them, and it is the subject (mubtada').

Page 149

His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿يَمُدُّونَهم في الغَيِّ﴾ is its predicate (khabar). The raised pronoun refers to the devils, and the object pronoun refers to the subject. That is: the devils assist them in error, by adorning it for them and driving them toward it. On this reading, the predicate is a description that does not refer back to the subject it belongs to (jārin ʿalā ghayr man huwa lahu), and there is a disagreement among the scholars of the two cities (Basra and Kufa) as to whether the pronoun must be made explicit (ibrāz al-ḍamīr) in such a case, just as with the disputed attributive (ṣifa). It has also been said that the first pronoun refers to the brethren and the second to the devils, and the meaning is: the brethren of the devils supply the devils with following and obedience. On this reading the predicate does refer to its own subject, and the prepositional phrase is attached to what precedes it. It is also permitted for it to be in a position of ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the agent or from the object.

Nāfiʿ recited (﴿يُمِدُّونَهُمْ﴾) with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a kasra on the mīm, from al-imdād, while the majority recite with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the mīm.

Abū ʿAlī said in al-Ḥujja, after mentioning this: The general usage in the revelation of what is praised and recommended is amdadtu on the form af‘ala, such as His saying, exalted: ﴿أنَّما نُمِدُّهم بِهِ مِن مالٍ وبَنِينَ﴾ and ﴿وأمْدَدْناهم بِفاكِهَةٍ﴾ and ﴿أتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمالٍ﴾. And what is contrary to that is on madadtu, as He said: ﴿ويَمُدُّهم في طُغْيانِهِمْ يَعْمَهُونَ﴾. Thus they speak with what indicates that the correct form is the fatḥa on the yāʾ, as the majority held. The basis of Nāfiʿ's reading is that it is like ﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ and ﴿فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرى﴾.

al-Jaḥdarī recited (﴿يُمادُّونَهُمْ﴾) from the pattern of mufāʿala, and it is figurative here, as if the devils were helping them by inciting them and making sins easy for them, while these people help the devils by following and obeying them.

﴿ثُمَّ لا يُقْصِرُونَ﴾: i.e., they do not hold back nor desist from their misguidance until they completely bring them to ruin. It is from aqṣara, meaning to cease and refrain, as in the line of poetry:

sama laka shawqun baʿda mā kāna aqṣara
(Longing has risen in you after it had ceased.)

It is also permitted for the pronoun to refer to the brethren, and this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī, and al-Jubbāʾī held this view, meaning: then these people do not desist from error nor hold back, like the righteous. It is also permitted that by the brethren is meant the devils, with the plural pronoun attached to it first, the object second, and the agent third returning to the ignorant ones in His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿وأعْرِضْ عَنِ الجاهِلِينَ﴾. That is: the brethren of the ignorant ones, who are the devils, support the ignorant ones in error, then the ignorant ones do not desist from that. The predicate on this reading also refers to what it belongs to, as in some of the earlier possibilities, but the first is preferable for the sake of the contrast (muqābala).

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar recited (﴿يَقْصُرُونَ﴾) with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the ṣād, from qaṣara, and it is also figurative for refraining.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 203:

﴿When you do not bring them a sign﴾ from the Qur'an, when revelation was delayed, as related from Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Zajjaj; or a sign they had proposed, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim. ﴿They say: "Why have you not fabricated it?"﴾ That is, why did you not gather it and concoct it from your own self as a forgery? Or: why did you not take it from Allah, the Exalted, by asking Him for it? This is a mockery on their part, may Allah, the Exalted, curse them. From what we have mentioned it becomes known that ijtaba (to choose, to gather) has two meanings: "to gather" and "to take." The intended sense varies according to the disagreement over the interpretation of the verse. It is related from 'Ali ibn 'Isa that ijtiba' in origin means "extraction," and from it comes jibayat al-kharaj (the collection of land tax). It was also said that its origin is "gathering," from "jabaytu al-ma'a fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the pool), and from it the pool is called jabiyah because it gathers water. This is the view of al-Raghib. In al-Durr al-Masun: jaba al-shay' means he gathered the thing deliberately. For this reason, ijtabaytuhu has come to mean "I chose it."

Al-Farra' said: one says ijtaybtu al-kalam, ikhtalaqtuhu and irtajaltuhu when you composed it from your own self; and likewise ikhtara'tuhu according to Abu 'Ubaydah. Ibn Zayd said: these letters are used by the Arabs for speech that a man begins without having prepared it beforehand in his mind. Whoever makes the origin something that does not reject its use in the other sense as a metaphor is not hidden. ﴿Say⦆ in reply to them: ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord﴾, without my having any part in it at all. This is in the sense of restricting his condition, upon him be prayer and peace, to following what is revealed to him, by directing the restriction to the act itself in relation to its counterpart, which they had imposed upon him, upon him be prayer and peace. It is not in the sense of restricting his following, may Allah, the Exalted, bless him and grant him peace, to what is revealed to him by directing the restriction in relation to another object, as is common in usage. It is as if it were said: I do nothing but follow what is revealed to me from Him, the Exalted, without disagreement or proposing. In mentioning the title of Lordship together with its addition to his pronoun, upon him be prayer and peace, there is much to note.

﴿This﴾ is a reference to the glorious Qur'an, indicated by what is revealed to me. ﴿Are insights from your Lord﴾: that is, they are in the position of insights for hearts, by which one sees the truth and perceives what is right; or they are clear proofs and luminous evidences that suffice without anything else. The statement is thus an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh). I have verified what is in it in the fullest manner in al-Tiraz al-Mudhhab. Or it contains a metonymy (majaz mursal), where the effect is named for the cause. It is also permitted that the insights are a metaphor for the Qur'an guiding creation to perceive the realities. In that case "this" is the subject and "insights" is its predicate; the predicate of a singular subject is given in plural because it comprises verses and surahs, each of which is made an insight. "Min" (from) is attached to an omitted element that functions as an adjective of "insights," conveying its magnificence, meaning: insights that come from Him, the Exalted. Mentioning the attribute of Lordship together with its addition to their pronoun is to emphasize the obligation of believing in it. His statement, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ is conjoined to "insights." Their tanwin is for magnification. Placing the adverbial phrase before them and following them with His statement, exalted is He: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is to signify that the Qur'an being insights is established with respect to all, and by it the proof is established against everyone. As for its being guidance and mercy, it is specific to the believers, since they are the ones who draw from its lights and gather from its lights. This is contrary to what the statement of some implies, that the three are for the believers. Al-Nisaburi said in his tafsir: the insights are for those of the eye of certainty, guidance for those of the knowledge of certainty, and mercy for others among the righteous who follow, in the fullest manner; and all are for a people who believe. Al-Khazin mentioned something similar and claimed that it is one of the subtleties, but this is against the apparent meaning, indeed it can hardly be accepted. This sentence, as appears, is part of the statement commanded to be said.

The verse has been cited by those who do not permit ijtihad for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; but there is room for scrutiny in this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 204 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.﴾ This is guidance toward the path to success through the sublime benefits alluded to, which the Qur'an contains. Listening (al-istima') is well known. The lam (in *lahu*) may be taken as the lam of causation (ajaliyya), or as meaning *ila* (to), or as an extra particle (sila), meaning: "listen to it." Al-inssat (silence) means keeping quiet. It is said: *nasata yunsitu*, *anssata*, and *intasata*, when one is silent. The noun is *al-nusta* with a damma. It is also said, as al-Azhari said: *anssatahu* and *anssata lahu* when one is silent for him and listens to his speech. It is also said *anssatahu* when one silences him. The conjunction (of listening and silence) is for emphasis on the matter of the Qur'an. The command is given a reason in His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿so that you may receive mercy﴾, meaning: so that you may attain the mercy, which is the utmost of its fruits.

The verse is evidence for Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) that the follower (ma'mum) does not recite, neither in a silent (sirriyya) nor in an audible (jahriyya) prayer, because it demands the obligation of listening when the Qur'an is recited in the prayer and elsewhere. The proof for permissibility of listening and for leaving it has been established elsewhere, so the obligation of silence remains in force for the audible recitation. Likewise, in the silent recitation, we know it is being recited (by the imam).

Numerous reports support this. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Mujahid, who said: "A man from the Ansar recited behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the prayer, and so the verse was revealed: 'And when the Qur'an is recited, etc.'"

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he led his companions in prayer, and he heard people reciting behind him. When he finished, he said: "Has the time not yet come for you to understand? Has the time not yet come for you to reflect? ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, as Allah, exalted is He, has commanded you."

[p. 151]

Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "There is no recitation behind the imam."

He also narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The imam was only appointed to be followed. So when he says the takbir, say the takbir, and when he recites, be silent.'"

He also narrated from Jabir: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever has an imam, then the imam's recitation is a recitation for him.'"

If this hadith is authentic, it must specify the generality of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So recite what is easy of it﴾, and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no prayer except with recitation," according to the opponent's method, absolutely, so the follower is excluded. And according to our method too, because that generality has already been specified in part, namely the one who catches the bowing (al-mudrik fi al-ruku'), by consensus (ijma'). Therefore it is permissible to specify further the follower by the aforementioned hadith. Likewise, the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the one who prayed badly (al-musi' salatahu): "Say the takbir, then recite what is easy for you of the Qur'an," are understood as referring to situations other than following an imam, in order to harmonize the evidences. Indeed, it may be said that recitation is established for the follower by the Law, since the imam's recitation is for him. If he recited too, he would have two recitations in one prayer, and that is not prescribed.

The discussion remains about the authentication of the report. It has been transmitted through many chains, raised (marfu') to the Prophet (ﷺ) from Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him), and it has been declared weak. But those who declared it weak, such as al-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi, and Ibn Adi, acknowledged that the raising to the Prophet (ﷺ) is not established, and that the correct version is a mursal, because the memorizers (huffaz), such as the two Sufyans, Abu al-Ahwas, Shu'ba, Isra'il, Sharik, Jarir, Abu al-Zubayr, Abd ibn Humayd, and other people, transmitted it from Musa ibn Abi Aisha, from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, from the Prophet (ﷺ), omitting (the Companion) and reporting it as a mursal. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) once also transmitted it as a mursal. In this case we can say: the mursal is a proof according to most of the scholars. So it suffices for us in what concerns practice according to our opinion. And as an argument ad hominem (ilzam), by establishing the proof for the authority of the mursal as well. And, supposing we concede that it is not authoritative, Imam (Abu Hanifa) raised it through a sound chain (sanad).

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan narrated in his Muwatta', saying: "Abu Hanifa, Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Abi Aisha informed us, from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Whoever prays behind an imam, then the imam's recitation is a recitation for him.'"

And their statement that the memorizers whom they listed did not raise it is not correct. Ahmad ibn Mani' said in his Musnad: "Ishaq al-Azraq informed us, Sufyan and Sharik narrated to us, from Musa ibn Abi Aisha, from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, from Jabir, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Whoever has an imam, then the imam's recitation is a recitation for him.'"

Then he said: "Jarir narrated to us from Musa, from Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ)," and he mentioned it without mentioning Jabir. Abd ibn Humayd also narrated it, saying: "Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, al-Hasan ibn Salih narrated to us, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ)," and he mentioned it. The chain of the first hadith of Jabir is on the condition of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and the second is on the condition of Muslim. These, Sufyan, Sharik, Jarir, and Abu al-Zubayr, raised it through sound chains. So their counting among those who did not raise it is invalid. If a trustworthy transmitter (thiqa) reports alone, it must be accepted, because raising (rafa') is an addition, and the addition of a trustworthy transmitter is accepted. How much more so when he did not report alone. And a trustworthy transmitter may sometimes transmit a hadith with a full chain and at other times as a mursal.

Ibn Adi narrated it from the Imam (Abu Hanifa) (may Allah be pleased with him) in his biography, and in it he mentioned a story. Abu Abdullah al-Hakim narrated it with its chain: Abu Muhammad ibn Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Hamdan al-Sayrafi told us, Abd al-Samad ibn al-Fadl al-Balkhi told us, Makki ibn Ibrahim told us, from Abu Hanifa, from Musa ibn Abi Aisha, from Abdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi, from Jabir ibn Abdullah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, and a man behind him was reciting. A man from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) began forbidding him from reciting in the prayer. When he finished, the man approached him and said: 'Do you forbid me from reciting behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' They disputed until they mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever prays behind an imam, then the imam's recitation is a recitation for him.'"

In a narration of Abu Hanifa: "That happened in the Dhuhr or the 'Asr prayer," and it is that "a man recited behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Dhuhr or the 'Asr prayer, so he gestured to him and forbade him. When he finished, he said: 'Do you forbid me?'" and the hadith continues. Yes, Jabir narrated the place of the ruling alone at times, and the whole narration at other times. It contains the rejection of recitation behind the imam, because it was reported in support of that Companion's prohibition of it absolutely, in silent and audible prayers. Especially in Abu Hanifa's narration, the story was in a silent prayer, not a permission to do or abandon it. Thus it conflicts with what is narrated in some versions of the hadith: "What is the matter with me, that I am disputed in the Qur'an?"

[p. 152]

And the statement that the recitation is required: "There must be recitation of al-Fatiha," as well as what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: "We were behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Fajr prayer. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited, and the recitation became difficult for him. When he finished he said: 'Perhaps you recite behind your imam?' We said: 'Yes, that is what we do.' He said: 'Do not do so except with the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha), for there is no prayer for one who does not recite it.'"

The prohibition is given precedence because the absolute prohibition takes priority when there is conflict, and because of the strength of its chain, for the hadith of prohibition is more authentic. Thus the rejection by the fanatics is invalid, and so is the weakening by some of them of such a figure as the Great Imam (Abu Hanifa) (may Allah be pleased with him), despite his strictness in transmission to the utmost degree, to the extent that he stipulated remembrance (al-tadhakkur) for its permissibility after the narrator knows that the narration is in his own handwriting. The memorizers did not stipulate this. And his two companions did not agree with him. Moreover, the report has been strengthened by many other narrations from Jabir, even though they are weak, and by the positions of the Companions too, such as Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Ibn Mas'ud.

Muhammad (al-Shaybani) narrated from Dawud ibn Qays ibn Ajlan that Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I wish there were a stone in the mouth of the one who recites behind the imam." A similar statement is narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

It is also narrated from Ali (may Allah honor his face), though there is some discussion about it, that he said: "Whoever recites behind the imam has erred from the fitra (natural way)."

Al-Sha'bi said: "I met seventy people of Badr, all of whom prohibited the follower from reciting behind the imam." Some of our companions have claimed the consensus of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) on this. Perhaps what he meant is the consensus of many of their great ones. Otherwise it is open to question, and the claim that he meant the tacit consensus (ijma' sukuti) is also not valid.

Some people held that the follower recites when the imam recites silently, and does not recite when he recites audibly. This is the view of Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, al-Zuhri, Malik, Ibn al-Mubarak, Ahmad, and Ishaq, and it is narrated from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). Their argument, as it is said, is that the verse indicates the command to listen to the recitation of the Qur'an, and the Sunna indicates the obligation of reciting behind the imam. So we applied the implication of the verse to the audible prayer and the implication of the Sunna to the silent prayer, in order to harmonize the evidences.

Others said: he only recites in the silent prayer, because one is not called a listener (mustami') in it. This was objected to: even if we concede that he is not called that, we do not concede that he is not called a silent one (munsit) while knowing the recitation. And we do not concede that the Sunna indicates the obligation of reciting behind the imam. Without establishing that, it is like pulling out thorns with one's hands (kharTu al-qatad). Moreover, the rule is to act on the stronger of the two evidences, and what the stronger one requires is only prohibition. From here, the narration attributed to Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him), that it is recommended to recite al-Fatiha as a precaution, is weak, since it opposes what the Imam and Abu Yusuf went to, namely disliking recitation because of the threat (of punishment) in it. The truth is that his view is like theirs. For he said in the book al-Athar, after a report was attributed to Alqama ibn Qays: "He never recited at all, neither in what is recited aloud nor in what is not recited aloud. We take by this, so we do not see reciting behind the imam in any prayer, whether audible or not, and one should not recite behind him in any of them." He mentioned something similar in his Muwatta'. Al-Sarakhsi said: "The prayer of the one who recites behind the imam is invalid according to a group of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), among whom, it is said, is Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas." In the narration of al-Muzani from al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him), he recites in both audible and silent prayers. In the narration of al-Buwayti, he recites al-Fatiha in silent prayers and adds a surah in the first two units, and in audible prayers he recites only al-Fatiha. The well-known position among the Shafi'is is that the follower who hears the imam in an audible prayer has no surah, but listens instead. If he is too far to hear, or hears a sound whose letters he cannot distinguish, or the prayer is silent, he recites according to the more correct view.

The cause of revelation was not recitation in the prayer, but another matter. Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that they used to speak during the prayer, and so it was revealed. Its meaning is the prohibition of speaking, not of recitation. Some people interpreted the Qur'an as referring to the sermon (khutba). The command to listen is either for obligation or for recommendation. According to us, silence during the sermon is obligatory, with detail on the issue. Mujahid (may Allah be pleased with him) and others narrated that the verse concerns the prayer and the sermon on Friday. And in the statements of our companions there is what indicates the obligation of listening when the Qur'an is recited aloud, absolutely.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 7, verse 204 (part 2 of 2):

It says in al-Khulasa (a work of Hanafi jurisprudence): "A man is writing fiqh (jurisprudence), and beside him a man is reciting the Qur'an, so that he cannot hear the Qur'an. The sin is upon the reciter. Accordingly, if he recites aloud on the roof at night while the people are asleep, he commits a sin." This is an explicit statement of the obligation in its general form. The reason given is that the ruling follows the general wording of the text, not the specific occasion of its revelation. The word *idha* ("whenever") here is universal, and most conditional clauses in the Qur'an introduced by it are universal. The meaning of "listening" (*istima'*) in the verse is the one that comes first to mind. Al-Zajjaj said that it means acceptance and response. In this sense it is a metaphor, as stated explicitly in al-Asas (Zamakhshari's *Asas al-Balagha*). From the same usage: "God hears the one who praises Him" (*sami'a Allahu liman hamidah*), and "the amir heard the speech of so-and-so." Al-Allama al-Tibi preferred this view and said: "This fits the composition of the noble passage better, both before and after it, and it encompasses more meanings and opinions. When God mentioned, by implication, that the polytheists only mocked the Qur'an and cast it behind their backs, because they had lost insight, lacked guidance and mercy, and their condition was contrary to that of the believers, He commanded the believers to do something more than merely listening: to accept it, act upon what is in it, hold fast to it, and not go beyond it, making the ruling depend on those attributes. For this reason it was said: when the Qur'an is recited, the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in order to add emphasis to the causal link. That is, 'O believers, when it has become clear that you are not like these obstinate ones, then hold fast to this Book, which combines all the attributes of perfection, which guides to the straight path and leads to the station of mercy and nearness. So listen to it, strive to take from it and act upon what is in it, so that the desired goal may be achieved and that you may be shown mercy.'" This includes the obligation to remain silent during prayer, by way of a stronger inference, since prayer is a place of intimate communication, and listening is to the one speaking. On this basis, silence is also required when the Messenger (ﷺ) recites. The passage is clear that the address in the verse is to the believers; indeed, it is an explicit text on this point.

Some scholars said: the address in it is to the disbelievers. This is because the Qur'an being insight, guidance and mercy only becomes manifest under a particular condition: when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to them at the time of its revelation, they listened to him and remained silent, so that they might understand its meanings and excellences, acknowledge its inimitability, and thereby be content without seeking other miracles. This is supported by God's words at the end of the verse, "so that you may be shown mercy," on the basis that this is an expression of hope (*tarajji*), which suits the condition of the disbelievers and not the condition of the believers, who have already attained mercy with certainty, as in His words: "a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe." It is answered that the mercy hoped for here is different from that mercy. And even if it is granted that it is the same, the granting of hope by the Generous One is binding, so no difference remains. The building of the verb in the passive voice indicates that the matter depends on recitation by whoever the reciter is. The verse contains evidence of the exaltation of the status of the Qur'an that is plain to see.

From this point, some companions (of the school) said: it is recommended for one who wishes to recite it outside prayer to wear his best clothes, wear a turban, and face the qibla as a sign of honour toward it. The same applies to knowledge. If he recites while lying down, there is no harm, since this is a form of remembrance, and God has praised those who remember Him standing, sitting and lying on their sides. He should fold his legs during recitation and not stretch them out, because that is a breach of good manners. If he recites while walking, or while weaving or doing similar work, then if his heart is present and not occupied, it is not disliked; otherwise it is disliked. He should not recite while his private parts are exposed, nor if someone in his presence is in that state, even if that person is his wife. Some disliked reciting in the bathhouse and on the road. Al-Nawawi said: "Our school does not dislike it in these two places, but it is disliked in the latrine and in the grindstone house while it is turning, according to al-Sha'bi, and this is what our school requires." The discussion of the etiquette of recitation and what is fitting for the reciter is lengthy, and al-Suyuti's *al-Itqan* contains a considerable portion of it. If you have it, refer to it there.

The sentence, according to what their statements indicate, may be part of the speech that was commanded to be said, and it may be a fresh statement from God, the Exalted. It has been said: on the first view, His words, glorified and exalted be He:

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾ is coordinated with (*qul*, "say"). On the second reading, there is a shift (*tajrid*) of address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the command is general to every act of remembrance, for concealment is closer to sincerity (*ikhlas*) and nearer to acceptance. In some reports: "Allah the Exalted says: 'Whoever remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself, and whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than it.'" Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: The meaning of remembering within oneself is that one should know the meanings of the invocations that he utters with his tongue, keeping in mind the attributes of perfection, might, greatness and majesty. This is because remembrance by the tongue, if empty of remembrance by the heart, is as if it were without benefit. Indeed, a group said that mere verbal remembrance has no reward at all, and whoever utters the good word without attending to its meaning, or ignorant of it, is not counted a believer in the sight of Allah the Exalted. It has been said: the address is to the listener of the Qur'an, the remembrance is the Qur'an, and the meaning is the command to the follower (*ma'mum*) to recite silently after the imam has finished his recitation. But this is far-fetched, even if one adheres to the view of al-Imam.

The words of Allah, glorified and exalted, ﴿in humility and fear﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), by interpreting it as an active participle, i.e., *mutadarri'an* (humbly) and *kha'ifan* (fearful), or by supposing an omitted genitive, i.e., "possessing humility and fear." That it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*) is not appropriate.

Some have permitted that this be a verbal noun (*masdar*) of a verb other than the one mentioned, but this is nothing (of substance). The original of *khifah* is *khufah*. As for *duna* in the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿and below the loudness of speech﴾, it is an adjective modifying an omitted circumstantial object: i.e., "and speaking words below loudness," because *duna* does not inflect (*la tatasarraf*) according to the well-known view. It is coordinated with *tadarru'an* (humbly). It has been said: there is no need for what was mentioned, and it is coordinated with its circumstance; the meaning is: remember Him humbly and moderately.

It has been said: the coordination is with the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿within yourself﴾, but in the sense: remember Him with remembrance within yourself and with remembrance by your tongue, below loudness. By loudness is meant raising the voice excessively, and what is below it is another kind of loudness. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it is that one makes himself hear. Al-Imam said: The meaning is that the remembrance should fall between loudness and whispering, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent in it﴾. The words of Ibn Zayd indicate that by loudness is meant the opposite of remembrance within the self, and the verse, in his view, is an address to the follower who is commanded to listen attentively: i.e., "Remember your Lord, O listener, within yourself, and do not raise your voice in remembrance."

﴿in the mornings﴾: *al-ghuduww* is the plural of *ghudwah*, as in the Qamus; and in the Sihah, *al-ghuduww* is the opposite of *al-rawah* (evening), and *qad ghada yaghdu ghuduwwan* (he went out in the morning). The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿bil-ghuduww﴾ mean "at the mornings," plural of *ghadwah*, which is the time between the dawn prayer and the rising of the sun. So He expressed the time by the verbal noun, as one says: "I came to you at sunrise," i.e., at the time of its rising. This is explicit that *ghuduww* is a verbal noun, not a plural. On this basis, a plural noun may be supposed with it, i.e., "the times of the mornings," to match His words, glorified and exalted, ﴿and the evenings﴾. It is, as al-Azhari said, the plural of *asl*, and *asl* is the plural of *asil*, meaning the time between the afternoon and the setting of the sun. So it is a plural of a plural, not for the paucal number, and it is not the plural of *asil*, because *fa'il* is not pluralized as *af'al*. It has been said: it is a plural of it, because it may be pluralized in that form, as *yamin* (oath) and *iman*. It has been said: it is a plural of *asl* as a singular, like *'unuq* (neck), and it is also pluralized as *usˤlan*. The prepositional phrase is connected to *udhkur* (remember). These two times were singled out for remembrance. It has been said: because at the morning the living being turns from sleep, which is like death, to wakefulness, which is like life, and the world transforms from darkness, which is a non-existential nature, to light, which is an existential nature. In the evening the matter is reversed. Or, because they are two times of leisure, so remembrance in them is more closely attached to the heart. It has been said: because they are two times in which the angels alternate over the children of Adam. It has been said: the purpose is not specification, but the continuity and constancy of remembrance, i.e., "remember at every time."

Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd al-Sadusi recited *wal-iṣal* (and the ending), which is the verbal noun of *asala*, when one enters the evening (*asil*). It matches *ghuduww* on the basis of the view that it is singular and a verbal noun. So reflect upon this. ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted.

[Page 155]

[Page 155]

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾: they are the angels of the Exalted Assembly. The meaning of "with" here is nearness to Allah, the Exalted, through closeness and good pleasure, not nearness of place, since Allah is exalted above that. It has also been said that the meaning is "at the Throne of your Lord." ﴿They are not too proud to worship Him﴾, but perform it as they have been commanded. ﴿And they glorify Him﴾, that is, they declare Him far above whatever is unfitting for the presence of His majesty, in the most eloquent manner. ﴿And to Him they prostrate﴾, that is, they single Him out with the utmost worship and humility, and they do not associate anything with Him, may His majesty be exalted. This is an allusion to those among the accountable beings other than them, as the placing of "to Him" (lahu) at the front indicates. It is also permissible to derive from the whole statement, as al-'Allama al-Tibi preferred, that it is a reason for what precedes, meaning: "Perform worship with sincerity as you have been commanded. If you do not perform it in this way, then We are free of you and of your worship. Indeed, We have honored servants, of such and such a nature." On this reading, the placement is for the sake of the verse's end rhyme (fasila). Because of the allusion in the verse, prostration was prescribed at this verse, to humble those who refuse and those who were alluded to. It has been said: The command to prostrate has come in verses in which a command to prostrate is given, so that one complies with the command; or in which the refusal of the disbelievers to prostrate is related, in opposition to them; or in which the prostration of prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, is related, so that one follows their example. This last is of the second category by way of allusion, or of the final category by way of explicit statement.

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in his prostration for this, as Ibn Abi Shayba narrated from Ibn 'Umar: "O Allah, to You my body has prostrated, in You my heart has believed. O Allah, grant me knowledge that benefits me and deeds that raise me."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related, and he (al-Tirmidhi) authenticated it, from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in the prostration of the Qur'an at night, many times: "My face has prostrated to the One who created it and split its hearing and its sight by His power and His strength. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators."

It is also reported from her: "No Muslim prostrates to Allah, the Exalted, with a prostration except that Allah raises him by it a degree, or removes from him by it a sin, or both of these for him together."

Muslim, Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws, weeping and saying: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is Paradise. I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so for me is the Fire.'"

The verse has been used as evidence that concealing remembrance (dhikr) is better. This agrees with what Ahmad related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best remembrance is the hidden."

This verse also reproaches the ignorant Sufis of our time for what they do, which is deemed reprehensible by the Shari'a, by reason and by custom. "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return."

[Page 156]

This (and from the category of allusive interpretation (ishara), meaning the esoteric reading of verses): ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul﴾, which is the spirit (ruh), ﴿and from it He created its mate﴾,

[Page 156 continues]

which is the heart (qalb). ﴿So that he might find rest with her﴾, that is, that he might incline towards her and be at peace. The spirit used to perceive from the heart the gentle breezes of divine graces. ﴿When he covered her﴾, that is, when he had intercourse with her. This is an allusion to spiritual marriage. The Sufis say that it pervades all existing things: you do not see any disparity in the creation of the All-Merciful.

﴿She bore a light burden﴾: at the beginning, through the appearance of the slightest trace of human attributes in the spiritual heart.

﴿Then when it became heavy﴾: the traces of attributes grew and multiplied. ﴿They both called upon Allah, their Lord﴾, because they feared the transformation of the luminous spiritual attributes into the dark attributes of the soul, ﴿saying: If You give us a righteous one﴾, fit for servitude, ﴿we will certainly be among the thankful.﴾ ﴿Then when He gave them a righteous one﴾ according to the natural disposition of the faculties, ﴿they assigned to Him partners in what He had given them﴾, that is, they made their offspring partners with Allah, the Exalted, in what He had given their offspring. Among them are the worshippers of the belly, among them the worshippers of the luxurious cloak, and among them those who worship the dirham and the dinar.

﴿Indeed those you call upon besides Allah﴾, whatever they may be, ﴿are servants like you﴾ in helplessness and in having no effect. ﴿So call upon them﴾ for whatever matter you wish. ﴿Let them answer you, if you are truthful﴾ in ascribing influence to them. ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ This is a question in the manner of denial, meaning: they have no feet with which to walk; rather, it is by Allah, mighty and majestic, for it is He who causes them to walk. The same is to be said regarding what follows.

﴿Say: Call upon your partners, then plot against me﴾ if you are able. ﴿Indeed my protector is Allah, who revealed the Book, and He protects the righteous﴾, that is, whoever stands by it in a state of uprightness. ﴿And you see them looking at you, yet they do not see﴾ the truth, nor your reality, because they are blind in heart in reality. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers. ﴿Take what is easy﴾, that is, what is easy for them to bear, and do not burden them with what is hard for them. ﴿Enjoin what is good﴾, that is, the fair way, ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾, so do not repay them for their ignorance.

It is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: There is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of noble character than this verse.

It has been said: This is due to the strength of its indication of monotheism (tawhid). For whoever witnesses the Owner of forelocks and His disposal of His servants, and that they do what they do or abstain from it by Him, glorified and exalted, and not by themselves, will not oppose them, nor contend with them over their obligations, nor become angry at the commanding and forbidding, nor be harsh, but will show forbearance towards them. ﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan should prompt you, then seek refuge in Allah﴾, by witnessing and presence, for then you will see that no act belongs to anyone other than Him, glorified be He. This points to what befalls a person at times of anger, and indicates its treatment by seeking refuge. Some have said: Anger only arises in a person when he finds something ugly in the one he is angry with, and then believes that he himself is capable while the other is incapable. When a light from the world of intellect is revealed to him, he realizes that the one he is angry with only committed that act because Allah, the Exalted, created in him a motive, and the eternal Word had already preceded concerning him, so there is no way for him to abandon it. At that point his anger changes. It has been reported: Whoever knows the secret of Allah, the Exalted, in predestination, calamities become light for him. So seeking refuge in Allah, the Exalted, in meaning, is a request for refuge in Him through unveiling that light.

﴿Indeed those who fear Allah﴾, that is, who guard against polytheism, ﴿when a passing thought from Satan touches them﴾, a momentary impulse from him, by attributing the act to someone other than Allah, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿they remember﴾ the station of tawhid and the witnessing of acts as coming from Allah, the Exalted, ﴿and then they see clearly﴾: the effective agency of Allah, the Exalted, and no devil or any other doer besides Him, glorified be He, in their sight. ﴿And their brothers﴾, that is, the brothers of the devils among the veiled ones, ﴿are drawn on by the devils into error﴾, which is the attribution of the act to the pure one (?), ﴿and then they do not refrain﴾ from obstinacy, contention and disputation. And ﴿they say: Why do you not fabricate it?﴾, meaning: why do you not gather it from your own self? ﴿Say: I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord﴾, because I am standing by it, not by myself.

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it﴾, that is, to the Qur'an, with your outward ears, ﴿and be silent﴾ with your inward senses. It is also permissible that the pronoun in "to it" refers to the Lord, glorified be He, meaning: when the Qur'an is recited, listen to the Lord, may His majesty be exalted, for He is the speaker and the one addressing you through it.

﴿That you may receive mercy﴾, through true hearing, or through the mercy of the manifestation of the Speaker in His speech by His attributes and acts.

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾, by adorning yourself with whatever attributes of Allah, the Exalted, it is possible to adorn oneself with. It has been said that this is in the sense of: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾.

[Page 157]

﴿In humility and fear﴾, according to the difference of the situation, ﴿and without loudness﴾, that is, without this becoming apparent from you, but rather you remain mentioning Him in your heart, ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾, that is, the times of the manifestation of the light of the spirit, and the times of the dominance of the attributes of the soul.

﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ at any time, heedless of witnessing the essential Oneness. Some of the great ones have said: His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, in humility and fear﴾, is an allusion to the highest station, which is the share of the arrived ones who witness; His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And without loudness﴾, is an allusion to the middle station, which is the portion of those travelling towards the station of witnessing; and His saying, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾, is an allusion to the station of those descending among the wayfarers. The mention of fear indicates the sensing of the awe of majesty, as one said:

I long for Him, and when He appears I lower my gaze out of reverence for Him,
Not out of fear but out of awe, and as a safeguard for His beauty.

They have mentioned that the state of the beginner and the wayfarer depends on the judgment of the shaykh, for he is the physician of the diseases of the heart, and so he knows best the treatment. He may see raising the voice in dhikr as a remedy where cutting off thoughts and the soul's inner talk depends on it. In "Awarif al-ma'arif" by al-Suhrawardi, may his secret be sanctified: The servant continues to repeat this word upon his tongue while his heart agrees, until it becomes rooted in him, removing inner talk, and its meaning takes the place of it in the heart. When the word takes hold and becomes easy on the tongue, the heart absorbs it, and then the remembrance becomes the remembrance of the Essence. This remembrance is witnessing, unveiling and direct vision, and that is the ultimate aim of seclusion. What has been mentioned may also be attained through recitation of the Qur'an, when one increases recitation and strives for the heart to agree with the tongue, until recitation flows on the tongue and takes the place of inner talk, and ease enters the servant's recitation and prayer. End quote.

It is also related from him what amounts to this: The servant's constitution resembles a large city, and his limbs and members are like its inhabitants. The servant, when he turns to remembrance, is like a caller who has climbed a minaret at the gate of the city intending to make the call to prayer audible to the people of the city. So the one who truly remembers intends to awaken his heart and to inform its parts and components through the remembrance of his tongue. He speaks with part of himself and hears with all of himself, until the word passes from the tongue to the heart, and it is illumined by it and attains the benefit of the states. Then the light of the heart is reflected onto the outer form, and it adorns itself with the beauty of good deeds. End quote.

﴿Indeed those who are with your Lord﴾: and they are those who have passed away and remain through Him, glorified and exalted be He, the people of uprightness. ﴿They are not too proud to worship Him﴾, because they are not veiled by selfhood (ananiyya). ﴿And they glorify Him﴾ by negating it. ﴿And to Him they prostrate﴾ through complete annihilation (fana') and the effacing of what remains. Allah, the Exalted, is the Everlasting; there is nothing in existence besides Him.

* * *

Surat al-Anfal is Medinan, as related from Zayd ibn Thabit and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and this is also found in a report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he was asked about it (the surah) and the scholar (Ibn 'Abbas) said: That is the surah of Badr. In another report he said: It was revealed concerning Badr. It has also been said that it is Medinan except His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾, the verse; for it was revealed in Mecca according to Muqatil. It is countered that it is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that this very verse was revealed in Medina. Some have tried to reconcile the two statements in a way that is not free from scrutiny. Others have excepted His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you﴾, the verse. Ibn al-'Arabi and others authenticated this, and it is supported by what al-Bazzar related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it was revealed when [he] embraced Islam.

Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). In the Shami count it has seventy-seven verses, and in the Basri and Hijazi counts seventy-six. In the Kufi count it has seventy-five. The point of its connection to Surat al-A'raf is that the latter contains: ﴿And enjoin what is good﴾, and this surah contains many instances of what is enjoined. The latter also mentions the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them) with their peoples, while this surah mentions the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) and what took place between him and his people. In that surah, He, glorified and exalted is He, detailed the stories of the family of Pharaoh and their like and what befell them, and in this one He summarised that, saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Like the custom of the family of Pharaoh and those before them, who denied the signs of Allah, so Allah seized them for their sins. Indeed Allah is strong and severe in punishment﴾. There, He alluded to the bad assumption of the disbelievers regarding the Qur'an in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say, "Why do you not fabricate one?"﴾. Here He stated this explicitly in His saying, majestic is His glory: ﴿And when Our signs are recited to them, they say, "We have heard. If we willed, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ In the preceding surah He, majestic is His state, explained that the Qur'an is guidance and mercy for a people who believe, and He followed that with the command to listen to it and the command to remember Him, and here He, majestic and exalted is He, explained the state of the believers when it is recited and their state when Allah, blessed is His name, is mentioned, in His saying, mighty is the One who speaks: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His signs are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely﴾. There are other connections besides these. The apparent view is that its placement here is tawqifi (divinely directed), and so is the placement of Bara'a after it; in this respect they are like the rest of the surahs, and many scholars held this view, as has passed in the introductions.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned that the placing of this surah here was not by a directive from the Messenger (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) to the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), as is the preferred view for the rest of the surahs, but rather by the ijtihad (independent judgement) of Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him). It would appear at first glance that the fitting arrangement would be to place al-A'raf after Yunus and Hud, since each of them includes the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them), and they are all Meccan in revelation, especially as the hadith was narrated concerning the merit of the seven long surahs, and they counted the seventh as Yunus, and it was called by that name, as al-Bayhaqi related in al-Dala'il. Thus placing it after two surahs from al-A'raf is a placing of a counterpart with the rest of its counterparts. Moreover, Surat al-Anfal is short in comparison with al-A'raf and Bara'a. This was already questioned long ago by the scholar of the Ummah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said to Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him): "What led you to resort to al-Anfal, which is among the mathani, and to Bara'a, which is among the mi'in, and join them together, not writing the basmala between them, and placing them among the long seven?" Then he mentioned Uthman's answer. We have already related the report in full, question and answer. Then he said: I say: Uthman's purpose in this is fulfilled by matters that Allah opened for him, namely:

First: He placed al-Anfal before Bara'a despite its brevity, because it contains the basmala, so he placed it first so that it would be like a fragment of it and its opening, and Bara'a, because it lacks the basmala, would be like its completion and remainder. For this reason a group of the early scholars said: they are one surah.

Second: He placed Bara'a here for the sake of length, since there is no surah longer than it after the six preceding surahs; that suffices as a connection.

Third: He interposed the two surahs within the long seven, whose order was known in the earliest era, to indicate that this matter came not from divine directive, and that the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) died before explaining both of them. So they were placed here like a borrowed placement. This is unlike placing them after the long seven, which would give the impression that this is their place by divine directive, and this is not supposed under this arrangement, because the order of the seven is known.

Look at this subtle point which Allah opened, and which no diver can plumb.

Fourth: Had he postponed them and put Yunus first, and placed Hud after Bara'a as in the codex of Ubayy, in observance of the connection of the seven and the juxtaposition of some with others, something else more emphatic in connection would have been lost, along with what we have pointed out. The more fitting thing for Surat Yunus is that it be followed by the five surahs after it, because of what they share in terms of connections: the stories, the opening with (Alif-Lam-Ra), the mention of the Book, their being Meccan, the proportion of their lengths (apart from al-Hijr), and their being named after a prophet, while al-Ra'd is the name of an angel, which is fitting alongside the names of the prophets (peace be upon them). These are several connections of linkage between Yunus and what follows, and they are more emphatic than this single consideration of placing Yunus after al-A'raf. For some of these reasons Surat al-Hijr was placed before al-Nahl despite being shorter than it. Had Bara'a been postponed after these six surahs, the connection would have been very distant because of its length after several surahs shorter than it, unlike placing Surat al-Nahl after al-Hijr, since al-Nahl is not as long as Bara'a.

The placing according to the openings in the arrangement is also witnessed by what we have mentioned: the placing of al-Hijr before al-Nahl for the sake of the connection of (Alif-Lam-Ra) before it; and the earlier placing of Al 'Imran before al-Nisa' despite being shorter, because of its connection to al-Baqarah in the opening (Alif-Lam-Mim), and the succession of the Ta-Sin surahs and the Ha-Mim surahs, and the succession of al-'Ankabut, al-Rum, Luqman and al-Sajda, since each opens with (Alif-Lam-Mim). For this reason al-Sajda was placed before al-Ahzab, which is longer than it. This is what Allah opened to me.

Then it is mentioned that Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) placed in his codex al-Baqarah, al-Nisa', Al 'Imran, al-A'raf, al-An'am, al-Ma'ida and Yunus, observing the long seven, placing the longest first and then the next longest. Then he followed with the mi'in, placing Bara'a, then al-Nahl, then Hud, then Yusuf, then al-Kahf, and so on in order of length, and he placed al-Anfal after al-Nur.

The connection is that each is Madani and includes rulings. In al-Nur is: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession in the earth﴾, and in al-Anfal: ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land﴾, and so on. The connection between the two verses is not hidden, since the first includes the promise of what was realised and mentioned in the second. So reflect. End of quotation.

I say: Allah has bestowed upon this lowly servant what He did not bestow upon that noble master, and all praise is due to Allah for it, in that He caused me to understand the connection of this surah with what precedes it, which he did not explain. Furthermore, what he said about the absence of tawqif in this arrangement is extremely far-fetched, as is understood from what we have presented in the introductions. The question of the scholar and Uthman's answer (may Allah be pleased with them both) are not explicit on that point. What he, may God have mercy on him, mentioned in the first of the matters Allah opened to him does not, on its apparent sense, accord with the apparent sense of the scholar's question (may Allah be pleased with him), since that question indicates that omitting the basmala from Bara'a is also a matter of ijtihad, whereas what he mentioned implies the opposite. His claim that Yunus is the seventh of the long seven is not an agreed matter; rather it is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr and a narration from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). In a narration in al-Hakim it is al-Kahf. A group, as al-Suyuti said in his Itqan, held that the first of the long seven is al-Baqarah and the last is Bara'a, and Ibn al-Athir in al-Nihaya restricted himself to this view. It is also reported from some that the seventh is al-Anfal and Bara'a, based on the view that they are one surah, and al-Firuzabadi mentioned this in his Qamus. What he mentioned concerning the second matter is rendered unnecessary by the reason Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) gave. Al-Nahhas in his Nasikh related from him that he said: "Al-Anfal and Bara'a were called the two companions in the time of the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him); therefore I placed them among the long seven." What he mentioned about observing the openings in the arrangement is not consistent, since al-Jinn, al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas all open with "Qul", with the separation of several surahs between the first and second, and the separation of two surahs between the second and third. After all this, what he mentioned is not free from scrutiny, as will not be hidden from the careful reader. So reflect.
